inside: Yakuza groups placed workers in the subcontracting chains of the state-funded clean-up and took part of their pay.

n: Scam-city builders partnered with Myanmar army's Karen border force
rank: commander, Karen Border Guard Force under the Myanmar army
d: Chinese-run crime groups built scam centres in Myanmar in partnership with Colonel Saw Chit Thu, leader of the Karen Border Guard Force, a militia placed under the Myanmar army. In 2017 he partnered with She Zhijiang's Yatai group to build Shwe Kokko and also dealt with Wan Kuok-koi's Dongmei Group over Saixigang; Wan, a former leader of the 14K triad, was sanctioned by the US Treasury in 2020. Saw Chit Thu received the junta's Thiri Pyanchi honour in November 2022. The UK sanctioned him in December 2023 and the US later did the same, for links to forced labour in scam centres. She Zhijiang was extradited from Thailand to China on 10 November 2025.
cite: UK sanctions designation (December 2023); US Treasury designations; reporting collected by Wikipedia
who: Yatai (She Zhijiang) and Dongmei (Wan Kuok-koi) groups
inside: Chinese crime groups partnered with the commander of an army-controlled militia, who let them build scam centres on the land his force held.

n: Iraq tax heist network had PM's office director and MP inside
rank: General Commission for Taxes and the Prime Minister's office
d: A network around businessman Nour Zuhair Jassim drew on officials inside Iraq's state, including the director of the Prime Minister's office, to take about $2.5 billion from a General Commission for Taxes account in 2021–22. The money left through 247 cheques paid to five front companies posing as oil firms owed tax refunds. In late 2024 a Baghdad court sentenced 10 people: Nour Zuhair in absentia to 10 years, former MP and finance-committee head Haitham al-Jubouri, Raed Juhi, former director of Prime Minister Mustafa al-Kadhimi's office, and a tax-commission director general and his deputy. Several former senior tax and Rafidain Bank officials have not been charged.
cite: Baghdad criminal court verdicts, November–December 2024, reported by The National
inside: A businessman's network used officials inside the tax commission and the prime minister's office to pay $2.5 billion of tax money to its front companies.

n: UN panel finds gang member on Haitian council and police aiding gangs
rank: former legislators, a municipal commissioner and police officers
d: Haiti's armed gangs have people inside the state: the UN Security Council's panel of experts on Haiti, in a report covering October 2025 to July 2026, says at least one member of the Cité Soleil municipal commission set up on 25 May 2026 is an active member of the Brooklyn gang, and that serving police officers supply gangs with weapons. It accuses former Kenscoff legislator Alfrédo Junior Antoine of arming youth groups and sponsoring a January 2025 attack that killed more than 100 people, and former senator Nenel Cassy of controlling a criminal group in Miragoâne. The 'historic use of gangs' by former senator Youri Latortue and ex-lawmaker Prophane Victor fuels violence in the Artibonite ahead of elections, it says. Antoine denied his gang connections to the panel by email. Cassy sent the panel no reply but told the Associated Press 'I am a pacifist', called the report incorrect and unfounded and asked the experts to retract his name.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, final report pursuant to Security Council resolution 2794 (2025), S/2026/714, 8 September 2026 (reissued 12 October 2026), para. 37 (police collusion), para. 43 (Cité Soleil municipal commission), paras. 48-51 (Antoine, including his emailed denial), paras. 52-59 (Cassy, including the Panel's unanswered letter), para. 62 (Artibonite); Associated Press via WLRN, 8 October 2026 (https://www.wlrn.org/americas/2026-10-08/report-offers-new-insight-into-haitian-gangs-as-general-election-looms), for Cassy's response by telephone
who: Viv Ansanm and other Haitian gangs
inside: Haiti's gangs have a member on a municipal commission and police officers who supply them with weapons and information.

n: PCC crime group's money ran two São Paulo city bus firms
rank: city bus concession companies
d: The PCC (Primeiro Comando da Capital), Brazil's largest criminal organisation, had its money in two São Paulo bus companies that held city contracts, state prosecutors allege. In April 2024 Operation Fim da Linha alleged that Transwolff (132 lines, about 583,000 passengers a day) and UPBus (158 buses) laundered PCC money; the firms had received more than R$800 million in public funds the year before. The city took over both companies on 9 April 2024, and that month the São Paulo courts accepted charges of criminal organisation, money laundering, extortion and misappropriation against 19 of those investigated. The UPBus president was arrested in December 2024. Both concession contracts were ended; Transwolff has not operated in the city since December 2025, and Alfa Rodobus took UPBus's place.
cite: São Paulo Public Prosecutor's Office (MPSP), Operation Fim da Linha; Exame, 17 April 2024 (19 defendants); Diário do Transporte, 17 September 2026 and 13 February 2026
inside: The PCC's money was inside two bus companies holding city contracts, which allegedly laundered its drug and robbery proceeds while taking public funds.
undone: No one has been convicted. The charges accepted in April 2024 have not been tried, and the defendants are presumed innocent. A later operation, Vectura Corrupta, rested on a provisional ruling of 4 September 2026 by a judge of the São Paulo appeal court that allowed 13 temporary arrests and searches, refused to freeze property and did not treat the allegations as proven; among those named were a former president of SPTrans, the city transport authority, and a former president of the city council, Milton Leite, described in police statements as the real owner of Transwolff. Leite has previously denied any link to criminal activity, and the report records that no statement from his defence, or from the other people under investigation, was in the material it was based on. Transwolff is challenging the city's intervention in court.

n: Rizzuto Mafia took a cut of Montreal public works contracts
rank: mayors of Montreal and Laval
d: The Rizzuto family, Montreal's Mafia, took a share of the city's public construction contracts through firms that also paid political parties, witnesses told Quebec's Charbonneau Commission. The commission (2011–2015) was a public inquiry into collusion and corruption in public construction contracts and organised-crime infiltration of the industry. During the inquiry Montreal mayor Gérald Tremblay resigned, and interim mayor Michael Applebaum and Laval mayor Gilles Vaillancourt were later convicted or pleaded guilty in related corruption cases. The commission reported on 24 November 2015.
cite: Commission of Inquiry on the Awarding and Management of Public Contracts in the Construction Industry (Charbonneau Commission), final report, November 2015
who: Rizzuto Mafia family and construction cartels
inside: The Mafia took a share of Montreal's public contracts through construction firms that also paid political parties, and mayors were convicted in related cases.

n: Mafia families controlled hiring on the New York docks
rank: port hiring and dock labour
d: Mafia families controlled much of the hiring of dock workers at the port of New York and New Jersey, a state crime commission found before 1953. That year the two states created the Waterfront Commission of New York Harbor to fight criminal influence over that hiring, and it licensed and screened dock workers for 70 years. New Jersey moved to leave the agreement between the states in 2018, and after the US Supreme Court allowed it in 2023 the commission was dissolved on 17 July 2023. New Jersey State Police took over its role at New Jersey ports, and New York set up a new waterfront commission.
cite: Waterfront Commission Compact (1953); US Supreme Court, New York v. New Jersey (2023)
who: American Mafia families on the docks
inside: Mafia families controlled hiring at the New York docks, deciding who worked there, until the states set up a commission to screen workers.

n: South African police minister accused of colluding with syndicate
rank: Minister of Police and national police leadership
d: A criminal syndicate had senior South African police officials working with it, including Police Minister Senzo Mchunu, KwaZulu-Natal police commissioner Lt Gen Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi alleged on 6 July 2025. Mchunu was placed on leave and President Ramaphosa set up the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry. A R228 million police health-services contract had gone to businessman Vusimuzi 'Cat' Matlala's company in 2024; he faces corruption, fraud and money-laundering charges. The commission's interim report, submitted on 17 December 2025, found prima facie evidence of criminal conduct and corruption by serving and former officers of the police and of the Ekurhuleni metro police and recommended criminal referrals and discipline; Ramaphosa accepted the recommendations. By July 2026, 13 police officers faced criminal charges, including National Commissioner Fannie Masemola on a public-finance charge.
cite: Madlanga Commission interim report, 17 December 2025, reported by The Star, 29 January 2026; National Prosecuting Authority charges, Daily Maverick, 5 July 2026; Business Day, 14 July 2026 (parliamentary ad hoc committee draft report); Minister of Police statement, 6 July 2025, reported by eNCA and Sowetan, 6 July 2025
inside: A police commissioner alleges the police minister and senior officers worked with a criminal syndicate, while a linked businessman won a police contract.
undone: The commission says it has made no findings and that those implicated will be allowed to reply. The interim report named no politician among those who should face criminal charges, and Mchunu, his chief of staff Cedric Nkabinde, the suspended deputy national commissioner Shadrack Sibiya and Brown Mogotsi were left off that list. A parliamentary ad hoc committee's draft report, deliberated on 14 July 2026, found no evidence that Mchunu entered a corrupt agreement or acted on a cartel's instructions when he disbanded the Political Killings Task Team in December 2024, while recording unresolved integrity and accountability concerns about how he did it; it also found the evidence did not prove Sibiya acted for Matlala. Mchunu rejected Mkhwanazi's allegations as baseless in a statement on 6 July 2025, saying they were made without evidence, and is presumed innocent. He is out of office, called the suspended police minister in the January 2026 report, with Firoz Cachalia holding the post. The charges against the 13 officers and against Matlala have not been tried.

n: 'Construction mafia' bribes and threatens South African councillors
rank: ward councillors and municipal contracts
d: Extortion groups calling themselves 'business forums' try to capture ward councillors, the local elected officials, by bribery or threats, sometimes by joining local party branches, the Institute for Security Studies reported in October 2021. The forums demand a cut, often 30%, of public construction projects and shut down sites that refuse. The civil engineering contractors' body SAFCEC estimated that by March 2019 at least R25.5 billion of projects had been disrupted or halted. The ISS said three Tshwane councillors had been killed in under four years in killings linked to such syndicates. The National Prosecuting Authority agreed to prosecute violent extortion under the Prevention of Organised Crime Act.
cite: Institute for Security Studies, ISS Today, 25 October 2021; SAFCEC estimates
inside: Extortion groups bribe or threaten local councillors, sometimes by joining their party branches, to take a cut of public building projects.

n: Black Axe-linked group paid to 'protect votes', given 80 state posts
rank: state government posts and election campaigns
d: The Neo Black Movement of Africa (NBM), which the BBC linked to the Black Axe confraternity, was given 80 government roles after it was paid to 'protect votes' in Nigeria's 2012 Edo governorship election, according to leaked documents in a BBC Africa Eye investigation of December 2021. The documents suggested 35 million naira went to the NBM. Black Axe is a Nigerian confraternity, a secretive student-born brotherhood, that police in several countries treat as an organised crime group. Former members told the BBC that members hold posts in state assemblies and executives and are hired by politicians for election violence. The NBM denies any link to Black Axe.
cite: BBC Africa Eye, 'Black Axe' investigation, December 2021
inside: A group linked to Black Axe was paid to 'protect votes' in a state election and then given 80 posts in that state's government.

n: 'Ndrangheta ties lead Italy to dissolve Reggio Calabria council
rank: mayor and city council of a provincial capital
d: 'Ndrangheta clans, the Calabrian mafia, had ties to councillors in Reggio Calabria, leading the Italian government on 9 October 2012 to dissolve the city council for mafia infiltration. Some councillors were suspected of links to clans during the centre-right administration of Giuseppe Scopelliti, mayor from 2002 to 2010. Mayor Demetrio Arena and all 30 councillors were removed and three commissioners ran the city. It was the first time the government of an Italian provincial capital had been dismissed over organised-crime links.
cite: Italian Council of Ministers dissolution decree, 9 October 2012 (Law 164/1991)
inside: 'Ndrangheta clans had ties to Reggio Calabria councillors, and the state dissolved the whole council for mafia infiltration.

n: Chongqing gangs paid the city's deputy police chief for protection
rank: executive deputy head of the Public Security Bureau; head of the Judicial Bureau
d: Criminal gangs in Chongqing, a city of over 30 million in south-west China, paid bribes to Wen Qiang, for 16 years executive deputy head of its Public Security Bureau (the police force) and then head of its Judicial Bureau, to protect them. His case came out in a campaign against organised crime run from October 2009 to 2011 by the city's party chief Bo Xilai and police chief Wang Lijun, which arrested 4,781 suspects, including 19 alleged crime bosses, hundreds of triad members, six district police chiefs and other officials. Wen was convicted of taking bribes and protecting criminal gangs and executed on 7 July 2010. Lawyers and scholars raised concerns about forced confessions and due process in the campaign's trials; Bo Xilai was himself jailed for life in 2013.
cite: Chongqing courts (2010); reporting collected by Wikipedia
inside: Chongqing's gangs paid the city's deputy police chief, who used his post to protect them for years.

n: François Pérol: Rothschild banker oversaw a bank merger, then ran it
rank: Élysée deputy secretary-general; CEO of Groupe BPCE
d: François Pérol, a French Treasury official, moved from the bank Rothschild & Cie into the president's office, where he followed a bank merger he had advised on, and then took charge of the merged bank. As a Rothschild managing partner from 2005 to 2007 he advised Banque Populaire on creating Natixis. As deputy secretary-general of the Élysée under Nicolas Sarkozy he followed the 2008–09 merger of Banque Populaire and the Caisses d'Epargne, and in February 2009 he became head of the merged group, BPCE. He was prosecuted for illegal taking of interest (prise illégale d'intérêts), the offence of an official taking a stake in a business he supervised. The Paris criminal court acquitted him on 24 September 2015 and the Paris Court of Appeal confirmed that on 30 June 2017.
cite: Tribunal correctionnel de Paris, 24 Sept 2015; Cour d'appel de Paris, 30 June 2017 (Acteurs publics)
inside: A former Rothschild banker in the president's office followed a merger he had advised on and then took charge of the merged bank; he was prosecuted and acquitted.

n: Pujo Committee: Morgan-linked men held 341 company directorships
rank: boards of 112 corporations
d: Bankers linked to J. P. Morgan & Co. sat on the boards of 112 corporations at once, giving the group a say inside companies it lent to. A 'directorship' is a seat on a company's board, which oversees management. A House Banking subcommittee led by Arsène Pujo, with counsel Samuel Untermyer, investigated this 'money trust' in 1912-13 and questioned Morgan himself. Its 1913 report found 180 individuals linked to the group holding 341 directorships in those 112 corporations, which had $22.2 billion in resources, and the 20 largest banks holding 42.9% of US banking resources. It named bankers including Paul and Felix Warburg, Jacob Schiff, William Rockefeller and Benjamin Strong. Its findings fed the Federal Reserve Act and the 1914 Clayton Antitrust Act, whose limits on interlocking directorates remain law.
cite: House Committee on Banking and Currency, Pujo Committee report (1913); Wikipedia 'Pujo Committee'
who: J. P. Morgan & Co. and allied banks
inside: Bankers from the Morgan group sat on the boards of 112 companies at once, giving the bank a say inside the companies it lent to.

n: Bankers secretly drafted the Federal Reserve plan at Jekyll Island
rank: National Monetary Commission (banking reform bill)
d: Senior Wall Street bankers secretly drafted the law to set up a US central bank. In November 1910 Senator Nelson Aldrich, chairman of the National Monetary Commission, took Assistant Treasury Secretary A. Piatt Andrew, Henry Davison of J.P. Morgan & Co., Frank Vanderlip of National City Bank, Paul Warburg of Kuhn, Loeb & Co. and his secretary Arthur Shelton to the Jekyll Island Club in Georgia; other accounts add Benjamin Strong of Bankers Trust. Their plan was published in January 1911 as the Aldrich Plan, with no mention of its origin; participants did not admit the meeting until the 1930s. Congress never voted on it, but the Federal Reserve's history says the Jekyll Island plan 'laid a foundation for what would eventually be the Federal Reserve System', created in 1913.
cite: Gary Richardson & Jessie Romero, 'The Meeting at Jekyll Island', Federal Reserve History (Federal Reserve Board); Wikipedia 'Benjamin Strong Jr.'
who: Morgan, National City and Kuhn, Loeb bankers
inside: Wall Street bankers secretly wrote the draft of the national banking law for the senator chairing the commission, laying the base for the Federal Reserve.

n: Quigley: Milner Group held half of Britain's Dawes Plan delegation
rank: Reichsbank reorganisation and reparations schedule
d: Historian Carroll Quigley writes that the Milner Group, a British network of officials and financiers known through its Round Table journal, had 'half of the British delegation' on the 1924 Dawes committee, the ten experts who reset German war reparations. Britain's two experts were Sir Josiah Stamp and Sir Robert Kindersley, Lazard Brothers chairman and senior colleague there of Round Table leader Robert Brand. Quigley adds that 'the chief influence was that of J. P. Morgan and Company'. The plan set a rising reparations schedule, put the Reichsbank, Germany's central bank, under a board of seven creditor-state and seven German members independent of government, and gave Germany an 800-million-mark loan, about half raised through Wall Street bond issues. German right-wing parties attacked its limits on sovereignty. The attribution is Quigley's.
cite: Wikipedia 'Dawes Plan'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 241–242
inside: Creditor states got seven seats on the board of Germany's central bank under the Dawes plan, drawn up by a panel that included Lazard's chairman.

n: Evelyn Baring ran Egypt's finances for its European creditors
rank: Controller-General (1879); agent and consul-general (1883–1907)
d: Evelyn Baring, of the Barings banking family, became the British official controlling Egypt's finances while Barings Bank held a significant stake in Egyptian debt. After the Khedive Ismail, Egypt's ruler, went bankrupt in 1876, Britain and France imposed 'Dual Control', putting their own controllers over Egypt's finances; no conflict of interest was raised at the time. Baring pressed for Ismail's removal, which the powers obtained in 1879. After Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 he returned as agent and consul-general (1883–1907), the effective ruler of Egypt, and kept its revenues committed to paying its European creditors.
cite: Wikipedia 'Evelyn Baring, 1st Earl of Cromer'
inside: A member of the Barings banking family controlled Egypt's finances and kept its revenues committed to paying its European creditors, among them Barings.

n: Wallenberg bank hid German Bosch's ownership of American Bosch
rank: Swedish government trade delegations
d: Stockholms Enskilda Bank, the Wallenberg family's bank in neutral Sweden, held German-owned companies on paper so that the German firm Bosch kept control of them during the Second World War. In 1939–41 the bank bought Bosch subsidiaries, including the American Bosch Corporation, on condition that Bosch could buy them back after the war. The US government treated this as 'cloaking' enemy property (hiding the real owner behind a front), seized American Bosch in 1943 and in 1945 blacklisted the bank until 1947. At the same time the Swedish government used the bank's heads for its trade talks: Jacob Wallenberg dealt with Germany, and Marcus Wallenberg Jr. chaired the Swedish side of the Swedish–British commission (1939–43). Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau Jr. regarded Jacob Wallenberg as strongly pro-German.
cite: Wikipedia 'Stockholms Enskilda Bank', 'Marcus Wallenberg (1899–1982)', 'Wallenberg family' (citing G. Aalders, The Art of Cloaking Ownership, 1996)
inside: The Wallenberg bank held German Bosch's American company on paper, so the German firm kept hidden control of it during the war.

n: Robert Rubin: Goldman co-chair to Treasury, then Citigroup
rank: National Economic Council director; Treasury Secretary
d: Robert Rubin moved from Goldman Sachs into the US posts that set financial policy, then to Citigroup, a bank whose merger needed a change in the law he had argued for. After 26 years at Goldman, ending as co-chairman (1990–92), he ran Bill Clinton's National Economic Council (1993–95) and was Treasury Secretary (1995–99). He called the Glass–Steagall separation of commercial and investment banking obsolete; its repeal in 1999, pushed by Sanford Weill to legalise the Travelers–Citicorp merger, came at the end of his term. Rubin joined Citigroup in 1999 as executive committee chairman and was paid $126 million there to 2009. In 2001 he phoned a Treasury official seeking help for Citigroup client Enron, which a Senate staff inquiry found not illegal. Citigroup needed a federal rescue in 2008.
cite: Wikipedia 'Robert Rubin'
inside: A former Goldman co-chairman as Treasury Secretary argued for repealing the banking law the industry wanted gone, then joined the bank whose merger needed it.

n: Henry Paulson: Goldman CEO to Treasury; AIG rescue paid Goldman $12.9bn
rank: Treasury Secretary (2006–09)
d: Henry Paulson went from chairman and chief executive of Goldman Sachs to US Treasury Secretary in July 2006, and in that post ran a rescue whose largest beneficiary was Goldman. On joining he sold about $600 million of Goldman stock under ethics rules, with capital-gains tax deferred. In September 2008 he and the Federal Reserve rescued the insurer AIG, whose trading partners were then paid in full; Goldman was the largest recipient of public funds passing through AIG, about $12.9 billion. The Special Inspector General for TARP, the programme's watchdog, reviewed these payments in November 2009. The New York Times reported in August 2009 that Paulson spoke with Goldman chief Lloyd Blankfein some 24 times in the week of the AIG rescue, two calls before he obtained an ethics waiver.
cite: SIGTARP report on AIG counterparty payments (Nov 2009); NYT, Morgenson & Van Natta, 9 Aug 2009; Wikipedia 'Henry Paulson'
inside: Goldman's former chief ran the AIG rescue as Treasury Secretary, which paid Goldman $12.9 billion of public money in full.

n: Ex-Goldman economist ran the New York Fed that supervised Goldman
rank: Federal Reserve Bank of New York supervision of Goldman
d: William Dudley, Goldman Sachs's chief US economist until 2007, was president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the regulator that supervises Goldman, from 2009 to 2018. Carmen Segarra, a New York Fed examiner placed at Goldman from October 2011, said she found Goldman had no firm-wide conflict-of-interest policy, was pressed by superiors to change her findings and was fired after seven months. In September 2014 she released recordings, broadcast by ProPublica and This American Life, of supervisors deferring to Goldman over a Santander deal they called 'legal but shady'. Her whistleblower suit was dismissed on legal grounds.
cite: Wikipedia 'Carmen Segarra', 'William C. Dudley'; ProPublica / This American Life, Sept 2014
inside: A former Goldman economist led the regulator that supervises Goldman, and recordings show its supervisors deferring to the bank.

n: JPMorgan hired Chinese officials' relatives to win business
rank: Chinese government officials and state-owned company executives
d: JPMorgan Chase, the US bank, hired around 100 relatives and friends of Chinese government officials and state-company executives so that those officials would steer business to it. The 'Sons and Daughters' programme was run by its Hong Kong subsidiary from 2006 to 2013 and bypassed the bank's normal hiring process. The US Securities and Exchange Commission said the bank won more than $100 million in business this way. In November 2016 JPMorgan agreed to pay $264 million to settle civil and criminal charges under the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, which bans paying foreign officials, or giving them something of value, to win business.
cite: SEC and US Department of Justice settlements, 17 Nov 2016; OCCRP; Wikipedia 'JPMorgan Chase'
inside: JPMorgan hired about 100 relatives and friends of Chinese officials so that those officials would steer business to the bank.

n: Mozambique officials and Credit Suisse bankers bribed over hidden loans
rank: Finance ministry and state companies (hidden state guarantees)
d: Mozambican officials and Credit Suisse bankers took bribes and kickbacks to arrange $2.2 billion of state-guaranteed loans hidden from parliament and the IMF. In 2013-14 three state companies borrowed $622 million from Credit Suisse and $535 million from Russia's VTB for tuna fishing and maritime security projects with the shipbuilder Privinvest. The US Justice Department said at least $200 million went in bribes and kickbacks; the banker Andrew Pearse got about $45 million. When the loans surfaced in 2016 the IMF and World Bank froze support; one study estimated two million people were pushed into poverty. Mozambique's Constitutional Council declared the loans void (2019, 2020). In October 2021 Credit Suisse pleaded guilty to wire fraud in the US, was fined almost $500 million and forgave $200 million of Mozambique's debt.
cite: US DOJ plea agreement (Oct 2021); UK FCA; Mozambique Constitutional Council (2019, 2020); Wikipedia 'Tuna bonds'
inside: Privinvest and Credit Suisse bankers paid officials to arrange $2.2 billion of state-guaranteed loans hidden from parliament and the IMF.

n: Espírito Santo money linked to ex-PM Sócrates in corruption trial
rank: Prime Minister (José Sócrates, 2005–11)
d: Portuguese prosecutors say money from the Espírito Santo banking group reached José Sócrates, prime minister from 2005 to 2011. Ricardo Salgado led Banco Espírito Santo (BES), of a banking family close to power since the Salazar dictatorship, and was nicknamed 'Dono Disto Tudo' ('owner of all this'); BES collapsed in 2014. In the case known as Operation Marquês, Sócrates was charged with receiving undue payments, Salgado with three counts of corruption and eight of money laundering. A judge threw out most charges in April 2021, but the Lisbon Court of Appeal reinstated them in January 2024 and trial began on 3 July 2025; all defendants are presumed innocent. In a separate case from the same investigation, Salgado's breach of trust sentence was raised to eight years on appeal in 2023.
cite: Lisbon Court of Appeal, 25 Jan 2024 and order of 24 Feb 2026; Tribunal Central Criminal de Lisboa (trial from 3 July 2025); Observador, 11 November 2025; ECO, 25 February 2026
who: Banco Espírito Santo / Espírito Santo group (Ricardo Salgado)
inside: Prosecutors say the Espírito Santo group's money reached the prime minister, charging its head with corruption and the prime minister with taking undue payments.
undone: The trial is still running and no verdict has been reached. There are 21 defendants and 117 charges in all, which the defendants have generally denied; Salgado faces eight counts of money laundering and three of active corruption, one of them naming Socrates as the person corrupted. On 11 November 2025 the presiding judge, Susana Seca, warned that some charges risked lapsing on time limits, and the court later specified the Vale do Lobo and Caixa Geral de Depositos corruption counts against Socrates, Armando Vara, Rui Horta e Costa and Jose Diogo Gaspar Ferreira, during the first half of 2026. On 24 February 2026 the Lisbon Court of Appeal rejected as wholly unfounded a request to end the case against Salgado because of his Alzheimer's disease, saying his health would be weighed if he is convicted and sentence falls to be served. All defendants are presumed innocent.

n: Cuba's spy Ana Montes was the DIA's top Cuba analyst
rank: senior analyst, Defense Intelligence Agency
d: Cuba's intelligence service recruited Ana Belén Montes while she was a graduate student, and she went on to become the leading analyst on Cuba's military at the US Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA), the Pentagon's intelligence arm, which she joined in 1985. From inside the agency she passed classified information to her Cuban handlers until her arrest on 21 September 2001. She pleaded guilty in 2002, was sentenced to 25 years and was released on 6 January 2023.
cite: US District Court, Washington DC, guilty plea Oct 2002; Wikipedia 'Ana Montes'
inside: Cuba's intelligence service recruited a woman who became the US military's top Cuba analyst and passed it secrets from inside the agency.

n: 'Qatargate': Netanyahu aides suspected of being paid to promote Qatar
rank: prime minister's office aides
d: Israeli police suspect that two men close to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took money to promote the image of Qatar, a Gulf state that mediates in the Gaza war and hosts Hamas's political office. In March–April 2025 police arrested Netanyahu adviser Jonatan Urich and former spokesman Eli Feldstein on suspicion of being paid through Third Circle, the firm of US lobbyist Jay Footlik, which was registered under the US Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA). Channel 12 reported that Feldstein drew a salary from Footlik while working for Netanyahu. Netanyahu was questioned as a witness, not a suspect, and called it a political witch hunt. In May 2026 prosecutors announced a separate indictment of Urich over leaking a classified document.
cite: Israel Police and State Attorney investigation, 2025; Malay Mail/AFP explainer 3 Apr 2025; Arab News 28 May 2026
org_note: foreign_state = Qatar
inside: Aides to Israel's prime minister are suspected of being paid through a lobbyist's firm to promote Qatar while working in his office.
undone: Nobody has been charged in the Qatar strand of the case. On 22 June 2026 Israeli media reported that prosecutors were working towards a decision on a broad indictment that would also cover a former senior Mossad official and the retired major general Yoav 'Poly' Mordechai, questioned as a suspect over bribery and contact with a foreign agent; Calcalist reported that he brokered Israeli arms and cyber deals with Qatar for brokerage fees worth millions of shekels. The Attorney General and the State Attorney had not ruled, and no indictment had been filed. The separate indictment of Urich over leaking a classified document has not been tried. All the suspects are presumed innocent.

n: Saudi Arabia paid Twitter manager Ahmad Abouammo for users' data
rank: Twitter Middle East partnerships manager
d: Saudi officials paid Ahmad Abouammo, a Twitter employee, to take data from the company's systems that helped them identify and locate users they were interested in. Abouammo managed Twitter's relations with Middle East journalists and celebrities in 2013–2015 and received a $42,000 watch and two $100,000 wire transfers. A San Francisco federal jury convicted him in August 2022, and he was sentenced to three and a half years in December 2022. A second ex-employee, Ali Alzabarah, left the US before he could be charged.
cite: US District Court, Northern District of California, verdict Aug 2022 and sentence Dec 2022
org_note: foreign_state = Saudi Arabia
inside: Saudi officials paid a Twitter employee to take data from the company's systems that helped them identify and find users.

n: McLaren report: Russia's FSB inside the Moscow anti-doping lab
rank: WADA-accredited Moscow laboratory and Sochi 2014 testing
d: Russia's FSB security service and Ministry of Sport worked through the Moscow laboratory accredited by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), the body that sets drug-testing rules for world sport, to hide doped athletes. Richard McLaren's reports for WADA in July and December 2016 found a 'state-directed failsafe system' involving the ministry, the national team centre, the FSB and the laboratory. FSB-linked staff opened supposedly tamper-proof sample bottles at the 2014 Sochi Olympics to swap urine. More than 1,000 Russian competitors in over 30 sports benefited between 2011 and 2015, and the 'disappearing positive' method hid at least 643 positive samples.
cite: McLaren Independent Investigation Reports to WADA, 18 July and 9 Dec 2016
org_note: org = target body; infiltrator is fsb
inside: Russia's security service and sport ministry worked through the lab meant to enforce world anti-doping rules, swapping samples to hide doped athletes.

n: FIFA voters allegedly paid to back Russia for the 2018 World Cup
rank: FIFA executive committee members
d: People seeking Russia's 2018 World Cup allegedly paid members of FIFA's executive committee, the 22-member board that chose World Cup hosts, to vote for Russia. FIFA is the world governing body for football, based in Switzerland. The committee chose Russia (2018) and Qatar (2022) in December 2010. A US indictment unsealed in April 2020 alleges that Jack Warner of Trinidad and Tobago received about $5m and Guatemala's Rafael Salguero about $1m to vote for Russia. The 2020 charges were brought against media executives; the voters named were already charged or dead, so these bribes have not been tried. Russia called the claims baseless.
cite: US District Court, Eastern District of New York, superseding indictment unsealed 6 April 2020
inside: People seeking Russia's World Cup allegedly paid FIFA executive committee members to vote for Russia as host.

n: FIFA voters allegedly paid to back Qatar for the 2022 World Cup
rank: FIFA executive committee members
d: People seeking Qatar's 2022 World Cup allegedly bribed members of FIFA's executive committee, the board of football's world governing body that chose World Cup hosts in December 2010. The April 2020 US indictment alleges that Brazil's Ricardo Teixeira, Paraguay's Nicolás Leoz and an unnamed co-conspirator received bribes in return for their votes for Qatar. Separately, Qatari FIFA executive Mohamed bin Hammam was banned for life in 2012, and leaked emails published by the Sunday Times in 2014 showed him making payments of $10,000 to $200,000 to football officials before the 2010 vote. Qatar denies wrongdoing.
cite: US District Court, E.D. New York, superseding indictment April 2020; FIFA Ethics Committee bans 2011–12; Sunday Times 'FIFA Files' June 2014
inside: People seeking Qatar's World Cup allegedly paid FIFA executive committee members in return for their votes for Qatar.

n: Tokyo 2020 bid paid firm tied to IOC voter's son
rank: IOC member and Japanese Olympic Committee president
d: Tokyo's 2020 Olympic bid committee paid about $2m in 2013 to Black Tidings, a Singapore company tied to Papa Massata Diack, son of IOC member Lamine Diack, at the time African votes in the International Olympic Committee were being sought. The IOC picks Olympic host cities by a vote of its members. French financial prosecutors opened a corruption investigation of Tsunekazu Takeda, president of the Japanese Olympic Committee (JOC), in December 2018. A JOC panel concluded the payments were not bribes but could not interview key people. Takeda denied wrongdoing and stepped down from the JOC and IOC in 2019.
cite: French Parquet National Financier investigation, 2018–19
inside: Tokyo's bid paid a firm tied to the son of an IOC member while it sought IOC votes, and French prosecutors opened a corruption case.

n: Hungarian spies at Hungary's EU mission tried to recruit Commission staff
rank: European Commission staff
d: Hungarian intelligence officers posing as diplomats at Hungary's Permanent Representation in Brussels, its embassy to the EU, tried to recruit Hungarians working at the European Commission, the EU's executive body. Der Spiegel, Direkt36, De Tijd and others reported this in October 2025. A Commission letter leaked in July 2026 confirms that the mission ran such a network from 2012 to 2018, though no serious breaches were found. Olivér Várhelyi, Hungary's EU ambassador from 2015 to 2019 and now a Commissioner, denies knowing; the Commission's May 2026 findings largely cleared him.
cite: European Commission internal investigation, findings May 2026 and letter to MEPs; Euronews 2 July 2026
org_note: foreign_state = Hungary; target body eu
inside: Hungarian spies posing as diplomats tried to recruit Hungarians working at the European Commission to work for them from inside it.

n: Egyptian intelligence's man in the German government press office
rank: employee of the Federal Government Press Office
d: Egypt's General Intelligence Service had a man inside Germany's Federal Press Office, which runs the German chancellor's communications. The man, named as Amin A., an Egypt-born German citizen, worked in its visitor service from 1999. Federal prosecutors charged him in November 2020 with helping the Egyptian service from at least 2010 by compiling reports on German media coverage and, in 2014–2015, helping an attempt to recruit a source, in exchange for favours for his family. Germany's interior minister said he had no access to sensitive data.
cite: German Federal Prosecutor General, indictment Nov 2020; BfV annual report 2019
inside: Egypt's intelligence service had an employee of Germany's government press office report to it and help an attempt to recruit a source.

n: Indian RAW officers cultivated Australian politicians and an insider
rank: politicians, a state police service, cleared officials
d: Officers of India's foreign intelligence service, RAW, cultivated Australian politicians and a state police service and recruited an Australian security-clearance holder with access to defence technology. ASIO, Australia's domestic security agency, disrupted the group, and two RAW officers were expelled in 2020 after seeking secrets on defence projects, airport security and trade. In a March 2021 speech ASIO chief Mike Burgess described a foreign 'nest of spies' that had also cultivated a foreign embassy and monitored a diaspora community, without naming the country. In April 2024 Australian media and the Washington Post reported it was India.
cite: ASIO Director-General annual threat assessment, March 2021; ABC, The Australian, Washington Post, April 2024
inside: India's foreign intelligence service recruited an Australian clearance holder with access to defence technology and cultivated politicians and a state police service.

n: Haqqani network, called an arm of Pakistan's ISI, runs Taliban security
rank: interior ministry and Kabul security
d: The Haqqani network, which the US military's top officer called an arm of Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), now holds senior posts in Afghanistan's Taliban government. The network is a militant group within the Taliban, designated a terrorist organisation by the US in 2012. In September 2011 Admiral Mike Mullen told the US Senate it 'acts as a veritable arm' of the ISI. After the Taliban took Kabul in 2021 the network was given control of Kabul's security, and its leader Sirajuddin Haqqani became the Taliban government's interior minister. Pakistan denies ties.
cite: US Senate Armed Services Committee testimony of Adm. Mike Mullen, 22 Sept 2011; US FTO designation 7 Sept 2012
inside: The Haqqani network, which the top US military officer called an arm of Pakistan's spy agency, now runs the Taliban government's interior ministry and Kabul's security.

n: North Korean IT workers placed inside 300+ US companies via laptop farm
rank: remote IT staff positions in US companies
d: North Korea got its IT workers hired, under false identities, inside more than 300 American companies. It places such workers in remote jobs abroad to earn money for the state. Arizona resident Christina Chapman ran a 'laptop farm' for three years: she kept company laptops at her home so the North Korean workers appeared to be working from the US. The scheme generated more than $17m for the North Korean government. She was sentenced to eight years in federal prison in 2025.
cite: US federal court, sentence July 2025
inside: North Korea got its workers hired inside more than 300 US companies under false identities, earning over $17 million for its state.

n: UN experts: Rwanda commands M23 and placed Rwandans over eastern Congo
rank: provincial governments of North and South Kivu
d: Rwanda's army commands the M23 armed group and has placed Rwandans in charge of state functions in the parts of eastern Congo it holds, according to the UN Group of Experts, which monitors sanctions on Congo for the Security Council. M23, whose political arm is the AFC, took Goma in January 2025 and Bukavu after. The experts reported in June 2025 that Rwandan reinforcements backed the capture of Goma and that officials said President Kagame decided to take both cities. They described a 'systematic effort to dismantle existing State authority': new governors appointed, Rwandans placed over mining, tax, banking and border control, and 18 customary chiefs removed. A later report, public in mid-2026, put 14,000 to 18,000 Rwandan soldiers in the Kivus at the end of December 2025 and said Kagame's defence adviser James Kabarebe coordinated with the AFC/M23 and with former president Joseph Kabila.
cite: UN Security Council Group of Experts on the DRC, final report June 2025; Africanews, 2 July 2026, on the experts' later report; UN Group of Experts on the DRC, S/2026/466, paras. 100-101 and annex 19 (Kagame interview with Jeune Afrique, 26 March 2026)
org_note: foreign_state = Rwanda
inside: UN experts say Rwanda's army commands M23 and placed Rwandans over mining, tax, banking and border control in the eastern Congo areas it holds.
undone: These are the findings of a monitoring body appointed by the Security Council, not of a court. The later report named the Rwandan generals said to command the forces in North and South Kivu. No court has ruled on Rwanda's command of M23. In an interview with Jeune Afrique on 26 March 2026, summarised in the experts' annex 19, President Kagame rejected Rwanda's responsibility for the conflict, called it a Congolese political problem and denied that Rwanda was directing or sponsoring Kabila, while admitting that operations beyond Rwanda's borders included deploying troops and materiel and coordinating with AFC/M23, which he said were defensive measures. The Group of Experts wrote to the Government of Rwanda on 2 April 2026 seeking clarification of its support to AFC/M23 and was awaiting a reply when it reported.

n: Cuba took over restructuring of Venezuela's military counterintelligence
rank: military intelligence (DIM, later DGCIM)
d: Under secret agreements, Cuba oversaw the rebuilding of Venezuela's military intelligence service and placed Cuban officers to inspect its units. Documents seen by Reuters show that on 26 May 2008 Venezuela's defence minister and Cuba's deputy defence minister signed two agreements: Cuba would oversee the restructuring and train Venezuelan officers in Havana, and an eight-member Cuban team (GRUCE) would inspect units. The service, renamed DGCIM in 2011, shifted to watching Venezuela's own soldiers and grew to at least 1,500 agents. Reuters published this in August 2019. After US forces seized Maduro in January 2026, Reuters reported Cuban advisers being removed from DGCIM posts and withdrawing.
cite: Reuters special report 'How Cuba taught Venezuela to quash military dissent', 22 Aug 2019; Reuters reporting Feb 2026
inside: Under secret agreements Cuban officers oversaw the rebuilding of Venezuela's military intelligence and inspected its units, which turned to watching Venezuela's own soldiers.

n: Samherji allegedly paid Namibian ministers for fishing quotas ('Fishrot')
rank: fisheries minister and justice minister
d: Samherji, one of Iceland's largest fishing companies, paid Namibian officials to obtain horse-mackerel fishing quota, according to documents released by WikiLeaks on 12 November 2019 and its former Namibia manager Jóhannes Stefánsson. A quota is a government licence to catch a set amount of fish. Fisheries Minister Bernhardt Esau and Justice Minister Sacky Shanghala resigned the next day, and in December 2019 they and four associates (the 'Fishrot Six') were arrested and charged with racketeering (running a criminal enterprise), corruption, fraud and money laundering under Namibia's Prevention of Organised Crime Act. Samherji's statement of 12 November 2019 put the alleged bribes on Stefánsson alone, saying other senior staff were unaware of his actions; records later showed that he never controlled the Cyprus accounts the money passed through and that the payments ran on for three years after he left.
cite: Fishrot Files (WikiLeaks, Kveikur/Al Jazeera, Stundin), Nov 2019; Namibian Anti-Corruption Commission and Prosecutor-General arrests and charges, Dec 2019–Feb 2020; Icelandic District Prosecutor investigation into Samherji
inside: Samherji paid Namibian officials, including the fisheries and justice ministers, to obtain fishing quotas from the state.
undone: No verdict has been reached and the accused are presumed innocent. New Era reported on 16 April 2026 that the main trial, which had been set to start that week, was on hold before Judge Marelize du Plessis of Namibia's High Court, with the matter postponed to 24 April 2026 while Sakeus Shanghala sought leave to appeal the refusal of his application for her to recuse herself and a co-accused's lawyer asked that the trial proceed despite the pending interlocutory applications. Ten people were arrested in the case, among them Shanghala, Bernhardt Esau, James Hatuikulipi, Mike Nghipunya, Ricardo Gustavo and Otneel Shuudifonya. Iceland's District Prosecutor also opened an investigation into Samherji.

n: Bashar Kiwan ran Comoros's passport sales; ex-president jailed for life
rank: former president
d: Syrian-French businessman Bashar Kiwan helped run the Comoros government's passport-sale programme, under which much of the money never reached the state treasury. Under the 2008 'economic citizenship' law, Comoros sold passports in bulk to stateless people (bidoon) living in the Gulf, with Gulf money paying for them. Prosecutors said the programme brought in about 200 million dollars. On 28 November 2022 a court in Moroni, the capital, sentenced former president Ahmed Abdallah Sambi to life in prison for high treason and related charges; Kiwan was tried with him.
cite: Comoros State Security Court verdict, 28 Nov 2022 (as summarised on Wikipedia)
who: Bashar Kiwan and Gulf-funded passport buyers
inside: An outside businessman helped run the Comoros passport-sale programme, and much of its money never reached the treasury.

n: Zuneth Sattar's firms won Malawi police and army contracts via officials
rank: vice president, police inspector general, ministers
d: Companies linked to Zuneth Sattar, a UK-based businessman, won 16 contracts worth over $150 million from Malawi's police and the Malawi Defence Force between 2017 and 2021, and the Anti-Corruption Bureau said he paid officials to secure them. The bureau reported in June 2022; President Chakwera said 84 people were named and withdrew Vice President Saulos Chilima's delegated powers. Former police chief George Kainja and lands minister Kezzie Msukwa were arrested. In November 2022 the bureau arrested Chilima, alleging he received $280,000 and other items for helping two Sattar-linked firms win contracts. Chilima pleaded not guilty and denied the charges; a court dropped them on 7 May 2024 after the state filed notice to discontinue the case, giving no reasons, and he died in a plane crash the following month.
cite: Malawi Anti-Corruption Bureau report to the President, June 2022; President Chakwera's address, 21 June 2022; Al Jazeera, 'Malawi vice president arrested by anti-corruption bureau', 25 Nov 2022; BBC News, 'Malawi's Vice-President Saulos Chilima charged with corruption', 25 Nov 2022; BBC News, 'Malawi vice-president corruption charges dropped', 7 May 2024
inside: Sattar's companies paid Malawian officials, including allegedly the vice president, to win police and army contracts; his charges were later dropped.

n: Guinea-Bissau's navy and army chiefs charged in US cocaine cases
rank: former navy chief; army chief of staff
d: US prosecutors charged the heads of Guinea-Bissau's navy and army with offering their positions to help cocaine traffickers. Guinea-Bissau, in West Africa, has served since the mid-2000s as a transit point for South American cocaine headed to Europe. On 2 April 2013 the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) arrested former navy chief José Américo Bubo Na Tchuto at sea in a sting; he pleaded guilty to drug conspiracy in New York. An indictment unsealed on 18 April 2013 charged army chief Antonio Indjai with offering to store cocaine for the FARC, the Colombian guerrilla group, and sell it weapons; he stayed in Bissau and was not arrested. In February 2022 President Umaro Sissoco Embaló blamed Na Tchuto, by then back home, for a failed attack on the government palace.
cite: US Attorney SDNY indictments, April 2013; Na Tchuto guilty plea; Al Jazeera, 11 Feb 2022
inside: Guinea-Bissau's navy and army chiefs offered to use their commands to move and store cocaine for traffickers.

n: Hezbollah financiers got Gambian state monopolies under Jammeh
rank: president
d: Businessmen the US designates as financiers of Hezbollah got control of state monopolies in Gambia through President Yahya Jammeh. Hezbollah is the Lebanese Shia party and armed group; 'designated' means placed on a US sanctions list. OCCRP, a journalist network, reported on 27 March 2019 ('Great Gambia Heist') that Lebanese businessman Mohamed Bazzi was one of Jammeh's closest associates and received monopolies including the fuel supply. Ali Charara, also designated, paid 35 million dollars for half of the state telecoms firms Gamtel and Gamcel, and OCCRP estimated over 100 million dollars from Gambian telecoms reached Hezbollah. Jammeh left office in 2017.
cite: OCCRP, 'Jammeh's Taiwanese Alliance and the Hezbollah Laundromat', 27 Mar 2019; US Treasury designations of Bazzi and Charara
inside: Hezbollah-linked financiers got state monopolies and half the state telecom firms through the president, sending over $100 million towards Hezbollah.

n: Burmeister & Wain debarred for paying Mauritian officials in power tenders
rank: state electricity board tender officials
d: Burmeister & Wain Scandinavian Contractor, a Danish power-plant builder, paid members of the Mauritian administration through intermediaries during tenders for the Saint-Louis power station of the Central Electricity Board, Mauritius's state power company. The African Development Bank, which lends for such projects, reached that finding 'on the balance of probabilities' in June 2020 and debarred the firm for 21 months, meaning it could not bid on bank-funded projects.
cite: African Development Bank sanctions decision, June 2020
inside: The Danish power-plant builder paid Mauritian officials through intermediaries during tenders for the state power company's station.

n: Telecom firms paid Karimova over a billion for Uzbek licences
rank: president's daughter
d: Three foreign telecom companies paid entities controlled by Gulnara Karimova, elder daughter of the late Uzbek president Islam Karimov, to get into the Uzbek mobile market; what they got in return were licences and radio frequencies from the state. VimpelCom (2016, 795 million dollars), Telia (2017, 965 million dollars) and MTS (2019, 850 million dollars) settled US foreign-bribery cases over those payments; the figures are what each paid to settle. Uzbek prosecutors put her kickbacks at 869.3 million dollars, and OCCRP, a network of investigative journalists, reported in 2015 that she had taken over a billion dollars from Scandinavian and Russian telecom firms. She was convicted in Uzbekistan in 2017 and 2020 and remains in prison; Switzerland dropped its own trial in 2026.
cite: US DOJ/SEC FCPA resolutions with VimpelCom (2016), Telia (2017) and MTS (2019); Uzbek court verdicts 2017, 2020
inside: Three telecom companies paid entities of the president's daughter to get licences into the Uzbek mobile market.

n: Businesspeople bribed Marshall Islands lawmakers for a 'special region' law
rank: members of parliament; former president
d: Cary Yan and Gina Zhou, China-born businesspeople who had bought Marshallese passports, paid tens of thousands of dollars from about 2016 to 2020 to Marshall Islands officials, including legislators, to pass a law creating a semi-autonomous 'Rongelap Atoll Special Administrative Region'. Both pleaded guilty in New York; Zhou was sentenced in February 2023 and Yan to 42 months in May 2023. In December 2023 the US State Department barred former president Kessai Note and MP Mike Halferty from entering the US for taking those bribes; Note denies it.
cite: US DOJ sentencing release, 16 May 2023; US State Department 7031(c) designation, Dec 2023; OCCRP investigation
inside: Two businesspeople paid Marshall Islands lawmakers to pass a law creating a semi-autonomous region they wanted.

n: Micronesian president accuses China of 'political warfare'
rank: president and senior officials
d: Micronesia's outgoing president, David Panuelo, accused China of bribing and threatening officials in the Federated States of Micronesia to keep the Pacific country aligned with Beijing, or neutral, in any war over Taiwan. He made the accusation in a 13-page letter in March 2023 and called it 'political warfare'. He wrote that he had considered switching diplomatic recognition to Taiwan. China rejected the claims.
cite: Letter of President David Panuelo, 9 Mar 2023, as reported by Reuters and CNN
inside: Micronesia's president says China bribed and threatened officials to keep the country aligned with Beijing in any war over Taiwan.

n: Getax charged with bribing Nauru politicians for phosphate
rank: MPs and ministers
d: Getax Australia, a Gold Coast phosphate trader, is charged by Australian federal prosecutors with conspiring to bribe politicians in Nauru, a Pacific island state whose main export is phosphate, between 2007 and 2012 to win phosphate deals. The case has been repeatedly delayed. In a related case Sydney businessman Mozammil Bhojani pleaded guilty to paying over 120,000 dollars to a Nauruan MP and a minister and was jailed in 2018.
cite: Australian Federal Police investigation; NSW District Court sentence of Bhojani, 2018
inside: Getax is charged with bribing Nauruan politicians to win phosphate deals, and a linked businessman admitted paying an MP and a minister.
undone: Getax has not been tried and is presumed innocent. It faces one count of conspiring to bribe a foreign public official, prosecutors alleging it sought to bribe Nauruan government officials for favourable deals over Nauru's phosphate reserves. It applied to the Queensland District Court for a permanent stay of the prosecution and, in support, subpoenaed the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade for documents on the Australian Federal Police investigation. In R v Getax Australia Pty Ltd [2025] QDC 38, reported on 21 March 2025, the court set that subpoena aside and ordered Getax to pay the department's costs.

n: Australian detention subcontracts paid firms tied to Nauru's leaders
rank: justice minister; later president
d: Firms tied to Nauru's leaders received subcontracts worth millions under Australia's offshore asylum centre on Nauru, which Australia pays contractors to run. A 2023 investigation for the Sydney Morning Herald and The Age found banking records showing over 120,000 dollars in suspect payments to justice minister David Adeang, and about 2.6 million dollars to a company of Lionel Aingimea, later president. It said Australia's Home Affairs department had been warned of bribery allegations since 2010. The reporters stressed they were not claiming the payments were bribes, only that they should be scrutinised. Detailed questions were sent to Adeang and Aingimea and neither responded; Adeang has previously called bribery allegations over the earlier Getax matter 'baseless' and said they had been 'consistently disproven'.
cite: Sydney Morning Herald / The Age investigation, July 2023
inside: Reporters found that firms tied to Nauru's leaders got subcontracts under Australia's asylum centre and suspect payments reached its justice minister, though they did not call them bribes.

n: Paladin's Manus contract: 'visa' payments alleged as bribes
rank: senior PNG officials (unnamed)
d: Paladin, a company paid 530 million Australian dollars from 2017 to 2019 to run Australia's asylum centre on Manus Island in Papua New Guinea, sent money to a businessman close to senior PNG officials, according to its former director Ian Stewart. He told the Sydney Morning Herald and The Age in 2023 that over 3 million dollars went to a Singapore account of that businessman, and that a 1.5 million dollar invoice marked 'Visas' was a bribe. Paladin's former chief executive, David Saul, said he was not aware of any improper payment to any politician or official, that the businessman had a legitimate marketing relationship with Paladin and was paid far less than claimed, and that on visas Paladin 'paid nothing to any official and got nothing from them'.
cite: Sydney Morning Herald / The Age investigation, July 2023
inside: A former director of Australia's Manus contractor says it paid over $3 million to a businessman close to senior PNG officials, including a bribe invoiced as 'Visas'.

n: Albanian interior minister Tahiri and his cousin's cannabis group
rank: former interior minister
d: Saimir Tahiri, Albania's interior minister until 2017 and so in charge of its police, was tied to his cousin Moisi Habilaj's cannabis-trafficking group. Italian police arrested Habilaj in October 2017 in a probe into an Albanian-Italian group moving over 3.5 tonnes of cannabis, and wiretaps mentioned Tahiri. On 19 September 2019 Albania's Serious Crime Court convicted him of abuse of office and sentenced him to 3 years and 4 months, but dropped the drug-trafficking and organised-crime charges.
cite: Albanian Serious Crime Court verdict, 19 Sep 2019; Italian Guardia di Finanza operation, Oct 2017
inside: Albania's interior minister, in charge of its police, was charged over ties to his cousin's cannabis-trafficking group; the drug charges were dropped and he was convicted of abuse of office.

n: Croatian PM Sanader convicted of taking €10m from MOL for control of INA
rank: prime minister
d: Hungary's oil company MOL paid Croatian Prime Minister Ivo Sanader a 10 million euro bribe to give it management control of Croatia's national oil company INA, Croatian courts found. MOL is a Hungarian company in which the state has influence. The courts found the payment came from MOL chief executive Zsolt Hernádi. A 2012 verdict was quashed in 2015, but Sanader was convicted again in 2020 and the Supreme Court confirmed it in 2021. Hungary has not handed Hernádi to Croatia and MOL denies the bribe.
cite: Zagreb County Court verdict 2020, upheld by the Croatian Supreme Court 2021
inside: Hungary's oil company paid Croatia's prime minister €10 million to give it management control of Croatia's national oil company.

n: Lithuanian president impeached over Russian donor Borisov
rank: president
d: Yuri Borisov, a Russian businessman who ran the helicopter firm Avia Baltika, reportedly gave about 400,000 dollars to Rolandas Paksas's 2002 presidential campaign and then received Lithuanian citizenship by Paksas's decree. On 31 March 2004 the Constitutional Court found Paksas had broken the constitution and his oath, and on 6 April 2004 the Seimas, Lithuania's parliament, removed him, the first European head of state impeached. The European Court of Human Rights later found his lifetime ban from parliament disproportionate.
cite: Constitutional Court of Lithuania ruling, 31 Mar 2004; Seimas impeachment vote, 6 Apr 2004
inside: A Russian businessman reportedly funded the president's campaign and was then granted Lithuanian citizenship by that president's decree.

n: Yorgen Fenech's 17 Black and Malta's prime minister's office
rank: PM's chief of staff and energy minister
d: Yorgen Fenech, a Maltese businessman, owned 17 Black, a Dubai company that leaked papers showed was expected to pay Panama companies held by the prime minister's chief of staff Keith Schembri and minister Konrad Mizzi. Journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia had exposed the companies; she was murdered in 2017. Fenech was arrested in November 2019 and indicted in 2021 for commissioning her murder; Schembri and Mizzi resigned. A 2021 public inquiry found the state created an 'atmosphere of impunity', and a magisterial inquiry led to charges over 17 Black against Fenech, Schembri and Mizzi. On 2 September 2026 a jury in Valletta found Fenech not guilty of complicity in the murder and of criminal association.
cite: Public inquiry into the death of Daphne Caruana Galizia, report July 2021; Maltese indictments
inside: A businessman's Dubai company was set up to pay secret companies of the prime minister's chief of staff and the energy minister.
undone: On 2 September 2026 a nine-member jury at the Law Courts in Valletta found Fenech not guilty of complicity in the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia and of criminal association, by eight votes to one on each charge; the prosecution was expected to appeal. He is therefore not guilty of those charges. Keith Schembri, who testified over three days in late July 2026 and denied any involvement, has not been charged over the murder. The report of the acquittal records no other charge against Fenech, and no verdict in the 17 Black proceedings was found.

n: 'Monacogate': Rybolovlev graft case over courting officials closed
rank: public prosecutor and senior officials
d: Dmitry Rybolovlev, a Russian billionaire who owns AS Monaco football club, was suspected of courting Monaco officials, including former public prosecutor Jean-Pierre Dreno, to get favourable treatment. The suspicion rested on messages from the phone of his lawyer Tetiana Bersheda. In November 2018 he was made a formal suspect in a corruption and influence-peddling probe. The case against Dreno and Rybolovlev was dismissed in 2023, and in February 2025 Monaco's courts closed it, ruling the phone data unlawfully obtained after a European Court of Human Rights finding.
cite: Monaco investigating judges 2018–2023; European Court of Human Rights judgment, June 2024; Monaco court ruling, Feb 2025
inside: A billionaire was suspected of courting Monaco officials, including the public prosecutor, to get favourable treatment; the courts later closed the case.

n: 'Conto Mazzini': businessmen paid San Marino politicians for licences
rank: former state secretaries and party leaders
d: Construction and banking entrepreneurs paid San Marino politicians to obtain building permits and banking licences, prosecutors said, with cash drawn from an account in the name of 'Giuseppe Mazzini' at Banca Commerciale Sammarinese. Twenty-one former political figures, including former state secretaries (ministers) Fiorenzo Stolfi and Claudio Podeschi, went on trial in 2015 for criminal association to launder bribes; about 200 million euros were seized. Several were convicted in 2017, and an appeal court upheld most convictions in March 2022 with lower sentences.
cite: San Marino criminal court, 2017; appeal ruling, March 2022; Freedom House 'Freedom in the World' 2023
inside: Construction and banking entrepreneurs paid San Marino ministers and party leaders to obtain building permits and banking licences.

n: Patria armoured-vehicle bribery case against Janez Janša
rank: prime minister
d: Patria, a Finnish state-owned arms maker, paid bribes partly aimed at Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša to win a 278 million euro deal for 135 armoured vehicles signed in 2006, Finnish broadcaster YLE alleged in 2008. A Ljubljana court sentenced Janša to two years in 2013, but the Constitutional Court annulled the verdict and the case lapsed in 2016. In Finland the defendants were acquitted on appeal; Austria convicted one middleman.
cite: Ljubljana District Court, 5 June 2013; Constitutional Court of Slovenia, 2015; Finnish and Austrian proceedings
inside: The Finnish arms maker allegedly paid bribes partly aimed at Slovenia's prime minister to win the armoured-vehicle deal his government signed.

n: Stanford paid Antigua's bank regulator to look away, US charges
rank: head of the Financial Services Regulatory Commission
d: R. Allen Stanford paid Leroy King, head of Antigua's Financial Services Regulatory Commission, the body that supervised Stanford's bank, more than 100,000 dollars in bribes to ignore the bank's real assets and help obstruct an SEC investigation, according to a June 2009 US indictment. Stanford ran Stanford International Bank from Antigua and was convicted in the US of a 7 billion dollar fraud. The SEC is the US securities regulator. Antigua extradited King to Houston on 12 November 2019.
cite: US DOJ indictment (S.D. Texas, June 2009); DOJ release on extradition, 12 Nov 2019
inside: Stanford paid the head of Antigua's bank regulator to ignore his bank's real assets and help obstruct a US investigation.

n: Iranian donor got Dominica diplomatic post, Al Jazeera reports
rank: prime minister
d: Iranian businessman Alireza Monfared gave hundreds of thousands of dollars to Dominican Prime Minister Roosevelt Skerrit's 2014 campaign in return for an ambassadorship and a diplomatic passport, Al Jazeera reported in November 2019; a witness said Skerrit handed it over in Kuala Lumpur. Dominica, a Caribbean island state, sells citizenship; OCCRP found about 7,700 buyers by 2023, including Afghanistan's former spy chief and sanctioned Russians. Monfared was later jailed in Iran for oil-revenue theft. Skerrit denies any trade.
cite: Al Jazeera Investigative Unit, 27 Nov 2019; OCCRP/Government Accountability Project, 11 Oct 2023
inside: An Iranian businessman reportedly gave money to the prime minister's campaign in return for a Dominican ambassadorship and diplomatic passport.
undone: The account has never been tested in a court or by any public inquiry. It rests on Al Jazeera's undercover filming and the word of one witness, no charge has been reported against Skerrit, and he denies any trade. He is presumed innocent.

n: Odebrecht paid 92 million dollars in Dominican bribes for public works
rank: public works minister
d: Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction company, paid 92 million dollars in bribes in the Dominican Republic to win public works, it admitted to the US in 2016. In October 2021 a Dominican court convicted businessman Ángel Rondón, named as the channel for the bribes, and former public works minister Víctor Díaz Rúa; four other defendants were acquitted. An appeal court upheld both convictions on 19 May 2023.
cite: US DOJ plea agreement with Odebrecht, Dec 2016; Dominican court verdict Oct 2021, upheld 19 May 2023
inside: Odebrecht paid $92 million in Dominican bribes through a businessman to win public works, and the public works minister was convicted.

n: Investor says he paid Grenada's PM; diplomatic posts for kickbacks alleged
rank: prime minister
d: Investor Eric Resteiner claimed he paid about half a million dollars to Grenada's Prime Minister Keith Mitchell, Al Jazeera reported in November 2019; Mitchell said he received only 15,000 dollars for travel costs. Grenada sells citizenship and has given ambassador titles to foreign businessmen. US businessman Leo Ford said a partner was offered a diplomatic post for kickbacks on state projects, which the government denies.
cite: Al Jazeera Investigative Unit, 27 Nov 2019
inside: An investor says he paid Grenada's prime minister, and another businessman says a partner was offered a diplomatic post for kickbacks on state projects; the government denies both.

n: Mohamed gold family bribed Guyanese officials, US says
rank: permanent secretary, customs officials
d: Guyanese gold traders Nazar Mohamed, his son Azruddin and their firm Mohamed's Enterprise bribed customs officials, paid officials for favourable treatment in court matters and bribed to win state contracts, the US Treasury said on 11 June 2024 when it sanctioned them. It said they left over 10,000 kg of gold off customs declarations in 2019–2023 and evaded more than 50 million dollars in duty. It also sanctioned Mae Thomas, permanent secretary (the top civil servant) of the home affairs ministry from 2020 to 2023, for taking cash and gifts in return for contract, gun-permit and passport favours. The Mohameds deny wrongdoing.
cite: US Treasury OFAC press release JY2401, 11 June 2024
inside: Gold traders bribed customs officials and a top home affairs civil servant for duty evasion, court favours and state contracts.

n: Honduran president Hernández took trafficker bribes to protect cocaine
rank: head of state
d: Drug traffickers paid Juan Orlando Hernández, president of Honduras from 2014 to 2022, millions of dollars in bribes to protect US-bound cocaine shipments, a New York jury found. Several convicted traffickers testified that they had paid him. He was convicted in the Southern District of New York of conspiracy to import cocaine and related weapons counts, and sentenced to 45 years in June 2024. His brother, a former congressman, was convicted in the same district in 2018. He was granted a full US presidential pardon on 1 December 2025 and released the same day; Honduras then asked Interpol, the international police network, to execute a 2023 domestic arrest order written to take effect if US authorities freed him.
cite: US v. Hernandez, S.D.N.Y., verdict March 2024, sentence June 2024; presidential pardon 1 December 2025; Honduran Ministerio Publico arrest order, December 2025; Al Jazeera, 'Honduras ex-president sentenced to 45 years for helping drug traffickers', 26 June 2024
undone: Pardoned by the US president in December 2025; released the same day.
inside: Drug traffickers paid the president of Honduras millions of dollars to protect their US-bound cocaine shipments.

n: Sinaloa Cartel paid Mexico's security chief García Luna
rank: security minister
d: The Sinaloa Cartel paid Genaro García Luna, Mexico's Secretary of Public Security from 2006 to 2012 and the cabinet minister who ran the federal police, in exchange for protection from arrest, safe passage for its shipments and warnings of coming operations. He held the post during the militarised phase of the drug war. A US federal court in the Eastern District of New York convicted him in February 2023 on all five counts, including continuing criminal enterprise (running a large drug operation), and sentenced him in 2024. In May 2025 a US court ordered him and his wife to pay Mexico more than $2.4 billion in a civil suit over public contracts, the largest financial judgment attached to any official on this map.
cite: US v. Garcia Luna, E.D.N.Y., verdict February 2023, sentence 2024; US civil judgment for the Government of Mexico, May 2025
inside: The Sinaloa Cartel paid the minister in charge of the federal police for protection, safe passage for its shipments and warnings of operations.

n: Medellín Cartel paid Panama's ruler Noriega for protection
rank: head of state
d: Manuel Noriega, Panama's military ruler and head of state from 1983 to 1989, took money from the Medellín Cartel as protection money, bribes or shares of profits, and a 1988 US indictment said he turned Panama into a shipping platform for South American cocaine bound for the US. After the US invasion removed him, a Miami federal court convicted him in 1992 on eight of ten counts of drug trafficking, racketeering (running a criminal enterprise) and money laundering. On 10 July 1992 he was sentenced to 40 years. It was the earliest case in which a sitting head of state's control of the security apparatus was prosecuted as a trafficking enterprise.
cite: US v. Noriega, S.D. Fla., 1992; Wikipedia, 'Manuel Noriega' (conviction on eight of ten counts; sentence 10 July 1992)
inside: The Medellín Cartel paid Panama's military ruler, who turned the country into a shipping platform for its cocaine.

n: Guinea-Bissau's navy chief Na Tchuto offered his post to traffickers
rank: armed forces chief
d: José Américo Bubo Na Tchuto, chief of staff of Guinea-Bissau's navy, offered to use his position to help move cocaine into the United States. He was taken in a sting by the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) in international waters and pleaded guilty in New York to conspiring to import cocaine. The country's air force chief was indicted in the same operation. Guinea-Bissau, in West Africa, has been a transit point for South American cocaine headed for Europe.
cite: US v. Na Tchuto, S.D.N.Y., plea 2014
inside: Guinea-Bissau's navy chief offered to use his command to help traffickers move cocaine into the United States.

n: Parapolítica: AUC paramilitaries' collusion with Colombia's Congress
rank: legislature
d: Colombia's AUC paramilitaries, armed groups that were themselves among the country's largest cocaine traffickers, colluded with members of Congress, and roughly 30% of the Congress was investigated, charged or convicted over it. The scandal is known as 'parapolítica' and was prosecuted by the Supreme Court of Justice from 2006. By April 2012, 139 members of Congress were under investigation; five governors and 32 legislators had been convicted. A later review by the Inspector General's office counted more than 500 elected officials investigated over a decade.
cite: Supreme Court of Justice proceedings from 2006; Human Rights Watch; Procuraduria General
inside: AUC paramilitaries colluded with members of Colombia's Congress, and dozens of legislators and governors were convicted over it.

n: Bolivia's anti-drug police chief sold protection for cocaine loads
rank: counter-narcotics chief
d: René Sanabria, former commander of Bolivia's national anti-narcotics force (FELCN) and from 2009 head of an elite drug intelligence unit inside the Interior Ministry, sold protection to cocaine shippers. He was taken in a sting by the US Drug Enforcement Administration: his group agreed to protect Miami-bound cocaine loads for a 50,000 payment, and one container shipment was seized on arrival. He pleaded guilty in Miami and was sentenced on 23 September 2011 to 14 years; his co-defendant got nine.
cite: US v. Sanabria-Oropeza and Foronda-Azero, S.D. Fla., pleas June 2011, sentences 23 September 2011
inside: Bolivia's former anti-drug police chief, then running a drug intelligence unit, sold protection to cocaine shippers.

n: H-2 cartel used Nayarit's attorney general Veytia
rank: state prosecutor
d: The H-2 cartel used Edgar Veytia, attorney general (chief prosecutor) of the Mexican state of Nayarit, to serve it from 2013 to 2017, US prosecutors established. He directed officers to wiretap and arrest rival traffickers, released the cartel's members from custody and assisted acts of violence. He had campaigned on the claim that there was no room for organised crime in Nayarit. He pleaded guilty in Brooklyn to a conspiracy to import heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine and marijuana, and on 26 September 2019 was sentenced to 20 years with $1 million in forfeiture. Two months earlier the US Treasury had sanctioned his governor, Roberto Sandoval.
cite: US v. Veytia Cambero, E.D.N.Y., guilty plea 2019, sentence 26 September 2019 before Judge Carol Bagley Amon
inside: The H-2 cartel used Nayarit's chief prosecutor, who had officers arrest its rivals and released its members from custody.

n: Tamaulipas governor Yarrington took $3.5m in bribes for state business
rank: state governor
d: Tomás Yarrington, governor of the Mexican state of Tamaulipas from 1999 to 2005 and a presidential candidate, admitted taking more than $3.5 million in bribes; US prosecutors said they came from individuals and private companies in Mexico in exchange for deals with the state government. He fled Mexico in 2012, was arrested in Italy in 2017 and extradited to the US the following year. He pleaded guilty in 2021 to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and was sentenced in March 2023 to nine years. Charges of conspiracy to import cocaine and marijuana and of bank fraud were dismissed under the plea. He was released in November 2024 after a sentence adjustment for time served and returned to Mexico in April 2025 to face a second laundering case.
cite: US v. Yarrington Ruvalcaba, S.D. Tex., plea 25 March 2021, sentence 15 March 2023; Bureau of Prisons release records, 2024; Fiscalia General de la Republica proceedings, 2025; US Attorney's Office, S.D. Texas, 'Former Mexican governor and presidential candidate sentenced for money laundering', March 2023
inside: Companies paid the governor of Tamaulipas more than $3.5 million in return for deals with his state government.

n: 'Metastasis': traffickers paid Ecuador's judges, prosecutors and police
rank: judiciary and police
d: Drug traffickers paid judges, prosecutors, police commanders and prison officials in Ecuador to fix cases and protect them, a case known as 'Metastasis'. It came to light from the decrypted phone of a trafficker. After 28 days of hearings the National Court sentenced 20 of 21 defendants on 25 November 2024 to between three and ten years, with public service treated as an aggravating factor. The former president of the Judiciary Council, which oversees Ecuador's judges, drew nine years and four months for delaying a habeas corpus in favour of a trafficker's brother for money; another judge was convicted over a release order priced at $200,000. Two fugitives, a former legislator and a businessman, are subject to extradition requests to Venezuela and the United States.
