On 1 April 1941 they and Rashid Ali al-Gaylani overthrew the regent's government and set up a 'National Defence Government'. Britain invaded in the Anglo-Iraqi War that followed; the plotters fled, and all four were later returned to Iraq and executed.
cite: Golden Square (Iraq) (Wikipedia)
inside: A cabal of pro-Axis army officers decided which Iraqi governments survived, then overthrew the government in 1941 with encouragement from German and Italian envoys.

n: Orange Order members held every Northern Ireland premiership, 1921–69
rank: Prime Minister and cabinet of Northern Ireland
d: The Orange Order, a Protestant fraternal society, held a formal place inside Northern Ireland's ruling Ulster Unionist Party: when the Ulster Unionist Council was formed in 1905 the Order had 50 of its 200 seats, a link it kept until 2005. From 1921 to 1969 every Prime Minister of Northern Ireland was an Orangeman, all but three cabinet ministers were, and 87 of the 95 MPs who never reached cabinet were members. Prime Minister James Craig said in 1934 that he was 'an Orangeman first and a politician and a member of this parliament afterwards' and spoke of 'a Protestant Parliament and a Protestant State'. The Unionist party, led by Orangemen, governed without interruption until direct rule from London in 1972.
cite: Orange Order (Wikipedia, citing Ulster Unionist Council history and Craig's 1932–34 speeches)
inside: The Orange Order held formal seats in the ruling party's governing council, and its members held nearly every cabinet post in what its premier called a Protestant state.

n: IRB faction inside Ireland's National Army purged after 1924 mutiny
rank: National Army command; defence minister
d: After the Irish Civil War, the Irish Republican Brotherhood, a secret oath-bound society, re-formed in 1923 as a faction inside the Free State's National Army, backing Minister for Defence Richard Mulcahy against a rival group of officers, the 'Old IRA'. The rivalry over the IRB's hold on army posts led to the Army Mutiny of 1924. In its aftermath Mulcahy resigned and Kevin O'Higgins, acting head of government, dismissed other IRB members from the army. The IRB then dissolved itself, and the episode helped establish civilian control over the Irish army.
cite: Irish Republican Brotherhood (Wikipedia)
inside: A secret oath-bound society re-formed as a faction holding posts inside Ireland's National Army, and the fight over its grip on those posts led to the 1924 mutiny.

n: Bavarian Illuminati placed members in state bodies until banned in 1785
rank: Civic and state governing bodies; court officials
d: The Illuminati were a secret society founded on 1 May 1776 by Adam Weishaupt, a professor at the University of Ingolstadt in Bavaria, and four students. It recruited heavily among lawyers, academics, churchmen and officials, and its members came to hold seats in many civic and state governing bodies, where some court officials reportedly favoured fellow members. About 650 members can be verified at the end of 1784, and the true total was perhaps about 1,300. Elector Charles Theodore banned it and other secret societies by edicts from 1784; the edict of 2 March 1785 effectively ended it. The government seized its papers in 1786–87 and published them in 1787.
cite: Illuminati (Wikipedia)
inside: The Illuminati recruited officials into a secret society, and its members came to hold seats in state bodies where some reportedly favoured fellow members.

n: Carbonari officers forced a constitution on the King of Naples
rank: Army regiments and state officials
d: The Carbonari were a secret revolutionary society whose members in the Kingdom of Naples included nobles, priests, landlords, government officials and army officers. On 1 July 1820 two officers, Michele Morelli and Joseph Silvati, led cavalry regiments towards Nola, and General Guglielmo Pepe and many other officers and officials joined. King Ferdinand I agreed to grant a constitution and a parliament. The Holy Alliance sent an Austrian army in February 1821 that defeated the movement; Morelli and Silvati were sentenced to death and Pepe went into exile.
cite: Carbonari (Wikipedia, citing Villari 1911)
inside: A secret revolutionary society had officers and officials among its members, and they led army regiments to force the King of Naples to grant a constitution.

n: La Cagoule: secret society funded by industrialists infiltrated French army
rank: Army officers; later Vichy's Milice
d: La Cagoule was a secret far-right society founded in 1936 by Eugène Deloncle, organised in military-style cells whose members swore an oath on pain of death. It was funded by industrialists including L'Oréal founder Eugène Schueller and Louis Renault. Through Georges Loustaunau-Lacau's Corvignolles network it infiltrated parts of the French army to obtain weapons, and it carried out assassinations and the bombing of two employers' buildings on 11 September 1937 to blame communists. It planned to overthrow the Popular Front government in November 1937; police had infiltrated it, and about 70 men were arrested. Member Joseph Darnand later led the Vichy regime's Milice.
cite: La Cagoule (Wikipedia)
inside: A secret far-right society funded by industrialists got inside parts of the French army through an officers' network in order to obtain weapons for a planned coup.

n: US envoy Poinsett used York Rite lodges to reshape Mexico's cabinet
rank: President Victoria's cabinet
d: Joel Roberts Poinsett, the first United States minister to Mexico, promoted the York Rite branch of Freemasonry there, which was tied to US political interests and became one of three competing Masonic strands in Mexican politics. He used his connection with the York Rite lodges to pressure President Guadalupe Victoria into removing allies such as Lucas Alamán from his cabinet. Some historians call this the first US 'soft' coup in Latin America, saying it installed a compliant government that dropped plans for a naval expedition against Spanish-held Cuba and Puerto Rico. Poinsett became caught up in Mexico's political turmoil and was recalled in 1829–30.
cite: Joel Roberts Poinsett (Wikipedia)
inside: The United States' envoy used Masonic lodges tied to US interests to press Mexico's president into removing ministers, reshaping the cabinet in Washington's favour.

n: Irish bishops' secret objections killed a health scheme; minister resigned
rank: Cabinet health policy
d: Ireland's Catholic bishops, led by Archbishop John Charles McQuaid of Dublin, steered the cabinet of Taoiseach John A. Costello to drop the Mother and Child Scheme, Health Minister Noël Browne's 1950 plan for free health care for mothers and children up to 16. On 5 April 1951 McQuaid told Costello the scheme was 'opposed to Catholic social teaching', and Costello told McQuaid he would accept the Church's view even if it brought down the government. Browne was left alone in cabinet and resigned on 11 April 1951. The next day The Irish Times published the private correspondence between the bishops and ministers, revealing how far the hierarchy had decided government policy.
cite: Mother and Child Scheme (Wikipedia)
inside: Catholic bishops secretly told the Irish cabinet what Church teaching allowed, and the government dropped its own health scheme rather than defy them.

n: Jamaat-e-Islami activists given judicial jobs under Zia, Pakistan
rank: Judiciary; cabinet (information ministry)
d: Jamaat-e-Islami, Pakistan's main Islamist movement, became seen as the ideological and political arm of General Zia-ul-Haq's military government after 1977, with members at times holding cabinet posts including information and broadcasting. Journalist Owen Bennett-Jones writes that 'tens of thousands of Jamaat activists and sympathisers were given jobs in the judiciary', and that these appointments kept Zia's Islamisation agenda alive after his death in 1988. Jamaat also backed Zia's support for the war against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan. Zia later distanced himself from the party over elections.
cite: Jamaat-e-Islami Pakistan (Wikipedia, citing Owen Bennett-Jones, Pakistan: Eye of the Storm)
inside: An Islamist movement placed tens of thousands of its activists in judicial jobs under a military ruler, and they kept his Islamisation agenda going after his death.

n: Brotherhood leader Turabi made Sudan's attorney general; Islamists placed
rank: Attorney General and Justice Minister
d: Hassan al-Turabi, who had taken control of Sudan's Muslim Brotherhood and led its political arm, the Islamic Charter Front, was brought back by President Gaafar Nimeiry under a 1977 'National Reconciliation' and made Justice Minister and Attorney General in 1979. His movement took a 'top down' approach, placing party members in high posts in government and the security services. Turabi became Nimeiry's foreign-affairs adviser in 1983 and was instrumental in institutionalising sharia law in northern Sudan; Nimeiry's September 1983 laws imposed it on the whole country and set off renewed civil war in the south. This groundwork preceded the 1989 coup that Turabi is alleged to have designed.
cite: Hassan al-Turabi; Gaafar Nimeiry (Wikipedia)
inside: The Muslim Brotherhood's leader was made attorney general and his movement placed its members in high government and security posts, where they pushed in sharia law.

n: Sudan's Free Officers took power in 1969; Nimeiry led their council
rank: Revolutionary Command Council; head of state
d: Sudan's Free Officers were a clandestine group of army officers on the Egyptian model. On 25 May 1969 Colonel Gaafar Nimeiry, commanding the Khartoum garrison, joined other Free Officers in overthrowing the civilian government of Ismail al-Azhari, in what they called the 'May Revolution'. Nimeiry made himself chairman of their Revolutionary Command Council and ruled Sudan until 1985, later bringing Islamists into government and imposing sharia law across the country in September 1983.
cite: Gaafar Nimeiry (Wikipedia)
inside: A clandestine group of army officers used the Khartoum garrison to overthrow Sudan's civilian government, and its own council then ruled the country.

n: Heritage's 1981 Mandate: about 60% of 2,000-plus proposals begun in a year
rank: Reagan cabinet; Interior Secretary; NEH chair
d: The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank in Washington, wrote a 20-volume, roughly 3,000-page programme for Ronald Reagan's incoming administration, Mandate for Leadership, with more than 2,000 recommendations for moving the federal government in a conservative direction. Reagan handed out copies at his first cabinet meeting, and the administration hired contributors including James G. Watt, who became Secretary of the Interior, and William Bennett, who became chair of the National Endowment for the Humanities and later Education Secretary. According to its authors, about 60 percent of the proposals had been implemented or begun by the end of Reagan's first year. Heritage has produced a Mandate for each new conservative administration since, most recently Project 2025.
cite: Mandate for Leadership (Wikipedia, citing Washington Post 16 Nov 1980 and New York Times 2002)
inside: A think tank wrote a programme for the incoming government, its contributors were hired into top posts, and about 60 percent of its proposals were acted on.

n: PNAC think tank's signatories took 10 posts in Bush's Iraq-war government
who: Project for the New American Century
rank: Vice President; Defence Secretary; Deputy Defence Secretary
d: The Project for the New American Century (PNAC), a Washington think tank founded in 1997 by William Kristol and Robert Kagan, called in an open letter to President Clinton in January 1998 for the removal of Saddam Hussein; signatories included Donald Rumsfeld, Paul Wolfowitz, Elliott Abrams and John Bolton. Ten of the 25 people who signed its 1997 statement of principles then served in George W. Bush's administration, among them Vice President Dick Cheney, Defence Secretary Rumsfeld and Deputy Defence Secretary Wolfowitz; Scooter Libby became Cheney's chief of staff and Bolton UN ambassador. Shortly after 11 September 2001 PNAC urged Bush to remove Saddam, and its members supported the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Some scholars argue its influence on the decision has been exaggerated.
cite: Project for the New American Century (Wikipedia, citing Abelson and Parmar)
inside: Members of a think tank that campaigned to remove Saddam Hussein took senior posts in the Bush government, which then invaded Iraq, though some scholars question its influence.

n: ADF lawyers wrote Mississippi's abortion law that ended Roe v. Wade
rank: State legislation; Mississippi Attorney General's legal team
d: Alliance Defending Freedom (ADF), a Christian conservative legal organisation, wrote the model for Mississippi's 15-week abortion ban, a law designed to provoke a legal challenge to Roe v. Wade. When it was challenged, ADF lawyers joined the Mississippi Attorney General's legal team to defend it, and in Dobbs v. Jackson (2022) the Supreme Court overturned Roe and Casey and returned abortion law to the states. ADF says it authored at least 130 bills in 34 states in 2022, of which more than 30 became law, and its members wrote model 'bathroom bills'. Former ADF attorney Mike Johnson became Speaker of the House of Representatives on 25 October 2023.
cite: Alliance Defending Freedom (Wikipedia, citing ADF 'Who We Are', The Nation, NBC News 2021, CBS News 2023)
inside: A Christian legal group wrote the model for a state abortion law and then joined the state's own legal team to defend it up to the Supreme Court.

n: Scientology's secret Project Normandy aimed to take control of Clearwater
rank: Clearwater city government and local media
d: The Church of Scientology ran a secret operation, Project Normandy, to take control of Clearwater, Florida, by infiltrating city offices and local media. A front group, the 'United Churches of Florida', bought the Fort Harrison Hotel for $3 million, which became the church's headquarters. A 'Top Secret' internal document of 5 December 1975 set the aim of working out whom to penetrate and 'handle' to establish 'area control'. The plan was found in a 1977 FBI raid on Scientology offices and reported by the Clearwater Sun in November 1979. The church had also tried to entrap Mayor Gabriel Cazares in a sex scandal and staged a fake hit-and-run; he sued, and the church settled in 1986. Clearwater remains its main base.
cite: Project Normandy (Wikipedia, citing Clearwater Sun 3 Nov 1979)
inside: The Church of Scientology drew up a secret plan to penetrate and 'handle' Clearwater's city offices and local media so it could control the town.

n: Fundación Mediterránea economists took over Argentina's economy ministry
rank: Ministry of Economy
d: Domingo Cavallo used the Fundación Mediterránea, a business-funded think tank in Córdoba, to prepare a team of economists to take over Argentina's economy, and backed Carlos Menem's 1989 presidential bid. Cavallo, who had briefly led the central bank in 1982, became Economy Minister in February 1991 and brought that team into the ministry. On 1 April 1991 he signed the Convertibility law that fixed the peso at one US dollar, and he served until 1996. Recalled as minister in March 2001, he froze bank deposits in late November 2001, measures known as the 'corralito', shortly before Argentina's economic collapse and record debt default.
cite: Domingo Cavallo (Wikipedia)
inside: A business-funded think tank trained a team of economists that took over Argentina's economy ministry and carried out its own programme there.

n: ICMI under minister Habibie moved Muslim intellectuals into Suharto's state
rank: Civil service and central ministries; vice-presidency
d: The Indonesian Association of Muslim Intellectuals (ICMI) was formed in 1990 under B. J. Habibie, then Minister of Research and Technology, with President Suharto's permission as he courted Islamic support. In return for backing the regime, ICMI gained influence over policy and administration: its members moved into the civil service and central ministries, and it helped set up religious courts, Bank Muamalat and the newspaper Republika. By 1994 it had about 80,000 members. Critics, including groups in Nahdlatul Ulama, called it a lobby for Suharto's regime and a vehicle for Habibie, who became vice-president in 1998 and then president when Suharto resigned.
cite: Indonesian Association of Muslim Intellectuals (Wikipedia)
inside: A Muslim intellectuals' association moved its members into the civil service and ministries, and used that place to set up religious courts and an Islamic bank.

n: Sasson report: state ministries built illegal settler outposts
rank: Housing, defence, education and energy ministries; WZO settlement division
d: An official report commissioned by Prime Minister Ariel Sharon and written by former senior prosecutor Talia Sasson, published on 8 March 2005, found that Israeli state bodies had spent millions of shekels supporting unauthorised West Bank settlement outposts, against the government's own rules. The Defence Ministry approved trailers to start outposts; the Housing Ministry supplied 400 mobile homes, some placed on private Palestinian land; the World Zionist Organization's settlement division, the Education Ministry and the Energy Ministry also helped. The settler movement Gush Emunim, founded in 1974, and its building arm Amana drove the outposts, and Amana received about 100 million shekels in state money in 2013–2015. In 2017 Gush Emunim co-founder Pinchas Wallerstein was appointed to head a committee on legalising outposts.
cite: Sasson Report; Gush Emunim (Wikipedia)
inside: An official report found state ministries funding the settler movement's illegal outposts against the government's own rules, and a movement co-founder later headed a committee on legalising them.

n: CIA directed Iran's 1953 coup, including bribes to members of parliament
rank: Prime minister and parliament (Majlis)
d: The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), with British help, bribed members of Iran's parliament and organised the security forces to remove Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh in August 1953, after he nationalised Iran's oil. A CIA internal history released by the National Security Archive in August 2013 says the coup 'was carried out under CIA direction as an act of US foreign policy'. The plan, codenamed TPAJAX, also included propaganda against Mossadegh, persuading the Shah to cooperate and stirring up demonstrations. General Fazlollah Zahedi replaced Mossadegh, and the CIA arranged to pay his new government $5 million within days. The Shah ruled as a close US ally until the 1979 revolution.
cite: Foreign Policy, 19 Aug 2013; Al Jazeera, 20 Aug 2013 (CIA history released by the National Security Archive)
inside: The CIA bribed members of Iran's parliament and organised its security forces to remove the prime minister who had nationalised Iran's oil.

n: CIA secretly funded Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party
rank: Ruling party (LDP) and its members
d: The CIA secretly gave money to Japan's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), which has governed Japan for most years since 1955, and to its members during the 1950s and 1960s. Former intelligence officers described the payments to The New York Times in 1994: the aim was to make Japan a bulwark against communism and undermine the Japanese left, and the CIA also recruited informers inside the party. In July 2006 the State Department's official history series, Foreign Relations of the United States, formally acknowledged the covert funding for the first time, saying it was meant to keep an LDP-led government in power. Some money also went to moderate Socialists. The LDP denies receiving it.
cite: New York Times News Service via Deseret News, 9 Oct 1994; Japan Times, 20 Jul 2006 (FRUS vol. XXIX part 2)
inside: The CIA secretly funded Japan's ruling party and its members and recruited informers inside it, to keep a government friendly to the United States in power.

n: CIA paid over half of Frei's campaign costs in Chile's 1964 election
rank: Presidential election and Congress
d: The CIA paid slightly more than half the cost of Eduardo Frei's Christian Democratic campaign in Chile's 1964 presidential election, without Frei being told. The US Senate's Church Committee, which investigated US intelligence abuses, set this out in its 1975 report 'Covert Action in Chile 1963–1973'. It counted about $13.4 million spent in that decade, $8 million of it on elections and party support, including money for chosen congressional candidates in 1965 and 1968–69 and about $4 million for opposition parties in 1971–73. The CIA also funded the newspaper El Mercurio. On 15 September 1970 President Nixon ordered the CIA to help organise a military coup against the elected president, Salvador Allende.
cite: US Senate Select Committee on Intelligence Activities (Church Committee), 'Covert Action in Chile 1963–1973', 1975
inside: The CIA secretly paid more than half of a presidential campaign and funded chosen congressional candidates, so Chile's elected officials owed their seats partly to US money.

n: CIA handed 'bags of money' to Italian politicians before the 1948 vote
rank: Christian Democrat and allied candidates
d: The CIA delivered cash to chosen Italian politicians — Christian Democrats, Republicans and other pro-American parties — to pay campaign costs such as posters and pamphlets before Italy's April 1948 general election. F. Mark Wyatt, a CIA officer involved, described the 'bags of money' in a later interview and said guidance on whom to back came partly from Christian Democrat leader Alcide De Gasperi. The Christian Democrats won about 48% of the vote and the Communist-led Popular Democratic Front 31%. A US Defense Department draft history says the CIA then gave an average of $5 million a year in covert aid in Italy from the late 1940s to the early 1960s.
cite: F. Mark Wyatt interview, CNN Cold War series (National Security Archive); US DoD draft history cited in 'CIA activities in Italy'
inside: The CIA paid the campaign costs of chosen Italian politicians, so the parties that won and governed had been financed by US intelligence.

n: CIA-funded Gehlen Organization became West Germany's spy service, the BND
rank: Foreign intelligence service (BND)
d: The Gehlen Organization, a spy network built after 1945 by Reinhard Gehlen, the Wehrmacht's former intelligence chief on the Eastern Front, worked with the newly created CIA from 1947, and the CIA supplied its money, cars and aircraft. On 1 April 1956 the organisation was turned into West Germany's official foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), with Gehlen as its first president until 1968. It employed hundreds of former Nazi Party members, and Gehlen told a Bundestag committee in 1953 that about 40 of its staff came from the SS and SD, the Nazi party's armed and security branches. The CIA's own declassified history describes the relationship.
cite: CIA history 'CIA and the Origins of the BND, 1945–49' (declassified); Wikipedia, 'Gehlen Organization'
inside: The CIA funded and equipped a spy network that then became West Germany's official intelligence service, giving it a hand in building that service from the start.

n: CIA paid King Hussein of Jordan millions a year for 20 years
rank: King
d: The CIA made secret yearly payments of millions of dollars to King Hussein of Jordan for about 20 years, The Washington Post reported in February 1977. Hussein had been king since 1952, so the payments covered most of his reign up to then. President Jimmy Carter halted them a few days before the story ran. The report gave no exact figure. It appeared while Washington was still dealing with the Senate Church Committee's 1975–76 inquiry into the CIA, and US officials began assessing what the disclosure would mean for relations with Jordan, a close US ally in the Middle East.
cite: Washington Post, Feb 1977, as reported by Jewish Telegraphic Agency, 22 Feb 1977
inside: The CIA secretly paid Jordan's king millions of dollars a year for about twenty years, putting the head of a state on a foreign spy service's payroll.

n: CIA delivered bags of cash to Afghan President Karzai's office
rank: President's office
d: The CIA delivered cash in bags to the office of Afghanistan's President Hamid Karzai for more than a decade from the start of the 2001 war, The New York Times reported in April 2013, citing sources who put the total at tens of millions of dollars. The sources said much of it went on to Karzai's relatives, associates, politicians and warlords. Karzai confirmed receiving what he called 'small amounts' and said he was grateful; his palace said the money was used for charitable purposes. Some Afghan senators called the payments a breach of national sovereignty. Karzai had earlier admitted taking similar cash from Iran.
cite: New York Times, 28 Apr 2013; NPR, 1 May 2013
inside: The CIA delivered bags of cash to the Afghan president's own office for more than a decade, and much of it went on to his politicians and warlords.

n: Iran paid cash to Afghan President Karzai's chief of staff
rank: Presidential chief of staff
d: Iran's government gave bags of cash to Umar Daudzai, chief of staff to Afghanistan's President Hamid Karzai, The New York Times reported in October 2010, describing a steady stream of money meant to buy his loyalty and promote Iran's interests inside the presidential palace. Karzai confirmed the payments two days later. He said Iran handed over €500,000 to €700,000 at a time, once or twice a year, and that the money was transparent and paid for the costs of running the president's office. The payments reportedly stopped after Karzai signed a strategic partnership agreement with the United States.
cite: New York Times, 23 Oct 2010; Foreign Policy, 25 Oct 2010; NPR, 1 May 2013
inside: Iran's government paid cash to the Afghan president's chief of staff to buy his loyalty and push Iran's interests inside the presidential palace.

n: CIA paid Peru's spy chief Vladimiro Montesinos at least $10 million
rank: De facto head of National Intelligence Service (SIN)
d: The CIA gave Vladimiro Montesinos, unofficial head of Peru's National Intelligence Service (SIN) under President Alberto Fujimori, at least $10 million in cash from 1990 to September 2000, plus surveillance equipment, the Center for Public Integrity reported in 2001. The money went to a narcotics intelligence unit that Montesinos founded and personally controlled. When the CIA reported his alleged corruption, other US agencies told it to keep working with him. Military intelligence sources said CIA-supplied equipment was used to tap opposition figures, journalists and officers. Montesinos fled after a September 2000 video showed him paying a $15,000 bribe, and Fujimori resigned on 20 November 2000.
cite: Center for Public Integrity, 28 Jul 2001
inside: The CIA paid Peru's spy chief at least $10 million, and equipment it supplied was used by his service to tap opposition figures and journalists.

n: Panama's military ruler Manuel Noriega was on the CIA payroll
rank: Military ruler
d: Manuel Noriega, commander of Panama's armed forces and the country's de facto ruler in the 1980s, was paid at least $300,162 by the CIA for passing it secrets and carrying out other US intelligence operations, according to court documents disclosed in May 1991 ahead of his drug-trafficking trial in Miami. US forces had invaded Panama in December 1989 and taken him to the United States. The disclosure showed that the man in charge of Panama's military and intelligence apparatus had been a paid US source while he also took money from drug traffickers. He was convicted in April 1992.
cite: Tampa Bay Times, 31 May 1991; The Nation, 'April 9, 1992: Manuel Noriega Is Convicted'
inside: The CIA paid the commander of Panama's armed forces to pass it secrets and carry out US intelligence work, so the country's ruler was a US source.

n: CIA funded Burnham's party to unseat Cheddi Jagan in British Guiana
rank: Premier (1964 election)
d: The CIA secretly funded Forbes Burnham's and Peter D'Aguiar's parties to remove the elected leftist premier Cheddi Jagan in British Guiana, the British colony that became Guyana. The State Department's official history records about $2.08 million approved for covert action there from 1962 to 1968: money and campaign expertise before the December 1964 election, funds linked to the 1964 general strike and help registering opposition voters, while Washington urged Britain to adopt proportional representation and delay independence. The anti-Jagan coalition won in 1964 and the CIA kept funding Burnham as premier. He became the first prime minister of independent Guyana in May 1966.
cite: US State Department, Foreign Relations of the United States 1964–68, vol. XXXII, editorial note 370
inside: The CIA secretly funded opposition parties to remove an elected premier, then kept funding the man who replaced him as head of government.

n: CIA's LITEMPO network counted two future presidents of Mexico
rank: President (Díaz Ordaz, Echeverría)
d: Winston Scott, CIA station chief in Mexico City from 1956, recruited 12 agents inside the Mexican government between 1956 and 1969 under a programme called LITEMPO, an unofficial channel for sensitive political information. Documents published by the National Security Archive in October 2006 identify Gustavo Díaz Ordaz, president from 1964 to 1970 and a personal friend of Scott, as LITEMPO-2, and Luis Echeverría, then a deputy minister at the interior ministry (Gobernación) and president from 1970 to 1976, as LITEMPO-8. Fernando Gutiérrez Barrios of the DFS, Mexico's political police, was LITEMPO-4. The network was active during the 1968 Tlatelolco massacre of students, on which Scott's reporting proved inaccurate.
cite: National Security Archive, Electronic Briefing Book No. 204, 18 Oct 2006
inside: A CIA station chief recruited agents inside the Mexican government, including two men who became president, to pass the United States political information.

n: Guatemalan colonel linked to two killings was a paid CIA source
rank: Army lieutenant colonel
d: Lieutenant Colonel Julio Roberto Alpirez of Guatemala's army was a paid CIA source at the time of two killings he was linked to: that of US citizen Michael DeVine near his ranch in June 1990, and the disappearance and apparent murder in 1992 of guerrilla Efraín Bámaca Velásquez, husband of American lawyer Jennifer Harbury. In April 1995 the acting CIA director, William Studeman, admitted the agency had failed to tell Congress what it knew. Reports said the CIA paid Alpirez up to $44,000 after learning of his alleged role in the DeVine case. The President's Intelligence Oversight Board reviewed the CIA's Guatemalan relationships in a report of 28 June 1996.
cite: Los Angeles Times via Spokesman-Review, 6 Apr 1995; Intelligence Oversight Board, Report on the Guatemala Review, 28 Jun 1996
inside: The CIA had a serving Guatemalan army officer on its payroll as a source, and kept paying him after learning he was linked to a killing.

n: CIA funded Mobutu and Congo's governments after moving against Lumumba
rank: Head of government and army chief
d: From August 1960 the CIA ran a covert political programme in the Congo, first to keep Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba out of power and then to keep chosen pro-Western leaders in office. The State Department's official history records covert funds to Joseph Mobutu's College of Commissioners from late 1960 and payments to Mobutu himself until September 1966. The CIA also paid for the 1961 parliamentary session that approved Cyrille Adoula's government, then funded that government through two parliamentary crises. About $11.7 million was approved for covert action in the Congo from 1960 to 1968, $5.8 million of it for political action. Mobutu ruled the country from 1965 to 1997.
cite: US State Department, Foreign Relations of the United States 1964–68, vol. XXIII, editorial note 1
inside: The CIA paid Mobutu and Congo's chosen leaders and even funded a parliamentary session, to keep pro-Western men running the government.

n: Sarkozy convicted of conspiring to seek Gaddafi's money for 2007 campaign
rank: Interior minister, later President
d: Aides to Nicolas Sarkozy, then France's interior minister, met Libya's intelligence chief Abdullah al-Senussi, brother-in-law of the ruler Muammar Gaddafi, in secret in 2005 to seek money for Sarkozy's 2007 presidential campaign, a Paris court found. On 25 September 2025 it convicted Sarkozy of criminal conspiracy covering 2005–2007 and sentenced him to five years in prison, the first such sentence for a former French president. Claude Guéant received six years and Brice Hortefeux two. The court acquitted Sarkozy of corruption and illegal campaign financing, saying there was no proof Libyan money reached the campaign. The case began with a 2012 Mediapart report. Sarkozy denies wrongdoing and is appealing.
cite: Al Jazeera, 25 Sep 2025; PBS NewsHour, 25 Sep 2025
inside: A Paris court found Sarkozy's aides met Libya's intelligence chief in secret to seek Gaddafi's money for his presidential campaign, but found no proof the money arrived.

n: Saddam's Iraq allegedly paid the head of the UN Oil-for-Food programme
rank: Head of UN Oil-for-Food programme
d: Benon Sevan, the UN official who ran the Oil-for-Food programme, allegedly took about $160,000 in bribes from Saddam Hussein's government. The programme let sanctioned Iraq sell limited amounts of oil to buy food and humanitarian goods; Iraq abused it by selling oil on the black market and bribing officials. An independent inquiry led by former US Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker made the allegations public in August 2005. In January 2007 US prosecutors in New York indicted Sevan for bribery and conspiracy to commit wire fraud, saying the money came through the brother of former UN Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali. Kofi Annan had suspended Sevan in 2005. He denies the charges and lives in Cyprus.
cite: Jurist, Jan 2007; Independent Inquiry Committee (Volcker), interim report, Aug 2005
inside: Saddam Hussein's government is alleged to have bribed the UN official in charge of the Oil-for-Food programme, the body meant to police Iraq's oil sales.

n: East German spy Günter Guillaume was Chancellor Brandt's personal aide
rank: Personal assistant to the Chancellor
d: Günter Guillaume, an agent of East Germany's foreign intelligence service, the HVA (part of the Stasi, the East German Ministry of State Security), became a personal assistant to West German Chancellor Willy Brandt, giving East Berlin a source inside the head of government's office. He was supervised by the HVA's chief, Markus Wolf. West German authorities arrested Guillaume on 24 April 1974, and Brandt, whose policy of opening relations with East Germany had defined his government, resigned as chancellor on 6 May 1974, less than two weeks later.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Guillaume affair'; Deutschlandmuseum, 'A spy at the heart of the West German government', 24 Apr 1974
inside: East Germany's foreign intelligence service placed its agent as a personal assistant to West Germany's chancellor, giving it a source inside his office.

n: Stasi agent rose to deputy head of the BND's Soviet section
rank: Deputy head, BND Soviet section
d: Gabriele Gast, on the books of East Germany's foreign intelligence service, the HVA, since 1968, joined West Germany's foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), on 1 November 1973. She worked in the section analysing the Soviet Union and by 1986 was its deputy head; her reports went to the Chancellor's office and the foreign and defence ministries. She passed the HVA copies of 49 detailed Western intelligence reports, including analysis of the Reagan–Gorbachev summit. Exposed after East Germany's collapse, she was arrested in September 1990 and sentenced in 1991 to six years and nine months in prison. She was released on probation in 1994.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Gabriele Gast' (Bavarian High Court sentence, 1991)
inside: East Germany's intelligence service had an agent rise to deputy head of a section of West Germany's spy service, passing it that service's secret reports.

n: SPD chief whip Karl Wienand convicted of spying for East Germany
rank: SPD parliamentary chief whip
d: Karl Wienand, chief whip of the Social Democratic Party (SPD) in West Germany's parliament, the Bundestag, from 1967 to 1974, was convicted in 1996 by the Düsseldorf regional court of spying for East Germany's Ministry of State Security (the Stasi). He was sentenced to two and a half years and fined the 1 million Deutschmarks he had received. In 1973 Wienand had admitted paying Christian Democrat MP Julius Steiner 50,000 marks to abstain in the 1972 no-confidence vote against Chancellor Willy Brandt. The Federal Court of Justice rejected his appeal in 1997, and President Roman Herzog commuted the prison term to probation on health grounds. Wienand denied spying until his death in 2011.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Karl Wienand' (Düsseldorf regional court, 1996)
inside: East Germany's secret police paid the governing party's chief whip in West Germany's parliament, who was convicted of spying for it.

n: Israel ran US Navy intelligence analyst Jonathan Pollard as a spy
rank: Navy intelligence analyst
d: Jonathan Pollard, a US Navy intelligence analyst hired in 1979, passed classified material to Israel from June 1984 until the FBI arrested him on 21 November 1985, just after he left Israel's embassy in Washington. His handler was Rafi Eitan, head of Lekem, an Israeli scientific-intelligence bureau. Israel paid him $10,000 in cash at the start and then a salary that reached $2,500 a month. He was sentenced to life in prison on 4 March 1987. Israel apologised in 1987, gave him citizenship in 1995 and admitted in 1998 that he had been its agent. He was paroled on 20 November 2015.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Jonathan Pollard' (US District Court sentence, 1987)
inside: Israeli intelligence paid a US Navy intelligence analyst a salary to pass it classified material his own government was meant to keep.

n: Nasser's son-in-law and Sadat's aide Ashraf Marwan was a Mossad source
rank: Presidential aide, Secretary for Foreign Relations
d: Ashraf Marwan, son-in-law of Egypt's President Gamal Abdel Nasser and later part of President Anwar Sadat's inner circle, offered his services at Israel's embassy in London in 1969 and was taken on as a source by Mossad, Israel's foreign intelligence service, in 1970. He passed Egyptian war plans and minutes of high-command meetings and warned of the coming 1973 war. In February 1974 Sadat made him Secretary to the President for Foreign Relations. His role was revealed in 2002; some argued he was a double agent, but historian Uri Bar-Joseph's work established him as a genuine Mossad spy. He died after falling from his London balcony on 27 June 2007.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ashraf Marwan' (Uri Bar-Joseph, The Angel; inquest, 2010)
inside: Israel's foreign intelligence service took on the Egyptian president's son-in-law as a source, and he passed it Egypt's war plans and high-command minutes.

n: Mossad agent Eli Cohen entered Syria's ruling circle under a false name
rank: Syrian ministers and army officers
d: Mossad trained Eli Cohen, an Egyptian-born Israeli, and gave him the identity of a Syrian businessman, Kamel Amin Thabet. He lived in Buenos Aires from 1961, presenting himself as a source of money for Syria's Ba'ath Party, and moved to Damascus in February 1962. There he hosted ministers, businessmen and officers, lent money to officials and heard them discuss army plans, and he reported Syrian positions on the Golan Heights and a plan to divert the Jordan River's headwaters. He was reportedly on a short list for deputy defence minister. Syrian security caught him on 24 January 1965; a military court sentenced him to death and he was hanged in Damascus on 18 May 1965.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Eli Cohen'
inside: Mossad planted an agent under a false identity in Syria's ruling circle, where he heard officials discuss army plans and reported them to Israel.

n: Labour minister John Stonehouse was a Czechoslovak agent, MI5 history says
rank: Minister (Technology; Posts and Telecommunications)
d: John Stonehouse, a Labour MP who served in Harold Wilson's governments as Minister of Technology, Postmaster General and Minister of Posts and Telecommunications between 1967 and 1970, allegedly began spying for Czechoslovakia in 1962. In 1969 Wilson told him of a defector's claim that he was a Czechoslovak agent, which Stonehouse denied. The official history of MI5, Britain's security service, published in 2009, supported the allegation, and in December 2010 it emerged that Margaret Thatcher had agreed in 1980 to keep the matter quiet because there was not enough evidence for a trial. In March 1968 Stonehouse had negotiated a technology cooperation agreement with Czechoslovakia.
cite: Christopher Andrew, The Defence of the Realm (MI5 authorised history), 2009; Wikipedia, 'John Stonehouse'
inside: Czechoslovak intelligence allegedly ran a serving British minister as its agent, and he negotiated a technology agreement with Czechoslovakia while in office.

n: Conservative MP Ray Mawby sold Commons information to Czechoslovak spies
rank: Member of Parliament, ex-minister
d: Ray Mawby, Conservative MP for Totnes from 1955 to 1983 and assistant Postmaster General in 1963–64, was paid by Czechoslovakia's military intelligence service under the code name 'Laval'. He received £100 for each piece of information and signed a receipt for one payment. He handed over hand-drawn floor plans of the Prime Minister's office in the House of Commons and details of who guarded it, lists of parliamentary committees and information on fellow politicians, and promised to ask questions in the Commons for his handlers. The meetings ran for about a decade and ended in November 1971. The BBC revealed the case on 28 June 2012 from Czech security files.
cite: BBC, 28 Jun 2012 (Czech security service files); Wikipedia, 'Ray Mawby'
inside: Czechoslovak military intelligence paid a British MP for information on Parliament and the Prime Minister's office, and he promised to ask questions for his handlers.

n: State Department analyst Kendall Myers spied for Cuba for decades
rank: Analyst, Bureau of Intelligence and Research
d: Walter Kendall Myers worked as a Europe analyst in the US State Department's own intelligence unit, the Bureau of Intelligence and Research (INR), which prepares analysis for the Secretary of State, from 2000 until he retired in 2007. US authorities charged that he and his wife had spied for Cuba for nearly three decades. They were arrested in June 2009 after an FBI undercover operation, and in July 2010 he was sentenced to life in prison without parole. Cuba's intelligence service thereby had a source inside the department that sets US policy towards Cuba.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Walter Kendall Myers' (US District Court, Jul 2010)
inside: Cuban intelligence had an analyst inside the US State Department's own intelligence bureau as its source for nearly three decades.

n: Rwandan officer James Kabarebe commanded Congo's army in 1997–98
rank: Army chief of staff
d: James Kabarebe, a Rwandan army officer, was chief military strategist of the rebellion that brought Laurent-Désiré Kabila to power in Kinshasa on 17 May 1997, and Kabila then made him chief of staff of the Congolese army. While he held the post, units in eastern Congo recruited more Banyamulenge, Banyarwanda and former Rwandan army troops. Fearing a coup, Kabila dismissed him around 27 July 1998. On 4 August 1998 Kabarebe led an airborne assault on Kitona air base with about 3,000 Rwandan and Ugandan soldiers, starting the Second Congo War's push on the capital; Zimbabwean, Namibian and Angolan forces stopped them from taking Kinshasa.
cite: Wikipedia, 'James Kabarebe'
inside: A Rwandan army officer was made chief of staff of Congo's army, and under him its eastern units filled with troops tied to Rwanda before he led an invasion.

n: Apartheid police spy became deputy director of a Geneva aid fund
rank: Deputy director, International University Exchange Fund
d: Craig Williamson, an officer of apartheid South Africa's Security Branch police, persuaded the director of the International University Exchange Fund (IUEF), a Geneva-based body that paid scholarships for African students with money largely from Swedish donors, to make him deputy director in the late 1970s. The post gave him a way into the banned African National Congress (ANC). He diverted IUEF money to a covert South African operation called 'Long Reach' and used it to set up a news agency that recruited journalists for counter-intelligence. He was exposed in 1980. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission later gave him amnesty for bombings including the 1982 letter-bomb killing of Ruth First.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Craig Williamson' (TRC amnesty decisions 1999–2000)
inside: An apartheid police spy got himself made deputy director of a Geneva aid fund and diverted its donor money into South African covert operations.

n: French mercenary Bob Denard commanded the Comoros presidential guard
who: Bob Denard and French secret services
rank: Presidential Guard commander
d: Bob Denard, a French mercenary who worked for France's secret services, led the 1978 coup that returned Ahmed Abdallah to power in the Comoros and then commanded the islands' Presidential Guard for about eleven years, gaining business interests and Comorian citizenship. The islands also served as a base for getting round the embargo on apartheid South Africa. In 1989 Abdallah ordered the guard disarmed and was shot dead shortly afterwards; French paratroopers took Denard out of the country, and he was later acquitted over the killing for lack of evidence. In 1995 he led another coup, ended by French troops, and the court that later tried him recognised the secret services' role.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Bob Denard'
inside: A mercenary working with France's secret services commanded the Comoros presidential guard for eleven years, and used that post for his business interests.

n: Syria's spy chief Ghazi Kanaan picked Lebanon's candidates and officials
rank: Lebanese elections, security and judicial appointments
d: Ghazi Kanaan headed Syrian military intelligence in Lebanon for about twenty years from 1982, during Syria's 1976–2005 military presence there. He vetoed anti-Syrian candidates and pushed pro-Syrian ones onto electoral lists, drew the boundaries of fourteen electoral districts after the 1989 Taif Agreement, and shaped security and judicial appointments; the head of Lebanon's General Security agency reported directly to him. His deputy Rustum Ghazaleh succeeded him in 2002. After former prime minister Rafik Hariri was assassinated in February 2005 and the UN Security Council called for foreign forces to leave, Syria withdrew its troops by 30 April 2005. Kanaan died of a gunshot wound in October 2005.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ghazi Kanaan'; Wikipedia, 'Syrian occupation of Lebanon'; UN Security Council Resolution 1559, 2 Sep 2004
inside: Syria's military intelligence chief in Lebanon picked electoral candidates and security and judicial appointees, and Lebanon's General Security head reported to him.

n: Iran hanged ex-deputy defence minister Alireza Akbari as an alleged MI6 spy
rank: Former deputy defence minister
d: Iran convicted Alireza Akbari, who had been deputy defence minister under Ali Shamkhani and an adviser to the Iranian navy, of spying for Britain's foreign intelligence service, MI6. Iranian officials said he passed information on 178 Iranian figures, including the nuclear scientist Mohsen Fakhrizadeh. His death sentence was announced on 11 January 2023 and his execution by hanging on 14 January. Akbari and his family denied the charge; in a recording later released by the BBC he said he had been drugged, held in solitary confinement and tortured into confessing. Britain's foreign secretary called the allegations politically motivated and the execution barbaric.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Alireza Akbari'; BBC, Jan 2023
inside: Iran says Britain's foreign intelligence service recruited a former deputy defence minister to pass it information on Iranian figures; he said his confession was forced.

n: US intelligence used UN weapons inspectors' mission to eavesdrop on Iraq
rank: UN Special Commission (UNSCOM)
d: US intelligence used eavesdropping gathered with the help of UNSCOM, the UN Special Commission set up to find and destroy Iraq's banned weapons, to listen to communications of the units guarding Saddam Hussein, The Washington Post and The Boston Globe reported in January 1999. The Post said UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan had convincing evidence of it. Sources said the monitoring was partly meant to help inspectors find weapons, but Annan reportedly believed Washington used it to penetrate Saddam's security. UNSCOM's chief, Richard Butler, denied that the US had used the commission, and US officials declined to comment.
cite: Reuters via Christian Science Monitor, 7 Jan 1999 (Washington Post, Boston Globe)
inside: US intelligence used a UN weapons-inspection mission to listen in on Saddam Hussein's security units, turning an international body's work to its own purposes.

n: CIA-backed exile Ayad Allawi chosen as Iraq's interim prime minister
rank: Interim Prime Minister
d: Ayad Allawi's exile group, the Iraqi National Accord, worked with the CIA from 1992 and received US covert aid reported at $5 million in 1995 and $6 million in 1996. The CIA backed its 1996 plan for Iraqi generals to move on Baghdad; Saddam's agents infiltrated the plot and many participants were executed. After the 2003 US invasion, Allawi sat on the US-appointed Iraqi Governing Council, and in December 2003 he met CIA officials at Langley to plan Iraq's new domestic intelligence service. On 28 May 2004 the Governing Council unanimously chose him as interim prime minister of the government that took over sovereignty from the US-led occupation in June 2004.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Ayad Allawi' (citing Wurmser; Cockburn and Cockburn)
inside: A CIA-funded exile was made Iraq's interim prime minister after planning Iraq's new domestic intelligence service with CIA officials.

n: Chile's secret police chief Contreras was a CIA contact, paid in 1975
rank: Head of DINA secret police
d: Manuel Contreras headed DINA, the secret police of General Augusto Pinochet's military government, from 1973 to 1977. A CIA report released on 19 September 2000 shows US policymakers authorised CIA contact with him from 1974 to 1977, and the agency made him a one-time payment in 1975, although US intelligence reports by then named him as the main obstacle to a better human rights policy in Pinochet's government. The CIA kept the relationship until 1977, despite reportedly holding intelligence that he ordered the 1976 killing of exiled Chilean diplomat Orlando Letelier in Washington. Chilean courts later convicted Contreras in many cases; at his death in 2015 his sentences totalled 529 years.
cite: CIA, 'CIA Activities in Chile' (Hinchey report), 19 Sep 2000; Wikipedia, 'Manuel Contreras'
inside: The CIA kept contact with and paid the head of Chile's secret police, putting the dictatorship's security chief in a relationship with US intelligence.

n: CIA officer gave South Vietnam's coup generals $42,000 to topple Diệm
rank: Army generals
d: CIA officer Lucien Conein acted as the link between the US embassy and the South Vietnamese generals planning to overthrow President Ngô Đình Diệm, told them the US would not intervene to stop a coup, and gave them 3 million piastres, about $42,000, to reward units that joined. A State Department cable to Ambassador Henry Cabot Lodge had already said US policy was not to try to stop a coup and authorised the embassy to explore a change of leader. The generals moved on 1 November 1963 in Saigon; Diệm and his brother Ngô Đình Nhu were killed the next day after surrendering. A succession of military governments followed.
cite: Wikipedia, '1963 South Vietnamese coup' (Pentagon Papers; FRUS)
inside: A CIA officer gave South Vietnam's generals money to reward the army units that joined their coup against the president.

n: Greek junta leader Papadopoulos was Greek intelligence's link to the CIA
rank: Junta leader and prime minister
d: Georgios Papadopoulos, the army officer who led Greece's military coup on 21 April 1967 and became the junta's leader, had served from 1959 to 1964 in KYP, the Greek intelligence service, as its main contact with the CIA's top officer in Greece. Some sources describe him as on the CIA payroll from the 1950s. In 1973 The Observer accused the CIA of engineering the coup and reported that US military aid officials in Athens knew him as 'the first CIA agent to become Premier of a European country'. At his 1973 confirmation hearing, CIA director William Colby denied both claims but said the agency had 'worked with' him in his official role.
cite: The Observer, 1 Jul 1973; William Colby confirmation hearing, 1973; Wikipedia, 'Georgios Papadopoulos'
inside: Papadopoulos was Greek intelligence's main contact with the CIA, and some sources say he was on its payroll before he led the coup and ran the junta.

n: CIA cash briefcases for Chamoun's candidates in Lebanon's 1957 election
rank: Parliament (Chamber of Deputies)
d: CIA money paid for selected candidates backed by President Camille Chamoun in Lebanon's June 1957 parliamentary election. CIA officer Wilbur Crane Eveland later wrote that he regularly drove to the presidential residence with 'a briefcase full of Lebanese pounds' to be spent on the campaign; American oil companies working in Lebanon also contributed. Independents, nearly all of them pro-Chamoun, won 51 of the 66 seats. The result left Chamoun's opponents with little representation in parliament, and the following year Lebanon fell into a political crisis in which US Marines landed near Beirut.
cite: Wilbur Crane Eveland, Ropes of Sand (1980); Wikipedia, '1957 Lebanese general election'
inside: The CIA funded the president's chosen candidates in Lebanon's election, so the parliament that resulted was largely made up of members it had paid for.

n: Suitcase of Venezuelan cash allegedly meant for Argentina's 2007 campaign
rank: Presidential campaign
d: On 4 August 2007 Argentine police seized $790,550 in undeclared cash from Guido Alejandro Antonini Wilson, who arrived in Buenos Aires on a chartered plane that also carried representatives of Venezuela's state oil company, PDVSA. In December 2007 the FBI arrested men it accused of acting as Venezuelan government agents and trying to pay Antonini $2 million to stay silent. Two of them pleaded guilty in Miami and, with US prosecutors, said the money was meant for the presidential campaign of Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, who won that October. Both governments called for investigations; nothing was proven in Argentina, and the Argentine case was closed in 2015 under the statute of limitations.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Maletinazo' (US District Court, Miami, 2008)
inside: Two men who pleaded guilty in Miami said Venezuelan government cash flown into Buenos Aires was meant for a presidential campaign; nothing was proven in Argentina.

n: CIA kept Castillo Armas on its payroll, then made him Guatemala's ruler
rank: President
d: The CIA chose Carlos Castillo Armas, an exiled Guatemalan army officer, to lead its operation against President Jacobo Árbenz, whose land reform had expropriated land held by the US-based United Fruit Company. It planned to give him $225,000 for an abandoned 1952 plot, then kept him on its payroll at $3,000 a week. In June 1954 he led about 480 CIA-trained fighters into Guatemala; Árbenz resigned on 27 June, and after US-brokered talks Castillo Armas joined the ruling junta and took it over in July. The US recognised his government on 13 July 1954. He ruled until a presidential guard shot him dead on 26 July 1957.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Carlos Castillo Armas'; Wikipedia, '1954 Guatemalan coup d'état' (declassified CIA and State Department records)
inside: The CIA kept an exiled officer on its payroll and backed his invasion, and he then took over Guatemala's ruling junta.

n: CIA gave about $1 million to Indonesia's Masyumi party in the 1955 election
rank: Masyumi party (parliamentary election)
d: According to former CIA officer Joseph Smith's 1976 memoir, 'Portrait of a Cold Warrior', the CIA secretly gave about $1 million to Masyumi, a centrist Islamic party, during Indonesia's 1955 parliamentary election, the country's first, to reduce support for President Sukarno and the Communist Party of Indonesia. Masyumi won 57 seats, tying the Indonesian National Party (PNI) for the most, with 20.92% of the vote, a result below expectations. No party won a majority, and the PNI's Ali Sastroamidjojo formed a coalition government that included Masyumi. The amount rests on Smith's account and has not been independently confirmed.
cite: Joseph Burkholder Smith, Portrait of a Cold Warrior (1976), pp. 110–111; Wikipedia, '1955 Indonesian legislative election'
inside: The CIA secretly gave about $1 million to an Indonesian party, which then joined the coalition government; the figure rests on one former officer's memoir.

n: RAW joint secretary Rabinder Singh fled to the US as a suspected CIA mole
rank: Joint secretary, Research and Analysis Wing
d: Rabinder Singh, a former army major, rose in India's foreign intelligence agency, the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW), to joint secretary at its New Delhi headquarters, covering Southeast Asia. Counter-intelligence officers noticed him photocopying documents unrelated to his work, put him under surveillance and tapped his phones, suspecting he worked for the CIA. He disappeared in May 2004, reportedly via Nepal, and India dismissed him that year. A former RAW officer's book says he flew to the US from Kathmandu under a false identity; reports said the CIA arranged his US passports, which has not been officially confirmed. Interpol refused India's 2007 request for a red corner notice.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Rabinder Singh (intelligence officer)'
inside: A senior officer of India's foreign intelligence agency was suspected of working for the CIA, copying documents unrelated to his job before fleeing to the US.

n: British officers and MI6 removed Oman's sultan and installed his son
rank: Sultan
d: Britain planned and carried out the 23 July 1970 palace coup in Salalah that removed Sultan Said bin Taimur of Oman and installed his son Qaboos. Oman's armed forces were under de facto British command: Brigadier John Graham, their overall commander, briefed the Arab officers of the Desert Regiment who carried out the coup, and British officials sent Qaboos, then under house arrest, cassette tapes setting out the plan. Accounts based on British records say MI6, the Foreign Office and the Ministry of Defence planned it and Prime Minister Edward Heath approved it. Britain denied involvement for forty years, saying its officers had acted on their own. An RAF plane flew the deposed sultan out.
cite: The Guardian (Ian Cobain), 2016; Mark Curtis, 'Britain's coup in Oman, 1970', 2016; Wikipedia, '1970 Omani coup d'état'
inside: British officers commanding Oman's armed forces had its soldiers carry out a palace coup that Britain had planned, replacing the sultan with his son.

n: Bolivia's interior minister Antonio Arguedas said the CIA had recruited him
rank: Interior minister
d: Antonio Arguedas, Bolivia's interior minister under President René Barrientos, said in 1968 that the CIA had recruited him in 1965, and gave details of CIA staff and their activities in Bolivia, a US State Department record shows. By his own account he had also smuggled a copy of the diary of Che Guevara, killed in Bolivia in October 1967, to Fidel Castro and then fled the country. US diplomats suspected Barrientos might have prompted his anti-CIA statements to shift blame for the diary leak onto the United States. Arguedas was brought back and tried for treason and espionage, survived three assassination attempts and took refuge in Mexico's embassy in 1969.
cite: US State Department, FRUS 1964–68, vol. XXXI, doc. 179; Time, 23 Feb 1970
inside: Bolivia's interior minister said the CIA had recruited him, so the official in charge of the country's security had been working for US intelligence.

n: Orellana network had the chiefs of Peru's property registry
rank: Head, registrar and IT chief of SUNARP
d: A criminal network run from the Lima law firm of Rodolfo Orellana got senior officials of Peru's national property registry, SUNARP, to work for it. Between 2009 and 2013 the firm changed the recorded owners of disputed land and sold 47 plots through front men, with the registry's former head Álvaro Delgado Scheelje, a registrar and its IT chief smoothing the paperwork. In February 2020 a Lima court convicted 19 people of criminal association and bribery: Orellana's sister Ludith got 10 years and the three registry officials 6 years and 8 months each. Orellana himself faces a separate laundering trial.
cite: Andina, 8 Feb 2020; LP Derecho, 11 Feb 2020
inside: A criminal law firm got the head of Peru's property registry and other officials to work for it, changing recorded land ownership so the firm could sell plots.

n: Traffickers bought early release from Peru's presidential pardons board
rank: Head of the presidential pardons commission
d: Convicted drug traffickers paid officials of the commission that advised President Alan García on pardons and sentence reductions, a case known in Peru as the 'narcoindultos' (narco-pardons). Between 2006 and 2011 more than 5,000 prisoners had sentences commuted or were pardoned, a disproportionate number of them traffickers. A congressional commission found the programme had been used to collect bribes from traffickers. In December 2015 a court sentenced the commission's head, Miguel Facundo Chinguel, García's former lawyer, to 13 years and 8 months for criminal conspiracy and taking bribes for the early release of at least three traffickers. Six lower commission officials were also convicted.
cite: Peru Reports, Dec 2015; InSight Crime, 'Can Peru Congress make narco-pardons case stick'
inside: Drug traffickers paid officials of the presidential pardons board, and the board then recommended early release for traffickers.

n: Cocaine groups paid port security, dockers and customs contacts at Callao
rank: Port security chief, customs contacts, police
d: Cocaine trafficking groups paid people inside Callao, Peru's main seaport, to get drugs onto ships. An investigation by La República, reported by InSight Crime in 2015, quoted a former trafficker saying the port's security chief charged about $20,000 for entry and dockworkers took at least $10 per kilo. Corrupt workers loaded the cocaine after containers had cleared customs, and contacts inside customs warned traffickers hours ahead if a container was picked for a second check. Infiltration of the police and customs was given as one reason why less than 20% of the cocaine moving through Callao was detected. Peru's former anti-drug police chief said 80% of the country's cocaine left through Callao and Paita.
cite: InSight Crime, 22 May 2015, citing La República
inside: Cocaine groups paid the port's security chief, dockworkers and customs contacts, who loaded drugs and warned them of checks.

n: Paraguayan deputy Ulises Quintana accused of serving trafficker 'Cucho'
rank: Member of the Chamber of Deputies; prosecutors; police
d: Prosecutors say the cocaine network of Reinaldo 'Cucho' Cabaña had a member of Paraguay's Chamber of Deputies, three prosecutors and seven police officers working for it. In September 2018 anti-drug agents mounted Operation Berilo, more than 33 raids that took in Cabaña, the deputy Ulises Quintana, several police officers, prosecutors' assistants and a prosecutor. The accusation, filed in September 2019 and confirmed in May 2022, charges Quintana with criminal association under the drug law and with laundering drug money, on the allegation that the network financed his campaign for the chamber and that he used his influence to move its cash through police checkpoints. He was sent for trial with Cabaña and 21 others at the end of March 2026.
cite: ABC Color, 19 September 2025, for the accusation of September 2019 confirmed in May 2022, the charges, the fourteen attempted preliminary hearings and the bad-faith reprimand; La Nación (Paraguay), 27 February and 2 March 2026, for the restored detention and the judge's reasons, and 1 April 2026 for the referral of Cabaña, Quintana and 21 others to trial and the release on alternative measures; Diario Vanguardia, 1 April 2026, for the three charges dismissed; Hoy and Amambay Ahora, 1 April 2026, for the conditions of release and the scale of Operation Berilo; Última Hora, 2 April 2026, for the prosecutor's claim that the network financed the campaign
inside: A trafficker's network financed a congressman's campaign, and prosecutors say the congressman then intervened to get the trafficker released.
undone: Eight years on, no trial has been held and Quintana denies the charges. Getting as far as the preliminary hearing took fourteen attempts, and in September 2025 the judge formally reprimanded Quintana and his lawyers for litigating in bad faith with delaying motions; in February 2026 the same judge restored both men's pre-trial detention, saying the motions showed an unwillingness to submit to the process. Once the preliminary hearings ended, three of the five charges against Quintana were dismissed for want of an accusation - influence trafficking, illicit enrichment and complicity in drug trafficking - and he and Cabaña left Tacumbú prison on alternatives to detention, Cabaña with an electronic tag and Quintana free to move but barred from within a kilometre of the border. The oral trial, where the prosecution has to prove any of it, had not begun when this was checked on 14 November 2026.

n: PCC paid Paraguayan prison staff as 75 inmates walked free
rank: Prison staff, Pedro Juan Caballero
d: The Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC), Brazil's largest prison gang, which also controls cocaine routes through Paraguay, got staff at the prison in Pedro Juan Caballero, on the Brazilian border, to help its members escape. In January 2020 at least 75 inmates, many of them PCC members, left over several days through a tunnel and, according to officials, the main gate. Interior Minister Euclides Acevedo said people working in the jail were complicit, and Justice Minister Cecilia Pérez said prisoners had reportedly offered staff $80,000 for help. Pérez ordered the entire prison staff fired. The escape showed how far the PCC had reached into Paraguay's prisons.
cite: OCCRP, 21 Jan 2020; AP, Jan 2020
inside: A Brazilian prison gang reportedly paid staff at a Paraguayan prison, who then helped at least 75 inmates, many of them its members, escape.

n: Paraguayan deputy Lalo Gomes charged with laundering drug money
rank: Member of the Chamber of Deputies
d: Paraguayan prosecutors charged Eulalio 'Lalo' Gomes, a Colorado Party member of the Chamber of Deputies from Pedro Juan Caballero, with laundering money from international drug trafficking. In July 2024 Brazilian media alleged he had helped Brazilian drug figures including Luiz Carlos da Rocha, alias 'Cabeça Branca'. On 19 August 2024, hours after the charges were filed against him, his son and three others, Gomes was shot dead when anti-drug police raided his home; officials said agents had been fired on. His family disputes that account. Prosecutors also charged an alleged front man and two officials of Zeta Banco.
cite: Ámbito / EFE, 19 Aug 2024; ABC Color, 19 Sept 2024
inside: Prosecutors charged a sitting deputy with laundering international drug money, and Brazilian media alleged he helped Brazilian drug figures; he was killed before any trial.

n: Gambling boss paid Rosario's chief prosecutor; senator charged as leader
rank: Regional chief prosecutor, Rosario; provincial senator
d: Leonardo Peiti, who financed illegal gambling in Santa Fe province, paid the prosecutors who were supposed to investigate him. In November 2025 a Rosario court sentenced Patricio Serjal, former head of Rosario's prosecutors, to nine years for taking bribes to leave Peiti alone; an office employee who passed the payments up got five years, and deputy prosecutor Gustavo Ponce Asahad had already been convicted. Peiti told the court he gave $200,000 to Peronist senator Armando Traferri for his campaign. Prosecutors charged Traferri as head of the network, but his fellow legislators kept his immunity in place for about four years. The court called him the central figure of the network's political side.
cite: La Política Online, 7 Nov 2025; La Capital (Rosario)
inside: An illegal gambling boss paid the head of Rosario's prosecutors to leave him alone, and funded a senator charged as the network's political leader.

n: Alvarado clan had Rosario police chiefs and a prosecutor's employee
rank: Heads of police brigades and a police station; prosecutor's office employee
d: The criminal group of Esteban Alvarado, a Rosario drug and car-theft boss later sentenced to life, had senior officers of Santa Fe's police working for it. Between 2019 and 2021 courts convicted six officers, among them the head of the investigations police's operations brigade, the former head of the judicial division and a police station chief, of criminal association; each got three years and a six-year ban from office. They warned the gang of raids, passed it information from the unit investigating its rivals Los Monos, and steered murder inquiries toward rival gangs. An employee of a prosecutor's office who leaked a tapped phone to the group got one year.
cite: La Capital (Rosario), 21 Feb 2022
inside: A drug gang had senior Santa Fe police officers working for it, warning it of raids and steering murder inquiries towards its rivals.

n: Mendoza federal judge Walter Bento sold rulings to detainees
rank: Federal judge, Mendoza
d: People held on serious charges, including drug trafficking and smuggling, paid a network led by Walter Bento, the most powerful federal judge in Mendoza, Argentina, for house arrest or release. Federal judges in Argentina handle drug-trafficking cases. After a trial lasting two and a half years, Mendoza's Federal Oral Tribunal No. 1 found Bento and about twenty others guilty in February 2026 of illicit association, bribery, money laundering and illicit enrichment. Bento was sentenced to 18 years and fined 540 million pesos; his wife got six years and his son five. He had been detained since late 2023.
cite: Diario de Cuyo, 3 and 7 Feb 2026
inside: Traffickers and smugglers paid a federal judge's network, and the judge granted them house arrest or release.

n: Bagdad gang paid Panamanian police for checkpoints and escorts
rank: National Police sub-lieutenant and paid officers
d: Bagdad, a Panamanian gang federation, got officers of the National Police to work for it, according to prosecutors in Operation Neptuno. In April 2021 a police sub-lieutenant was charged as a key member: prosecutors said he shielded the group's cases, opened checkpoints, escorted vehicles carrying drugs and guarded its meetings in Chame and Playa Blanca. A notebook seized in the case allegedly listed police officers of various ranks and the sums they were paid for information. Nineteen members were charged with criminal association, money laundering and corruption of public officials. Bagdad has been linked to at least 27 killings in two years, including 13 inmates at La Joya prison.
cite: Panamá América, 11 Apr 2021
inside: A gang federation paid police officers, including a sub-lieutenant who opened checkpoints and escorted its drug shipments.
undone: A trial court convicted six of those prosecuted in Operation Neptuno of criminal association and acquitted fifteen, La Prensa reported, setting a sentencing hearing for the six on 19 August; the report gives no date for the verdict itself. Those convicted were named as Ricardo Gonzalez, Gustavo Gonzalez, Carlos Cornejo, Luis Montenegro, Rigoberto Jaramillo and Ernesto Lasso. The report does not say whether the police sub-lieutenant was among the convicted or the acquitted, so the case against the officers remains unresolved. Those acquitted were found not guilty, and anyone still awaiting trial is presumed innocent.

n: Two colonels arrested for tipping off trafficker 'César el Abusador'
rank: Two colonels and three other officers
d: The cocaine and laundering network of César Emilio Peralta, known as 'César el Abusador', had officers inside the Dominican security forces who warned it of action against it. In August 2019 Dominican authorities and the US DEA raided properties linked to the network, but Peralta escaped. About two weeks later, two colonels and three other officers were arrested on suspicion of leaking the arrest warrant and the planned raids to Peralta and his lieutenants, reportedly in return for a large payment in dollars. Investigators also looked at why an immigration alert was sent late. Peralta was later caught in Colombia in a joint operation with the United States.
cite: Dominican Today, Sept 2019; InSight Crime
inside: A cocaine network paid officers inside the Dominican security forces, who leaked its leader's arrest warrant and the planned raids.

n: Operation Falcón: cocaine network reached a Dominican state agency head
rank: Director of Comunidad Digna; a deputy
d: A Santiago-based cocaine and laundering network that authorities say moved more than $500 million had a serving government official and a congressman among its contacts. In September 2021 Dominican prosecutors, the drug agency DNCD and the US DEA carried out more than 80 raids. Those arrested included Juan Maldonado Castro, a four-term former deputy appointed in 2020 as director of the state programme Comunidad Digna; he was suspended by decree. Deputy Héctor Darío Féliz was accused of trying to move a man wanted for extradition so he could avoid arrest, but was not detained because of his parliamentary immunity. President Luis Abinader said the operation would continue 'whoever falls'. The trial of 70 defendants opened in Santiago in April 2026.
cite: Diario Libre, 8 Sept 2021; El Caribe, Sept 2021
inside: A cocaine network counted a state agency head and a congressman among its contacts, and the congressman tried to help a man avoid extradition.
undone: No verdict has been reached and the accused are presumed innocent. On 6 March 2025 a judge of the Fifth Investigating Court of the Santiago judicial district sent 31 accused to trial, and eased the conditions of six of them from house arrest with an electronic tag to periodic reporting and a travel ban. The trial opened before the Third Collegiate Court of the Santiago Judicial District, judges Ingrid Liberato, Deyanira Mendez and Kimberly Tatis, where the prosecution began reading an indictment covering 70 defendants, individuals and companies, on 10 April 2026; the hearing was suspended to 16 April. Maldonado Castro is among the accused.

n: Ex-army captain Quirino says drug money funded Fernández's campaign
rank: Presidential campaign and foundation of Leonel Fernández
d: Quirino Ernesto Paulino Castillo, a former Dominican army captain and drug trafficker, claims his drug money reached the campaign of Leonel Fernández, president from 2004 to 2012. Paulino was extradited to the United States on drug charges in 2005 and released in 2014. In a February 2015 television interview he said he funded Fernández's campaign from 2002 to 2004, gave more than $155,625 to Fernández's foundation FUNGLODE, and was owed about $500,000 used for the party nomination contest, and that Fernández knew the money was 'dirty'. He offered to take a polygraph test. His release after reported negotiations with US authorities raised questions about his credibility, and the claims have not been tested in court.
cite: Americas Quarterly, 10 Feb 2015; InSight Crime
inside: A convicted trafficker claims his drug money funded a Dominican president's campaign and foundation, with the president's knowledge; the claim has not been tested in court.

n: Fugitive Figueroa Agosto held Dominican state ID and officers' help
rank: DNCD drug agency officers; intelligence directorate
d: José David Figueroa Agosto, a Puerto Rican drug trafficker on the run from US justice, lived in the Dominican Republic for about ten years under false names with help from inside its security agencies. When he was found he held a valid card from the national intelligence directorate, the DNI, and six gun permits issued by the interior ministry and the armed forces. After his girlfriend Sobeida Félix was arrested and $4.6 million seized in 2009, raids found a member of his group holding the original file of the DNCD drug agency's intelligence unit. A captain was accused of treason for reportedly taking $10,000. Figueroa was later sentenced to 209 years in prison in the United States.
cite: El Día, 4 Jan 2010; Acento
inside: A fugitive trafficker got help from inside Dominican security agencies, which issued him an intelligence card and gun permits and leaked a drug-agency file.

n: Costa Rica investigates 116 police over links to drug gangs
rank: 116 officers of the Ministry of Public Security
d: An internal intelligence report found that drug trafficking gangs had officers of Costa Rica's police working for them. On 5 August 2026 President Laura Fernández announced that 116 officers of the Ministry of Public Security were under investigation; Security Minister Gerald Campos said the report named 122 people and that the force had more than 38 active corruption cases. Officers were allegedly tied to drug trafficking, migrant smuggling and alcohol smuggling, some escorted criminals, and some coordinated clandestine landings of aircraft reportedly carrying drugs. The report had reached officials of the previous government in April, and Campos said no investigation was ordered then. The case goes to prosecutors.
cite: Revista EyN / AFP, 6 Aug 2026
inside: Drug gangs had Costa Rican police officers working for them, escorting criminals and coordinating clandestine drug flights.

n: Guanacaste police chief arrested for helping a drug-flight network
rank: Head of the Fuerza Pública delegation in Nandayure
d: A drug trafficking group in Guanacaste, Costa Rica, had the local police commander passing it information, according to the OIJ judicial police. In July 2024 the OIJ arrested the head of the Fuerza Pública delegation in Nandayure, a 19-year veteran, and another officer, together with ten other people, in the case known as Caso Coraza. Investigators say the group flew drugs abroad in small planes from clandestine airstrips, including one at a Guanacaste hotel, and laundered money by trading cattle for cash. The OIJ carried out 29 raids, including at two police delegations, and seized 15 vehicles and more than 600 head of cattle.
cite: Teletica, 1 July 2024; CRHoy, July 2024; CRHoy, 5 March 2026
inside: A drug-flight network had the local police commander passing it information while it flew drugs out of clandestine airstrips.
undone: Nobody has been charged in court.
