As of 5 March 2026 the case was still in the investigation phase, with no indictment, trial date or verdict reported, and three suspects had been let out of pre-trial detention: one on a property guarantee, two to house arrest, each time over the prosecution's objection. The report does not say what stage the case against the Nandayure police commander has reached. All the suspects are presumed innocent.

n: Rotterdam customs officer waved cocaine containers through for 7.5%
rank: Customs officer selecting containers for inspection
d: Cocaine importers paid a Dutch customs officer at Rotterdam port, Gerrit G., to keep their containers out of inspection. He worked in the pre-arrival unit that chooses which containers are scanned, and removed his clients' shipments from that selection, taking 7.5% of the value of the drugs. He was arrested in April 2015 after police intercepted 400 kilos of cocaine; investigators found €1.1 million in cash at his flat and €1 million in bank accounts, and estimated he earned at least €3.5 million. In July 2017 the Rotterdam court sentenced him to 14 years, and the Hague appeals court upheld 14 years in May 2020. Two men were convicted of bribing him.
cite: DutchNews, 4 July 2017; Gerechtshof Den Haag, 18 May 2020
inside: Cocaine importers paid a customs officer in the unit that picks containers for scanning, and he removed their shipments from inspection.

n: Criminals reported in management of Securitas's Rotterdam port guards
rank: Securitas port guards and managers
d: A cocaine network got its people inside Securitas, the security company guarding parts of Rotterdam port, according to the Algemeen Dagblad. Two Securitas guards were arrested in summer 2020, suspected of helping move cocaine, passing information to criminals and arranging logistics so that smuggling containers were not searched, in an inquiry covering 4,000 kilograms. A third suspect, believed to have directed them in dozens of transports, fled abroad. AD's sources said criminals held management positions at the firm and deliberately recruited corrupt guards. The evidence came from EncroChat, an encrypted phone service police had broken into. Securitas said the accusations went against its values and that staff are screened.
cite: NL Times / AD, 13 Jan 2021; NOS
inside: A cocaine network got people into management at the port's security firm, who recruited guards to keep its containers from being searched.

n: Taghi network paid a senior Utrecht police officer for searches
rank: Senior police officer, Midden-Nederland
d: The criminal organisation of Ridouan Taghi, then the Netherlands' most wanted drug trafficker, had a high-ranking Utrecht police officer searching police systems for it. According to the Algemeen Dagblad in July 2019, the officer was paid thousands of euros, several times, to look up people and photographs and pass the results to the gang. The allegation came from Nabil B., the crown witness against Taghi's network. The officer was dismissed and the Rijksrecherche, which investigates police misconduct, opened an inquiry.
cite: NL Times / AD, 10 July 2019
inside: A drug trafficking organisation paid a senior police officer to search police systems for it and pass on what he found.

n: Prosecutors suspect underworld placed a trainee in Amsterdam police
rank: Trainee police officer, Amsterdam
d: Dutch prosecutors suspected that criminals had deliberately placed one of their contacts inside the Amsterdam police. Mehmet A., a 22-year-old trainee officer who had earlier worked as a guard at a detention centre, searched police systems from December 2017 for dozens of drug dealers, cash-machine bombers and motorcycle gang members, and sold the results at €250 a name. Buyers included two cannabis-trading brothers and the No Surrender motorcycle club. He was arrested in November 2018 after an anonymous tip. At his trial in March 2019 the prosecutor said an encrypted PGP phone given to him by a criminal pointed to his being 'positioned by the underworld', though there was no hard proof, and asked for 45 months.
cite: NL Times, 6 Mar 2019
inside: Prosecutors suspect criminals placed a contact as a police trainee, and he searched police systems for drug dealers and gangs and sold them the results.

n: Dutch police officer sold underworld 'subscriptions' to case files
rank: Police officer with case-file access
d: Criminal suspects in the Netherlands paid a police officer, Mark M., for regular access to confidential police files about them. For about four years, until his arrest in September 2015, he used login details for the BlueView police information system to read criminal case files and passed them to contacts in the underworld, some of whom paid 'subscriptions'. He claimed he looked up the information as a hobby. In February 2018 the Den Bosch district court sentenced him to five years in prison, though it cleared him of bribery. Dutch police reported 18 officers suspended for leaking information in one year as the problem grew.
cite: DutchNews, 19 Feb 2018; DutchNews, May 2017
inside: Criminal suspects paid a police officer for regular access to confidential police files about them, which he read and passed on for four years.

n: Amsterdam court desk worker sold personal data to a bombing suspect
rank: Information desk employee, Amsterdam district court
d: A man suspected of explosions and arson in The Hague and a shooting in Waalwijk got a worker inside the Amsterdam district court to supply him with confidential personal data. Sana C., who worked at the court's information desk with access to several systems holding personal details, was paid up to €700 per transaction. Police found her in 2024 during another investigation, with a court envelope holding six people's details and dozens of printouts. In May 2026 the court in Zwolle sentenced her to four years, one suspended, also for extorting almost €100,000 from a man, and banned her from public service for seven years. The buyer is thought to be hiding in Morocco.
cite: DutchNews, 28 May 2026
inside: A bombing suspect paid a worker at the Amsterdam court's information desk to supply him with people's confidential personal data.

n: 'Airport broker' recruited Schiphol staff to move Suriname cocaine
rank: Logistics and transport staff at Schiphol firms
d: A cocaine network used an 'airport broker' to recruit staff of companies working at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, whose security passes let them move drugs past controls. In 2024 the Royal Marechaussee, the Dutch military police who guard the airport, arrested six men aged 32 to 51 in logistics, transport and parcel delivery jobs, suspected of smuggling cocaine hidden in pallets from Suriname. A former airport worker allegedly linked the broker with the others; police said several areas of work had to be involved to get the drugs out. €124,000 in cash and cryptocurrency was seized. About 60,000 people work at Schiphol, all screened.
cite: DutchNews, 31 May 2024
inside: A cocaine network used a broker to recruit staff of firms at Schiphol airport, whose security passes let them move drugs past controls.

n: Antwerp drugs squad team leader arrested for leaking to gangs
rank: Chief inspector, Federal Judicial Police drugs department
d: Belgian investigators suspect that drug gangs had a source at the heart of Antwerp's fight against cocaine. In June 2023 a chief inspector and team leader in the drugs department of the Federal Judicial Police in Antwerp was arrested on suspicion of breaching professional secrecy by passing sensitive information to criminal gangs. Brussels investigators searched his home on the orders of an Antwerp judge, and he was released on conditions after questioning. He had been instrumental in dismantling the 'Mixers' gang, which had accused him of corruption. The Antwerp prosecutor's office said it was too early to draw conclusions.
cite: Brussels Times / De Standaard, 7 June 2023
inside: Belgian investigators suspect drug gangs had a team leader in Antwerp's federal drugs police passing them sensitive information.

n: Antwerp judge: gangs have inside staff in port, customs, police, courts
rank: Customs, police, municipal and prison staff
d: An Antwerp investigating judge wrote in October 2025 that cocaine networks had got people inside Belgium's state at many levels. In an open letter published on the website of Belgium's courts, the judge, one of 17 in Antwerp, said their investigations had led to the arrest of key port employees, customs officers, police officers, counter staff in several municipalities, and justice staff in prisons and in the courthouse. Moving one container could earn a port worker over €100,000. The judge, who had spent four months in a safe house after threats, warned that Belgium was turning into a 'narco-state'. Justice Minister Annelies Verlinden said she understood the concerns.
cite: Brussels Times, 27 Oct 2025; Maritime Executive, Oct 2025
inside: An Antwerp judge reported that cocaine networks had paid people inside the port, customs, police, town halls, prisons and courts to work for them.

n: Fake sick notes freed Guinea-Bissau's record cocaine traffickers
rank: Appeal Court judges; prison staff and doctors
d: Traffickers convicted over Guinea-Bissau's largest cocaine seizure, 1,869 kg found in 2019 in Operation Navara, got out of prison with help from inside the justice system, the Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime reported. In April and May 2021 several were released on medical grounds that police later found were invented; officers said the Supreme Court's vice-president had authorised the release, and a judge ordered junior prison officials and doctors detained. In October 2020 the Court of Appeal had cut ringleader Braima Seidi Ba's 16-year sentence to six years in a ruling reportedly driven by bribes; one judge dissented. Seidi Ba was never detained. In 2022 the Supreme Court's criminal chamber acquitted him and Ricardo Ariza Monges of all charges and upheld the other ten convictions.
cite: Global Initiative, West Africa Risk Bulletin 1, 2021; Lusa via Noticias ao Minuto, 1 July 2022 (Supreme Court acquittal of Braima Seidi Ba and Ricardo Ariza Monges)
inside: Cocaine traffickers got judges, prison officials and doctors to act for them, cutting a ringleader's sentence and releasing others on invented medical grounds.
undone: No one has been tried over the false medical certificates or the alleged bribes, and the reported detentions of prison officials and doctors produced no verdict that could be found. Seidi Ba and Monges, tried in absentia and on the run since 2019, were acquitted by the Supreme Court in a ruling the Portuguese news agency Lusa reported on 1 July 2022, so the convictions against them no longer stand and both are presumed innocent. The same ruling ordered seized assets forfeited to the state, returned other property to its owners and lifted the freezes on bank accounts.

n: 'Cherif Cocaine' said to fund Niger's ruling party and enjoy protection
rank: Ruling PNDS party; senior officials
d: Cherif Ould Abidine, an Agadez transport businessman known locally as 'Cherif Cocaine', was reported to have financed Niger's ruling party and to have been protected by officials at the highest levels. A 2018 Global Initiative study by Peter Tinti, based on fieldwork in Agadez and Niamey, said it was an open secret that he enjoyed such protection and that he reportedly funded political campaigns, notably those of the PNDS party of President Mahamadou Issoufou. He reportedly also won a French government contract to carry military supplies to the Madama base near Libya. He died in 2016. The study said illicit money in Niger's electoral politics was almost certainly real but hard to document.
cite: Global Initiative, 'Drug trafficking in northern Niger', 18 June 2018
inside: A researcher reported that a cocaine-linked businessman funded Niger's ruling party's campaigns and was protected by officials at the highest levels, though this is hard to document.

n: Senegal's police chief removed over report linking him to drug ring
rank: Director-General of National Police
d: A report by the head of Senegal's anti-drug police office accused his predecessor, Abdoulaye Niang, of being implicated in a Senegalese and Nigerian drug trafficking ring while he ran that office. By then Niang had become director-general of the national police. In July 2013 President Macky Sall relieved him of his duties so that he could defend himself. The report's author, Commissioner Cheikhna Keïta, had sent his findings to the authorities from February. A government inquiry said it found no evidence against Niang. The affair raised questions about whether traffickers had protection at the top of the police.
cite: AP via Star Tribune, 26 July 2013; Dakaractu
inside: Senegal's anti-drug chief accused his predecessor, by then national police chief, of working with a drug ring while running the anti-drug office; an inquiry found no evidence.

n: Fraudster Hushpuppi paid Nigerian 'supercop' Abba Kyari to jail a rival
rank: Deputy Commissioner of Police and team leader
d: Ramon Abbas, an internet fraudster known as Hushpuppi, used payments to Abba Kyari, a Nigerian deputy police commissioner who led a special investigation team under the Inspector-General of Police, to have a rival locked up. US court documents filed in 2021 said that after a co-fraudster, Vincent Chibuzo, tried to cheat Abbas over a scheme targeting Qatari businessmen, Kyari's team arrested Chibuzo, and Abbas sent Kyari about N8 million in two bank transfers. US prosecutors indicted Kyari and a court issued an arrest warrant. Nigeria's Police Service Commission suspended him from 31 July 2021. Kyari denied taking money.
cite: ICIR Nigeria, July 2021; TheCable, 1 Aug 2021
inside: A fraudster paid a senior Nigerian police officer, whose team then arrested the fraudster's rival.

n: Kenyan troops in Somalia accused of sugar and charcoal deals with al-Shabaab
rank: Kenya Defence Forces in Somalia
d: A November 2015 report by the rights group Journalists for Justice said Kenya Defence Forces units deployed in southern Somalia to fight al-Shabaab had become part of a sugar and charcoal smuggling cartel that included the militant group. The cartel was said to earn about $50 million a year, and the report argued that the trade helped keep al-Shabaab alive nearly four years after Kenya entered Somalia. Charcoal exports from Somalia were banned by the UN Security Council because they funded al-Shabaab. President Uhuru Kenyatta dismissed the report and the military denied the claims and asked for evidence.
cite: Business Daily, 12 Nov 2015; Citizen Digital, Nov 2015
inside: Smuggling profits drew Kenyan army units sent to fight al-Shabaab into a sugar and charcoal cartel that included the group, so the troops' trade helped fund it, the report alleged.

n: Maputo kidnapping gangs had police and justice staff inside
rank: Police officers; justice-sector employees
d: Gangs that kidnap businesspeople and their families for ransom in Mozambique's capital have people inside the police and justice system. In January 2023 Nelson Rego, director-general of SERNIC, the national criminal investigation service, said publicly at its anniversary ceremony that employees of the bodies that administer justice were involved in kidnappings. Arrests followed: in May 2024 SERNIC detained two officers of Maputo's 23rd police precinct over the abduction of an eight-year-old girl from her primary school, for whom the kidnappers had demanded 200,000 meticais.
cite: AIM, 10 Jan 2023; AIM, 7 May 2024
inside: Kidnapping gangs had police officers and justice staff on their side, so people meant to investigate abductions were themselves taking part in them.

n: Gold smuggling case reached Zimbabwe's spy agency and police
rank: CIO intelligence operatives; senior police officers
d: A gold smuggling syndicate had officers of Zimbabwe's Central Intelligence Organisation (CIO) and the police helping it move gold out through the main airport, according to police. In October 2020 Henrietta Rushwaya, president of the Zimbabwe Miners Federation, was stopped at Harare's Robert Mugabe International Airport with about 6 kg of gold worth $330,000 in her hand luggage, allegedly bound for Dubai. Six more people were arrested, among them two CIO operatives, a police superintendent and a detective chief inspector, as well as a businessman she said had supplied the gold. Rushwaya was remanded in custody while the case continued.
cite: VOA Zimbabwe, 29 Oct 2020; NewsDay
inside: A gold smuggling syndicate had intelligence and police officers working for it, so state security staff helped move gold out through the main airport.

n: Thabo Bester bribed private prison staff to fake his death and escape
rank: G4S warders and CCTV contractor at Mangaung prison
d: Thabo Bester, a convicted rapist and murderer, is alleged to have paid staff at Mangaung Correctional Centre, run for the South African state by G4S, to help him escape in 2022 by faking his death in a cell fire with a corpse. Prosecutors say a G4S security supervisor and the technician who ran its cameras were each promised R2.5 million and paid R40,000, and other staff offered smaller sums. Bester and his partner, Dr Nandipha Magudumana, were arrested in Tanzania in April 2023. Several G4S staff were charged with corruption, arson and defeating the ends of justice; charges against Motanyane Masukela were withdrawn on 17 June 2025. The trial of Bester, Magudumana and six others, put off five times, is set for 19 April to 18 June 2027 in the Free State High Court.
cite: GroundUp, 28 Aug 2026; OFM, 17 Jun 2025; Sunday Times, 7 May 2023
inside: An escaping prisoner and his associates paid staff of the company running the prison, so the guards and camera operator helped fake his death instead of keeping him locked up.
undone: Nobody has been tried over the escape. The trial was postponed again on 28 August 2026, to April 2027, and all the accused are presumed innocent. Magudumana's Constitutional Court challenge to her arrest in Tanzania and return to South Africa was heard in May 2026 and judgment was reserved.

n: Nafiz Modack convicted of paying a police brigadier to recover cars
rank: SAPS brigadier
d: Nafiz Modack, a Cape Town figure whom police describe as an underworld boss, paid a senior police officer to use his command for him. Between 2011 and 2013 Brigadier Kolindhren Govender of the South African Police Service received R146,000 from Modack and in return told officers under him to recover vehicles that belonged to Modack. Govender pleaded guilty to 51 corruption counts in December 2019. Modack was convicted of corruption in June 2025 and in September 2025 sentenced by the Cape Town Regional Court to 10 years, three suspended. He is separately on trial for the 2020 murder of anti-gang detective Charl Kinnear and is accused of paying an anti-gang unit sergeant for information.
cite: Daily Maverick, 21 Sept 2025; Daily Maverick, 18 June 2020
inside: An underworld boss paid a police brigadier, who then ordered officers under his command to recover the boss's cars, putting police resources at his service.

n: 28s gang boss Stanfield got gun licences through police registry staff
rank: Officers at the SAPS Central Firearm Registry
d: Ralph Stanfield, whom police describe as a leader of the Cape Town prison gang the 28s, obtained firearm licences for himself and his family with help from officers inside the police's Central Firearm Registry, the office that approves gun licences. Stanfield, his wife and his sister were arrested in June 2014 along with registry officers. The Supreme Court of Appeal ruled in December 2019 that the Stanfields had obtained their licences unlawfully. Their criminal case, with three former police officers and 18 others, was postponed repeatedly, withdrawn, reinstated and then withdrawn again in September 2024 without any of it being tried. The case was one of several showing gang figures getting guns and licences from inside the police, including a colonel who sold police-stored weapons to gangs.
cite: Daily Maverick, 18 June 2020, and 4 August 2021, for the charges and the Supreme Court of Appeal ruling; News24, 17 September 2024, for the withdrawal of the firearms case; Daily Maverick/amaBhungane, 8 March 2026, for the withdrawal and the former registry officers' later employment; eNCA, 19 October 2026, and Sunday Times, 11 November 2026, for the current High Court trial and the not-guilty pleas
inside: A prison gang leader got officers inside the police firearm registry to approve gun licences for him and his family that the courts later ruled unlawful.
undone: The prosecution over the licences is gone. The case, which at its largest ran to more than a hundred charges against Stanfield, his wife Nicole Johnson, his sister and the registry officers, was withdrawn in the Cape Town Regional Court in September 2024, so the allegations were never tested. What survives is the Supreme Court of Appeal's finding of December 2019 that the licences had been obtained unlawfully. Court papers in the abandoned case had set out that five firearm licences were approved for Stanfield, four for his wife and two for his sister, with one registry officer capturing the applications and another approving them. Stanfield has been in custody since September 2023 and went on trial in the Western Cape High Court on 19 October 2026 with his wife and twelve others on about 42 other charges, including racketeering, murder and fraud, to which they pleaded not guilty; that trial is separate from the licences and nothing in it has been proved. Reporting in March 2026 found that two of the former registry officers who were arrested in 2014 were later working for a private security company that dealt with Stanfield. Checked on 14 November 2026.

n: UAE spy chief's firm secretly bought 49% of Trump family crypto company
rank: Largest outside shareholder and board seats, World Liberty Financial
d: An Abu Dhabi company backed by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE's national security adviser and brother of its president, secretly bought 49% of World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's cryptocurrency venture, the Wall Street Journal reported on 31 January 2026. Aryam Investment 1 agreed to pay $500 million, half upfront; Eric Trump signed four days before the January 2025 inauguration, and the deal was not disclosed. Executives of G42, the UAE artificial-intelligence firm Tahnoon chairs, helped manage Aryam and took seats on World Liberty's board. The report said $187 million went to Trump family entities. In November 2025 the US government approved sales of advanced Nvidia chips to G42. The White House and World Liberty said the deal did not influence policy.
cite: The Block, citing Wall Street Journal (1 Feb 2026)
inside: The UAE security adviser's firm is reported to have secretly bought 49% of the president's family company and put its executives on the board, before US chip approvals for his AI firm.

n: North Korea chose UNDP's local staff and took their pay in hard currency
rank: UNDP country office, Pyongyang
d: North Korea's government placed its own nominees in the Pyongyang office of the UN Development Programme (UNDP), the UN's main aid agency, and took the money paid for them. A 2008 report by the US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations found most local staff were North Koreans chosen by the government, against UNDP policy; their salaries went to the government in convertible currency with no check on what staff received. Officials had to be present at site visits, and in 2002 the government moved $2.72 million of its own funds abroad through a UNDP account. Four audits since 1999 had found problems but were kept from UNDP's own board. UNDP suspended its North Korea operations in March 2007 after the government refused new controls.
cite: US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations report (Jan 2008), via NK Economic Watch (24 Jan 2008)
inside: North Korea's government placed its own nominees as staff in the UN aid agency's Pyongyang office and took their pay, so the UN office served the government's control and income.

n: UN Libya envoy León negotiated UAE job while leading Libya peace talks
rank: UN Special Representative for Libya
d: While Spanish diplomat Bernardino León led the UN's Libya peace talks, the United Arab Emirates, which backed one side in Libya's civil war, offered him a highly paid job. Leaked emails reported by the Guardian in November 2015 showed that, months into his UN post, León wrote to the UAE foreign minister that his plan would 'completely delegitimise' the rival Tripoli parliament, that his moves had been 'consulted with' the UAE-backed side, and that 'I can help and control the process while I am there.' On 4 November 2015 the UAE named him first director-general of its state-backed Emirates Diplomatic Academy, and the UN replaced him with Martin Kobler. The Tripoli government said the hiring cast doubt on the talks; León said his emails were misrepresented.
cite: Al Jazeera (6 Nov 2015); The New Arab, citing the Guardian (5 Nov 2015)
inside: While leading UN peace talks, the envoy negotiated a well-paid job with the UAE, which backed one side, and wrote that he was steering the process in that side's favour.

n: Saudi 'Special Committee' kept 2,700 Yemeni leaders on its payroll
rank: Yemeni president, tribal, party and army leaders
d: Saudi Arabia ran its Yemen policy through the Special Committee, a body of its Council of Ministers that has paid Yemeni leaders since 1962. In June 2012 the Yemeni paper Al-Sharea printed part of a list of about 2,700 tribal, political and military figures it said received monthly Saudi payments totalling 56 million riyals, with ex-president Ali Abdullah Saleh, Sheikh Sadeq al-Ahmar and General Ali Mohsin reported at the top; the ruling party and the Islah party denied it, and MPs demanded an explanation. Saudi cables from 2010–2012 later published by Drop Site News show the committee authorising 50 million riyals for tribes fighting the Houthis and directing named sheikhs and a serving brigade commander.
cite: Global Voices (12 June 2012), citing Al-Sharea; Drop Site News, Saudi cables (2025)
inside: A Saudi government committee kept thousands of Yemeni political, tribal and military leaders on monthly pay and directed named sheikhs and a serving brigade commander.

n: Ex-Al Jazeera reporter Fahad Yasin ran Somalia's spy agency for Qatar (alleged)
rank: Director, National Intelligence and Security Agency
d: Somali media and analysts allege that Qatar placed an ally at the head of Somalia's security apparatus. Fahad Yasin, a journalist for Qatar's state-funded Al Jazeera Arabic in Mogadishu from 2005 to 2011, became chief of staff to President Mohamed Abdullahi 'Farmaajo' in 2017, deputy head of the National Intelligence and Security Agency (NISA) in 2018 and its director from August 2019 to September 2021, then national security adviser. Commentators said he had channelled Qatari money into the 2012 presidential vote, and Garowe Online reported he coordinated sending Somali recruits to Eritrea who were told they would train in Qatar. Qatar denied funding Somalia through him. The prime minister suspended him in 2021 over the murder of NISA officer Ikran Tahlil, and he was replaced in May 2022.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Fahad Yasin Haji Dahir' (citing Reuters, BBC Somali, Garowe Online); Garowe Online, 'Qatar denies claims of funding Somalia through Fahad Yasin'
inside: Qatar is alleged to have had its ally run Somalia's intelligence agency, through which Qatari money and Qatar-linked recruitment of Somali soldiers were reportedly arranged; Qatar denies it.

n: Azerbaijani Laundromat paid UNESCO chief's husband €345,000
rank: Spouse of UNESCO Director-General; later EBRD board
d: Shell companies in the Azerbaijani Laundromat, a $2.9 billion scheme that moved money from Azerbaijan's ruling circle, paid €345,000 between 2012 and 2014 to Kalin Mitrev, husband of UNESCO Director-General Irina Bokova, OCCRP reported in September 2017. One payment of €20,000 arrived on 25 October 2013, three days after UNESCO, the UN's cultural agency, hosted an exhibition requested by a foundation chaired by Mehriban Aliyeva, the Azerbaijani president's wife. Mitrev, by then Bulgaria's director on the board of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, said the money was for consultancy on a flood project and was declared. Bokova said she knew nothing of his business. Bulgaria's chief prosecutor and revenue agency opened checks.
cite: OCCRP, Azerbaijani Laundromat profile 'Kalin Mitrev' (Sept 2017); bne IntelliNews (Sept 2017)
inside: Azerbaijani ruling-circle money was reported paid to the UNESCO chief's husband, one payment arriving days after UNESCO hosted an exhibition requested by the Azerbaijani first lady's foundation.

n: Ex-MP Lintner convicted of bribing a Bundestag member for Azerbaijan
rank: Bundestag member and PACE delegate Karin Strenz
d: Azerbaijan used former German MP Eduard Lintner to pay a sitting member of the Bundestag, Germany's parliament, to promote its interests at the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), a human-rights body of national MPs. OCCRP's Laundromat records showed Lintner, a CSU deputy for 33 years and a PACE delegate until 2010, received €819,500 from Laundromat companies in 2012–2014. In July 2025 the Munich Higher Regional Court found he bribed public officials on Azerbaijan's behalf, the first such verdict against a German lawmaker, and gave him a nine-month suspended sentence; it found CDU MP Karin Strenz, who died in 2021, took money from his company and from Azerbaijani officials. Lintner called it legitimate lobbying and is appealing.
cite: OCCRP (30 July 2025); OCCRP, 'The Influence Machine' (2017); JAMnews (2025)
inside: Azerbaijan paid a former German MP to bribe a sitting MP, so a member of a European human-rights assembly promoted Azerbaijan's interests there, a court found.

n: Pakistani intelligence recruited Indian diplomat Madhuri Gupta
rank: Second secretary, Indian High Commission in Islamabad
d: Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), its main spy agency, recruited Madhuri Gupta, a second secretary at India's High Commission (embassy) in Islamabad, and she passed it information, an Indian court found. Indian police arrested her in 2010 after six months of surveillance. On 18 May 2018 a New Delhi court convicted her of spying and wrongful communication of information, saying she had passed 'categorically sensitive information, which could have been useful to the enemy country', and sentenced her to three years in prison. She had already spent about 21 months in custody. Gupta denied the charges, saying colleagues had falsely implicated her, and her lawyer said she would appeal.
cite: Al Jazeera (20 May 2018); Business Standard/PTI (18–19 May 2018)
inside: Pakistan's spy agency recruited an Indian diplomat inside India's embassy in Islamabad, who passed it sensitive information her government was meant to keep.

n: Pakistani agent drew missile secrets from Indian defence lab director Kurulkar
rank: Director of a DRDO laboratory
d: A Pakistani intelligence operative posing as a woman online drew information from Pradeep Kurulkar, director of a laboratory of India's Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), the state body that designs its missiles and weapons, Indian investigators say. Kurulkar was arrested in Pune on 3 May 2023 after a complaint from DRDO's own vigilance department. On 30 June 2023 Maharashtra's Anti-Terrorism Squad filed a 1,837-page charge sheet under the Official Secrets Act, and reports of it said he discussed Indian missile systems with the operative. Investigators, not Kurulkar, describe the contact as a 'honey trap', a seduction set up to extract secrets. At his bail hearing Kurulkar argued that the information he is said to have passed was already in the public domain.
cite: Free Press Journal, 15 April 2026 (Bombay High Court bail refusal); PTI via The Hitavada, 16 April 2026 (Kurulkar's public-domain argument); Punekar News, 13 July 2026 (trial opens before Pune sessions court); Onmanorama, 8 July 2023
inside: A Pakistani intelligence operative drew a director of India's weapons-research body into contact and obtained discussion of Indian missile systems, investigators allege.
undone: Kurulkar has not been convicted. A Pune court refused him bail in December 2023. The Bombay High Court refused him bail again on 15 April 2026, Justice Shivkumar Dige noting that he had been in contact with a Pakistani intelligence operative and could abscond if released. A Pune sessions court completed the framing of charges on 18 June 2026, and the trial opened before Sessions Judge P. Y. Ladekar on 13 July 2026 with the examination of the first prosecution witness. No verdict has been reached, the allegations are untested, and he is presumed innocent.

n: Pakistani handlers paid 11 Indian Navy sailors for naval secrets
rank: Serving Indian Navy personnel
d: Pakistani intelligence agencies paid serving Indian Navy personnel for information, through two Indian businessmen who sent money to the sailors' bank accounts on the handlers' instructions, India's National Investigation Agency (NIA) says. Fifteen people were arrested, 11 of them serving Navy personnel; the NIA took over the case from Andhra Pradesh police in December 2019 and charged 14 people in June 2020. The NIA said Mohammad Haroon Lakdawala and Imran Yakub Giteli, who had relatives in Pakistan, met intelligence operatives there and funded the payments from cross-border trade. In October 2025 a court sentenced the two to five and a half and six years, bringing convictions in the case to four. Related arrests continued into 2023.
cite: The News Minute (18 Oct 2025); The South First (2023)
inside: Pakistani intelligence paid serving Indian Navy sailors through middlemen, so people inside the navy passed it the information the navy was meant to keep secret.

n: Aide to Indian MP held for passing documents to Pakistan's High Commission
rank: Personal assistant to a Rajya Sabha MP
d: Pakistan's High Commission (embassy) in New Delhi paid an Indian MP's assistant for official documents, Delhi police said. In October 2016 police caught Mehmood Akhtar, a Pakistani in the High Commission's visa section, receiving military documents from two men; India ordered him to leave, and Pakistan expelled an Indian diplomat in return. Days later the Crime Branch detained Farhat, personal assistant to Munavvar Saleem, a Samajwadi Party member of the Rajya Sabha (India's upper house), saying he had handed official documents to Akhtar for money after making contact with the High Commission some years earlier. Saleem sacked him and said he regretted employing him.
cite: The News Minute (30 Oct 2016); Business Standard/IANS (29 Oct 2016)
inside: Pakistan's embassy in Delhi paid an Indian MP's assistant, who used his place in the MP's office to hand over official documents.

n: Letter says North Korea paid Pakistan's army chief $3m for nuclear help
rank: Chief of Army Staff
d: North Korea paid Pakistan's army chief and another senior general to approve passing nuclear-weapons technology to it, according to a 1998 letter that Pakistani scientist A.Q. Khan released and the Washington Post reported in July 2011. The letter, apparently signed by North Korean Workers' Party secretary Jon Byong-ho, said $3 million had gone to General Jehangir Karamat, then Chief of Army Staff, and $500,000 plus jewellery to Lieutenant-General Zulfiqar Khan. Western intelligence officials told the Post the letter was authentic. Pakistani officials called it a fake, and both generals denied it; Karamat said he 'was not in the loop'. Pakistan's centrifuge technology is known to have reached North Korea.
cite: Express Tribune/Reuters, citing Washington Post (8 July 2011)
inside: North Korea is said to have paid Pakistan's army chief and another general to approve passing it nuclear-weapons technology, according to a letter both men deny.

n: A.Q. Khan took Urenco centrifuge designs from the Netherlands to Pakistan
rank: Translator at Urenco's Dutch partner
d: Pakistani metallurgist A.Q. Khan, working inside the Dutch side of Urenco, the European uranium-enrichment consortium, took its centrifuge designs to Pakistan's nuclear programme. From 1972 he worked at FDO, a subcontractor to Urenco's Dutch partner, and visited the Almelo enrichment plant many times without official clearance. In late 1974 he was given the German G-1 and G-2 centrifuge designs to translate and had 16 days of unsupervised access. He left for Pakistan on 15 December 1975 with copied blueprints and contacts for nearly 100 suppliers, and in 1976 began centrifuge work there. A Dutch court convicted him in absentia of nuclear espionage in 1983; the verdict was overturned in 1985 for a faulty summons. The designs later reached Iran, Libya and North Korea.
cite: Carnegie Endowment, 'A.Q. Khan Nuclear Chronology' (Sept 2005)
inside: Working inside the Dutch partner of the European enrichment consortium, Khan copied its centrifuge designs and supplier contacts and took them to Pakistan's nuclear programme.

n: North Korea's Ilsimhoe cell reached the Democratic Labor Party's leadership
rank: Deputy, Democratic Labor Party standing committee
d: A group called Ilsimhoe, taking orders from North Korea's ruling Workers' Party, had members inside South Korea's Democratic Labor Party (DLP), then a party with seats in the National Assembly, and passed the North information on the party's core membership. South Korea's National Intelligence Service arrested its founder Michael Jang and DLP central committee member Lee Jeong-hun on 24 October 2006. In April 2007 a Seoul court convicted five people of spying: Jang got nine years, Lee six, and Choi Gi-yeong, a former DLP vice secretary-general, four. The court rejected the charge that they formed a spy ring; the Supreme Court later upheld that they received the Workers' Party's orders. The case split the DLP.
cite: Daily NK, 'Michael Jang and the Ilsimhoe Scandal'; Joongang Ilbo via Free Korea (16 Apr 2007)
inside: A group taking orders from North Korea's ruling party had members inside a South Korean parliamentary party and passed the North information on its core membership.

n: Wangjaesan ring passed South Korean political intelligence to the North
who: North Korean Workers' Party liaison department
rank: Politician's secretary
d: A South Korean group called Wangjaesan, acting for North Korea's Workers' Party, gathered political intelligence in the South, and one member worked as secretary to a politician, a Seoul court heard. Prosecutors said its leader, a 49-year-old activist named Kim arrested in August 2011, met North Korean agents in China and Japan and in 2001 took orders from the Workers' Party's foreign liaison department to recruit more agents. In February 2012 the Seoul Central District Court sentenced Kim to nine years under the National Security Law and four others to two to seven years for leaking political information. The court rejected the charge that they had run an anti-state organisation for two decades.
cite: Korea JoongAng Daily (23 Feb 2012)
inside: A ring acting for North Korea's ruling party gathered South Korean political intelligence, with one member working as a politician's secretary.

n: North Korean-directed Chungbuk cell tried to recruit regional politicians
rank: Regional politicians and civic leaders (recruitment targets)
d: Three members of a group called Chungbuk Dongjihoe, acting on orders from North Korean agents, worked to recruit politicians and labour and civic figures in South Korea's North Chungcheong province, a court found. Prosecutors said the group swapped encrypted instructions and reports with the agents, collected local political information and received about $20,000 in operating funds. In February 2024 the Cheongju District Court sentenced the three, including chairman Son Mo, to 12 years each under the National Security Act. Their arrests in 2021 were among several cases in which South Korean prosecutors said North Korea tried to build networks reaching into parties and local politics.
cite: Asia Economy (16 Feb 2024); Korea JoongAng Daily (2021)
inside: A group taking orders and money from North Korean agents set out to recruit South Korean regional politicians and civic figures and collected political information for the North.

n: North Korean agent posing as a defector lectured at army bases
rank: South Korean army officers and bases
d: North Korea placed an agent, Won Jeong-hwa, inside South Korea's military circles by having her pose as a defector. Under that cover she gave 52 lectures at military bases, and prosecutors said she dated a South Korean army officer and used the relationship to make him work for her. She passed the North the locations of key military installations, lists of North Korean defectors and personal details of South Korean officers; business cards and photos of 23 officers were found among her belongings. She was arrested in July 2008, and in October 2008 the Suwon District Court sentenced her to five years in prison.
cite: NBC News/AP (15 Oct 2008); Korea Times (15 Oct 2008)
inside: North Korea placed an agent posing as a defector inside South Korean military circles, where she used an army officer to pass the North military secrets.

n: North Korean hacker paid a South Korean army captain in crypto
rank: Army captain; joint command system login
d: A North Korean agent known as 'Boris' used cryptocurrency to recruit a serving South Korean army captain, through a South Korean crypto-exchange operator, Lee. From 2021 Lee, following Boris's Telegram instructions, gave the captain a watch with a hidden camera and a hacking device called Poison Tap; the captain filmed secret material and handed over login details for the Korean Joint Command and Control System, the military's command network. The hacking attempt failed. The captain was paid about 48 million won and Lee about 700 million won in bitcoin. Both were arrested in April 2022. The captain, Kim, was sentenced to ten years, and in December 2025 the Supreme Court upheld Lee's four-year sentence.
cite: Korea Times (29 Apr 2022); Korea JoongAng Daily (28 Dec 2025)
inside: A North Korean agent paid a serving South Korean army captain in cryptocurrency to film secret material and hand over logins to the military's command network.

n: Chongryon finance chief took ¥837m from Korean credit union in Tokyo
rank: Chogin Tokyo credit union
d: Chongryon, the association of pro-North Korean residents in Japan that serves as Pyongyang's de facto embassy, controlled a network of Korean credit unions called Chogin and drew money out of them. Kang Yong-gwan, former head of Chongryon's finance bureau, took 837 million yen from the Chogin Tokyo credit union in 13 transactions between 1994 and 1998. Chogin Tokyo collapsed in 1999. Police arrested Kang in November 2001 and searched Chongryon's headquarters; other Chogin chairmen were arrested in the following weeks over illicit loans. In March 2004 the Tokyo District Court sentenced Kang to six years in prison for embezzlement, and his appeal was rejected in October 2005.
cite: Japan Times (29 Nov 2001; 27 Mar 2004; 7 Oct 2005)
inside: Chongryon, Pyongyang's de facto embassy in Japan, controlled a network of Korean credit unions and its finance chief drew hundreds of millions of yen out of one of them.

n: Oman says it broke up a UAE spy network in its government and army
rank: Omanis including government employees
d: Oman said in January 2011 that it had uncovered a spy network run for the United Arab Emirates that targeted 'Oman and the way its government and military work'. Its state news agency said several Omani nationals had been arrested about two months earlier, some of them government employees, and would be sent to court. The UAE denied any link and said it would cooperate with any transparent investigation. The case showed tension between two Gulf neighbours that are both members of the Gulf Cooperation Council.
cite: Al Jazeera (31 Jan 2011)
inside: Oman said the UAE ran a spy network that included Omani government employees, working inside the state to report on how its government and army operate.

n: Afghan intelligence arrests officials and a general spying for Pakistan's ISI
rank: Foreign ministry diplomat; senior bureaucrats; an army general
d: Afghanistan's intelligence service, the National Directorate of Security (NDS), said in 2012 that Pakistan's spy agency, the ISI, and Iran had agents inside the Afghan government. In February 2012 it reported arresting four officials, including a senior diplomat in the Foreign Ministry's Asia section said to work for Pakistan's military intelligence. On 1 August 2012 NDS head Rahmatullah Nabil told parliament that 15 government employees, including senior bureaucrats and a military general, had been arrested for spying, and that some had confessed to working for the ISI or Iran. He also said insurgent infiltrators inside the security forces had been caught planning assassinations.
cite: RFE/RL (28 Feb 2012); RFE/RL (2 Aug 2012)
inside: Pakistan's spy agency and Iran had agents among Afghan government employees, including a Foreign Ministry diplomat and a general, who spied for them.

n: Operation Midnight Jackal: ISI officers worked to topple Bhutto in parliament
rank: National Assembly members (no-confidence vote)
d: Officers of Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), the military's spy agency, worked to bring down Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto by winning over her own party's members of the National Assembly before a no-confidence vote. Between 28 September and 6 October 1989, Brigadier Imtiaz Ahmed and Major Mohammed Amir met two PPP MNAs, Arif Awan and Rasheed Bhatti, at a Rawalpindi house to get them to defect to the opposition alliance. The civilian Intelligence Bureau had bugged the house and recorded the talks. Army chief General Mirza Aslam Beg retired both officers at Bhutto's request. The motion failed. In 1994 Bhutto's second government arrested Imtiaz and planned treason charges.
cite: The Herald (Aug 1994, republished by Dawn, 2018)
inside: Officers of the military spy agency tried to win over members of the prime minister's own party in parliament so they would defect and vote her out.

n: Qatar flew EU transport chief Hololei free while he negotiated its air deal
rank: Director-General for Transport, European Commission
d: Qatar and its state airline paid for flights and holidays for Henrik Hololei, head of the European Commission's transport department, while he negotiated the EU–Qatar aviation agreement that opened Europe's skies to Qatar Airways. The trips, from 2015 to 2021, were revealed by Politico in 2023, and Hololei left the post in March 2023. An inquiry by OLAF, the EU anti-fraud office, concluded he shared confidential details of the deal with Qatar; a 2025 Commission disciplinary procedure found unauthorised gifts, conflicts of interest and breaches of confidentiality, and on 29 January 2026 the Commission terminated his contract. The European Public Prosecutor's Office opened a criminal corruption investigation in late 2024. The agreement, signed in 2019, remains in force.
cite: bne IntelliNews (Jan 2026); ERR News (2025); FDD (7 Nov 2024)
inside: Qatar and its state airline paid for flights for the EU official negotiating their aviation deal, and he shared confidential details of the talks with Qatar, an EU inquiry found.
undone: The European Public Prosecutor's Office investigation was still open in February 2026. No charges have been brought, no court has ruled, and Hololei is presumed innocent. The Commission's decision was a disciplinary one over administrative breaches, not a criminal finding.

n: Gülen followers won Turkey's judicial board, then picked top judges
rank: Supreme Board of Judges and Prosecutors (HSYK); Court of Appeals
d: Followers of Fethullah Gülen, a Turkish preacher whose Hizmet movement placed members in state jobs, gained seats on the Supreme Board of Judges and Prosecutors (HSYK), the body that appoints and moves Turkey's judges, in its 2010 election, and then used it to fill the top courts. Ahmet Hamsici, a former HSYK deputy chairman, said in a 31-page testimony after the 2016 coup attempt that Gülen wanted at least 140 Court of Appeals seats for his followers; the board agreed on 108, and about 107 of those named were appointed. The government, then allied with the movement, had bargained over the posts. In the 2014 HSYK election non-Gülenist candidates won and the government declared the movement's hold ended.
cite: Hürriyet Daily News, 18 Nov 2016 (Hamsici testimony); Daily Sabah, 13 Oct 2014
inside: Gülen followers won seats on the board that appoints Turkey's judges and then used it to place about 107 of the movement's people in the top appeals court.

n: Leaked 2010 civil-service exam questions helped place Gülen followers
rank: State recruitment exam (KPSS) question unit
d: People working in the question-preparation unit of Turkey's state testing body leaked the 2010 Public Personnel Selection Exam (KPSS), the test about 808,000 people sat for civil-service jobs, and prosecutors say the questions went to followers of the Gülen movement so its members could be hired into the state. Prosecutors confirmed that general-culture, skills and education questions were seized at least 12 days before the test, and about 2,600 suspects were investigated. In 2019 an Ankara court sentenced 70 defendants, most of them wives of military officers linked to the movement, to between seven months and 14 years. A separate 2010 police promotion exam case led to 735 arrests.
cite: Hürriyet Daily News, 12 May 2016; Daily Sabah, 14 Feb 2019
inside: Leaked civil-service exam questions went to Gülen followers so the movement could get its members hired into state jobs, prosecutors say.

n: Gülen-linked judges removed for cheating on Turkey's 2012 judge exam
rank: Judges and prosecutors
d: Followers of the Gülen movement entered Turkey's courts as judges and prosecutors through a 2012 entrance exam whose questions had been leaked, according to the country's judicial board. After an opposition CHP deputy, Atilla Kart, complained that 20 named candidates had seen the questions, expert reports from prosecutors and the national testing centre (ÖSYM) found the candidates had marked the same questions wrong. In June 2015 the Supreme Board of Judges and Prosecutors (HSYK) dismissed 37 judges and prosecutors on that evidence. The board linked the suspects to the movement, which was already accused over the 2010 civil-service exam leak. The case was used as evidence of a wider practice of placing members in state institutions.
cite: Daily Sabah, 11 Jun 2015
inside: Gülen followers became judges and prosecutors through a leaked entrance exam, placing the movement's members inside Turkey's courts, the judicial board found.

n: Gülen-linked prosecutor summoned Turkey's spy chief in 2012 'MİT crisis'
rank: Istanbul special prosecutor and police chiefs
d: Prosecutors and police chiefs that a Turkish court later tied to the Gülen movement used their posts to target the head of the national intelligence agency (MİT). On 12 February 2012 Istanbul prosecutor Sadrettin Sarıkaya, running a probe into the Kurdish KCK network, summoned MİT undersecretary Hakan Fidan over his talks with the PKK. Prime Minister Erdoğan ordered Fidan not to appear and passed a law requiring the prime minister's permission to prosecute intelligence officers. On 3 March 2021 the Istanbul 23rd High Criminal Court gave 10 of 18 defendants, including former police chiefs Yurt Atayün and Ali Fuat Yılmazer, aggravated life sentences for attempting to overthrow the government. Sarıkaya was jailed.
cite: Turkish Minute, 3 Mar 2021; Hürriyet Daily News (Sarıkaya arrest)
inside: Prosecutors and police chiefs tied by a court to the Gülen movement used their posts to summon and target the head of Turkey's intelligence agency.

n: Gülen-linked gendarmes and prosecutors stopped Turkish spy-agency trucks
rank: Gendarmerie commanders and Adana prosecutors
d: Gendarmerie officers and prosecutors whom Turkish courts tied to the Gülen movement used their posts in 2014 to stop and search trucks of the national intelligence agency (MİT) heading to Syria near the border, against government orders to let them pass. The government said the search was part of the movement's campaign from inside the state. On 28 June 2019 Ankara's 16th High Criminal Court convicted seven gendarmes and prosecutors of obtaining and disclosing confidential state documents. Former Adana chief prosecutor Süleyman Bağrıyanık received over 22 years, prosecutors Ahmet Karaca and Aziz Takcı 26 years each, and former brigadier general Hamza Celepoğlu about 20 years.
cite: Hürriyet Daily News, 29 Jun 2019
inside: Gendarmes and prosecutors tied to the Gülen movement used their posts to stop intelligence-agency trucks against government orders, which the government said served the movement's campaign.

n: Court ties Istanbul police intelligence chiefs to Hrant Dink murder
rank: Istanbul police intelligence chief and deputy
d: An Istanbul court ruled in March 2021 that the 2007 killing of Hrant Dink, an Armenian-Turkish newspaper editor, was carried out in line with the aims of the Gülen movement, which it found had members inside the police and security services who let the plot go ahead. Of 76 defendants, former Istanbul police intelligence chief Ramazan Akyürek and his deputy Ali Fuat Yılmazer were given life sentences for premeditated murder, as were two former Istanbul interior-ministry officers. A former Trabzon commander, Ali Öz, got 28 years. The gunman, Ogün Samast, had been sentenced in 2011. Other defendants were convicted of membership of what Ankara calls 'FETÖ' and of destroying documents.
cite: Voice of America (AP), Mar 2021; Duvar English
inside: A court found Gülen movement members inside the police and security services let the plot to kill Hrant Dink go ahead in line with the movement's aims.

n: Aide to Turkey's armed forces chief confessed to bugging for Gülenists
rank: Aide-de-camp to the Chief of General Staff
d: Lieutenant Colonel Levent Türkkan, aide-de-camp to Turkey's Chief of General Staff Hulusi Akar, told investigators after the July 2016 coup attempt that he had been a follower of the Gülen movement since school and had carried out its orders inside the military. He said movement members gave him the questions for his 1989 military academy entrance exam, and that he planted listening devices in the office of the previous chief, Necdet Özel, with a device supplied by a contact at Türk Telekom. State media published the confession as key proof of the movement's role. On 23 May 2017 he told an Ankara court the statement was false and given under torture; photos had shown him bruised.
cite: Hürriyet Daily News, 21 Jul 2016; Stockholm Center for Freedom, 24 May 2017
inside: The armed forces chief's aide said the Gülen movement placed him in the military through leaked exam questions and had him bug the previous chief's office; he later retracted it.

n: Menzil Sufi order said to fill Turkish police posts vacated by Gülenists
rank: Police appointments; health and energy ministers
d: Menzil, a branch of the Naqshbandi Sufi order, moved its followers into Turkish state posts emptied by the purge of Gülen followers, according to journalists and the order's own leader. The book Metastaz by Barış Terkoğlu and Barış Pehlivan says that from 2014 new police recruits came largely from Naqshbandi and other sects, with Menzil dominant, and T24 reported police promotions made by reference to Menzil membership. Menzil chief Fevzeddin Erol told Sözcü that health minister Recep Akdağ and energy minister Taner Yıldız were members and that the order had 'men everywhere in the state'. Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu denied it, and a court ordered T24's article removed.
cite: Foreign Policy, 15 Jan 2020
inside: Journalists and the order's own leader say the Menzil order moved its followers into Turkish police and state posts, with police promotions made by reference to membership.

n: RSS sends its own organiser to run the BJP as 'general secretary'
rank: BJP national general secretary (organisation)
d: The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation, places one of its full-time organisers, called pracharaks, inside India's ruling BJP as its general secretary (organisation), a post reserved by convention for senior RSS men. In July 2019 the RSS recalled Ram Lal after 13 years in the post and replaced him with B. L. Santhosh. The holder makes sure the BJP leadership carries out the RSS chief's instructions, reports to the RSS head and mobilises RSS workers at elections. In 2004 the then holder, Sanjay Joshi, drafted a resolution against party leader L. K. Advani over his praise of Jinnah, and Advani was forced to resign as party president.
cite: ThePrint, Jul 2019; Asian Age, 14 Jul 2019
inside: The RSS places one of its own organisers in the ruling BJP's top organisational post, where he makes sure the party carries out the RSS chief's instructions.

n: Liberhan inquiry: RSS groups and UP government enabled Babri demolition
rank: Uttar Pradesh chief minister, bureaucracy and police
d: The Liberhan Commission, a 17-year official inquiry into the 1992 demolition of the Babri Mosque at Ayodhya, found that the RSS and its allied groups, together with Uttar Pradesh's BJP government, made it possible. Its report, given to the prime minister on 30 June 2009, named the RSS, VHP, Bajrang Dal, BJP and Shiv Sena, and called chief minister Kalyan Singh the 'pivotal figure'. It said his government transferred officers who opposed the plan, worked through handpicked bureaucrats, and that about 90% of the police sent to guard the mosque were sympathisers, the rest told not to use force. The demolition was followed by violence that killed hundreds.
cite: ThePrint, summary of Liberhan Commission report (2009)
inside: An official inquiry found RSS-family groups worked with a state government that moved aside opposing officers and used sympathetic police, so the state let the mosque be demolished.

n: VHP officials made public prosecutors in Gujarat 2002 riot trials
rank: Special public prosecutors in riot cases
d: Gujarat's government appointed lawyers from the Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP), a Hindu nationalist body in the RSS family, as public prosecutors in trials over the 2002 Gujarat riots, in which VHP members were among the accused. Citizens for Justice and Peace told the Supreme Court that Dilip Trivedi, general secretary of the VHP's Mehsana unit, prosecuted the Sardarpura massacre case and that Chetan Shah, a VHP supporter, handled the Gulbarga Society case. A Special Investigation Team report of 17 May 2010 said political affiliation appeared to have influenced the appointments. In 2021 Kapil Sibal told the court that 55 accused were bailed after Trivedi's appointment.
cite: Zee News (Supreme Court hearing, Oct 2003); LiveLaw, 11 Nov 2021
inside: Gujarat appointed VHP lawyers to prosecute riot cases in which VHP members were accused, putting the group's people in charge of cases against its own members.

n: RSS history wing's leader made chair of India's history research council
rank: Chair, Indian Council of Historical Research
d: Y. Sudershan Rao, head of the Andhra Pradesh branch of the Akhil Bharatiya Itihas Sankalan Yojana (ABISY), a history body set up by the RSS, was made chair of the Indian Council of Historical Research (ICHR), the state body that funds and directs historical research, in July 2014. In March 2015 three ABISY-linked historians were nominated to the council on his recommendation. Critics, including historian Romila Thapar, said he had no peer-reviewed publications and saw the appointments as placing RSS-aligned people in state institutions. Rao said the Ramayana and Mahabharata were accurate history and announced a study of whether Adam's Bridge was man-made. He served until 2017.
cite: Wikipedia (Yellapragada Sudershan Rao, citing Indian press); Tribune, 27 Nov 2015
inside: The leader of an RSS history body was made head of the state history research council and brought in more of that body's historians, critics say to serve the RSS line.

n: VHP men took 9 of 11 key seats on the state-formed Ram temple trust
rank: Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust
d: The Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP), the Hindu nationalist body that led the campaign for a Ram temple at Ayodhya, took control of the trust India's government formed on the Supreme Court's orders to build it. In February 2020, nine of the 11 trustees with a decisive role were from the VHP or RSS, including its chairman Nritya Gopal Das, a member of the VHP's guidance council, and general secretary Champat Rai, a VHP vice-president. Former Modi aide Nripendra Misra chaired the construction committee, and four ex-officio members are senior government officers. Only two trustees had no RSS or VHP link.
cite: IANS via Lokmat Times, 21 Feb 2020; The Week, 19 Feb 2020
inside: VHP and RSS figures took nine of eleven decisive seats on the state-formed trust building the Ayodhya temple, the project the VHP had campaigned for.

n: Army officers and Harkat-ul-Jihad plotted Islamist coup in Pakistan, 1995
rank: Army general headquarters
d: Serving Pakistani army officers working with Qari Saifullah Akhtar, chief of the militant group Harkat-ul-Jihad al-Islami, planned to seize power from inside the army in 1995. They intended to storm a corps commanders' meeting at army headquarters in Rawalpindi on 30 September, kill Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, the army chief and other leaders, and proclaim an Islamic caliphate with Major General Zahirul Islam Abbasi as its emir. Officers were detained on 26 September 1995 after Akhtar turned informer, and weapons and uniforms were seized. A court martial gave Abbasi seven years and Brigadier Mustansir Billah 14 years; two colonels were dismissed and jailed.
cite: Dawn (Supreme Court appeal coverage, Feb 2022); Wikipedia (Zahirul Islam Abbasi)
inside: A militant group's chief worked with serving army officers on a plan to seize power from inside the army by killing the country's leaders.

n: Saudi-inspired Madkhali Salafis entrenched in Libya's forces and mosques
rank: Special Deterrence Force; LNA brigades; religious endowments authority
d: Followers of Rabee al-Madkhali, a Saudi cleric whose ultra-conservative Salafi teaching demands obedience to rulers, built positions inside both of Libya's rival governments after 2011, the International Crisis Group reported in April 2019. In Tripoli they are strong in the Special Deterrence Force (Rada), nominally under the interior ministry and given a national remit by decree in May 2018. In the east they form units of Khalifa Haftar's Libyan National Army and dominate the eastern religious endowments authority, which runs mosques and issues fatwas. In late 2018 the Tripoli government named a Madkhali-sympathetic head of its endowments office; a former official estimated most Tripoli mosques were under Madkhali influence.
cite: International Crisis Group, Addressing the Rise of Libya's Madkhali-Salafis, 25 Apr 2019
inside: Followers of a Saudi-inspired Salafi current hold posts in Libyan security units and run the eastern religious authority that controls mosques and issues fatwas.

n: Al-Shabaab agents inside Mogadishu's city hall, spy agency and chamber
rank: Mogadishu mayor's office; intelligence agency (NISA)
d: Al-Shabaab, the al-Qaeda-linked Islamist insurgency, placed agents inside Somalia's institutions. On 24 July 2019 a blind woman using a false name, who worked as a disability coordinator in the office of Mogadishu mayor Abdirahman Omar Osman, blew herself up at a security meeting there, killing six officials; the mayor died of his wounds on 1 August. Al-Shabaab said the target was UN envoy James Swan. The National Intelligence and Security Agency (NISA) later paraded a government band singer it said was al-Shabaab's accountant, and the government dissolved the Chamber of Commerce board after finding the group had representatives on it.
cite: Daily Nation (Nairobi), Jan 2020; Al Jazeera, 25 Jul 2019
inside: Al-Shabaab placed its agents in Somali institutions, including a worker in the Mogadishu mayor's office who bombed a meeting there and members on the Chamber of Commerce board.

n: Unification Church members signed up en masse to South Korea's ruling party
rank: People Power Party membership and leadership vote
d: A South Korean special counsel found that about 3,500 Unification Church followers joined the then-ruling People Power Party (PPP), about 3,100 of them between October 2022 and March 2023, ahead of the party convention that chose its leader. Prosecutors raided the firm holding the PPP membership list on 18 September 2025 and matched about 120,000 names against 1.2 million church records. Several people were then charged under the Political Parties Act, among them Kim Keon-hee, the church's leader Han Hak-ja and its former world headquarters head Yun Young-ho. At the first hearing, at the Seoul Central District Court on 21 August 2026, all denied the charges; Kim's lawyer said there was no evidence of a conspiracy and that the roughly 2,400 members enrolled may not have affected the result.
cite: Korea JoongAng Daily, 26 Sep 2025; The Fact, 21 August 2026 (first hearing, Seoul Central District Court); Daum/news report of the Seoul Central District Court judgment of 28 January 2026
inside: A special counsel found thousands of Unification Church followers joined the ruling party before its leadership vote, which prosecutors suspect was an effort to choose the party's leader.
undone: No verdict has been reached. The case is at its first-hearing stage, the next sitting was set for 28 August 2026, and the defendants are presumed innocent. The court separated the trial of a co-defendant, Jeon Seong-bae, from Kim Keon-hee's at his request. Party figures said the overlap between the two membership lists was statistically expected, and the law requires proof that members were coerced. The suspicion that the church first sought to help lawmaker Kweon Seong-dong and then backed Kim Gi-hyeon, who won the leadership, has not been tested at trial. In a separate case on different facts, the same court convicted Kweon on 28 January 2026 of taking 100 million won in illegal political funds from the church in January 2022, sentencing him to two years with 100 million won forfeited; he said he would appeal. Yun Young-ho was given one year and two months in that case.

n: Assembly of God pastor Everaldo allegedly steered Rio's health posts
rank: Rio de Janeiro State Health Secretariat; Cedae; Detran
d: Everaldo Pereira, an Assembly of God pastor and national president of the Social Christian Party (PSC), was arrested on 28 August 2020 in Operation Tris in Idem, a federal police inquiry into corruption in Rio de Janeiro state's health secretariat during the COVID-19 pandemic under PSC governor Wilson Witzel. Reports cited by Congresso em Foco said Everaldo, who held no government post, was the most powerful figure in Witzel's government and influenced appointments to the Health Secretariat, the state water company Cedae and the vehicle agency Detran. Witzel was suspended from office the same day and later removed. Everaldo had baptised Jair Bolsonaro in the Jordan River in 2016.
cite: Congresso em Foco, 28 Aug 2020 (citing O Dia); Channels TV/AFP, 28 Aug 2020
inside: A pastor and party chief with no government post is reported to have controlled appointments in Rio's health secretariat and other state bodies, which were then under corruption investigation.

n: Greek junta's officers in Cyprus's National Guard overthrew Makarios
rank: Cypriot National Guard command
d: Greece's military government used the Greek officers it had posted to Cyprus's army, the National Guard, to overthrow the Cypriot government. About 650 Greek officers were serving in the National Guard, and the junta also supplied, controlled and funded EOKA-B, an armed group that wanted Cyprus joined to Greece. On 2 July 1974 President Makarios wrote publicly to the Greek president demanding the officers' withdrawal and accusing the junta of plotting against him. On 15 July, on orders from junta leader Dimitrios Ioannidis, the National Guard attacked the presidential palace and installed Nikos Sampson. Turkey invaded on 20 July and came to hold 37 per cent of the island, which remains divided.
cite: Library of Congress Country Studies, 'Cyprus: The Greek Coup and the Turkish Invasion'; Wikipedia, '1974 Cypriot coup d'état'
inside: Greece's junta used the Greek officers it had posted inside Cyprus's National Guard to turn that army on the Cypriot president and overthrow him.

n: KGB 'home Russians' cultivated Finland's leaders, including Kekkonen
rank: President and party leaders
d: The Soviet KGB assigned its officers in Helsinki to individual Finnish politicians and officials, who each came to have a personal Soviet contact known as a 'kotiryssä', or 'home Russian'. Dozens of KGB officers worked under diplomatic cover at the Soviet embassy. Viktor Vladimirov, a KGB general posted there in 1955–60, 1970–71 and 1977–84, began the system and dealt with elite politicians, including President Urho Kekkonen. A former Soviet diplomat later said Vladimirov reported straight to the Soviet leadership and backed Ahti Karjalainen to succeed Kekkonen. The public learned of the system through a 1981 book. It is tied to 'Finlandization', the bending of Finnish policy to Moscow's wishes; Helsingin Sanomat reported in 2015 that the practice had almost ended.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Kotiryssä' (citing Helsingin Sanomat 2003, 2009, 2015; Koivisto memoirs); Barents Observer (5 Nov 2012)
inside: The Soviet KGB gave Finnish politicians and officials personal KGB contacts and worked on the country's leaders, linked to Finnish policy bending to Moscow's wishes.

n: TV figure 'Boki 13' bribed North Macedonia's special prosecutor
rank: Head of the Special Prosecution Office
d: Bojan Jovanovski, a television personality known as 'Boki 13', used his closeness to Katica Janeva, head of North Macedonia's Special Prosecution Office, to sell the country's richest man, Jordan Orce Kamčev, milder treatment in his criminal case. The Special Prosecution Office had been set up to pursue high-level crimes after a wiretapping scandal. Kamčev had been detained in November 2018 on extortion and money-laundering charges and was released in March 2019. In July 2019 Jovanovski and his security chief were arrested at the Greek border carrying €1.5 million. In June 2020 a court found he had bribed Janeva with €50,000 and jailed him for nine years; Janeva got seven years for misuse of office.
cite: OCCRP (22 Jun 2020); RFE/RL (2020)
inside: A TV personality bribed the head of the special prosecution office to sell a tycoon milder treatment in his criminal case, so a prosecutor's decisions served the payers.

n: Serbian intelligence officer gave instructions to a Macedonian MP
org_label: Serbian Security Information Agency (BIA) and Russian intelligence
rank: Member of parliament
d: Leaked files of Macedonia's own counter-intelligence service say a Serbian intelligence officer at Serbia's embassy in Skopje steered a pro-Russian Macedonian MP. The documents, prepared in 2017 for the service's director and published by OCCRP partners on 4 June 2017, say Goran Živaljević of Serbia's Security Information Agency (BIA) gave instructions to Ivan Stoilković, an MP who led the Democratic Party of Serbs in Macedonia, a partner in the ruling coalition, and that Stoilković was in contact with Russian diplomats. They also say three officers of Russia's foreign intelligence service (SVR) worked from the Russian embassy and tried to recruit current and former army and interior ministry staff. Stoilković declined to discuss the contacts; Serbia said Živaljević broke no rules.
cite: OCCRP / Spooks and Spin (4 Jun 2017)
inside: North Macedonia's counter-intelligence files say a Serbian intelligence officer gave instructions to a coalition MP, while Russian intelligence officers tried to recruit army and interior ministry staff.

n: Tycoon Savvidis paid Macedonian politicians to fight the name deal
rank: Politicians from several parties
d: Ivan Savvidis, a Russian-Greek billionaire and former member of Russia's parliament for the ruling United Russia party, paid at least €300,000 to opponents of the agreement that renamed Macedonia 'North Macedonia', a deal needed for it to join NATO. According to Macedonian interior ministry documents seen by OCCRP partner IRL, the money, some carried in cash across the Greek border, went to more than a dozen Macedonian politicians from several parties, to new nationalist groups and to football hooligans linked to the opposition VMRO-DPMNE party, ahead of protests in which a petrol bomb was thrown at parliament. Greece separately expelled two Russian diplomats for paying opponents of the deal. Savvidis did not answer reporters' questions; Moscow denied the claims and called Athens' expulsion of the diplomats unfounded.
cite: OCCRP (16 Jul 2018); Eurasia Review (18 Jul 2018)
inside: A Russian-Greek billionaire paid Macedonian politicians from several parties to oppose the name deal Macedonia needed to join NATO, according to interior ministry documents; he did not answer reporters' questions.

n: Mafia banker Michele Sindona became the Vatican's financial adviser
rank: Financial adviser to the Holy See
d: Michele Sindona, a Sicilian banker who laundered heroin money for Mafia families, was hired by the Holy See to manage its investments. After Italy ended the Vatican's tax exemption on Italian investment income in 1968, the Holy See took Sindona on as financial adviser, and his work with the Vatican Bank (the IOR) began in 1969; large sums moved from his banks through the Vatican to Swiss banks. He was also a member of the secret P2 Masonic lodge. When his Franklin National Bank in New York failed in 1974, the Vatican lost an estimated 35 billion lire. In 1986 an Italian court jailed Sindona for life for ordering the 1979 murder of Giorgio Ambrosoli, liquidator of his banks; he died of cyanide poisoning in prison days later.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Michele Sindona'; Wikipedia, 'Institute for the Works of Religion'
inside: A banker who laundered Mafia money was made the Holy See's financial adviser, giving him control of Vatican investments through which large sums moved from his banks.

n: Polish communist secret police had an informant in the Vatican
rank: Pope John Paul II's circle
d: Poland's communist Security Service (SB), the secret police, had an informant close to Pope John Paul II in Rome. In April 2005, weeks after the Pope's death, Poland's Institute of National Remembrance, the state body that holds communist-era police files, announced that about 700 pages showed Father Konrad Hejmo, a Dominican priest who ran pastoral care for Polish pilgrims at the Vatican, had been a secret collaborator under the code names 'Hejnal' and 'Dominik' during the 1980s. Hejmo's Dominican superior, who reviewed the files, called them convincing. It was not established how much secret information he passed on. The case was part of a wider picture of communist services trying to watch the Polish-born Pope.
cite: NBC News / Associated Press (Apr 2005); Mail & Guardian (28 Apr 2005)
inside: Poland's communist secret police had a priest working inside the Vatican's pastoral care for Polish pilgrims as its secret informer near the Pope.

n: Iranian agents worked alongside Bosnian Interior Ministry staff
rank: Interior Ministry and AID intelligence agency
d: Iran built a presence inside Bosnia's wartime security apparatus. On 15 February 1996 NATO-led troops raided a ski chalet at Fojnica that they called a terrorist training cell, arresting three Iranians and several Bosnians who worked for the Interior Ministry, and finding explosives, weapons and models of UN buildings. Western officials said the Bosnian intelligence agency AID, under former interior minister Bakir Alispahić, worked largely beyond government control and close to Iran, one of Bosnia's few wartime allies. The United States made ending Iran's military role a condition of a $400 million programme to train and equip the Bosnian army, and demanded that AID be shut down.
cite: Christian Science Monitor (12 Mar 1996)
inside: Iranian agents worked alongside Bosnian Interior Ministry staff, and the Bosnian intelligence agency operated close to Iran and largely beyond government control.

n: MG Baltic bribed Lithuania's Liberal leader and parties for votes
rank: Liberal Movement leader and Labour Party MP
d: MG Baltic, one of Lithuania's largest business groups, paid politicians and their parties to get decisions it wanted in parliament. On 12 May 2016 anti-corruption officers searched Eligijus Masiulis, leader of the Liberal Movement, and detained MG Baltic vice-president Raimondas Kurlianskis; prosecutors said Masiulis had taken a bribe from Kurlianskis, and €242,000 was found in his possession. A lower court acquitted everyone in 2022, but the Court of Appeal convicted them in 2023 and the Supreme Court made it final on 24 October 2024. Masiulis got five and a half years in prison, Labour MP Vytautas Gapšys four years and three months, and Kurlianskis five and a half years. The Liberal Movement, the Labour Party and MG Group were fined as organisations.
inside: A business group paid a party leader and other MPs to get the decisions it wanted in parliament, and courts convicted them of bribery.

n: Russia's GRU recruited a Lithuanian Air Force officer
rank: Air Force officer, Šiauliai airbase
d: Sergey Moiseyenko, an army surgeon at a military hospital in Šiauliai who worked for Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, recruited a Lithuanian Air Force officer in 2012. The officer, Sergej Pusin, served at Šiauliai airbase, which hosts NATO's Baltic air-policing mission, and was paid 500 to 1,000 euros at secret meetings in Moiseyenko's garage. Moiseyenko passed Russian intelligence copies of Lithuanian defence ministry documents and personal files of airbase officers, and sought details of NATO flights and training. He was detained in late 2014 and a Šiauliai court sentenced him to ten and a half years; appeals failed. Lithuania pardoned him in November 2019 as part of a spy swap with Russia.
cite: LRT (15 Nov 2019)
inside: Russia's military intelligence paid a Lithuanian Air Force officer at a NATO airbase to pass defence documents and officers' files.

n: FSB officer tried to recruit Lithuania's presidential guards
rank: VIP Protection Department
d: Nikolai Filipchenko, an officer of the Kaliningrad branch of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) who used a false identity, tried to recruit officers of Lithuania's VIP Protection Department, the unit that guards the president, in order to plant listening devices in the office and home of President Dalia Grybauskaitė. Lithuanian authorities said the operation aimed at infiltrating state institutions, law enforcement and intelligence services.
