inside: Prosecutors said a crime group's jailed bosses received privileged information from the city official in charge of fighting them; he admitted meeting its leaders while holding the post.
cite: El Espectador, High Court upholds sentence, May 2018; Infobae, 9 Mar 2022

n: Peace-court prosecutor took money to delay ex-FARC Santrich's extradition
rank: Support prosecutor, JEP peace tribunal
d: Prosecutors say emissaries of Jesús Santrich, a former FARC commander wanted by the United States, paid a prosecutor inside the JEP, the tribunal set up by the peace deal to judge the war. Carlos Julián Bermeo was filmed taking cash in a Bogotá hotel in 2019, in transactions said to reach US$40,000, and investigators said he agreed to delay Santrich's extradition by at least three months. In September 2022 a court convicted him of bribery at first instance and sentenced him to eight years, while acquitting him of conspiracy and influence peddling. Bermeo said he would appeal. A fugitive, he was recaptured in Bogotá on 15 March 2024 with US Marshals support. No appeal result was found.
inside: Prosecutors say people acting for a former guerrilla leader paid a prosecutor inside the peace tribunal to slow his extradition case; a court convicted the prosecutor of taking the bribe.
cite: Noticias RCN, 9 Sep 2022; Vanguardia, 15 Mar 2024; El Colombiano, Mar 2024

n: Buenaventura port smugglers allegedly had a prosecutors' team leader
org_label: Buenaventura port smuggling and drug networks
rank: CTI team coordinator, Attorney General's Office
d: Prosecutors allege that smuggling networks linking Colombia's main Pacific port, Buenaventura, with Cali and Bogotá had a man inside the CTI, the Attorney General's Office's investigative police. Francisco Javier Martínez, alias Pacho Malo, coordinated the CTI team in Buenaventura that handled drug and smuggling cases. Undercover CTI agents gathered material on him from 2020 to 2022. He was arrested in Medellín on 22 February 2024 for criminal conspiracy. The agents also said deputy attorney general Martha Mancera and another senior official favoured him. An inquiry into Mancera was closed in January 2024 for lack of evidence and reopened in May 2025. She denies the claims and says the agents are lying.
inside: Prosecutors allege smuggling networks had the very officer leading local drug and contraband inquiries; agents claim senior prosecutors shielded him, which remains unproven and is denied.
cite: Vanguardia, capture, 22 Feb 2024; El Tiempo, inquiry reopened, 24 May 2025
undone: No trial outcome has been reported. Martinez denied the charges when he was detained and was sent to prison pending the case; he is presumed innocent. The reopened inquiry into Martha Mancera has produced no charge that could be confirmed, and she denies the claims.

n: AUC commander Mancuso allegedly chose the rectors of the University of Córdoba
rank: Rector and governing board, state university
d: The AUC paramilitary army under Salvatore Mancuso allegedly took control of the University of Córdoba, a state university in Montería, by pressing its governing board over who became rector. Recordings raised in Congress by Gustavo Petro in 2004 reportedly show Mancuso pressing board members over the 2000 vote. On 18 February 2003 board members, unions and the acting rector met him at a camp in Santa Fe de Ralito; four who attended later voted for Claudio Sánchez Parra as rector. Victims' lawyers count over 277 abuses against the university community and say collective agreements were ended. In 2008 Mancuso confessed to murders of staff and students. Prosecutors sent Sánchez to trial in 2019; the sources cited give no verdict or defence.
inside: Prosecutors and victims allege a paramilitary commander pressed a state university's board to elect his preferred rector, so its leadership and labour policy served the armed group.
cite: Semana, 8 May 2004; El Heraldo, 15 Feb 2019

n: Ex-commander says AUC gained votes on the University of Sucre's board
who: AUC, Héroes de Montes de María bloc
rank: Governing board, state university
d: A former AUC paramilitary commander says his bloc copied what Salvatore Mancuso did at the University of Córdoba and got inside the University of Sucre, a public university in Sincelejo. Edwar Cobos, alias Diego Vecino, told a Justice and Peace prosecutor in May 2011 that between 2001 and 2005 the group had the votes of the students' and graduates' board representatives. He named Jáder Castilla and Yahir Acuña, then a city councillor and later a member of the Chamber of Representatives, said this helped elect Rafael Peralta as rector, and said the group proposed its vice-rector in exchange for those votes. The prosecutor said he would send copies for criminal inquiries. The report carries no response from Acuña and no verification.
inside: A former paramilitary commander claims his group won board votes at a public university to choose its rector and vice-rector; this has not been shown in court.
cite: El Heraldo, 9 May 2011

n: Convicted Magdalena governor Trino Luna told peace court of AUC control there
rank: Governor of Magdalena, 2004-2007
d: Trino Luna Correa, governor of Magdalena department from 2004 to 2007, was convicted in the 'parapolítica' scandal, the prosecutions of politicians allied to the AUC paramilitary army. In July 2022 Colombia's peace tribunal, the JEP, accepted him and he pledged to explain the AUC's influence over public administration, its control of elections in Magdalena and its funding by local businesses. He also made claims about national figures, including that the AUC financed the campaign of Mario Iguarán, Attorney General from 2005 to 2009, through commanders Macaco and Jorge 40. The JEP told him he must provide evidence for his statements. Those claims are unproven; the report carries no reply from those he named.
inside: A governor convicted over paramilitary ties has told a tribunal that the AUC influenced Magdalena's administration and elections; his wider claims about national officials remain unproven.
cite: Publimetro, on the JEP's decision of 12 Jul 2022, 14 Jul 2022

n: Mancuso told peace court the DAS gave his men targets at Córdoba's university
rank: DAS state intelligence collaborators
d: Salvatore Mancuso, a former AUC paramilitary commander, told Colombia's peace tribunal, the JEP, in Montería in May 2023 that staff of the DAS, the state intelligence agency, worked for his group. He said the DAS supplied information about professors' supposed guerrilla links at the University of Córdoba, on which the group decided to kill three named teachers and students. He also said the DAS ran illegal phone taps and moved his men in Córdoba and Norte de Santander, and that he had DAS collaborators from 1988 and 1989. He said the group had also infiltrated the student body through a student leader. The report gives Mancuso's account only, with no independent check or reply.
inside: A paramilitary commander testifies that state intelligence staff gave his group names and transport, so agency information chose whom his men killed; this is his account.
cite: El Universal (Cartagena), 17 May 2023

n: Paraguay's arms-control officers accused over guns for PCC and CV; Brazil acquitted four
who: Arms network supplying PCC and Comando Vermelho
rank: Directorate of War Material (DIMABEL)
d: Prosecutors in Brazil and Paraguay allege an arms-trafficking network had officers at DIMABEL, the Paraguayan military agency that controls and registers weapons, to supply Brazilian buyers, chiefly the PCC and Comando Vermelho gangs. In November 2025 Brazilian prosecutors reported that a federal court had sentenced four officers (a general, a colonel, a captain and a lieutenant) to terms of up to 7 years 6 months. Paraguayan press reported in April 2026 that all four were acquitted, with a Brazilian regional federal court clearing General Jorge Orué Roa and Colonel Bienvenido Fretes, and Brazil dropped their extradition. Paraguayan prosecutors allege those two and General Arturo González Ocampos took gifts or payments linked to the importer International Auto Supply. A judge ordered trial in May 2025; no verdict was found.
inside: Prosecutors allege officers in the agency licensing weapons imports helped, for gifts or payments, a network whose guns were meant for Brazilian gangs; a Brazilian court acquitted four of them.
cite: Ministério Público Federal (Brazil), 6 Nov 2025; ABC Color, 7 Dec 2024, 9 May 2025 and 21 Apr 2026; Última Hora, 21 Apr 2026

n: Clan Rotela allegedly bribed guards and set shifts at Paraguay's Tacumbú
rank: Guards and managers, Tacumbú prison
d: The Clan Rotela, a Paraguayan crime group led by Armando Rotela, allegedly took over the running of Tacumbú, the country's main prison, by bribing and threatening its staff. Former Justice Minister Ángel Barchini testified that guards protected the clan under threats and bribery. A guard said staff lost control in 2021 and clan members decided shift changes. Prison director Luis Esquivel says his security chief pressed him to open the gates during a revolt on 10 October 2023, when he was seized and stabbed. About 2,500 police and soldiers retook the jail on 18 December 2023, and over 300 phones were seized. Prosecutors indicted Rotela and eight others in December 2024; in May 2025 a judge sent the case to trial.
inside: Prosecutors and witnesses say a crime group bribed and threatened prison staff until it set guards' shifts, so the staff protected the gang they were guarding.
cite: ABC Color, on the indictment, 22 Dec 2024; Última Hora, 27 Jun 2025

n: Trafficker 'Tavi' Celis funded Paraná's mayor, then got a municipal unit
rank: Mayor, councillor and security official, Paraná
d: A drug-selling group led by Daniel 'Tavi' Celis got inside the city government of Paraná, capital of Argentina's Entre Ríos province, by financing the 2015 campaign of Sergio Varisco, who won knowing where the money came from, a court found. Once elected, Varisco, councillor Pablo Hernández and security official Griselda Bordeira let the clan keep trafficking and gave it unrestricted control of Municipal Unit No. 2. On 30 December 2019 a federal court convicted 26 people, sentencing Varisco to six and a half years and Celis to 13. Varisco said he was 'absolutely innocent' and appealed; Celis, in his last words to the court, accused Varisco of breaking a political pact but did not link him to trafficking. Six other defendants were acquitted.
inside: A drug group paid for a mayor's campaign; judges found that in office he and his officials let it keep trading and gave it a municipal unit.
cite: La Capital, 31 Dec 2019; El Litoral, 22 Dec 2020, for the cassation chamber rejecting every defence appeal; Crónica, 31 December 2019 (https://www.cronica.com.ar/amp/policiales/El-ex-intendente-de-Parana-condenado-por-narcotrafico-rompio-el-silencio-20191231-0017.html), for Varisco's denial and Celis's last words
undone: The Federal Criminal Cassation Chamber rejected every defence appeal on 22 December 2020 and confirmed the verdicts.

n: Montonero guerrilla served as a conscript inside Formosa's army regiment
rank: Conscript, Regimiento de Infantería de Monte 29
d: The Montoneros, an Argentine guerrilla movement, had one of their own inside an army regiment before attacking it. According to Infobae's account, drawing on Ceferino Reato's book, Luis Roberto Mayol was a Montonero who had served as a conscript at Regiment 29 in Formosa. On 5 October 1975 about 50 Montoneros tried to seize 200 weapons there, planning to bring in attackers on a hijacked airliner. They expected little resistance, but conscripts fought back. Infobae counts 32 dead, including 10 conscripts; El Litoral counts 28. The sources do not set out exactly what Mayol passed on.
inside: A guerrilla movement had a member serving as a conscript in the regiment it raided for weapons; published accounts call him its infiltrator, without detailing his role.
cite: Infobae, 27 Nov 2018; El Litoral, on Operación Primicia; Wikipedia, Operation Primicia

n: Tupamaros recruited a sailor who opened Uruguay's naval training centre
rank: Second-class sailor, Centro de Instrucción de la Marina
d: The Tupamaros, Uruguay's urban guerrilla movement, had a sailor working for them inside the navy's training centre in Montevideo. According to an account in the Cuban journal Pensamiento Crítico, second-class sailor Fernando Gorin (also spelled Garin), on guard duty that night, gave the signal in late May 1970, disarmed the roof sentry and helped subdue the duty petty officer. Militants identifying themselves as police were let in. They locked up the personnel and left with over 300 long arms. Uruguayan police files, held in the Sitios de Memoria archive, list about 300 rifles, 170 revolvers and 30 pistols taken, and date the raid 27 May; the journal says 29 May. Gorin went underground. Fernán Pucurull, a Tupamaro named as a raider, was killed days later.
inside: A guerrilla movement recruited a serving sailor, who used his guard post to open a naval base to its fighters, so the navy's own weapons went to the movement.
cite: Pensamiento Crítico no. 43, Havana, Aug 1970; Sitios de Memoria Uruguay, file on Fernán Pucurull

n: US says Venezuelan diplomat Ghazi Nasr al Din used his post to fund Hizballah
rank: Chargé d'affaires in Damascus; embassy post in Lebanon
d: The US Treasury said in June 2008 that Hizballah, the Lebanese armed movement, had a supporter inside Venezuela's diplomatic service. Ghazi Nasr al Din had been chargé d'affaires at Venezuela's embassy in Damascus, then director of political aspects at its embassy in Lebanon. Treasury said he used his position as a diplomat, and as president of a Shi'a Islamic centre in Caracas, to support Hizballah financially. It said he advised donors on fundraising, gave them bank details so deposits went directly to Hizballah, and arranged members' travel, including a January 2006 trip to Caracas. He was designated under US terrorism sanctions, with Fawzi Kan'an and two travel agencies. This is a US finding, not a court verdict.
inside: The US Treasury says an armed movement's supporter sat in Venezuela's diplomatic service and used that post to raise money for it and arrange its members' travel.
cite: US Treasury press release hp-1036, 18 Jun 2008

n: Communist and MIR ties to Venezuelan officers behind the 1962 Carúpano rising
rank: Marine battalion and National Guard officers
d: Venezuela's Communist Party (PCV) and the Revolutionary Left Movement (MIR) had links with serving officers who rose against President Rómulo Betancourt in Carúpano on 4 May 1962. Captain Jesús Molina Villegas, Major Pedro Vegas Castejón and Lieutenant Héctor Fleming Mendoza led a marine battalion and a National Guard detachment. Accounts name PCV and MIR figures involved, including Congressman Eloy Torres and Douglas Bravo. Loyal forces retook the town within a day; one count gives 56 dead and over 400 arrested. Betancourt suspended the activities of both parties by decree, and a second rising followed at Puerto Cabello a month later.
inside: Two left-wing parties had ties with serving officers, who then turned their units against the government, according to accounts of the rising.
cite: El Ciudadano, on the Carupanazo; Wikipedia, El Carupanazo

n: Illegal gold miners allegedly got tip-offs from Peruvian police: 96 officers in 37 cases
rank: Peruvian National Police, sub-officers to colonel
d: Police officers in Peru have been accused of working for illegal gold-mining networks, according to an Ojo Público report on cases reviewed by the Police Disciplinary Tribunal. From 2019 to 2024 at least 37 cases implicated 96 officers, 36 of them in La Libertad, home of the Pataz mining area, where 13 mine workers were killed. Officers were accused of leaking operations to miners, stealing gold and altering custody of seized ore. They included a colonel and two commanders. Cases rose from 2 in 2019 to 16 in 2024, but only six ended with sanctions fully upheld, and eight ended in acquittal. Illegal miners also use a government registry, Reinfo, to avoid controls.
inside: Disciplinary cases accuse police officers of leaking operations to illegal miners and tampering with seized ore, so that officers sent to stop the mining served it instead.
cite: Ojo Público via Actualidad Ambiental, 28 May 2025; La República, 15 Sep 2026

n: Peru's police chief accused of selling protection to gold miners
who: Informal gold miners and a mining firm
rank: Head of Arequipa police region; later national commander
d: Witnesses allege that informal gold miners in Arequipa had Víctor Zanabria on their side when he led the region's police; he later became commander general of Peru's National Police. The Sunday programme Panorama, reported by RPP in May 2025, cited an anonymous officer and a protected collaborator. They claim he belonged to a group selling police protection in mining disputes, tipped off armed miners before operations, and took payment in cash and gold, and that officers listed at Arequipa posts really worked at a mine for 250 soles a day. Zanabria replied that the Public Ministry archived the case because the collaborator gave a date when he was in Jordan. The claims come from unnamed sources and were not independently verified.
inside: Unnamed witnesses claim gold miners paid a regional police chief for protection and warnings; he says prosecutors closed the case, and nothing is proven.
cite: RPP, citing Panorama, 12 May 2025

n: Bolivia probed whether police warned trafficker Marset before he fled in 2023
rank: Anti-narcotics force (FELCN) and Santa Cruz police
d: Bolivia's government investigated in 2023 whether the Uruguayan cocaine trafficker Sebastián Marset had help inside its police. Marset left Santa Cruz on 29 July 2023. Four days later he sent a video thanking Ismael Tito Villca, director of the FELCN, the anti-narcotics force, for alerting him to leave in time. Government Minister Eduardo del Castillo said he could not rule out police help and that prosecutors and even judges might have favoured Marset. Villca and two other senior officers testified as witnesses, and the police high command publicly backed Villca. Marset's video is a trafficker's own claim; the report cited shows no finding against any officer.
inside: A minister said a trafficker may have had help inside police and courts, after he thanked the anti-drug chief for a warning; this is unproven, and police backed the chief.
cite: Montevideo Portal, 29 Aug 2023

n: Airbus money reached SriLankan Airlines' chief via his wife's shell firm
rank: Chief executive of state-run SriLankan Airlines
d: Airbus, the European planemaker, used a shell company to pay the head of state-run SriLankan Airlines during the 2013 sale of 10 aircraft. The UK Serious Fraud Office's 2020 settlement with Airbus described a US$2 million bribery arrangement through a Brunei firm in the name of chief executive Kapila Chandrasena's wife. Sri Lanka's bribery commission alleges the money went further. Chandrasena reportedly said Rs 60 million reached former president Mahinda Rajapaksa, then retracted this, alleging intimidation; he was found dead in May 2026. Prosecutors allege Rs 100 million reached his son Namal, who denies it and was in remand from September 2026. The order for four A350s was terminated at a reported US$116 million.
inside: Airbus paid the chief of the state airline buying its planes; Sri Lankan investigators allege the money also reached the president's family, which Namal Rajapaksa denies.
cite: News 1st, 12 May 2026; Daily FT, 9 May and 30 Sep 2026, and 6 Oct 2016; EconomyNext, 4 Sep 2026; The Sunday Times (Sri Lanka), 13 Sep 2026; Daily FT, 20 Mar 2026

n: SNC-Lavalin accused of bribing for Padma Bridge job; executives acquitted
rank: Communications minister and Bridges Division officials (alleged)
d: The World Bank accused SNC-Lavalin, a Canadian engineering firm, of conspiring to bribe Bangladesh's communications minister Syed Abul Hossain and other officials to win the consultancy job on the Padma Bridge. In June 2012 the bank cancelled its US$1.2 billion credit, citing a corruption conspiracy. None of this was proven. Bangladesh's Anti-Corruption Commission cleared all the accused in September 2014. In Canada, a judge excluded the wiretap evidence, prosecutors called no evidence, and in February 2017 three former SNC-Lavalin executives were acquitted. The bank also barred the firm from its projects for 10 years. Bangladesh finished the bridge with its own money in 2022.
inside: The World Bank alleged a Canadian firm tried to buy a minister and officials to win a state bridge contract, but Bangladeshi and Canadian proceedings cleared the accused.
cite: The Daily Star (Bangladesh), Feb 2017; Wikipedia, Padma Bridge graft scandal (World Bank statements, 2012)

n: Medical colleges allegedly paid India's health ministry staff and inspectors
org_label: Private medical college owners and middlemen
rank: Health Ministry officials, National Medical Commission inspectors and board member
d: Owners of private medical colleges allegedly paid officials inside India's Health Ministry and the National Medical Commission (NMC), the body that decides which colleges may teach doctors. In July 2025 the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) named 34 people, among them eight ministry officials, a National Health Authority official, five NMC inspection doctors and board member Jeetu Lal Meena. The CBI alleges ministry staff photographed confidential files and sold inspection dates and inspectors' names. Colleges could then prepare ghost teachers, fake patients and tampered fingerprint attendance. Three inspectors allegedly took Rs 55 lakh for a favourable report on one institute. Eight people were arrested, and none of the allegations has yet been proven in court.
inside: The CBI alleges private college owners paid ministry staff and inspectors for leaked inspection files and favourable reports, so the regulator of doctor training served those it regulates.
cite: PTI via The Week, 4 Jul 2025; Medical Dialogues, 7 Jul 2025

n: Rolls-Royce accused of paying Indian officials over Hawk jet deal
rank: Unnamed Defence Ministry, HAL and tax officials (alleged)
d: Rolls-Royce, the British engine maker, is accused of paying intermediaries whose money reached Indian public servants during India's purchase of Hawk trainer jets. In May 2023 the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) booked the company, its then India director Tim Jones and arms dealer Sudhir Choudhrie, along with unidentified officials of the Defence Ministry and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL). Its case says tax officials were paid to block inquiries, and that about GBP 1.85 million went to an intermediary to retrieve a seized list of agents, which could have ended the contract. A 2017 UK court judgment found Rolls-Royce concealed its Indian intermediaries from 2005 to 2009. The Indian allegations have not been tested in court.
inside: The CBI alleges Rolls-Royce's money reached defence and tax officials through intermediaries, so that purchases and tax inquiries inside the Indian state served the company.
cite: ThePrint, 29 May 2023 (citing the CBI FIR and Southwark Crown Court judgment of 17 Jan 2017)
undone: No charge sheet, trial or verdict has been reported since the CBI registered its case in May 2023, and those named are presumed innocent.

n: Kashmir police officer Davinder Singh caught driving Hizbul militants
rank: Deputy Superintendent of Police, Jammu and Kashmir
d: Davinder Singh, a Deputy Superintendent of Police in Jammu and Kashmir, is accused of working for Hizbul Mujahideen, an armed group fighting Indian rule in Kashmir. On 11 January 2020 police stopped a car on the Srinagar-Jammu road and found him with two Hizbul militants; weapons and explosives were recovered. The National Investigation Agency's July 2020 charge sheet alleges he sheltered a commander in Jammu, moved militants in his own vehicle and helped obtain arms from across the border. It also alleges Pakistani High Commission officials in New Delhi were grooming him for sensitive information. The Lieutenant Governor dismissed him in May 2021. The reports cited give no trial verdict.
inside: Prosecutors say an armed group and Pakistani officials had a serving police officer on their side, using his rank and vehicle to protect and move militants.
cite: The Quint, 6 Jul 2020 and 21 May 2021; The Wire, 6 Jul 2020
undone: No verdict has been reached and Singh is presumed innocent. He faces trial on national security charges before the Special NIA Court in Jammu and is held in Kot Bhalwal Jail. Republic reported on 25 July 2026 that the court refused his plea for 20 days' interim bail but granted him custody parole so that he could attend a religious ceremony in Srinagar from 27 to 30 July 2026, returning to the jail by the evening of 31 July, and that his regular bail appeal was pending before the High Court.

n: About 80 Kashmir state staff dismissed as alleged militant collaborators
rank: Police, prisons, schools, hospitals, J&K Bank and other state bodies
d: Jammu and Kashmir's authorities say groups such as Hizbul Mujahideen and Lashkar-e-Taiba have supporters on the state payroll; about 80 employees were dismissed in the five years to October 2025, among them two sons of Hizbul's leader said to have handled its funding, constables, teachers, a prisons deputy superintendent and a J&K Bank chief manager. A task force set up in April 2021 selects cases. Article 311 lets the government dismiss staff without an inquiry on security grounds, so the allegations are not tested first. The Kashmir Times counted 79 dismissals by March 2025, 20 to 25 of them challenged in court and none reversed. On 30 May 2026 the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh held that such decisions get only limited judicial review. Mehbooba Mufti and trade unions call the dismissals arbitrary.
inside: Officials allege armed groups kept people in state jobs who passed information and handled funds for them; the dismissals came without inquiry, so most claims remain unproven.
cite: Scroll, Jul 2021; Kashmir Life, 6 Nov 2023 and 31 May 2026; Kashmir Times investigation (dismissals under Article 311(2)(c)); ETV Bharat, 30 Oct 2025
undone: The allegations behind these dismissals have not been tested at a trial. Dismissal under Article 311(2)(c) is an administrative act taken without an inquiry; most court challenges were still pending when last reported, no one dismissed has been reinstated, and on 30 May 2026 a division bench restored a constable's 2007 dismissal, holding that the government's satisfaction is open to only limited judicial review.

n: Serving Pakistani navy officers helped militants try to seize a frigate
rank: Pakistan Navy officers at Karachi Naval Dockyard
d: Serving Pakistan Navy officers worked with militants to try to seize the frigate PNS Zulfiqar at Karachi Naval Dockyard on 6 September 2014. The attackers came aboard in uniform showing service cards. Al-Qaeda's South Asian branch claimed the attack and said it meant to turn the ship's missiles on American and Indian naval vessels, though the Pakistani Taliban also claimed it. A closed navy tribunal sentenced five officers to death in 2016 for terrorist links, mutiny, conspiracy and bringing weapons into the dockyard. One officer's father said the charge named Islamic State links. The navy has refused to release its inquiry report. In December 2024 the Islamabad High Court lifted a stay on the executions.
inside: A militant group had serving navy officers on its side, and a navy tribunal found they conspired and brought weapons into the dockyard to seize a warship.
cite: Nukta, Dec 2024; Asia Times, Jun 2016; The Express Tribune, May 2016

n: Energy firm staff charged over papers taken from India's oil ministry
rank: Petroleum ministry files, via paid suppliers and government staff
d: Executives of Indian energy companies are accused of paying for confidential papers taken from the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, which sets rules and awards for their industry. In February 2015 Delhi Police arrested staff of Reliance Industries, Reliance ADAG, Essar, Cairn India and Jubilant Energy. The April 2015 charge sheet named 13 people, including two men described as government employees and a casual defence ministry worker. Police said two brothers, arrested outside Shastri Bhavan, the building housing the ministry, were paid Rs 2.5 lakh a month for documents. Charges were theft, trespass, forgery and conspiracy; the Official Secrets Act was not then used. The reports cited give no trial outcome or company statements.
inside: Police allege energy firms' staff paid for confidential papers from the ministry that governs them, with government workers among those charged in the scheme.
cite: Free Press Journal; The Quint; The News Minute, 18 Apr 2015; Business Standard/IANS, 20 Apr 2015; Millennium Post, 20 Apr 2015

n: Gold smugglers allegedly reached Kerala chief minister's top civil servant
org_label: Gold smuggling network using UAE consulate baggage
rank: Principal secretary to Kerala's chief minister
d: A gold smuggling network allegedly had help from M. Sivasankar, principal secretary to Kerala's chief minister. In July 2020 customs officers found about 30 kg of gold in diplomatic baggage addressed to the UAE consulate, which is normally cleared without inspection. They arrested P.S. Sarith, a former consulate employee, who named Swapna Suresh, another former employee. Investigators alleged Sivasankar pressed customs to clear baggage without checks and took commission on a state housing scheme. He was arrested in October 2020, spent 98 days in jail, and had his suspension revoked in January 2022. In April 2023 the Kerala High Court refused him bail in the housing case; in January 2024 the Supreme Court granted medical bail without ruling on the merits. No verdict was found.
inside: Investigators allege smugglers got the chief minister's senior aide to press customs to pass their consignments; the reports cited show no court finding on that allegation.
cite: ThePrint, Dec 2020; The News Minute, 5 Jan 2022; Onmanorama, 13 Apr 2023; DT Next, 19 Jan 2024

n: Police tipped off gangster Vikas Dubey before he ambushed eight officers
rank: Chaubeypur police station and senior Kanpur police
d: Gangster Vikas Dubey had police in Uttar Pradesh's Kanpur district passing him information, a state inquiry found. Shortly after midnight on 3 July 2020, eight policemen who went to arrest him in Bikru village were ambushed with gunfire from rooftops. Dubey was killed by police on 10 July. A three-member Special Investigation Team then reported a nexus between police, administration officials and Dubey. Its 3,500-page report said officers gave him tip-offs, that his phone records showed policemen in regular contact over the previous year, and that police failed to secure convictions in his pending cases. It recommended action against 80 police personnel and left the decision to the government.
inside: A crime boss had police officers in contact and on side, and the state inquiry found their tip-offs and inaction protected him instead of enforcing the law.
cite: The Week, 5 Nov 2020

n: Staffer at India's Moscow embassy accused of passing secrets to ISI
rank: Security assistant, Indian embassy in Moscow
d: Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), its main spy agency, allegedly paid a Ministry of External Affairs employee posted at India's embassy in Moscow for confidential information. The Uttar Pradesh Anti-Terrorist Squad arrested Satendra Siwal, 26, on 3 February 2024 after summoning him to its Meerut unit while he was home on leave. He joined the service in 2018 and went to Moscow in 2021; ThePrint describes him as multi-tasking staff, and a ministry source as a security assistant. The squad says he had passed strategically sensitive information to ISI operatives since 2021. The report gives no amount for the payments. The report cited does not cover any trial.
inside: Police say Pakistan's spy agency paid a foreign ministry employee inside an Indian embassy, so information the ministry was meant to protect went to Pakistan.
cite: ThePrint, Feb 2024
undone: No charge sheet, trial or verdict has been reported since the arrest in February 2024, and Siwal is presumed innocent.

n: HAL fighter-jet plant supervisor arrested as alleged ISI source
rank: Assistant supervisor, HAL Aircraft Division
d: Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), its main spy agency, allegedly obtained information from inside Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), the state-owned firm that builds India's military aircraft. In October 2020 the Maharashtra Anti-Terrorism Squad arrested Deepak Shirsath, 41, an assistant supervisor who had worked for 15 years at HAL's Aircraft Division near Nashik. Police say he sent details of Indian fighter aircraft, the factory at Ozar, the nearby airbase and restricted areas over WhatsApp and social media. An officer said he confessed; that claim comes from police. A case was registered under the Official Secrets Act, and phones and memory cards went for forensic testing. The report cited does not give a verdict.
inside: Police allege Pakistan's spy agency recruited a long-serving supervisor inside India's state military aircraft maker to pass it details of fighters and the plant.
cite: Scroll, 9 Oct 2020

n: Two Indian ordnance factory staff accused of leaking output data to ISI
rank: Junior works manager and chargeman at ordnance factories
d: Pakistani agents allegedly recruited staff inside two Indian ordnance factories, the plants that make ammunition and weapons for the armed forces. In March 2025 the Uttar Pradesh Anti-Terrorism Squad arrested Ravindra Kumar, a chargeman at Hazratpur in Firozabad, and Kumar Vikas, a junior works manager at Kanpur. Both allegedly dealt with a social media contact called 'Neha Sharma', which police believe was a false identity. Police say they passed production reports, stores records, requisitions, machine layouts and staff attendance sheets, for money. Kumar Vikas was booked under the Official Secrets Act. The squad says Pakistani handlers use such identities to approach central government staff. The reports cited do not cover any trial.
inside: Police allege Pakistani intelligence used a fake online identity and money to recruit staff at two arms factories, who then sent it production data.
cite: The Week, 15 Mar 2025; India TV, 19 Mar 2025

n: Engineer with Mumbai naval dockyard access accused of spying for Pakistan
rank: Contractor's engineer with access to Mumbai naval dockyard
d: A Pakistani intelligence operative allegedly recruited an engineer whose job, the police say, gave him access to warships at the naval dockyard in south Mumbai. The Maharashtra Anti-Terrorism Squad arrested Ravindra Verma, 27, of Thane on 28 May 2025. He worked as a junior service engineer for a defence technology firm and went aboard naval ships and submarines. The squad alleges an agent posing as a woman on Facebook drew him in, and that he sent sketches, diagrams and audio notes about warships and submarines in return for money from accounts in India and abroad. Verma pleaded innocence in a bail application, saying the allegations must be proven at trial.
inside: Police allege a Pakistani operative recruited a contractor's engineer with access to the navy's dockyard to pass it details of ships and submarines; he pleads innocence.
cite: PTI via The Week, 25 Jun 2025

n: Coast Guard boat welder allegedly paid Rs 200 a day by Pakistani handler
org_label: Pakistani handler using the name Sahima
rank: Welder working on Coast Guard boats at Okha jetty
d: A Pakistani handler allegedly recruited a welder who worked on Indian Coast Guard boats at Okha jetty in Gujarat. The Gujarat Anti-Terrorist Squad announced the arrest of Deepesh Gohel, 33, on 29 November 2024. Police say a Facebook contact called Sahima, who claimed to work for the Pakistan Navy, approached him about seven months earlier. He allegedly sent the names and movements of ships stationed at Okha for Rs 200 a day, with about Rs 42,000 moving through his associates' accounts. Gujarat police reported a similar arrest in Porbandar a month before. He was booked for criminal conspiracy against the state. The reports cited do not cover any trial.
inside: Police allege a Pakistani handler paid a worker with access to Coast Guard boats to report which ships were at the base and how they moved.
cite: Free Press Journal/ANI, 30 Nov 2024; News Arena India; Patrika, May 2025

n: Cochin Shipyard subcontract workers accused of leaking navy ship data
rank: Insulation workers at Udupi Cochin Shipyard
d: Pakistani handlers allegedly recruited subcontract workers at Udupi Cochin Shipyard, part of the Indian shipbuilder Cochin Shipyard, to send them details of naval ships. The chief executive of Cochin Shipyard reported a security breach at Malpe police station in Karnataka in November 2025. Police then arrested Rohit and Santri, insulation workers employed by the subcontractor Shushma Marine. They allege Rohit sent ship identification numbers, repair schedules and details of sensitive infrastructure, continuing after a transfer with Santri's help. A third man was later held for allegedly supplying SIM cards and one-time passwords for the WhatsApp accounts. All three face Official Secrets Act charges, and none has been proven in court. Police reported a further arrest in February 2026.
inside: Police allege Pakistani handlers recruited a subcontractor's staff working inside a state shipyard, who passed them details of naval vessels under repair there.
cite: Scroll, Dec 2025; ETV Bharat, Feb 2026

n: Rajasthan official, a former minister's ex-aide, accused of working with ISI agents
rank: Assistant administrative officer, district employment office
d: Police in Rajasthan allege that Shakur Khan, an assistant administrative officer at the employment office in Jaisalmer, a district on the Pakistani border, passed sensitive information to Pakistan's Inter-Service Intelligence (ISI). Police arrested him in June 2025 after detaining him on 28 May. They say he kept in contact with staff at Pakistan's High Commission in New Delhi, including one expelled by India that May, visited Pakistan without reporting it, met ISI agents and sent information over WhatsApp. He had been personal assistant to former minister Saleh Mohammed; Congress said that link does not implicate the minister. The arrest came amid a wider wave of at least 16 spying arrests.
inside: Police allege a Rajasthan government employee in a border district dealt with Pakistan's spy agency and its embassy staff and sent them sensitive information.
cite: Scroll, 4 Jun 2025

n: Embraer paid $800,000 to win a jet sale to Mozambique's state airline
rank: Transport Minister; state airline LAM
d: Brazilian aircraft maker Embraer paid $800,000 in bribes to secure the sale of two aircraft to LAM, Mozambique's state airline, in 2009. The money was booked as "sales commissions" and paid in two $400,000 instalments to Xihivele, a shell company set up by the go-between Mateus Zimba, through an account in Portugal. In September 2021 Maputo City Court sentenced the former transport minister, Paulo Zucula, and Zimba to ten years each, and ordered them to pay Mozambique 70.7 million meticais. Both defence teams planned to appeal. LAM's former chairman, Jose Viegas, was acquitted for insufficient evidence and an expired time limit; the attorney general said it would appeal. Embraer admitted paying bribes in several countries and paid about $225 million in US and Brazilian fines.
inside: A foreign aircraft maker sent bribes through a shell company while Mozambique's state airline bought its planes, and a court jailed the transport minister and the go-between.
cite: MarketScreener/AIM, 14 Sept 2021; ch-aviation, Sept 2021

n: Chinese timber traders claimed Mozambique's agriculture ministers helped them
rank: Minister of Agriculture (current and former)
d: Chinese timber traders told undercover investigators that they benefited from help by Mozambique's agriculture ministers, whose ministry oversees the forests, according to a February 2013 report by the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA), a campaign group. EIA linked the trader Mofid to minister Jose Pacheco and the trader Senlian to his predecessor Thomas Mandlate. A trader, Liu Chaoying, said Pacheco was "like brothers" with him and came to him for money. Both ministers denied involvement. EIA put 2012 lost revenue at almost $30 million. Prosecutors opened an investigation. EIA's 2014 follow-up said the anti-corruption office, apparently prompted by donors, found no evidence that Mozambicans held shares in either firm, and called officials' role in illegal exports beyond its scope. Mofid's licence was suspended for a year.
inside: EIA alleges Chinese log exporters had the ministers who oversee Mozambique's forests on their side, so smuggled timber left the country untaxed; both ministers denied it.
cite: EIA, 3 May 2013; EIA, First Class Crisis, July 2014; Wood Floor Business, 2013

n: Mofid accused of paying Mozambique customs and forest agents at Pemba
rank: Customs and forest checkpoint agents
d: Mofid, a Chinese-linked timber company in northern Mozambique, was accused of paying state agents to get its timber through. In January 2017, days after a ban on raw log exports took effect, the reporting outlet Oxpeckers described about 30 containers from Mofid and its associate Peng Pai being loaded at Pemba harbour. Drivers said the cargo had no export permits and alleged that customs agents were paid to offload it. An unnamed employee alleged that Mofid's general manager, Vicky Lau, paid cash to agriculture and environment agents at checkpoints for seized illegal timber. The provincial agriculture department had cancelled Mofid's licence, but the report alleged it kept operating through other companies. Lau and Mofid did not answer questions. The report mentions no charges.
inside: Drivers and an employee allege a timber firm paid customs and forest agents, so the officers meant to stop illegal logs let them through or sold them on.
cite: Oxpeckers (Estacio Valoi), 10 Jan 2017

n: Chinese timber firms allegedly bribe officials along Mozambique's export route
rank: Officials on the timber route; ruling Frelimo party
d: Chinese timber businesses pay Mozambican officials to move wood to port, according to a May 2024 report by the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA), a campaign group. A former official, quoted anonymously, described sharing in the bribes. EIA says inspections of protected rosewood rarely happen because of corruption, and that the ruling Frelimo party gains campaign funds from Chinese investment, making it reluctant to crack down. China takes more than 90% of Mozambique's wood despite a log export ban in place since 2017. EIA also estimates that about 30% of timber from Cabo Delgado province comes from insurgent-held forests, a claim analysts dispute. China's embassy in Washington and the environment minister did not answer VOA. An attorney general's report to parliament links forest crime to corruption.
inside: EIA alleges Chinese timber firms pay Mozambican officials, so those officials move banned wood to port and inspections of protected rosewood rarely happen.
cite: VOA, 17 May 2024, citing EIA
undone: Nothing here has been tested. No prosecution of a Chinese timber firm or a Mozambican official has been reported from the EIA report, the companies and officials are unnamed, and the firms and the governing party are presumed innocent. A search in Portuguese found no court case arising from it.

n: Mukula rosewood traffickers allegedly reached Zambia's president and ministers
rank: President's circle, ministers, state forestry firm ZAFFICO
d: Timber traffickers supplying China allegedly used Zambia's state forestry company, ZAFFICO, as cover and shared profits with people around President Edgar Lungu, according to the Environmental Investigation Agency's 2019 report "The Mukula Cartel". Mukula is a protected rosewood. EIA named Lungu's daughter Tasila, Lands Minister Jean Kapata and Justice Minister Given Lubinda. It estimated over 50 containers a month left illegally from June 2017 to May 2019, with about $7.5 million a year in bribes and informal fees, and said a Chinese trader gave $40,000 worth of campaign outfits. President Lungu dismissed the report as fake news and the ruling Patriotic Front's media director called it treasonous. Tasila Lungu, Lubinda and Kapata sued EIA in 2021; Lungu later withdrew. Transparency International Zambia says most prosecutions are still ongoing.
inside: EIA alleges timber traffickers paid their way to Zambia's ministers and a state company, which then covered their log exports; the officials named deny it.
cite: Daily Monitor/AFP, Dec 2019; Lusaka Times repost of EIA, The Mukula Cartel, 2019; Transparency International Zambia; News Diggers, 'Dismissing Mukula report as fake news disheartening - EIA', 19 Dec 2019; Open Zambia, 'EIA defends Mukula cartel expose coverage', 20 Jan 2020

n: Hong Kong businessman Sam Pa allegedly funded Zimbabwe's spy agency
rank: Central Intelligence Organisation
d: Hong Kong-based businessman Sam Pa, a member of the Queensway Syndicate, gave Zimbabwe's Central Intelligence Organisation (CIO), the state spy agency, money and equipment in return for access to diamonds, cotton and property, according to CIO sources quoted in a June 2012 Global Witness report. One CIO document put the support at $100 million and 200 pick-up trucks. Global Witness, a campaign group, said CIO members jointly controlled a company with Pa, Sino Zimbabwe Development, and called the money apparent off-budget financing, meaning it sat outside the state budget. On 14 April 2014 the US Treasury sanctioned Pa and the company, citing their role in undermining democracy and facilitating corruption. The Global Witness summary records no reply from Pa, the company or the CIO.
inside: Global Witness alleges a foreign businessman paid Zimbabwe's spy agency and went into business with its members, winning access to diamonds and other sectors.
cite: Global Witness, 11 June 2012, with April 2014 update on US Treasury sanctions

n: Malawi police food contractor paid K145m into an account the president signed
rank: Police finance director; ruling party account
d: Businessman Zameer Karim's company Pioneer Investments won a 2015 contract to give Malawi's police 500,000 ration packs, and a leaked Anti-Corruption Bureau report alleged it then paid MK145 million into a ruling party account. President Peter Mutharika was its sole signatory. The report, leaked in June 2018, alleged Karim sought a 20% price rise, and that loans of about MK3.8 billion were taken with police as guarantor using a forged signature. Karim also claimed K466 million extra. Karim and police finance director Innocent Bottoman were charged and pleaded not guilty; Bottoman died in July 2021. Mutharika called the money an honest donation. The party refunded it and later apologised when a civil appeal was withdrawn. In October 2021 the High Court ordered the trial resumed; no verdict was found.
inside: The Anti-Corruption Bureau alleges a contractor got an inflated police food deal with a police finance chief's help, then paid money into the president's party account.
cite: amaBhungane/Daily Maverick, 1 Apr 2019; The Nation (Malawi); The Nation (Malawi), 21 Oct 2021

n: Malawi minister accused of favouring maize trader Transglobe, then acquitted
rank: Minister of Agriculture
d: A presidential inquiry found that Malawi's agriculture minister, George Chaponda, acted suspiciously in favour of a private maize trader, Transglobe, during a food shortage reported to affect 6.5 million people. The inquiry, led by retired Chief Justice Anastasia Msosa, found he personally asked the state grain buyer Admarc to buy from Transglobe, and that Zambia then licensed Transglobe for half of a 100,000-tonne contract. It said the timing could not be put down to coincidence and did not rule out corruption. Chaponda was arrested on 19 July 2017 with Transglobe's representative Rashid Tayub. A magistrate acquitted him in 2018 on charges including illegally holding foreign currency at his home, and the High Court later upheld the acquittal.
inside: An inquiry found a minister pressed a state grain buyer on behalf of a private trader and suggested possible corruption, but a court acquitted him.
cite: The Nation (Malawi) on the Msosa commission report; The Nation on High Court ruling

n: German firm and Lesotho minister accused of forging a solar deal past Cabinet
rank: Minister in the Prime Minister's Office
d: Lesotho's anti-corruption directorate charged Robert Frazer of the German company Frazer Solar and former minister Temeki Tšolo with fraud and abuse of power over a solar deal signed in September 2018. Prosecutors allege they forged it after Cabinet refused it. Before parliament's Public Accounts Committee in July 2021 Tšolo denied any wrongdoing, saying his signature had been forged and that he had been set up: 'I was not aware I signed any contract with Frazer Solar.' The Principal Secretary for Energy, Themba Sopeng, testified that Tšolo had personally approved the deal with then prime minister Thabane's backing. Lesotho's High Court declared the agreement unlawful in November 2022, then dismissed the criminal case, saying the prosecution appeared to have lost interest.
inside: Prosecutors allege a foreign company and a minister together pushed through a contract Cabinet had not approved, leaving Lesotho facing a €50 million claim from the company.
cite: Lesotho Tribune, 15 May 2026; Kingdom of Lesotho v Frazer Solar GmbH and Others (438/2024) [2026] ZASCA 75, 22 May 2026; Public Eye (Lesotho), 11 Nov 2022; Public Eye (Lesotho), 8 October 2024 (https://publiceyenews.com/2024/10/08/tsolos-legal-woes-escalate/), for Tšolo's denial before the Public Accounts Committee and Sopeng's contrary testimony
undone: The criminal case has produced no verdict. It was dismissed once, revived by the Court of Appeal on 15 May 2026, and awaits a rehearing before a different High Court judge. Parliament's Public Accounts Committee had opened its own inquiry in 2021 into who signed the agreement. The sources cited report no bribe. Frazer and Tšolo are presumed innocent. On 22 May 2026 South Africa's Supreme Court of Appeal dismissed Lesotho's appeal against the €50 million arbitration award, which stands, while rescinding the order making it enforceable there. The stored Lesotho Tribune report of 15 May 2026 says Tšolo had not responded publicly to that day's ruling.

n: Nuctech's alleged $12.8m 'commission' to a Namibian commissioner's firm ended in acquittals
rank: Public Service Commission member
d: Namibian prosecutors alleged that Chinese state-owned scanner maker Nuctech inflated the price of a roughly $55.3 million deal with the finance ministry so it could pay at least $12.8 million in "commission" to Teko Trading. Teko was owned by Teckla Lameck, a serving member of the Public Service Commission, which oversees state employment, and her partner Jerobeam Mokaxwa. Prosecutors said Teko had no role in the deal. The Anti-Corruption Commission arrested them and Nuctech's Africa representative, Yang Fan, in July 2009. Nuctech had been led until 2008 by Hu Haifeng, son of China's then president, though the case did not allege he was involved. The three were later found not guilty of fraud and corruption.
inside: Prosecutors alleged a Chinese firm paid millions to a company owned by a Namibian public service commissioner on a state deal, but the three accused were acquitted.
cite: AFP via Solar Daily, 21 July 2009; The Namibian; NBC News Namibia

n: Lesotho's deputy army commander says security staff help famo gangs
rank: Security agency and police members
d: Members of Lesotho's security agencies escort and associate with famo gangs, deputy army commander Matela Matobakele said in July 2024, without naming anyone. Famo is a Basotho music style whose rival groups are blamed for killings. He spoke after a famo musician and a radio presenter working for peace between the groups were shot dead in Maseru on the weekend of 20 July 2024. An earlier police minister, Lepota Sekola, had also said some officers were allegedly involved in the gangs. In June 2024 the government outlawed 12 famo groups, a move criticised by the opposition All Basotho Convention and Democratic Congress, which a Transformation Resource Centre report says have strong relations with some famo gangs. In 2022 the then ABC leader, Nkaku Kabi, backed the Terene famo faction at a rally.
inside: Lesotho's own deputy army commander says members of the security agencies escort criminal famo gangs, putting state officers at the gangs' service; he named nobody.
cite: Lesotho Times, 27 July 2024; Africa Press Lesotho; Sowetan, 30 August 2022 (Kabi's rally); Transformation Resource Centre, Lesotho monthly report, June 2024

n: Mining minister took $8.5m from China International Fund, US jury found
rank: Minister of Mines and Geology
d: Executives of China Sonangol and China International Fund (CIF), Chinese-linked companies, paid Guinea's mines minister, Mahmoud Thiam, $8.5m to win rights in the country's mining sector. Thiam, minister in 2009 and 2010, negotiated many terms of a joint venture with CIF. Sam Pa, head of CIF, sent $3m to Thiam's Hong Kong account about two weeks before the shareholders' agreement was signed. The bribes aimed to secure the companies' place as first shareholder in a national mining company that would take over Guinea's stakes in mining projects. A New York jury convicted Thiam of money laundering, and in August 2017 he received seven years in prison. A US appeals court upheld the judgment in August 2019.
inside: Chinese-linked companies paid the minister negotiating with them, and he used his post to steer Guinea's government into agreements giving those companies rights over its mining stakes.
cite: US Department of Justice, 25 August 2017; US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, United States v. Thiam, 5 August 2019

n: Panalpina and oil firms paid Nigeria Customs officials to ignore import rules
who: Panalpina, Shell, Transocean, Tidewater, Noble, GlobalSantaFe
rank: Nigeria Customs Service officials
d: Panalpina, a Swiss freight company, and oil-sector firms paid officials of the Nigeria Customs Service through brokers to set aside import rules, according to US regulators. From about 2002 to 2007, GlobalSantaFe paid for documents showing its drilling rigs had left Nigerian waters, when they had never moved. Noble obtained eight temporary import permits with false papers. Tidewater reimbursed a broker about $1.6m for such payments, and a Shell unit used a broker to obtain preferential customs treatment. Invoices called the bribes 'special handling' or 'local processing' fees. In November 2010 the firms settled with the US Justice Department and Securities and Exchange Commission. The total for all seven companies in the settlements exceeded $236m.
inside: Foreign companies paid customs officers through brokers, so Nigeria's customs officials supplied false papers and set aside import rules for those companies' rigs and vessels.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission, 4 November 2010; National Law Review, 'Record FCPA settlements', 2010

n: Parker Drilling paid an agent to influence a Nigerian customs panel
rank: Temporary Import Panel on customs duties
d: Parker Drilling, a Houston drilling company, paid an agent to influence a Nigerian government panel that was reviewing its customs and tax compliance. Nigeria set up the Temporary Import Panel in late 2002 to check whether its customs service had collected the duties owed. The panel fined Parker $3.8m. From January to May 2004 Parker sent the agent $1.25m instead of paying. The agent reported spending part of it on items including entertaining officials, and his emails mentioned contacts at the Ministry of Finance, the State Security Service and the president's office. The fine fell to $750,000. In April 2013 Parker agreed to an $11.76m penalty under a deferred prosecution agreement, in which charges are dropped if it complies, and paid the US securities regulator $3.05m plus $1.04m in interest.
inside: A US drilling company paid an agent $1.25m to influence the government panel judging it, and the panel's $3.8m fine against the company was cut to $750,000.
cite: US Department of Justice, 16 April 2013

n: Airbus used an official's relative in Ghana plane deals; Ghana found no bribery
rank: High-ranking elected official (identified and cleared in Ghana's inquiry)
d: UK court papers said Airbus hired a close relative of a high-ranking elected Ghanaian official as its business partner while selling Ghana C-295 military transport planes. Ghana signed for two aircraft in August 2011. Commissions of about €5m were allegedly promised or paid. When the arrangement failed Airbus's checks, staff allegedly routed payments through a Spanish company with no Ghana links. Airbus agreed a record £3bn settlement with France, the UK and the US in 2020, covering several countries, including failure to prevent bribery in Ghana. In August 2024 Ghana's Special Prosecutor closed its inquiry, finding no evidence that John Mahama, identified as the official, took bribes, and no basis to say he was induced to favour Airbus. It also cleared the relative and his associates.
inside: UK court papers allege Airbus placed a decision-maker's relative as its paid partner to win Ghanaian aircraft purchases; Ghana's Special Prosecutor found no evidence of bribery and charged nobody.
cite: Citi Newsroom, February 2020 (UK court statement of facts); Office of the Special Prosecutor of Ghana report, 8 August 2024, via Modern Ghana; Ghana News Agency, 9 Aug 2024

n: Latin American cocaine cells paid off Guinea-Bissau's military, GI-TOC reports
rank: Senior military figures
d: Latin American cocaine traffickers were paying Guinea-Bissau's military for protection by about 2006, according to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research group. Its 2022 study says each of three trafficking cells was 'protected by, and paying off, the military'. It says that by the 2005 elections 'military and political protection of the trade went right to the top'. It reports that senior military figures consolidated their control of the bulk transit of cocaine and kept a share of the profits, reportedly between 13% and 15%. The report names no individual for these payments. These are the group's findings from its sources, and not a court verdict.
inside: GI-TOC reports that foreign cocaine traffickers paid Guinea-Bissau's military for protection, so army figures guarded and then took a share of the traffickers' transit trade.
cite: Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), 'Cocaine politics in West Africa: Guinea-Bissau's protection networks', 2022

n: Sanctions: Mali ruling-party MP coordinated armed blockade of peace talks
who: Arab Movement of Azawad (MAA), pro-government wing
rank: Member of the National Assembly
d: Mohamed Ould Mataly sat in Mali's National Assembly for the party of President Keita, the RPM, while being an influential member of an armed group, the pro-government wing of the Arab Movement of Azawad (MAA). He was a former mayor of Bourem and its member of parliament. The UN listed him in July 2019 for obstructing Mali's 2015 peace deal. According to the listing summaries, he and the MAA wing's military chief of staff coordinated an armed blockade of regional consultations in Gao in November 2018, which stopped discussion of key parts of the deal. The UN imposed a travel ban, then an asset freeze on 19 December 2019. The US and EU followed with sanctions.
inside: An influential member of an armed group held a ruling-party seat in parliament, and sanctions listings say he helped organise an armed blockade that stopped talks on the peace deal.
cite: UN Security Council Mali sanctions list, via Hong Kong SFC, December 2019; Kharon Brief, December 2019; Arab News/AFP, 10 July 2019

n: Sanctions: armed-group member advised Kidal's governor, controlled aid
who: HCUA, an armed group in the CMA coalition
rank: Special adviser to the Governor of Kidal
d: Ahmed Ag Albachar, an influential member of the armed group HCUA, became special adviser to the Governor of Kidal in northern Mali in early 2018, according to the UN sanctions list. He also chaired the humanitarian commission of Kidal's regional administration. The list says he mediated between the Coordination of Movements of Azawad (CMA), the rebel coalition, and Ansar Dine, a designated terrorist group. Sanctions findings summarised by Kharon, a sanctions research firm, say he used his role to control all aid and development projects in the region and to intimidate and extort aid organisations. He co-owned a transport company that NGOs were authorised to use in Kidal. The UN listed him in July 2019 and froze his assets that December.
inside: A member of an armed group held a post advising the regional governor, and sanctions findings say he used his position to control and extort aid projects in Kidal.
cite: UN Security Council Mali sanctions list, via Hong Kong SFC and Government of Jersey annex; Kharon Brief, December 2019

n: Papers said Nigerian generals aided Boko Haram; defence chiefs denied it
rank: Ten generals and other senior officers (unnamed, reported)
d: Nigerian newspapers reported in June 2014 that courts-martial had found ten generals and five other senior officers guilty of giving arms and information to Boko Haram, the Islamist armed group. The Leadership daily, citing unnamed military sources, named none of them. Defence headquarters said there was 'no truth whatsoever' in the report. The Interior Minister, Abba Moro, told the BBC the trials were 'good news'. Soldiers had told AP that some senior officers were helping the group, and officers' information allegedly helped it ambush convoys and attack barracks. John Campbell of the US Council on Foreign Relations wrote that the credibility of the claims remained unresolved. The sources cited show no published verdict or names.
inside: Newspapers alleged senior army officers secretly supplied Boko Haram with arms and information, helping it attack troops; the Defence Headquarters denied this and no officer was publicly named.
cite: Al Jazeera, 4 June 2014; Council on Foreign Relations, John Campbell, 5 June 2014

n: Nigerian army commander said soldiers were selling arms to Boko Haram
rank: Soldiers and a brigade commander (unnamed)
d: Nigerian soldiers sold arms and ammunition to Boko Haram, the armed group they were fighting, according to the army's own commander in the north-east. Maj-Gen Lucky Irabor said in 2016 that some soldiers had been making the sales, calling them a betrayal of the Nigerian people. Three weeks earlier the army had said a tribunal was trying 16 officers and troops for offences including theft and sale of ammunition. A front-line soldier told AP his brigade commander was on trial in secret in Maiduguri, and that his artillery brigade had received only one of 21 anti-aircraft guns assigned to it. The army was investigating the guns. The sources do not report a verdict or say where the guns went.
inside: Boko Haram's money reached soldiers inside the Nigerian army, the theatre commander said, and they sold it army weapons and ammunition meant for use against the group.
cite: AP via The Herald, September 2016

n: Nigeria held 18 soldiers and 15 police over alleged arms sales to militants
who: Boko Haram, ISWAP and criminal buyers (alleged)
rank: Serving soldiers and police officers
d: Serving Nigerian soldiers and police officers have been arrested on suspicion of selling arms to the armed groups they were sent to fight, according to a Daily Trust article listing the cases. On 29 May 2025, Operation Hadin Kai, the army's north-east campaign against Boko Haram and its offshoot ISWAP, arrested 18 soldiers and 15 police officers for allegedly selling arms to terrorists and other criminals. On 2 September 2025 a lance corporal in Marte, Borno State, was arrested with 711 rounds he allegedly meant for terrorists. On 27 September a soldier and a police officer were held over arms allegedly being smuggled to Boko Haram and ISWAP. These are allegations, and the article reports no outcome.
inside: The arrests allege that armed groups obtained weapons through paying soldiers and police officers who were posted to fight them and had access to security force arms.
cite: Daily Trust, 'Soldiers, stop the gunrunning', 2025

n: Salt Lake City's 2002 bid paid cash and favours to IOC members
org_label: Salt Lake City Olympic bid committee
rank: International Olympic Committee members
d: The International Olympic Committee's members vote on which city hosts the Olympic Games. The committee seeking the 2002 Winter Games for Salt Lake City spent over $16 million and flew more than 70 of the roughly 100 IOC members to Utah. Members' relatives got jobs at First Security Corporation Bank, arranged by Spencer Eccles, and help into the University of Utah by Jim Jardine, while Intermountain Health Care provided medical facilities and treatment during visits. The scandal broke on 24 November 1998 with a report on a letter showing tuition paid for a member's child. The IOC expelled six members, four resigned and ten more were sanctioned, the first corruption expulsions in its history. Bid leaders Tom Welch and David Johnson were acquitted of all US charges in December 2003.
inside: A city's bid committee put money, jobs and university places in the hands of the officials who voted on hosting, and the vote went its way.
cite: IOC Ad Hoc Commission report, 1999; New York Times, 6 December 2003, on the acquittal of Welch and Johnson
undone: Five organisers were tried in the United States and acquitted in December 2003.

n: CONCACAF president Jeffrey Webb pleaded guilty and forfeited $6.7m
org_label: Traffic and other sports marketing companies
rank: President of CONCACAF and FIFA vice-president
d: CONCACAF, based in Miami, governs football in North and Central America and the Caribbean and sells tournament rights such as the Gold Cup. Jeffrey Webb, its president and a FIFA vice-president, was among 14 officials charged on 27 May 2015 in the US racketeering case built around sports marketing companies paying football officials for media and marketing contracts. He pleaded guilty on 23 November 2015 to racketeering conspiracy, wire fraud conspiracy and money laundering conspiracy, and agreed to forfeit more than $6.7 million. Prosecutors estimated about $150 million in bribes across the case, at least $110 million of it tied to the 2016 Copa America Centenario. FIFA banned him from football for life in September 2016, and his sentencing was postponed repeatedly.
inside: Marketing firms' money reached the president of the confederation that sells regional tournament rights, and those contracts were steered to the payers.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 3 December 2015, on the EDNY superseding indictment and guilty pleas

n: Colombia's football federation chief Luis Bedoya admitted FIFA bribes
org_label: sports marketing companies in the US FIFA case
rank: FIFA executive committee member and CONMEBOL vice-president
d: Luis Bedoya led Colombia's national football federation, sat on FIFA's executive committee and was a vice-president of the South American confederation CONMEBOL. He waived indictment and pleaded guilty in the United States on 12 November 2015 to a two-count information charging racketeering conspiracy and wire fraud conspiracy, in the case over payments by sports marketing companies for tournament rights, and agreed to forfeit all funds on deposit in his Swiss bank account, among other funds. No amount has been given for that forfeiture. Reuters reported in May 2016 that he was banned from football for life. He cooperated with prosecutors and no sentence has been reported. On his own admission he took money from firms doing business with the competitions he helped govern.
inside: Rights-buying companies paid a man who voted inside FIFA and CONMEBOL, so decisions on their contracts were taken by someone on their payroll.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 3 December 2015, on Bedoya's 12 November 2015 guilty plea; Reuters, 6 May 2016, on the life ban

n: UNOPS executive director accused of steering $60m to a businessman's firms
rank: Executive director, UN Office for Project Services (UNOPS)
d: The UN Office for Project Services, UNOPS, manages construction and procurement projects for the UN system. US prosecutors allege that Vitaly Vanshelboim, a Ukrainian who joined the UN in 1992 and became a UNOPS executive director, took bribes to divert nearly $60 million in agency funding to companies linked to British businessman David Kendrick. A UN tribunal valued his benefits at over $3 million and ordered him to repay $58.8 million. He was sacked in January 2023 and arrested in Alicante in March 2025. On 21 October 2025 Spain's National High Court approved extradition on three of six charges: bribery as an agent of an organisation receiving federal funds, honest-services wire fraud and money laundering. His lawyers had three days to appeal; no transfer to US custody has been reported.
inside: Prosecutors say a businessman's payments bought a senior UNOPS official, who then sent the agency's project money to that businessman's firms.
cite: Associated Press, 21 October 2025, on Spain's National High Court extradition ruling (read via infonews.ca); EFE report of the same ruling; Associated Press, Oct 2025 (Spanish extradition approved); UN Dispute Tribunal UNDT/GVA/2023/020, judgment published Feb 2025; Inner City Press, 5 Nov 2026
undone: No conviction. Vanshelboim was dismissed by UNOPS in early 2023. In October 2023 the UN Dispute Tribunal found blatant misconduct, ordered him to repay $58.8 million - the loss UNOPS sustained on the Kendrick deals, not his own benefit - and withheld his pension. He was arrested in Spain in March 2025 on a warrant from the Southern District of New York, and Spain's National Court approved his extradition in October 2025 on bribery, wire fraud and money laundering. The US indictment covers at least September 2015 to around August 2023. On 26 October 2026 the UN Appeals Tribunal refused a reporter access to the briefs in his internal case. He is presumed innocent.

n: Nigeria's election staff jailed over cash before the 2015 vote
rank: INEC deputy director and a second commission official
d: Nigeria's Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, runs elections and its staff count and collate the votes. On 28 June 2019 the Jigawa State High Court in Gumel, before Justice Yusuf Birnin-Kudu, convicted two INEC officials on three of six counts and discharged them on the other three. Auwal Jibrin, a deputy director in Dutse, was jailed for six years and Garba Ismaila for seven. The court found that Jibrin and Ismaila dishonestly received 45 million naira out of 250 million naira handed out in Jigawa State before the 2015 presidential election. The EFCC says that money came from about $115 million disbursed by the then petroleum minister Diezani Alison-Madueke, who has not been convicted in the matter, and that it was meant to influence the result.
inside: Money the anti-corruption agency traced to a serving minister was paid to the officials running the vote count, so the commission's own staff worked to shape the result.
cite: EFCC press release, June 2019, and ICIR Nigeria, 1 July 2019, on the 28 June 2019 judgment

n: Football boss Mamic accused of paying three Croatian judges for rulings
rank: Judges of the Osijek County Court
d: USKOK, Croatia's anti-corruption office, indicted six at the Zagreb County Court: the football executive Zdravko Mamic, his brother Zoran, Osijek County Court judges Darko Kruslin, Zvonko Vekic and Ante Kvesic, and Natasa Sekulic, on bribery, influence-peddling and money-laundering charges. The case began when Mamic, his conviction final, sent USKOK a USB drive accusing the three judges. Prosecutors say he met Vekic in 2017-2019 in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Dubai, met Kruslin at Maksimir stadium in November 2016, and gave Vekic at least 370,000 euro for himself, Kruslin and Kvesic, who allegedly promised an acquittal, a dismissal of charges and return of a 7 million kuna guarantee. Kruslin had presided over the chamber that gave Mamic six and a half years for siphoning 116 million kuna from Dinamo Zagreb.
inside: Prosecutors say a football executive facing trial paid judges in the court hearing his cases, so the court's decisions would be made to suit him.
cite: N1 (Croatia), 7 June 2023; USKOK indictment, confirmed by the indictment chamber of the Zagreb County Court as reported by Dnevnik.hr; no trial verdict found as of November 2026
undone: No verdict has been reached and all the accused are presumed innocent. The indictment chamber of the Zagreb County Court confirmed USKOK's indictment, which it reported as covering Zdravko and Zoran Mamic, the judges Darko Kruslin, Ante Kvesic and Zvonko Vekic, Natasa Sekulic and the businessman Drago Tadic, on charges of bribery, trading in influence and money laundering. No trial date was reported, and Zdravko Mamic's request to move the case from the Zagreb court to Osijek was still before the High Criminal Court.

n: Malta's ex-PM and hospital concession bosses charged over privatised hospitals
org_label: Vitals Global Healthcare and Steward Health Care
rank: Prime Minister, chief of staff and a former minister
d: Maltese prosecutors charged former prime minister Joseph Muscat, former chief of staff Keith Schembri and former minister Konrad Mizzi, with 19 other people and companies, over the 2015 contract handing three public hospitals to private concessionaires. Charges include money laundering, fraud, conspiracy, bribery and corruption in public office. Steward Malta Management's legal representative, David-Joseph Meli, was charged with corrupting Muscat, Schembri and Mizzi. A magistrate's four-year inquiry produced a 1,200-page report, and charges were filed on 28 May 2024. A civil court had already annulled the concession, citing fraud and collusion between concessionaires and senior officials. All pleaded not guilty, Muscat calling the charges laughable. The charges have not been tried; in February 2026 a court turned down Muscat's human rights application over how he was drawn into the inquiry.
inside: A court found the hospital concessionaires and senior officials colluded; prosecutors say the companies paid the prime minister's circle, who then handed them public hospitals.
cite: OCCRP, May 2024; Malta magisterial inquiry; civil court annulment; The Maltese Herald, 20 February 2026

n: Aprilia's mayor sent to trial over a 2018 mafia vote deal; council dissolved
rank: Mayor and council of Aprilia
d: Lanfranco Principi was placed under house arrest on 3 July 2024 in Operation Assedio, one of 25 custody orders sought by Rome's anti-mafia prosecutors against a group led by Patrizio Forniti, and resigned as mayor of Aprilia the next day. The charges are external complicity in a mafia association, political-mafia electoral exchange, bid rigging and trading in influence. Prosecutors say the deal was struck at the 2018 council elections, when at least 200 of the 453 preference votes Principi received were delivered by two businessmen inside the association in return for works, contracts and hirings; he became deputy mayor, and was elected mayor in 2023. One cited act is a direct award of 48,678 euro for cleaning street gullies in November 2018.
inside: At least 200 of a councillor's 453 preference votes were delivered by a mafia group, prosecutors say, and paid back with direct awards and hirings once he reached the town hall.
cite: Editoriale Domani, Quotidiano Nazionale and La Verità, 3-4 July 2024, on the arrest and the charges; Latina Tu, 12 July 2024, on the specific acts and the vote figures; Il Caffè, 2025, on the immediate trial listed for 10 June 2025; L'Indipendente, 19 April 2025, on the dissolution
undone: No verdict. Principi declined to answer at his guarantee interrogation on 12 July 2024. The Tribunal of Latina ordered an immediate trial for him and nineteen others, with the first hearing on 10 June 2025, and the Court of Cassation has upheld the existence and mafia character of the association in rejecting a co-defendant's release application. In April 2025 the cabinet dissolved Aprilia's council for mafia infiltration; the interior ministry then barred Principi and the former mayor Antonio Terra from standing for office. He remained under house arrest into 2026, allowed to work remotely. A further bid-rigging investigation into the local public transport tender, naming both former mayors, has closed without a charging decision. He is presumed innocent.

n: Court convicts nine over cocaine moved through Portugal's Leixoes port
rank: Port employees at Leixoes
d: Portugal's public prosecutors charged 13 people and one company with criminal association, drug trafficking, possession of a prohibited weapon and money laundering, and Porto's criminal investigation court sent them to trial. Prosecutors said employees of the port of Leixoes, near Porto, were paid 10,000 and 40,000 euro to help move cocaine, and a diver and an importer from Brazil were among the defendants. Those two challenged the case for procedural nullities and insufficient evidence; the court rejected the challenge. Seizures at Leixoes of 78 kilograms in May 2023 and 91 kilograms in October 2023 were valued at about 4.2 million euro. On 17 July 2026 the Porto court convicted nine of the 13 defendants, acquitted four, imposed terms from suspended sentences to 17 years and fined the company 48,000 euro.
inside: Prosecutors said a cocaine network bought the help of the port's own workers, so the people handling containers moved the drugs through for it.
cite: Portugal Resident on the Porto Regional Attorney General's Office indictment; Observador, 17 July 2026, on the judgment

n: UN panel: UAE pays Yemeni brigades and controls the guard forces at its own bases
rank: Amaliqah Brigades, Guards of the Republic, Tihamah Brigades and base guard forces
d: The UAE originally recruited, trained and paid most forces affiliated with the Southern Transitional Council, a situation the UN Panel of Experts on Yemen said had evolved since 2015, finding in January 2021 that it had scaled down its direct control over most of them. The UAE provides some payments to the Amaliqah Brigades, Guards of the Republic and Tihamah Brigades; some brigades also draw salaries from Yemen's government. A footnote records the Panel's finding that the UAE directly controls the Yemeni guard forces at its own bases at Balhaf and Rayyan. Yemen's government told the Panel that Emirati money and weapons continued to reach the Security Belt and Shabwani Elite Forces. The UAE told the Panel it does not support any unilateral action by any party to the conflict.
inside: UN investigators say a foreign state pays units inside Yemen's own forces and directly commands the guard forces at its own bases.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2021/79 (25 January 2021), paras. 31-32 and 52 and footnote 13
