n: Foreign service paid an Azerbaijani to get back into its spy agencies
rank: Reserve officer of the state security service
d: Azerbaijan's State Security Service said in December 2018 that Bahruz Yusifzade, a reserve officer who had left the state security service, arranged meetings with officers of a foreign special service, who reached him through a foreign national he had himself once recruited. The service said he was instructed to seek a position inside Azerbaijan's intelligence agencies and was found to have taken money from foreign intelligence services. He was arrested and prosecuted for treason under article 274 of the criminal code. The country behind the recruitment was not named. The account comes from the State Security Service alone; no independent account of the case, and no trial outcome, has been published.
inside: Azerbaijan's State Security Service says a foreign spy service paid a former officer and told him to win a post back inside its intelligence agencies.
cite: Trend.az, 'State Security Service unveils multi-stage espionage against Azerbaijan', 27 December 2018

n: Iran paid a serving Israeli soldier to photograph army bases
rank: Soldier, Givati Brigade, Israel Defense Forces
d: A soldier in the Israeli army's Givati Brigade was arrested in September after allegedly being in contact with Iranian intelligence from about July 2025 and sending photographs and video of sites in Israel, including the inside of army bases, together with information on weapons the army uses. Prosecutors say he did it in exchange for financial compensation. The investigation was run by the Shin Bet internal security service, the investigative military police and the defence ministry's security directorate, and a court cleared the details for publication in January 2026. He is charged with contact with a foreign agent, passing information to the enemy, impersonation and obstruction of justice. The case has not yet been decided.
inside: Prosecutors say Iranian intelligence paid a serving soldier to photograph inside the bases he was posted to and send the pictures out.
cite: Tzvi Jasper, Jerusalem Post, 15 January 2026 (mirrored by Yahoo News)

n: US prosecutors say $10m from South Africa's 2010 bid reached FIFA's Jack Warner
rank: FIFA vice-president
d: FIFA's executive committee members voted on World Cup hosts. US prosecutors allege that before the vote, officials of FIFA, the South African government and the bid committee were prepared to arrange $10 million for the Caribbean Football Union to help South Africa win the 2010 tournament. Because the bid could not pay from government funds, the indictment says the money came from FIFA tournament funds, wired from a FIFA account in Switzerland in three payments on 2 and 31 January and 7 March 2008 into accounts controlled by Jack Warner, a FIFA vice-president, in the Caribbean Football Union's name. Warner has maintained his innocence. Trinidad and Tobago's High Court stayed his extradition in September 2025, finding it flawed, and permanently halted it in July 2026; he never stood trial.
inside: Prosecutors say a national bid got millions into the accounts of the FIFA official who controlled a bloc of votes.
cite: US Department of Justice indictment, Eastern District of New York, May 2015, as analysed by Daily Maverick, 27 May 2015

n: Honduras: CONCACAF chief Hawit and federation head Callejas admit bribes
org_label: sports marketing companies in the US FIFA case
rank: CONCACAF president; president of the Honduran football federation and member of FIFA's Television and Marketing Committee
d: Alfredo Hawit, a Honduran who became president of the regional confederation CONCACAF and a FIFA vice-president, was arrested in Zurich on 3 December 2015 on suspicion of bribery, at the hotel where seven officials had been arrested that May, and later pleaded guilty in the US case in which sports marketing companies paid football officials for media and marketing rights. Rafael Callejas, a former president of Honduras who ran the Honduran football federation and sat on FIFA's Television and Marketing Committee, also pleaded guilty, in a plea the Department of Justice announced in March 2016. Callejas died in US custody on 4 April 2020, before he could be sentenced. The wider prosecution brought 41 arrests and charges against 18 individuals and two corporations, with bribes estimated at $150 million.
inside: Companies that bought football rights paid two Honduran officials, one of them CONCACAF's president, and both admitted taking the money.
cite: US Department of Justice press releases, 11 April 2016 (plea by a former high-ranking FIFA and CONCACAF official) and 28 March 2016 (plea by the former president of the Honduran soccer federation), as listed in the 2015 FIFA corruption case file

n: Costa Rica's federation president Eduardo Li pleaded guilty in FIFA case
org_label: sports marketing companies in the US FIFA case
rank: President of the Costa Rican football federation; FIFA executive committee member-elect
d: Eduardo Li was president of Costa Rica's national football federation and had been elected to FIFA's executive committee when he was arrested in May 2015. He pleaded guilty in the United States on 7 October 2016, admitting he had taken more than $500,000 in bribes. The prosecution described sports marketing companies, among them Traffic, paying officials of CONCACAF and its member federations for the rights to matches and tournaments, including qualifying games sold by national federations. Li's plea is one of more than a dozen guilty pleas by football officials and executives in the same investigation, which the US estimated involved about $150 million in bribes across the whole case. He has not been sentenced and has asked the US court to vacate the conviction.
inside: Marketing companies' money reached the head of Costa Rica's federation, whose body sold the match rights those companies bought.
cite: Associated Press, 7 October 2016; US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, court records

n: A contractor paid the finance director of a US Africa development agency
rank: Director of Financial Management, US African Development Foundation
d: The US African Development Foundation is a federal agency funding enterprises in Africa. On 30 January 2026 federal prosecutors charged its financial management director, Mathieu Zahui, by criminal information with accepting gratuities from a foundation contractor and lying to a federal investigator. Prosecutors said the contractor, who owned a Kenya-based company, paid him $12,000 in cash. From June 2020 to December 2023 Zahui arranged for the foundation to route vendor payments through that company, including invoices for work it did not perform, approved mark-ups of 17 to 66 per cent, and caused at least $617,625 to be paid to it. He denied receiving any benefit when interviewed in 2024. He pleaded guilty on 23 February 2026 and was sentenced on 27 May 2026 to four months and a $12,000 forfeiture.
inside: A contractor's cash bought the official who controlled the agency's payments, and he routed the agency's money through that contractor's company.
cite: US Attorney, District of Columbia, press releases, 30 January 2026 (charge) and 27 May 2026 (sentencing)

n: Bangladesh's former election chief arrested over the 2018 'midnight' vote
rank: Chief Election Commissioner
d: Bangladesh's 11th parliamentary election, held on 30 December 2018 under the Election Commission led by KM Nurul Huda, returned a sweeping Awami League victory and is known locally as the 'midnight' election, for ballot boxes said to have been filled with sealed papers the night before polling. After Sheikh Hasina's government fell, a BNP national executive committee member filed a case on 22 June 2025 naming 24 people, among them three former chief election commissioners - Kazi Rakibuddin Ahmad, Huda and Kazi Habibul Awal - and their commissioners, over the 2014, 2018 and 2024 elections. The prosecution says Huda helped keep Hasina in power and that election officials were directed to stuff ballot boxes.
inside: The case alleges a governing party controlled the officials heading the election commission, who then ordered the count fixed in its favour.
cite: Prothom Alo, 23-27 June 2025; The Business Standard, 1 July 2025 (bail refused and the statement to the magistrate); Daily Observer, 2 July 2025
undone: No trial or verdict. Huda was arrested at his Uttara home on 22 June 2025 after being seized by a crowd and handed to police; a Dhaka court granted four days' remand and extended it by four more on 27 June, and on 25 June the case was widened to add sedition, fraud and embezzlement. He then gave a voluntary statement to a Dhaka magistrate admitting that the 2018 election was manipulated - but placing it on the intelligence agencies and on the commission's then secretary, Helal Uddin Ahmed, saying the commission was kept in the dark and 'there was nothing I alone could do'. So he admits the rigging and denies directing it, which is why this record stays coded possible. Bail was refused on 1 July 2025.

n: Novomatic accused of buying a seat on Casinos Austria's board for an FPO man
rank: Chief financial officer, Casinos Austria
d: In March 2019 Peter Sidlo, a Freedom Party (FPO) district councillor in Vienna with no gaming or executive background, was made chief financial officer of Casinos Austria, a third owned by the Austrian state through its holding company OBAG, with Novomatic then a large shareholder on 17.19 per cent (no longer a holder). In early 2026 Austria's corruption prosecutor, the WKStA, charged Johann Graf, founder of the gambling machine maker Novomatic, its former chief executive Harald Neumann, and Heinz-Christian Strache, then vice-chancellor and FPO leader, with trading in influence, and asked for a corporate fine against Novomatic. Prosecutors allege Graf and Neumann backed Sidlo's appointment in return for the FPO pushing government to open the casino market and repeal Vienna's ban on gaming arcades. Novomatic calls the allegations groundless.
inside: Prosecutors say a gambling firm helped put a party loyalist into a state-owned casino company's boardroom in exchange for laws the firm wanted changed.
cite: Casino.org, 3 March 2026; World Casino Directory, 2 March 2026, on the WKStA indictment filed at the Vienna Regional Court for Criminal Matters (Causa Casinos); ORF Wien, 17 Apr and 27 May 2026; Heute, 27 Oct 2026, on the 25 November 2026 continuation
undone: No verdict has been reached. The trial was to open in early March 2026, but Strache and Novomatic challenged the assigned judge and she was excluded for the appearance of bias; with a new judge the trial opened at the Vienna Regional Court for Criminal Matters on 19 May 2026. The first days went to a separate life-insurance charge against Strache, to which he pleaded not guilty on 27 May 2026, calling the accusations baseless. The Casinos strand itself is listed to continue on 25 November 2026, a date still ahead. On that count Strache faces a maximum of two years. A separate strand, over 240,000 euro of Novomatic sponsorship paid to an FPÖ-linked institute, was dropped by the WKStA in July 2024. All deny wrongdoing and are presumed innocent.

n: Five Greek border police charged with running crossings for smugglers
rank: Special border guard unit, Evros border
d: Five officers of a special border guard unit in north-eastern Greece were arrested in Didymoteicho and held in custody pending trial, accused of working with four smugglers of undetermined nationality operating from Turkey. Authorities said the officers helped with at least 12 crossings bringing in at least 100 people, and took a share of what the smugglers charged. Internal affairs had been watching them since October 2022, and wiretapped calls produced more than 2,000 pages of transcripts; about 26,000 euro in cash and nearly 60 mobile phones were seized when they were arrested. They testified before an examining magistrate in Orestiada in June 2023, and the case had not been tried as of that date.
inside: Prosecutors say a smuggling ring had the border guards themselves on its payroll, so the unit guarding the crossing arranged the crossings for it.
cite: Associated Press / WTOP, June 2023
undone: No trial has been reported. A search in Greek found coverage only of the May 2023 arrests, the June 2023 pre-trial custody order and the magistrate's hearing, so the charges remain untested and the five officers are presumed innocent.

n: Tremestieri Etneo council dissolved after ex-mayor's vote-exchange sentence
who: Mafia group (none named for this town in the source)
rank: Mayor and council of Tremestieri Etneo
d: The Italian cabinet dissolved the council of Tremestieri Etneo, a town in the province of Catania in Sicily, for mafia infiltration on 27 March 2025, together with San Luca in Calabria and Poggiomarino in Campania. A few days earlier its former mayor, Santi Rando, had been sentenced at first instance to eight years for political-mafia vote exchange at the 2015 municipal election, the offence of obtaining votes through a criminal group in exchange for favours once in office; an Italian first-instance sentence is not final. Dissolution hands a town to government commissioners and is ordered when an inquiry finds organised crime has conditioned the administration. San Luca, dissolved for confirmed criminal-organisation conditioning, had seen no candidates stand at its June 2023 municipal elections.
inside: A court has sentenced the former mayor at first instance over votes exchanged with a mafia group, and the government dissolved the council.
cite: L'Indipendente, 19 April 2025, which reports the 27 March 2025 dissolutions in background

n: Houthi defence procurement chief attached to the Tehran office
who: Houthi supply network operating from Iran (per the UN Panel)
rank: Director of procurement, Houthi-appointed Ministry of Defence
d: Major General Muhammad Ahmad al-Talibi is procurement director at the defence ministry run by the Houthi authorities in Sanaa. The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen said in October 2024 that he is attached to the Houthi office in Tehran and in charge of illicit shipment of materiel to the Houthis through a network of individuals and entities, and that he arranges training for Houthi combatants in Iran. The Panel places him in a liaison cell monitoring transfers from Iranian naval ports. Its case study 6 says that in 2022 he ordered a Yemeni customs broker clearing smuggled materiel to move to Djibouti; an annex to the same report dates the move to August 2023. Press material annexed to the report notes Tehran has always denied arming the Houthis.
inside: UN investigators say the man buying weapons for the defence ministry in Sanaa is attached to an office in Tehran, so purchasing serves the supply route from Iran.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2024/731 (11 October 2024), paras. 77-79 and case study 6; the Iranian denial from press material annexed to the same report

n: MAN manager accused of paying Turkmenistan's state oil chief 8.4m euros
org_label: MAN Ferrostaal and MAN GHH Gas & Oil
who: MAN Ferrostaal and MAN GHH Gas & Oil, then both part of the MAN group
rank: Head of the state oil company Turkmennebit, and decision-makers in the oil ministry
d: German prosecutors say a former MAN manager, not publicly named, transferred 8.4 million euros between 2002 and 2007 into accounts controlled by Saparmammet Veliev, then head of the state oil company Turkmennebit. A 1999 decree of leader Saparmurat Niyazov had ordered Turkmennebit to let MAN build a compressor station in oil fields near the Iranian border. The prosecution says decision-makers in the Turkmen government asked at least five per cent of the contract. A Munich court heard in January 2015 that the minister expected that five per cent, that about eight million euros was taken by people in the oil ministry, and that a Ukrainian competitor lost out; it convicted a Berlin middleman, a long-standing Siemens sales agent in Turkmenistan, who drew up sham consultancy contracts to carry the money.
inside: A German group paid into Turkmenistan's oil ministry and the state oil company that oversaw the work, and got the contract to build a gas compressor station.
cite: RFE/RL, 'Former German Manager On Trial For Bribing Of Turkmen Oil Officials', 11 December 2019, for the 8.4 million euros into Veliev's accounts, the 1999 Niyazov decree and the prosecution's five per cent; Abendzeitung Munchen, 'Minister bestochen: Mittelsmann verurteilt', 29 January 2015, for the middleman's conviction and sentence, the minister's five per cent, the eight million taken in the oil ministry and the 232 million euro contract; OECD Working Group on Bribery, Phase 4 report on Germany, for the bogus construction invoices, the joint venture that issued them, the investigation opened in July 2009 and the 10 million euro fine of December 2011; Transparency International, Exporting Corruption progress report 2012, for the compressor station being in Turkmenistan
undone: No Turkmen official has been charged in anything published, and the court report does not say whether the ministry officials faced proceedings. The two published outcomes are against the German side: MAN Ferrostaal agreed with the Munich prosecutors in December 2011 to a fine of 10 million euros, 500,000 as punishment and 9.5 million of confiscated gain, for the negligent failure to supervise rather than for bribery; and the middleman was convicted in January 2015 under a plea agreement, after a confession, receiving one year and six months suspended with 20,000 euros to pay. The OECD records one conviction for foreign bribery in the case and seven other people resolving their cases without one. The former MAN GHH Gas & Oil manager's own trial opened in Munich in late 2016, was postponed for his ill health and resumed in December 2019, where his defence asked that it be stopped as time-barred; no verdict has been found in anything published, so whether it ended in one is not known here. The contract value is given as 233 million German marks in the 1999 decree reported by RFE/RL and as 232 million euros by the court reporting of 2015, and the two cannot both be right. Veliev was dismissed in 2005 and died in prison in October 2017, serving 24 years for corruption.

n: Myanmar's home affairs minister investigated over scam-syndicate bribes
rank: Minister of Home Affairs and chair of the anti-scam supervisory committee
d: Lieutenant General Tun Tun Naung, home affairs minister in Myanmar's military government, chaired the Central Supervisory Committee on Combating Telecom Fraud and Online Gambling, the body set up to eliminate scam centres, formed on 10 December of the preceding year. He had earlier served as minister of border affairs. Mizzima reported that he had come under investigation for allegedly taking bribes from illegal online scam syndicates, and that he was removed as home affairs minister on 31 January 2025, a year after taking the post, with the National Defence and Security Council returning him to his original military duties. The report gives no evidence for the allegation, no charge has been made public, the syndicates were not named, and its sources say he has not been given a new assignment.
inside: One report says the scam operators paid the minister who chaired the committee set up to close their centres, with no evidence given.
cite: Mizzima, 'Former Home Affairs Minister investigated for alleged ties to online scam operations', undated copy at mizzimaenglish.blogspot.com

n: Three Israeli soldiers and a civilian charged with working for an Iranian handler
rank: Three serving soldiers and a civilian
d: The Haifa District Prosecutor's Office charged three Israeli soldiers and a civilian in May 2026 with working for an Iranian intelligence handler. Prosecutors say the soldiers are suspected of acting for the handler before they enlisted, and that some approached him on their own initiative to carry out missions. The group photographed and sent images of train stations, shopping centres and security cameras, and material on the Israeli Air Force's Technological College in Haifa, where some had studied. They were asked to obtain weapons, and some damaged property as part of the tasks. One defendant recruited the others. The four were arrested in March after an investigation by the Shin Bet, military intelligence's Unit 8200, the Israel Police's Lahav 433 and the military police. The case has not been decided.
inside: Prosecutors say some were already acting for an Iranian handler before they enlisted, so the service had recruits inside the army.
cite: JNS, 'Civilian, three IDF soldiers charged with spying for Tehran', 9 May 2026

n: Marketing firms bought CONMEBOL's president Juan Angel Napout
org_label: Traffic, Torneos y Competencias and Full Play
rank: President of CONMEBOL and FIFA vice-president
d: CONMEBOL, in Luque outside Asuncion, runs South American football and sells television and marketing rights to its tournaments. A Brooklyn jury convicted Juan Angel Napout, its president and a FIFA vice-president, of racketeering conspiracy and two counts of wire fraud conspiracy on Friday 22 December 2017, the Department of Justice announcing it on 26 December. Prosecutors showed principals of the marketing companies Traffic, Torneos y Competencias and Full Play paid him millions of dollars for his support on rights to editions of the Copa America, and that on Copa Libertadores rights Torneos paid through Full Play as an intermediary. A third defendant, Manuel Burga of Peru, was acquitted. Judge Pamela Chen remanded Napout, gave him nine years in August 2018, and the Second Circuit upheld the conviction in June 2020.
inside: Marketing companies put bribe money in the pocket of the man running South American football, and the rights to its tournaments went to them.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, press release, 26 December 2017, on the jury verdict of Friday 22 December 2017; sentencing August 2018; United States v. Napout (2d Cir., June 2020)

n: Chile's football federation president Sergio Jadue pleaded guilty
org_label: sports marketing companies in the US FIFA case
rank: President of Chile's ANFP (national football association) and a CONMEBOL vice-president
d: Sergio Jadue ran Chile's ANFP, the national football association, and was a vice-president of CONMEBOL, the South American confederation that sells the rights to the Copa America and Copa Libertadores. Waiving indictment, he pleaded guilty in the United States on 23 November 2015 to a two-count information of racketeering conspiracy and wire fraud conspiracy, in the case in which the marketing companies Traffic, Torneos y Competencias and Full Play paid officials for those rights, and he agreed to forfeit all funds in his US bank account. FIFA banned him from football for life in May 2016. His US sentencing has been postponed repeatedly, most recently in October 2023, and he has not been sentenced. A Santiago court later closed the separate Chilean case against him as time-barred.
inside: Marketing companies' payments reached the head of Chile's football association, who also held a vice-presidency at the confederation selling those tournament rights.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, court records; Reuters, 23 November 2015; La Tercera on the Chilean case being closed

n: Nicaragua's federation head and FIFA officer Julio Rocha pleaded guilty
org_label: sports marketing companies in the US FIFA case
rank: President of the Nicaraguan football federation; FIFA development officer
d: Julio Rocha Lopez was president of Nicaragua's football federation and later a FIFA development officer. He pleaded guilty in the United States to racketeering conspiracy and wire fraud conspiracy, each carrying up to 20 years, in a case the Department of Justice announced on 7 December 2016. The prosecution concerned sports marketing companies paying officials of CONCACAF and its member federations for the rights to matches and tournaments. Rocha's plea put the scheme inside FIFA's own development arm. He was banned from football for life about two months before he died of cancer in January 2018, under house arrest in the United States and due to be sentenced in Brooklyn federal court on 2 February. He was never sentenced.
inside: Rights-buying firms paid an official who had run Nicaragua's federation and then held a FIFA development post, placing their interests inside both bodies.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, release of 7 December 2016; Inside World Football, 15 January 2018

n: Traffickers' payments reached the head of Mexico's Interpol office
rank: Head of Mexico's Interpol National Central Bureau
d: A national central bureau connects a country's police to Interpol, through which forces exchange information across borders. In Mexico's 2008 Operation Clean House (Operacion Limpieza), Ricardo Gutierrez Vargas, director for international police affairs and Interpol at Mexico's Federal Investigative Agency and, an Interpol website says, head of its National Central Bureau, was put under house arrest on suspicion of passing police information to traffickers. Rodolfo de la Guardia Garcia, the agency's former second-in-command, was held over a suspected leak to the Sinaloa cartel for monthly payments. The former federal police commissioner Gerardo Garay and three other Public Safety Department officials were also detained, on undisclosed allegations. Interpol sent a team to check whether its database information reached cartels. Both Interpol chiefs were later acquitted, prosecutors unable to support the charges.
inside: Prosecutors suspected traffickers were paying the officials who ran Mexico's link to international policing, turning that channel to the gangs' use; both were later acquitted.
cite: Associated Press via NBC News, 2008 (undated copy); El Universal, 27 February 2014, for the acquittals

n: 41 Romanian police and customs officers indicted over cigarette route
org_label: Cigarette-smuggling network running loads from Serbia
rank: Moravita customs post and border police
d: Romania's anti-corruption prosecutors indicted 41 police and customs officers working at the Moravita crossing, on the country's western border with Serbia. Prosecutors said the officers took money to wave through an organised cigarette-smuggling operation, which moved loads worth about 3.3 million euro. Officers were allegedly paid between 100 and 900 euro per shift, and the smuggling ran almost daily. One officer was already in temporary arrest. On the prosecutors' case, the smuggling network had bought the control function at the crossing itself.
inside: Prosecutors say a smuggling ring paid almost the whole staff of a border post, so the officers meant to search lorries let its cigarettes through.
cite: HotNews.ro, 16 June 2011

n: Bulgaria's gambling regulators charged as members of Bozhkov's crime group
rank: State Gambling Commission - head of control activities and a commission member
d: Bulgarian prosecutors charged the State Gambling Commission's head of control activities and a former commission member, identified by the court only as T.M. and P.G., named in local media as Todor Markov and Plamen Georgiev, with taking part in an organised criminal group headed by the gambling businessman Vasil Bozhkov. The commission licenses and inspects betting operators. Police raided it twice in January 2020, questioned 16 officials, and both men were placed under house arrest in February 2020. Bozhkov, charged in absentia with extortion and attempted bribery after leaving the country, denies wrongdoing and called the accusations ridiculous; no response from the two regulators is reported. He returned in August 2023, and in April 2024 prosecutors sent the case to court, with nine co-defendants including officials of the now-dissolved commission.
inside: Prosecutors say Bulgaria's richest gambling operator had the regulator's own inspection chief inside his criminal group, so the body policing him answered to him.
cite: OCCRP, 13 February 2020; Bulgarian National Radio, 23 April 2024
undone: No verdict has been reached and the defendants are presumed innocent. The case is being tried at the Sofia City Court, where at a hearing reported on 22 January 2026 the court was still waiting for conclusions on new expert examinations, only some of which were ready, and adjourned the case to 4 March; it also refused Bozhkov's request to lift his travel ban, finding no change in circumstances. Bozhkov is charged as an instigator acting in complicity with officials of the State Gambling Commission who, prosecutors say, let gambling fees under the Gambling Act go uncollected in full.

n: Russia's GRU sought Slovak parliament's secret reports via an MP's aide
rank: Parliamentary staff and classified annual reports
d: Slovak police and Special Prosecutor Daniel Lipsic announced on 15 March 2022 that Bohus Garbar, a former correspondent for the pro-Russian website Hlavne spravy, was charged with espionage and bribery. Police said that from about April 2021 he was an intelligence contact for Russia's GRU, and that he sought parliament's classified material, including the annual reports of Slovakia's secret services, through Jozef Mihalcin, an assistant to a lawmaker, and Bohus M., in the Slovak Intelligence Service until late 2021. Both were released without charge. Four Slovaks were accused in all; Lipsic said Garbar and a second defendant, Pavel Bucka, accused of passing NATO material since 2013, could face four to 13 years. In 2023 the court approved a plea bargain: three years suspended for three, and a 15,000 euro fine.
inside: Russian military intelligence used a journalist to reach a parliamentary aide and an intelligence service officer, to get the secret annual reports of Slovakia's spy agencies.
cite: Radio Slovakia International (STVR), 15 March 2022 and 1 March 2023

n: Poggiomarino mayor arrested over alleged mafia pact; council dissolved
rank: Mayor and council of Poggiomarino
d: Maurizio Falanga, then mayor of Poggiomarino in the province of Naples, was arrested in October, accused of taking part in a political-mafia pact - the Italian offence of trading votes delivered by a criminal group for favours from the person elected. On 27 March 2025 the Italian cabinet dissolved the town's council for mafia infiltration and handed it to government commissioners. Dissolution is ordered when an official inquiry finds that organised crime has conditioned a local administration's decisions. Poggiomarino was one of several councils in Campania, Lazio and Calabria dissolved in the same period. The allegations against Falanga have not been proven in court.
inside: Prosecutors say a mafia group and the mayor struck a deal over votes, so the town hall's decisions were open to the group that helped elect him.
cite: L'Indipendente, 19 April 2025 (reporting the 27 March 2025 cabinet session)

n: UN panel: Hezbollah-linked expert said to guide Houthi revenue committee
rank: Adviser to the Houthi committee on revenue and military spending
d: The United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen reported in October 2024 that a special committee had recently been set up to augment the Houthis' revenue and to plan military spending, including on weapons, allegedly under the guidance of a high-profile expert known as Abu Radwan, linked to the Radwan forces of the Lebanese armed movement Hizbullah. He reportedly provides advice on increasing customs duties, taxes, levies and telecommunications tariffs, and enhanced collections from telecommunications companies by almost 35 per cent. The same report places General Abdulreza Shalai of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Quds Force, and his deputy, a senior Hizbullah cadre, in the Houthi command and control structure, advising and assisting Abdulmalik al-Houthi. The report records no response from Hezbollah.
inside: UN investigators say a Hezbollah-linked expert is alleged to guide the committee raising Houthi customs duties, taxes and telephone tariffs and planning military spending.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2024/731, paras. 72 and 108 (October 2024)

n: Fake research jobs used to recruit Philippine defence staff for China
rank: Civilian employees of the defence department, navy and coast guard
d: In March 2026 Philippine investigators said civilian analysts at the Department of National Defense, the navy and the coast guard were recruited through fake research work. People posing as research staff found their resumes on sites like LinkedIn, commissioned geopolitical analysis, then asked about troop rotations, resupply schedules for the BRP Sierra Madre at Ayungin Shoal and personnel names at West Philippine Sea detachments. They reportedly passed material for more than two years, paid up to 100,000 pesos through e-wallets, messages hidden in a modified Tetris app. The National Security Council tied the operation to China and said it had terminated it, calling those involved low-level analysts who had confessed, and the case closed, involving three, though one report names four.
inside: Investigators say handlers posing as research clients paid defence and coast guard staff, so insiders passed out the navy's resupply plans.
cite: Daily Tribune, 'Spy recruitment ABCs targeting Pinoys bared', 8 March 2026

n: Taliban men inside Afghan army and police killed 115 troops in three months
rank: Soldiers and police inside the Afghan National Defence and Security Forces
d: Insider attacks are cases in which Afghanistan's security forces are targeted by Taliban infiltrators within their ranks. The Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction, the US auditor of Afghan war spending, reported on 30 April 2021 that such attacks rose 82 per cent in the first quarter of 2021 and that casualties from them roughly doubled. Coalition figures cited in the report counted 31 insider attacks in those three months, killing 115 Afghan military personnel and wounding 39. SIGAR said some of the underlying data is classified. All attacks on Afghan security forces were up 37 per cent on the same period a year earlier. The government fell in August 2021.
inside: The Taliban got its own fighters enlisted in the army and police, so soldiers on the state's payroll attacked the forces they had joined.
cite: SIGAR, Quarterly Report to the United States Congress, 30 April 2021, as reported by Al Jazeera

n: Launderers used a Citibank manager inside the bank in Singapore
rank: Relationship manager, Citibank Singapore
d: Wang Qiming, a relationship manager at Citibank in Singapore - the employee who opens and handles client accounts - got two years in October 2025, the longest term in the city's largest money-laundering case, with about 3 billion Singapore dollars seized. The court heard he helped the convicted launderer Su Baolin open an account and handle illicit cash, and forged transaction documents, cheating Citibank of over 8.5 million Singapore dollars in deposits. He pleaded guilty to four of ten charges; his lawyer said he would appeal, arguing he took only 700 to 800 Singapore dollars commission per transaction and did not benefit. The judge found he deliberately disguised the source of funds. Singapore's regulator penalised nine financial institutions over lapses in the case, including Citigroup's and Julius Baer's local units.
inside: The syndicate's money came through a banker inside Citibank who opened its accounts and faked the paperwork the bank used to check clients.
cite: Bloomberg, 'Ex-Citi Banker Gets Longest Sentence in Singapore Launder Case', 23 October 2025, republished by SWI swissinfo.ch

n: Brazil's football federation chief Jose Maria Marin took rights bribes
rank: President of the Brazilian Football Confederation (CBF)
d: The Brazilian Football Confederation, the CBF, runs football in Brazil and sells the rights to its competitions. Jose Maria Marin, its former president, was convicted in federal court in Brooklyn in December 2017 of racketeering conspiracy, three counts of wire fraud conspiracy and two counts of money laundering conspiracy. The court heard Traffic and the Brazilian marketing company Klefer paid him over the Copa do Brasil, the CBF's own cup competition, and that he accepted or agreed to accept millions of dollars in bribes in connection with the media and marketing rights to the Copa America and Copa Libertadores. He was sentenced on 22 August 2018 to four years in prison, a $1.2 million fine and $3,335,593 in forfeiture, and FIFA banned him from football for life in April 2019.
inside: Companies buying the rights to Brazilian and South American tournaments paid the head of the federation that sells the rights to its own competitions.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, press releases, 26 December 2017 and 22 August 2018

n: Venezuela's football federation president Rafael Esquivel pleaded guilty
org_label: sports marketing companies in the US FIFA case
rank: President of the Venezuelan football federation 1988-2015; vice president of CONMEBOL
d: Rafael Esquivel was president of Venezuela's national football federation from 1988 to 2015 and was vice president of CONMEBOL, the South American confederation, when he was arrested on 27 May 2015 in the US racketeering case. On 10 November 2016 he pleaded guilty in federal court in Brooklyn to racketeering conspiracy, three counts of wire fraud conspiracy and three counts of money laundering conspiracy, admitting he had taken millions of dollars in bribes from sports marketing companies in connection with the sale of media and marketing rights to tournaments including the Copa Libertadores and the Copa America. He agreed to forfeit more than $16 million. FIFA banned him from football for life in November 2017. No sentence has been reported.
inside: The companies buying South American tournament rights paid Venezuela's federation president, who was also a vice president of the confederation selling those rights.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, press release, 10 November 2016

n: US Imagina bribed Caribbean and Central American football officials for rights
rank: Officials of the Caribbean Football Union and four Central American federations
d: US Imagina, a Florida media company formerly Media World, majority-owned by the Barcelona group Mediapro, buys sports media rights. On 10 July 2018 it pleaded guilty to two counts of wire fraud conspiracy over two senior executives' part in schemes to pay more than $6.5 million in bribes to officials of the Caribbean Football Union and four Central American federations for World Cup qualifying rights. It paid $5,279,000 in forfeited proceeds, a $12,883,320 fine and $6,655,000 in restitution to those federations, about $24.8 million in all. Its chief executive Roger Huguet and the executive Fabio Tordin had pleaded guilty, the pleas unsealed in December 2015. Gerard Romy, Mediapro's co-chief executive, was indicted on 53 counts in March 2020 and was still at large as of 2024; those charges are untested.
inside: A broadcaster paid the football officials who controlled the rights it wanted, so the people selling those rights were working for the buyer.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, press release, 10 July 2018

n: Indonesia's ruling party bribed an election commissioner for a seat
rank: Commissioner of the General Elections Commission (KPU)
d: Indonesia's General Elections Commission, the KPU, decides who takes seats in parliament. On 25 July 2025 the Jakarta Corruption Court sentenced Hasto Kristiyanto, a senior figure in the governing Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle, to three years and six months and a 250 million rupiah fine for bribery. The judges found he handed 400 million rupiah, about $24,500, to the KPU commissioner Wahyu Setiawan to get a seat vacated by a lawmaker-elect's death in March 2019 given to a fellow party member, Harun Masiku. He was acquitted of obstruction of justice over the search for Masiku, a fugitive since January 2020. His party said the prosecution was politically motivated. Parliament approved an amnesty on 31 July 2025, he left prison the next day, and the KPK then ended the case.
inside: A governing party's cash bought a serving election commissioner, so the body that allots parliamentary seats awarded one to the party's man.
cite: Jakarta Post, 25 July 2025; Antara, 2 August 2025; Indonesian police news service, 2 August 2025

n: 66 officers at Romania's Siret border post indicted over smugglers' bribes
org_label: Organised smuggling networks at the Ukrainian border
rank: Siret customs post and border police
d: Anti-corruption prosecutors sent 62 border police officers and four customs officers from the Siret crossing, on Romania's border with Ukraine, for trial at the Suceava Appellate Court. They were charged with taking bribes, offering bribes and supporting criminal networks. Prosecutors said the police officers received or accepted money and goods worth 3,643,513 lei so that organised crime networks could pass the crossing without being checked. Forty-nine of those charged were in temporary arrest, that is pre-trial detention, and 17 were at liberty. Prosecutors alleged that the networks had bought the cooperation of officers at the post. The charges were untested when the file was sent to court, and the outcome of the Suceava case has not been traced.
inside: Prosecutors say smuggling networks paid dozens of officers at one border crossing, so the state's own checks there worked for the smugglers.
cite: Mediafax / HotNews.ro, 27 April 2011

n: Bulgarian prosecutor arrested as part of the Balbuzanov crime group
rank: Prosecutor, Pleven Regional Prosecutor's Office
d: Dimitar Zahariev, a prosecutor at the Pleven Regional Prosecutor's Office, was arrested on 6 June 2017 inside Sofia's Palace of Justice, where he was due in a trial. The Specialized Prosecutor's Office accused him of providing logistics to an organised criminal group headed by Kamen Balbuzanov, known as 'The Hook', which investigators said was broken up at the end of 2016; he also faced a charge of blackmailing a local doctor. A prisons department employee was taken into custody in Pleven in the same case, accused of threatening a witness. A prosecutor decides which cases are brought and how they are run, so a criminal group with a prosecutor inside can shape whether its members are charged. Last known position: the June 2017 arrest; the later outcome is unverified.
inside: A crime group is alleged to have had a serving prosecutor working for it, giving it a say inside the office that decides who gets charged.
cite: The Sofia Globe, 6 June 2017; BNT, 6 June 2017

n: Caserta city council dissolved for Camorra infiltration
rank: City council and departments of a provincial capital
d: The Italian cabinet dissolved the city council of Caserta, a provincial capital near Naples, for Camorra infiltration in 2025 and put an extraordinary commission in charge for 18 months. Italian law allows a council to be dissolved when an inquiry finds organised crime has conditioned its decisions. Inspectors had been inside the administration since the previous August. The inquiry pointed to figures connected to the Belforte clan backing the coalition that won the election. Two former members of the city executive, Massimiliano Marzo and Emiliano Casale, an official, Francesco Biondi, and eight others, including council employees and businessmen, are under investigation for alleged corruption, falsification and vote-buying; those allegations are untested. The mayor, Carlo Marino, called the decision political and said he would challenge it before the TAR Lazio.
inside: Inspectors found a Camorra clan's people had backed and reached inside a city administration, so council decisions and jobs were shaped to suit the clan.
cite: L'Indipendente, 19 April 2025; Council of Ministers decree

n: Bosnia's special police chief held over drug cartel ties
rank: Head of the Federation Special Police Unit; acting director of the Federation Police Directorate
d: On 22 April 2024 Bosnia's State Investigation and Protection Agency detained 22 people in Operation Black Tie 2 on suspicion of organised crime, drug trafficking and money laundering. Oslobodjenje named Mustafa Selmanovic, head of the Federation's Special Police Unit, and Vahidin Munjic, acting director of the Federation's Police Directorate, among them; Dnevni avaz named businessmen and a hospital manager in Zenica. Several special police officers allegedly acted as bodyguards for Edin 'Tito' Gacanin in 2016. The US Treasury blacklisted his 'Tito and Dino' clan in March 2023, alleging close links to the Kinahan cartel. Rotterdam sentenced him in absentia in November 2023 to seven years and a one million euro fine; arrested in Dubai in 2022 and bailed in January 2024, his whereabouts are unknown. No charges have been traced.
inside: Suspects detained on suspicion of drug trafficking and money laundering included the heads of the federation's special police unit and police directorate, whose officers allegedly guarded the cartel's leader.
cite: OCCRP, April 2024; SIPA, RFE/RL

n: UN sources place a Quds Force general over Houthi military commands
rank: Adviser to the Houthi leader, supervising aerospace and naval forces
d: Several confidential sources told the United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen, in its October 2024 report, that General Abdulreza Shalai of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Quds Force plays a predominant role: operating under the title jihad assistant, he advises and assists the Houthi leader Abdulmalik al-Houthi and allegedly supervises the aerospace forces, meaning missiles and drones, the naval forces and all military regions, along with mobilisation and logistics. His deputy is described as a senior Hezbollah cadre, and the Panel reports that Hezbollah takes part in Houthi decision-making. The Panel also reports that Iraqi armed groups have sent experts and combatants to Yemen since 2015, and that the Popular Mobilization Forces recently trained about 80 Houthi combatants at the Bahbahan centre in Jurf al-Sakhr, in Iraq.
inside: UN investigators report a foreign officer at the top of the Houthi command, where Iran's Quds Force is said to shape its missile and naval forces.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2024/731, paras. 14, 20 and 72 (October 2024)

n: Azerbaijan's security service says a ministry department head spied for foreign agencies
rank: Department head, Ministry of National Security
d: Azerbaijan's State Security Service said in December 2018 that Zakir Ismayilov, born in 1959, a former department head who held other senior posts in the former Ministry of National Security, was recruited by foreign intelligence agencies under a pseudonym and passed them information from his posts, personnel information and other secret data while in office. After retiring in 2015 he is said to have reported on changes in Azerbaijan's security agencies and methods that could be used against them. He was arrested and prosecuted for treason under article 274 of the criminal code. The service did not name the country involved, and named a second man, Bahruz Yusifzade, prosecuted under the same article. The claim rests on the service's own statement; the accused's response and the outcome are not known.
inside: Azerbaijan's security service says a foreign spy service recruited a serving department head inside its own ministry, who passed out personnel files and other secrets.
cite: Trend.az, 'State Security Service unveils multi-stage espionage against Azerbaijan', 27 December 2018

n: 78 Lao border officers disciplined for waving Chinese nationals through
rank: Police and immigration officers at the Boten checkpoint
d: Laos disciplined 78 officers, 77 serving police and immigration officers and one former officer, for taking bribes to let Chinese nationals cross at Boten, on the Chinese border, without visas or passports. Most of those punished worked in Bokeo province's Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone, a gambling and tourism hub for Chinese visitors, though the Boten checkpoint itself sits in Luang Namtha province. A Luang Namtha provincial police notice of 7 June 2023 set out the penalties: five officers lost their Lao People's Revolutionary Party membership and their jobs or pensions, and 73 were suspended from the party for six months, demoted or moved. All had to sign notes acknowledging the penalty. A provincial official told Radio Free Asia it was kept quiet because of the many ongoing investigations.
inside: People paying to cross unchecked had bought the officers at the border post, so Laos's own immigration control let them in and out unrecorded.
cite: Radio Free Asia, 'Laos punished 78 border security officers for bribery in June', 6 November 2023

n: Fish exporter and a Tunisian customs officer jailed over false exports
rank: Customs executive at the Dhehiba border post
d: The financial-corruption chamber of the Tunis Court of First Instance sentenced a former customs executive posted at the Dhehiba crossing to five years in prison, and the owner of a group of companies exporting tuna and sardines to seven years, in a judgment delivered late on 2 October 2025. They were convicted of misuse of office and falsification of customs documents for private interests, to the detriment of the administration: the officer had applied the customs revenue office stamp to two declarations recording exports of tuna and sardines that had never passed through the Dhehiba post, giving them an appearance of regularity. Neither man was named in the ruling as reported. The report rests on a single judicial source, and no appeal outcome has been traced.
inside: An exporter had the customs officer at the border stamp paperwork for shipments that never crossed, so the state certified exports that did not exist.
cite: Diwan FM, reported by Tunisie Numerique, 'Tunisie - Corruption douaniere: 5 ans de prison pour un ancien cadre, 7 ans pour un homme d'affaires', 3 October 2025

n: Suppliers put a UN procurement chief on their payroll for contracts
rank: Chief of the Commodity Procurement Section, UN Procurement Division
d: Sanjaya Bahel ran the commodity procurement section of the UN Procurement Division, which buys goods and services for the organisation's operations worldwide. A jury convicted him on 7 June 2007 of mail and wire fraud, conspiracy and accepting corrupt payments, and on 1 April 2008 he was sentenced to 97 months in prison. He had helped companies owned or represented by the businessman Nishan Kohli and his relatives win contracts worth tens of millions of dollars, giving them inside information, advice on bid prices and help with UN problems, and ghost-writing their correspondence with the UN. In return he received cash, first-class flights, a computer and a discounted three-bedroom apartment, benefits worth hundreds of thousands of dollars. He forfeited $103,500 and the apartment.
inside: Suppliers paid the official who decided UN purchases, so the UN bought from them on terms he shaped from inside the buying office.
cite: US Attorney, Southern District of New York, sentencing release, 1 April 2008

n: World Bank staff took kickbacks to steer Africa contracts to Swedish firms
org_label: Swedish consultants and companies in World Bank tenders
rank: World Bank trust funds manager and task manager
d: The World Bank lends money for projects in poorer countries and its staff manage the contracts. Ramendra Basu, a World Bank trust funds manager, conspired between 1997 and 2000 with a Swedish consultant and others to steer Bank-financed contracts for work in Ethiopia and Kenya to particular Swedish companies, taking $127,000 in kickbacks. He also helped the consultants bribe a Kenyan government official, arranging a $50,000 wire transfer abroad for the official's benefit. Basu pleaded guilty on 17 December 2002 and was sentenced on 22 April 2008 to 15 months in prison. A colleague, task manager Gautam Sengupta, pleaded guilty to the same charges in February 2002 and was sentenced in February 2006. Sweden prosecuted and convicted the consultants.
inside: Contractors paid World Bank staff who chose who won Bank-funded work, so the loans bought services from the firms that paid them.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 22 April 2008

n: Romania's ex-transport minister sent to trial over an RAR bribe offer
rank: Former Minister of Transport; director of the Romanian Automobile Registry
d: The Romanian Automobile Registry, RAR, is the state body that certifies vehicle roadworthiness. In September 2025 it opened a public procurement worth about 23 million lei including VAT for maintenance of the equipment used to test and diagnose vehicles. Anticorruption prosecutors say that between September and November 2025 Catalin Daniel Buse, administrator of Euro Quip International SRL, which wanted its framework agreement renewed, promised RAR's director general 6 per cent of the contract's value - about 1.3 million lei - and that Alexandru-Razvan Cuc, a former Social Democrat transport minister, brokered the approach as a private intermediary. The director general, Mihai Alecu, reported it and is a witness, so no official was bought.
inside: A former transport minister is accused of brokering a 6 per cent cut to the head of the body that certifies vehicle roadworthiness; the official reported the offer instead.
cite: DNA communiqués of 16 December 2025 and 9 February 2026, reported by Radio Europa Liberă România, HotNews and Digi24; Ziare.com, 5 February and 13 November 2026
undone: No verdict. The National Anticorruption Directorate detained Cuc and Buse for 24 hours on 16 December 2025, Buse for giving a bribe and Cuc for complicity in giving a bribe, and on 9 February 2026 sent both for trial while they were held in preventive arrest; the file went to the Bucharest Tribunal. Cuc says the whistleblower provoked him into the offer and has asked the court to refer a question to the Constitutional Court. Both are presumed innocent. Because the offer was reported rather than accepted, this record describes an attempt on the institution, not a completed capture of it.

n: Houthis run Yemenia Airways through loyalists and hold its $100m
rank: Operational management of the state airline
d: Yemenia Airways is Yemen's state-owned airline; its board of directors sits in Aden under the internationally recognised government. The United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen reported in October 2024 that the Houthi movement took over the running of the company in Sanaa through loyal staff and refused to recognise the Aden board, and that aircraft were detained at Sanaa airport on 25 and 26 June 2024. On instructions from the Houthi-appointed finance ministry, the central bank branch in Sanaa told commercial banks to suspend the airline's payments, leaving about 100 million dollars of its money under Houthi control for more than a year.
inside: An armed movement put its own people in charge of a state airline whose legal board sits elsewhere, and the company's cash then stayed in its hands.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2024/731, paras. 115-118 (October 2024)
undone: The Panel's next final report, S/2025/650 of 17 October 2025, said that as at 1 August 2024 the Houthis still held $120 million belonging to Yemenia Airways frozen, and that the company had no information about the state of that money because its access to its own financial and administrative systems in Sana'a was blocked. The same report said Israeli strikes on Sana'a international airport in May 2025 destroyed Yemenia aircraft there, including two in one attack and the last remaining one in a later strike, leaving the airline with no working aircraft in Sana'a and three in Aden. This is the finding of a UN panel, not of any court, and no case has been brought over it.

n: Foreign bidders and two Nepali telecom regulators convicted over contract
org_label: Nuemera SDN Berhad, Namaste Global Communication and OSI Consulting joint venture
rank: Chairmen of the Nepal Telecommunications Authority
d: Nepal's Special Court convicted two former chairmen of the Nepal Telecommunications Authority, Digambar Jha and Purushottam Khanal, a Malaysian national, Mohammad Nur Amin, and a joint venture of the Malaysian firm Nuemera SDN Berhad, Namaste Global Communication of Singapore and OSI Consulting of India, on 6 March 2025. The authority regulates telecoms and was setting up a Mobile Device Management System to stop grey-market phone imports. In June 2019 it disqualified the lowest bidder, which had offered 7.66 million dollars, and gave the contract to the joint venture. Nepal's anti-corruption commission alleged inflated cost estimates, manual bids in breach of the procurement law, fabricated documents and collusion to hide the partners' shortcomings. The court put the loss to the state at 232 million rupees. Fourteen other defendants were acquitted.
inside: A foreign consortium got the regulator's own chairmen to disqualify the cheapest bidder and hand it the phone-tracking contract instead.
cite: Kathmandu Post, 'Court convicts Nepali officials, foreign firms in MDMS corruption case', 7 March 2025

n: Seven Kuwaiti judges jailed for taking gifts from a laundering suspect
rank: Seven serving judges
d: Kuwait's Court of Cassation upheld seven-year prison terms for seven judges who took vehicles and gifts from Fouad Salehi, an Iranian national arrested by the interior ministry in August 2020 and accused of money laundering and of bribing Kuwaiti officials. Investigators said his communications linked him to ten judges. It was the first time Kuwait lifted judicial immunity, and the Court of Appeal ordered the seven dismissed from the bench and the gifts returned. Two businessmen were given twelve years each with fines, a lawyer ten years and a government department head seven. One judge's acquittal was upheld. The ruling was reported in October 2023.
inside: A money-laundering suspect handed cars and gifts to serving judges, putting his network inside the court that would decide cases touching it.
cite: Gulf News, 'Kuwait landmark verdict: Seven judges sentenced to seven years over bribery scandal', 20 October 2023

n: Huawei and ZTE men convicted over $10m to a former Algerie Telecom executive
rank: former Algerie Telecom executive
d: An Algerian court sentenced two ZTE executives, Dong Tao and Chen Zhibo, and Huawei's Xiao Chunfa to ten years in jail in their absence for corruption and influence peddling, with international arrest warrants issued, fines of three million dinars each and a two-year ban on the firms from public tenders. Mohamed Boukhari, a former executive of the state operator Algerie Telecom, and a businessman, Chami Madjdoub, each got 18 years and a five million dinar fine over suspicious payments and money laundering between 2003 and 2006. The report alleges the Chinese executives paid $10m into offshore accounts set up by Madjdoub for Boukhari. The Register attributes these details to the French-language site Presse-DZ and does not independently verify them.
inside: Two Chinese telecoms suppliers allegedly routed $10m to an executive of Algeria's state operator, whose contract decisions then favoured them.
cite: The Register, 12 June 2012, citing Presse-DZ

n: Chinese loggers reported bribing Congolese officials over concessions and over-quota logging
org_label: Wan Peng and Booming Green (Booming Group)
rank: officials controlling forest concession allocation and harvest oversight
d: The Environmental Investigation Agency's October 2024 report examines two Chinese-owned loggers in the Democratic Republic of Congo: Wan Peng and Booming Green, of the Booming Group. An insider said Wan Peng got a concession during the moratorium on new industrial concessions, in place since 2002, by buying an old one and bribing officials: 'Yeah, we have bribed the General, equivalent to the military chairman in China', which the report calls an apparent reference to General Gabriel Amisi Kumba, unconfirmed independently. Another insider described payments covering over-quota harvesting and misdeclared species, naming no recipients. A January 2024 government audit documented illegalities at two Wan Peng subsidiaries, Congo King Baisheng and Congo Sunflower, including acquisition through influence peddling and in violation of regulations, and a fraudulent acquisition by Booming Green in Mai-Ndombe.
inside: Logging firms allegedly paid officials to obtain concessions during a moratorium and to cover harvesting above quota and misdeclared species.
cite: Environmental Investigation Agency, 'Until the Last Log', October 2024

n: Armed group commander Johnson Olony made one of South Sudan's deputy army chiefs
rank: Deputy Chief of Defence Forces, SSPDF (one of several such posts)
d: The UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan reported, in its final report of 1 July 2025, that Johnson Olony was made an SSPDF Deputy Chief of Defence Forces in January 2025, one of several such posts, and that his Agwelek forces are being integrated into the army. The Panel says the appointment carried responsibility for dismantling illegal checkpoints and disarming civilians, and that his presence in Malakal in February 2025 led to further mobilisation among local youth. Reporting that he was deployed to disarm Nuer youth and seize checkpoints along the Sobat River came from local observers, corroborated by photographs on file with the Panel. The army has continued integrating defectors from the National Salvation Front and the Agwelek forces under Olony, who secured his own agreement in 2023.
inside: An armed group's commander was made one of the army's deputy chiefs and his own fighters were integrated into its ranks.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan, final report S/2025/442, 1 July 2025

n: Wagner proxies given ministerial posts in the Central African Republic
rank: livestock minister; delegated minister for disarmament
d: The Sentry's June 2023 report says Hassan Bouba, appointed livestock minister in the Central African Republic, has been acting as a Wagner proxy, and that Hamza Gilbert Toumou Deya was awarded the position of delegated minister in charge of disarmament for working in the interest of President Faustin-Archange Touadera and Wagner. It also says a former anti-Balaka member nicknamed Yarkopa was appointed head of Unite 124, a unit the report says has not been publicly acknowledged, with several sources saying the Wagner-linked figure Wananga helped secure the appointment. The report says Wagner's top country representatives also serve as Touadera's special advisers. Its findings rest largely on confidential documents and interviews with named and unnamed sources.
inside: A foreign paramilitary group's proxies were given cabinet and command posts, the report says, including a livestock minister it describes as acting for Wagner.
cite: The Sentry, 'Architects of Terror', June 2023

n: Four Jamaican narcotics detectives charged under the Anti-Gang Act
org_label: Unnamed criminal organisation cited in the charge
rank: Firearms and Narcotics Investigation Division detectives
d: Four members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force's Firearms and Narcotics Investigation Division, Detective Sergeant James Dawes, Detective Corporal Tamela Anderson, Detective Constable Shane Givans and Constable Lakarie Barrett, were charged on 8 April 2025 after a Director of Public Prosecutions ruling earlier that week. The charges are facilitating the commission of a serious offence by a criminal organisation, forgery, uttering forged documents and perverting the course of justice. It is alleged that in 2023 the officers were investigating a Trelawny woman for suspected drug trafficking and she was taken into custody; her mother said a policeman told her the daughter would be released if money was paid, and she was freed without charge. It was reportedly discovered that the four accused had prepared the forged document used to release her.
inside: Prosecutors say serving narcotics detectives forged a document to free a trafficking suspect, and charged them with helping a criminal organisation from inside the police.
undone: Each officer was offered J$2m bail at the Supreme Court, after an application by attorneys Christopher Townsend and Chadwick Berry, and the case was set to return to court on 21 May 2025. Their lawyer argued there is no evidence of gang involvement.
cite: Radio Jamaica News (RJR), 10 April 2025

n: Costa Rica arrests two judges and an investigator over a trafficking group
rank: criminal court judges and an OIJ agent
d: Costa Rican prosecutors arrested two criminal judges, named only by the surnames Valverde and Ramirez, one of whom reportedly coordinates the Pococi criminal court, and an agent of the Organismo de Investigacion Judicial, the judicial police, surnamed Rojas. The arrests came on 1 September 2026 in a raid on the Juzgado Penal de Pococi, in Limon province. The Fiscalia Adjunta de Probidad, Transparencia y Anticorrupcion says the three used their posts to collaborate with the group led by Alejandro Arias Monge, known as Diablo, who was captured on 24 July 2026 in Sarapiqui, and which it describes as trafficking drugs locally and internationally. It is investigating whether they accepted gifts and neglected their duties. The suspected offences are procuring impunity in drug cases, bribery, bribe-giving and misuse of public resources.
inside: Prosecutors say a trafficking group reached inside a criminal court and the judicial police, so judges and an investigator worked to keep its members out of prison.
cite: Observador.cr, September 2026

n: Palau land authority chairman accused of leasing to a Chinese national for payment
org_label: Chinese national leasing Palauan public land
rank: chairman of Aimeliik's State Public Land Authority; Speaker of the House of Delegates
d: The US State Department's 2023 human rights report for Palau says local media covered the chairman of Aimeliik's State Public Land Authority, Clarence Sriderio Renggulbai, reporting that he leased land in September 2022 to a Chinese national without proper approvals and received direct payment. The same report says that on 4 August the Office of the Special Prosecutor charged House of Delegates Speaker Sabino Anastacio with misconduct in public office for leasing land without a business license. The report gives no amounts, does not name the lessee, and gives no outcome for either matter. The accounts were also collected in a U4 Anti-Corruption Helpdesk review of corruption in Pacific island countries, which does not name the officials.
inside: A Chinese national is reported to have paid a Palauan state land authority chairman directly, and public land was leased without the proper approvals.
cite: US Department of State, 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Palau; also U4 Anti-Corruption Helpdesk, Caitlin Maslen, 3 February 2026

n: US money-laundering charges: bribes alleged to have won CLAP food contracts
org_label: Contractors led by Alvaro Pulido Vargas
who: contractors led by Alvaro Pulido Vargas
rank: Venezuelan officials including Jose Gregorio Vielma-Mora
d: A federal grand jury in Florida charged five people in October 2021 with money laundering, alleging that from about July 2015 Alvaro Pulido Vargas and three others bribed Venezuelan officials, among them their co-defendant Jose Gregorio Vielma-Mora, to win CLAP contracts and inflated the costs to cover the payments. The bribery is alleged underlying conduct rather than a charge. A separate 2023 information names the buyer: COBISERTA, owned and controlled by the state of Tachira. On about 14 October 2016 it gave Pulido Vargas's Group Grand Limited a contract for about 10 million boxes at $34 each, some $340 million. Vielma-Mora, Tachira's governor from about 2012 to 2017, oversaw COBISERTA's contracting. Orlando Alfonso Contreras Saab, who forwarded his bribes, pleaded guilty in November 2023 and was sentenced in February 2024.
inside: Prosecutors say contractors paid the governor who oversaw a Venezuelan state food buyer, which then awarded them $340 million of contracts at inflated prices.
undone: The Justice Department announced on 11 October 2026 that Pulido Vargas was in the Southern District of Florida to face the 2021 charges, with an initial appearance set for 13 October 2026. Each of the five counts carries a maximum of 20 years. No disposition is recorded for the other defendants.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 21 October 2021; US Department of Justice press release 26-1168, 11 October 2026. US Department of Justice, criminal information in United States v. Orlando Alfonso Contreras Saab, Southern District of Florida, case 23-20364-CR-RUIZ/BECERRA, docketed 11 September 2023, paragraphs 3, 7, 10 and 12; DOJ Fraud Section FCPA case page for the same matter, giving the guilty plea of 2 November 2023 and the sentence of 16 February 2024

n: Yara offered a fertiliser ministry official's son a paid engagement
rank: Additional Secretary and Financial Adviser, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers
d: In the same case, Norway's Supreme Court said Yara International's then chief legal officer and a colleague offered a representative engagement to the son of an Indian official, Additional Secretary and Financial Adviser in the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers and a government-appointed board member of KRIBHCO, a fertiliser cooperative 67 per cent owned by the Indian state. The offer was linked to the father's position: a US$250,000 lump sum plus 50 cents a tonne of Yara fertiliser sold in India. A later draft replaced the lump sum with US$3 million, in US$1 million instalments for 2007 to 2009. On 16 October 2007 US$1 million went to Krystal Holdings & Investments Limited's Hong Kong account, a British Virgin Islands company whose beneficiaries were the official's and his son's spouses.
inside: Yara's money was aimed at an official who advised India's fertiliser ministry and sat on a state-owned producer's board, to strengthen Yara's position there.
cite: Supreme Court of Norway, HR-2017-1776-A, judgment of 15 September 2017 (official English translation)

n: Banker settled SEC case alleging $2.5m reached Ghanaian officials and MPs over a power plant
org_label: Asante Berko and a Turkish energy company
who: a Turkish energy company and the banker Asante Berko
rank: members of the Ghanaian parliament and officials approving a power plant
d: The US Securities and Exchange Commission charged Asante Berko, a former executive of a foreign-based subsidiary of a US bank holding company, on 13 April 2020 with violating the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act's anti-bribery provisions. The complaint, filed in the Eastern District of New York, says Berko arranged for his client, a Turkish energy company, to send at least $2.5 million to a Ghana-based intermediary, which used it to bribe Ghanaian officials into approving an electrical power plant project. The intermediary allegedly paid more than $200,000 to various other officials, and Berko more than $60,000 himself to members of Ghana's parliament and other officials. The SEC also alleged he misled his employer's compliance staff about the intermediary's role, and said those staff kept the firm out of the transaction.
inside: The SEC says a banker channelled a client's money to Ghanaian MPs and officials so they would approve the power plant his client wanted built.
undone: Berko consented to a final judgment on 23 June 2021, permanently enjoining him from violating the FCPA anti-bribery provision, Section 30A of the Exchange Act, and ordering $275,000 in disgorgement plus $54,163.92 in prejudgment interest, $329,163.92 in all. The litigation release records no admission.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission press release 2020-88, 13 April 2020; SEC litigation release 25121, 23 June 2021

n: Church circulated notices recruiting believers as Diet members' secretaries
rank: secretary to a House of Representatives member
d: Shimbun Akahata obtained notices it says Unification Church members circulated in spring 2013 among second-generation believers, recruiting them as secretaries to Japan's lower house members. One, headed House of Representatives secretary recruitment, said a young believer already secretary to a lower house member had made contact, and asked readers to introduce candidates, describing the lawmaker, not a believer, as strict and promising for a party's future plans. Neither notice names the lawmaker or the party. Another, addressed to students wanting to become politicians, said a lower house member elected in Kanagawa prefecture - written with a question mark - was looking for secretaries. The paper reported the church has sent believers as campaign workers and secretaries, and that its sources say it sought closeness to LDP and other lawmakers.
cite: Shimbun Akahata, 17 October 2022
inside: The church circulated notices recruiting second-generation believers into jobs as lawmakers' secretaries, seeking to place its people in Japan's parliamentary offices.

n: Chinese timber group Dejia reported bribing Gabonese ministers
rank: government ministers in Gabon and the Republic of Congo
d: A 2019 report by the Environmental Investigation Agency, a campaign group, said Dejia, described as one of China's most influential groups of affiliated timber companies in Africa, regularly bribed Gabonese and Congolese ministers to access timber concessions and manage them without controls. Mongabay, reporting the claim in May 2023, said the agency also found that illegally sourced Dejia timber reached the European Union and the United States, and that the practices cost Gabon millions of dollars.
inside: A Chinese timber group is reported to have paid ministers who hand out logging rights, so its concessions were granted and left unchecked.
cite: Mongabay, 10 May 2023, citing Environmental Investigation Agency, Toxic Trade: Forest Crime in Gabon and the Republic of Congo and Contamination of the U.S. Market (2019)

n: Haftar-linked men took over Benghazi's Bank of Commerce and Development
org_label: Khalifa and Saddam Haftar's circle and the financier Ahmed Gadalla
rank: chairmanship and de facto control of a commercial bank
d: The Sentry's April 2026 report says figures linked to Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar's forces forced Jamal Tayeb Abdel Malek, founder of Benghazi's Bank of Commerce and Development, to surrender his shares in 2022. Wassim al-Zway, a Haftar loyalist, became chairman on paper, while the report says genuine authority flowed to Saddam Haftar's circle and the Dubai-based financier Ahmed Gadalla, who became the bank's de facto chief. Russia's state printer Goznak began shipping billions in dinar banknotes to Haftar's camp as early as May 2016, roughly 14 billion dinars entering circulation this way, and after 2023 occasionally smuggled pallets of high-grade notes in. Injections of unauthorised dinars reached about 10 billion in circulation by October 2025, mainly in two categories of new 50-dinar notes, which the report says Gadalla oversaw distributing.
inside: An armed faction's financiers took a commercial bank's shares and chairmanship, so its money and banknote supply served the Haftar family's forces.
cite: The Sentry, 'Eastern Libya's Top Money Man', April 2026

n: Uganda police convicted of guarding a gold fraud syndicate's refinery
org_label: alleged gold fraud syndicate around Real Sunnex Ltd
rank: four police constables, called counter-terrorism officers in the article's photo caption
d: Uganda's Police Disciplinary Court convicted four police constables on 29 August 2026 after they left their assigned beats and, police say, self-deployed to support a gold fraud syndicate, guarding an illegal gold refinery linked to a $4m fraudulent transaction. Police Spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke said two of them, Kulutu Ayubu and Waiswa Benon, were recommended for dismissal and two, Waiswa Siraj and Emorut Razak, for discharge. A Dubai-based businessman complained in July 2025 that Asiimwe Moses and others operating under Real Sunnex Ltd had taken $4m from him in a bogus gold deal, and police said the syndicate was preparing to take a further $4m. A sting led to 16 arrests, and the four officers and 12 civilian suspects are being processed for criminal trial; no denials are reported.
inside: A fraud ring had serving police officers guarding its fake-gold refinery, so state force protected the swindle instead of stopping it.
cite: Daily Monitor (Uganda), 31 August 2026

n: Wagner firms granted CAR mining permits; report says they shaped mining law
rank: mining ministry decisions and state mining company GEMINCA
d: The Sentry's June 2023 report says Wagner-affiliated companies Lobaye Invest, Midas Ressources and Diamville were granted mining licences and export authorisations in the Central African Republic, which it calls de facto authorisations to exploit and loot the country's wealth for protecting Faustin-Archange Touadera. It says the Ndassima deposit's exploitation permit was transferred to Midas in 2020, apparently without legal basis, and that Midas reportedly obtained a decree and a mining convention, the decree confirming a 25-year gold exploitation permit; a December 2020 note from the mines minister to Touadera described Midas as a Russian company. It also says Wagner tried to influence the revision of mining legislation, citing a confidential document by alleged Wagner authors recommending the state control artisanal miners and make state company GEMINCA the main buyer.
inside: Wagner's companies were granted state mining permits by decree, and The Sentry says Wagner worked to shape the mining law that would govern them.
cite: The Sentry, 'Architects of Terror', June 2023

n: Bahamas defence force officer sold patrol positions to traffickers
org_label: Cocaine conspiracy prosecuted in the Southern District of New York
rank: chief petty officer, Royal Bahamas Defence Force
d: Darrin Alexander Roker, 56, a former chief petty officer in the Royal Bahamas Defence Force, pleaded guilty in a New York court to one count of cocaine importation conspiracy. He told the court he gave traffickers information on where Bahamian law enforcement vessels were so their boats could avoid interception, and prosecutors say he was paid 20,000 dollars. He is the first of thirteen defendants to plead guilty. Prosecutors allege the conspiracy moved tons of cocaine through the Bahamas into the United States between 2021 and 2024 and also included police officers; Chief Superintendent Elvis Nathaniel Curtis and former sergeant Prince Albert Symonette are accused of taking bribes to move shipments through Nassau. Roker faced up to twenty years and a $1 million fine.
inside: Traffickers paid a serving naval officer for the positions of Bahamian patrol boats, turning the force meant to stop them into their lookout.
undone: At a hearing on 21 January 2026 before Judge Gregory Woods, Roker was sentenced to 48 months in prison. Prosecutors had sought at least five years and called his stage-four metastatic prostate cancer a powerful mitigating factor.
cite: Eyewitness News Bahamas (undated), 'Former Defence Force Officer Pleads Guilty in U.S. Cocaine Smuggling Case'; sentence from ZNS Bahamas, 22 January 2026, and Tribune242, 19 January 2026
