n: Operation Leviathan: traffickers' people inside Costa Rica's Moin container port
org_label: Cocaine export network using the Moin container terminal
rank: border police officers and terminal staff at Moin
d: Costa Rica's organised crime prosecution unit, FAEDO, says a network used the Moin container terminal at Limon, operated by APM Terminals, to ship cocaine to Europe and the United States. Investigators say ten border police officers let containers in and out without triggering alerts, allegedly for payment, alongside thirteen private security officers, twelve tractor-unit drivers, crane operators and operational supervisors. The group charged about $250,000 a shipment, whatever the quantity of cocaine, hiding loads under 60 kilos in refrigeration units or removing containers, loading them at properties in Limon and returning them, a method investigators call mete y saca. The investigation has run since 2023; on 28 July 2026 the Fiscalia, with the PCD and OIJ, made 65 raids and 43 arrests. The reporting does not accuse APM Terminals itself.
inside: Prosecutors allege border police and terminal staff at Costa Rica's main container port were paid to let the network's containers pass unchecked.
cite: Observador.cr, 28 July 2026

n: Alstom Power paid Lithuanian power station officials and politicians
rank: officials of a state power station and senior politicians
d: Alstom Power Ltd, the British arm of the French engineering group Alstom, pleaded guilty at a London court on 10 May 2016 to conspiring to corrupt officials at a Lithuanian power station and senior Lithuanian politicians. The Serious Fraud Office said the Alstom companies paid more than EUR 5 million in bribes across the investigation, to secure EUR 325 million of contracts, including two Lithuanian contracts worth EUR 240 million, one of them to upgrade the burners at the Lithuanian Power Plant, and falsified records to get past anti-bribery checks. Alstom Power Ltd was ordered to pay GBP 18,038,000 in total: a GBP 6,375,000 fine, GBP 10,963,000 compensation to the Lithuanian government and GBP 700,000 in prosecution costs.
inside: Alstom's money reached officials of a state power station and senior politicians, who then awarded the firm EUR 240 million of Lithuanian power contracts.
undone: Two men had been jailed on this charge set as of December 2018: John Venskus (3 years 6 months, sentenced 4 May 2018) and Goran Wikstrom (2 years 7 months, sentenced 9 July 2018, plus GBP 40,000 costs). Nicholas Reynolds, Alstom Power's former global sales director, was convicted at Blackfriars Crown Court on 19 December 2018 and sentenced on 21 December 2018 to 4 years 6 months, with GBP 50,000 in costs.
cite: UK Serious Fraud Office, 'Five convictions in SFO's Alstom investigation into bribery & corruption to secure EUR 325 million of contracts', 19 December 2018; SFO, 'Former Alstom Power Global Sales Director sentenced to 4.5 years for corruption', 21 December 2018

n: Scoular paid Mexican border inspectors to pass its grain trains
org_label: The Scoular Company, a US agricultural trader
rank: Mexican officials inspecting shipments at the border
d: The Scoular Company, an agricultural supply chain firm in Omaha, Nebraska, entered a three-year deferred prosecution agreement with the US Justice Department on one count of conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. Between 2013 and 2019 Scoular authorised third-party customs brokers to bribe Mexican officials at the border so its trains of corn and other products crossed despite inspections finding dirt, soil and other impurities. The brokers paid about $2,000 per train and invoiced it back to Scoular as reinspection fees. In all Scoular authorised more than $400,000 in bribes, avoided more than $6.5 million in fees and costs, and agreed to a $9,769,521 penalty and $414,351 in forfeiture. Scoular got no credit for voluntary disclosure, the department said, because its disclosure was neither voluntary nor timely.
inside: The firm's brokers paid Mexican border inspectors, so the state's own inspection decisions let its failed grain shipments through.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 17 July 2026

n: SNC-Lavalin paid $22.5m to the McGill hospital's chief and a manager
rank: chief executive and a senior manager of the McGill University Health Centre
d: The McGill University Health Centre is a public hospital group in Montreal. An agreed statement of facts says the engineering firm SNC-Lavalin paid $22.5 million that Arthur Porter, the centre's chief executive, and the senior manager Yanai Elbaz received to rig bidding on the $1.3 billion contract to build a new hospital; Porter funnelled the money through a shell company and Elbaz took his share through his own. Elbaz pleaded guilty in December 2018 to accepting a bribe and got 39 months. The former SNC-Lavalin executive Riadh Ben Aissa was sentenced to 51 months for using forged documents. The former chief executive Pierre Duhaime pleaded guilty on 1 February 2019 to helping a public servant commit breach of trust. Porter died in 2015 while a fugitive in Panamanian custody.
inside: The contractor's money bought the hospital's own chief executive and a senior manager, who then shaped the tender so the firm won the building contract.
undone: On 1 February 2019 a Quebec judge accepted a joint Crown and defence recommendation and sentenced Duhaime to 20 months of house arrest, 240 hours of community service and a $200,000 donation to a fund compensating crime victims, with no jail time; 14 of the 15 original charges against him were withdrawn.
cite: The Canadian Press via Global News, 1 February 2019; sentence from CBC News, 1 February 2019

n: Prosecutors allege Equalize paid serving police and tax-police officers for database files
rank: Guardia di Finanza marshal; state police superintendent and inspector; Carabinieri NCO
d: Milan prosecutors allege that the private intelligence firm Equalize had serving officers of Italy's state agencies on its payroll to pull confidential files. Named as suspects in October 2024 were Giuliano Schiano, a Guardia di Finanza maresciallo assigned to the DIA in Lecce; Marco Malerba, a Polizia di Stato sovrintendente at the Rho-Pero commissariato; Roberto Bonacina, a Polizia di Stato ispettore at the border police office at Orio al Serio airport; and Saverio Penna, a Carabinieri non-commissioned officer in the investigative unit in Milan. Open reported that Schiano and Malerba were regularly paid by the investigations firm for non-public information about the targets of the dossier operations, drawn from the interior ministry's SDI database and the tax agency's Punto Fisco system, and that Malerba's son was hired off the books.
cite: Open, 27 October 2024; Milano Finanza, 21 July 2026; ANSA via La Voce di New York, 9 April 2026
inside: Prosecutors say a private firm put serving police and tax-police officers on its payroll so state databases were searched for its paying clients.
undone: The four officers have not been tried. In April 2026 Milan prosecutors asked for Equalize's former owner Enrico Pazzali to be committed for trial and closed a second strand covering 81 suspects; in July 2026 they sought trial for 74 defendants, with 832 people named as alleged victims of the spying, and six plea agreements were filed for a judge to weigh. The position of a Guardia di Finanza general was severed and sent to Rome. The reports read do not say whether the four officers are among the 74, and all are presumed innocent.

n: US and UK sanction Kamlesh Pattni over bribes in Zimbabwe's gold trade
org_label: Kamlesh Pattni's gold and diamond network
rank: officials in Zimbabwe (Al Jazeera reported bribery at the national gold refinery)
d: The United States and the United Kingdom sanctioned the Kenyan-British businessman Kamlesh Pattni, freezing assets, confiscating property and imposing travel bans, reported on 10 December 2024. The US Treasury listed 27 companies and individuals in his network and said he had allegedly bribed officials in Zimbabwe for illicit profits from its gold and diamond trade. Al Jazeera's 2023 undercover investigation reported bribery at Zimbabwe's national gold refinery and smuggling through Harare airport. Pattni told undercover reporters his Zimbabwean businesses relied on political support from President Emmerson Mnangagwa and that an employee paid the president regular bribes; Mnangagwa did not respond to requests for comment. Pattni denied involvement in money laundering and criminal wrongdoing in Kenya, saying he was never convicted there, and said he believed the undercover reporters were investors.
inside: A foreign gold dealer allegedly bribed Zimbabwean officials, and Al Jazeera reported bribery at the state refinery and smuggling through Harare airport.
cite: Al Jazeera, 10 December 2024

n: Libyan state bank's $300m deposit backed loans to a Haftar fixer's firms
org_label: Ahmed Gadalla's companies and Haftar-aligned bankers
rank: the last central bank governor under Qadhafi, later aligned with the Haftar family, as chairman of a UAE bank; Libyan Foreign Bank guarantee deposit
d: The Sentry's April 2026 report says Farhat Benqdara, Qadhafi's last central bank governor and later a Haftar family ally, became chairman in 2018 of Al-Masraf, the Arab Bank for Investment and Foreign Trade, Abu Dhabi, backed by central bank governor Sadiq al-Kabir, whose votes through the state-owned Libyan Foreign Bank secured it. In 2019 Al-Masraf lent $300m to three Dubai companies linked to the financier Ahmed Gadalla - JTA General Trading LLC, al-Mored Oasis General Trading LLC and AMAA General Trading LLC - against a $300m Libyan Foreign Bank guarantee deposit. The report says the money funded Haftar's failed Tripoli offensive and likely bankrolled Wagner mercenaries. Benqdara blamed about $375m in 2020 impairment charges on Covid-19, which the report says masked the truth. Gadalla did not respond to The Sentry.
inside: One faction's man chaired a foreign bank while a Libyan state bank's deposit backed the loan, so public money financed their own war, the report alleges.
cite: The Sentry, 'Eastern Libya's Top Money Man', April 2026
undone: A $70m partial repayment was made in 2021, leaving about $230m of the loan outstanding as of January 2025.

n: US sanctions Liberia's chief prosecutor over bribes to drop cases
org_label: money launderers and criminal suspects paying for case outcomes
rank: Solicitor General and Chief Prosecutor of Liberia
d: On 15 August 2022 the US Treasury designated three senior Liberian officials under Executive Order 13818. It said Sayma Syrenius Cephus, then Solicitor General and Chief Prosecutor, took bribes to have cases dropped, worked to halt money laundering investigations for personal financial gain, shields money launderers and helps clear them through the courts, and intimidated other prosecutors to quash investigations. It also named Nathaniel McGill, Minister of State for Presidential Affairs and Chief of Staff to President George Weah, who Treasury said took kickbacks for steering contracts to firms he had an interest in, and Bill Twehway of the National Port Authority, said to have diverted $1.5 million in vessel storage fees into a private account and awarded a Port of Buchanan cargo contract to a company he secretly formed.
inside: Paying people facing prosecution bought the office that decides prosecutions, so Liberia's own chief prosecutor dropped their cases, Treasury says.
cite: US Department of the Treasury, press release, 15 August 2022; Executive Mansion of Liberia, 16 August 2022
undone: President George Weah suspended the three men with immediate effect on 16 August 2022 to let them face investigation, naming each one's principal deputy to act in their place.

n: Ethiopia charges fuel traders and the petroleum authority's deputy chief
org_label: fuel trading companies, including Yegna Petroleum
rank: Deputy Director General, Petroleum and Energy Authority
d: Ethiopian federal prosecutors charged 13 people, including senior officials and business figures, over fuel contraband before the Federal High Court, reported 7 May 2026. The first defendant is Dibara Fufa, Deputy Director General of the Petroleum and Energy Authority; others are Shumalem Birhane, director general of a fuel supply enterprise, Bereket Worku, and Yegna Petroleum's unnamed owner and manager. Prosecutors allege officials issued unauthorised fuel permits, helped sell 466,058 litres of white diesel to gold producers, gave one defendant access to over 1.2 million litres without legal justification and removed 1.9 million litres from oversight, and that Yegna Petroleum's owner got a distribution licence illicitly. Alleged losses are 8.4m, 22.5m, 21.3m and 17.8m birr, over 70 million in all. The hearing was adjourned to 18 May 2026 for preliminary objections.
inside: Prosecutors say fuel traders worked through the officials who issue permits, so the regulator's own decisions opened the taps for them.
cite: Fidel Post (Ethiopia), 7 May 2026; Capital (Ethiopia), 10 May 2026

n: Bahamas customs officer charged over payments from a contractor
rank: chief customs revenue officer
d: Pamela Williams, a chief customs revenue officer with the Bahamas Customs Department, stationed in Exuma, was charged on 19 May 2026 in Freeport Magistrate's Court with 77 counts covering 58,045 dollars: nineteen counts each of bribery, extortion, money laundering and fraud by false pretences, and one of fraudulent breach of trust. Prosecutors allege that between March 2023 and April 2025 she solicited and obtained payments without lawful authority as a public servant, including 56,320 dollars by cheque from Costal Systems Bahamas Ltd for unauthorised services and 1,725 dollars by three cheques from Geoffrey C. Lawes. She was not required to plead; bail was refused, her attorney given leave to apply to the Supreme Court, the matter adjourned to 26 September for voluntary bill of indictment proceedings. These are allegations.
inside: Prosecutors allege a contractor paid a senior customs officer $56,320 by cheque for services she had no lawful authority to give.
cite: The Tribune (Nassau), 20 May 2026

n: Two ex-PDI officers convicted of feeding a Chilean ketamine gang
rank: detectives, Policia de Investigaciones
d: Two former officers of Chile's investigative police (Policia de Investigaciones) were convicted at the Arica guarantee court after accepting the facts in an abbreviated procedure. Leoncio Oporto Duhart used his institutional login on the police BRAIN system to look up active arrest warrants against two men identified as leaders of Los Kussy Boys and passed it by messaging app, with photographs of evidence including seized cash; 2,200,000 pesos was paid into his account. He was convicted of criminal association, improper passive bribery, disclosure of secrets and illegal possession of firearm parts and ammunition, and got about five years. Claudio Solans Marchant ran a price list for reserved police information starting at 300,000 pesos, and was convicted of criminal association, active bribery and illegal firearm possession, getting just over four years.
inside: A drug gang paid a serving detective for police warrants and evidence, so Chile's investigative police warned the traffickers it was meant to catch.
cite: El Desconcierto opinion column, 7 August 2026, citing El Mostrador

n: Odebrecht paid Ecuador's Comptroller General over $10m to drop fines
rank: Comptroller General
d: Carlos Ramon Polit Faggioni was Ecuador's Comptroller General, the official guarding public funds against fraud. A Miami federal jury convicted him on 23 April 2024 of money laundering conspiracy, concealment money laundering and transactions in criminally derived property. The US Justice Department said that from 2010 to 2015 he solicited and received over $10 million in bribes from the Brazilian construction group Odebrecht, and in exchange removed fines and did not impose fines on Odebrecht's Ecuadorean projects. In about 2015 he also took a bribe to help a businessman win state insurance contracts. From about 2010 until at least 2017 a conspirator acting at Polit's direction moved the bribe money through Florida companies registered to friends and associates, often without their knowledge, and into buying and renovating Florida property.
inside: Odebrecht's money captured the official meant to audit it, so Ecuador's own spending watchdog cancelled the fines on the firm's projects.
cite: US Department of Justice press releases, 24 April 2024 (conviction) and 1 October 2024 (sentencing)
undone: He was sentenced to ten years in prison on 1 October 2024 and ordered to forfeit $16.5 million.

n: Okokrim charges Petronor unit over bribes tied to Congo's president
org_label: A Norwegian subsidiary of Petronor E&P ASA
rank: the President of Congo and close family members
d: Okokrim, Norway's economic crime authority, said on 26 January 2026 it had indicted two Norwegian citizens for gross corruption and gross accounting violations, and a Norwegian company, a wholly owned subsidiary of the Oslo-listed Petronor E&P ASA, for gross corruption. Okokrim says that from 2016 the accused applied for and obtained a share in Republic of Congo oil licences, and that bribes of particularly high value are linked to Congo's President and his close family. Norway has no jurisdiction over the recipients, so their liability was not considered. The case began with a suspicious transaction to a Monaco bank; Monaco's financial intelligence unit investigated, then sought legal assistance from Norway. Okokrim closed separate market manipulation suspicions against the individuals, the company and Petronor's former chairman without charges, for insufficient evidence.
inside: Okokrim alleges bribes of particularly high value are linked to Congo's president and his close family, and the Norwegian company then obtained a share of the country's oil licences.
cite: Okokrim press release, 26 January 2026

n: Canadian firm's bribes aimed at a Philippine police equipment deal
rank: officials deciding a Philippine National Police procurement (no post or official named in the release)
d: Ultra Electronics Forensic Technology Inc., a Montreal company, was charged with two counts of bribing Republic of the Philippines officials under section 3 of Canada's Corruption of Foreign Public Officials Act and one count of fraud under section 380 of the Criminal Code. The conduct ran from 2006 to 2018, to secure procurement of a ballistic identification system for the Philippine National Police. Quebec's Superior Court published a remediation agreement on 16 May 2023: the company pays a $6,593,178 penalty, a $659,318 surcharge and forfeits $3,296,589, and must follow an anti-bribery programme supervised for four years by an external auditor it pays for. The prosecution is stayed and the charges are to be withdrawn once the company meets its obligations, which include reporting to the Public Prosecution Service on implementation.
inside: The company paid Philippine government officials over twelve years in a scheme aimed at winning the national police force's contract for a ballistic identification system.
cite: Public Prosecution Service of Canada news release, 17 May 2023

n: SAP fined $222m; bribes offered to Tanzania Ports Authority officials
rank: top officials of the Tanzania Ports Authority
d: The German software company SAP was fined $222m by US authorities over bribery of government officials in several African countries, including Tanzania, in a report dated 15 January 2024. The article says SAP is linked to offering bribes to top officials at the Tanzania Ports Authority, the state body running the country's ports, in 2014/2015 to win a tender, and is alleged to have colluded with Tanzania Ports Authority insiders to obtain preferential treatment on other government deals that were meant to go to competitive bidding. The report does not name the officials or the tender, and says SAP offered bribes without stating whether payments were received. No response from the company appears on the page. The underlying US resolutions with SAP SE were announced on 10 January 2024.
inside: A software supplier is alleged to have colluded with insiders at the state ports authority to obtain preferential treatment on deals meant for competitive bidding.
cite: The Citizen (Tanzania), 15 January 2024; underlying US Department of Justice and SEC resolutions with SAP SE, 10 January 2024

n: Report says Haftar-aligned chairman used Libya's National Oil Corporation for the family
org_label: Khalifa Haftar's Libyan Arab Armed Forces network
rank: chairman of the National Oil Corporation
d: The Sentry's April 2026 report says Farhat Benqdara, the last central bank governor under Qadhafi and from 2018 a key economic adviser to Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar and his sons, chaired Libya's National Oil Corporation from 2022 to 2025, and that the Haftar family used the corporation to help evade the United Nations arms embargo on Libya, including securing an Irish private military contractor. The report says the NOC sold crude to the Chinese trader Unipec in August 2022 at what it calls an abnormal discount, and separately that stages of a Chinese drone acquisition programme were financed not by monetary payments but through illicit oil schemes. Haftar's forces did not respond. The Sentry says it used interviews, documentary research and financial forensic analysis, and that some sources are unnamed.
inside: An armed faction's own adviser ran the state oil company, so its oil sales and contracts were used to arm that faction, the report says.
cite: The Sentry, 'Eastern Libya's Top Money Man', April 2026; UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, paras. 97 and 101 (pp. 29-30) and annex 9 paras. 4-9 (pp. 64-65)
undone: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya reached the same conclusion from its own investigation in March 2026, which raises this from a single NGO report to a corroborated intergovernmental finding. The Panel found that Bengdara, while chairman of the National Oil Corporation, colluded with armed group actors to allocate oil service contracts to newly created entities associated with them and to divert Libyan oil and gas revenues, and that he designed a system using corporation-owned companies abroad, including Mediterranean Oil Services in Dubai and Murzuq Oil Services in London, as gatekeepers for funding and contracts. It records that his appointment was backed by the Haftar family after he facilitated the diversion of $300 million from Al-Masraf Bank in 2019, and that he resigned with effect from 16 January 2025.

n: Botswana's mining minister acquitted over a licence-for-millions charge
org_label: Sieyuan Electric Botswana and New Energy Company
who: Sieyuan Electric and New Energy Company
rank: Minister of Mineral Resources, Green Technology and Energy Security
d: Botswana's Directorate on Corruption and Economic Crime alleged that on or about 17 April 2024 Lefoko Maxwell Moagi, then minister of minerals and energy, accepted valuable consideration of 4,706,000 pula as a reward for signing eight base-metal prospecting licences for New Energy (Pty) Ltd in the Ghanzi, Tsabong and Tutume districts. Investigators traced money from New Energy through Wisecreatives Investments, whose sole director was a Chinese national, and Riders (Pty) Ltd, and found a Wisecreatives bank card in a vehicle at his Ramotswa home. On 29 October 2026 a Gaborone regional magistrate acquitted and discharged him, finding no case to answer, and the prosecution is appealing.
inside: A mining minister was accused of taking 4.7 million pula routed through two companies for signing eight prospecting licences, and was acquitted with no case to answer.
cite: Botswana Daily News and 2nd Republic News, 20-21 January 2026 (arraignment); Mmegi, June-August 2026 (trial and no-case submission); 2nd Republic News and Mmegi, 5 November 2026 (acquittal of 29 October 2026 and the DPP's appeal); Mmegi, 'I have always maintained my innocence – Moagi', after the ruling of 29 October 2026 (https://www.mmegi.bw/ampArticle/124563), for Moagi's response; Botswana Daily News, 'Witness Exonerates Lefoko From BPC Tendering Process', for the wording of the second charge
undone: Moagi was arraigned on 20 January 2026 on one count under section 25(1) of the Corruption and Economic Crime Act and reserved his plea. His counsel argued on a no-case submission that every deposit in the bank records was labelled a loan, that nothing showed the money was a reward for the licences, and that the funds were never at his disposal. Regional Magistrate Mareledi Dipate acquitted and discharged him on 29 October 2026, and the Director of Public Prosecutions lodged an appeal on 5 November 2026, saying the magistrate misapplied the law. A separate trial continues, on two counts of corruption and money laundering over Botswana Power Corporation tenders won by the Chinese contractor Sieyuan Electric Botswana, where he is accused of obtaining 100 heifers and a bull worth 417,500 pula bought with money the state says was disguised as a loan. Speaking to reporters after the acquittal, Moagi said he had always maintained his innocence on every matter brought against him.

n: Global Fund: bid collusion needed a Madagascar procurement official
org_label: malaria grant suppliers bidding to Madagascar's health programme offices
rank: procurement unit official at the health projects support office (UGP)
d: The Office of the Inspector General of the Global Fund, which finances health programmes, investigated procurement under five malaria grants to Madagascar and released its report on 3 January 2014, having begun work in April 2012. Reviewing $12.2m of about $70.8m disbursed, it found non-compliant expenditure, over-priced goods and collusion among suppliers, with about $1.16m of non-compliant spending including $462,670 of over-pricing. In a 2010 restricted national tender for indoor residual spraying supplies and equipment, run by UGP, the government's support office for health sector projects, contracts worth $640,146 were compromised, with slightly more than half charged above market rates; the Inspector General said such practices needed the collusion of a procurement unit official. SALAMA was removed as a principal recipient and its grant is in closure.
inside: Suppliers rigged bids for malaria contracts, which the inspectors said required an official inside the UGP, the government's support office for health sector projects, to work with them.
cite: Aidspan / Global Fund Observer, 8 January 2014, on the Global Fund OIG report of 3 January 2014

n: Operation Lobo: security firm Senase accused of paying state security staff
rank: security directors, officers and coordinators at state utilities and agencies
d: Dominican prosecutors accuse the private guarding company Senase, Servicio Nacional de Seguridad Integral S.R.L., of paying 108,080,359.92 Dominican pesos in bribes to security staff inside state bodies so its contracts stayed in force, paperwork moved quickly and objections or audits were avoided. The accusation covers 2012 to 2025, names ten people and four companies, charging bribery, criminal association, fraud against the state and money laundering. Those accused include the company's representative Quilvio Bienvenido Rodriguez Gonzalez, former security directors of the electricity distributors EdeSur and EdeEste, former security officers at EdeNorte, a member of EdeEste's security department, a former security director and assistant at the child-care agency Inaipi, and a former security coordinator at the health insurer Senasa. The operation began in July 2025; prosecutors have requested trial, not yet reached.
inside: Prosecutors say a guarding company put money in the pockets of the officials who oversaw its own contracts, so state bodies kept buying from it unchecked.
cite: Acento (Santo Domingo), 15 July 2026, Ministerio Publico accusation in Operation Lobo

n: Samoan immigration officer jailed for selling passports to non-Samoans
rank: assistant immigration officer
d: David Nomeneta Uaine, a former assistant immigration officer from Tuana'i, was convicted in Samoa's Supreme Court on 28 charges including corruption, bribery, forgery and using false documents, and was sentenced by Justice Tafaoimalo Leilani Tuala-Warren to four years in prison, all sentences concurrent. While in post in 2016 and 2017 he lodged and processed six applications for Samoan passports for people who were not Samoan; five were approved. He was allegedly paid with money sent to him from overseas, which the judge described as not significant amounts but as going to him personally, and the judge found the offending premeditated, sophisticated and deliberate, spread over six months, with his level of criminality high. The Samoa Observer brought the passport sales to the immigration office's attention in September 2017.
inside: Buyers abroad paid an immigration officer to push through Samoan passports for people with no right to them, using the state's own document system.
cite: Samoa Observer, 31 May 2019 (sentencing date confirmed by RNZ Pacific, 31 May 2019)

n: J&F bribed BNDES and Petros executives and a legislator for state finance
rank: BNDES and Petros executives and a senior legislative official
d: J&F Investimentos S.A., the Brazilian company behind meatpacker JBS, pleaded guilty on 14 October 2020 in federal court in Brooklyn to conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and agreed to a criminal penalty of $256,497,026. The US Justice Department said the conspiracy ran from 2005 to 2017, and that from 2005 to 2014 J&F paid more than $148 million in bribes to high-level Brazilian officials, including a then high-ranking executive at BNDES, Brazil's state development bank, which provided hundreds of millions in financing. A high-ranking executive of state-controlled pension fund Petros was paid more than $4.6 million for approving a merger benefiting J&F, and J&F paid approximately $25 million to a high-ranking official in the legislative branch to secure hundreds of millions in financing from Caixa Economica Federal.
inside: J&F's payments reached executives inside Brazil's state development bank and a state pension fund, which approved its financing and a merger, and a legislator who secured it financing from Caixa.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 14 October 2020

n: Strukton paid $31m through an agent for Riyadh metro work
rank: a high-ranking member of the ruling family
d: The Dutch public prosecution service said on 30 March 2026 that the construction company Strukton had accepted a 10 million euro settlement over foreign bribery of officials and forgery of documents in building a metro line in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Between February 2013 and June 2021 Strukton paid about US$31 million to a company acting as its agent, to bribe a high-ranking member of the ruling family; the payments helped Strukton win part of the metro contract. Its final export credit insurance application to Atradius Dutch State Business N.V. said it had paid the agent US$1.5 million when the agreed amount was US$27.5 million, concealing the bribes; Strukton also gave false information to its external auditor. The investigation into several former employees is complete and prosecutors intend to charge some.
inside: Strukton paid about $31m to an agent in order to bribe a senior member of the Saudi ruling family, and won part of the Riyadh metro contract.
cite: Openbaar Ministerie (Netherlands) news release, 30 March 2026

n: IT firm paid a Frankfurt chief prosecutor for the state's data work
org_label: A German IT company and its owner
rank: chief public prosecutor in Frankfurt, a corruption investigator
d: Frankfurt's regional court convicted an IT entrepreneur of bribery in twenty cases on 17 December 2025, giving him an 18-month suspended sentence and confiscating 44,200 euro; the verdict is not yet final. The court heard that the city's former chief public prosecutor, himself a corruption investigator, awarded contracts to firms he secretly held stakes in, among them the man's company, which had done his data backup and processing work for about two years, and in autumn 2014 told him to pay one euro for every billed hour or get no more orders. He paid cash from his private account, about once a quarter in sums of 1,000 to 5,000 euro, roughly 66,000 euro in all, handed over on walks in a park, until the prosecutor was arrested in summer 2020.
inside: A senior Frankfurt prosecutor demanded a cut of every billed hour from an IT firm he kept giving the state's data contracts.
cite: hessenschau (Hessischer Rundfunk), 17 December 2025
undone: The prosecutor was sentenced to six years in spring 2023 and released on probation in December 2025. A business partner received almost three years and a prosecutor who worked with him was fined. Hessen is suing for 6.6 million euro, the revenue the IT firm earned from his orders in the offence period.

n: Church renaming allowed after 18 years; church-linked editor bought the minister's tickets
rank: Minister of Education; Agency for Cultural Affairs
d: In 2015 the Agency for Cultural Affairs let the Unification Church register a new name, the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification. Jiji Press reported on 5 August 2022 that Kihei Maekawa, head of the agency's religious affairs division in 1997 and vice education minister in 2015, told an opposition-party hearing that the agency reversed an 18-year policy of not accepting renamings, that he was overruled, that he was 100 per cent sure the intent behind it was the education minister Hakubun Shimomura's, and that external power was at work. Shimbun Akahata reported on 4 September 2022 that an editor of the church-linked paper Sekai Nippo bought 40,000 yen of tickets to Shimomura's 2013 and 2014 fundraisers. Shimomura said in 2022 that he felt responsible for the renaming.
cite: Jiji Press, 5 August 2022 (Maekawa testimony); Shimbun Akahata / Japan Press Weekly, 4 September 2022 (https://www.japan-press.co.jp/s/news/?id=14271); The Japan Times, 5 August 2022
inside: A church-linked paper's editor bought tickets to the education minister's fundraisers, and his ministry reversed an 18-year refusal to let the church change its name. No source connects the two.

n: RSF-linked firms took a majority stake in Sudan's Al Khaleej Bank
org_label: companies linked to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
rank: majority shareholding in a commercial bank
d: Companies linked to Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary force led by the Dagalo family, bought a majority stake in Al Khaleej Bank in Khartoum in 2019, according to The Sentry's October 2025 report. A Dubai firm, Al Jil Alqadem General Trading, held bank shares; the report says Abdulrahim Dagalo owned it and that by late 2024 it was held by Mazin Fadlalla and Abozer Habib. In a Treasury release of 31 January 2024 the United States called Al Khaleej Bank an essential part of the RSF's efforts to finance its operations. The report rests on interviews, documentary research and corporate registry records in the UAE and Sudan, some sources unnamed for their safety. It says Abozer Habib declined to comment, citing legal proceedings, and Mazin Fadlalla did not respond.
inside: An armed force bought control of a commercial bank through front companies, so a licensed bank's accounts and transfers served its war financing.
cite: The Sentry, October 2025

n: Logging firms paid South Sudan's army, security and intelligence officers
org_label: logging companies, including Santos Petroleum and Timber Ltd and Aguet Trading (the Panel identified at least three South Sudanese and Ugandan companies)
rank: SSPDF, National Security Service, Military Intelligence and county officials
d: The final report of the United Nations Panel of Experts on South Sudan, dated 1 July 2025, says that in some cases individual foreign businesspeople have been identified as the owners and financiers of illegal logging, and names the companies Santos Petroleum and Timber Ltd and Aguet Trading. It says logging deals were negotiated directly with communities, county officials and security forces, including the SSPDF, the National Security Service, Military Intelligence and the opposition SPLA-IO, depending on the area, and cites a document from December 2023 in which a company agreed to pay local officials $5,000 per truck. Local chiefs and communities might receive only a few hundred dollars, with the rest going to county officials and security actors. The Panel reports these findings for 2023 to 2025.
inside: Timber operators reportedly paid county officials and the army, intelligence and security services they negotiated logging deals with.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan, final report S/2025/442, 1 July 2025

n: Charges dropped against Ugandan officers accused of spying for Rwanda
rank: seven serving army and police officers
d: Seven senior Ugandan security officers were accused of allegedly sharing classified information with Rwandan authorities. The case was heard by the General Court Martial at Makindye in Kampala, chaired by Brigadier General Robert Freeman Mugabe. On 16 April 2024 prosecutors told the court they had instructions to discontinue all charges, and the officers were freed. The report names no formal charge beyond that allegation. The visible portion of the report does not say what information was said to have been shared, or why the case was dropped, and the allegations were never tested at trial.
inside: Prosecutors alleged Rwanda was receiving classified Ugandan material from serving officers inside Uganda's army and police; the charges were later dropped.
cite: New Vision (Uganda), 17 April 2024

n: Arms dealer's company held power of attorney for Niger's defence ministry
org_label: Aboubacar Hima's arms companies (TSI, Brid A Defcon)
rank: power of attorney on behalf of the Ministry of Defence
d: A confidential audit by Niger's army inspectorate, reported by OCCRP, found TSI, a company founded by Nigerien arms broker Aboubacar Hima, gained power of attorney for the Ministry of Defence, letting it approve weapons deals and issue end-user certificates. Before getting that power, Hima had in 2018 issued Russia's Rosoboronexport an end-user certificate for the ministry. The audit covered about $1bn of military spending from 2011 to 2019 and found problems in contracts worth over $320m; Hima handled at least three quarters of the purchases reviewed, about $240m. Companies run by a second intermediary, Aboubacar Charfo, used fake bids, the audit saying the winner was known in advance. Hima's lawyer, Marc Le Bihan, declined to answer questions, said Hima could not be reached and was not being prosecuted over it.
inside: An arms dealer's company was given the ministry's own signing power, so it could approve and certify the weapons deals he was selling.
cite: OCCRP, 6 August 2020, citing Niger's Inspection Generale des Armees audit

n: Panama's presidential guard and prosecution staff convicted in an airport cocaine ring
rank: officials of the SPI, the Ministerio Publico, Senan and private airport security
d: The investigation began in 2021. At trial, which opened on 1 June 2025, judges Kathia Rodriguez, Ilka Castillo and Raul Vergara found twenty defendants guilty of conspiracy to traffic drugs and three of those also guilty of money laundering, as reported on 24 July 2026. Those convicted include officials of the Servicio de Proteccion Institucional, which guards the presidency, the Ministerio Publico, the air and naval service Senan, and private security at Tocumen airport. The network was led by Fernando Mendoza. Insiders changed the colillas, or identifying tags, on suitcases bound for terminals in France, Spain and other European countries.
inside: A trafficking network had officials of the presidential guard, the prosecution service, the air and naval service and airport security working inside Tocumen.
undone: Sentences had not been set when the verdict was reported. The court must still fix each one, and they are expected to range between 8 and 12 years.
cite: La Prensa (Panama), 24 July 2026

n: Samoan national jailed for bribing a New Zealand immigration contact
rank: staff contact, Immigration New Zealand office in Samoa
d: In April 2025 a Samoan national was jailed for four years at Auckland District Court and ordered to pay $4,000 to the victims, after pleading guilty to twelve representative charges: five of aiding and abetting breach of visa conditions, six of exploitation of unlawful migrants and one of corruption of a public official. RNZ reported that the person had bribed a contact at Immigration New Zealand's office in Samoa for favourable treatment on visa applications for those workers. The person's name was suppressed on an interim basis. A U4 Anti-Corruption Helpdesk overview of corruption in Pacific island countries records the case as bribing a government official and helping others to break visa rules.
inside: A broker paid a contact inside New Zealand's immigration office in Samoa, so visa applications got favourable treatment and workers entered illegally.
cite: RNZ, 7 April 2025; U4 Anti-Corruption Helpdesk, Caitlin Maslen, Overview of corruption and anti-corruption in Pacific island countries, 3 February 2026

n: Trader accused of bribing Venezuela's state food buyer CASA
rank: officials of the state food company CASA and PDVSA joint ventures
d: US prosecutors alleged Naman Wakil, a Syrian national and lawful permanent resident living in Miami, paid bribes from 2010 until at least September 2017 to officials of CASA, the Venezuelan state-owned and state-controlled company that buys the country's food, and of joint ventures between the state oil company PDVSA and foreign firms in the Orinoco belt. The Justice Department said the bribes won at least $250 million in contracts to sell food to CASA and to do business with the PDVSA joint ventures, including at least $30 million in highly inflated contracts to supply those joint ventures. He was arrested in Miami on 3 August 2021 and charged with conspiring to violate and violating the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and with money laundering. The allegations were never tested at trial.
inside: Prosecutors said the businessman's bribes reached buyers inside Venezuela's state food company and the PDVSA joint ventures that then awarded him contracts.
undone: Wakil died in his sleep on 24 July 2023, before his trial; his lawyer Howard Srebnick confirmed the death to Voice of America. On 8 January 2025 US District Judge Melissa Damian entered final judgment in a civil forfeiture action, forfeiting over $20 million in proceeds of the scheme to the United States. The 2025 forfeiture release describes Wakil as a Venezuelan national; the 2021 charging release called him a Syrian national.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 4 August 2021; US Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida, 10 January 2025; Voice of America, 25 July 2023

n: Yara's bribe to the son of Libya's de facto oil minister
who: Yara's former chief legal officer, acting on behalf of Yara International ASA
rank: de facto oil minister and chair of the National Oil Corporation
d: Yara International ASA is an Oslo-listed fertiliser group, 36.2 per cent state-held. Norway's Supreme Court ruled on 15 September 2017 on Yara's former chief legal officer, convicted of gross corruption. Norwegian courts found that in about early 2007 he agreed, on Yara's behalf, to pay at least US$4.5 million to the son of Libya's de facto oil minister, who chaired the board of the state-owned National Oil Corporation, with which Yara was negotiating. About US$1.5 million was paid into a Swiss account on 29 March 2007, prepaid through subsidiary Nitrochem and recovered through excess invoicing between October 2007 and May 2008. It coincided with a heads of agreement signed in April 2007. The Court of Appeal raised his sentence to seven years and the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal.
inside: Yara's money went to the family of the man running Libya's state oil company, to win his goodwill in the deal he was deciding.
cite: Supreme Court of Norway, HR-2017-1776-A, judgment of 15 September 2017 (official English translation)

n: Church papers describe Hagiuda as its hotline into the LDP
rank: LDP acting secretary-general; former Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry
d: Tansa reported on 3,212 pages of internal Unification Church reports to its World Headquarters, which it calls the TM Report. It casts Koichi Hagiuda, now LDP acting secretary-general and former trade and education minister, as a hotline between the church and the Liberal Democratic Party. Eiji Tokuno, then church president in Japan, wrote in a September 2020 report that he had met Prime Minister Shinzo Abe five times, that Hagiuda arranged the meetings and was usually present, and that one, on 2 July 2019, was to ask the church to support the candidate Tsuneo Kitamura in the upper house election. Hagiuda's secretary said on 31 January 2026 that he has no direct connection to the church as an organisation, but may have met people from an affiliated group, the Family.
cite: Tansa, The True Mother Files, 27 January 2026 (Japanese original 1 February 2026)
inside: Church records cast a senior LDP figure as its standing channel into the party leadership, arranging meetings with the prime minister and asking the church for votes.
undone: The church's public relations department called the documents extremely lacking in credibility on 16 January 2026.

n: Businessman's money reached Benin's presidential guard commander
rank: head of the presidential guard
d: Olivier Boko, a businessman and long-time friend of President Patrice Talon, and Oswald Homeky, a former sports minister, were each sentenced to 20 years in prison by the financial crimes and terrorism court in Cotonou for conspiracy against state security and corruption of a public official. Special prosecutor Elonm Mario Metonou said Homeky was arrested in September 2024 while handing six bags of money to the head of the presidential guard, Colonel Djimon Dieudonne Tevoedjre, who told the court Homeky had contacted him to foment a coup. The three men, including Boko's brother-in-law Rock Nieri, convicted in absentia, were ordered to pay 60 billion CFA francs ($95m) in damages. Defence lawyers walked out before the verdict; opposition figures accuse Talon of using the courts against opponents.
inside: A businessman's money was handed to the officer commanding the president's own guard, prosecutors say, to turn that unit against the president.
cite: Africanews, 31 January 2025

n: Russian officers placed over CAR's presidential security and police
rank: security adviser to the president; Russian control of the police security partnership
d: A report by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, published in February 2025, says Vitali Perfilev operated in 2023 as a security adviser to President Faustin-Archange Touadera, dealing with security and military matters. It says that from December 2023 Denis Pavlov, presented as a diplomat but in reality an officer of Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service, took control of the security partnership with the General Directorate of the Central African National Police; Canada sanctioned Pavlov in February 2024. The report says Wagner took control of the Ndassima gold mine through Midas Ressources, sanctioned by the United States in June 2023, and quotes a Ministry of Mines official saying operations there have been totally opaque, with ministry staff unable to carry out environmental checks.
inside: Russian intelligence and Wagner men sit inside the presidency's security circle and run the police partnership, so Central African security decisions follow Moscow.
cite: Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, February 2025

n: Wahda Bank issued $55m in uncovered cheques under a Haftar financier's sway
org_label: Ahmed Gadalla and the Haftar family network
rank: board seat and reported tacit control of a commercial bank
d: The Sentry's April 2026 report says that in May 2024 Benghazi's Wahda Bank issued certified cheques worth about 300 million dinars, roughly $55m, across 151 accounts without sufficient funds, in what it calls zero-clearing incidents. Multiple sources described the Dubai-based financier Ahmed Gadalla as holding tacit control of the bank at the time, and the report says he sits on its board. In a separate episode in April 2024, Benghazi's National Commercial Bank approved letters of credit worth 400 million dinars, about $88m, without matching dinar deposits, with paperwork involving a Turkish company linked to Fauzi al-Muqla, whose wife is the sister of Saddam Haftar's wife; sources say Gadalla already held sway over that bank. Wahda Bank, the National Commercial Bank and Muqla did not respond.
inside: A faction's financier sat on bank boards and reportedly controlled them, so banks created money and credit for people close to the Haftars.
cite: The Sentry, 'Eastern Libya's Top Money Man', April 2026

n: Wagner officers took command of Central African army units
rank: command of army battalions and the presidential guard
d: The Sentry, an investigative group, reported in June 2023 that an internal note of November 2021 by the European Union's External Action Service said most deployed units of the Central African Armed Forces were operating under direct command or supervision by Wagner mercenaries. The report says Wagner has exclusive control over some units, including Territorial Infantry Battalion 7, made up of former self-defence group members and ex-militiamen incorporated in early 2021, and that military sources described battalions 8 to 12 as largely controlled by Wagner. All 11 military sources it spoke to said Russian commanders give operational orders outside the capital. A former executive said of Wagner's country head Vitalii Perfilev: 'Vitali has the full green light on the army, he does not ask Touadera for approval.'
inside: A Russian paramilitary company's officers command Central African army units, so the state's own soldiers take orders from a foreign private force.
cite: The Sentry, 'Architects of Terror', June 2023

n: Importer bribed a Vanuatu customs officer to let a container pass
rank: customs border officer
d: Zhiqiong Huang pleaded guilty in Vanuatu's Supreme Court to two counts of corruption and bribery of officials under section 73(2) of the Penal Code, and was convicted on both. She handed customs border officer Jules Sesai 1,500,000 vatu in cash on 25 July 2025 to help release container APZU 2114608, consigned to Santo Nambawan Stores, and offered a further 1,000,000 vatu that month to steer him against physically inspecting it. On 28 July she telephoned customs officer Pakoa Tom asking him to cancel the inspection. The inspection went ahead on 6 August 2025 and found undeclared cigarettes, with duty assessed at 143,820,550 vatu. She was sentenced on 24 March 2026 to 24 months on each count, twelve months immediate and twelve suspended, and fined 1,000,000 vatu.
inside: An importer paid a customs border officer to release and not inspect her container, so the checks that would have found undeclared goods were called off.
cite: Public Prosecutor v Zhiqiong Huang, Supreme Court of Vanuatu, 24 March 2026

n: Florida supplier's $532,000 bought Bolivia's Minister of Government
org_label: A Florida-based equipment supplier and its owners
rank: Minister of Government
d: Arturo Carlos Murillo Prijic was Bolivia's Minister of Government, the cabinet post in charge of the police and internal security. The US Justice Department says he received at least $532,000 in bribes from a Florida-based company in return for helping it secure a contract worth about $5.6 million in 2019 to supply tear gas and other non-lethal equipment to Bolivia's Ministry of Defense. He was charged in the Southern District of Florida on 7 December 2021, pleaded guilty on 20 October 2022 to conspiracy to commit money laundering with a Foreign Corrupt Practices Act violation as the underlying offence, and was sentenced on 4 January 2023 to 70 months in prison. A related case charged Sergio Rodrigo Mendez Mendizabal, Luis Berkman, Bryan Berkman and Philip Lichtenfeld.
inside: A US supplier's payments put Bolivia's security minister on its side, and he helped it win a $5.6 million state order for tear gas.
cite: US Department of Justice, case page United States v. Arturo Carlos Murillo Prijic; US Department of Justice press release, 4 January 2023

n: SAP bribed Indonesian fisheries ministry and telecoms agency officials
rank: Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries and a state telecoms agency
d: SAP SE, the German business software company, admitted that between about 2015 and 2018 it paid bribes through agents to Indonesian officials to gain advantages on contracts with Indonesian government bodies. The US Justice Department named two of those bodies: Kementerian Kelautan dan Perikanan, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, and Balai Penyedia dan Pengelola Pembiayaan Telekomunikasi dan Informatika, a state-owned and state-controlled telecommunications and information accessibility agency. SAP was charged in the Eastern District of Virginia with conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and entered a three-year deferred prosecution agreement announced on 10 January 2024, paying a criminal penalty of $118.8 million and administrative forfeiture of $103,396,765. The same resolution covered a separate scheme in South Africa.
inside: SAP's agents paid officials inside an Indonesian ministry and a state telecoms agency, which then bought the company's software.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 10 January 2024

n: UK brokers paid Ecuador's state insurers' chairman $2.8m for reinsurance
org_label: Tysers Insurance Brokers and H.W. Wood, UK reinsurance brokers
who: UK reinsurance brokers Tysers and H.W. Wood
rank: chairman of Seguros Sucre and Seguros Rocafuerte
d: Two British reinsurance brokers, Tysers Insurance Brokers Limited and H.W. Wood Limited, agreed on 20 November 2023 to three-year deferred prosecution agreements with the US Justice Department on charges of conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. Between 2013 and 2017 they agreed, through employees and third-party agents, to pay about $2.8 million in bribes to the then chairman of two Ecuadorian state-owned insurers, Seguros Sucre S.A. and Seguros Rocafuerte S.A., and to three other Ecuadorian officials, in order to win and keep reinsurance business. Tysers paid a $36 million penalty and forfeited about $10.5 million; H.W. Wood paid $508,000 because it could not pay more. Juan Ribas Domenech, former chairman of both insurers, pleaded guilty on 16 September 2020.
inside: The brokers' money reached the chairman of two Ecuadorian state insurers, who then steered their reinsurance business to the two firms.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 20 November 2023

n: Gorrin accused of bribing officials for PDVSA currency contracts
rank: high-level officials deciding PDVSA currency contracts
d: A federal grand jury in the Southern District of Florida indicted Raul Gorrin Belisario, a Venezuelan television news network owner, on 23 October 2024 on one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. US prosecutors allege that between 2014 and 2018 he and others paid bribes to high-level Venezuelan officials to obtain foreign currency exchange loan contracts with PDVSA, Venezuela's state-owned energy company, then moved the proceeds through the US financial system and foreign bank accounts using shell companies, buying real estate, yachts and other luxury items in Florida. The Justice Department called it a $1.2 billion laundering scheme and over $1 billion in ill-gotten gains. Gorrin has denied the accusations and the indictment is an allegation.
inside: Prosecutors say Gorrin's bribes bought senior officials' decisions inside Venezuela's state oil company, which handed his side lucrative currency contracts.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 23 October 2024; San Juan Daily Star, February 2026, on the reported detention in Caracas; Revista E&N, February 2026
undone: Gorrin has not been tried on any of the United States charges, which run back to an indictment in 2017, and he is presumed innocent. Reports in early February 2026 said Venezuelan security agents had detained him overnight in Caracas, at about the time Alex Saab was arrested; those reports rested on anonymous sources, a representative for Gorrin said he was free the same evening, and one account described the status of both men as unclear. Whether he is in custody, and whether he has been or will be handed to the United States, is not established. He is not known to face charges in Venezuela.

n: Balt paid a senior doctor at a French state hospital to buy its devices
org_label: Balt SAS, a French medical device maker
rank: a physician in a senior role at a state-owned public hospital
d: The US Justice Department announced in March 2026 that it had resolved a foreign bribery investigation into Balt SAS, a medical device company headquartered in France, over payments to a physician who served in a senior role at a state-owned public hospital in France. Because Balt reported itself, cooperated and made changes, the department declined to prosecute and Balt agreed to pay about $1.2 million in disgorgement; France's Parquet National Financier reached a coordinated resolution. A grand jury in California indicted David Ferrera, an executive at Balt's US subsidiary, and Marc Tilman, a consultant, on 4 March 2026. Prosecutors allege that from about 2017 into 2023 they paid the official so the hospital would buy Balt's embolization coils.
inside: The company's payments reached a senior doctor inside a French public hospital, who then had the hospital buy that company's medical devices.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, March 2026

n: Berlin senator convicted after an agency staged her wedding free
rank: Senator for Health, Care and Gender Equality
d: Berlin's regional court convicted Dilek Kalayci, the city state's former Senator for Health, Care and Gender Equality, of passive bribery on 4 April 2025. In 2019 she had a Berlin advertising agency plan and organise her wedding, including invitation cards, worth 6,240 euro, and the agency never invoiced her. The court found that her department then hired the same agency for a campaign to recruit nursing staff, a contract she personally influenced, and that the agency received about 250,000 euro from the department in 2020 and 2021. Kalayci received a suspended sentence of one year and six months and had 6,240 euro confiscated; the agency head, Thomas E., received one year and three months, suspended. The verdict can still be appealed.
inside: An advertising agency's free work on a minister's wedding bought her influence, and her department then awarded that agency a 250,000 euro campaign contract.
cite: Landgericht Berlin I press release 13/2025, 4 April 2025

n: Deere's Thai unit bribed the air force and two road departments
org_label: Deere & Company (John Deere) and Wirtgen Thailand
rank: officials of the Royal Thai Air Force, Department of Highways and Department of Rural Roads
d: The US Securities and Exchange Commission announced on 10 September 2024 that Deere & Company, the Illinois maker of agricultural and heavy equipment, would pay nearly $10 million to settle Foreign Corrupt Practices Act charges. From at least late 2017 through 2020 its wholly owned subsidiary Wirtgen Thailand bribed Thai government officials at the Royal Thai Air Force, the Department of Highways and the Department of Rural Roads to win multiple government contracts, and also paid employees of a private company. The bribes took the form of cash, international travel and visits to massage parlours, and were booked as legitimate expenses. The subsidiary made about $4.3 million in profits. Deere paid about $5.4 million in disgorgement and interest and a $4.5 million penalty without admitting or denying the findings.
inside: The firm's Thai subsidiary paid officials inside the air force and two roads departments, which then awarded it their government equipment contracts.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission press release 2024-124, 10 September 2024

n: Philips China's staff shaped hospital tenders with hospital directors
rank: public hospital directors handling procurement
d: The Securities and Exchange Commission announced on 11 May 2023 that Koninklijke Philips N.V., the Amsterdam-based medical technology group, would pay more than $62 million over sales of medical diagnostic equipment in China. The SEC found that a district sales manager at Philips China gave funds to a hospital director to help with procurement, and that employees discussed tailoring technical specifications with hospital directors so that only Philips China and two other manufacturers would qualify. Employees, distributors or sub-dealers also prepared extra bids using rival manufacturers' products to make public tenders look legitimate and meet the minimum number of bids required under Chinese law. Philips paid $15 million in civil penalties and more than $47 million in disgorgement and interest without admitting or denying the findings.
inside: The company's staff worked with directors inside Chinese public hospitals to write tender specifications only its own equipment could meet.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission press release 2023-92, 11 May 2023

n: A $2.7m bribe scheme reached Ukraine's Supreme Court chief
rank: Chairman of the Supreme Court and Grand Chamber judges
inside: A businessman's money reached the head of Ukraine's highest court, which then overturned the ruling and returned the plant's shares to Ferrexpo AG, restoring his control.
d: Kostiantyn Zhevaho, a businessman, sought to bribe Grand Chamber judges of Ukraine's Supreme Court to overturn a 2022 appellate ruling that took Poltava Mining and Processing Plant shares from Ferrexpo AG and so from his control. The bribe totalled $2.7m, of which Chief Justice Vsevolod Kniaziev knew of $2m; it passed through the lawyer Oleh Horetskyi, who also entered a plea agreement, and the notary Kyrylo Horburov. Kniaziev had a hearing delayed while the money was collected, and after the Grand Chamber overturned the ruling on 19 April 2023 he joined another judge's dissent to conceal his interest. He was detained on 15 May 2023 after $1.34m was delivered to his flat.
undone: On 8 June 2026 the High Anti-Corruption Court approved a plea agreement and jailed Kniaziev for five years with confiscation of property and a three-year ban on judicial and law-enforcement posts, the term reduced below the statutory eight to twelve years because he cooperated and testified against other participants.
cite: Transparency International Ukraine, 'Unprecedented Case: Head of the Country's Highest Judicial Body Receives Custodial Sentence for Corruption'

n: Kremlin advisers worked inside Moldova's Socialist Party
rank: advisers to the president and senior Socialist Party figures
inside: Russian operatives advised Moldova's then governing party and its president's campaign and funded pro-Russian parties, pressing party members to take guidance from Moscow; Treasury says the effort failed.
d: On 26 October 2022 the US Treasury designated nine individuals and 12 entities over Russian interference in Moldova, saying Russia's efforts to influence the 2020 and 2021 elections failed. It said Olga Grak and Leonid Gonin advised ex-president Igor Dodon during the 2020 campaign, and that Yuriy Gudilin and Grak pressed Party of Socialists members to accept Russian guidance, promising to weigh in favourably with the Russian Presidential Administration. Treasury said Russia-based businessman Igor Chayka worked with Kremlin press secretary Dmitry Peskov on plans to undermine President Maia Sandu, and that the Russian government used Chayka's companies as a front to funnel money to collaborating parties, some earmarked for bribes and electoral fraud. Gudilin, a political technologist and ex-FSB officer, was designated for coordinating election influence in 2020 and 2021.
cite: US Department of the Treasury press release, 26 October 2022

n: Onyshchenko's gas firms got tax deferrals from Ukraine's tax chief Nasirov
rank: Head of the State Fiscal Service
inside: A member of parliament's gas companies got the head of Ukraine's tax service to grant unlawful tax deferrals, and examinations found the state may have lost over two billion hryvnia.
d: NABU alleges that the then member of parliament Oleksandr Onyshchenko organised a scheme in which gas from the state producer Ukrgazvydobuvannya was sold through fictitious exchanges to companies he controlled at below-market prices and resold at market rates. Prosecutors say Roman Nasirov, head of the State Fiscal Service, Ukraine's tax and customs authority, issued unlawful instructions granting three of those companies instalment repayment of tax debt and subsoil use fees; regional directorate heads submitted false reports claiming the companies faced bankruptcy risks when no such risks existed. Two forensic economic expert examinations confirmed that his actions between May 2015 and March 2016 may have caused the state to forfeit over UAH 2 billion in revenue.
undone: Nasirov was convicted of abuse of office in late 2025, the case file giving both 31 October and 4 November, and sentenced to six years' imprisonment, a UAH 17,000 fine and a three-year ban on holding certain posts. His co-defendant Volodymyr Novikov, a former State Fiscal Service department head, was acquitted, and a forgery charge against Nasirov was dropped in September 2023 on the statute of limitations, leaving the conviction resting on abuse of office alone. On 2 April 2026 the appeal chamber partly granted the defence appeals and amended the verdict, removing references to Liudmyla Solotva's testimony and recalculating pre-trial detention, but left the sentence unchanged; the Supreme Court opened cassation proceedings on 9 April 2026, so the conviction is not final. A separate charge of taking a UAH 722 million bribe, joined with proceedings against his father-in-law Oleksandr Hlimbovskyi, is pending.
cite: Transparency International Ukraine, HACC case file 52017000000000218

n: Developer leased 18 hectares near Kyiv after cadastre data changed
rank: officials of the regional State Land Cadastre
inside: A developer allegedly had officials inside the state land register change the records, so the register itself delivered a large lease to his company.
d: NABU's report records a case, exposed in September 2025, in which officials of the regional State Land Cadastre allegedly manipulated cadastral data so that a developer's company got a lease over 18 hectares near Kyiv, where the Stolychnyi market is located. The report values the land at UAH 160 million. The cadastre is the official register of land plots, their boundaries and permitted uses, so altering entries can change what may be built on a site and who may use it. The plots were split among nine strawmen who resold them to companies linked to the same developer, and were seized at SAPO's request. The developer, the former MP said to be involved and the cadastre officials are all unnamed in the report, and the allegations are unproven.
cite: National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine, investigations section of its report for the second half of 2025

n: Cyprus report: Rybolovlev's lawyers hired a judge's wife; officials helped
rank: president of Nicosia District Court; deputy attorney general; Limassol CID head
d: Cyprus's Anti-Corruption Authority report, 'Mafia State' after Makarios Drousiotis's book, covers seven cases. Days after interim orders of 9 and 14 October 2013 favoured Andreas Neocleous & Co clients including Dmitry Rybolovlev, the firm hired the wife of Nicosia District Court president Charis Solomidou on 1 November 2013. His 9 July 2014 recusal ruling named her employer as A. Neocleous Trust Company Ltd; investigators concluded, on the balance of probabilities, he intentionally concealed it. Former deputy attorney general Rikkos Erotokritou did not forward the Elena Rybolovleva complaint police file to the attorney general, and ensured it returned to police quickly, against standard procedure. Former Limassol CID head Ioannis Sotiriadis allegedly delayed returning her passport. It recommends criminal investigation of Solomidou for bribery and Rybolovlev for influence peddling, finding no guilt.
inside: Cyprus's Anti-Corruption Authority found a Russian businessman's law firm put a judge's wife on its payroll and reached prosecutors and police, so decisions went the firm's clients' way.
cite: Politis (en.politis.com.cy), Michalis Hadjistylianou, 17 June 2026
undone: The authority's findings, in a confidential final report of more than 3,000 pages, went to the attorney general as criminal referrals in June 2026. No one has been charged, no court has ruled on any of it, and the authority said that everyone named is presumed innocent.

n: Mauritius drugs inquiry tied a minister and a deputy speaker to traffickers
rank: Minister for Gender Equality; Deputy Speaker
d: The Commission of Inquiry on Drug Trafficking in Mauritius, chaired by the former judge Paul Lam Shang Leen, opened on 15 November 2015, questioned more than 300 people, released its findings in late July 2018 and called for further in-depth investigations. Roubina Jadoo-Jaunbocus, a lawyer and Minister for Gender Equality, resigned after the commission accused her of meeting jailed traffickers who were not her clients, and alleged she was complicit in money laundering and had arranged a money transfer to a trafficker. Deputy Speaker Sanjeev Teeluckdharry, like her a member of the governing MSM, resigned after being implicated. The prime minister said both disputed the findings and would take legal action, and that Jadoo-Jaunbocus could return to her post if she cleared her name in court.
inside: An official inquiry alleged a serving minister had met jailed traffickers who were not her clients and had helped move money for one; she and the deputy speaker both resigned.
undone: On 13 August 2024 the Privy Council allowed an appeal by Coomaravel Pyaneandee, a lawyer criticised in the same report (Pyaneandee v Lam Shang Leen [2024] UKPC 27), declaring that passages about him on pages 232-233 breached fairness and natural justice because he was never told the gist of the case against him, and ordering that they be disregarded and a link to the judgment be added to the published report. Whether any court challenge, prosecution or reinstatement followed for Jadoo-Jaunbocus or Teeluckdharry could not be confirmed.
cite: Africanews, 28 July 2018

n: San-Pedro's criminal police chief convicted in a cocaine network
rank: commissaire of the criminal police, San-Pedro
inside: A trafficking ring had the officer who ran criminal investigations in the port city on its side, so the police force meant to stop the cocaine was part of it.
d: Karamoko Dosso, a former commissaire of the criminal police in the Ivorian port of San-Pedro, was among nineteen convicted of drug trafficking and criminal association by the pole penal economique after a record seizure of more than two tonnes of cocaine in Abidjan and San-Pedro in April 2022. Thirteen appealed. The Abidjan appeal court confirmed ten-year sentences for five, including Miguel Devesa, a former Spanish police officer described as the network's organiser, and cut five to five years, Dosso's among them and that of Cesar Ouattara, a former regional elected official from San Pedro. Three defendants were acquitted, among them the cook Bartolo Priolo, and four companies, including Italia Service, were cleared of tax fraud; Italia Service's director, Maurizio Coco, said he served 37 months in custody before the acquittal.
undone: Devesa's lawyer, Me Zakaria Toure, called the sentence harsh and announced an appeal to the Court of Cassation, so the sentences are not final.
cite: Fraternite Matin via AllAfrica, 29 July 2025, on the Abidjan appeal court ruling of 28 July 2025 (the article itself gives no year)

n: Brunei's major crimes chief took a Malaysian contractor's pickup truck
org_label: Liew Say Koo (Say Koo (Liew) construction and L & E Contractor)
rank: head of the Major Crimes Investigation Unit, Royal Brunei Police Force
inside: A barred Malaysian contractor got the head of the police major crimes unit to press immigration to let him back in, in exchange for a vehicle.
d: Superintendent Hj Khairur Rijal Hj Abu Salim, former head of the Royal Brunei Police Force's Major Crimes Investigation Unit, was convicted of corruption and abuse of power at the Magistrate's Court in Bandar Seri Begawan on 31 January 2019. The court found he corruptly accepted a Toyota Hilux from Liew Say Koo, a Malaysian contractor, for helping him re-enter Brunei after he was barred following a two-year sentence for a 2007 conviction for killing his wife. Of 36 re-entry requests sent to immigration between 2011 and 2013, 14 went while he was abroad on training. He said he had borrowed the vehicle over three years as an unmarked surveillance car and that Liew was a police informant; the magistrate found it modified to stand out and Liew's informant role exaggerated.
undone: Sentencing of Khairur Rijal was deferred, the court taking two weeks from the verdict to consider it; this source does not record the sentence imposed and no later source for it could be found. Liew Say Koo was sentenced to 18 months for abetting.
cite: The Scoop (Brunei), 1 February 2019

n: Airline's $35,000 bribe to four Kyiv Court of Appeal judges
rank: four judges of the Kyiv Court of Appeal
inside: Prosecutors say four appeal judges received $35,000 from an airline's representative to release two aircraft held as evidence, so the court's decision served the company rather than the case.
d: Ukraine's anti-corruption bureau NABU and the specialised prosecutors SAPO allege four judges of the Kyiv Court of Appeal received $35,000, offered by Tetiana Polishchuk of Aircompany Constanta PrJSC, to cancel the seizure of two An-74TK-100 aircraft held as evidence in a case about obstructing the armed forces. The seizure of one aircraft was lifted in November 2023, and the judges, Viacheslav Dziubin, Ihor Palenyk, Viktor Hlynianyi and Yurii Slyva, were detained on 29 November 2023; searches reportedly found $10,000 with Dziubin, $25,000 with Palenyk and $8,300 each with Slyva and Hlynianyi. The High Council of Justice removed them from judging and later dismissed all four. SAPO referred the case to court on 20 September 2024; the register shows proceedings continuing through May 2026 with no verdict. The allegations are unproven.
cite: Transparency International Ukraine, HACC case No. 991/10365/24 (proceeding No. 52023000000000547)

n: Businessman's $20m in bribes to Armenia's finance minister
rank: former Minister of Finance
inside: A businessman allegedly paid Armenia's finance minister more than $20m, and in return his company is said to have been given favourable tax treatment.
d: On 8 July 2024 the US Department of Justice announced a settled civil forfeiture action over a Holmby Hills mansion in Los Angeles bought in 2011 by a trust benefiting the sons of Gagik Khachatryan, then Armenia's most senior official for taxes and customs and later finance minister. The sons called the money loans; the United States alleges the loans, repeatedly extended without repayment, were covers for bribe payments. Gibson Dunn's FCPA review names the payer as the businessman Sedrak Arustamyan, said to have paid more than $20m in exchange for favourable tax treatment for his company. The United States will sell the property, keep 85% of the net proceeds and pass the rest to the sons. The alleged payments are the subject of pending criminal prosecutions in Armenia.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 8 July 2024; Gibson Dunn, '2024 Year-End FCPA Update'

n: Company founder convicted of bribing a Kazakh state enterprise branch head (ruling not final)
who: a private company bidding on boiler-house work
rank: head of a branch of a state-owned enterprise
inside: A company's owner paid an official running part of a state enterprise to get a favourable state review, but the scheme was stopped before the review was given.
d: A court in Astana convicted three people over a bribe offered to secure a favourable state review for a project to reconstruct 21 boiler houses. According to Orda.kz, the founder of a private company offered 73.5 million tenge in total, and a middleman passed 12.2 million tenge of it to a government official who headed a branch of a state-owned enterprise. The offer was made in the autumn of 2024 and law enforcement exposed the scheme before the deal was completed. All three defendants pleaded not guilty and asked for acquittal: the businessman was given eight years, the official eleven years and the intermediary eighteen months. The report, published on 9 July 2025, says the ruling had not yet come into legal effect, and no appeal outcome is recorded.
cite: Orda.kz, 9 July 2025

n: A network of 200 firms was shielded inside Ukraine's State Tax Service
org_label: a money-laundering hub operating 200 controlled firms
who: operators of a network of 200 controlled firms
rank: the former head of the State Tax Service and the deputy head of the Poltava Regional Tax Office
inside: Operators of a network of 200 paper companies were allegedly shielded by the former head of the national tax service, so the service ran no audits.
d: NABU's report for the second half of 2025 records a case about a money-laundering hub with billion-hryvnia turnovers, whose members operated a network of 200 controlled firms that mass-produced fictitious tax invoices so other businesses could cut their tax. The report says the operation was shielded by the former head of Ukraine's State Tax Service and the deputy head of the Poltava Regional Tax Office, who helped the hub's companies obtain favourable rulings and guaranteed no tax audits or control measures would be conducted. It puts the forged sales at UAH 15 billion between 2020 and 2023, 'scheme-based' VAT at more than UAH 2.3 billion, and the tax revenue shortfall at UAH 147 million. The officials are not named and no payment to them is stated. The allegations are unproven.
cite: National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine, report for the second half of 2025, investigations section (the page's own footer and archive URL instead say 2026)

n: Cyprus law firm bribed the deputy attorney general; he was jailed, the firm fined
rank: Deputy Attorney General of Cyprus
d: In February 2017 the Assize Court found Rikkos Erotokritou, Cyprus's former deputy attorney general, guilty of bribery, abuse of power, corruption and conspiracy, giving him three and a half years for bribery, eighteen months for abuse of power. The Andreas Neocleous law firm LLC, then among the island's largest, was convicted of bribery, conspiracy and corruption and fined 70,000 euros; the founder's son, Panayiotis Neocleous, got two and a half years, and Andreas Kyprizoglou, a partner in Erotokritou's firm, eighteen months suspended for conspiracy to defraud.
