The prosecution argued efforts to ensure a raid on the Providencia trust went unpunished showed a conspiracy between Erotokritou and Panayiotis Neocleous over Erotokritou's application to have his loan written off. The investigation began with a probe attorney general Costas Clerides ordered in 2015.
inside: A large law firm bribed the state's second-ranking prosecutor; prosecutors said he worked to keep a raid on the Providencia trust from being punished.
undone: The Supreme Court heard the appeals in December 2017 and was to rule separately on whether Erotokritou held constitutional immunity from prosecution, which could have collapsed the case; neither source records the outcome. President Anastasiades pardoned Panayiotis Neocleous in 2018.
cite: Financial Mirror, 15 December 2017; OCCRP

n: Monaco's top judge charged over a 136 million euro award to developer Caroli
rank: President of the Supreme Court of Monaco
d: Didier Linotte led Monaco's Supreme Court for eleven years until Prince Albert II ended his mandate in August 2023. In 2020 that court, sitting as a bench of seven, ordered the Monegasque state to pay the developer Caroli nearly 136 million euros plus interest after Monaco withdrew from the Esplanade des Pêcheurs development; five of the seven voted for it. Prosecutors charged Linotte in June 2025 with trading in influence, passive corruption, illegal taking of interest in an organised group and money laundering, over acts they place in Monaco and France from 25 November 2011 to 13 July 2023. They are examining consultancy he is said to have continued through the firm Alma Marceau Transactions, including for Vinci, while sitting on the court.
undone: No trial has been held. The prosecutor general opened a preliminary inquiry in November 2021, after the hacked 'Dossiers du Rocher' leaks; the Monegasque state joined the proceedings in July 2024, saying it had found facts revealing Linotte's partiality. He was held for two days on 23 and 24 June 2025 and charged on 25 June, left at liberty under judicial supervision but barred from leaving Monaco. His lawyer calls the suggestion of outside influence on the judgment a fable, points out that the ruling was collegial, and says the consultancy was compatible with his status and ended in 2017 at the prince's request; he has filed motions in Monaco's court of appeal and a complaint to the European Court of Human Rights. Linotte is presumed innocent.
inside: The president of Monaco's highest court is accused of selling his influence while his bench ordered the state to pay a developer nearly 136 million euros.
cite: Monaco-Matin, 25 June 2025, and Monaco Hébdo, 1 July 2025, on the charges and the dates the prosecutor general gave; AFP via Paradis Fiscaux et Judiciaires, June 2025; Monaco Life, 26 June 2025

n: Cocaine traffickers paid a Salvadoran prisons aide for favours, prosecutors say
rank: aide in the General Directorate of the Bureau of Prisons
d: Wilfredo Hernandez Molina, for about a decade an aide to El Salvador's vice minister of security Osiris Luna Meza and an assistant in the prisons directorate on $2,500 a month, was arrested on 30 May 2023 on bribery accusations and illicit association, with a prisons fish-farming instructor, Mario Chavarria Ayala. Prosecutors say they sold early release, improved living conditions, unauthorised family visits and entry to Mariona prison, a transfer to the Baptist Hospital for detained trafficker Marvin Antonio Ramos (the report gives both 18 March 2022 and 18-20 January 2022), and funeral leave for Angel Alexander Bonilla Carranza. In a wiretapped call Walter Ramos said a visit would cost $5,000 to $6,000. He had no formal authority over prison staff; the report attributes his influence to his closeness to Luna.
inside: Prosecutors say traffickers' payments reached an aide inside the prisons directorate, so the prison service granted them visits, hospital stays and leave other inmates could not get.
undone: El Faro reported the case in July 2023 and no later outcome is recorded; the same report notes that two earlier investigations into Hernandez Molina never went to trial.
cite: El Faro, July 2023

n: Business associates' gifts bought favour from Brunei's work pass chief
org_label: business associates, including Daiecharm Deco Sdn Bhd and BT Employment Agency
who: business associates, including Daiecharm Deco and BT Employment Agency
rank: Senior Chief Immigration Officer, Head of the Work Pass Section
inside: Business owners who needed work passes gave gifts to the officer heading the work pass section, and the court found he showed them preferential treatment.
d: Seruji bin Haji Setia, a former Senior Chief Immigration Officer and head of Brunei's Work Pass Section, which approves permits for foreign workers, was convicted on 12 October 2024 on five counts of graft under Section 165 of the Penal Code, Chapter 22, and sentenced on 28 October 2024 to three years, effective from his remand date of 12 October. The court heard business associates gave him carpets, sofa cushion covers, car seat covers and BND100 in cash on multiple occasions, including Daiecharm Deco Sdn Bhd's managing director and BT Employment Agency's manager, and found he had shown preferential treatment to certain business owners, calling it a severe abuse of authority. The report does not say which payer gave what, nor which work-pass decisions were involved.
cite: Borneo Bulletin, 28 October 2024

n: Hotels and an events firm bought favour inside Brunei's tourism ministry
org_label: two hotels and an event management company
who: two hotels and an event management company
rank: Deputy Permanent Secretary for Tourism, Ministry of Primary Resources and Tourism
inside: Two hotels let the tourism ministry's deputy secretary defer his bills and the court found he favoured them in return; an events firm paid into his own account.
d: Wardi Mohd Ali, Deputy Permanent Secretary for Tourism at Brunei's Ministry of Primary Resources and Tourism until suspended in February 2021, was convicted on 23 July 2025 of misconduct in public office under section 12B of the Prevention of Corruption Act, Chapter 131. The Magistrate's Court found he had been or remained favourably disposed to two hotels for being allowed not to pay immediately on checking out between 18 June 2020 and 23 February 2021, accumulating unpaid invoices of about BND5,000, and let an event management company running a ministry event under his purview transfer funds into his personal account three times. Prosecution witnesses said his position was a factor in the hotels' deferring payment. The court called his actions deliberate, without reasonable justification and a serious abuse of power.
undone: The court revoked his bail. Sentencing submissions were set for 30 July 2025 and the sentence is not recorded in this source; the offence carries a fine of up to BND30,000 and/or up to seven years in prison.
cite: Borneo Bulletin via The Star (Malaysia), 24 July 2025

n: Suppliers' alleged $500,000 bribe for a Ukrainian deputy minister
org_label: EPG LLC and Techno Train LLC
rank: Deputy Minister of Communities and Territories Development (the case file also calls him former Acting Minister)
inside: Prosecutors say contractors' money was meant for a deputy minister so that ministry procurement went to predetermined suppliers at inflated prices.
d: Prosecutors allege a USD 500,000 bribe intended for Vasyl Lozynskyi, a deputy minister in Ukraine's Ministry of Communities and Territories Development, whom the case file also calls former acting minister. USD 400,000 of it came from Lviv with Roman Kitner, who allegedly collected part of the bribe there from Ihor Politar; the remaining USD 100,000's source is unestablished. The money is tied to alleged 7-10% kickbacks on 2022 heating-season equipment purchases: the Cabinet transferred UAH 1.68 billion, UAH 1.41 billion of it to procurement by the state institute UkrNDIvodokanalproekt under direct contracts with predetermined suppliers at prices allegedly inflated by 25 to 30%. Co-defendants include Serhii Kryvyi of Techno Train LLC, who allegedly used companies he controlled, and his subordinate Mykhailo Lukashyk, who allegedly prepared the inflated bids.
undone: The case file says Lozynskyi was detained on 21 January 2023 while receiving a bribe, though its own narrative says NABU searched the intermediary and he was not able to receive the money. He was dismissed on 22 January 2023 and released on UAH 2.5 million bail on 21 July 2023. The trial opened at the High Anti-Corruption Court on 16 May 2024 and is still running; the only verdict on file is the approval, on 18 December 2024, of the plea agreement of Oleksandr Kroshko (also spelled Kroshka), former director of EPG LLC, who admitted giving a bribe. On 21 January 2026 the court severed and suspended the case of co-defendant Mykhailo Lukashyk, who was serving in the military. Lozynskyi is charged under Articles 368(4) and 369(4) of the Criminal Code.
cite: Transparency International Ukraine, HACC Decided case file, proceeding No. 52022000000000280 (HACC case No. 991/4139/24)

n: Russian bank and officials got inside Kyrgyzstan's Keremet Bank
who: Russian state bank PSB and Russian officials
rank: Keremet Bank management and ownership
inside: Russian officials and a sanctioned Russian state bank coordinated with officials inside a Kyrgyz bank, and the state sold control of it to a firm linked to a Russian oligarch.
d: On 15 January 2025 the US Treasury designated Kyrgyzstan's OJSC Keremet Bank under E.O. 14024, as amended by E.O. 14114, for conducting or facilitating significant transactions, or providing services, involving Russia's military-industrial base. Treasury said that since at least summer 2024 Keremet officials have coordinated with Russian officials and the sanctioned Russian state bank Promsvyazbank on a sanctions evasion scheme in which Keremet would make cross-border transfers for PSB; neither the Keremet nor the Russian officials are named. It said the Kyrgyz finance ministry sold a controlling stake in the bank in 2024 to a firm strongly linked to a Russian oligarch tied to the Russian government, intending to create a sanctions evasion hub. Treasury also said the US-designated Russian-Moldovan oligarch Ilan Shor joined discussions about the bank's role.
cite: US Department of the Treasury press release, 15 January 2025

n: Ukraine's court administration chief jailed over a company's Supreme Court case
who: Forvater Plus LLC, the company whose case was at issue
rank: Head of the State Judicial Administration of Ukraine
inside: An intermediary's payments reached the official running Ukraine's court administration over a company's Supreme Court case; the court then partly granted the company's appeal.
d: Oleksii Salnikov was acting head of Ukraine's State Judicial Administration, which runs the courts' finances and staffing, from September 2021, formally appointed in April 2022 and dismissed in December 2023. Investigators say the former businessman Oleksii Honchar, the prosecution's key witness, approached him about a case before the Supreme Court's Administrative Cassation Court in which Forvater Plus LLC challenged the geology service's inaction over its application for a special subsoil permit without auction. They say Salnikov told him on 27 February 2023 that the case could be settled for $5,000, and that on 5 March 2023, under law enforcement supervision, Honchar handed him $5,000 at a restaurant and, after Salnikov said a further sum was needed, another $2,500 shortly afterwards. The court partially granted the company's appeal in December 2023.
undone: On 6 August 2025 the High Anti-Corruption Court convicted Salnikov of abuse of influence under Article 369-2(2), having acquitted him of fraud under Article 190(2) and reclassified the incitement-to-bribery charge brought under Article 369(4), and sentenced him to three years in prison with a three-year ban on holding posts in state and local government bodies. The defence argued the case was a provocation and that the money was for a vehicle for the Armed Forces. The parties were expected to appeal to the HACC Appeals Chamber, and no appeal outcome is recorded, so the conviction is not final on this source.
cite: Transparency International Ukraine, HACC Decided analytics on the Salnikov verdict

n: Prosecutors say a supplier's 1.9m lari reached Georgia's defence minister and PM
who: a businessman supplying the military hospital
rank: Minister of Defence and former Prime Minister
inside: Prosecutors say a supplier's cash reached the defence minister and the prime minister, and that the ministry's classified bidding was rigged on the minister's orders.
d: In September 2026 Georgia's Prosecutor's Office charged defence minister (2021-2024) Juansher Burchuladze and his relative Vasil Mkheidze over the purchase of medical equipment for the Giorgi Abramishvili Military Hospital under classified procurement rules in late 2022. Prosecutors say Mkheidze demanded a 10% cash kickback on the contract; the businessman sought guarantees higher up, and Burchuladze allegedly reached an understanding with then prime minister Irakli Garibashvili, who demanded his own cut, vouching for the chosen businessman. They say 1,900,000 lari was paid in instalments, Mkheidze keeping 400,000 and passing 1,500,000 to the minister, who kept 750,000 and passed 750,000 to Garibashvili. Burchuladze allegedly ordered his deputy Giorgi Khaindrava and procurement chief Vladimer Ghudushauri to rig the bidding. Across three contracts GEL 18,484,960 was charged against a market value of GEL 11,499,705.
undone: Former prime minister Irakli Garibashvili has been charged in the same matter. Burchuladze is charged under Article 338 of the Criminal Code and Mkheidze under Articles 25 and 338, and both are already serving sentences in separate criminal convictions. Both have proposed guilty pleas: Burchuladze five years, three in prison and two suspended, with a GEL 1,000,000 fine; Mkheidze four years and two months, one year two months in prison and three years suspended, with a GEL 100,000 fine. The prosecution says both cooperated and will seek summary judgment at the initial hearing, and puts the damage to the state at GEL 6,985,255.
cite: First Channel Georgia (1TV), 8 September 2026, reporting the Prosecutor's Office

n: El Salvador's ex-attorney general jailed for faking a case to favour businessman Rais
who: Enrique Rais, the businessman prosecutors say was favoured
rank: Attorney General of El Salvador
d: On 22 August 2025 the Tribunal Tercero de Sentencia in San Salvador sentenced Luis Antonio Martinez Gonzalez, El Salvador's former attorney general, to ten years: five for procedural fraud and five for failing to investigate. Prosecutors had asked for fifteen. The prosecution service accused Martinez of favouring the businessman Enrique Rais by using false evidence in cases involving the lawyer Mario Calderon, who represents the querella, and Claudia Herrera, a victim. Also convicted were Julio Adalberto Arriaza Gonzalez, former director of the Fiscalia's office for defending society's interests, who got five years for fraude procesal after his charge was changed from actos arbitrarios, and Francisco Grimaldi, who got six for fraude procesal under concurso real, tried for two separate cases. Asked about the ruling, Martinez said 'no comment'.
undone: The sentence is first-instance and no appeal outcome has been checked. The report records no verdict for Enrique Rais, whose role is the prosecution service's accusation rather than an adjudicated finding. The verdict came nine years to the day after Martinez and Rais were first arrested in the case in 2016.
inside: Prosecutors say the attorney general used the national prosecution service's own cases, built on false evidence, to favour the businessman Enrique Rais.
cite: Diario El Mundo, 22 August 2025

n: Document fixers allegedly bribed staff inside Malta's identity agency for ID cards
rank: officials of Identita, Malta's identity agency
d: Identita, formerly Identity Malta, is the Maltese state agency that issues identity cards and residence permits. Former member of parliament Jason Azzopardi alleges officials there helped non-EU nationals obtain valid ID cards and residence permits on false documents, putting the number at 18,000. He names the car dealer Bernard Attard as a broker who allegedly asked non-EU nationals for bribes running into thousands of euros, and alleges that Marija Spiteri, who worked at the agency's Brexit desk, used to input the foreign nationals' details into the system and let them into the office after hours so their photographs could be taken. Spiteri, a former Identita employee, and Attard were later arraigned and charged with money laundering, human trafficking, fraud and forgery; bail was refused and their assets frozen.
undone: No verdict has been reached. The compilation of evidence against Spiteri and Attard continues before Magistrate Donatella Frendo Dimech, and both are presumed innocent. Sources privy to Identita's workings reportedly disputed that the number of false cards was as high as 18,000, and said the agency had long been aware of fake identity cards; in court the prosecution said police investigations had uncovered only seven forged cards, and Identita's former head of compliance, Claudio Spiteri, confirmed that figure and said he had never heard the larger number mentioned. Police charged three Egyptian nationals with fraudulently obtaining ID cards; two pleaded guilty and were jailed six months each, while the third, Moustafa Ata Moussa Darwish, did not plead guilty and his case is ongoing. It remains unclear whether any serving Identita officials are under investigation.
inside: A former MP alleges that a ring selling papers paid staff inside the state identity agency, so it issued real ID cards and residence permits to the ring's clients.
cite: MaltaToday, report by Kurt Sansone (the page carries no publication date); MaltaToday court reports on the arraignment of Maria Spiteri and Bernard Attard and on the compilation of evidence before Magistrate Donatella Frendo Dimech

n: Indian technicians captured traffic inside Mauritius Telecom's cable station
rank: Baie-Jacotet submarine cable landing station
d: Mauritius Telecom is the island's main, state-controlled telecommunications company, and the Baie-du-Jacotet landing station is where the SAFE submarine cable carrying Mauritius's internet traffic comes ashore. A report by Girish Guddoy, Chief Technical Officer, revealed by Teleplus, says that on 15 April, with no year given on the page, a team of Indian technicians connected their tools to several internet links on the SAFE cable there and carried out a two-minute data capture on each, and that the tools were then removed. Guddoy says he told the chief executive, Sherry Singh, at once; the report was submitted before Guddoy resigned and was handed to Mauritius Telecom's acting chief executive. The article calls the sniffing alleged.
inside: Indian technicians were allegedly inside the state telecoms company's cable landing station, connecting tools to the country's main internet links and capturing data from each.
cite: Le Mauricien, 22 July 2022; L'Express/allAfrica, 16 April 2025
undone: Nothing has been established in court. Singh made the claim publicly on 1 July 2022; on 11 July the then prime minister complained to police that it was false news and said he had never authorised any foreign party to install interception equipment. Five complaints went to the Central Criminal Investigation Department, 23 people were questioned between July 2022 and February 2025, and no one had been arrested as of April 2025, when the government said it would bring in foreign investigators.

n: Brunei narcotics officer fed his drug supplier the bureau's secrets
rank: Assistant Narcotics Officer II, Narcotics Control Bureau
inside: A drug supplier had a source inside the drug squad, an officer who passed on confidential bureau information seven times, seeking cut-price drugs and to shield him from enforcement.
d: Muhammad Ali Iskandar bin Mustapha, an Assistant Narcotics Officer II in Brunei's Narcotics Control Bureau, disclosed confidential bureau information to his drug supplier on seven occasions between June and August 2023, seeking drugs at a reduced price and to shield the supplier from enforcement action. The supplier is not named and the report does not say whether money changed hands. He denied the charge on 19 March, then pleaded guilty on 26 December, and was sentenced on 7 January 2025 to two years and eight months in prison under section 12(B) of the Prevention of Corruption Act (Chapter 131), with two further offences taken into consideration. The sentence was reported the following day.
cite: Borneo Bulletin, 8 January 2025

n: Eight airport police charged over a trafficking network at Dakar's airport
org_label: a Senegalese and Sierra Leonean trafficking network
rank: police officers serving at Blaise Diagne International Airport
inside: A trafficking network allegedly paid officers on duty at the international airport 20,000 CFA francs a head to board travellers, making border policing part of the route.
d: Eight police officers at Blaise Diagne International Airport, outside Dakar, were arrested and charged on 4 December 2020 with complicity in migrant trafficking, document fraud and corruption, in a case the Brigade de Recherches de Faidherbe built against a network described as run by Senegalese and Sierra Leonean nationals, said to operate between Diamniadio and the Boune road. Hosts and facilitators said the officers helped travellers board flights for 20,000 CFA francs each. Police found 87 women from Sierra Leone and Guinea who were to be flown from the airport to work in the Gulf countries, reportedly as prostitutes or domestic workers, each saying they had paid more than 7,000,000 leones. The officers were granted provisional release pending a hearing on the merits; the drivers were held pending trial.
undone: The status is as of December 2020: the officers were charged and granted provisional release pending a hearing on the merits, and no outcome of that hearing is recorded six years on. Ndarinfo is relaying a report by Liberation; the Liberation original was not retrieved.
cite: Ndarinfo, 7 December 2020, citing Liberation

n: Coal buyers and hauliers paid officials inside Mongolia's state coal firm
org_label: coal buyers, transport companies and Chinese intermediaries
rank: Erdenes Tavan Tolgoi management, customs and border officials
inside: Coal buyers and haulage firms allegedly worked with managers inside Mongolia's state coal company and with customs officers, so state coal was sold and shipped on terms that suited them.
d: State coal company Erdenes Tavan Tolgoi was alleged to have undervalued coal against its market price in offtake contracts with Bodi International LLC, while transport companies were alleged to have overvalued their services. Bottlenecks at the railway, customs and the border militia gave officials opportunities to demand bribes. Thousands protested in Sukhbaatar Square in front of parliament in December 2022, and a former chief executive of the company, Gankhuyag Battulga, was charged with money laundering along with 11 others.
undone: By October 2025 the Prosecutor's Office reported 124 cases investigated against 156 individuals and three legal entities, 108 individuals charged, 88 found guilty, five sentenced to between two years and five years and nine months in prison, 80 fined, and 63 barred from public office for two to seven years, with 20 trials pending and 40 investigations continuing. Those figures are aggregate for the coal case and are not tied to the named company officials or firms above.
cite: U4 Anti-Corruption Resource Centre, 'The coal theft case', U4 Brief 2024:4, 27 February 2024; The Star (Go Go Mongolia/ANN), 7 October 2025, thestar.com.my/aseanplus/aseanplus-news/2025/10/07/five-people-sentenced-to-prison-and-80-fined-for-coal-crimes-in-mongolia

n: FSB paid a Ukrainian cabinet secretariat department head for secret files
rank: head of a department of the Cabinet of Ministers Secretariat
inside: Russia's security service recruited and paid a department head inside the office that serves Ukraine's government, so secret files from his own desk went to Moscow.
d: Ukraine's SSU reported on 21 June 2022 detaining a department head in the Cabinet of Ministers Secretariat and a directorate head at the Chamber of Commerce and Industry. The SSU said the FSB recruited the first man in 2012 on a trip to Russia and tasked him with collecting secret material, printed or photographed onto a flash drive: the state of Ukraine's defences, the arrangement of the state border and the personal data of law enforcement officers. The chamber official was his liaison, meetings arranged through a closed Telegram channel, and sent material to Russia by encrypted channels. The FSB reportedly paid $2,000 to $15,000 a task at meetings in temporarily occupied Crimea or abroad, where the chamber official usually collected it, paying the cabinet official his share in Kyiv.
undone: Both men were declared suspects of treason under Article 111 of the Criminal Code, which carries 12 to 15 years, and were remanded in custody. The cited report is from June 2022 and carries no trial result; the current stage is unverified.
cite: Hromadske, 21 June 2022, reporting the Security Service of Ukraine

n: Food firm's $55,000 bribe freed its invoices inside Kharkiv's tax office
rank: head of a department of the Main Directorate of the State Tax Service in the Kharkiv region
inside: A company's money was offered to a department head inside the regional tax office so that the commission would take the firm off a risk list and unblock its trading.
d: On 18 January 2024 Ocean Foods LLC went on the tax service's risk-criteria list, blocking its tax invoices and nearly halting its business. A company representative asked Olena Zubko for help; she had no authority and brought in Vitalii Hovorukha, who offered $55,000, to be shared among those involved, to an acquaintance heading a department of the State Tax Service's Kharkiv Main Directorate, so the commission would delist the company. Searches followed on 14 February and property was seized on 12 March. Both signed plea agreements with the specialised anti-corruption prosecutor on 12 August 2024, trial opened on 19 August, and both were convicted of aiding and abetting bribery on 21 August - the case page also gives 22 August - with one-year and two-year probationary terms and assigned duties.
cite: Transparency International Ukraine, HACC case file 52024000000000324

n: Fenech paid Malta's police anti-money-laundering chief, prosecutors say
rank: head of the police anti-money-laundering unit
d: Ray Aquilina, then head of the Maltese police's anti-money-laundering unit, is accused of taking a corrupt benefit from the businessman Yorgen Fenech at a time when his own unit was meant to be investigating Fenech's Dubai company 17 Black. Prosecutors say Fenech arranged the transfer of an apartment in Birżebbuġa to Aquilina at a significantly reduced price, with Aquilina's parents appearing as the buyers before donating it to him. Investigators told the court that Aquilina had looked up Fenech's name and identity card on the police database on eleven separate occasions. Aquilina was first arrested in 2021 in a wider probe into officials suspected of leaking information from the Caruana Galizia murder investigation to suspects. No conduct year is established, so this record is filed under that arrest.
inside: The head of the police anti-money-laundering unit is accused of taking a cut-price flat from the businessman his own unit was supposed to be investigating.
undone: No verdict. Aquilina, Fenech and the notary Mario Bugeja were charged on 15 January 2025 and all three pleaded not guilty; Aquilina faces corruption, perjury, revealing official secrets and money laundering, Fenech complicity in corrupting a public officer and money laundering, and Bugeja money laundering. On 12 February 2025 Magistrate Rachel Montebello found enough prima facie evidence and committed all three for trial. Fenech's acquittal on the Caruana Galizia murder charges in September 2026 has no bearing on this case, which turns on different offences and different evidence. Aquilina had taken a management post at Enemalta after retiring from the police and no longer holds it. All are presumed innocent.
cite: The Malta Independent, 12 February 2025; MaltaToday and Newsbook, 15 Jan 2025 (arraignment); TVM News, 12 Feb 2025 (committed for trial); Lovin Malta, Sep 2026, on the murder acquittal not binding this case

n: UK charges Peter Virdee with bribing Antigua's tourism and energy minister
rank: Minister of Tourism, Economic Development, Investment and Energy
d: Britain's National Crime Agency charged Peter Virdee, 50, also known as Hardip Singh, with bribing a foreign public official, named in the charge as Asot Michael, a Member of Parliament and Government Minister of Tourism, Economic Development, Investment and Energy for Antigua and Barbuda. Virdee's company PV Energy Ltd was charged with failing to prevent bribery over the same conduct, which the agency says took place between January 2015 and July 2017 and was intended to benefit PV Energy. Virdee appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 23 May 2024 and was bailed to appear at Southwark Crown Court on 20 June 2024. The agency described the investigation as multi-million pound, gave no bribe figure, and hedged only that it is alleged.
inside: A British energy company is accused of paying Antigua's energy minister, so the minister's decisions on power projects would serve the company.
undone: Virdee and PV Energy pleaded not guilty in a London court, reported on 9 July 2025. No trial outcome has been reported; both are presumed innocent.
cite: National Crime Agency press release, 23 May 2024 (via wired-gov.net republication; the NCA newsroom original could not be opened); Global Investigations Review, 9 July 2025

n: PdVSA and FMLN mayors co-owned Alba Petroleos; its boss became vice-minister
rank: deputy foreign minister; 18 municipal mayors
d: Alba Petroleos was set up in El Salvador in 2006 as a joint public-private venture: Venezuela's state oil company PdVSA held 60 per cent and eighteen FMLN mayors 40 per cent, financed by Venezuelan loans to the mayors between 2010 and 2015. InSight Crime calls Jose Luis Merino, an FMLN political commission member, the primary middleman between the FMLN and the Venezuelan government and Alba's public face, with his brother Sigfredo the listed founder while Merino controlled it behind the scenes. In late October 2016 President Salvador Sanchez Ceren had Foreign Minister Hugo Martinez create an ad-hoc post for Merino, which became a vice ministry of foreign affairs.
inside: A foreign state oil company owned a Salvadoran firm jointly with serving mayors, and its chief go-between was then made a deputy foreign minister.
undone: In June 2017 fourteen members of the US Congress from both parties asked the US Treasury to investigate Merino under the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act. Responding to earlier accusations by Senator Marco Rubio in 2016, the FMLN condemned what it called defamatory and baseless claims against one of its best leaders; the article reports no response from Merino to the 2017 letter.
cite: InSight Crime investigation, 2018 (updated 2025)

n: Brunei immigration officer paid to wave travellers out of the country
rank: immigration officer
inside: An outsider paid an immigration officer to break the rules she enforced, so border control worked for whoever paid rather than the state.
d: Hajah Nurul Huda, also known as Hajah Rusiati binti Abdullah, a former Brunei immigration officer, pleaded guilty to four charges under Section 6(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, Chapter 131, and got two years, two charges running consecutively and two concurrently. She took BND500 in bribes, in cash and by bank transfer, from an Indonesian national between October 2023 and July 2024, bypassing immigration rules so foreign nationals could leave Brunei without required re-entry permits. Malaysian Immigration at the Miri ICQ found discrepancies in a foreign national's travel records and a person concealed in a vehicle, and referred the case to Brunei's Anti-Corruption Bureau. Her defence cited her early plea, cooperation and the small sum; the judge said corruption, however small, is contagious and cannot be taken lightly.
cite: Borneo Bulletin (Fadley Faisal), 'Ex-immigration officer jailed for corruption', April 2025; the page carries no printed date beyond a site header of 15 April 2025 and says the sentence was passed the previous day

n: Kyiv judge Chaus took bribe money to fix a criminal verdict
who: a defendant seeking a suspended sentence
rank: judge of the Dniprovskyi District Court of Kyiv
inside: Money from outside the court reached a judge so that a defendant before him would be given a suspended sentence instead of prison.
d: Mykola Chaus was a judge of the Dniprovskyi District Court in Kyiv. Transparency International Ukraine records that an investigation opened in August 2016 after NABU caught him accepting a bribe, and that he was convicted in 2023 of soliciting a bribe of $100,000; its account gives the sum caught in 2016 as $150,000 and does not reconcile the two figures. The benefit was a suspended sentence for a pensioner accused of trading diphenhydramine. The case was referred to court in November 2021. He was sentenced to ten years in prison with full confiscation of property, reduced on appeal in 2025 to eight and a half years, and the case is under cassation review. The record does not say who handed over the money.
cite: Transparency International Ukraine, 'Real prison terms for real crimes: which high-level officials have been convicted'

n: Money allegedly aimed at prosecutors and judges to close a NABU case
org_label: a suspect in a NABU case
rank: a prosecutor of the Prosecutor General's Office, with SAPO officials and HACC judges named as targets
inside: A man under investigation allegedly paid a prosecutor and lawyers to buy decisions from the prosecutors and judges handling his own case, turning the anti-corruption system against itself.
d: NABU's report on its investigations records a case in which a prosecutor of the Prosecutor General's Office, together with two lawyers said to have acted as intermediaries, allegedly took money from a suspect in a NABU case to have that case closed, through bribes said to be intended for officials of the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office and judges of the High Anti-Corruption Court. The report says the sum demanded rose from $2 million to $3.5 million and that $200,000 was received, between February and September 2025, and that the scheme was exposed in October 2025. SAPO supervises corruption prosecutions and the High Anti-Corruption Court tries them, so these are the bodies meant to be beyond reach. Those involved are not named and the allegations are unproven.
cite: National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine, investigations section of its semi-annual report

n: Waste firm Helector bribed Cypriot mayors and planning officials
rank: mayor of Larnaca; municipal financial controller; town planning engineers
d: Helector, a waste management company that ran the landfills at Marathounda in Paphos and Koshi in Larnaca, was convicted in February 2020 of bribing Cypriot public officials. The case involved 83 charges of bribery, corruption, conspiracy and money laundering: the company overcharged municipalities by reporting higher waste volumes, and officials took bribes to look the other way. Convicted with it were Andreas Louroudjiatis, the former mayor of Larnaca, who received five years in prison; Demetris Patsalides, financial controller of Paphos municipality; and town planning engineers Michalis Pantis and Giorgos Koullapis. Helector was fined 201,000 euros. On 20 July 2022 the Supreme Court rejected all the appeals and convicted a further town planning engineer, Antonis Kourouzides, whom the lower court had acquitted.
inside: A waste contractor paid the municipal and planning officials who were supposed to check its invoices, so the councils kept paying it for waste it had not handled.
cite: Cyprus Mail, 20 July 2022

n: Brunei logistics firm's manager had a customs inspector bribed
rank: customs inspection officer, Royal Customs and Excise Department
inside: A freight company reached into the customs service that inspects its cargo by having its own staff bribe the inspecting officer.
d: Chin Chee Vun, 55, then general manager of the freight company Sivli Logistics Sdn Bhd, was convicted of instigating a subordinate to bribe a customs inspection officer in Brunei's Royal Customs and Excise Department, part of the Ministry of Finance and Economy, in October 2021. A Senior Magistrate's Court had acquitted him; the Public Prosecutor appealed, and the High Court in Bandar Seri Begawan reversed the acquittal and sentenced him to 24 months in prison, reported in September 2024. The report does not state the amount involved or what the company gained, and records no response from him.
cite: The Star (Malaysia), 25 September 2024, on the Brunei High Court ruling

n: Glencore bribed officials of Cameroon's state oil and refining firms
rank: officials of Société Nationale des Hydrocarbures (SNH) and Société Nationale de Raffinage (SNR, also known as Sonara)
d: Glencore, a commodity trader, paid bribes to officials of Société Nationale des Hydrocarbures and Société Nationale de Raffinage, Cameroon's state oil and refining companies, for favourable treatment in allocating and selling crude and buying oil products. The English court's sentencing remarks put the Cameroon bribes at EUR 10,532,712 between 1 March 2012 and 1 March 2015: EUR 4,187,820 disguised as service fees under an agent's contract and EUR 6,344,892 in cash from Glencore's Swiss cash desk. Glencore's UK arm pleaded guilty at a London court in June 2022 to seven counts, five of bribery, and was fined £182,935,392 in total, £56,881,245 of it for the Cameroon count. The judge said: 'I am making no findings of any kind against any specific individual'; individuals remained under Serious Fraud Office investigation, uncharged.
cite: Sentencing remarks, R v Glencore Energy UK Ltd, judiciary.uk; UK Serious Fraud Office case page, updated 1 May 2026
inside: A trading company's cash reached officials inside Cameroon's state oil and refining companies, which then gave Glencore favourable terms on the country's crude.

n: Eswatini registrar gave an alleged South African crime boss an identity
rank: assistant regional civil registrar, Ministry of Home Affairs
d: Nonhlanhla Malambe, an assistant regional civil registrar in Eswatini's Ministry of Home Affairs, was convicted of dishonesty and corruption by the civil service commission over a scheme giving citizenship documents to Vusimuzi 'Cat' Matlala, a South African businessman described as an alleged underworld figure. On 12 February 2024 she registered a birth certificate for 'Vusimuzi Dlamini', entered as replacing an older version, which the commission said falsely implied a long-standing registration; an ID card followed on 20 February. The certificate falsely named Thembi Christinah Zulu as his mother. Interpol asked Eswatini to verify the ID number after Dlamini's South African arrest; audits linked the account used to Malambe. The state alleges Matlala used it to pose as an Eswatini prince; he denied holding an Eswatini ID before South African MPs.
cite: TimesLIVE, 24 October 2026
inside: Eswatini's civil service commission found an assistant registrar guilty of corruption over a manufactured birth certificate and ID card for Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala, an alleged South African underworld figure.

n: Angola's central bank and sovereign fund moved $500m to a London firm
org_label: Jorge Gaudens Sebastião and a private foreign company headquartered in London
who: a private foreign company headquartered in London
rank: Governor and managing director of Banco Nacional de Angola; president of the Sovereign Fund
d: Angola's Supreme Court convicted four men in August 2020 over the irregular transfer of US$500 million from the central bank, Banco Nacional de Angola, to a private foreign company headquartered in London, said to be for a strategic investment fund for projects in Angola. José Filomeno dos Santos, president of the Sovereign Fund of Angola and a son of the former president, received five years in all for fraud and influence peddling. Valter Filipe, the former central bank governor, was convicted of continued embezzlement and fraud; the reports give no sentence for him. António Samalia Bule, its former managing director, got five years, and the businessman Jorge Gaudens Sebastião six. All were acquitted of money laundering.
inside: A private company headquartered in London received a US$500m transfer out of Angola's central bank; the Supreme Court convicted the bank's governor, its managing director and the sovereign fund's president.
undone: The defendants' extraordinary appeal of unconstitutionality suspended the ruling, and on 3 April 2024 the Constitutional Court declared the 2020 conviction unconstitutional, finding breaches of legality, the presumption of innocence, the adversarial principle and the rights of defence, chiefly the Supreme Court's refusal to admit a letter from former president José Eduardo dos Santos, and removed the fraud-by-defraudation count from the framework. The Supreme Court plenary reheard the record, including that written testimony, and on 9 July 2024 reinstated the convictions, holding that the former president's authorisation of the transfer did not exclude the defendants' responsibility; two judges dissented.
cite: Ver Angola (Lusa), 29 November 2021; Ver Angola, 4 April 2024; Ver Angola, 9 July 2024

n: US sanctions Liberia's presidential chief of staff over investors' bribes
org_label: investors and business owners dealing with the Liberian government
rank: Minister of State for Presidential Affairs and Chief of Staff to the President
d: On 15 August 2022 the US Treasury designated three senior Liberian officials under Executive Order 13818, which builds upon and implements the Global Magnitsky Act. One was Nathaniel McGill, Minister of State for Presidential Affairs and Chief of Staff to President George Weah. Treasury said McGill is credibly accused of taking bribes from potential investors, bribing business owners, taking kickbacks for steering contracts to companies he held an interest in, and manipulating public procurement processes to award multi-million dollar contracts. It says he solicited bribes from government office seekers and regularly distributes thousands of dollars in undocumented cash to other government officials. Also designated were Solicitor General and Chief Prosecutor Sayma Syrenius Cephus and the National Port Authority's managing director Bill Twehway. The release records no response from them.
inside: Treasury says bribes from investors and business owners reached the chief of staff to Liberia's president, who it says steered and rigged state procurement.
undone: allAfrica reported on 9 December 2023 that McGill, by then senator-elect for Margibi County, had earlier been sanctioned by the United States. Whether the designation is still in force was not confirmed.
cite: US Department of the Treasury press release, 15 August 2022; allAfrica, 9 December 2023

n: Prosecutors say a borrower's 1.7m birr bribe reached a Commercial Bank of Ethiopia chief
org_label: an unnamed borrower of the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia
rank: Vice-President, CBE Noor, Commercial Bank of Ethiopia (described in the report as the former CBE Noor executive)
d: Federal prosecutors charged Nuri Hussein, vice president for CBE Noor, the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia's interest-free unit, with receiving 1.7 million birr in bribes, in cash and in kind, from a borrower to facilitate a loan; the report also calls him the former CBE Noor executive. They accuse him of abusing his official authority and making the proceeds appear legitimate, and charge his sister-in-law, Rihana Workineh, with helping present the payments as lawful. The charges were put on 31 March 2026 before the Fourth Anti-Corruption Bench of the Federal High Court's Lideta Division, which kept Nuri in custody after his lawyers asked for more time to file objections, and adjourned to the following week. He had earlier been granted bail, upheld by the Federal Supreme Court. No plea is recorded.
inside: Prosecutors say a borrower's money reached the executive who ran the state bank's interest-free arm, and that the loan the borrower wanted was then facilitated.
cite: Addis Fortune, hearing of 31 March 2026

n: Financier Mpinganjira tried to buy Malawi's election-case judges
rank: High Court judges sitting as the Constitutional Court
d: Thomson Mpinganjira, founder of FDH Financial Holdings Limited and one of the richest people in Malawi, faced six charges under the Corrupt Practices Act and was convicted on 10 September 2021 on two counts of offering an advantage to a public officer under Section 24(2), the officers being Justices Michael Atanazio Tembo and Healey Potani. AFP reported that he was recorded offering financial inducements to one of the judges sitting as a Constitutional Court in the challenge to Malawi's 2019 presidential election, the allegation being that he sought their support for the then president, Peter Mutharika; the court found widespread irregularities and ordered a fresh election. High Court Judge Dorothy DeGabrielle sentenced him to nine years on each count, concurrently.
inside: A financier's money was offered to the judges deciding a presidential election case, to swing the court's ruling to the sitting president.
undone: Then president Lazarus Chakwera pardoned him under Section 89(2) of the Constitution on 6 July 2025, as one of 37 inmates pardoned during the Independence celebrations, and his appeal to the Supreme Court of Appeal was withdrawn by a notice dated 15 September 2025.
cite: Nation (Malawi) on the withdrawal of the appeal; AFP via Nile Post, 6 October 2021

n: Smugglers paid Kosovo border police to wave contraband trucks through
rank: border police officers serving in the Leposavić area
d: Smugglers moving goods between Serbia and Kosovo used serving Kosovo border police to pass lorries unchecked. In January 2019 BIRN's programme Justice in Kosovo broadcast footage from two petrol stations and a retail store in Leposavić of officers taking up to €200 to pass contraband lorries; the prosecution alleged 20 to 150 euros a vehicle, shared with officers on duty. In May 2020 the Special Prosecutor's Office charged 33 people, mostly Kosovo police, with offences including illegal firearms possession, later dropping the bribery counts. On 27 October 2023 Prishtina's Basic Court convicted 13 of the accused officers - the report gives their number as both 19 and 20 - imposing 23 years in total, terms from three years to 18 months, and two-year bans on public office after release.
undone: Of the rest, six were acquitted for lack of evidence, one had charges withdrawn, 11 accused were separated from the case and one defendant died; the bribery counts in the May 2020 indictment had already been dropped.
inside: A cross-border smuggling network had Kosovo's own border police on its side, so the state officers meant to search its lorries let them through instead.
cite: Prishtina Insight (BIRN Kosovo), 27 October 2023

n: Three Serbian interior ministry members convicted of aiding Šarić's group
rank: members of the Ministry of the Interior (MUP)
d: Three members of Serbia's Ministry of the Interior, which runs the police, were convicted of aiding the criminal group of Darko Šarić, head of an international criminal organisation, of abuse of official position and disclosure of confidential information. In April 2025 Šarić was sentenced to six years for planning a murder and discrediting a cooperating witness, in proceedings against him and his associates. Radio Slobodna Evropa set the verdict alongside an earlier episode: in 2014 five heads of police administrations were removed after Šarić named one of them in court as a corrupt policeman, the state leadership citing their alleged involvement in politics and the media and alleged contacts with the drug dealer then on trial; the dismissed officers said it was a staged media campaign by criminals.
inside: A drug-trafficking organisation had interior ministry members passing it confidential information, and a court convicted three of them for helping it.
undone: The report, a June 2026 retrospective, does not name the three, give their posts or sentences, or say whether the April 2025 verdict is final or under appeal.
cite: Radio Slobodna Evropa (RFE/RL), 2 June 2026

n: Finnish border guard paid to hand police files to a convicted drug offender
org_label: Timo Erkki Sakari Tulokas, convicted separately in a large drug case
who: a convicted drug offender buying police data
rank: border guard (rajavartija, also called merivartija in the report) in a military post, Finnish Border Guard
d: On 30 August 2024 Helsinki District Court sentenced Jim Markku Koskenmäki, in a Finnish Border Guard military post since 1995, to two years and six months for breach of official secrecy, aggravated dereliction of duty, aggravated bribe-taking, an aggravated firearms offence and a drug use offence, and stripped his military rank. The court found Timo Erkki Sakari Tulokas, who the previous year received more than ten years in a separate large drug case, asked him to search official registers for secret material on serious and organised crime, including live investigations, and paid him at least €1,820, his aim being to further organised criminal activity. The two agreed he would report any investigative measures aimed at Tulokas or people he named. Koskenmäki denied most charges and Tulokas all of his.
inside: A man convicted in a large drug case paid a serving border guard for the police's own files on organised-crime investigations, including live ones.
undone: The 30 August 2024 judgment was not legally final and could be appealed to the court of appeal; Tulokas received eight months, for aggravated bribery and incitement to breach of official secrecy and to aggravated dereliction of duty. No appeal-court ruling was found.
cite: Yle, 30 August 2024

n: Carabinieri report far-right group's proselytism reaching serving Italian soldiers
rank: three serving Italian Army soldiers posted in or near Turin
d: Carabinieri investigators in Turin reported serving Italian Army soldiers increasingly present at a far-right group's meeting place, which the paper frames as hypothesised neo-fascist proselytism that would have reached armed-forces circles. The inquiry into 'La Barriera - Avanguardia Torino' sent seventeen activists to a preliminary hearing on 11 March 2026 on charges of apologia di fascismo, the Italian offence of glorifying fascism, over Fascist-era rituals and slogans and racist and antisemitic remarks at its gatherings. Months of surveillance of the venue by the Carabinieri's ROS unit recorded soldiers the reports describe as holding extremist views. Three on active service in or near Turin were identified; one, the case papers say, reportedly attended an operational meeting with two leaders and, in autumn 2024, taken part in some initiatives. None was investigated.
inside: Investigators report that serving army soldiers, described as holding extremist views, turned up ever more often at a neo-fascist movement's Turin meeting place; one took part in its activities.
cite: Il Fatto Quotidiano, 6 March 2026; ANSA via L'Adige, 11 March 2026
undone: Nothing has been decided. The preliminary hearing opened in Turin on 11 March 2026, with prosecutors asking that the seventeen be sent to trial for apologia di fascismo; reporting of that hearing records no ruling and no further date, and the accused are presumed innocent. The Carabinieri's ROS unit had sealed the group's premises, the Edoras cultural circle on via Tibone, in July. At least three serving soldiers are said to have attended the circle and some of its events, but none of them is under investigation and nothing has been established against them.

n: Icelandic billionaire accused of paying a serving police officer to spy
org_label: Björgólfur Thor Björgólfsson and the security firm PPPSF
rank: traffic warden, Reykjavík Metropolitan Police
d: Lúðvík Kristinsson, a traffic warden with the Reykjavík Metropolitan Police, has been relieved of duty, and Iceland's state prosecutor is investigating evidence that he carried out paid private surveillance while on police duty between September and December 2012, logging about 60 hours of it; the firm logged about 850 hours over the three months. RÚV's investigative programme Kveikur reported that the billionaire Björgólfur Thor Björgólfsson allegedly financed the surveillance through PPPSF, a security firm founded by two former police officers, Jón Óttar Ólafsson and Guðmundur Haukur Gunnarsson, with the lawyer Birgir Már Ragnarsson alleged to have brokered it. Those watched were former Landsbanki shareholders behind a class action over the bank's 2008 collapse; Björgólfsson allegedly wanted to know whether the businessman Robert Wessman was behind it.
cite: Iceland Monitor, April 2025, reporting RÚV's Kveikur
inside: A billionaire litigant allegedly paid a serving Reykjavík police officer, through a private security firm, to watch his legal opponents in 2012 while the officer was on police duty.

n: US Treasury says Tagwirei's gifts to Zimbabwe's leaders won state contracts
rank: President and First Vice-President; senior government officials
d: On 5 August 2020 the US Treasury designated the Zimbabwean businessman Kudakwashe Regimond Tagwirei and Sakunda Holdings, where he is chief executive and a founding director, for being owned or controlled by him. Treasury said he has utilized his relationships with high level Zimbabwean officials to gain state contracts, and provided high priced items, such as expensive cars, to senior-level Zimbabwean government officials. A government audit prompted a 2019 parliamentary inquiry after about $3 billion disbursed under Command Agriculture, a state farm subsidy championed by President Emmerson Mnangagwa and largely financed by Sakunda, could not be accounted for. Designating him again on 4 March 2024, Treasury said Mnangagwa has benefited from his corrupt network and that he has provided high-value gifts to senior government members to gain access to resources.
inside: The US Treasury says a businessman's cars and high-value gifts to senior Zimbabwean officials won his company state contracts, and that the president benefited from his corrupt network.
cite: US Department of the Treasury press releases, 5 August 2020 (sm1082) and 4 March 2024 (jy2154, https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jy2154)

n: Botswana's top civil servant jailed over a pension fund deal
rank: Permanent Secretary to the President
d: Carter Morupisi, Botswana's Permanent Secretary to the President, was found guilty of money laundering and corruption by the High Court in Gaborone, before Judge Mokwadi Gabanagae, on 16 November 2022. The South African businessman Tim Marsland, described as his alleged corruptor, is alleged to have given him a Toyota Land Cruiser worth about 700,000 rand in exchange for facilitating a 500 million pula transaction from the Botswana Public Officers Pension Fund to the asset manager Capital Management Botswana; the vehicle was forfeited to the state. On appeal, reported 7 December 2024, the Court of Appeal sentenced him to 18 months for money laundering and to five and seven years on the corruption counts, to run concurrently; a 130,000 pula fine imposed at trial was to be refunded if paid.
inside: An asset manager's principal is alleged to have given Botswana's top civil servant a Land Cruiser, and he facilitated the 500 million pula pension fund transaction that paid the firm.
undone: Marsland, who was fighting extradition from South Africa, allegedly shot and killed himself at his home in Kliprivier, Gauteng, on 10 April 2025; an inquest was opened.
cite: Botswana Daily News, 7 December 2024; The African Mirror, 8 December 2024 and on Marsland's death in 2025

n: Chinese firm's proprietors paid Gambia's fisheries chief to free detained vessels
rank: Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Fisheries
d: Dr Bamba Banja, permanent secretary at the Gambia's fisheries ministry, accepted 100,000 dalasi from a Chinese private company in September 2018 to free a vessel detained for illicit fishing. The High Court, before Judge B.A. Bakre, convicted him of economic crime, official corruption and a public officer receiving property to show favour. He was given a two-year mandatory jail term, a fine of one million dalasi for causing economic loss to the government or two further years in jail, 100,000 dalasi or one year, and 50,000 dalasi or six months. He denied the allegations in his defence. The Point, reporting the conviction of 8 March 2023, said the money came from the proprietors of Golden Lead Company Limited, who wanted their detained vessels freed.
inside: A Chinese company's payment reached the civil servant running Gambia's fisheries ministry, in exchange for freeing a vessel detained for illicit fishing.
undone: President Adama Barrow pardoned Banja and 36 others on 19 January 2024.
cite: The Standard (Gambia), 9 March 2023; The Point (Gambia), 9 March 2023 (https://thepoint.gm/africa/gambia/headlines/ex-ps-banja-jailed-fined-d1000000) and on the pardon (https://thepoint.gm/africa/gambia/headlines/barrow-pardons-ex-ps-banja-others)

n: Kenya's anti-counterfeit chair charged over payments from two companies
org_label: Hongda Automotive Limited and UNIPRO Limited
rank: board chair, Anti-Counterfeit Authority
d: The Anti-Counterfeit Authority is the Kenyan body that polices fake goods. Prosecutors say its board chairman, Josphat Gichunge Kabeabea, a former member of parliament for Tigania East, asked a Chinese investor, Du Zhisheng, for 5 million shillings on 11 November 2025 so that he would hold off arresting and charging him over allegedly counterfeit motor vehicle spare parts, then sought a further 1 million and 300,000 shillings and received 144,500 shillings through a mobile number registered to a third party. Investigators also recorded an October 2025 allegation that he demanded 10 million shillings from UNIPRO Limited and received 8 million by threatening to accuse it of trading counterfeit goods.
inside: The chairman of the body that polices counterfeit goods is accused of charging importers to hold off arresting them, so the check on fake car parts was not applied.
undone: No verdict. The Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission recommended charges on 14 November 2025 and the Director of Public Prosecutions approved them on 17 November, under section 6(1)(a) read with section 18 of the Anti-Bribery Act 2023 and the Proceeds of Crime and Anti-Money Laundering Act. Kabeabea was arraigned at the Milimani Anti-Corruption Court on 17 November 2025 before Principal Magistrate Celesa Okore, pleaded not guilty to five counts, and was released on a 2 million shilling bond or 1 million cash bail, ordered to surrender his passport and barred from contacting witnesses or commenting publicly. The case was listed for mention on 8 December 2025. Conviction carries up to ten years. He is presumed innocent.
cite: Capital FM and Nation, 17 November 2025; The Standard and K24, 17 November 2025, on the charge sheet and bail terms; Tukio, 17 November 2025, on the separate UNIPRO allegation

n: Freetown customs officers demanded a bribe to clear an exporter's container
org_label: Sigismond Tommy Mei, operations assistant at Bollore Logistics; container of exporter Juan Ruiz
who: a freight forwarder and a mineral exporter
rank: customs officers at Queen Elizabeth II Quay
d: Akmed Karim and Mary Banya, Sierra Leonean customs officers of the National Revenue Authority formerly at Queen Elizabeth II Quay in Freetown, were convicted on two counts of soliciting and accepting an advantage under section 28(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act No. 12 of 2008. On 28 February 2019 they solicited 2.5 million old leones from Sigismond Tommy Mei, an operations assistant at Bollore Logistics, to clear a 40-foot container owned by Juan Ruiz, an American businessman. The High Court, before Justice Aiah Simeon Allieu, a Court of Appeal judge sitting as a High Court judge, convicted them on 18 December 2025 and sentenced each to three years or a 60,000 new leone fine. Both had pleaded not guilty. Premier Media reported a third officer charged over Ruiz's boat was acquitted.
inside: A freight forwarder's payment reached two customs officers at Freetown's main quay, who had refused to release an American exporter's container until it was paid.
cite: Sierra Leone Anti-Corruption Commission press release ACC/PR/25/020, 23 December 2025; Premier Media (Sierra Leone), 19 December 2025, on the judgment of 18 December 2025

n: Illegal gambling ring paid Kosovo police economic-crime investigators
rank: investigators, Kosovo police directorate for economic crimes and corruption
d: Prosecutors allege an illegal gambling operation paid two investigators in Kosovo police's economic crime unit to leave it alone. Lavdim Osmani and Lutfi Menxhiqi were arrested in February 2020, Osmani in a 1,300-euro sting. The June 2020 indictment alleged they agreed in November 2019, with the cooperating witness D.H., not to investigate illegal gambling, took 1,500 then 3,000 euros from Driton Berisha and 3,000 more in January 2020, and that Menxhiqi passed on planned inspections. In February 2022 Pristina's basic court jailed them for six and a half and five and a half years, fining each 4,000 euros; the court of appeals annulled that judgement in May 2023 and ordered a retrial. Both pleaded not guilty at the retrial; in January 2025 Menxhiqi said he never took the money.
inside: Prosecutors say gambling operators bought the two police investigators assigned to economic crime, so the unit meant to shut them down protected them instead.
undone: At the retrial, reported on 30 April 2025, the Pristina court again convicted both, jailing Osmani for six years and Menxhiqi for five, fining each 4,000 euros and barring them from public office for five years; the verdict could be appealed within 30 days.
cite: Transparency International, Corruption cases with social impact in the Western Balkans and Turkey (case updated January 2025); Periskopi, 30 April 2025, on the retrial verdict

n: Police say Puls club's people paid Štip tax inspectors to hide inspections
org_label: owners of the Puls nightclub in Kočani
rank: tax controllers and inspectors, Public Revenue Office regional directorates
d: Police say those behind the Puls club in Kočani paid tax officials to warn of inspections; a fire there on 16 March 2025 killed 60 people. On 20 November 2025 Kočani police announced eight arrests and charges against eleven, three detained earlier. Two tax controllers at the Štip directorate's Regional Tax Inspectorate, D.P. and D.D., were reported for taking a bribe under Article 357, having abused access to data on unannounced inspections to warn the club's responsible person for unlawful gain and gifts; that person, M.J., son of the club's actual owner, was reported for giving a bribe, and the owner, D.J., for forgery. Six more tax officials in Štip and Strumica were reported for abuse of office, letting Puls and the MMMM Cafe skip inspections and proper fiscalization.
inside: Police say the club owner's son paid tax controllers inside the Public Revenue Office, so officials with access to inspection plans tipped the club off instead.
cite: Ministry of Interior, Republic of North Macedonia, press release, 20 November 2025; Euronews, 4 April 2025, on the fire

n: Montenegrin police and intelligence officers jailed with the Kavač clan
rank: a former intelligence officer and a police officer
d: Two Montenegrin security officials were convicted alongside the Kavač clan's leader, the Kotor-based group originally allied with the Škaljari clan in smuggling South American cocaine into Europe. In a verdict OCCRP reported on 24 July 2026, a special panel of Podgorica's Higher Court, using intercepted Sky app messages, handed the clan's fugitive leader Radoje Zvicer 40 years in absentia for aggravated murder and other charges, and sentenced ten co-defendants, a combined 148 years. Petar Lazović, a former intelligence officer, got 20 years, was also convicted of smuggling for financial gain, fined 100,000 euros and ordered to forfeit 32,000 euros; Ljubo Milović, a fugitive police officer, got 19 years, a 100,000 euro fine and forfeiture of 31,800 euros. OCCRP reported the feud between the clans has allegedly corrupted police and politicians.
inside: A cocaine-trafficking clan had a police officer and an intelligence officer among its co-defendants, and a court jailed both on drug and smuggling charges.
cite: OCCRP, 24 July 2026

n: Bitumen supplier paid Thimphu city officials to sign for undelivered barrels
rank: engineer and procurement officer, Thimphu Thromde
d: In 2019 Bhutan's Anti-Corruption Commission found that an engineer and a procurement officer at Thimphu Thromde had allegedly colluded with Bhutan Bitumen Industries over short deliveries of bitumen emulsion. On an order of 75 barrels the company was asked to keep 25 back and deposit Nu 75,000 into the officials' accounts; they verified and paid for all 75, and the Commission found the deposit was made. The same pattern followed on two further orders. The officials were charged with two counts of abuse of functions, three company officials with two counts of participating in an offence, and the money was to be restituted. It also faces ten counts of active bribery of foreign public servants over alleged payments of Nu 3 M to Sikkim officials, and three of tax evasion.
undone: The Commission forwarded the case to the Office of the Attorney General in October 2019. No prosecution, plea or verdict has been reported since, and a search found no later outcome, so the charges remain untested allegations.
cite: Bhutan Broadcasting Service, 16 October 2019
inside: A supplier allegedly put money into the bank accounts of the city government's own buyers, who then signed off and paid for bitumen the company had never delivered.

n: Treasury says Zimbabwe's president shields gold and diamond smugglers and takes bribes
org_label: unnamed gold and diamond smuggling networks (no payer named in the release)
who: unnamed gold and diamond smuggling networks (no payer named in the release)
rank: President of Zimbabwe
d: On 4 March 2024 the US Treasury designated 11 Zimbabweans and three companies under the Global Magnitsky order, the day it ended its older Zimbabwe sanctions programme. Treasury said President Emmerson Mnangagwa gives gold and diamond smugglers a protective shield, directed officials to sell gold and diamonds in illicit markets, and takes bribes for his services; the release names no payer. He was designated for corruption and as a leader of an entity whose members engaged in serious human rights abuse. Kudakwashe Tagwirei, a businessman designated in August 2020, reportedly gave high-value gifts to senior government members. Obey Chimuka, Fossil Agro and Fossil Contracting, designated in December 2022 under E.O. 13469, were re-designated under E.O. 13818: Chimuka for acting for Tagwirei, Fossil Contracting for Chimuka's control of it.
inside: Treasury says Mnangagwa gives smugglers a protective shield and takes bribes for it, and has directed officials to sell gold and diamonds in illicit markets; the release names no payer.
cite: US Department of the Treasury press release, 4 March 2024

n: Businessman accused of offering Namcor managers N$2.5m over fuel stations
rank: managers, since described by the paper as former managers, of Namcor, the state petroleum corporation
d: Namcor is Namibia's state-owned National Petroleum Corporation. In July 2022 its trading arm, Namcor Petroleum Trading and Distribution, bought the rights to nine service stations at Namibian Defence Force bases from Enercon Namibia for N$53.2 million. The state alleges Peter Elindi, then an Enercon shareholder, offered N$2.5 million that month to two Namcor managers, Cedric Willemse and Jennifer Hamukwaya, to induce them to abuse their positions and facilitate the purchase. Elindi is also charged with fraud, prosecutors alleging he misled Namcor into believing he could sell stations encumbered to the Ministry of Defence and Veterans Affairs until 2031. Namcor sued Enercon in the High Court in April 2024 to void the agreement and recover the money. Elindi denied the bribe allegation, calling the case a witch-hunt.
undone: In April 2026 fourteen accused, Elindi among them, pleaded not guilty to 75 charges under the Anti-Corruption Act and the Prevention of Organised Crime Act before Magistrate Eliud Nakulonda in the Windhoek Magistrate's Court, offering no plea explanation and leaving the state to prove its case. The matter was postponed to 28 October 2026 for a decision by the Prosecutor General. No trial has begun and no verdict has been reached; all the accused are presumed innocent.
inside: Prosecutors say a fuel company's shareholder offered two managers of Namibia's state oil firm N$2.5m so it would buy his nine filling stations.
cite: The Namibian, bail hearing report (no date on page); New Era, April 2026 (Windhoek Magistrate’s Court plea proceedings)

n: Gold scheme paid a Kenyan senator $700,000, investigators report
who: Zandi, named in the report as handing over the cash
rank: Senator, later Speaker of the National Assembly
d: A September 2023 report by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, drawing on an account by a Kenyan gold transporter and broker and what it calls an apparent internal report by Kenyan security services that the researchers could not independently verify, concerns a non-existent 4.6-tonne gold consignment, Zlivia, supposedly brought to Nairobi in February 2018. It says that in Dubai Moses Wetang'ula, then a senator, reportedly asked for US$2 million, claiming a senior Kenyan cabinet secretary demanded it to secure the consignment's release, and that in January 2019 Zandi handed US$700,000 in cash to him and the businessman Zaheer Jhanda. Jhanda, contracted to handle the consignment's documentation, taxes and customs, said he was hired only to advise. Both men had previously denied wrongdoing; Wetang'ula called the affair a non-issue.
undone: Police gave notice of warrants in June 2020, but the researchers found no evidence of any detention. No charge, trial or verdict has been reported, and Wetang'ula was elected Speaker of the National Assembly in late 2022 and still held the post.
inside: A fake-gold scheme's cash reached a senator who, the report says, asked for US$2 million in Dubai to get the consignment released, citing a demand from a senior cabinet secretary.
cite: Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, 'All that glitters', September 2023

n: Addax paid $2.1m to a Nigerian state oil manager over drilling rights
rank: General Manager, Upstream Division, Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation
d: Paulinus Okoronkwo, a dual US-Nigerian citizen, was upstream division general manager at the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC), the state oil company. In October 2015 Addax Petroleum, a Swiss-based Sinopec subsidiary, wired $2,105,263 into his Los Angeles law firm's client trust account as consultancy fees for a settlement with NNPC over Addax's drilling rights. The engagement letter bore a fake Lagos address, and prosecutors said the trust account created the false impression the money belonged to a client, and it was a bribe for his influence over more favourable terms. A jury convicted him in August 2025 of three counts of transactional money laundering and one each of tax evasion and obstructing justice. He was sentenced to 87 months, with $923,824 restitution to the Internal Revenue Service and $1,039,997 forfeited.
undone: The sentence was announced on 23 February 2026, and the State Bar of California suspended his law licence in January 2026. The release records no appeal and no charge against Addax.
inside: An oil company's $2.1m, routed through a law firm, reached the state oil manager handling its drilling-rights settlement, US prosecutors said.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Central District of California, press release, 23 February 2026

n: Trucking director accused of paying a Zambian provincial official K8,000
rank: Deputy Permanent Secretary for Copperbelt Province
d: Zambia's Anti-Corruption Commission said in a release of 6 January 2025 that it had arrested Yusuuf Saiid Abdidahir, 45, a director of Gaban Trucking and Trading Limited, and charged him with one count of corrupt practices under the Anti-Corruption Act No. 3 of 2012, for allegedly offering 8,000 kwacha to the unnamed Deputy Permanent Secretary for Copperbelt Province. The money was allegedly offered to free a truck and two trailers the Zambia National Service impounded in Ndola over an attempt to smuggle 1,392 bags of mealie meal into the Democratic Republic of Congo. The truck was later handed to the Zambia Revenue Authority. The commission said the conduct took place between 1 November and 27 December 2024, and that Abdidahir had been released on bond and would appear in court.
undone: No court outcome has been reported. A second search for developments after the January 2025 charge found no plea, trial, conviction or acquittal, so the charge remains untested and Abdidahir is presumed innocent.
inside: A haulier allegedly offered money to the unnamed deputy head of a provincial administration so that his smuggling-seized truck would be let go.
cite: Zambia Anti-Corruption Commission media release, 6 January 2025

n: Head of Moldova's Central Customs Bureau detained over payments to clear imports
org_label: unnamed payers (the source identifies no importers or companies)
who: unnamed payers (the source identifies no importers or companies)
rank: head of the Central Customs Bureau
d: On 21 May 2025 Moldova's National Anti-corruption Centre and prosecutors in Bălți announced that they had detained the head of the Central Customs Bureau and a customs broker in a case of passive corruption in aggravating circumstances. According to preliminary data of the investigation, the two, with other people whose identity the centre said could not be disclosed, allegedly received over 40,000 dollars in several instalments to facilitate the passage of goods across the customs border, including goods for the Transnistrian segment, and to omit detection of multiple legal violations. A close relative of the accused, alleged to have acted as an intermediary, was later detained for 72 hours, as was the head of the Căușeni internal customs post, and financial means of about 1.1 million lei were detected.
undone: The case was still under investigation by prosecutors in Bălți at the centre's June 2025 update. No indictment, trial or court decision has been reported, and no payer has been named.
inside: Investigators say unnamed payers, with the bureau's own head, allegedly bought the passage of imports across Moldova's customs border and the overlooking of breaches.
cite: National Anticorruption Centre, Republic of Moldova, press releases of 21 May 2025 and 25 June 2025 (the 21 May date appears in the companion release on the intermediary's arrest)

n: Spain's Supreme Court dissolved ANV as an instrument of ETA
rank: 337 council seats in the Basque Country and 93 in Navarre
d: On 17 September 2008 the Supreme Court's Sala 61 ruled unanimously, the court's president saying there were no dissenting opinions, to outlaw Acción Nacionalista Vasca (ANV) and wind it up, on suits by the Fiscalía and the Abogacía del Estado; the dissolution of its municipal groups follows from the ruling, with the details left to the execution phase. The same proceeding concerned the Partido Comunista de las Tierras Vascas (PCTV), which the government's final reports likewise called an instrument of ETA. The Abogacía del Estado argued ANV was a “mere instrument or tool of ETA-Batasuna”, and a pendrive seized from an alleged ETA member, Gorka Murillo, headed “Elecciones 2007. Pasos a dar en el ámbito jurídico”, reportedly showed Batasuna directing ANV's candidacy process and campaign for the 2007 municipal elections.
undone: The Constitutional Court dismissed ANV's amparo appeal against the Supreme Court judgment, dated 22 September 2008, in STC 31/2009 of 29 January 2009, leaving the party's dissolution final.
inside: Spain's courts found an armed separatist movement was running a party that held hundreds of council seats, putting its people inside local government.
cite: Legal Today (Europa Press), 17 September 2008; later outcome: Tribunal Constitucional, STC 31/2009, 29 January 2009

n: Crime bosses got Macedonian passports from interior ministry staff
org_label: Škaljari clan and other criminal organisations
who: Škaljari clan and other crime groups
rank: eleven staff of the interior ministry's administrative affairs department
d: In April 2021 the opposition party VMRO-DPMNE, citing a whistleblower, said ministry employees issued documents to organised crime figures, among them Jovan Vukotić, head of Montenegro's Škaljari clan, who got a passport in December 2017 as 'Georgi Andonov'; the party said about 200 false-identity documents, issued between December 2017 and January 2021, went to people in criminal organisations. Within a week prosecutors charged eleven officials of the ministry's administrative affairs department in Skopje, ten with abuse of office and authority and one with instigation; the case covered 215 passports, 214 to foreign nationals and one to a North Macedonian. Seven admitted guilt, five at the first hearing on 5 May 2021 at Skopje's Basic Criminal Court; the court imposed seven prison sentences of one to three years and four suspended.
undone: Transparency International's page says the appellate court upheld the sentences but gives no date, and no later source confirming that outcome could be found; first-instance sentencing was reported in June 2021.
inside: Criminal organisations obtained real state passports under false names from officials inside the interior ministry, so the state itself concealed who they were.
cite: Transparency International, Corruption cases with social impact in the Western Balkans and Turkey, 'The Double Affair' (case updated August 2021)

n: Bhutan trading firm's bribe fixed an agriculture ministry tender
rank: Senior Livestock Production Officer, Ministry of Agriculture and Forests
d: Samten, chief executive of Sai Trading Partner, paid Nu 1 million to Tshewang Tashi while Tshewang was a Senior Livestock Production Officer at Bhutan's Ministry of Agriculture and Forests. According to the Anti-Corruption Commission's investigation in 2017 and 2018, the payment was to obtain privileged information and fix the tender for a modern hatchery project in Samrang, Samdrupjongkhar.
