cite: Controladoria-Geral da União release of December 2023 as carried by Agência Gov, 'CGU e AGU assinam acordo de leniência pela 1ª vez com empresa de pequeno porte', for the years, the Banco do Brasil rural credit programme, the figure and the quotation from the secretary for private integrity; the Acordos de Leniência dataset of Brazil's Portal da Transparência, process 00190.104707/2022-18, for the agreement being recorded as fulfilled

n: Foster Wheeler got inside help from a Petrobras manager for UFN-IV
rank: A manager in Petrobras's engineering department
d: Petrobras, Brazil's state oil company, tendered the design of a gas-to-chemicals complex it called UFN-IV. Foster Wheeler Energy, a British engineering business, won it. The US Justice Department says it offered and paid bribes to decision-makers at Petrobras through intermediaries including an Italian agent, and that it won the contract by obtaining confidential documents, inside information and secret assistance from a manager in Petrobras's engineering department. The Securities and Exchange Commission puts the bribes at about 1.1 million dollars. On 25 June 2021 the comptroller-general, the attorney-general and federal prosecutors settled for 86,196,063.32 reais, of which 67,273,820.43 went back to Petrobras and the rest was fines. The Commission put the whole coordinated resolution, across the American, British and Brazilian authorities, at more than 43 million dollars.
inside: An engineering company paid for confidential documents and secret help from a manager inside Petrobras, and won the design contract he helped decide.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission, 'SEC Charges Amec Foster Wheeler Limited With FCPA Violations Related To Brazilian Bribery Scheme', 25 June 2021, for the UFN-IV contract, the 1.1 million dollars, and the coordinated resolution of more than 43 million dollars, which that order says covers the American, British and Brazilian authorities together; the US Department of Justice's criminal information, for the bribes to decision-makers at Petrobras, the Italian agent, and the confidential documents, inside information and secret assistance from a manager in Petrobras's engineering department; Controladoria-Geral da União and Advocacia-Geral da União, 'CGU e AGU celebram acordo de leniência de R$ 86 milhões com empresas por ilícitos em projeto com a Petrobras', 25 June 2021, for the Brazilian figures and the share returned to Petrobras

n: Stericycle paid officials at the health bodies holding its waste contracts
rank: Officials of institutions of the SUS, the national health service
d: Stericycle, a US medical-waste company, paid officials at bodies of Brazil's national health service, the SUS, which held its waste contracts through Brazilian subsidiaries. The US Justice Department and Securities and Exchange Commission found its staff made hundreds of payments across Brazil, Mexico and Argentina, usually in cash and set as a percentage of what the government customers owed, and kept spreadsheets of which had been paid, under code words including 'CP' for commission payment. Brazil's comptroller-general and attorney-general settled on 20 April 2022 for 109,698,073.80 reais, about 65 million of it compensation, 41 million the Clean Company Act fine and 2,853,015.49 the improbity fine. The announcement gives no years; the group found the conduct itself and reported it in 2018. It served a two-year compliance monitorship, and in April 2025 the US charges were dismissed with prejudice seven months early, prosecutors saying it had fully complied.
inside: A waste company paid officials at the national health service bodies that held its hospital waste contracts and owed it the money its payments were reckoned against.
cite: Advocacia-Geral da União and Controladoria-Geral da União, 'CGU e AGU celebram acordo de leniência de R$ 109 milhões com empresas por ilícitos na coleta de lixo hospitalar em unidades de saúde', 20 April 2022, for the figure, the six companies, the hospital waste contracts with bodies and entities of the SUS and the improbity fine - that release gives no years; Saud Advogados' English note on the same announcement for the split of the Brazilian sum; Maeda, Ayres & Sarubbi, on the group's own internal investigation and its self-report to the CGU in 2018; Willkie Compliance Concourse, 22 April 2022, on the US Justice Department's account of the spreadsheets naming the government customers paid and the code words, and its April 2025 note on the motion to dismiss; Morrison Foerster and Miller & Chevalier, on the dismissal with prejudice in April 2025 and the certification that preceded it; Waste Management's Form 10-Q for 2025, for its acquisition of Stericycle in November 2024 and the dismissal

n: Brokers imposed on France's state shipbuilder took its arms commissions
org_label: Ziad Takieddine and Abdul Rahman El-Assir
rank: DCN International, the state shipbuilder's export arm, and the second state-held company that negotiated the Saudi sale
d: DCN was France's state shipbuilder. In autumn 1994, shortly before France signed a 5.41 billion franc contract to sell Pakistan three Agosta-B submarines, Renaud Donnedieu de Vabres, special adviser in the cabinet of defence minister François Léotard, had two Franco-Lebanese businessmen, Ziad Takieddine and Abdul Rahman El-Assir, added as intermediaries to that deal and to the 19 billion franc Sawari II sale of three La Fayette frigates to Saudi Arabia. Both contracts were negotiated by companies held by the state, and both were close to finished. A car bomb in Karachi in May 2002, which killed eleven French DCN employees, reopened the matter in France. Investigating judges reported in 2014 that the network of intermediaries had been paid 327 million euros in commissions on the two contracts.
inside: A defence minister's office put two private brokers inside the contracts of two state arms companies, which then paid them commissions on deals already all but signed.
undone: A Paris court convicted six people in June 2020. On 4 March 2021 the Cour de justice de la République, which tries ministers, acquitted prime minister Édouard Balladur and gave Léotard a two-year suspended sentence and a 100,000 euro fine for complicity in the misuse of corporate assets, finding he had played a central and driving part in imposing a network of needless intermediaries on two state-held companies; his appeal was rejected on 4 June 2021. On 21 January 2025 the Paris appeal court acquitted Balladur's 1995 campaign director Nicolas Bazire, holding the link between the commissions and that campaign unproven, and convicted the other five: Takieddine's five years were confirmed and the rest of the sentences reduced, El-Assir taking four years. Takieddine died in Beirut on 23 September 2025 without having been extradited.
cite: Compendium of Arms Trade Corruption (World Peace Foundation), case file L'affaire Karachi, as published on corruption-tracker.org, which distinguishes court findings from reporting; tribunal correctionnel de Paris, 15 June 2020; Cour de justice de la République, 4 March 2021, and Cour de cassation, 4 June 2021; Paris appeal court, 21 January 2025, reported by Agence France-Presse

n: A British broker's payments reached the officer selling Norway's warships
rank: a naval officer handling vessel sales at Forsvarets logistikkorganisasjon, the Norwegian armed forces' logistics agency
d: Forsvarets logistikkorganisasjon buys and disposes of equipment for the Norwegian armed forces. Bjørn Stavrum, the naval officer there who handled the sale of the armed forces' decommissioned vessels, took nearly a million kroner in 2013 from CAS-Global, a British company registered in 2008 that was buying them. CAS-Global bought six missile torpedo boats and the supply ship KNM Horten in 2012, telling Norwegian officials it would own the vessels itself; all seven went on to Nigeria, to Global West Vessel Services, a firm reported to be controlled by the former militia leader known as Tompolo. The sales became public in Norway in 2014. Økokrim, Norway's economic crime authority, charged Stavrum with aggravated corruption, embezzlement, breach of trust, theft and breaking the export control act.
inside: The buyer's money reached the officer inside Norway's defence logistics agency who handled the warship sale, so the state sold its ships through the company paying him.
undone: Oslo district court sentenced Stavrum to four years and eight months in 2017. The appeal court convicted him on every count in October 2018 and set the term at four years and three months, with just over 2.7 million kroner in compensation to the armed forces and a further million kroner confiscated; part of the case went to the Supreme Court on how the Export Control Act applies, and the conviction is final. On the British side, the City of London police's overseas anti-corruption unit had arrested four people by May 2017 without charging anyone.
cite: Forsvarets forum, on the final conviction, the four-year-three-month term and the confiscation; OCCRP, on the 154,000 US dollars paid into Stavrum's account in two instalments in 2013 and on Global West Vessel Services; Oslo tingrett 2017 and lagmannsrett October 2018 judgments as reported by NRK, Aftenposten and Dagbladet; Compendium of Arms Trade Corruption (World Peace Foundation), case file on CAS-Global Ltd and the private Nigerian coast guard fleet

n: Ballast Nedam's airfield bribes reached the Saudi royal house, the FIOD found
rank: members of the Saudi royal house, and the air force that bought the airfield work
d: Ballast Nedam is a Dutch construction company. At the end of 2012 it settled with the Dutch prosecution service for 17.5 million euros over what the service called payments to foreign agents on large projects in Saudi Arabia and Suriname between 1996 and 2003, keeping the case out of court. Parts of the investigation file were later shown to the broadcaster HUMAN, and on that account the Dutch fiscal investigation service believed the company had paid at least half a billion dollars to members of the Saudi royal house and other highly placed Saudis, who were given cover names in its records. For the conversion of two airfields the Saudi air force paid 580 million dollars, which investigators believed covered 331 million of commissions on work worth about 249 million.
inside: A Dutch builder's money is said to have reached the ruling house that controls Saudi contracting, and the air force then bought its airfield work at twice the estimated cost.
undone: No court has ruled on who received the money: the settlement ended the case against the company. Two former Ballast Nedam managers were prosecuted over the Saudi payments, and three accountants and their firm were investigated for concealing the bribery of foreign officials by issuing a clean audit opinion and filing no fraud report; the firm settled, and a court barred the prosecution of the three accountants, which the appeal court upheld. An investigating judge agreed to hear a Saudi witness, but the Dutch foreign ministry refused permission on the ground that such questioning could disturb relations with Saudi Arabia.
cite: Openbaar Ministerie settlement with Ballast Nedam of December 2012, 17.5 million euros, as reported by NOS and Transparency International Nederland; FIOD investigation file as shown to Omroep HUMAN for the documentary 'Inzake Saoedi-Arabië' (2017), reported by NOS, Cobouw and HUMAN; De Bont Advocaten on the appeal court upholding the bar on prosecuting the three accountants

n: Mammoet Salvage paid an Iraqi MP to reach the oil minister
who: Mammoet Salvage B.V., then part of SHV Holdings
rank: a member of Iraq's parliament, used as a route to the minister of oil
d: Mammoet Salvage is a Dutch salvage company, then part of the SHV group. On 28 April 2021 it accepted a settlement offer from the Dutch prosecution service, one of five group companies that together paid 41,621,000 euros, and the prosecution service said it had bribed a senior foreign official: a member of Iraq's parliament. The company paid the parliamentarian into a private account in Switzerland. The purpose, on the prosecution service's account, was to reach Iraq's minister of oil through him and so settle a dispute with an Iraqi state oil company. Invoices were issued in the name of the parliamentarian's own company for services that did not match what was done, which made them false.
inside: A Dutch salvage firm paid a member of Iraq's parliament into a Swiss account to reach the oil minister and settle its dispute with the state oil company.
undone: No court has ruled on the payments: the settlement ended the case against the company, and because the investigation found no unlawful gain from the Iraqi payments it paid a fine only, with no confiscation. The prosecution service said it suspected several people connected to Mammoet Salvage and intended to prosecute some of them, and that it had also named an accounting firm as a suspect in an investigation that was not then complete. The parliamentarian is not named in the announcement, and nothing published shows the money reaching the minister.
cite: Openbaar Ministerie news release of 28 April 2021 announcing transactions with Econosto Mideast, Econosto, ERIKS, CMK Mammoth Gulf and Mammoet Salvage, totalling 41,621,000 euros, which sets out the Iraqi payments and the use of false invoices

n: Schenker paid customs officers at St Petersburg to speed Ford's freight
org_label: Schenker, then Deutsche Bahn's logistics arm
who: Schenker, the logistics company then owned by the German state railway Deutsche Bahn
rank: customs officers at the port of Saint Petersburg
d: Schenker is a freight and logistics company, at the time owned by Deutsche Bahn, the German state railway. Between 2010 and the middle of 2012 it paid customs officers at the port of Saint Petersburg to clear its containers faster, so that car parts arrived on time at Ford's plant near the city. The payments ran through Trans-Business, a Russian subcontractor. Deutsche Bahn reported the matter itself, after an anonymous tip reached its compliance officer, and in 2016, four years into the investigation, the Cologne public prosecutors closed the case against the company for a fine of 2 million euros: 1.7 million as confiscated gain, which a prosecutor said equalled the payments they treated as bribe money, and 300,000 euros as punishment, held down because the company had cooperated.
inside: A German logistics firm paid customs officers at a Russian port to wave its client's freight through faster, and was fined in Germany for it.
undone: No court has ruled on who took the money. The fine ended the case against the company and the proceedings against its employees were ended for payments rather than verdicts, so no Russian customs officer is named in anything published. Deutsche Bahn said the breaches were those of a Russian Schenker company since liquidated, and declined to name the staff involved or to confirm what its own inquiry had found. The Cologne prosecutors were still examining the part played by Ford, two of whose employees were suspected of knowing of the payments; Ford said it was unaware of any wrongdoing by its staff, and the US Securities and Exchange Commission had opened an inquiry of its own. The OECD's annex dates the court decision to September 2016 and Deutsche Bahn announced the fine on 7 October 2016.
cite: Automotive Logistics, 'DB Schenker pays out over allegations of bribery in Russia; Ford still under investigation', October 2016, for the fine, its two components and the prosecutor's statements; automobil-produktion.de, 18 August 2015, for the Trans-Business route and the suspicion against two Ford employees; OECD Working Group on Bribery, Phase 4 report on Germany, Annex 1C, for the grounds under sections 334 and 335 of the criminal code

n: MAN Turbo paid 9m euros for a Kazakh state gas pipeline contract
who: MAN Turbo, the industrial machinery division of the German group MAN
rank: the people in charge of Kazakhstan's state gas transport company
d: MAN Turbo built gas turbines and compressors for MAN, the German engineering and truck group. Its chief executive paid about 9 million euros in 2004 to the people running a Kazakh state gas company, to win the contract for a pipeline compressor station, the plant that keeps gas moving. He told the Munich court the head of the Kazakh contract partner had demanded a market entry fee and would otherwise give the work to a competitor; he bargained it down from 12 million euros and sent it to shell companies. MAN Turbo announced in December 2005 an order of more than 80 million euros from Intergas Central Asia, the state gas transport company, for its first compressor station in Kazakhstan. He confessed and was convicted in June 2010.
inside: A German manufacturer's money reached the people running Kazakhstan's state gas pipeline company, which then gave it the contract they had threatened to award elsewhere.
undone: No Kazakh was ever named. The recipients are described in the German proceedings only as the decision-makers at Kazakh state enterprises and as the head of the contract partner, who one report said fronted for influential Kazakh clans, and no Kazakh proceedings over the contract have been found. The prosecutors charged bribery of a foreign official, but the court convicted him under the commercial bribery provision, which treats the person paid as a business counterparty rather than an official; German law at the time did not clearly cover the staff of a foreign state company. The indictment put the payments between 2005 and 2008 while his confession put the payment in 2004. German reporting abbreviates his surname, which the Associated Press gave in full. That the contract was the Intergas Central Asia compressor station rests on matching the court's description to MAN Turbo's own announcement of the order; no published document names both.
cite: Legal Tribune Online, 28 June 2010, for the conviction and the two-year suspended sentence; dpa via leinetal24.de, 28 June 2010, for the conviction being under the commercial bribery provision and for the Kazakh pipeline order; ddp via techfieber.de, 11 December 2009, for the indictment and the prosecutors' statement that the decision-makers at the Kazakh state enterprises acted in breach of duty; NZZ (ddp) on the opening of the trial in June 2010 for the market entry fee demanded by the contract partner's head, the bargaining down from 12 million euros and the shell companies; Automobilwoche (dpa) for the pipeline modernisation and for Siemens and General Electric as the competitors; energie-und-management.de, 16 December 2005, for MAN Turbo's order from Intergas Central Asia; busplaner.de, 11 December 2009, and vol.at, 10 December 2009, for the 75.3 million euro fine on MAN Turbo and the finding that officials and customers' staff had been bribed with the division chief's involvement

n: MAN's bus orders from Tunisia's trade ministry ran on consultancy fees
who: MAN, the German truck and bus maker
rank: Tunisia's ministry of trade
d: MAN is a German maker of trucks and buses. In June 2011 a Munich court convicted a former sales director of its foreign subsidiaries, who admitted winning orders worth hundreds of millions of euros by paying more than 1.5 million euros to those placing them between 2003 and 2006, and gave him one year and ten months suspended and a 60,000 euro penalty. Prosecutors had charged four counts of especially serious commercial bribery and one of bribing a foreign official. The reporting names four customers: a large bus order in Lisbon, paid through a sham consultancy contract with a shell company, an Italian local transport company, a municipal transport company in Oslo, and Tunisia's trade ministry, whose business ran the same way. One of the orders was for 1,000 buses.
inside: A German bus maker paid the customers that placed its orders through a sham consultancy contract, and one of those customers was a Tunisian ministry.
undone: No Tunisian official is named in anything published, and neither the amount paid in Tunisia nor the date of its order is reported; the court reporting says only that the ministry's business ran like the Lisbon one. Which of the five counts was the foreign-official charge is not reported either, though the trade ministry is the only state body among the four customers named. The two reports differ over whether the order of 1,000 buses was the Lisbon one or the Tunisian one. The manager is not named and left MAN in 2009. No Tunisian proceedings have been found.
cite: autohaus.de (dpa), 27 June 2011, for the charges, the confession, the four customers including the Tunisian trade ministry and the sham consultancy contract through a shell company; autoservicepraxis.de (dpa), 29 June 2011, for the sentence of one year and ten months suspended, the 60,000 euro penalty and the order of 1,000 buses

n: South Sudan's security service sat on the board of the state oil company
org_label: South Sudan's National Security Service and its Internal Security Bureau
rank: a seat on the board of Nilepet, the state oil company, and agents among its staff
d: Nilepet is South Sudan's state oil company. The United Nations Panel of Experts on South Sudan reported in 2016, and confirmed in April 2019, that Akol Koor Kuc, director general of the Internal Security Bureau of the National Security Service, held a seat on Nilepet's board, and that members of the company's staff were active agents of the service. The panel found that the service had placed agents inside other large South Sudanese companies too, among them the Dar Petroleum Operating Company and the Bank of South Sudan, and that it ran commercial ventures of its own. Global Witness published a 2016 letter instructing Nilepet's managing director to pay 1,516,720 US dollars towards security service expenses, citing a letter signed by Akol Koor days earlier.
inside: A state security service put its director on the board of the national oil company and its agents among the staff, and the company's oil money then paid the service's bills.
undone: No court has ruled on any of it, and the findings are an inquiry's rather than a verdict's. South Sudan's government, answering a report by The Sentry, said that Akol Koor as director general of the Internal Security Bureau was lawfully a non-executive member of Nilepet's board and that this represented no personal or preferential interest; it also said Nilepet's day-to-day affairs were run by a management team headed by a managing director appointed by the president. The panel reported in 2016 that arms purchases financed by Nilepet appeared to have bypassed the National Legislative Assembly entirely and had circumvented the army's own weapon supply and accounting mechanisms, and that weapons reached a militia through Akol Koor's bureau; those are the panel's findings and have not been tested in court. Dates differ on when the board seat began: the panel put it at 2016 and said at least since then, while sources interviewed by Global Witness put it at least as early as 2014. Akol Koor was summarily dismissed as director general on 2 October 2024 after thirteen years and replaced by Akec Tong Aleu; his appointment as governor of Warrap State was revoked when he arrived in Juba, and in November 2024 a gunfight broke out at his home when soldiers were reported to have come to arrest him. Nothing published says the service's agents left the companies, which is why this is recorded as still felt rather than over.
cite: United Nations Security Council, Final report of the Panel of Experts on South Sudan, S/2019/301, 9 April 2019, for the board seat held since at least 2016, the staff who were active agents, and the agents placed inside Dar Petroleum Operating Company and the Bank of South Sudan; the panel's earlier final report, S/2016/70, 26 January 2016, for the board seat and the arms purchases that bypassed the legislature; Global Witness, 'Capture on the Nile', for the 2016 payment letter and for its own sources dating the seat to 2014; the South Sudanese government's published response to The Sentry's report for the denial; Radio Tamazuj, 2 and 3 October 2024, and Sudans Post, 10 October 2024, for the dismissal and the replacement

n: Smith & Ouzman's money reached Mauritania's interior ministry over ballot printing
rank: Secretary-general of the interior ministry, which runs elections
d: The same British security printer convicted over Kenya was convicted of paying officials in Mauritania. A Southwark jury found in December 2014 that Smith & Ouzman and two of its directors corruptly agreed to payments totalling 395,074 pounds to officials in the two countries between November 2006 and December 2010, to win contracts for ballot papers and certificates; the company was ordered to pay 2.2 million pounds. On the Mauritanian side the body was the interior ministry, which organises elections. Its secretary-general, Mohamed El Hadi Macina, was arrested in February 2016 and charged with corruption, misappropriation of state property and breach of trust, and the court issued an international arrest warrant for the company's chairman. The outcome of the Mauritanian trial has not been traced.
inside: A foreign printing company's money reached the official running the ministry that organises Mauritania's elections, and the printing contracts went to the company; a British court convicted the company.
cite: Serious Fraud Office case page, Smith and Ouzman Ltd (relevant jurisdictions: Ghana, Kenya, Mauritania, Somaliland); Associated Press, 'Mauritania charges official with corruption, issues warrant'

n: A Turkish builder bought two successive US State Department contracting officers
org_label: Deniz Turkkan and his Turkish construction company
rank: Two contracting officers in the State Department's Office of Acquisitions Management
d: A Turkish construction magnate held the same seat inside American embassy construction twice over. Zaldy Sabino, a contracting officer in the State Department's Office of Acquisitions Management, was convicted in October 2019 on 13 counts of conspiracy, bribery, honest services fraud and false statements, and sentenced in February 2020 to 87 months. Prosecutors said he took at least 521,863 dollars in cash from Deniz Turkkan between 2012 and 2016 while supervising contracts to Turkkan's partners in Iraq, Turkey and Yemen, among them a 142 million dollar embassy power plant, and that he concealed the relationship on his financial disclosure forms and in a security reinvestigation. His predecessor in the same post, Steven Graves, admitted taking money from Turkkan and was jailed for 15 months.
inside: A foreign builder paid the two officials who in turn held the same contracting post, and his partners won the embassy construction they supervised; both officials were convicted.
cite: US Department of Justice, 'State Department Contracting Officer Sentenced to Prison for Bribery and Procurement Fraud Scheme', 14 Feb 2020; Washington Post, 14 Feb 2020

n: Fresenius gave Angola's military services director a stake in its arm
rank: Director of Military Services; state hospital nephrologists
d: Fresenius Medical Care, a German dialysis company listed in New York, sold dialysis kits to Angolan military hospitals. From 2008 to 2010 its Portuguese unit paid Angola's Director of Military Services a commission of 20 per cent on those sales, and in June 2010 it handed a 35 per cent stake in its Angolan subsidiary to Angolan nephrologists, including that official, without payment and without any check on them; the shares were transferred in January 2012. Two state hospital doctors were also paid monthly retainers, and $559,972 went out for temporary storage with no contract behind it. Fresenius settled with the US Securities and Exchange Commission in March 2019; the order puts the benefit at over $10 million.
inside: Fresenius put a free shareholding in its own Angolan arm into the hands of the official deciding military hospital purchases, which kept buying its kits.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-85468, In the Matter of Fresenius Medical Care AG & Co. KGaA, 29 March 2019

n: Fresenius paid Spanish public hospital doctors who shaped its tenders
rank: publicly employed doctors at state-owned hospitals
d: Fresenius Medical Care's Spanish unit reached inside state-owned hospitals through the doctors who drew up and scored its tenders. In a 2011 tender run by a state-owned hospital in Valencia for a contract worth about $2 million, a doctor the company paid over $114,000 between 2008 and 2011 supplied it with draft specifications and proposed scores; the company also gave over $40,000 to the hospital's foundation and $51,600 more between 2012 and 2014. In 2015 it won 60 per cent of a tender worth about $3 million at a state-owned hospital in Torrecardenas after a second doctor agreed to support its bid. Six publicly employed doctors received over $3 million through a clinic purchase, a revenue share, leases and consulting deals. The SEC put the benefit at over $20 million.
inside: Fresenius paid the publicly employed doctors who drew up and scored its tender specifications, so Spain's state-owned hospitals bought dialysis supplies on terms set by their supplier.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-85468, In the Matter of Fresenius Medical Care AG & Co. KGaA, 29 March 2019

n: Fresenius paid Serbian doctors sitting on state health fund tender panels
rank: doctors on the Serbian Health Fund (RFZO) and other public tender commissions
d: Fresenius Medical Care sold dialysis products and ran clinics in Serbia, where purchases are decided by tender commissions of the Serbian Health Fund, known as the RFZO. Four doctors who worked both for the state and for Fresenius received over $329,000 while sitting on those commissions. The company also spent over $393,000 in 2008 on a conference trip to Philadelphia for doctors and routed over $170,000 through a transport vendor, and it paid over $1 million to speed up the privatisation of four clinics. The US Securities and Exchange Commission settled with the company in March 2019 and put the combined benefit from Serbia and Bosnia at over $10 million.
inside: Fresenius paid doctors who sat on the state health fund's tender commissions, so the panels deciding public dialysis purchases included people on its payroll.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-85468, In the Matter of Fresenius Medical Care AG & Co. KGaA, 29 March 2019

n: Fresenius paid a Brcko doctor who became mayor over a clinics tender
rank: member of the Brcko Assembly, later mayor
d: Bosnia held a government tender to set up and run dialysis clinics in Republika Srpska and the Brcko district. A government doctor who was elected to the Brcko Assembly in November 2008, and who later became mayor, was paid $80,850 in December 2008 by Fresenius Medical Care and over $1.3 million by 2009 under a consulting agreement that was later put in his wife's name. Over $957,000 went to a Bosnian healthcare executive for setting up clinics, with nothing to show services were done. The US Securities and Exchange Commission settled with the company in March 2019 and put the combined benefit from Serbia and Bosnia at over $10 million.
inside: Fresenius's consulting money went to a serving Brcko assembly member, later the district's mayor, while the government chose who would set up and run its dialysis clinics.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-85468, In the Matter of Fresenius Medical Care AG & Co. KGaA, 29 March 2019

n: Fresenius commissions were partly meant for officials at Mexico's IMSS
rank: officials of the Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social (IMSS)
d: The Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social, or IMSS, is Mexico's state-run social insurance agency and buys dialysis treatment for its patients. In January 2010 an IMSS tender awarded Fresenius Medical Care a share of that work at $92 per treatment. A contract the company signed with a Mexican distributor in December 2010 was backdated and labelled as advice, and $213,500 in improper commissions was paid, which the US Securities and Exchange Commission said was intended partly for IMSS officials. The order does not say the money reached them. Fresenius settled in March 2019 and the order puts the Mexican benefit at over $2 million.
inside: Fresenius's commissions were partly intended for officials of IMSS, Mexico's state health insurer, which had just awarded it a share of its dialysis treatment work.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-85468, In the Matter of Fresenius Medical Care AG & Co. KGaA, 29 March 2019

n: Fresenius paid Libreville public hospital executives per dialysis kit
rank: three executives of the Centre Hospitalier de Libreville
d: The Centre Hospitalier de Libreville is Gabon's main public hospital. Between October 2007 and 2009 three of its government executives were paid a kickback on every dialysis kit the hospital bought from Fresenius Medical Care, under sham consulting agreements; over $420,000 went to them directly and was booked as export commissions. From 2009 to 2012 a further $807,000 for them was routed through a West African supplier, which the company later turned into a purported distributor. Payments in Gabon came to about $2.3 million between 2007 and 2016. Fresenius settled with the US Securities and Exchange Commission in March 2019, which put the benefit from its West African schemes at over $40 million.
inside: Fresenius paid three executives of Gabon's main public hospital a cut of every dialysis kit it bought, so the hospital's purchasing served its own supplier.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-85468, In the Matter of Fresenius Medical Care AG & Co. KGaA, 29 March 2019

n: Microsoft Hungary won a tax agency tender with improper payment money
rank: National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV); an official of the Ministry of National Development
d: Microsoft sold software licences to the Hungarian state through resellers. Its Hungarian subsidiary asked for large discounts on the stated ground that the government needed them, did not pass them on, and the margin left with the resellers funded improper payments. NAV, Hungary's National Tax and Customs Administration, ran a tender for Microsoft licences that was re-launched on 25 March 2014 after an official of the Ministry of National Development was asked to help; a reseller won it in April 2014 on a gross margin of about 1.06 million euros, and two service agreements followed the same year. The US Securities and Exchange Commission found books-and-records and internal-controls breaches in July 2019 and put Microsoft's gain from the improper payments in Hungary at $13,780,733.
inside: Discounts Microsoft left with its resellers funded payments to officials, and Hungary's tax and customs administration relaunched its licence tender, which a reseller then won on Microsoft products.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-86421, In the Matter of Microsoft Corporation, 22 July 2019

n: A Microsoft reseller won Hungary's police licence tender on hidden margin
rank: ORFK, Hungary's National Police; an employee of the Office for Education
d: ORFK, Hungary's National Police, is an agency under the interior ministry. It launched a tender for Microsoft desktop licences on 1 September 2014, which was won by a third party Microsoft had not approved; the margin on it was about 1.56 million euros on a licence purchase of roughly 2.2 million euros, and services ran from March 2014 to April 2015. The same scheme covered OFI, the Hungarian Office for Education, where an engagement worth about $3.5 million in revenue ran in 2014 and 2015 and an OFI employee supplied consulting services through a third party under a false name. The US Securities and Exchange Commission settled with Microsoft in July 2019 over books-and-records and internal-controls breaches.
inside: The margin Microsoft left with unapproved resellers paid for business with Hungary's national police and education office, whose licence tenders were then won on Microsoft products.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-86421, In the Matter of Microsoft Corporation, 22 July 2019

n: Contractors paid Eletronuclear's president over Brazil's Angra 3 reactor
rank: former president and former officers of Eletronuclear
d: Eletronuclear is the nuclear power subsidiary of Eletrobras, the electricity company 51 per cent owned by the Brazilian federal government, and it awarded the contracts to build the Angra 3 reactor. Private Brazilian construction companies rigged the bidding and, through inflated prices and sham invoices, paid about $9 million to Eletronuclear's former president and other former officers: about $4.1 million to the president, partly through at least 28 invoices from one contractor, and about $4.9 million to the others. Two per cent of the contract value went to officials of two of Brazil's largest political parties. The civil construction contract was about $4.6 billion and the assembly contract about $1.1 billion; work stopped in 2015. Eletrobras settled with the SEC in December 2018 for $2.5 million.
inside: Contractors' money reached the officers running Brazil's state nuclear builder, so the reactor contracts and their inflated prices were settled in the payers' favour.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-84973, In the Matter of Centrais Eletricas Brasileiras S.A. - Eletrobras, 26 December 2018

n: Beam's Indian arm paid excise officials for licences and state liquor orders
rank: state excise officials; staff of government depots and retail stores
d: Beam Inc, the American spirits maker now part of Suntory, sold its drinks in India through Beam Global Spirits and Wine (India). From 2006 to 2012 its staff and third-party promoters paid officials in fourteen Indian states for label registrations, warehouse licences, prompt inspections at its Behror bottling plant and sales orders in government-run liquor shops. In 2011 one million rupees, about $18,000, went to a senior excise official and the registration of a ready-to-drink product was approved within weeks. Over $550,000 went to a promoter in Delhi and over $1.5 million to a promoter handling the Canteen Stores Department, the Ministry of Defence body that runs India's armed-forces shops, for orders at its depots and stores and prominent shelf placement.
inside: Beam's money went to the state excise officials who grant its product licences and to staff of government liquor shops, who then approved and ordered its drinks.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-83575, In the Matter of Beam Inc., 2 July 2018; US criminal information, United States v. Beam Suntory Inc., N.D. Ill., filed 21 October 2020 (https://www.justice.gov/media/1107851/dl?inline)
undone: The US Securities and Exchange Commission found books-and-records and internal-controls breaches in July 2018 and ordered about $8.2 million in disgorgement, interest and penalty. A US criminal information over the same payments was filed against Beam Suntory in the Northern District of Illinois on 21 October 2020. Beam paid over $19 million.

n: Otis paid intermediaries over Baku's municipal lift contracts
rank: a senior official of Baku Liftremont
d: Baku Liftremont is a municipal entity that buys and maintains the lifts in Baku's public housing. Between 2012 and 2014 Otis Russia, part of the American group United Technologies, sold to it through four intermediaries: ten Liftremont contracts between March 2012 and August 2014 worth $14.6 million, with a spread of at least $11.8 million between what Otis charged the intermediaries and what Liftremont paid, part of it intended for Liftremont officials. Nine contracts were won through intermediaries between February 2013 and December 2014. A senior Liftremont official is described in the order but not named. The US Securities and Exchange Commission found anti-bribery, books-and-records and internal-controls breaches in September 2018, and the company paid about $14 million.
inside: United Technologies' lift arm sold through intermediaries whose margin was partly meant for officials of Baku's municipal lift operator, which kept buying its lifts.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-84087, In the Matter of United Technologies Corporation, 12 September 2018

n: An engine maker's agent paid an Air China purchasing official
org_label: International Aero Engines / Pratt & Whitney (United Technologies)
rank: a former senior purchasing official at Air China Limited
d: Air China Limited is a state-owned airline. International Aero Engines, a venture in which United Technologies' Pratt & Whitney held a stake, won a contract to supply Air China in April 2009 and paid a sales agent about $55 million in commissions between 2009 and 2013, including $4.3 million in success fees for that contract. The agent made at least six payments totalling over $160,000 to a former senior purchasing official at Air China, who was later convicted of corruption in China. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's order of September 2018 found books-and-records and internal-controls breaches over this and other conduct, and United Technologies paid about $14 million.
inside: International Aero Engines' sales agent paid Air China's senior purchasing official, so the state-owned airline's engine contract went to the venture whose agent was paying him.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-84087, In the Matter of United Technologies Corporation, 12 September 2018

n: FMC's intermediary paid Iraqi state oil company officials for equipment deals
rank: two high-level officials of South Oil Company; officials at Missan Oil Company
d: South Oil Company is Iraq's state-owned oil producer in Basra, and Missan Oil Company is its counterpart in Maysan governorate; both owned by the Ministry of Oil, which approves their awards. From 2008 to 2013 FMC Technologies, now part of TechnipFMC, paid a Monaco-based intermediary $794,000, some used to bribe Iraqi officials. Two high-level South Oil Company officials were paid directly and a relative of an Iraqi official put on a retainer. South Oil Company awarded contracts 4165 to 4168 in February and March 2011, worth about $17 million, on which FMC made over $4 million in illicit profits; Missan awarded two contracts in 2009 and 2010 on 9 per cent commissions to the intermediary. The US Securities and Exchange Commission found anti-bribery and accounting breaches in September 2019.
inside: FMC Technologies' intermediary paid two senior officers of Iraq's state oil producer, which then awarded it the equipment contracts the oil ministry approved.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-87055, In the Matter of TechnipFMC plc, 23 September 2019

n: Quad's Peru unit paid statistics institute officials 13% of each order
rank: officials of the National Institute of Statistics and Information (INEI)
d: Quad/Graphics is an American printing company. From 2011 to January 2016 its Peruvian subsidiary paid bribes of about 13 per cent of each government work order to officials of Peru's National Institute of Statistics and Information, known as INEI, which runs the census and national surveys, and to officials at municipalities, using false invoices from four sham vendors. Over $1 million was paid out in Peru in this way, and the US Securities and Exchange Commission put the gain on the statistics institute's contracts at over $4.4 million. Its order of September 2019 found anti-bribery, books-and-records and internal-controls breaches for the Peruvian conduct, and the company paid $9,895,334.
inside: Quad's Peruvian arm handed back a share of every order to officials of the state statistics institute, which kept awarding it the printing work.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-87128, In the Matter of Quad/Graphics, Inc., 26 September 2019

n: Quad Peru paid education ministry officials to drop contract penalties
rank: officials of the Ministry of Education (MINEDU)
d: Quad/Graphics' Peruvian subsidiary printed for Peru's Ministry of Education, known as MINEDU. Between 2011 and 2015 it paid ministry officials to cut the penalties and extend the delivery dates on contracts it already held: over $117,000 through sham vendors and over $45,000 between June 2011 and May 2013 from a slush fund. The company avoided default and penalties and was enriched by over $970,000. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's order of September 2019 found anti-bribery, books-and-records and internal-controls breaches for the Peruvian conduct, and Quad/Graphics paid $9,895,334 in disgorgement, interest and penalty.
inside: Quad's money reached ministry officials, who then eased the penalties and deadlines in the state printing contracts the company was failing to meet.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-87128, In the Matter of Quad/Graphics, Inc., 26 September 2019

n: Quad Peru's law firm bribed judges in its own $12m tax case
rank: judges hearing the company's tax litigation, including appellate judges
d: SUNAT, Peru's tax authority, assessed Quad/Graphics' Peruvian subsidiary more than $12 million in value added tax, interest, penalties and fines. Between 2011 and 2013 the subsidiary paid a local law firm to bribe the judges hearing the case: $20,000 in 2011, an extraordinary fee in December 2012, a $407,100 invoice in April 2013 of which $230,000 was wired, and $108,488 in October 2013, with improper payments to the firm of about $209,752. The December 2012 payment appeared to produce a preliminary injunction; the attempt on the appellate judges failed and the firm refunded $173,181 in June 2013. SUNAT won its appeal in the summer of 2014 and Peru's Supreme Court ruled for Quad in March 2018. The SEC settled with the company in September 2019.
inside: Quad's Peruvian subsidiary paid a law firm to reach the judges hearing its own tax case, and one payment appeared to win it an injunction against the tax authority.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-87128, In the Matter of Quad/Graphics, Inc., 26 September 2019

n: Quad's China unit paid agents for a state printing firm's orders
rank: officials at Shaanxi Beiren Printing Machinery Co. Ltd
d: Quad/Tech Shanghai Trading Company, the Chinese arm of the American printer Quad/Graphics, sold printing control systems. From 2010 to 2015 it paid commissions of about 2 per cent of sales order values to sham sales agents who did no real work, invoiced as technical service fees, for officials at Shaanxi Beiren Printing Machinery Co. Ltd, a state-owned manufacturer, and for employees of other customers. About $182,000 was paid or promised and the unit was enriched by about $1,087,322. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's order of September 2019 found books-and-records and internal-controls breaches over the Chinese conduct.
inside: Quad's Chinese arm paid commissions to sham agents, partly for officials of a state-owned machinery maker, which kept ordering its printing control systems.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-87128, In the Matter of Quad/Graphics, Inc., 26 September 2019

n: Cognizant's builder paid a Tamil Nadu official for a Chennai permit
rank: a senior official of the state of Tamil Nadu; a local electricity board
d: Cognizant, an American IT company, built a campus of about 2.7 million square feet at Chennai for roughly 17,500 staff, starting work in 2011 before the required planning permit was issued. A senior government official of the Indian state of Tamil Nadu demanded $2 million, which Cognizant's construction firm paid in mid-2014; the permit came in November 2014 and Cognizant repaid the firm $2.5 million through falsified change orders between 2015 and 2016. Two senior US executives approved the payment and the method. Further bribes of about $770,000 bought an environmental clearance at Pune and $840,000 bought planning, power and environmental permits at Siruseri. The company settled with the SEC in February 2019 for about $25 million, with anti-bribery breaches found.
inside: Cognizant's construction firm paid the senior Tamil Nadu official who demanded $2 million, and the state then issued the planning permit its half-built Chennai campus needed.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-85149, In the Matter of Cognizant Technology Solutions Corporation, 15 February 2019; SEC press release 2019-12

n: Dun & Bradstreet's China units paid officials for restricted company files
rank: employees of the State Administration of Industry and Commerce and its provincial offices
d: Dun & Bradstreet, an American business data company, sells company credit information. From about 2006 to 2012 its Chinese subsidiaries obtained non-public financial statement files held by the State Administration of Industry and Commerce, the agency that registers companies, by paying its employees and using third-party agents; Chinese law restricts access to those files. Data from the National Bureau of Statistics was also used. One subsidiary, Shanghai Roadway, held data on over 150 million Chinese citizens, was raided by Shanghai police in March 2012 and convicted under China's data privacy law in January 2013. Of 1,036 customers whose decision-makers received payments, 156 were government agencies or state-owned firms. The SEC settled in April 2018 for about $9.2 million.
inside: Dun & Bradstreet's Chinese units paid employees of the agency that registers companies, who handed over restricted financial files the company was not entitled to obtain.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-83088, In the Matter of The Dun & Bradstreet Corporation, 23 April 2018

n: WPP's Indian agency paid officials of two state information departments
rank: Departments of Information and Public Relations, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh
inside: WPP's Indian agency paid officials of two states' information departments, including one who demanded kickbacks on contracts he supervised, and those departments awarded it the advertising work.
d: WPP is the world's largest advertising group. The US Securities and Exchange Commission found that its Indian subsidiary paid bribes to officials of the Departments of Information and Public Relations (DIPR) of the Indian states of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, the offices that buy government advertising, to win and keep campaign contracts between 2015 and 2017. Money moved through two vendors and an intermediary, one vendor passing over $1,000,000 on for DIPR officials. The order describes a senior DIPR official who demanded kickbacks on contracts he supervised, and says DIPR paid the subsidiary $1,588,480 for a campaign marking the June 2015 anniversary of Telangana's formation that never took place. WPP settled in September 2021 for over $19 million without admitting or denying the findings.
cite: SEC administrative order 34-93117, In the Matter of WPP plc, 24 September 2021

n: Adviser paid ISSPOL's risk director to place Ecuador police pension money
rank: Risk Director and Investment Committee member, ISSPOL
inside: The investment adviser Jorge Cherrez paid the risk director of Ecuador's police pension fund, who approved the contracts placing the fund's money with Cherrez's own companies.
d: ISSPOL is the pension fund of Ecuador's national police. The US Justice Department charged the investment adviser Jorge Cherrez Mino with paying more than $2.6 million in bribes to ISSPOL officials between about 2014 and 2020 to win and keep the fund's investment business, taking about $65 million in profits from one part of the scheme. At least $1,397,066 went to John Luzuriaga Aguinaga, the fund's Risk Director and a member of its investment committee, who reviewed and approved the contracts that sent ISSPOL money to Cherrez's companies and took cash, cheques in relatives' names and a debit card. Both were charged in Florida in February 2021. Luzuriaga was sentenced in December 2022 to 58 months in prison and ordered to forfeit $1.39 million.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 2 March 2021; Primicias, 21 December 2022

n: Brokers paid the chairman of Ecuador's state insurer Seguros Sucre
rank: Chairman of the board, Seguros Sucre S.A.
inside: Brokers paid the man who chaired the state insurer, so the state's insurance and reinsurance business was placed with the firms paying him.
d: Seguros Sucre was Ecuador's state-owned insurance company, which held most public bodies' policies. Juan Ribas Domenech chaired its board from 2013 to 2017 and was also an adviser to the then president. His US factual proffer says he accepted about $5,036,465 in bribes, routed through two introducer companies and laundered through US bank accounts, from insurance and reinsurance brokers in return for using his position to give them Seguros Sucre business, including the defence ministry policies for 2013-14 and 2014-15. He pleaded guilty in Florida in September 2020 to conspiracy to launder money and was sentenced in March 2021 to 51 months in prison. In June 2021 President Guillermo Lasso signed a decree ordering the insurer's liquidation, citing corruption over the previous fourteen years.
cite: US factual proffer, United States v. Juan Ribas Domenech, S.D. Fla.; DOJ press release, 23 March 2021; Primicias, 15 June 2021

n: Vendors paid Citgo's procurement manager more than $7m for contracts
who: Venezuelan businessmen and their supply firms
rank: procurement officer and manager, Citgo Special Projects Group
inside: Venezuelan suppliers paid the procurement manager who awarded contracts at Citgo, the refiner owned by Venezuela's state oil company, so its buying served the firms paying him.
d: Citgo Petroleum Corporation is a Houston-based refiner owned by Venezuela's state oil company, Petroleos de Venezuela S.A. Jose Luis De Jongh Atencio, a procurement officer and manager in Citgo's Special Projects Group, accepted more than $7 million in bribes between about 2013 and 2019 from the businessmen Jose Manuel Gonzalez Testino and Tulio Anibal Farias Perez and others, along with tickets to a World Series game, the 2015 Super Bowl and a concert, in return for helping their companies obtain Citgo contracts. He directed the money into shell companies in Panama and Switzerland, sometimes against false invoices, and bought Houston-area property. He pleaded guilty in March 2021 and was sentenced in January 2023 to 48 months in prison.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 23 March 2021; Stanford FCPA Clearinghouse enforcement action record (sentence of 25 January 2023)

n: Adoption agency staff bribed Ugandan High Court judges and registrars
rank: High Court judges and court registrars
inside: A foreign adoption agency paid court staff and judges, so Uganda's High Court handed guardianship of children to the agency's paying clients.
d: Robin Longoria, who ran part of an Ohio-based adoption agency's international programme, pleaded guilty in August 2019 to conspiring to violate the US foreign bribery law and commit wire and visa fraud. Fees paid to a Ugandan agent were passed as bribes to probation officers, for reports recommending a child be placed in an orphanage, to court registrars, so cases went to judges described as adoption-friendly, and to judges of Uganda's High Court, so the agency's US clients won guardianship of Ugandan children. False documents were then filed with the US State Department. In August 2020 prosecutors charged Debra Parris, the agency's former executive director Margaret Cole and the Ugandan lawyer Dorah Mirembe. Parris pleaded guilty on 17 November 2021, Cole in February 2022; Mirembe remained at large.
cite: US Department of Justice press releases, 29 August 2019 and 4 February 2022; DOJ FCPA enforcement actions list, 2020; US Department of Justice press release, 17 November 2021

n: Clear Media's gifts and travel renewed its Hangzhou bus-shelter concession
rank: Officials of the Hangzhou transit authority
d: Clear Media, the Chinese bus-shelter advertising arm then majority-owned by the US firm Clear Channel Outdoor Holdings, gave gifts, meals and entertainment to officials of the Hangzhou transit authority, the city body that granted its advertising concession. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's order of 28 September 2023 records that in December 2016 Clear Media spent about $12,800 entertaining officials and in January 2017 took a further $14,000 for that purpose because the concession had to be renegotiated; the concession was renewed the same month. The order covers payments from 2012 to 2017 and about $16.4 million of benefit to Clear Channel. The company paid $26,116,487 in disgorgement, interest and a civil penalty, neither admitting nor denying the findings.
inside: Clear Media gave gifts and entertainment to officials of the Hangzhou transit body that granted its bus-shelter concession, and that body renewed the concession in January 2017.
cite: US SEC order 34-98615, 28 Sep 2023

n: Clear Media kept its Shanghai transit concession off open tender
rank: Officials of the Shanghai public transit authorities
d: Clear Media, the Chinese bus-shelter advertising arm then majority-owned by Clear Channel Outdoor Holdings of the United States, cultivated officials of the Shanghai public transit authorities with gifts, entertainment and travel. It signed a ten-year concession agreement with those authorities in December 2016. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's order of 28 September 2023 records that a Clear Media executive told the company's own auditors that keeping a close relationship with the officials was meant to stop the concession going to open tender, where Clear Media would probably have lost on price. The order found anti-bribery, books-and-records and internal-controls violations, and Clear Channel paid $26,116,487 in all, neither admitting nor denying the findings.
inside: Clear Media's gifts and travel for Shanghai transit officials kept its bus-shelter concession out of open tender, and those authorities signed a ten-year agreement with it instead.
cite: US SEC order 34-98615, 28 Sep 2023

n: Gartner paid a firm tied to a SARS official, then won two contracts
rank: Senior officials of the South African Revenue Service
d: Gartner, a US research and advisory firm, paid a South African IT consultancy whose executive director was a close friend of a senior official of the South African Revenue Service, the national tax authority, after SARS officials told Gartner to use that firm. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's order of 26 May 2023 found the stated reason, meeting black economic empowerment requirements, was false, because Gartner's existing local sub-agents already qualified. SARS then awarded Gartner two contracts without competition: a roughly $1 million agreement signed on 5 February 2015 and a roughly $10 million follow-on signed on 31 July 2015, which a SARS commissioner had suggested. Gartner paid $675,974 in disgorgement, $180,790 in interest and a $1.6 million penalty.
inside: Gartner paid a consultancy run by a close friend of a senior South African Revenue Service official, and the tax authority awarded it two contracts without competition.
cite: US SEC order 34-97609, 26 May 2023

n: Frank's International's agent paid the Sonangol official awarding contracts
rank: Senior official of Sonangol responsible for contract awards
d: Frank's International, a Netherlands-based oilfield services company then listed in New York, used an Angolan sales agent to pass money to a senior official of Sonangol, Angola's state oil company, who was responsible for awarding contracts. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's order of 26 April 2023 found that the agent was taken on in November 2007 with no written contract and no checks, and that his businesses received about $5.5 million from Frank's Angolan operations between 2008 and 2014, some of it diverted to the official, who also got travel and entertainment in 2013 and 2014. Frank's kept contracts that were at risk and won eleven new ones. It paid about $8 million in disgorgement, interest and a civil penalty.
inside: Frank's International's Angolan agent passed money to the Sonangol official responsible for awarding contracts, and the state oil company kept its contracts in place and added eleven more.
cite: US SEC order 34-97381, 26 Apr 2023

n: Oracle Turkey's slush fund flew interior ministry officials to California
rank: Officials of Turkey's Ministry of Interior
d: Oracle's Turkish subsidiary used money hidden in excessive distributor discounts to pay for travel by officials of Turkey's Ministry of Interior. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's order of 27 September 2022 found that in May 2018 four unnamed ministry officials working on the 112 emergency-call project were flown to California, where the business meeting lasted about 15 to 20 minutes and the rest of the week was given to Los Angeles, Napa Valley and a theme park. Oracle received a large follow-on order on 31 May 2018, and the ministry required bidders to include Oracle products. Oracle paid $7,905,416 in disgorgement and interest and a $15 million penalty for conduct in Turkey, the United Arab Emirates and India.
inside: Oracle's Turkish arm paid for interior ministry officials' travel from hidden discount funds, and the ministry ordered more of its software and required bidders to include its products.
cite: US SEC order 34-95913, 27 Sep 2022

n: Oracle Turkey's middleman paid cash to Social Security Institute staff
rank: Officials of Turkey's Social Security Institute
d: Oracle's Turkish subsidiary directed cash to officials of Turkey's Social Security Institute, the state body that runs the country's pension and health insurance, through an intermediary connected to a 2016 deal with the institute. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's order of 27 September 2022 found that a 2017 database order was routed through a reseller to build a fund from an excess margin of about $1.1 million, and that an entity controlled by the intermediary received at least $185,605. From 2009 to 2019 the subsidiary used excess discounts and sham marketing payments to create such funds, which also paid for foreign officials' travel to conferences. Oracle paid $7,905,416 in disgorgement and interest and a $15 million penalty.
inside: Oracle's Turkish arm built hidden funds from reseller margins and sent money through an intermediary meant for officials of Turkey's state social-security body, which ordered its databases.
cite: US SEC order 34-95913, 27 Sep 2022

n: Honeywell's consultant paid a Sonatrach director over Arzew refinery terms
rank: Sonatrach downstream development director
d: Honeywell's Belgian unit held a contract to upgrade Zone 4 of the Arzew refinery near Oran, owned by Sonatrach, Algeria's national state oil company. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's order of 19 December 2022 found that a consultant paid Sonatrach's downstream development director $50,000 on 19 April 2011 and $25,000 on 28 December 2011 from a Swiss account. The director was a key decision-maker on the disputed construction schedule and penalty payments, and an amendment settling those terms was signed on 19 June 2011. About two weeks later Honeywell engaged a Monaco agent, paid $300,000 and booked it as a sales commission; the agent repaid part to the consultant. The SEC attributed $3,118,350 of disgorgement to the Algerian conduct.
inside: Honeywell's consultant paid Sonatrach's downstream development director, who decided the disputed Arzew schedule and penalties, and the amendment settling them was signed on terms the company wanted.
cite: US SEC order 34-96529, 19 Dec 2022

n: Tenaris paid a Petrobras tender manager to drop the international tender
rank: Senior manager in Petrobras procurement and tendering
d: Tenaris, a Luxembourg-based steel pipe maker, paid a high-ranking manager in the procurement and tender department of Petrobras, Brazil's state-controlled oil company, through its Brazilian subsidiary Confab Industrial. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's order of 2 June 2022 found that the manager used his authority to have Petrobras forgo an international tender for certain pipe and tube contracts, which left Confab as the only domestic supplier and allowed direct negotiation. About $10.4 million in bribes was paid between 2008 and 2013, routed through offshore entities and false consultancy contracts, with the manager taking about 0.5 per cent of Confab's revenue; Confab obtained more than $1 billion in Petrobras contracts. The manager pleaded guilty in Brazil. Tenaris paid $78.1 million.
inside: Tenaris paid a senior manager in Petrobras's tender department, who used his authority to drop the international tender, leaving its Brazilian unit to negotiate the pipe contracts directly.
cite: US SEC order 34-95030, 2 Jun 2022

n: KT's bribe to a Quang Binh official won it a provincial solar contract
rank: High-level official of the People's Committee of Quang Binh province
d: KT Corporation, South Korea's largest telecommunications operator and a company with shares traded in New York, paid a high-level official of the People's Committee of Quang Binh province, the provincial government in central Vietnam, to win a solar power project. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's order of 17 February 2022 found the official received $95,031 in 2014, and that the construction company that advanced the money was reimbursed about $200,000 in 2018 through a false arrangement. The order charged only the FCPA's books-and-records and internal accounting controls provisions. KT paid $2,263,821 in disgorgement, $536,457 in interest and a $3.5 million penalty for conduct in Vietnam and South Korea.
inside: KT Corporation paid a senior official of Quang Binh's provincial government, and that government awarded it the solar power project it was seeking.
cite: US SEC order 34-94279, 17 Feb 2022

n: KT paid a Vietnamese training official $550,000 for a colleges contract
rank: Official of the General Department of Vocational Training
d: KT Corporation, South Korea's largest telecommunications operator, paid an official of Vietnam's General Department of Vocational Training, part of the Ministry of Labor, Invalids and Social Affairs, to obtain a contract to equip vocational colleges. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's order of 17 February 2022 found that an agent fee of about 8.5 per cent included $550,000 for that official, and the contract was signed on 28 May 2015; a partner company was reimbursed about $775,000 in January 2017. When the Ministry of Finance held up an advance payment in 2015, KT staff paid ministry officials about $3,000 in cash and the advance was released. The order charged the books-and-records and internal controls provisions, and KT paid about $6.3 million.
inside: KT Corporation's agent fee included money for an official of Vietnam's vocational training department, which awarded it the colleges contract, and cash to finance ministry officials released its advance.
cite: US SEC order 34-94279, 17 Feb 2022

n: Jardine Lloyd Thompson disgorged $29m over Seguros Sucre contracts
rank: Officials of Seguros Sucre
d: Jardine Lloyd Thompson, a British insurance broker, paid bribes through a Florida intermediary to obtain and keep contracts with Seguros Sucre, Ecuador's state-owned insurance company. The US Justice Department closed the case on 18 March 2022 with a declination under its corporate enforcement policy, a decision not to prosecute conditioned on the company giving up its profits, and JLT disgorged about $29 million. The chief executive of its former Colombian subsidiary, Felipe Moncaleano Botero, and two intermediaries, Jose Vicente Gomez Aviles and Roberto Heinert, each pleaded guilty in 2020 in the Southern District of Florida to money laundering conspiracy. The same state insurer was also the target of schemes by the brokers Tysers and H.W. Wood, resolved in November 2023.
inside: Jardine Lloyd Thompson paid bribes through a Florida intermediary to officials of Ecuador's state insurer, which awarded and renewed the broker's contracts.
cite: US DOJ, 20 Nov 2023 (recording the 18 Mar 2022 JLT declination)

n: Corsa Coal's intermediary paid Al Nasr's chairman for $143m of coal orders
rank: Chairman of Al Nasr Company for Coke and Chemicals
d: Corsa Coal, a US coal producer, paid about $4.8 million to an Egypt-based intermediary that its own employees knew would use part of it to bribe Egyptian officials - among them, the Justice Department's declination letter says, the chairman of Al Nasr Company for Coke and Chemicals. The scheme ran from late 2016 to early 2020, bringing Corsa roughly $143 million in coal orders from Al Nasr and about $32.7 million in profit. Corsa reported itself, and in March 2023 the department declined to prosecute, taking $1.2 million rather than the whole profit. Frederick Cushmore Jr. pleaded guilty and awaits sentence. Charles Hunter Hobson was convicted by a jury in February 2026 of conspiring to and paying Egyptian officials through the intermediary's purported commissions, taking over $200,000 in kickbacks himself.
inside: Corsa's money reached officials at Egypt's state coke maker through an intermediary, and the company then bought about $143 million of Corsa's coal.
cite: US DOJ declination letter to Corsa Coal Corporation, 8 Mar 2023. US Department of Justice, 'Former Coal Company Executive Convicted in International Bribery and Money Laundering Scheme', 19 February 2026

n: EBRD consultant won six contracts while his partner worked inside the bank
org_label: Transport engineering consultant and his US consultancy company (both unnamed in the decision)
who: A transport engineering consultant and his US company
rank: EBRD consultancy contracts, with a bank operation leader involved
d: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, a development lender based in London, awarded six consultancy contracts between 2019 and 2020 to a transport engineer and his US company while an EBRD staff member who was his partner worked on those projects. In a decision of 19 June 2024 the bank's Enforcement Committee found he had concealed the conflict of interest, a fraudulent practice, and counted the involvement of bank staff as an aggravating factor. The staff member had forwarded his CV to colleagues and was the bank's operation leader on two of the contracts; she was dismissed in July 2021 after a compliance investigation. The panel found insufficient evidence that the two conspired. Fees came to about EUR 367,000; he is debarred until 30 December 2027.
inside: An outside consultant's partner sat inside the lender and led projects he was hired for, and six contracts worth about EUR 367,000 went to his own company.
cite: EBRD Enforcement Committee, Appeal Decision No. 1 (Appeal Case ECS 001-2023), 19 June 2024

n: Koenig & Bauer's payments reached Casa da Moeda's officials over tenders
rank: public agents of Casa da Moeda do Brasil, the state mint
d: Casa da Moeda do Brasil is Brazil's state-owned mint. Koenig & Bauer Banknote Solutions, a Swiss maker of banknote printing machines formerly called KBA-NotaSys, signed a leniency agreement with Brazil's comptroller-general and attorney-general over unlawful payments to public agents, in acts the agreement says were meant to frustrate the objectives of a tender and which affected contracts with the federal administration. The agreement names no official and does not date the acts; those details sit in a restricted annex. The company reported itself to the Swiss attorney-general in 2015 and was sanctioned in Switzerland on 23 March 2017 over conduct in Brazil, Morocco, Nigeria and Kazakhstan. The Brazilian agreement, signed on 5 October 2026, sets 69,218,854.26 reais to be paid to Casa da Moeda as compensation for damage.
inside: Koenig & Bauer paid Brazilian public agents in acts the leniency agreement says were meant to frustrate a tender, and it compensated the state mint for the resulting damage.
cite: Acordo de Leniencia (SEI 4121262) between the Controladoria-Geral da Uniao, the Advocacia-Geral da Uniao and Koenig & Bauer Banknote Solutions SA, signed 5 October 2026, clauses 2.1.4, 5.2, 6.1.1, 8.1.1, 8.3, 8.7; CGU list of leniency agreements signed, updated October 2026; OCCRP, 27 February 2017, on the Swiss settlement

n: Dredging firm paid Nigerian Ports Authority executives for dredging work
org_label: Dredging International Services (Cyprus), a DEME subsidiary
rank: Nigerian Ports Authority executives
d: The Nigerian Ports Authority is the federal body that runs Nigeria's ports. Dredging International Services (Cyprus), a subsidiary of Belgium's DEME group, was sentenced in Switzerland in late May 2017 to a fine of one million Swiss francs and ordered to repay 36 million francs of unlawful profit, after Swiss prosecutors proved it had bribed the authority's executives. OCCRP reported that more than 20 million dollars went to nine offshore companies over about five years from 2007, that three former authority officials, Adebayo Sarumi, Felix Ovbude and Abba Murtala Mohammed, together received 2.6 million dollars, and that the authority awarded the company dredging contracts worth 70 million dollars a year without the open bidding Nigerian law requires. Nigeria's then justice minister reportedly told Switzerland there was no case to investigate.
inside: Dredging International paid executives of the Nigerian Ports Authority, which awarded it dredging work worth $70 million a year without the open bidding Nigerian law requires.
cite: OCCRP, 'Four Ex-Nigerian Officials Named in Swiss Bribery Scandal', June 2017; Tages-Anzeiger listing of Swiss corporate convictions under article 102 of the Swiss criminal code; Blick, listing of Swiss companies convicted of corruption

n: PwC firms took procurement secrets from Ethiopian Electric Power officials
rank: procurement officials, Ethiopian Electric Power and Ethiopian Electric Utility
d: Three member firms of the accountancy network PwC - PricewaterhouseCoopers Associates Africa in Mauritius, PwC Kenya and PwC Rwanda - obtained confidential procurement information from officials working on a World Bank-financed Ethiopian power project and used it to influence who won consultancy contracts. One contract, awarded in 2019, was to introduce international accounting standards at Ethiopian Electric Power Corporation, the state electricity generator; the firms also sought to influence the award of a fixed-asset inventory contract for the Ethiopian Electric Utility, the state distributor. The World Bank's Integrity Vice Presidency investigated, and on 18 March 2026 the Bank debarred all three for 21 months under a settlement in which they admitted culpability. PwC Associates also misrepresented its experts' availability and qualifications and did not fully disclose its subconsultants.
inside: PwC's member firms got officials inside Ethiopia's two state electricity companies to hand over confidential bid information, and the consultancy contracts then went to PwC.
cite: World Bank Group, Integrity Vice Presidency, press release no. 2026/034/INT, 18 March 2026

n: Thai businessman and four EDL executives jailed for bribery in Laos
rank: four former senior executives, Electricite du Laos
d: The Vientiane Capital People's Court announced verdicts on 1 July 2026 in four corruption cases with 17 defendants. In one it found Aphichart Vannakul, a Thai businessman, and four former senior executives of Electricite du Laos (EDL), the state electricity company, guilty of embezzling state funds, abuse of office and bribery, and sentenced all five to life imprisonment. Aphichart was ordered to pay EDL more than US$24.8 million and the court authorised seizure and sale of his assets, including ten bank accounts, 11 land plots and a vehicle; if those fell short, the former executives' assets would be sold too. More than US$1 million in bribe payments was confiscated for the state. The case was linked to an EDL hydropower project, but no details of the project were made public.
inside: Aphichart Vannakul's payments reached four senior managers inside Laos's state electricity company, and the court ordered him to repay it over $24 million for the project they handled.
cite: The Nation (Thailand), 2 July 2026, reporting Vientiane Capital People's Court verdicts of 1 July 2026

n: Dana Minerals' $35m 'entry fee' for Madagascar's state chrome deposit
rank: board of Kraomita Malagasy (KRAOMA), the state chrome company
d: Kraomita Malagasy (KRAOMA), Madagascar's state-owned chrome company, negotiated in 2023 to hand exploitation of the Brieville chrome deposit to Dana Minerals Corporation, a foreign company, after the previous operator's contract was terminated. BIANCO, the national anti-corruption bureau, says US$35 million was requested through a Malagasy intermediary, presented as an entry fee for the award plus compensation for the earlier investor, and that an initial US$5 million went to an offshore account in Mauritius rather than to KRAOMA's official accounts. BIANCO says the decision to select Dana Minerals was taken at the level of KRAOMA's board, and found indications of corruption and money laundering involving five people and four companies. Three suspects were placed in pre-trial detention on 5 March 2026 and about US$4.75 million was repatriated. Nobody has been convicted.
inside: Dana Minerals' entry fee went through an intermediary to an offshore account rather than to Madagascar's state chrome company, whose board then awarded it the Brieville deposit.
cite: BIANCO (Bureau Independant Anti-Corruption, Madagascar), statements on the Brieville chrome investigation and the repatriation of USD 4.75 million, 28 March 2026

n: Swiss bribery probe into Gunvor's $1bn deal with Gabon Oil Company
rank: Gabon Oil Company, the state oil company
d: In June 2024 Gunvor, a Geneva commodity trader, lent Gabon Oil Company (GOC), the state oil company, US$1 billion to buy Assala Energy's six oil blocks from the US fund Carlyle, about a fifth of Gabon's output, taking exclusive rights to market the crude. In mid-May 2026 the Swiss Attorney General's Office searched Gunvor's Geneva offices in a criminal investigation against persons unknown for suspected bribery of foreign public officials over African oil contracts, notably in Gabon. Public Eye reported that Mohamed Dagdag, a French-Moroccan businessman, acted as intermediary alongside a former vice-president holding a presidential mandate to find investors and that intermediaries were paid out of inflated port-fee invoices. Gunvor said its internal investigation found the deal met the most stringent compliance standards.
inside: Swiss prosecutors suspect Gunvor's payments to intermediaries close to Gabon's presidency bought the state oil company's $1bn deal, which left Gunvor marketing Gabon's crude.
cite: Public Eye, 'Oil mega-deal in Gabon: Gunvor once again in the sights of the Swiss justice system', 2026; Swiss Office of the Attorney General search of Gunvor's Geneva offices, May 2026

n: Bourbon executives convicted over payments to Cameroon tax inspectors
rank: two tax inspectors, Cameroon tax administration
d: The criminal court in Marseille convicted three executives of Bourbon, a French group supplying marine services to the offshore oil industry, on 12 July 2024 for corruption of foreign public officials in Africa. Former chief executive Christian Lefevre received 30 months suspended, Gael Bodenes and former deputy director Laurent Renard 24 months, and each was fined 80,000 euros.
