Bodenes appealed, which suspends his conviction, and his lawyer said the facts are disputed. On the Cameroon part, the reporting says bribes of 150,000 euros, about 100 million CFA francs, were paid to two tax inspectors, and that the money served to make an 11 million euro tax debt owed by Bourbon disappear. The affair began in 2012 when Marseille customs found US$250,000 in cash in a former tax director's suitcase.
inside: Bourbon's executives were convicted of paying two Cameroonian tax inspectors, and reporting says the money made an eleven-million-euro tax claim against the group disappear.
cite: Journal du Cameroun, reporting the judgment of the tribunal correctionnel de Marseille, 12 July 2024

n: Try Pheap's logging consortium paid Cambodian national park officials
rank: National Park officials; Cambodian military units
d: On 9 December 2019 the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control designated Try Pheap, a Cambodian tycoon, for corruption, together with 11 Cambodia-registered companies he owns or controls. The designation says he used his network inside Cambodia to build a large-scale illegal logging consortium that depends on officials who protect his timber shipments, that he used the Cambodian military to enable his timber trafficking, and that Cambodian National Park officials were paid by him to keep his operations secret, which made it hard for local authorities to act against him. Timber was sold to buyers in Vietnam, China, Europe and Russia. The release gives no sums and no dates for the conduct, and the finding is the Treasury's own rather than a court's.
inside: US Treasury says Try Pheap paid Cambodia's national park officials and used army units, so the bodies meant to stop illegal logging protected his timber instead.
cite: US Department of the Treasury, press release sm849, 9 December 2019 (OFAC designations of Try Pheap and Kun Kim)

n: Cambodian foreign ministry officials accused of selling 12,000 visas
org_label: workers at online scam compounds and casinos
rank: former director-general and two officials, Ministry of Foreign Affairs
d: Cambodia's Anti-Corruption Unit said on 29 August 2026 that three former officials of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs took 12,000 visa stickers and sold visas to foreign workers at online scam compounds and casinos for US$300 to US$6,000 each, about US$3 million in all. They are named as Tho Samnang, a former director-general, Nop Ratha, a former deputy bureau chief, and Yos Rane, a contract officer. Nearly 200 foreign nationals were found with fraudulent visas in their passports. The three are charged with intentional destruction and embezzlement, abuse of power and money laundering, and three further charges were said to be in preparation. Courts froze and confiscated US$980,000 and US$250,000 said to have been laundered. The allegations have not been tried.
inside: Workers at Cambodia's scam compounds and casinos are accused of paying three foreign ministry officials for visas, so the ministry's own stickers admitted whoever paid.
cite: Asia Gaming Brief, 31 August 2026, reporting the Cambodian Anti-Corruption Unit statement of 29 August 2026

n: Julius Baer manager in Singapore filed a forged tax paper for a launderer
org_label: Fujian money-laundering network (Lin Baoying and others)
rank: relationship manager, Bank Julius Baer Singapore branch
d: Liu Kai, a relationship manager at the Singapore branch of the Swiss private bank Bank Julius Baer, handled the account of Lin Baoying, one of ten foreign nationals later convicted in Singapore's S$3 billion money-laundering case. In 2020 he sent her samples of Chinese tax documents, advised that a round income figure "would look suspicious", guided her edits to a certificate he suspected was forged, and submitted it to his own bank so her account would be approved. Singapore police charged him with using a forged document as genuine; on 24 October 2025 he was jailed for four months, and in March 2026 the Monetary Authority of Singapore barred him from the industry for seven years.
inside: Lin Baoying, of a Fujian laundering network, had her Julius Baer manager guide her edits to a forged tax certificate and file it past the bank's account checks.
cite: Singapore Police Force news release, 24 October 2025; Monetary Authority of Singapore prohibition orders, 17 March 2026 (reported 18 March 2026)

n: Julius Baer managing director laundered $1.2bn for the PDVSA network
org_label: PDVSA foreign-exchange embezzlement network (Francisco Convit Guruceaga and others)
rank: managing director and vice chairman, Bank Julius Baer
d: Matthias Krull was a managing director and vice chairman at the Swiss private bank Julius Baer, where his job was to attract wealthy Venezuelan clients. In 2016 one of those clients asked him to help launder the proceeds of a scheme that had embezzled about $1.2 billion from PDVSA, Venezuela's state oil company, by rigging its currency exchanges. Krull used Miami property and false investment schemes to disguise where the money came from. He pleaded guilty in August 2018 to conspiracy to launder money and was sentenced to ten years that October; after he cooperated with prosecutors, the same judge cut the term to three and a half years.
inside: A network that embezzled $1.2 billion from Venezuela's state oil company recruited Julius Baer's vice chairman, Matthias Krull, to disguise where its money came from.
cite: US Department of Justice release, 29 October 2018; The Real Deal, 24 March 2021

n: Julius Baer banker moved FIFA bribe money for a sports marketing firm
rank: relationship manager, Bank Julius Baer (Montevideo and Zurich)
d: Jorge Luis Arzuaga was a relationship manager for the Swiss private bank Julius Baer in its Montevideo and Zurich offices. Between February 2013 and May 2015 he agreed with executives of the Argentine sports marketing company Torneos y Competencias, including Alejandro Burzaco, to pass their bribes through accounts at his bank, moving about $25 million into a sub-account held for a senior FIFA official who was selling World Cup broadcasting rights. Arzuaga pleaded guilty in June 2017 and was sentenced in November 2020 to three years' probation. The bank itself admitted laundering more than $36 million and paid over $79 million under a 2021 deferred prosecution agreement.
inside: Torneos y Competencias had Julius Baer's own relationship manager route its bribes, so the bank's accounts carried about $25 million to a senior FIFA official.
cite: US Department of Justice, Eastern District of New York release, 27 May 2021

n: RCBC branch manager opened the accounts that moved the $81m bank theft
org_label: the network that laundered the Bangladesh Bank theft
rank: branch manager, Rizal Commercial Banking Corporation
d: Maia Deguito managed a branch of Rizal Commercial Banking Corporation (RCBC), a large Philippine bank, and one of her duties was screening transactions under the country's anti-money-laundering law. She allowed accounts to be opened on fictitious identity documents, without the face-to-face meetings the law requires, and $81 million stolen from Bangladesh's central bank by hackers in 2016 was moved through them. In 2019 a Makati regional trial court convicted her on eight counts of facilitating money laundering and sentenced her to 56 years in prison. The Court of Appeals upheld the conviction in a ruling reported in April 2023 and rejected her claim that the trial judge was biased.
inside: The people laundering a stolen $81 million had the branch manager inside RCBC open accounts on fake papers, defeating the bank's own identity checks.
cite: Philippine Star, 21 April 2023; Rappler, April 2023

n: Six Danske Estonia managers sold laundering services to criminal clients
org_label: non-resident clients from Russia, Azerbaijan and elsewhere
rank: foreign customer managers, Danske Bank Estonia international banking division
d: Estonian state prosecutors charged six former managers of Danske Bank's Estonian branch in April 2023 with large-scale money laundering between 2007 and 2015. The six worked in the branch's international banking division as managers for foreign customers. Prosecutors allege they ran their own laundering business inside the bank, hidden from other units: selling clients companies that concealed their real owners, advising them how to hide the electronic trail of transfers, preparing transfer papers for a fee and putting through transactions with no economic purpose. The sums alleged are about $1.61 billion and €6.07 million, tied to eight crimes in Russia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Switzerland, the United States and Iran. The trial opened at Harju County Court in November 2023 and all six denied the charges.
inside: Prosecutors say non-resident criminal clients paid six managers inside Danske's Estonian branch to hide their owners and transfers, so the branch put through transactions with no economic purpose.
cite: OCCRP, 19 April 2023; Baltic Times, 13 November 2023

n: Bribed TD Bank insider handed customer data to an account-takeover ring
rank: bank employee, TD Bank, N.A. and a second institution
d: Edward Low, a New York-based employee of TD Bank, took bribes of at least $26,700 from outside co-conspirators. Between January and May 2021 he used his access to pull confidential TD customer information and passed it to them; they used it to take over accounts and steal money, and he processed some of the transactions himself. Working at a second, unnamed institution in 2022, he falsified bank records so a co-conspirator could open an account for a shell company. Prosecutors put the fraud at more than $500,000. Low pleaded guilty in Newark on 17 February 2026 to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and making false bank entries, with sentencing set for July 2026.
inside: A fraud ring paid an employee inside two banks for customer records and false entries, so the banks' own systems opened accounts and released money to it.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey release, 17 February 2026

n: Operation Casablanca: 22 Mexican bank officers took cartel cash for commission
rank: banking officials at twelve Mexican commercial banks
d: US Customs agents spent nearly three years posing as money launderers for the Cali and Juárez cartels. They deposited drug cash into undercover accounts, wired it to Mexican banks and collected bank drafts in return. In May 1998 the United States announced the arrest of 22 banking officials from twelve Mexican commercial banks, and indicted the banks Bancomer, Banca Serfin and Confia for taking part; according to the indictment the officials knew the money was drug proceeds and took a commission. The operation brought 112 arrests and $35 million in seizures. The Federal Reserve recorded a US money-laundering conviction for Bancomer, closed its own case in December 2000, and required Bancomer to strengthen its controls.
inside: Posing as Cali and Juarez cartel launderers, US agents paid officers at twelve Mexican banks a commission to accept drug cash and wire it on; Bancomer was convicted.
cite: US Treasury Department release, 18 May 1998; Federal Reserve Board enforcement actions, 12 December 2000

n: Tribunal: Videocon's 64 crore rupees reached ICICI Bank's chief executive
rank: chief executive and managing director, ICICI Bank
d: ICICI Bank is one of India's largest private banks. In an order dated 3 July 2025 an appellate tribunal, upholding the Enforcement Directorate's seizure of her assets, found that its former chief executive Chanda Kochhar had accepted a bribe of 640 million rupees from the Videocon Group, routed through her husband Deepak Kochhar. The tribunal said she sat on the committee that sanctioned a 3 billion rupee loan to Videocon despite a conflict of interest, breaking the bank's own rules, and that Videocon moved the money to NuPower Renewables immediately after the loan was paid out. Videocon's chairman admitted that Deepak Kochhar controlled NuPower in practice. The tribunal criticised a 2020 decision that had released 780 million rupees of attached assets.
inside: A tribunal found Videocon's 640 million rupees reached ICICI's chief executive through her husband's company, and she sat on the committee that lent Videocon 3 billion rupees.
cite: Onmanorama, 22 July 2025; Free Press Journal, July 2025

n: CBI: PNB manager was paid to issue credit letters for Gitanjali Gems
rank: deputy manager, Punjab National Bank, Brady House branch, Mumbai
d: Gokulnath Shetty, a retired deputy manager of the state-owned Punjab National Bank, is the main accused in the fraud at the bank's Brady House branch in Mumbai linked to the jewellers Nirav Modi and Mehul Choksi. In October 2020 India's Central Bureau of Investigation booked him in a further case, alleging he took more than 10.8 million rupees in bribes between 2014 and 2017 from Rishika Financials, which arranged bank guarantees for Choksi's firm Gitanjali Gems. According to the CBI he issued letters of undertaking, which promise payment to overseas banks, on the word of Rishika's owner and sent them by SWIFT message without entering them in the bank's core accounting system, so the bank's own scrutiny was bypassed. He was arrested in March 2018; no verdict has been reported.
inside: The CBI alleges Rishika Financials paid a Punjab National Bank manager to issue Gitanjali Gems' payment guarantees on its word and keep them out of the bank's books.
cite: Press Trust of India via The News Minute, 20 October 2020

n: ED: DHFL paid Yes Bank's founder 600 crore rupees for a 3,700 crore deal
rank: co-founder and chief executive, Yes Bank
d: India's Enforcement Directorate alleges that Yes Bank, then one of the country's larger private banks, invested 37 billion rupees in debentures issued by the housing lender DHFL between April and June 2018, and that DHFL in return paid 6 billion rupees to DOIT Urban Ventures, a company linked to the bank's co-founder and chief executive Rana Kapoor, as a loan secured on property worth only 396.6 million rupees. Kapoor was arrested in 2020 and has since been granted bail. In 2026 a Mumbai court closed the money-laundering proceedings against DHFL itself, holding that the company was immune under insolvency law once its rescue plan was approved, while ruling that its former officers and others continue to be prosecuted.
inside: The Enforcement Directorate alleges DHFL paid 6 billion rupees to a company linked to Yes Bank's chief executive, after which the bank bought 37 billion rupees of DHFL debentures.
cite: Bar and Bench, 2026; Free Press Journal, 2026

n: PMC Bank's chairman and MD hid HDIL's bad loans behind 21,000 fake accounts
rank: chairman, managing director and directors, Punjab and Maharashtra Co-operative Bank
d: The Punjab and Maharashtra Co-operative Bank served depositors in Mumbai until the Reserve Bank of India took it over in September 2019 and froze withdrawals. Mumbai police's Economic Offences Wing filed a charge sheet of nearly 33,000 pages in December 2019 against five people: the bank's former chairman Waryam Singh, its former managing director Joy Thomas, a former director, and Rakesh and Sarang Wadhawan, promoters of the property company HDIL, named as the main accused. Police allege the bank's officials created about 21,000 fictitious accounts to hide loans made to HDIL and its group from the Reserve Bank, and received kickbacks from the promoters which they spent on property. A forensic audit put the bank's loss at about 67 billion rupees.
inside: Police allege HDIL's promoters paid kickbacks to PMC Bank's chairman and managing director, who hid the bank's loans to HDIL from the Reserve Bank behind 21,000 fictitious accounts.
cite: Business Today, 27 December 2019

n: CBI: companies paid Syndicate Bank's chairman to clear their credit
rank: chairman and managing director, Syndicate Bank
d: S K Jain was chairman and managing director of Syndicate Bank, a state-owned Indian bank. India's Central Bureau of Investigation arrested him on 2 August 2014 and alleges that Prakash Industries paid him more than 12.5 million rupees, through a chartered accountant acting as middleman and delivered via his brother-in-law, to approve the company's application for $20 million of overseas borrowing, and that a separate 5 million rupees came from Bhushan Steel over the clearing of credit facilities. Searches turned up cash, gold and deposits. The CBI charge sheet names Jain, Prakash Industries' chairman, the middleman and two others on conspiracy and corruption charges; the finance ministry suspended Jain. Both companies denied involvement, and no verdict has been reported.
inside: The CBI alleges Prakash Industries and Bhushan Steel paid Syndicate Bank's chairman through a middleman, to approve $20 million of overseas borrowing and clear credit facilities.
cite: Press Trust of India via DT Next, 3 December 2017

n: Bank of East Asia manager took HK$290,000 to open accounts for agents
rank: senior relationship manager, Bank of East Asia, Admiralty branch
d: Lai Chee-wai was a senior relationship manager at the Admiralty branch of the Bank of East Asia in Hong Kong, and opening client accounts was part of his job. Between December 2018 and March 2021 he took more than HK$290,000 from representatives of five intermediary companies that sell company-formation services, at HK$2,000 to HK$15,000 for each account opened for a client living outside Hong Kong. The bank required corporate applicants to attend a branch in person, so he and one intermediary submitted eight false immigration landing slips to make it appear clients were in Hong Kong. Hong Kong's anti-corruption commission brought the case; he pleaded guilty and was jailed for 18 months on 30 May 2024. Two intermediaries were jailed earlier.
inside: Company-formation intermediaries paid a Bank of East Asia manager per account and filed forged immigration slips with him, so clients who never came to Hong Kong became customers.
cite: Independent Commission Against Corruption (Hong Kong) press release, 30 May 2024

n: HSBC staff paid by agents opened 250 accounts, 70 flagged as laundering risks
rank: relationship and business managers, HSBC North Point branch
d: Three staff at the North Point branch of HSBC in Hong Kong took payments from the insurance agents Han Jie and Zhou Yinying for opening accounts for clients the pair referred. Lo Wing-hang, then an insurance specialist, agreed on HK$500 to HK$1,500 per account and paid a colleague, premier relationship manager Lo Cheuk-kim, HK$100 each; together they took more than HK$170,000. Premier business manager Wan Hui helped twelve clients for 6,000 yuan. About 250 referred clients had accounts opened, and the bank later flagged 70 of them as money-laundering risks and reported them to a law enforcement agency. Hong Kong's anti-corruption commission prosecuted; on 14 April 2026 two were jailed for ten and six months, with the third awaiting sentence.
inside: The insurance agents Han Jie and Zhou Yinying paid three HSBC branch staff per account, so 250 clients were taken on and the bank flagged 70 as laundering risks.
cite: Independent Commission Against Corruption (Hong Kong) press release, 14 April 2026

n: ICBC's Madrid staff convicted of banking for Chinese criminal groups
rank: director general and retail staff, ICBC Spain branch, Madrid
d: ICBC Spain is the Madrid branch of the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, opened in late 2010. In an agreed judgment reported on 2 July 2020, Spain's Audiencia Nacional convicted four former staff, among them the branch's director general, of money laundering. The court found they persistently ignored anti-money-laundering rules and gave the Chinese criminal groups known as Snake and Cheqia cover for their money: cash deposits of any size broken into smaller amounts, internal accounts without names, false documents and identity numbers, and invented invoices. The Snake group alone held 70 accounts there and paid in €41.59 million in cash between January 2011 and October 2012. Sentences ran from three to five months with fines of €22.7 million.
inside: The Snake and Cheqia criminal groups banked through ICBC Madrid's director general and staff, who split their cash and hid 41 million euros in nameless accounts.
cite: Consejo General del Poder Judicial (Spain), 2 July 2020

n: Wells Fargo banker opened funnel accounts for a Sinaloa laundering ring
rank: personal banker, Wells Fargo
d: Luis Fernando Figueroa, a personal banker at Wells Fargo, admitted he belonged to an organisation that laundered drug money from the United States to Mexico for the Sinaloa Cartel. He opened Wells Fargo accounts in the names of recruited nominees, which the ring used as "funnel accounts": couriers collected cash in Los Angeles, Chicago, Boston, New Jersey and New York and paid it in deposits of $22,000 to $45,000, and the money was then moved on to Mexico. About $19.6 million was laundered between 2014 and 2018. The FBI arrested him in November 2018 as part of an operation that brought eight arrests, and he pleaded guilty in federal court in San Diego in May 2019 to conspiracy to launder money.
inside: A Sinaloa Cartel laundering ring had one of its members working as a Wells Fargo banker, opening the nominee accounts its couriers paid $19.6 million into.
cite: La Opinión, 17 May 2019 (US Attorney's Office, Southern District of California)

n: Businessman accused of bribing Petropiar officers for inflated contracts
rank: senior officials of Petropiar's procurement division
d: From at least 2015 to May 2019 Rixon Rafael Moreno Oropeza, a Venezuelan businessman, paid bribes to senior officials of Petropiar, a joint venture between Venezuela's state-owned energy company and an American oil company, to obtain multimillion-dollar procurement contracts, according to an indictment returned in Miami in August 2022. Prosecutors said over $30 million in Petropiar contract payments went to accounts he controlled in South Florida, and that one contract for breathing devices, priced at about a hundred times their actual cost, brought him roughly $2.7 million. A senior Venezuelan government official was allegedly promised a $1 million bribe to install another person as a high-ranking official in Petropiar's procurement division. The Justice Department names none of the officials, and an indictment is only an allegation.
inside: Prosecutors allege Rixon Moreno Oropeza paid senior officials in Petropiar's procurement division, so the state oil venture bought from his companies at prices up to a hundred times cost.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 24 August 2022

n: Supplier's staff paid three PDVSA officials 3% of every invoice
org_label: Rafael Pinto Franceschi and Franz Muller Huber
rank: three PDVSA officials handling vendor business and payments
d: Rafael Enrique Pinto Franceschi, a sales representative for a Miami-based supplier to Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), Venezuela's state-owned energy company, and Franz Herman Muller Huber, the supplier's president, were indicted in Houston in February 2019 for conspiring to bribe three PDVSA officials. Prosecutors said that from about 2009 to 2013 Pinto alerted an official whenever PDVSA paid the supplier; the official then raised a fictitious invoice from a Panamanian shell company for 3 per cent of the payment, and Muller made sure it was paid into a Swiss account. In return the supplier received contracts, inside information and payment of overdue invoices. Pinto took over $985,000 in kickbacks and Muller over $258,000. Both pleaded guilty and were sentenced in May 2021, Pinto to two years and Muller to 20 months.
inside: A Miami supplier's president and sales representative paid three PDVSA officials three per cent of every invoice, so the state oil company gave them contracts, inside information and quick payment.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 26 February 2019; Stanford FCPA Clearinghouse case record 741

n: Shell-company pair paid PetroEcuador officials $4.4m and bought them homes
who: Armengol Cevallos Diaz and Jose Cisneros Alarcon
rank: PetroEcuador officials awarding oil services contracts
d: Armengol Alfonso Cevallos Diaz, an Ecuadorian businessman living in Miami, pleaded guilty in January 2020 to conspiring to pay $4.4 million in bribes, between 2012 and 2015, to officials of Empresa Publica de Hidrocarburos del Ecuador (PetroEcuador), the state-owned oil company. He admitted laundering money through Miami shell companies and bank accounts, buying Miami-area properties for certain PetroEcuador officials, and passing on bribes from an oil services company and from Ecuadorian contractors. The payments ran through O&G International Supplies, a company he created; its director, Jose Melquiades Cisneros Alarcon, agreed a plea in August 2019 and was sentenced in February 2020 to 20 months in prison and $4.4 million in forfeiture. The department said twelve people had by then been charged in the PetroEcuador investigation.
inside: Armengol Cevallos paid PetroEcuador officials $4.4 million and bought them Miami homes, so the state oil company's service contracts went to the contractors who paid.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 23 January 2020; A&O Shearman FCPA case record

n: Contractor paid PetroEcuador officials over $8m to win oil contracts
org_label: Jose L. De La Paz Roman
who: Jose L. De La Paz Roman
rank: PetroEcuador officials awarding contracts
d: Jose L. De La Paz Roman, a US national and a contractor to PetroEcuador, Ecuador's state-owned oil company, was accused of paying its officials more than $8 million between 2012 and 2016 to obtain contracts. He pleaded guilty in January 2019 and was sentenced to three years in prison, two years of supervised release and forfeiture of $2,145,000. His case was one of several brought in Florida over the same state oil company. Two former PetroEcuador officials who took bribes in the wider investigation, Roberto Barrera and Jose Raul De La Torre Prado, also pleaded guilty to conspiring to launder the money; Barrera was sentenced in 2019 to 23 months in prison, three years of supervised release and forfeiture of $150,000.
inside: Jose De La Paz Roman, a PetroEcuador contractor, admitted paying its officials over $8 million, so the state oil company's contracts went to him.
cite: A&O Shearman FCPA case record, United States v. Ramiro Luque Flores et al.

n: Hitachi gave the ruling ANC's funding vehicle a stake in its Eskom bids
rank: Eskom Holdings tender process
d: Hitachi, a Japanese engineering group, sold a 25 per cent stake in its South African subsidiary to Chancellor House Holdings, which the US Securities and Exchange Commission describes as a front company for the African National Congress, South Africa's governing party. That gave the party a share of the profits from any contract Hitachi won from Eskom Holdings, the state-owned electricity utility. Hitachi then won two power station contracts, paid Chancellor about $5 million in dividends, and paid a further $1 million in undocumented 'success fees' for its influence in the Eskom tender process. The SEC said Hitachi knew of the arrangement while bidding and encouraged Chancellor to use its political influence. In September 2015 Hitachi paid a $19 million penalty without admitting or denying the findings.
inside: Hitachi sold the ANC's front company a quarter of its South African arm, and the party's influence inside state utility Eskom helped it win two power station contracts.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission, press release 2015-212, 28 September 2015

n: Halliburton paid $3.7m to a firm owned by a Sonangol official's friend
rank: Sonangol official approving contract awards
d: Officials of Sonangol, Angola's state oil company, told Halliburton's management in 2008 that the US oilfield services company had to partner with more local Angolan-owned businesses to meet local content rules. A Halliburton vice president, Jeannot Lorenz, then arranged for it to retain a local firm owned by a former Halliburton employee who was a friend and neighbour of the Sonangol official who would approve contract awards. Halliburton paid the firm $3.705 million and outsourced more than $13 million of work to it, skipping competitive bidding and avoiding a control requiring committee review of contracts in high-corruption-risk countries. Sonangol approved seven subcontracts to Halliburton. In July 2017 Halliburton paid over $29.2 million to settle SEC books-and-records and internal-controls charges, and Lorenz paid $75,000.
inside: Halliburton paid $3.7 million to a firm owned by a friend of the Sonangol official who approved its contracts, and the state oil company approved seven subcontracts.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission, press release 2017-133, 27 July 2017

n: Key Energy paid a Pemex contract employee through a consulting firm
rank: Pemex contract employee in the department approving its contracts
d: Key Energy Services, a Houston oilfield services company, worked in Mexico through a subsidiary, Key Mexico, which held contracts with Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex), the state oil company. The SEC found that Key Mexico routed payments through a consulting firm tied to a Pemex contract employee who worked in the department that negotiated and approved Key Mexico's Pemex contracts, and that he supplied inside information. Key Mexico's country manager approved the consulting payments without telling head office and resigned in February 2014. A Key Energy senior vice president in Houston had suggested in 2011 seeking a further $90 million on the existing contract. In August 2016 Key Energy consented to a cease-and-desist order and disgorged $5 million; the SEC imposed no civil penalty, citing cooperation and the company's financial condition.
inside: Key Energy's Mexican arm paid a consulting firm tied to the Pemex employee in the department approving its contracts, and he supplied inside information on its deals.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission, order 34-78558, 11 August 2016

n: FLIR paid for a 20-night 'world tour' for Saudi interior ministry officials
rank: officials of the Saudi Arabia Ministry of Interior
d: FLIR Systems, an Oregon company that makes infrared cameras and sensing equipment, paid for travel and gifts for officials of Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Interior who had key roles in deciding to buy its products. In 2009 two employees of its Dubai office arranged a 20-night trip for Saudi officials with stops in Casablanca, Paris, Dubai, Beirut and New York City; one employee called it the 'world tour'. Between 2008 and 2010 FLIR paid about $40,000 more for Saudi travel, including New Year's Eve trips to Dubai. The SEC said FLIR earned more than $7 million in profits on sales influenced by the travel and gifts. In April 2015 it paid $9,504,584 to settle charges under the anti-bribery, books-and-records and internal-controls provisions.
inside: FLIR paid for a twenty-night trip and other travel for Saudi interior ministry officials who decided its sales, and earned over $7 million on them.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission, press release 2015-62, 8 April 2015

n: IAP used a shell firm to win Kuwait's surveillance planning contract
rank: Kuwait Security Program, Ministry of the Interior
d: IAP Worldwide Services, a Florida defence contractor, sought work on the Kuwait Security Program, a nationwide surveillance project, mainly CCTV, overseen by Kuwait's Ministry of the Interior. The programme had two phases: planning and feasibility, then the much larger installation contract. The US Justice Department said IAP and a vice president, James Michael Rama, formed a shell company called Ramaco in February 2006 to bid for the planning phase to hide IAP's role, so that IAP could shape the installation requirements to suit its own strengths. Ramaco won the roughly $4 million planning contract. Between September 2006 and March 2008 IAP and others paid a consultant about $1,783,688, understanding some would be used to bribe Kuwaiti officials. IAP paid $7.1 million under a non-prosecution agreement.
inside: IAP used a shell company to win the job of planning Kuwait's interior ministry surveillance programme, so the requirements for the big installation contract suited IAP itself.
cite: US Department of Justice, press release, 16 June 2015

n: Goodyear's Kenya unit bribed staff of state firms and ministries
rank: Kenya Ports Authority, Telkom Kenya and ministry staff
d: Goodyear, the US tyre maker, held a majority stake in a Kenyan subsidiary that the SEC found paid bribes to land tyre sales. The recipients were employees of the Kenya Ports Authority, the Armed Forces Canteen Organization, Nzoia Sugar Company, the Kenyan Air Force, the Ministry of Roads, the Ministry of State for Defense, East African Portland Cement Co. and Telkom Kenya Ltd., most of them state-owned companies or government bodies. Bribes in Kenya and Angola together came to more than $3.2 million over four years and were recorded as normal business expenses. Goodyear self-reported. In February 2015 it paid $14,122,525 in disgorgement and $2,105,540 in interest to settle books-and-records and internal-controls charges, and agreed to report on its remediation to the SEC for three years.
inside: Goodyear's Kenyan subsidiary paid employees of the Kenya Ports Authority, Telkom Kenya, the Air Force and two ministries, so those bodies bought its tyres.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission, press release 2015-38, 24 February 2015

n: Goodyear's Angola unit paid staff of Sonangol and other state firms
rank: Sonangol, Electric Company of Luanda and Catoca mine staff
d: Goodyear, the US tyre maker, owned a tyre distributor in Angola that the SEC found paid bribes to secure sales. The recipients were employees of Sonangol, the state oil company; the Catoca Diamond Mine, owned by a consortium that includes the national mining company Endiama E.P. and Russia's ALROSA; UNICARGAS; Engevia Construction and Public Works; the Electric Company of Luanda; and the National Service of Alfadega, the customs service. Payments also went to other local officials, such as police and city council officials. Bribes in Angola and Kenya together exceeded $3.2 million over four years and were booked as normal business expenses. Goodyear self-reported and in February 2015 paid more than $16 million in disgorgement and interest to settle SEC books-and-records and internal-controls charges.
inside: Goodyear's Angolan distributor paid employees of Sonangol, the Luanda power company, the Catoca diamond mine and the customs service, so those bodies bought its tyres.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission, press release 2015-38, 24 February 2015

n: PBSJ executive offered a Qatari Diar director a cut of a rail contract
rank: Director of International Projects, Qatari Diar
d: Walid Hatoum, a former officer of the international arm of The PBSJ Corporation, a US engineering firm, offered payments to the then Director of International Projects at Qatari Diar Real Estate Investment Company, which the Qatari government established to coordinate the country's real estate development. The official owned and controlled a local company through which the money was to pass. Hatoum offered an agency fee of 1.8 per cent of a Qatari light rail transit contract, about $640,000, and 3 per cent of a $25 million hotel resort project in Morocco, about $750,000. PBS&J International was awarded the $35.6 million rail contract in August 2009. The scheme was caught before any of the money was paid, and in January 2015 Hatoum settled SEC anti-bribery charges with a $50,000 penalty.
inside: A PBS&J executive offered Qatari Diar's director of international projects 1.8 per cent of a rail contract through his own company, and the state firm awarded PBS&J the work.
cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission, order 34-74112, 22 January 2015

n: Zimmer Biomet's Mexican unit paid customs officials to clear implants
rank: Mexican customs officials
d: Biomet 3i Mexico, a subsidiary of the US orthopaedic and dental implant maker Zimmer Biomet, paid bribes to Mexican customs officials through customs brokers and sub-agents so that it could import dental implants that lacked proper registration or labelling. Biomet had signed a deferred prosecution agreement with the US Justice Department in 2012 over bribery in Argentina, Brazil and China. The department said the company breached that agreement by continuing to use a Brazilian distributor known to have paid officials and by failing to fix its compliance programme. In January 2017 Zimmer Biomet entered a new three-year deferred prosecution agreement, paid a $17.4 million criminal penalty and accepted an independent compliance monitor for three years. Its subsidiary JERDS Luxembourg Holding pleaded guilty, and the SEC took $13 million more.
inside: Zimmer Biomet's Mexican subsidiary paid customs officials through brokers, so Mexico's customs service admitted dental implants that lacked proper registration or labelling.
cite: US Department of Justice, press release, 12 January 2017

n: HMT's sales agent paid officials to win PDVSA purchases
rank: Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) purchasing
d: HMT LLC, a US maker of storage tank equipment, disclosed to the US Justice Department that a sales agent it had retained to promote and sell its products in Venezuela had paid bribes to Venezuelan government officials in order to win purchases by Petroleos de Venezuela, S.A. (PDVSA), the state-owned and state-controlled energy company. The department's letter puts the bribes at about $500,000 across Venezuela and China, the Chinese payments being in exchange for purchases by Chinese state-owned enterprises that the letter does not name. In September 2016 the department closed its investigation under its Foreign Corrupt Practices Act pilot programme and required HMT to disgorge $2,719,412. No individual official is named, and the money passed through the agent rather than being shown to reach a named recipient.
inside: HMT's sales agent paid Venezuelan officials, the company told US prosecutors, so that the state oil company PDVSA would buy its storage tank equipment.
cite: US Department of Justice, Fraud Section letter to HMT LLC, 29 September 2016

n: Antwerp MPET terminal drivers moved a cocaine container for traffickers
rank: straddle carrier drivers, MSC PSA European Terminal (MPET)
d: Three men who drove container handlers and straddle carriers at the MPET terminal in Antwerp were convicted of cocaine trafficking by the Antwerp correctional court. On 4 December 2018 customs found a container of banana puree from Costa Rica that had been unloaded on 22 November and then disappeared; its seal stamps had been tampered with. The prosecution said the drugs were moved from the South American container into a European one to cut the risk of inspection. MPET's own system showed the men had not been ordered to move the container, and terminal camera footage implicated all three. They were sentenced to four, four and a half and six years, with fines, and EUR 957,000 in assets was seized.
inside: Men driving straddle carriers at Antwerp's MPET terminal worked for a cocaine network, so the terminal's own machines moved and emptied a container nobody had ordered moved.
cite: The Brussels Times with Belga, 21 October 2022

n: Traffickers pressured an Antwerp dock worker to switch a cocaine load
rank: dock worker, Antwerp quay 1742
d: Dutch customs in Rotterdam found about 1,160 kg of cocaine in sports bags in a container from Panama, took it out, replaced it with fake drugs and let the container travel on to Antwerp, where it was unloaded at quay 1742. On 27 September 2022 the dock worker Joao B.P. moved the container with a straddle carrier, ringed it with other containers and handled the transfer of the bags into another box. He admitted the drug trade had approached him, that he first refused, and that he gave in after threats to his family. On 1 June 2023 Antwerp prosecutors asked for five years, a EUR 24,000 fine and a ten-year port ban; the report does not give the verdict, due on 16 June 2023.
inside: Traffickers pressed an Antwerp dock worker, with threats to his family, into moving their container with his straddle carrier and screening the transfer of the drug bags.
cite: Flows (Belgian shipping trade press), 2 June 2023

n: Antwerp warehouse manager let cocaine extractors onto the AET quay
rank: warehouse manager, ACR Warehouse, Antwerp Euroterminal
d: The Antwerp correctional court convicted six men on 3 October 2026 over three attempts to import cocaine through the Antwerp Euroterminal in the Waaslandhaven. The insider was a 60-year-old manager at ACR Warehouse, a firm that takes in deliveries for ships in the port: he let the men who pull drugs out of containers onto the quay by having them pose as suppliers to his warehouse. A planner was to find the container holding 381 kg. In February 2025 police found 40 kg in an opened rice container, with a ladder left behind; in November 2025 three men were arrested, two hidden in wooden crates in a van. The organiser got nine years, the warehouse manager seven, and over EUR 1.4 million was forfeited.
inside: A cocaine ring used ACR Warehouse's manager inside Antwerp Euroterminal to bring its container extractors onto the quay as bogus suppliers, past the terminal's access controls.
cite: VRT NWS, 3 October 2026 (Antwerp correctional court)

n: Antwerp port company clerk fed a trafficker container codes and times
rank: clerk at a company in Antwerp port
d: An Antwerp criminal court sentenced a 30-year-old woman to six years for helping a cocaine trafficker. She was a clerk at a company based in the port, not named in the court reporting, and gave him container serial numbers, access codes, seal numbers, arrival times and cargo destinations. She also advised which containers would best hide a drug load. The offences ran from June 2020 to February 2021 and came to light through the investigation into criminals using the Sky ECC encrypted phone service. The trafficker, aged 27, got nine years and a EUR 40,000 fine, with EUR 1,150,000 confiscated from him and EUR 150,000 from her. Police seized 3,109 kg of cocaine from five containers in Rotterdam, London, Kapellen, Beveren and the Dominican Republic.
inside: A trafficker had a clerk inside an Antwerp port firm, so the company's own container records, codes and timings were used to choose and move his drug loads.
cite: VRT NWS, 23 December 2022 (Antwerp criminal court)

n: Antwerp port security officer turned cameras away for a container swap
rank: security officer at the Port of Antwerp
d: A 30-year-old security officer at the Port of Antwerp was sentenced on appeal to four years and a EUR 16,000 fine for his part in importing 455 kg of cocaine. He had turned the port's security cameras away so that a container swap would not be filmed. The cocaine was found on 22 June 2020 in the floor of a container from Ecuador; the swap had been done on the night of 19 to 20 June 2020 by a straddle carrier driver, who also changed the container-number stickers so the box would not be scanned. The driver and an accomplice were convicted in July 2021. The court first acquitted the security officer and prosecutors appealed; Sky ECC evidence showed he had been asked to take part and had agreed.
inside: A cocaine ring recruited the man guarding the port's cameras, so the system meant to watch the quay was pointed away while a drug container was swapped.
cite: The Brussels Times, 23 February 2023 (Antwerp Court of Appeal)

n: Ex-customs employee searched Dutch systems for cocaine importers
rank: customs employee, Dutch Douane
d: A 29-year-old man from Rotterdam, a former employee of the Dutch customs service, is accused of searching customs systems at others' request to find whether particular containers had been intercepted and what had happened to them, and of explaining how special customs units work. Prosecutors say most shipments he gave information about had already been seized, more than 4,000 kg of narcotics in all; for one container not yet inspected, holding 491 kg of cocaine worth about EUR 37 million, he can be prosecuted for the import itself. The case grew out of a large investigation into criminals' encrypted phones, which indicated a customs officer was being paid to query the systems. Seven years was demanded on 19 January 2022; the release does not give the verdict.
inside: Prosecutors say cocaine importers paid a former customs employee to query the service's own systems, so they learned which of their containers had already been intercepted.
cite: Openbaar Ministerie (Dutch Public Prosecution Service), 19 January 2022

n: Rotterdam customs officer's container data allegedly reached a smuggler
rank: customs officer with system access, port of Rotterdam
d: Dutch prosecutors accuse a 57-year-old customs officer from Capelle aan den IJssel of passing information about containers to an alleged drug smuggler. Over about a year, they say, a 49-year-old man from Rotterdam, described as the leader of the operation, repeatedly approached her 28-year-old son for information from the customs systems about shipments believed to hold drugs. The son asked his mother for it and also searched her laptop himself, passed it on and was paid, arranging for part of the money to reach her. The prosecution calls this passive bribery of a public official. The shipments were destined for the port of Rotterdam. On 14 May 2024 prosecutors demanded eight years for the officer, seven for her son and twelve for the 49-year-old.
inside: Prosecutors say a smuggling group paid a customs officer's son for her access, so Dutch customs' own records on suspect containers reached the people shipping them.
cite: Openbaar Ministerie (Dutch Public Prosecution Service), 14 May 2024

n: Rotterdam customs officer accused of selling importers information
rank: customs officer, port of Rotterdam
d: A 46-year-old customs officer in the port of Rotterdam is accused of passing confidential information to criminals so cocaine could be brought in through the port. Prosecutors say she set conditions on payment and on the quality of what she supplied, advised on risks and on the signals that appear in customs systems, and met the criminals in person, asking EUR 25,000 for each request. Her older sister is said to have kept the money and to have been the link to two other suspected cocaine traders; a large sum of cash was found at the officer's home. The investigation began in July 2022 on a tip to the criminal intelligence team. On 17 July 2025 prosecutors demanded six years for her and shorter terms for three co-defendants.
inside: Prosecutors say cocaine traders paid a serving Rotterdam customs officer EUR 25,000 a request for customs information on their containers and on the signals the systems show.
cite: Openbaar Ministerie (Dutch Public Prosecution Service), 17 July 2025

n: Rotterdam port worker rented out his ECT terminal pass to drug crews
rank: port worker with access to the ECT container terminal
d: The Rotterdam district court convicted a port worker with access to the ECT container terminal of preparing cocaine imports, and sentenced him to 22 months. He lent his access pass several times, for payment, to men who used it to get onto the terminal and take cocaine out of containers, arranged passes from other port workers, and told one of them where particular containers stood. He was given EUR 500 up front. His pass was blocked on 12 March 2013; days later customs were told three men had climbed a fence to get off the site, and the court found he had dropped them there. He said he believed he was helping a theft of electronics, but the court held he had accepted the chance it was cocaine.
inside: Cocaine crews paid a Rotterdam port worker to lend them his ECT terminal pass, so the company's own access control let them onto the quay to empty containers.
cite: Rechtbank Rotterdam, 31 March 2016, ECLI:NL:RBROT:2016:2415, via BijzonderStrafrecht.nl

n: ECT employee made false terminal passes and switched off its checks
org_label: A convicted drug importer who bought the passes
rank: employee of ECT, Rotterdam cargo-handling company
d: A 34-year-old woman from Rotterdam who had worked for thirteen years at ECT, a cargo-handling company in the port, made two false access passes that let people onto the terminal. She also disabled the company's control systems: the check matching a pass to a valid personnel number, and the one stopping two passes in the same name being on the site at once. A 32-year-old man paid her EUR 10,000 for the passes and says he resold them for EUR 12,000; he had an earlier conviction for importing hard drugs. An intruder caught on the site in summer 2018 led investigators to her; she was dismissed and arrested in December 2018. Prosecutors could not establish she knew the passes were for drug smuggling, and demanded 18 months, six suspended.
inside: Prosecutors say a drug importer paid a long-serving ECT employee EUR 10,000 for false passes, and she disabled the checks that would have caught them, opening the terminal.
cite: Openbaar Ministerie (Dutch Public Prosecution Service), 11 July 2019

n: Vlissingen bulk terminal's directors charged over cocaine landings
org_label: Cocaine importers using the port of Vlissingen
rank: three former directors of Bulk Terminal Zeeland
d: Dutch prosecutors accuse three former directors of Bulk Terminal Zeeland, a transshipment company founded in 2015 in the port of Vlissingen, of large-scale cocaine trafficking, forgery, money laundering and taking part in a criminal organisation. They say the company's facilities were offered, recommended and actually used to bring cocaine ashore, that the two younger directors were in contact with known drug criminals, and that the 61-year-old majority shareholder handled the laundering with a Lithuanian who moved large amounts of cash. Six completed or attempted imports are cited, of 100 to 2,188 kg each, hidden in cover cargo such as soy, aluminium or coal, from 2017. The investigation, Acropolis, began in April 2022. In June 2026 prosecutors demanded twelve years for each director. No verdict has been reported.
inside: Prosecutors say cocaine importers were in contact with Bulk Terminal Zeeland's three directors, who offered and used the Vlissingen firm's own quay to land six drug loads.
cite: Openbaar Ministerie closing demand, June 2026, via BijzonderStrafrecht.nl

n: Valencia cocaine network rigged the port's docker hiring and shifts
rank: Centro Portuario de Empleo, the port's stevedore hiring body
d: Spanish police say a cocaine network at the port of Valencia corrupted the hiring of dockers at the Centro Portuario de Empleo, the body that recruits stevedores for the port, rigging the entrance exams and falsifying applicants' drug tests so that its own people got the jobs. Once inside, members controlled work shifts so that contaminated containers were put in chosen places and police movements could be watched; some faked leave-of-absence papers so they could return to stevedoring after prison. Operation Spider, run by Investigating Court No. 15 in Valencia and announced on 26 September 2025, lasted eighteen months and ended in 81 arrests, among them union leaders, seventeen port workers, seventeen managers from five companies and a Guardia Civil officer. Police seized 4.5 tonnes of cocaine.
inside: Police say a cocaine network rigged the exams and drug tests at Valencia's stevedore hiring body, so its own members got dock jobs and chose the shifts.
cite: eldiario.es, 23 and 26 September 2025 (Policia Nacional; Juzgado de Instruccion 15 de Valencia)

n: Barcelona crane driver pulled cocaine from a container for a network
org_label: Cocaine network using the port of Barcelona
rank: stevedore operating the container crane, port of Barcelona
d: Spain's customs surveillance service says a network used the rip-off method at the port of Barcelona: cocaine is hidden in a container of legitimate cargo without the knowledge of the shipper or the consignee, and taken out at a later port. In late June 2025 a ship from Chile that had called in Ecuador docked at Fos-sur-Mer near Marseille, where French customs found 138.5 kg of cocaine in one container bound for Barcelona. It arrived there on 14 July under controlled delivery, and on 17 July investigators watched men open it and move the bags into a second container. A stevedore who worked the crane that moved and handled the containers was arrested on 26 July and a lorry driver on 24 July; four people were remanded in operation Leurre.
inside: Customs investigators say a cocaine network used the stevedore working the crane at Barcelona, so the port's own machinery moved the container its men opened and emptied.
cite: Agencia Tributaria (Spanish Tax Agency, Vigilancia Aduanera), 30 July 2025

n: 'Ndrangheta had the container scanner operator at Gioia Tauro
rank: Customs Agency scanner operator, Gioia Tauro
d: On 6 October 2022 the Guardia di Finanza, acting for the Reggio Calabria anti-mafia prosecutors, arrested 36 of 37 suspects over cocaine imports through Gioia Tauro, Italy's largest container port. Among them was Pasquale Sergio, an employee of the Customs Agency working as the scanner operator, accused of altering the X-ray results for a container that reached Gioia Tauro from Santos in Brazil on 18 December 2020 carrying 300 kg, for about three per cent of the value, roughly EUR 261,000. Fourteen dock workers were also arrested; prosecutors say they had drug containers moved to a quiet part of the terminal, transferred the cocaine into a second container, and used cloned seals. Four tonnes were seized.
inside: Prosecutors say 'Ndrangheta clans paid the customs scanner operator at Gioia Tauro about EUR 261,000 to alter the X-ray result for a container holding 300 kilos of cocaine.
cite: Il Fatto Quotidiano, 6 October 2022 (Guardia di Finanza; DDA Reggio Calabria)

n: Two Gioia Tauro customs officials arrested over 'Ndrangheta cocaine
rank: officials of the Customs and Monopolies Agency, Gioia Tauro
d: On 20 February 2024 the Guardia di Finanza arrested two officials of Italy's Customs and Monopolies Agency posted at Gioia Tauro, along with an employee of a shipping company; seven people are under investigation. Prosecutors at the Reggio Calabria anti-mafia directorate say the officials worked at the key inspection points, the scanner and the visual checks where containers are opened, and either altered the results or left irregularities unflagged so that large amounts of cocaine left the port. They are also said to have told South American traffickers how to pack cocaine in cover cargo, supplied seizure reports so the group could account for lost loads, and warned associates of coming operations. Five imports between June 2020 and October 2022 totalling more than three tonnes were identified.
inside: Prosecutors say 'Ndrangheta-linked traffickers had two customs officials at Gioia Tauro's scanner and inspection points, who passed the checks, supplied seizure reports and warned of coming operations.
cite: ShippingItaly and Unione Sarda, 20-21 February 2024 (Guardia di Finanza; DDA Reggio Calabria)

n: Five port workers charged with loading cocaine in a Guayaquil terminal
rank: forklift and tractor-trailer operators at a Guayaquil port company
d: On 25 October 2026 camera footage at a port in southern Guayaquil showed five workers leaving a restricted area without authorisation and, between roughly noon and half past, coordinating a crane, a flatbed trailer and a tractor-trailer, with vehicles placed so that they blocked the cameras' view while a container was loaded. Police dogs alerted on the container and officers found 889 kg of cocaine built into its structure; the box had been sealed with 24 pallets of canned tuna declared for France. Prosecutors charged two forklift operators, a boarding assistant, the man said to have recruited the others, and the tractor-trailer driver, who said he was to be paid USD 10,000. A judge ordered them detained and set a 30-day investigation.
inside: Prosecutors say cocaine exporters paid five workers at a Guayaquil port company, who used its crane and trailers and blocked its cameras while a container was loaded.
cite: Primicias (Ecuador), November 2026 (Policia Antinarcoticos; Fiscalia)

n: Suppliers paid Krakatau Steel's production director for equipment orders
org_label: PT Grand Kartech and PT Tjokro Bersaudara
rank: Director of Production and Technology, PT Krakatau Steel
d: Two equipment suppliers paid the production and technology director of PT Krakatau Steel, Indonesia's state-owned steelmaker, to approve their orders. The KPK, Indonesia's anti-corruption commission, arrested Wisnu Kuncoro in March 2019 after a handover of Rp20 million at a Jakarta shopping mall. Prosecutors said Kenneth Sutardja of PT Grand Kartech paid for approval of two 35-tonne boilers budgeted at about Rp24 billion, and Kurniawan Eddy Kuncoro of PT Tjokro Bersaudara paid over stacker and stockyard work worth about Rp13 billion, with a broker, Karunia Alexander Muskita, carrying the money. The payments set out in the indictment came to about Rp101.8 million and US$4,000. Sutardja was sentenced to 21 months and Kurniawan to 15 months; prosecutors asked for two years for Wisnu Kuncoro.
inside: Two equipment suppliers paid the production director of Indonesia's state steelmaker, so Krakatau Steel's approval of their boiler and stockyard orders served the firms selling them.
cite: CNN Indonesia, 14 August 2019; Antara (Bengkulu), 16 October 2019

n: Contractor paid PLN managers to inflate a Bukit Asam power plant job
rank: managers, PLN South Sumatra generation unit (UIK SBS)
d: Nehemia Indrajaya, director of the private contractor PT Truba Engineering Indonesia, worked with managers of PT PLN's South Sumatra generation unit to win and inflate a 2018 contract to retrofit the sootblowing system at the Bukit Asam coal-fired power station. PLN is Indonesia's state electricity company. The KPK said an engineering manager, Budi Widi Asmoro, picked Nehemia's firm before the tender, told the procurement planners to set the official estimate at the bid price without checking the market, and took Rp750 million; both bidders were companies Nehemia owned. The budget request rose from about Rp52 billion to Rp75 billion. The Palembang corruption court convicted Nehemia on 14 April 2025 and gave him six years, a Rp300 million fine and Rp17.5 billion in restitution.
inside: A contractor paid managers inside the state electricity company, so its tender and its price estimate were arranged to suit the contractor's own bid.
cite: CNBC Indonesia, 9 July 2024; Palembang District Court decision 70/Pid.Sus-TPK/2024/PN Plg, 14 April 2025

n: Fund manager got state pension firm Taspen to put Rp1tn in its fund
rank: President Director, PT Taspen
d: PT Taspen is the state-owned company that holds and invests the pensions of Indonesian civil servants. The Jakarta corruption court found that its president director, Antonius Kosasih, and Ekiawan Heri Primaryanto, president director of the private fund manager PT Insight Investment Management, acted together over Taspen's investments: Insight was appointed directly, with no tender, to run the I-Next G2 mutual fund, and Taspen put Rp1 trillion into that high-risk fund without adequate prior study. The court put the loss to the state at Rp1 trillion. On 6 October 2025 Kosasih was sentenced to ten years and Ekiawan to nine, each with a Rp500 million fine, and Kosasih was ordered to repay Rp29.2 billion along with sums in US and Singapore dollars.
inside: A private fund manager was appointed without any tender by the state pension company's own president director, so Taspen put a trillion rupiah into the manager's high-risk fund.
cite: Jawa Pos, 6 October 2025

n: Riza Chalid's terminal firm got inside Pertamina's fuel trading units
org_label: PT Orbit Terminal Merak and the Riza Chalid family's oil business
rank: directors, Pertamina Patra Niaga and Pertamina International Shipping
d: Muhammad Kerry Adrianto Riza, owner of the fuel terminal company PT Orbit Terminal Merak and son of the oil trader Mohammad Riza Chalid, was convicted alongside officials of Pertamina, Indonesia's state oil company. Prosecutors said he used his father's influence to win a Pertamina lease of his terminal that was not needed and did not meet standards, and had Pertamina's shipping arm charter three vessels from a company with no oil and gas transport licence. The Jakarta corruption court jailed him for 15 years on 26 February 2026 and ordered Rp2.9 trillion repaid; the Supreme Court rejected his appeal on 14 October 2026. Two private shipping brokers got 13 years each and three former Pertamina Patra Niaga directors six to nine. Riza Chalid has fled, under an Interpol red notice.
inside: An oil trader's family firm worked through Pertamina's own directors, so the state oil company's leasing and chartering decisions went to businesses the family controlled.
cite: Jakarta Globe, 12 May 2026; InvestorTrust, 26 February 2026; The Star, 16 February 2026; Okezone/RCTI+, 31 October 2026; Akurat, verdicts read 26-27 February 2026 (Tipikor Jakarta: the restitution order and the shipping brokers’ terms)

n: Contractors paid a Petronas Carigali executive for maintenance work
org_label: Faltech Engineering and other Petronas Carigali contractors
rank: construction executive, Petronas Carigali Sdn Bhd
d: Mohd Amal M. Razalan, a construction executive at Petronas Carigali Sdn Bhd, the exploration arm of Malaysia's state oil company, was charged by the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission in January 2023 with 41 corruption counts and five money-laundering counts covering RM9.65 million. Prosecutors said he took about RM9.4 million from four people, among them the director of Faltech Engineering Sdn Bhd, for certifying more than fifty job completion tickets for Petronas Carigali and for helping Faltech obtain the contract for civil and structural maintenance services. In November 2023 he pleaded guilty to one count of taking RM35,217.50 for helping a company secure structural maintenance work; the Shah Alam sessions court jailed him for a day and fined him RM177,000, and the remaining 44 charges were taken into consideration.
inside: Maintenance contractors paid an executive inside Petronas Carigali, the state oil company's exploration arm, and he admitted taking money to help a firm win structural maintenance work.
cite: Sinar Harian, 11 January 2023; Malay Mail, 8 November 2023

n: Suppliers delivered first and won Hanoi Heart Hospital's tenders after
org_label: Hoang Nga and Kim Hoa Phat medical supply companies
who: Hoang Nga and Kim Hoa Phat
rank: Director, Hanoi Heart Hospital
d: Nguyen Quang Tuan, director of Hanoi Heart Hospital, a public hospital, let two medical supply companies, Hoang Nga and Kim Hoa Phat, deliver cardiac intervention consumables before any tender was held, and then had the bidding paperwork put in order so that they won the contracts. The court found the inflated prices cost more than 53 billion dong. On 21 April 2023 a Hanoi court sentenced him to three years for breaking tender rules and did not bar him from practising medicine; he returned US$10,000 and paid about 6 billion dong. The director of Hoang Nga was given a suspended term of two and a half years and the chairman of Kim Hoa Phat a suspended two years. Twelve other people were sentenced in the same case.
inside: Two suppliers worked through the public hospital's own director, so its tenders were written up afterwards to confirm the suppliers that had already delivered.
cite: Tuoi Tre, 21 April 2023

n: AIC and Song Hong paid Bac Ninh's leaders for hospital equipment tenders
org_label: AIC Group and Song Hong Corporation
who: AIC Group and Song Hong Corporation
rank: provincial party secretary and chairman, Bac Ninh province
d: AIC Group, run by Nguyen Thi Thanh Nhan, and Song Hong Corporation paid the leaders of Bac Ninh province in northern Vietnam to win medical equipment tenders for six district hospitals. The Bac Ninh provincial court found on 1 November 2024 that Nhan paid 3 billion dong to the provincial party secretary, Nguyen Nhan Chien, and 1 billion dong to the provincial chairman, Nguyen Tu Quynh, and gave them holiday money of about 10 billion and 8.1 billion dong over several years. Song Hong's general director, La Tuan Hung, paid each of them 1 billion dong. AIC won three of the tenders, and losses were put at about 48.6 billion dong. Nhan, who has fled abroad, was given 13 years, Chien four and a half years and Hung two.
inside: AIC and Song Hong paid Bac Ninh province's party secretary and its chairman, so medical equipment tenders for six district hospitals went their way, AIC winning three.
cite: Tap chi Toa an Nhan dan, 1 November 2024

n: Contractors' money reached Vietnam's health ministry over hospital builds
org_label: Sao Nam Song Hong and other hospital contractors
who: Sao Nam Song Hong and other contractors
rank: Minister of Health and ministry project officials
d: Vietnam approved second campuses for Bach Mai Hospital and Viet Duc Friendship Hospital in 2014 for nearly 10,000 billion dong; both stood unfinished for years. On 27 May 2026 a Hanoi court convicted ten people over the projects. Nguyen Thi Kim Tien, health minister when they were approved, was given six years for mismanaging state assets and ordered to pay 108 billion dong; the court said she received 7.5 billion dong from subordinates. Nguyen Chien Thang, said by the court to have taken nearly 88.5 billion dong, received 30 years, and Nguyen Huu Tuan, said to have taken over 12 billion, 25 years. Le Thanh Thiem, director of the contractor Sao Nam Song Hong, got ten years for fraud. About 100 billion dong in contractors' bribes was ordered returned.
inside: Contractors' bribes reached officials running the health ministry's hospital building programme, so decisions on the Bach Mai and Viet Duc second campuses served the paying firms.
cite: Bao Dau Tu, 27 May 2026

n: Xuyen Viet Oil paid ministry and tax officials to keep its fuel licence
rank: Deputy Minister of Industry and Trade and department heads
d: Xuyen Viet Oil, a Vietnamese fuel importer, was not eligible to renew its petroleum import and export licence when it expired in June 2021, so its chair, Mai Thi Hong Hanh, paid officials to obtain it. A Ho Chi Minh City court found on 29 November 2024 that she paid bribes 22 times from 2016 to 2022, totalling over 31.5 billion dong, to eight former officials of the ministries of industry and trade and of finance and related bodies. She also kept petroleum price stabilisation fund money in her own account. Hanh was given 30 years, the former deputy industry and trade minister Do Thang Hai three years, and Le Duc Tho, former Ben Tre party secretary, 28 years. On appeal in May 2025 Hanh's total fell to 28 years.
inside: A fuel importer paid officials of the industry and trade and finance ministries, so the import licence it was no longer eligible for was renewed in its favour.
cite: LSVN, 29 November 2024; Sai Gon Giai Phong, 12 May 2025

n: Contractor and public works officials convicted over Cebu lamppost deal
rank: regional director and bids and awards committee, DPWH Region 7
d: Gerardo Surla, chairman of GAMPIK Construction and Development Inc, was convicted along with three officials of the Philippine Department of Public Works and Highways in Region 7 over a lamppost contract worth 35.634 million pesos, bid on 28 November 2006. The Sandiganbayan, the court that tries cases against public officials, convicted the regional director, Robert Lala, and two members of the bids and awards committee, Pureza Fernandez and Agustinito Hermoso, together with Surla, and put the overpricing at 12.63 million pesos. Each was sentenced to six years' imprisonment. The conviction was handed down on 29 September 2020 and the court has since affirmed it.
inside: A contractor acted together with the public works regional director and the committee judging the bids, so the award and the price paid served the contractor.
cite: Malaya Business Insight, September 2025

n: FIA: bankers opened 29 forged accounts that moved billions for Omni Group
org_label: Omni Group, Bahria Town Karachi and the Zardari group
rank: president and senior executives of Summit Bank, with Sindh Bank and United Bank accounts
d: Pakistan's Federal Investigation Agency accused senior bankers of opening 29 fake accounts at Summit Bank, Sindh Bank and United Bank for outside business groups. Its first information report alleges they "opened fake/forged accounts by fraudulently fulfilling the codal formalities", including by obtaining signatures, and that 4.5 billion rupees passed through the accounts in ten months. Fifteen parties, among them Bahria Town Karachi and Omni Pvt Ltd, are said to have deposited 2.855 billion rupees. Hussain Lawai, Summit Bank's president from 2008 to 2016, was detained on 6 July 2018 with the banker Taha Raza; he denies wrongdoing. In January 2025 a banking court in Karachi cleared 14 other accused for lack of evidence, while Lawai remained named in the FIA's final report; two accused died during the proceedings.
cite: Dawn, 7 July 2018; Dawn, 26 January 2025
inside: Investigators allege business groups including Omni and Bahria Town had Summit Bank officers open 29 forged accounts, so billions of rupees moved without the bank's identity checks.

n: Family Bank's anti-laundering officer convicted over stolen NYS millions
org_label: Josephine Kabura and the National Youth Service theft network
who: the National Youth Service theft network
rank: anti-money-laundering compliance manager, Family Bank
d: Charles Kamau Thiongo, the officer responsible for anti-money-laundering checks at Kenya's Family Bank, was convicted of helping Josephine Kabura launder 791 million shillings taken from the National Youth Service, a state youth training scheme, through three accounts at the bank. The court convicted him on three counts of aiding the laundering and failing to report suspicious transactions, and fined him 750,000 shillings or three years in jail in default. On 19 December 2022 Chief Magistrate Francis Andayi, at Milimani in Nairobi, acquitted the bank's former chief executive Peter Munyiri and two co-accused, finding the laundering unproved and the chief executive not the person obliged to report. The bank had been discharged in May 2019 after pleading guilty to six reporting failures and paying a 64.5 million shilling fine.
cite: People Daily (Kenya), report of the Milimani court judgment of 19 December 2022
inside: A network that stole from Kenya's National Youth Service was helped by Family Bank's own anti-laundering officer, so 791 million shillings moved through the bank unreported.

n: TD Bank's Florida banker issued 150 debit cards for a Colombia drug ring
org_label: narcotics money-laundering co-conspirators moving funds to Colombia
rank: retail banker, TD Bank, N.A.
d: Leonardo Ayala, 26, of Homestead, Florida, a retail banker at TD Bank, used his position between June and November 2023 to launder drug money to Colombia. He opened fraudulent accounts, issued more than 150 debit cards to shell companies and unblocked cards the bank had restricted for suspicious activity, taking more than $6,000 in bribes from co-conspirators. The cards were used for more than 12,000 cash machine withdrawals in Colombia, taking about $5.5 million out of the United States. He pleaded guilty to conspiracy to launder monetary instruments and to accepting bribes as a bank employee, and was sentenced to two years in prison and three years of supervised release. Federal prosecutors in New Jersey brought the case.
cite: Washington Times, 11 June 2026, reporting the US Attorney's Office for the District of New Jersey
inside: A drug money network paid a TD Bank employee to open false accounts and switch its blocked cards back on, so the bank's own controls were overridden.

n: KPK: Jepara bank's directors lent against 40 fictitious borrowers
rank: president director, business director and credit officers, BPR Jepara Artha
d: Indonesia's Corruption Eradication Commission named five suspects on 18 September 2025 over business lending at BPR Jepara Artha, a bank owned by the Jepara district government. Four are the bank's own officers, among them president director Jhendik Handoko and credit section head Ariyanto Sulistiyono. The fifth is an outside party, Mohammad Ibrahim Al'asyari, director of the company PT Bumi Manfaat Gemilang. The commission alleges that between 2022 and 2024 collateral was used for 40 fictitious borrowers, and puts the loss to the state at a minimum of 254 billion rupiah. Investigators seized 136 land and building plots worth about 60 billion rupiah, 11.5 billion rupiah in cash from Al'asyari and 1.3 billion rupiah from Handoko. All five were detained and the case is still being investigated.
cite: CNN Indonesia, 18 September 2025
inside: Investigators allege the director of an outside company worked with the Jepara district bank's own directors, so loans were booked against collateral for 40 borrowers who did not exist.

n: Bank of Baroda's South African branch head backed the Guptas' coal deal
rank: branch head and managers, Bank of Baroda South Africa
d: Bank of Baroda, an Indian state bank, was the last bank holding the accounts of the Gupta family's South African companies. Its South African branch head, Sanjiv Gupta, who is not known to be related to the family, issued a bank letter of assurance on 18 December 2015 promising full payment of the 2.1 billion rand, about $160 million, that the Guptas paid for the Optimum coal mine. India's Central Vigilance Commission is examining whether he had the authority to give it, and the bank has asked it to open penalty proceedings that could end in his dismissal. Reporting on the bank's records also found managers nullified suspicious activity alerts on a Gupta account, including eight filed on 13 and 14 April 2016. No criminal charges have been reported.
cite: OCCRP, GuptaLeaks investigation, 'India's Bank of Baroda Played a Key Role in South Africa's Gupta Scandal'
inside: The Gupta network's last remaining bank backed its coal mine purchase through its South African branch head, and managers there cancelled the suspicious-activity alerts on its account.

n: Catler-Uniservice's bribes reached YPFB's president over a gas plant
rank: President of YPFB, the state oil and gas company
d: YPFB, Bolivia's state oil and gas company, awarded the Catler-Uniservice consortium a contract worth 86 million US dollars to build a gas processing plant at Rio Grande, in Santa Cruz. Prosecutors said the consortium paid YPFB's president, Santos Ramirez, a close ally of President Evo Morales, to obtain and keep the work. The scheme surfaced in January 2009 when Uniservice's manager, Jorge O'Connor, was killed in a robbery in which 435,000 US dollars was taken, money said to have formed part of the payment. YPFB had already paid the consortium 16.5 million US dollars, of which only 9.4 million was recovered in machinery and equipment. In January 2012 a La Paz court jailed Ramirez for 12 years and convicted Catler's director, Agustin Melano, in absentia.
inside: The Catler-Uniservice consortium's payments reached the president of Bolivia's state oil company, which awarded it the 86 million dollar gas plant contract and paid out millions.
cite: eju.tv / ANF and ABI, 26-27 January 2012

n: AHMSA paid Lozoya before Pemex bought its idle fertiliser plant
rank: Director general of Pemex, the state oil company
d: Altos Hornos de Mexico (AHMSA), a steel group, sold its disused Agronitrogenados fertiliser plant to Pemex, the state oil company, in a deal agreed in 2013 with Pemex's then director, Emilio Lozoya. Mexico's federal prosecutor, the FGR, alleges AHMSA's owner Alonso Ancira made four transfers totalling about 3.5 million US dollars in 2012 to a company of Lozoya's sister, paying him in advance because he was expected to get the Pemex post. Specialists later called the plant scrap. Ancira was arrested in Spain in 2019, extradited to Mexico in February 2021 and released that April after agreeing to repay Pemex about 216.66 million US dollars in instalments; the FGR asked for his money-laundering trial to be suspended, not dropped. Proceedings against Lozoya and his sister were still running in 2026.
inside: AHMSA's money allegedly reached Emilio Lozoya before he took charge of Pemex, Mexico's state oil company, which then bought the steel group's disused fertiliser plant.
cite: La Razon, 20 April 2021; Excelsior/FGR filings, 2026

n: Firms paid for releases from the workers' fund Caixa managed
rank: Vice-president for government funds, Caixa Economica Federal
d: The FI-FGTS is a fund of about 32 billion reais built from Brazilian workers' housing-fund savings, managed by Caixa Economica Federal, the federal savings bank. Fabio Cleto, Caixa's vice-president for government funds and lotteries from 2011 to 2015, said in a plea deal he received weekly instructions from Eduardo Cunha, then speaker of the lower house, on how to vote in the fund's investment committee, and that companies paid for money to be released. Plea deals cross-checked against the fund's investments indicated bribes in 47.7 per cent of sums released to firms; Odebrecht, Eike Batista's LLX, Brado Logistica, Eldorado and Construtora Carioca are among those named. Cunha, the former minister Henrique Alves, Cleto and others were charged in October 2016. Cunha denied the accusations and challenged Cleto to prove them.
inside: Companies' payments allegedly reached the Caixa executive who voted on releases from the workers' housing fund, so the fund's money went to the firms that paid.
cite: Metropoles, August 2017; Congresso em Foco, 26 October 2016

n: Camargo Correa's ex-controller charged with paying Petros for a share deal
rank: Executives of Petros, Petrobras's pension fund
d: Petros is the pension fund of Petrobras, Brazil's state oil company, and holds the retirement savings of its workers. Federal prosecutors' Greenfield task force, set up to examine losses at state-company pension funds, charged Luiz Roberto Ortiz Nascimento, a businessman and son-in-law of Camargo Correa's founder who had controlled the construction group, with paying bribes to Petros executives between 2009 and 2014 so that the fund would buy shares in the bank Itau that Camargo Correa held. A federal court in Brasilia accepted the charge and made him a defendant. The report does not name the Petros executives said to have been paid, and does not give the sums paid or the value of the share purchase.
inside: Camargo Correa's former controller allegedly paid executives of Petros, Petrobras's pension fund, so that it would buy the Itau bank shares his group held.
cite: O Antagonista, on the Greenfield charge accepted by the Federal Court in Brasilia

n: Zelotes: Gerdau accused of steering its appeals inside the CARF tax tribunal
rank: Councillors of CARF, the finance ministry's tax appeals tribunal
d: CARF, the Conselho Administrativo de Recursos Fiscais, is the tribunal in Brazil's finance ministry hearing companies' appeals against tax assessments.
