In Operacao Zelotes, federal prosecutors charged fourteen people over CARF cases, among them Gerdau's former legal director Expedito Luz and two consultants to the steel group, Marco Biondo and Raul Schineider. Prosecutors allege that between 2011 and 2014 simulated consultancy contracts channelled money, that the handling and allotment of cases was manipulated, and that Gerdau's cases were steered to the first chamber of CARF's higher section to fall to councillor Jose Ricardo da Silva, named as the leader of a criminal organisation inside the tribunal. A Brasilia judge accepted the charges in October 2017. Gerdau denies offering or giving any improper advantage and says nothing was paid to the consultancies.
inside: Gerdau's money allegedly reached councillors of the finance ministry's tax appeals tribunal, where the steel group's own appeals were routed to the councillor prosecutors call the ringleader.
cite: IstoE Dinheiro, 31 October 2017 (MPF charges accepted)

n: Skanska's returns on gas pipeline contracts went to Enargas and a state trust
rank: Federal planning minister and public works secretary; Enargas and Nacion Fideicomisos
d: Skanska, a Swedish construction group, won contracts worth about 100 million US dollars to expand Argentina's Norte and Sur gas pipelines after the 2001 energy crisis. Recordings seized in a 2007 raid on its Buenos Aires offices caught a Skanska manager, Javier Azcarate, describing returns of three per cent of the contracts for the gas regulator Enargas, and two per cent for Nacion Fideicomisos, the state trust manager financing the works. Prosecutors said the contracts were steered through private tenders, with shell companies and false invoices disguising payments. The recordings led to the departure of Enargas's head, Fulvio Madaro. On 13 July 2026 a federal court gave Julio De Vido, former federal planning minister, and Jose Lopez, former public works secretary, five years each for passive bribery and fraudulent administration.
inside: Skanska paid shares of its pipeline contracts to the gas regulator and the state trust funding the works, and the planning minister and public works secretary took bribes.
cite: Perfil, 13 July 2026 (Tribunal Oral Federal No 4 verdict)

n: Causa Vialidad: 51 Santa Cruz road contracts steered to Lazaro Baez's firms
rank: Vialidad Nacional, the national roads agency, and its Santa Cruz district
d: Between 2003 and 2015, 51 road contracts in the southern province of Santa Cruz, paid with national money, went to companies owned by Lazaro Baez, a businessman close to the Kirchners. In December 2022 a federal court held this was fraudulent administration at the expense of the state and convicted Baez as a participant, with the former president Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner, the former public works secretary Jose Lopez, Nelson Periotti, former head of Vialidad Nacional, the national roads agency, and four officials of its Santa Cruz district and of the provincial roads body. Baez, Kirchner, Lopez and Periotti each got six years. The appeals court upheld the verdict in November 2023 and the Supreme Court confirmed it on 10 June 2025. Julio De Vido and three others were acquitted.
inside: Lazaro Baez's firms were favoured inside the national roads agency and its Santa Cruz district, which awarded them 51 road contracts the court found defrauded the state.
cite: Chequeado and iProfesional on the Corte Suprema ruling of 10 June 2025

n: An Ecopetrol contracts officer took $12,000 to qualify a failing bidder
rank: Leader of the Perforacion VTD unit, Ecopetrol
d: Ecopetrol is Colombia's majority state-owned oil company. Luis Edison Pachon Agudelo, who led its Perforacion VTD drilling unit, administering contracts and certifying bidders' experience, received 12,000 US dollars into a personal New York account. On 21 December 2009 he issued two revised certifications with altered dates, objects and values, which Ecopetrol's evaluation committee used to approve a company that had initially failed the minimum amount. That firm won contract 089 of 2010, worth 112,000 million Colombian pesos. A criminal court convicted him of bribery and ideological falsity in a public document, sentencing him to seven years and six months, as reported on 31 August 2026. The judgment calls the payment part of an international company's strategy of recruiting officials who could favour it; the company is unnamed.
inside: An international company's payment reached an Ecopetrol contracts officer, who issued altered experience certificates so it could qualify and win a 112 billion peso drilling contract.
cite: Publimetro Colombia, 31 August 2026

n: Coal firm's director paid the regent who moved its mining licence over
rank: Regent of Tanah Bumbu
d: Mardani H. Maming, head of the Tanah Bumbu district in South Kalimantan, signed Regent Decree No. 296 of 2011 transferring a coal mining and production licence from PT Bangun Karya Pratama Lestari to PT Prolindo Cipta Nusantara. In Indonesia a district head issues and transfers mining licences in his district. Prosecutors said he took no less than Rp 118 billion in gratuities from Henry Soetio, then director of PT Prolindo Cipta Nusantara, who died before the trial. The Corruption Eradication Commission arrested Maming in July 2022. The Banjarmasin high court gave him 12 years; the Supreme Court rejected his appeal on 1 August 2023 and in November 2024, on a review petition, cut the sentence to 10 years, a Rp 500 million fine and Rp 110.6 billion in replacement money.
inside: PT Prolindo's director paid the district head who issues mining licences in Tanah Bumbu, and the coal licence was transferred to that company by his decree.
cite: VOI, 5 November 2024 (Supreme Court review verdict No. 1003 PK/Pid.Sus/2024); The Jakarta Post, 31 July 2022

n: Riau governor took money to move oil palm estates out of forest zone
rank: Governor of Riau
d: Annas Maamun, governor of Riau in Sumatra, was convicted of taking Rp 500 million to put three oil palm estates into a letter revising the province's forest map, which would have moved them out of the state forest zone. Land inside that zone cannot legally be planted. The areas were 1,188 hectares in Kuantan Singingi, 1,124 in Rokan Hilir and 120 at Duri. The money came from Edison Marudut Siahaan and was handed over by Gulat Medali Emas Manurung, who chaired the Riau branch of the oil palm growers' association Apkasindo and was jailed for three years in February 2015. The Bandung corruption court gave Maamun six years in June 2015. President Joko Widodo pardoned a year of his sentence in 2019 and he was released in October 2020.
inside: Palm oil businessmen paid the governor of Riau, who agreed to revise the province's forest map so three of their estates fell outside the state forest zone.
cite: The Jakarta Post, 25 June 2015; Tempo, 26 November 2019 (presidential decree No. 23/G/2019)

n: Oil traders paid the head of Indonesia's upstream oil regulator
rank: Chairman of SKK Migas, the upstream oil and gas regulator
d: Rudi Rubiandini ran SKK Migas, the Indonesian state task force that regulates upstream oil and gas and handles the state's share of production. He was installed on 16 January 2013 and arrested the same year. The Jakarta corruption court found on 29 April 2014 that he had taken about US$1 million from Widodo Ratanachaitong, president director of the Singapore trading firm Kernel Oil Private Limited, passed through Kernel's operational director Simon Gunawan Tanjaya and Rubiandini's golf trainer Deviardi, in exchange for securing a win in an oil tender, and US$522,000 from Artha Meris Simbolon of Kaltim Parna Industri. He was sentenced to seven years and a Rp 200 million fine for bribery and money laundering, where prosecutors had asked for ten. He said he accepted the verdict.
inside: Kernel Oil's money reached the chairman of SKK Migas, the state body regulating upstream oil and gas, and the trader was secured a win in an oil tender.
cite: The Jakarta Post, 29 April 2014; Indonesia Investments, 29 April 2014

n: Mining firms allegedly paid Brazil's mining agency directors for rights
rank: directors of the National Mining Agency (ANM)
d: Brazil's federal police arrested a sitting director of the National Mining Agency, Caio Mario Trivellato Seabra Filho, on 17 September 2025 in Operacao Rejeito. The agency grants and polices mining rights across Brazil. The court order, from the third federal criminal court in Belo Horizonte, says Trivellato allegedly received R$2.7 million as an improper advantage and helped amend the agency's Resolution 85/2021. It alleges a former director, Guilherme Santana Lopes Gomes, obtained a mining authorisation in about 18 months where the process normally takes four to ten years, and signed a utilisation guide for Mineracao Boa Vista without the required environmental licence. A former regional manager in Minas Gerais is alleged to have taken benefits including cash. At least 42 mining companies are named. No one has been convicted.
inside: Mining companies allegedly paid directors of Brazil's national mining agency, which granted an authorisation in 18 months rather than years and amended its own licensing resolution.
cite: Agencia Infra, 17 September 2025 (court order, 3rd Federal Criminal Court, Belo Horizonte); Istoe Dinheiro, 17 September 2025

n: CBI: cybercriminals paid an Axis Bank manager to open mule accounts
org_label: a cyber-fraud network running 'digital arrest' scams
rank: branch manager, Axis Bank, Bandra Reclamation branch, Mumbai
d: India's Central Bureau of Investigation arrested Nitesh Rai, a manager at Axis Bank in Mumbai, on 11 November 2025, alleging he took illegal payments from cybercriminals and used his position to process account-opening forms. The agency says this created channels for moving and layering the proceeds of cybercrime, including 'digital arrest' frauds, in which callers posing as police tell victims they face arrest and must hand over money. Reporting on the case says Rs 10,000 was transferred into Rai's own Axis Bank account on 2 January 2025 in exchange for processing the forms, arranged by two men named in the complaint. The case was registered under the Prevention of Corruption Act; a Mumbai court remanded Rai to CBI custody.
inside: India's CBI alleges a cyber-fraud network paid an Axis Bank manager to process its account-opening forms, so the bank's identity checks let stolen money through.
cite: ThePrint, 12 November 2025; Free Press Journal, 22 December 2025

n: CBI: forged papers opened 13 mule accounts at a Punjab & Sind Bank branch
org_label: unidentified operators of 13 mule accounts routing cybercrime money
rank: branch head Vikas Wadhwa, Punjab & Sind Bank, Government Girls Senior Secondary School branch, Sriganganagar
d: In January 2026 India's Central Bureau of Investigation registered a case against the branch head of Punjab & Sind Bank, a state-owned bank, at its Government Girls Senior Secondary School branch in Sriganganagar, Rajasthan, and against 18 other people and firms. It alleges that 13 current accounts were opened in the names of firms that did not exist, using forged identity papers and false rent agreements, and that bank officials wrote fake site-visit and business-verification reports so the accounts would pass the bank's customer checks. About Rs 1,084 crore from cybercrime and other illicit activity was routed through them, the agency says. The allegations follow a preliminary enquiry and have not been tested in court.
inside: Outside operators allegedly used forged papers, and false reports by bank staff, to get thirteen accounts past Punjab & Sind Bank's identity checks and move cybercrime money through.
cite: The Hitavada, 17 January 2026; The Daily Pioneer, 17 January 2026

n: Ex-Bradesco managers accused of opening shell accounts for Rio doleiros
org_label: the doleiro network of Vinicius Claret and Claudio Barboza
rank: general managers of two Bradesco branches, Rio de Janeiro
d: On 28 May 2019 Brazil's federal police arrested Tania Maria Aragao de Souza Fonseca, a former general manager of a Bradesco branch in Rio de Janeiro, and sought a second former general manager, Robson Silva, in an operation called Bancarrota. Prosecutors say the two broke the bank's compliance rules to open accounts for seven shell companies set up for doleiros - unlicensed currency dealers - Vinicius Claret and Claudio Barboza, who were by then cooperating with investigators. Counting money in and out, R$989.6m passed through the Bradesco accounts, far more than at three other banks used. Prosecutors say the cash was used to supply bribes to political figures. Bradesco said it learned of the operation from the press and was cooperating.
inside: Prosecutors say the doleiros Vinicius Claret and Claudio Barboza got two Bradesco branch managers to break the bank's client checks, opening shell-company accounts for their money.
cite: Band B (Bandab), 28 May 2019

n: Stanbic Uganda managers charged over a forged-document raid on a client
org_label: men linked to Petrom Ltd and Famane Investments
rank: branch managers, Stanbic Bank Garden City and Freedom City branches, Kampala
d: Ugandan police said on 13 February 2023 that staff at two Stanbic Bank branches in Kampala had conspired with outsiders to take about US$1.8m from the account of a customer, Nile Energy. The Garden City branch manager is alleged to have made transfers of US$287,000 and US$295,000 to a company called Petrom Ltd, and a man using forged documents to pose as Nile Energy's director made withdrawals. A further transfer request of US$988,200 was stopped when the bank contacted the account holders, who said they had not authorised it. Twelve people were arrested and nine, including two branch managers, were to be charged with causing financial loss and money laundering at the Anti-Corruption Division. Police reported no payment to the staff.
inside: Police allege an outside ring worked with two Stanbic branch managers and used forged papers to defeat the bank's identity checks and move a customer's money out.
cite: UG Standard, 14 February 2023

n: Florida suppliers bribed Corpoelec chiefs for $60m of Venezuelan contracts
org_label: Miami supply companies run by Luis Alberto Chacin Haddad and Jesus Ramon Veroes
rank: President of Corpoelec and its director of procurement
d: Two businessmen whose supply companies were based in Miami paid officials of Corpoelec, Venezuela's state-owned national electricity company, to win its purchasing contracts. The US Justice Department said the bribes went to Luis Alfredo Motta Dominguez, who was Venezuela's minister of electrical energy and president of Corpoelec, and to Eustiquio Jose Lugo Gomez, Corpoelec's procurement director, and that more than $60m in contracts for forklifts, transformers, generators and lightbulbs followed, at prices prosecutors say were inflated. Luis Alberto Chacin Haddad and Jesus Ramon Veroes pleaded guilty on 24 June 2019 to conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and were each sentenced to 51 months and $5.5m in forfeiture. Motta Dominguez and Lugo Gomez were indicted on 27 June 2019 and remain charged.
inside: Two Miami suppliers pleaded guilty to paying the head of Venezuela's state electricity company and its chief buyer, so Corpoelec's purchasing contracts went to their own firms.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 27 June 2019; A&O Shearman FCPA Tracker, United States v. Veroes and Chacin Haddad

n: PDVSA's finance planning chief took $17m over loans and a currency deal
org_label: PDVSA joint-venture partners and the Convit money-laundering network
who: Joint-venture partners and a businessmen's network
rank: Executive director of financial planning
d: Abraham Edgardo Ortega, executive director of financial planning at Petroleos de Venezuela SA (PDVSA), the Venezuelan state oil company, admitted taking $17m from outside parties for decisions he made inside it. He pleaded guilty on 31 October 2018 in Miami to conspiracy to launder money, admitting $5m for giving priority loan status to a French company and a Russian bank that were minority shareholders in PDVSA joint ventures, and $12m for taking part in a scheme involving a PDVSA loan and a foreign-exchange contract through which, prosecutors said, $1.2bn was taken out of the company. The investigation was called Operation Money Flight. Ortega forfeited $12m and was sentenced in May 2021 to 28 months in prison.
inside: Companies holding stakes in PDVSA ventures and a businessmen's network paid its finance planning director, so the state oil firm's lending and currency decisions favoured the payers.
cite: US Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs press release on Ortega's guilty plea (plea entered 31 October 2018); Stanford FCPA Clearinghouse, United States v. Convit Guruceaga et al.

n: Clairfield's central bank fees came back to Suriname's governor
who: Clairfield, a Belgian corporate advisory firm
rank: Governor of the Central Bank of Suriname
d: Robert van Trikt, governor of Suriname's central bank, signed five contracts in 2019 with Clairfield, a Belgian corporate advisory firm, with fees of 360,000 to 2.5 million euros, half paid up front. The Brussels Company Court declared all five void: the governor had no power to sign them, and the court found that the high fees he granted Clairfield were substantially recovered by him through a private company, with payments also made to Orion NV, the accountancy firm in which he held shares. Clairfield was ordered to repay 2,552,932.59 euros plus interest. Van Trikt was convicted of corruption, money laundering, embezzlement and forgery; in January 2026 Suriname's Court of Justice upheld the corruption conviction, cut his sentence from eight years to six and ordered him to repay 625,000 euros.
inside: The Belgian firm Clairfield won five unlawful contracts from Suriname's central bank governor, and the Brussels court found he recovered much of its high fees through his own company.
cite: Central Bank of Suriname statement on the Brussels Company Court judgment, reported by Keynews (Suriname); Accountant.nl, 23 January 2026, on the Court of Justice appeal judgment of 19 January 2026

n: NAB charges two ex-Sindh Bank presidents over Rs29bn Omni loans
rank: presidents of Sindh Bank
d: Sindh Bank is owned by the government of Sindh province. On 9 December 2019 Pakistan's National Accountability Bureau filed a reference, its formal charge sheet, in an accountability court against twenty accused, among them Bilal Sheikh and Tariq Ahsan, both former presidents of the bank. The bureau alleges they helped approve, by illegal means, a loan of 29 billion rupees to companies of the Omni Group, the business group at the centre of Pakistan's fake bank accounts case. It says 25 billion rupees went unpaid and 1.84 billion reached three benami companies. Neither report says what the bankers received. In January 2023 the court was still weighing acquittal pleas and whether amendments to the accountability law left it jurisdiction.
inside: Prosecutors say the Omni Group got two presidents of state-owned Sindh Bank to approve 29 billion rupees of loans to its companies, most of it never repaid.
cite: Business Recorder, 'Fake bank accounts: NAB files reference against two ex-Sindh Bank presidents and others'; Dunya News, 9 December 2019; Business Recorder, 11 January 2023, on the acquittal pleas

n: PT INTI paid Angkasa Pura II's finance director for a baggage contract
rank: Finance Director, PT Angkasa Pura II
d: PT Angkasa Pura II is the state company that runs Indonesia's western airports, including Jakarta's main airport. In July 2019 the Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK) arrested its finance director, Andra Yastrialsyah Agussalum, as a staff member of the state electronics maker PT INTI handed over cash in South Jakarta. The payments, US$71,000 and S$96,700, about Rp1.99bn in total, were made so that INTI would be named to carry out the Rp86bn supply and installation of semi-automatic baggage handling systems for six airports. The Jakarta corruption court jailed Andra for two and a half years in April 2020; the Supreme Court raised it to four years in January 2021. INTI's president director, Darman Mappangara, was convicted of paying.
cite: ANTARA, 10 February 2021 (KPK execution of sentence); JPNN, 2 August 2019 (KPK sting and charges)
inside: The state electronics maker PT INTI paid the finance director of state airport company Angkasa Pura II, so the Rp86bn baggage-system contract went to INTI.

n: Contractors rigged the tender of Jasa Marga's elevated toll road company
org_label: PT Bukaka Teknik Utama and PT Waskita Karya
rank: President Director, PT Jasamarga Jalanlayang Cikampek
d: PT Jasamarga Jalanlayang Cikampek (JJC) is the state toll operator Jasa Marga's company for the elevated Jakarta-Cikampek II road, known as the MBZ toll road. Prosecutors said its president director, Djoko Dwijono, the chair of the Jasa Marga tender committee, Yudhi Mahyudin, the operations director of the private engineering firm PT Bukaka Teknik Utama, Sofiah Balfas, and a planning consultant, Tony Budianto Sihite, colluded to decide who would win the construction tender, then cut the volume and quality of steel girders and concrete. The indictment, read in April 2024, put the loss at Rp510bn. Djoko was jailed for three years in July 2024, raised to ten on appeal in October 2024; a Waskita Karya division head, Dono Parwoto, had five years raised to eight in July 2025.
cite: Bisnis.com, 15 October 2024 (appeal sentence, indictment figures); Dandapala, 22 July 2025 (Waskita appeal, co-defendants' roles)
inside: The contractors Bukaka and Waskita worked with the state toll company's own director and tender chair to settle who won, then cut the steel and concrete used.

n: Businessmen steered state insurer Jiwasraya's money into their own shares
org_label: Benny Tjokrosaputro's and Heru Hidayat's groups
who: Hanson International and Trada Alam Minera
rank: President Director and Finance Director, PT Asuransi Jiwasraya
d: PT Asuransi Jiwasraya was Indonesia's oldest state-owned life insurer. The Jakarta corruption court found that two listed-company owners, Benny Tjokrosaputro of Hanson International and Heru Hidayat of Trada Alam Minera, together with Joko Hartono Tirto of PT Maxima Integra, arranged for Jiwasraya's portfolio to be put into their shares and medium-term notes, directly and through investment-management contracts and mutual funds. Jiwasraya's president director Hendrisman Rahim, finance director Hary Prasetyo and investment head Syahmirwan took part. All six were jailed for life in October 2020 over losses of Rp16.8tn, and the Supreme Court rejected every cassation appeal on 24 August 2021. Policyholders lost access to their payouts.
cite: CNBC Indonesia, 27 October 2020 (verdicts for six defendants); ANTARA, 25 August 2021 (Supreme Court cassation rejected, 24 August 2021)
inside: The listed-company owners Benny Tjokrosaputro and Heru Hidayat got state insurer Jiwasraya's own directors to put policyholders' money into shares and funds that they controlled.

n: Share owners and fund managers got army insurer Asabri to buy their stock
org_label: Heru Hidayat, Benny Tjokrosaputro and Lukman Purnomosidi
who: Trada Alam Minera, Hanson International, Eureka Prima
rank: President Directors, PT ASABRI
d: PT ASABRI holds the pension and savings contributions of Indonesia's soldiers, police and defence ministry staff, deducted at 8 per cent of basic pay. The Jakarta corruption court found that from 2012 its directors met private parties and placed the fund's money in shares such as LCGP, MYRX and SUGI and in mutual funds managed by them, while secretly taking gifts from shareholders, brokers and investment managers working with ASABRI. On 4 January 2022 two former presidents director, Adam Damiri and Sonny Widjaja, were jailed for 20 years and two investment officials for 15, over a state loss the audit agency put at Rp22.7tn. Businessmen Heru Hidayat, Benny Tjokrosaputro and Lukman Purnomosidi were convicted separately.
cite: CNN Indonesia, 4 January 2022 (four ASABRI verdicts, scheme, loss figure); Hukumonline, 5 January 2022 (co-defendants, dissenting opinion)
inside: Share owners and fund managers, among them Heru Hidayat, paid the directors of soldiers' insurer ASABRI, so its pension money went into the stocks and funds they ran.

n: KPK: advertising agencies and Bank BJB's chief split a Rp222bn ad budget
rank: President Director, Bank BJB
d: Bank BJB is the regional development bank owned by West Java province and its districts. On 13 March 2025 the Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK) named five suspects over its advertising spending: the former president director, Yuddy Renaldi, the head of its corporate secretary division, Widi Hartono, and three men who control advertising agencies, Ikin Asikin Dulmanan, Suhendrik and Sophan Jaya Kusuma. Investigators allege that of Rp409bn spent on advertising between 2021 and 2023, Rp222bn was fictitious, with money paid to six agencies and part of it returned to the bank's corporate secretary division as an off-budget fund. No trial verdict has been reported.
cite: Bisnis.com, 16 May 2025 (suspects, agencies and sums); Bisnis.com, 13 March 2025 (KPK naming of suspects, Rp222bn)
inside: Three advertising agency owners are alleged to have billed province-owned Bank BJB for work never done, with part of the money returned to the bank's own managers.

n: A borrower and Bank Jatim's branch head ran Rp299bn of fictitious credit
rank: Head of the Jakarta branch, Bank Jatim
d: Bank Jatim is the development bank owned by East Java province. Prosecutors in Jakarta found that in 2023 and 2024 its Jakarta branch issued Rp299.39bn of fictitious credit to the Indi Daya Group, which applied through shell companies and offered work orders and invoices as collateral. The judge put the loss at close to half a trillion rupiah. On 9 January 2026 the Jakarta corruption court jailed the group's owner, Bun Sentoso, for 14 years, the branch head, Benny, for 11, a group director, Agus Dianto Mulia, for 12, and two staff for eight years each. Benny was ordered to repay Rp3.51bn, Bun Sentoso Rp204.1bn.
cite: Dandapala, 13 January 2026 (verdicts of 9 January 2026); Dandapala, 24 October 2025 (fictitious credit of Rp299.39bn, BPK audit); Bisnis.com, 16 May 2025 (investigation opened)
inside: The Indi Daya Group applied through shell companies, and province-owned Bank Jatim's own branch head, later ordered to repay Rp3.51bn, approved Rp299bn of credit on false collateral.

n: A channel company got Pelindo's Surabaya region to hand it dredging work
rank: Regional head and engineering division head, PT Pelindo Regional 3
d: PT Pelindo is Indonesia's state ports company. On 27 November 2025 prosecutors at Tanjung Perak in Surabaya detained six suspects over the dredging of the Tanjung Perak port basin: three Pelindo Regional 3 officers, named only by initials, and three directors of PT Alur Pelayaran Barat Surabaya. Prosecutors allege the Pelindo officers appointed that company directly although it had no dredging vessels or expertise, justifying it wrongly as a Pelindo affiliate, and that the cost estimate was inflated to about Rp200.58bn, with its scope written so the firm would qualify. The work was then passed to subcontractors. No verdict has been reported.
cite: Detik, 27 November 2025 (Kejari Tanjung Perak: six suspects, roles and allegations)
inside: Prosecutors allege PT Alur Pelayaran Barat Surabaya, which had no dredging vessels, was appointed directly by state port company Pelindo's own officers at an inflated price.

n: Riza Chalid's trading firms rigged tenders at Pertamina's Petral arm
org_label: Gold Manor, VeritaOil and Global Energy Resources
rank: Managing Director and head of trading, Pertamina Energy Services
d: Petral, Pertamina Energy Trading Ltd, bought crude oil and refined products for Indonesia's state oil company. On 9 April 2026 the Attorney General's Office named seven suspects over its purchasing between 2008 and 2015: the businessman Mohammad Riza Chalid, said to be the beneficial owner of the firms Gold Manor, VeritaOil and Global Energy Resources, a director of those firms, four Pertamina Energy Services traders and managers, and a former vice-president of Pertamina's integrated supply chain who later ran Pertamina International Shipping. Investigators say tenders were conditioned and the internal price estimate leaked, cutting competition and marking up prices. Riza Chalid is on the wanted list; five suspects were detained.
cite: Metro TV News, 9 April 2026 (Kejagung: seven suspects, firms named, alleged tender conditioning)
inside: Trading firms said to belong to Mohammad Riza Chalid are accused of getting Pertamina's buying arm Petral to leak its price limits, so their bids won.

n: A catalyst supplier paid Pertamina's processing director to drop a test
rank: Processing Director, PT Pertamina
d: Catalysts are the materials an oil refinery needs to turn crude into fuel. On 10 September 2025 the Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK) named four suspects over Pertamina's catalyst buying for 2012 to 2014: the director of the supplier PT MP, identified as GW, his child, who worked as the firm's operations manager, Pertamina's processing director for those years, identified as CD, and CD's child. Investigators allege the supplier, which had failed a required quality test and entered the tender under the name of Albemarle Corp, asked through the two children for the tender to be arranged, that the director then issued a policy removing the test requirement, and that PT MP won the USD14.4m Balongan contract while he took at least Rp1.7bn in fees.
cite: InfoPublik, 11 September 2025 (KPK: four suspects, scheme, contract value and fees)
inside: The supplier PT MP, which had failed a required quality test, is alleged to have paid Pertamina's processing director to drop that test, then won the contract.

n: Businessmen paid Inhutani V's chief to keep their forest deal running
rank: President Director, PT Inhutani V
d: PT Inhutani V is the state forestry company for part of Sumatra. On 9 April 2026 the Jakarta corruption court found its president director for 2021 to 2025, Dicky Yuana Rady, guilty of taking S$199,000 from two private businessmen, Djunaidi Nur and Aditya Simaputra, so that he would arrange for the company PT PML to carry on working with Inhutani V on the use of state forest areas in registers 42, 44 and 46 in Lampung province. He was jailed for four years and fined Rp200m, ordered to repay the S$10,000 he had spent, and a Jeep Rubicon bought for him was confiscated; the remaining S$189,000 was returned to the state.
cite: EmitenNews, 9 April 2026 (verdict, bribe, payers and the forest cooperation)
inside: The businessmen Djunaidi Nur and Aditya Simaputra paid the president director of state forestry company Inhutani V, so their firm PT PML kept working its state forest areas.

n: A borrower and a BRI manager drew Rp122bn against fictitious work orders
rank: Relationship manager, Bank Rakyat Indonesia
d: Bank Rakyat Indonesia (BRI) is one of Indonesia's largest state-owned banks. On 28 September 2026 the Jakarta corruption court jailed a borrower, Maria Lastry Gultom, for eight years and her daughter, Li Putri Nazara, for four, over credit drawn on work orders and contracts that prosecutors said were fictitious, some of them citing work for the home affairs, industry and youth and sports ministries. A government auditor's report dated 10 March 2026 put the loss at Rp122bn, which Gultom was ordered to repay. A former BRI relationship manager, Frengki Hasoloan Sianturi, had already been sentenced to two and a half years and ordered to repay Rp790m.
cite: Dandapala, 28 September 2026 (verdicts, loss figure and the bank manager's earlier sentence)
inside: The borrower Maria Lastry Gultom drew Rp122bn of credit from state-owned BRI on fictitious work orders, helped by a bank relationship manager since jailed for it.

n: Buenaventura port logistics workers hid cocaine in Spain-bound containers
who: Cocaine exporters using port logistics staff
rank: Workers of a transport and logistics firm operating inside Buenaventura port
d: Colombia's prosecution service charged three men who worked for a transport and logistics company operating inside the port of Buenaventura, the country's main Pacific container port. Prosecutors allege they collected cocaine packages near the port, strapped them to their bodies or hid them in compartments, and used their work passes to carry the drugs past port security checks. Inside, they allegedly took the packages to lavatories in the mooring area and loaded them into containers bound for Spain. The case rests in part on 26 kilograms of cocaine found in lavatory bins at the port on 4 February 2024. The three were arrested in April 2025 in Buenaventura and Candelaria and a judge ordered them held in prison. No verdict has been reported.
inside: Prosecutors say cocaine exporters used three men employed inside Buenaventura port, whose work passes carried the drugs past the security checks meant to stop them.
cite: El Heraldo / EFE, citing the Fiscalía General de la Nación, 19 April 2025

n: Operation Darsena Cero: customs officers and port workers in Panama's ports
who: Container-contamination network shipping cocaine to Europe
rank: Officials of the National Customs Authority and workers at Panama's port terminals
d: Panama's attorney general announced on 12 May 2026 that sixteen people had been detained in the provinces of Panama, Colon and Panama Oeste in an operation called Darsena Cero. Those held included port workers, transport operators and officials; the National Police said two of them were officers of the National Customs Authority, the agency that inspects cargo. Prosecutors allege the group contaminated export containers with drugs, and link it to more than five tonnes of cocaine and chemical precursors seized at Panama's port terminals, most of it in containers bound for Europe. The investigation began in 2023. One shipment cited was 1,152 packages hidden in a container declared as Salvadoran coffee. The detainees face international drug trafficking allegations; no trial outcome has been reported.
inside: A smuggling network allegedly reached inside the customs service and the port workforce, so the staff checking containers were working for the shippers instead.
cite: Ministerio Publico de Panama press release, 12 May 2026; Revista E&F/EFE, 13 May 2026

n: 'Major' Carvalho's gang recruited Paranagua terminal staff and lorry drivers
org_label: Sergio Roberto de Carvalho ('Major') trafficking group
who: Sergio Roberto de Carvalho's cocaine group
rank: Employees of the container terminal at the port of Paranagua
d: A trafficker who turned state's witness told Brazil's federal prosecutors and Federal Police how cocaine left the port of Paranagua, the main grain port in southern Brazil. Jorge Santos Zela, arrested in November 2020 and the head of one of two groups working the port, said the gang led by Sergio Roberto de Carvalho, a fugitive former Sao Paulo military police officer known as 'Major', recruited lorry drivers carrying export cargo and employees of the container terminal. Teams of three covered each of the port's four daily shifts, loading cocaine into containers already bound for the country the gang wanted, a step they called 'contamination'. About one load a month was shipped. His plea agreement was approved by the federal court, and the account came out of Operation Enterprise.
inside: A state's witness says Sergio de Carvalho's group recruited container terminal staff on each shift at Paranagua, so cocaine was loaded by the port's own workers.
cite: Banda B, reporting the approved plea agreement in Operation Enterprise, 27 August 2021

n: Tin Can Island dock workers moved a cocaine container for a Lagos syndicate
org_label: Lagos-South Africa drug syndicate named by the NDLEA
who: A drug syndicate shipping through Lagos
rank: Dock workers at the Five Star terminal, Tin Can Island port
d: Nigeria's National Drug Law Enforcement Agency said that in January 2024 it examined two containers that had arrived at the Five Star terminal of Tin Can Island port in Lagos from Durban in South Africa. It found cocaine, large quantities of the synthetic cannabis sold as 'Colorado', a pistol and ammunition. Among those arrested were Anjorin Idowu, a dock worker at the terminal, and Uzairu Ahmed Iguda, who was in charge of positioning and stacking containers there; investigators allege the two, with a third dock worker who went on the run, moved drugs and the pistol out of one container into an empty one. The clearing agent named on the consignment was also arrested. Three men said to be the organisers were placed on the agency's wanted list.
inside: The NDLEA alleges a Lagos drug syndicate used dock workers who position containers at Tin Can Island, so its load could be moved inside the terminal unchecked.
cite: The Guardian (Nigeria), reporting the NDLEA, February 2024

n: Smuggling syndicate paid Cathay Pacific check-in staff in Hong Kong
org_label: Human smuggling syndicate (unnamed by the ICAC)
rank: Customer services officer handling check-in for Cathay Pacific Airways
d: Hong Kong's Independent Commission Against Corruption found that a human smuggling syndicate had bought the cooperation of ground staff inside Cathay Pacific Airways at Hong Kong International Airport. Tsui Ying-kit, a customer services officer handling passenger check-in, conspired with two other ground crew to check the syndicate's travellers against the airline's computer system in advance, issue their boarding passes quickly and warn the syndicate if any of them was flagged for security checks. He took HK$1,000 to HK$2,000 per traveller, HK$18,000 in all, between September 2008 and August 2009. Arrested in 2009, he absconded while on bail and was charged only after returning to Hong Kong in July 2025. He pleaded guilty and was jailed for 20 months in July 2026.
inside: A human smuggling syndicate paid Cathay Pacific check-in staff to process its travellers quickly and warn it when one was flagged for security checks.
cite: ICAC Hong Kong press release, 2026

n: Balkan-Ecuadorian network bribed Guayaquil port officials and ships' crews
rank: Customs, police and military personnel posted at Guayaquil's ports
d: Ecuadorian prosecutors allege a network led by the Serbian-Montenegrin Jezdimir Srdan, working with Albanians, Serbs, Ecuadorians and the Ecuadorian gang Los Lobos, bribed officials at Guayaquil's two main port terminals and could recruit and pay military and police personnel posted at ports and airports. They say one customs chief took part in one of the shipments, and that chat records show bundles of US$100 notes handed to members of the security forces. The network was said to pay US$600 a kilo for cocaine moved by ship and, in one instance, US$1.6 million to a single vessel's crew. Cocaine was hidden in legitimate export cargo bound for Rotterdam, Antwerp and Hamburg. Srdan was arrested in Guayaquil in November 2024 and twelve people are being prosecuted for organised crime and drug trafficking.
inside: Prosecutors say Jezdimir Srdan's network paid customs officers, police and soldiers posted at Guayaquil's terminals, so the men inspecting export cargo let its cocaine through.
cite: Primicias, reporting the Fiscalia General del Estado hearing, 15 November 2025

n: Shabu importers reached Manila container port's x-ray and appraisal staff
org_label: Importers and trading firms named in the magnetic-lifter shabu complaints
rank: X-ray inspection, shift supervision, operator and appraisal staff, Bureau of Customs, Manila International Container Port
d: In August 2018 Philippine agents found methamphetamine, known locally as shabu, hidden in magnetic lifters at the Manila International Container Port, and more lifters abandoned at a warehouse in Cavite thought to have held about 1,618 kilograms. In December 2018 the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency filed a complaint with the Department of Justice naming 49 people and firms. Among them were four Bureau of Customs staff who held x-ray inspection, shift supervision, operator and appraisal roles at the container port, a former customs intelligence agent and a former police anti-illegal drugs chief, alongside importers, consignees and shipping agents. The alleged offences were drug importation, graft and obstruction of justice. The former customs commissioner was excluded for want of evidence, and the complaint was pending at the justice department.
inside: The drug agency's complaint accused importers of buying the customs staff who x-ray and appraise containers at Manila's port, so the drugs passed inspection.
cite: The Philippine Star, reporting the PDEA complaint filed with the Department of Justice, 14 December 2018

n: Fortaleza port coordinator and camera operator helped load a cocaine container
org_label: Cocaine exporters using the port of Mucuripe
rank: Coordinator at the Companhia Docas do Ceara and the port's security camera operator
d: Brazil's Federal Police arrested five people in Operation Palma in April 2025 over 435 kilograms of cocaine packed into a container of carnauba wax at the port of Mucuripe in Fortaleza. Two worked at the port: a coordinator employed for more than ten years by the Companhia Docas do Ceara, the state company that runs it, and a security camera operator employed by a contractor. Investigators suspect they helped traffickers open and reload the container unseen. The five were held under temporary arrest. The report says some cameras were switched off while a lorry was held up, and that the coordinator told staff to reverse the container's removal. Federal Revenue agents found 390 packages on 6 February 2025 in a shipment routed to Japan by way of Le Havre.
inside: Investigators suspect cocaine exporters used a Companhia Docas do Ceara coordinator and the port's camera operator, so a container could be opened and reloaded unseen.
cite: O Povo, reporting Operation Palma by the Policia Federal, 16 April 2025

n: Traders jailed for offering a Jebel Ali customs inspector Dh40,000
org_label: Two traders importing through Jebel Ali Port
rank: Customs inspectors at Jebel Ali Port
d: Dubai Criminal Court convicted a 45-year-old manager and his 46-year-old business partner, both Indian, of bribery after they asked customs inspectors at Jebel Ali Port to stamp shipment papers and to certify that two vehicles carrying musical instruments had passed inspection when they had not. Customs had confiscated the shipment. They offered Dh40,000. A 27-year-old Emirati inspector reported the offer to his superior and to the police, was told to play along, and met the two men the next day; they were arrested as he took the money, which the court confiscated. Both denied the charges and were sentenced to a year in jail followed by deportation. The attempt failed because the official reported it, so nothing was decided in the traders' favour.
inside: Importers tried to buy the inspectors who certify cargo at Dubai's main port, so their confiscated shipment would be signed off as checked.
cite: The National, reporting Dubai Criminal Court, 22 May 2017

n: Trader accused of paying a Dubai Customs officer to clear undervalued perfume
org_label: A British trader importing through Jebel Ali Port
rank: Dubai Customs employees at Jebel Ali Port
d: Dubai prosecutors accused a 45-year-old British trader of paying Dh3,000 to a 27-year-old Dubai Customs employee the night before a shipment arrived at Jebel Ali Port, so that branded perfumes would be cleared under a cheaper brand name. The cargo was declared at Dh32,000 but valued at more than Dh215,000, evading Dh10,769 in duty. A section head noticed the employee fetching and returning clearance papers, stopped the car after it had passed the gate and found seven cartons that did not match the papers. The employee admitted taking the bribe; a 22-year-old colleague who stamped the papers denied knowing about it and was accused of complicity, and the trader was accused of forging documents. The report, from November 2013, records no verdict.
inside: A British trader is accused of paying a Dubai Customs officer at Jebel Ali to clear his perfume shipment under a cheaper brand, cutting the duty due.
cite: Customs Today, reporting the Dubai prosecution, 11 November 2013

n: Marines and terminal guards charged over cocaine in a Guayaquil container
org_label: Cocaine exporters shipping through the Naportec terminal
rank: Four serving marines of Ecuador's navy and three private security guards at the Naportec terminal
d: Ecuador's prosecution service charged seven men over cocaine found in a container at the Naportec terminal in southern Guayaquil on the night of 8 September 2025. Four were serving members of the navy's marine infantry, posted at the port, and three were private security guards on shift at the terminal. Prosecutors allege the marines broke the container's security seals to put the drugs inside with the guards' help. Police dog handlers from the ports and airports investigation unit found 432 blocks, 491.6 kilograms of cocaine, in jute sacks in a container of tinned tuna bound for France by way of Belgium; the blocks were stamped with designer labels. All seven were ordered held in preventive detention.
inside: Prosecutors say cocaine exporters used four navy marines posted at the Naportec terminal and three private guards to break a container's seals and load 491 kilograms of cocaine.
cite: Expreso and Primicias, reporting the Fiscalia General del Estado, 9-10 September 2025

n: AIC rigged the tenders for Quang Ninh's children's hospital kit
rank: Quang Ninh Obstetrics and Paediatrics Hospital project board
d: AIC, a Hanoi equipment supplier, fixed the medical equipment tenders of the public Obstetrics and Paediatrics Hospital in Quang Ninh province from inside. On 26 October 2023 the Quang Ninh People's Court convicted 16 people. The court found that AIC's chairwoman, Nguyen Thi Thanh Nhan, had her project manager work with staff on the health department's project board to set the technical specifications, configurations and unit prices, while AIC's chief accountant altered the firm's 2010-2013 accounts so it appeared able to bid. AIC staff also filled out the rival bids. AIC took four of six packages, worth over 206 billion dong, and an affiliate took two; the state lost more than 50.6 billion dong. Nhan, a fugitive, was given 10 years, bringing her total to 30.
inside: The supplier AIC had the specifications and prices of a Quang Ninh state hospital's equipment tenders written by its own project staff, then won four of six packages.
cite: Tap chi Toa an nhan dan (the courts' journal), 26 October 2023; RFA Vietnamese, 23-24 October 2023

n: AIC paid Ho Chi Minh City's biotechnology centre chief for lab deals
rank: director, Ho Chi Minh City Biotechnology Centre
d: The supplier AIC bought the co-operation of the director of the Ho Chi Minh City Biotechnology Centre, a state research body, to win the contracts to equip its laboratories. On 12 July 2024 the city People's Court found that the director, Duong Hoa Xo, took 14.4 billion dong from AIC and agreed with the chairwoman, Nguyen Thi Thanh Nhan, to rig the bidding, which removed real competition. AIC won eight contracts to equip 12 laboratories at prices inflated by 40 per cent, and the state lost more than 94.6 billion dong. Xo was given 15 years and Nhan, tried in absentia, 24. A deputy director of the city's planning and investment department was given seven and a half years for abuse of power.
inside: AIC paid the director of Ho Chi Minh City's state Biotechnology Centre 14.4 billion dong, and he rigged its laboratory tenders so AIC won them at inflated prices.
cite: Sai Gon Giai Phong, 12 July 2024; RFA Vietnamese, 12 July 2024

n: AIC's rigged bids took 134 Ho Chi Minh City school equipment deals
rank: Ho Chi Minh City Department of Education and Training
d: AIC won 134 school equipment packages run by Ho Chi Minh City's education department and the district education offices under it. On 12 December 2025 the city People's Court convicted 16 people of breaking the bidding rules, finding losses of 142 billion dong. The former department director, Le Hong Son, was given three years, suspended; his deputy two and a half years; the head of AIC's project board seven years; and Nguyen Thi Thanh Nhan, who has fled abroad and is wanted on international warrants, eight years, for a combined 30. The indictment said AIC's affiliated firms filed deliberately weak bids against it and that Son signed off unlawful direct appointments and a bid evaluation team that never met.
inside: AIC took over a city education department's purchasing by filling the rival bids with its own firms, while the director signed off unlawful direct appointments.
cite: Tien Phong, 12 December 2025; VietNamNet, indictment report 2025

n: SCB's money bought the central bank's Ho Chi Minh City supervisors
who: Van Thinh Phat / Saigon Commercial Bank
rank: inspection and supervision unit, State Bank of Vietnam Ho Chi Minh City branch
d: Five officers of the State Bank of Vietnam's Ho Chi Minh City branch, the unit that supervised Saigon Commercial Bank day to day, took money from the bank and kept its condition out of their reports. Prosecutors said that from 2016 to September 2022 supervision teams filed more than 70 reports urging tighter or special control of the bank, which their superiors did not approve, and that the officers blocked or filed untruthful reports and narrowed inspections. They received sums of roughly 470 million to 1.8 billion dong. On 11 April 2024 the city People's Court gave the branch's deputy director 11 years and four colleagues three to seven years for abuse of office; on 3 December 2024 the appeal court cut several, the deputy director to eight years.
inside: Saigon Commercial Bank's money reached the central bank officers supervising it in Ho Chi Minh City, so its true condition stayed out of their official reports.
cite: Sai Gon Giai Phong, 11 April 2024 and 3 December 2024; VietnamFinance, November 2023

n: Viet A's 8% commission reached Hanoi's disease control centre
rank: director, Hanoi Centre for Disease Control
d: The test kit maker Viet A had the purchasing papers of Hanoi's Centre for Disease Control written around its own product, then paid the centre a commission. On 6 March 2024 the Hanoi People's Court found that the centre's director, Truong Quang Viet, who chaired its procurement council, told staff to build the specification around Viet A's Covid test kit so that Viet A would win. The centre bought 28,300 kits in 2020 for over 13 billion dong, and the budget lost more than 9.1 billion. Viet A's general director then paid an 8 per cent commission, over 1.3 billion dong, of which Viet took 500 million and the finance head over 800 million. Both were given suspended sentences and returned the money.
inside: Viet A paid an 8 per cent commission to officers of Hanoi's disease control centre, whose director had written the purchase specification so only Viet A could win.
cite: Tuoi Tre, 6 March 2024

n: Firms paid Thai Nguyen and Quang Nam officials over Covid flights
rank: provincial foreign affairs, health and people's committee offices
d: Travel firms running paid repatriation flights during the pandemic bought the provincial approvals they needed to land and quarantine passengers. On 27 December 2024 the Hanoi People's Court convicted 17 people in the second stage of the rescue flights case. A deputy director of Thai Nguyen's foreign affairs department was found to have taken bribes routed through a company he insisted be included, after pressing a tour operator to understate the contract price and pay the difference off the books; two Quang Nam department deputy directors took 450 and 400 million dong to get the province to accept self-paid quarantine, and a Hai Duong provincial office specialist 650 million. The appeal court cut several sentences on 16 June 2025.
inside: Companies needing landing and quarantine permits paid officers of three provincial administrations, which then approved the flights those companies were selling.
cite: Tap chi Toa an nhan dan, 27 December 2024; Sai Gon Giai Phong, 16 June 2025; Bao Dau Tu, trial report December 2024

n: Orthofix's Mexican unit paid IMSS officials for hospital supply contracts
rank: officials of the Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social (IMSS)
d: Orthofix International, a medical device maker, used its Mexican subsidiary Promeca to pay officials of the Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social (IMSS), the Mexican government-owned health care and social services institution, so that Orthofix products would win sales contracts with government hospitals. The payments, which Promeca staff called 'chocolates', ran from 2003 to 2010 and totalled more than $300,000, some handed to officials directly and some routed through front companies the officials owned. The scheme produced nearly $5m in profits. In July 2012 the US Securities and Exchange Commission announced a settlement of $5.2m, including $4,983,644 in disgorgement, and Orthofix paid the Justice Department a further $2.22m penalty.
inside: A device maker's money reached buying officials inside Mexico's state health institution, so IMSS hospitals bought its products.
cite: SEC press release 2012-133, 10 July 2012

n: HP's Russian unit paid to keep a contract with the federal prosecutor's office
rank: official of Russia's federal prosecutor's office
d: Hewlett-Packard's Russian subsidiary paid more than $2m, through agents and shell companies, to a Russian government official in order to keep a multi-million dollar contract to supply computer hardware and software to Russia's federal prosecutor's office. The payments ran from about 2000 to 2007. The scheme came out through a joint US and German investigation, and in April 2014 HP settled with the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Justice Department over conduct in Russia, Poland and Mexico. The Russian subsidiary pleaded guilty. The official who took the money was not named in the SEC's announcement.
inside: A computer company's money reached an official inside Russia's prosecution service, which then kept buying its hardware and software.
cite: SEC press release, 9 April 2014

n: HP's Polish unit gave cash and gifts to a police official for IT contracts
rank: official of Poland's national police agency
d: Hewlett-Packard's Polish subsidiary gave gifts and cash worth more than $600,000 to an official of Poland's national police agency so that the agency would award HP contracts for information technology products and services. The official was promised a share of the net revenue from the contracts, and the cash came from off-the-books accounts. The payments ran from about 2006 to 2010. The Securities and Exchange Commission announced the settlement in April 2014 as part of a wider resolution covering HP's conduct in Russia, Poland and Mexico; the Polish subsidiary admitted criminal conduct. The official was not named.
inside: A computer company's cash reached an official inside Poland's national police, and the force then awarded it technology contracts.
cite: SEC press release, 9 April 2014

n: Morgan Stanley banker and a Shanghai state firm's chairman shared secret deals
who: Garth Peterson, Morgan Stanley real estate
rank: chairman of Yongye Enterprise (Group) Co
d: Garth Peterson, who ran Morgan Stanley's Shanghai real estate business, arranged secret payments and joint investments with the chairman of Yongye Enterprise (Group) Co, a Chinese state-owned company that had influence over that business. Between at least 2004 and 2007 Peterson and the chairman split at least $1.8m disguised as finder's fees owed by Morgan Stanley funds to third parties, invested together in Chinese fast-food franchises, and Peterson secretly acquired an interest in the Jin Lin Tiandi Serviced Apartments, bought from a Morgan Stanley fund and worth about $3.4m. A compliance officer had warned him in 2004 that Yongye staff counted as government officials. He was dismissed in 2008, pleaded guilty and settled with the SEC in April 2012, giving up the apartment interest and $254,589.
inside: A bank's own dealmaker cut the chairman of a Chinese state company into his profits, and the state firm's influence then served the bank's Shanghai deals.
cite: SEC press release 2012-78, 25 April 2012

n: Two NGO heads bribed Marshall Islands legislators for a special region law
rank: members of the Marshall Islands legislature
d: Cary Yan and Gina Zhou, who ran a New York-registered non-governmental organisation, paid tens of thousands of dollars to elected officials of the Republic of the Marshall Islands, including members of its legislature, to win support for legislation creating the Rongelap Atoll Special Administrative Region, a semi-autonomous zone that would have benefited their own business interests. The scheme began around 2016 and ran until at least August 2020. Both were arrested in Thailand in November 2020 and later extradited to the United States. On 1 December 2022 each pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. No individual Marshallese official was named in the Justice Department's announcement.
inside: Two business promoters paid members of the Marshall Islands legislature so that it would pass a law creating a zone for their own venture.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 1 December 2022

n: Brokers paid a BANDES official to win Venezuela's state bank trading business
rank: senior official of BANDES, Venezuela's state development bank
d: Executives of the New York brokerage Direct Access Partners paid kickbacks to Maria de los Angeles Gonzalez de Hernandez, a senior official of the Banco de Desarrollo Economico y Social de Venezuela (BANDES), the Venezuelan state economic development bank, so that BANDES placed its bond trading business through their firm. The firm's chief executive Benito Chinea and managing director Joseph DeMeneses were charged in April 2014; Gonzalez de Hernandez pleaded guilty on 18 November 2013 to Travel Act and money laundering offences, and other participants pleaded guilty in August 2013. The case was brought by US prosecutors in New York after the brokerage's trading volumes with BANDES were examined.
inside: A brokerage's kickbacks bought a senior officer inside Venezuela's state development bank, which then routed its trading business to the payers.
cite: Gibson Dunn 2013 Year-End FCPA Update, 6 January 2014

n: Bechtel's man at Egypt's state power joint venture took $5.2m from bidders
rank: general manager of PGESCo, the Bechtel-EEHC joint venture
d: Asem Elgawhary was general manager from 1996 to 2011 of PGESCo, a joint venture between the US engineering firm Bechtel and EEHC, Egypt's state-owned and state-controlled electricity company. PGESCo helped EEHC find subcontractors, run tenders and award contracts for power projects. Elgawhary admitted taking $5.2m from three power companies and their consultants, paid into offshore accounts he controlled, to give those bidders an unfair advantage in the bidding for state power contracts; he spent $1.6m of it in cash on a house and did not declare the income. He was arrested in November 2013, indicted in February 2014 and pleaded guilty in December 2014 to mail fraud, money laundering conspiracy and obstructing US tax laws. Gibson Dunn's review of the period records him as a recipient of Alstom's bribery campaign.
inside: Power contractors' money bought the manager who ran tenders for Egypt's state electricity company, so their bids were favoured in state power contracts.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 4 December 2014; Gibson Dunn 2014 Year-End FCPA Update

n: PetroTiger's bosses paid an Ecopetrol employee for a $45m oil services deal
rank: employee of Ecopetrol, Colombia's national oil company
d: The two co-chief executives of PetroTiger Ltd, a British Virgin Islands oil services company, and its former general counsel paid $333,500 to David Duran, an employee of Ecopetrol, the Colombian national oil company, to win a $45m oil services contract from Ecopetrol. US prosecutors in New Jersey charged all three. The general counsel Gregory Weisman pleaded guilty on 8 November 2013, co-chief executive Knut Hammarskjold on 18 February 2014, and co-chief executive Joseph Sigelman pleaded guilty to conspiracy to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act on 15 June 2015, two weeks into his trial, with sentencing set for the next day.
inside: An oil services firm's payments bought an employee inside Colombia's state oil company, which then awarded the firm a $45m contract.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 15 June 2015

n: BizJet bribed Mexico's federal police and presidential air fleet for repair work
rank: officials of the Policia Federal Preventiva and the presidential air transport body
d: BizJet International Sales and Support, a Tulsa-based aircraft maintenance company owned indirectly by Lufthansa Technik, paid bribes to officials of Mexican government bodies to win contracts for aircraft maintenance, repair and overhaul. The Justice Department named the Policia Federal Preventiva, the Coordinacion General de Transportes Aereos Presidenciales, and the air fleets of the state governments of Sinaloa and Sonora. BizJet was charged in March 2012 with one count of conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, entered a three-year deferred prosecution agreement and paid an $11.8m criminal penalty; Lufthansa Technik agreed not to be prosecuted for three years. Four former BizJet executives were charged separately in 2013.
inside: An aircraft repair firm paid officials inside Mexico's federal police and presidential air fleet, which then sent it their maintenance work.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 14 March 2012

n: BizJet bribed Panama's civil aviation authority for aircraft maintenance work
rank: officials of the Autoridad Aeronautica Civil
d: Among the government bodies whose officials BizJet International Sales and Support paid for aircraft maintenance, repair and overhaul contracts, the Justice Department named the Republica de Panama Autoridad Aeronautica Civil, Panama's civil aviation authority. BizJet, a Tulsa-based company owned indirectly by Lufthansa Technik, was charged in March 2012 with one count of conspiring to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, entered a three-year deferred prosecution agreement and paid an $11.8m criminal penalty. The announcement did not name individual officials or give the value of the Panamanian contracts. Four former BizJet executives were charged separately in 2013.
inside: An aircraft repair firm's bribes reached officials inside Panama's civil aviation authority, which then gave it maintenance contracts.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 14 March 2012

n: Rolls-Royce joint venture paid officials at Lithuania's Ignalina nuclear plant
rank: high-level officials of the Ignalina Nuclear Power Plant
d: Data Systems & Solutions LLC, a Virginia-based firm that supplied instrumentation and control systems for nuclear plants, paid bribes to high-level officials of the Ignalina Nuclear Power Plant, a state-owned nuclear plant in Lithuania, to win contracts to perform services there. Some payments were made by subcontractors by cheque or wire transfer. The Justice Department filed a two-count criminal information in June 2012 charging conspiracy to violate and violation of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and a two-year deferred prosecution agreement under which the company paid an $8.82m criminal penalty. The department credited the company's own investigation and cooperation. No individual officials were named.
inside: A nuclear services firm's bribes bought senior managers inside Lithuania's state nuclear plant, which then awarded it service contracts.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 18 June 2012

n: Dallas Airmotive paid Brazil's air force and a governor's office for engine work
rank: officials of the Brazilian Air Force and the Roraima state governor's office
d: Dallas Airmotive Inc, an aircraft engine maintenance, repair and overhaul provider based in Grapevine, Texas, admitted bribing Latin American officials to win government contracts. Between 2008 and 2012 it paid officials of the Brazilian Air Force and of the Office of the Governor of the Brazilian state of Roraima, using front companies linked to the officials, third-party representatives it expected to pass the money on, and direct benefits such as paid holidays. The Justice Department filed a criminal information in Texas in December 2014 charging conspiracy to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and a substantive bribery count, under a deferred prosecution agreement with a $14m criminal penalty. No individual officials were named.
inside: An engine repair firm's money reached officials inside Brazil's air force and a state governor's office, which then sent it their maintenance contracts.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 10 December 2014

n: Dallas Airmotive paid Peruvian Air Force officials for engine maintenance work
rank: officials of the Peruvian Air Force
d: Among the bodies whose officials Dallas Airmotive Inc admitted bribing to win government aircraft engine maintenance, repair and overhaul contracts, the Justice Department named the Peruvian Air Force. The Texas-based company made the payments between 2008 and 2012 through front companies linked to officials, through third-party representatives it expected to pass money on, and by providing benefits such as paid holidays directly. In December 2014 it entered a deferred prosecution agreement, was charged with conspiracy to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and a substantive bribery count, and agreed to a $14m criminal penalty. The announcement did not name individual officials or the contracts' values.
inside: An engine repair firm paid officials inside Peru's air force, which then awarded it the force's maintenance work.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 10 December 2014

n: Dallas Airmotive paid San Juan province's governor's office in Argentina
rank: officials of the Office of the Governor of San Juan Province
d: Among the bodies whose officials Dallas Airmotive Inc admitted bribing to win government aircraft engine maintenance, repair and overhaul contracts, the Justice Department named the Office of the Governor of the San Juan Province in Argentina. The Texas-based company made the payments between 2008 and 2012 through front companies linked to officials, through third-party representatives it expected to pass money on, and by providing benefits such as paid holidays directly. In December 2014 it entered a deferred prosecution agreement, was charged with conspiracy to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and a substantive bribery count, and agreed to a $14m criminal penalty. No individual officials were named.
inside: An engine repair firm's money reached officials in an Argentine province's governor's office, which then gave it the provincial aircraft work.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 10 December 2014

n: Bio-Rad's agents were used to influence Russia's health ministry over contracts
rank: Russia's Ministry of Health
d: Bio-Rad Laboratories, a California maker of clinical diagnostic and life science products, retained agents in Russia primarily to influence the country's Ministry of Health and help the company win bids for government contracts, paying them commissions of between 15 and 30 per cent of Russian sales. The Securities and Exchange Commission said about $7.5m in bribes were paid over five years across Russia, Vietnam and Thailand, producing some $35m in illicit profits. In November 2014 Bio-Rad agreed to pay the SEC $40.7m in disgorgement and interest and the Justice Department a $14.35m criminal fine. No Russian officials were named.
inside: A diagnostics firm paid agents to work on Russia's health ministry, which then awarded it state contracts for its products.
cite: SEC press release, 3 November 2014

n: PDVSA contractor paid two senior Venezuelan prosecutors to drop its case
org_label: a PDVSA contractor named in the indictment as 'Contractor 1'
who: a contractor to Venezuela's state oil company PDVSA
rank: senior prosecutors in the Venezuelan Attorney General's Office
d: US prosecutors in Florida charged Daniel D'Andrea Golindano and Luis Javier Sanchez Rangel, two former senior prosecutors in the Venezuelan Attorney General's Office, with taking more than $1m in 2017 from a party the indictment calls Contractor 1, which held contracts with subsidiaries of Venezuela's state oil company PDVSA and was under investigation over them. The indictment says they agreed not to pursue criminal charges against Contractor 1 and others, and that the Attorney General's Office then did not seek charges. The money went to an account in southern Florida through false invoices purportedly for medical diagnostic equipment. The charges were announced on 8 March 2022; both men are in Venezuela and remain at large, and an indictment is only an allegation.
inside: Prosecutors say a state oil contractor's money bought two senior prosecutors, so Venezuela's prosecution service dropped the case against it.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 8 March 2022

n: Collection agents and a BNI branch head staged KUR loans in Jember
org_label: CV Jawara Tani and CV Idris Afnan Jaya
rank: Branch head, BNI Jember
d: KUR is Indonesia's subsidised credit scheme for small businesses, paid out through state-owned banks. On 8 July 2026 the East Java High Prosecutor's Office named three suspects over KUR lending at the Jember branch of the state-owned bank BNI: MFH, the former branch head, and two collection agents, AM of CV Jawara Tani and IIS of CV Idris Afnan Jaya. Prosecutors say the agents put forward unqualified fictitious borrowers, used other people's identities on the applications and had verification approved outside the rules, and that money meant for borrowers was used to cover bad loans and for themselves. A state audit puts the loss at Rp41,487,138,481, Rp12.59bn of it with the two agents. BNI says the case follows its own 2024 report.
cite: Kontan, 14 July 2026 (Kejati Jatim suspects, BPKP audit figure, BNI statement)
inside: Two outside collection agents reached state-owned BNI's Jember branch head, who approved verification outside the rules so their fictitious borrowers drew subsidised credit.

n: A third party and a state bank's Asahan branch head staged KUR loans
org_label: an unnamed third party in Asahan
rank: Branch head of a state-owned bank in Asahan
d: On 9 December 2025 the Asahan district prosecutors in North Sumatra named two suspects over micro KUR lending in 2022 at a state-owned bank: WF, 56, the former branch head, and TAS, 36, a field loan officer the prosecutors describe as a BRI mantri. Prosecutors say the lending was arranged from the start between the branch head, a third party they did not identify, and field officers. About 38 residents were asked for their identity cards for what they were told was KUR paperwork; not all had businesses, those questioned said they had never borrowed, and they were asked to sign documents and given Rp1m each. The loss is put at Rp2,443,675,922.
cite: Detik, 9 December 2025 (Kejari Asahan: two suspects, scheme, 38 residents, loss figure)
inside: Prosecutors say an outside third party worked with the state bank's branch head and field officers, so villagers' identity papers became loans the villagers never asked for.

n: A borrower and two branch heads used 16 nominees for a state bank's KUR
org_label: FS, the user of the KUR funds
rank: Branch heads, state-owned bank, Martapura
d: On 28 April 2026 the South Sumatra High Prosecutor's Office named three suspects over subsidised KUR lending between 2020 and 2023 at a state bank branch in Martapura, East Ogan Komering Ulu: KS, branch head in 2021 and 2022, SF, branch head from 2022 to 2024, and FS, who used the money. Prosecutors say the two branch heads told credit and legal supervisors to have analysts and account officers prepare feasibility papers for FS's business, and that the loans were applied for in the names of 16 borrowers to finance one project. The alleged loss is about Rp3.9bn. Investigators questioned 41 witnesses. KS and FS were detained; SF was not, because he was going on pilgrimage.
cite: Metro TV News, 28 April 2026 (Kejati Sumsel: three suspects, scheme, loss figure)
inside: Prosecutors say an outside borrower's project was financed through two successive branch heads, who had the bank's own analysts dress 16 nominee borrowers up as eligible.

n: A developer and BNI Pontianak staff drew Rp14bn on forged papers
rank: Senior relationship manager and credit risk manager, BNI Pontianak
d: PT Mulia Jaya Land, a West Kalimantan housing developer run by Wendy alias Asia, obtained a Rp9bn construction working-capital facility and a Rp3bn further facility from the state-owned bank BNI's credit centres in Pontianak. The Supreme Court found that supplier invoices were inflated so the firm avoided putting in its own 30 per cent, that another company's office address was used without its owner's knowledge, that working capital was worked out from draft accounts the accounting firm denied issuing. A state audit put the loss at Rp14,182,333,020. The Pontianak court released all the defendants in July 2023; on appeal the Supreme Court jailed Wendy for eight years with Rp14.1bn to repay, and the bank's senior relationship manager and credit risk manager for three years and two and a half.
cite: Dandapala, 6 January 2025 (Supreme Court cassation: scheme, loss figure, sentences)
inside: A developer got credit from state-owned BNI on forged and borrowed documents, through bank officers the Supreme Court convicted with it for waving the checks through.

n: A property firm and two Bank DKI branch heads lent on fake debtors
rank: Branch heads, Bank DKI
d: Bank DKI is the bank owned by the Jakarta city government. Between 2011 and 2017 the head of its Muara Angke sub-branch, M Taufik, and the head of its Permata Hijau branch, Joko Pranoto, paid out staged cash apartment loans to PT Broadbiz Asia using falsified borrower data: the people named as borrowers had never applied, and the loans had no collateral, so when they went bad the bank had nothing to recover against. The loss was put at about Rp39.15bn. On 10 August 2022 the Central Jakarta District Court jailed the two branch heads for four years each with Rp200m fines, and Broadbiz Asia's president director Robby Irwanto for ten years with Rp39.15bn to repay. The verdict was open to appeal when reported.
cite: CNN Indonesia, 11 August 2022 (verdicts of 10 August 2022, scheme, loss figure)
inside: A property company drew city-owned Bank DKI's apartment loans in the names of people who never applied, through two branch heads convicted alongside its director.

n: A data supplier paid BPR Samarinda's credit chief for fictitious loans
org_label: SN, a supplier of fictitious borrower data
rank: Head of credit division, BPR Kota Samarinda
d: BPR Kota Samarinda is a small municipal bank in East Kalimantan. On 3 December 2025 Samarinda police named two suspects over lending in 2019 and 2020: AS, head of the bank's credit division, and SN, who police say supplied fictitious prospective-borrower data, including data for eight borrowers against a single piece of collateral. Police say 15 fictitious credits worth Rp2.745bn were paid out, four of them against photocopied collateral papers, that repayments from three borrowers were misused and that a customer's deposit was paid out without the owner's approval. A state audit put the loss at Rp4,683,553,134. Police say SN received about Rp2.65bn and that a receipt for money passed from SN to AS is among the evidence; how much AS received is not stated.
cite: Detik, 4 December 2025 (Polresta Samarinda: suspects, scheme, loss figure, receipt among evidence)
inside: Police say the man who fed the municipal bank fictitious borrower data also passed money to its credit chief, who then let the loans through.

n: Two developers and Bank Jateng's Blora branch head funded fake projects
org_label: PT Lentera Emas Raya and PT Gading Mas Properti
rank: Branch head, Bank Jateng Blora
d: Bank Jateng is the development bank owned by Central Java province. Its Blora branch lent against two six-storey housing blocks, in Kalibata in Jakarta and in Bekasi, that did not exist; the applications came from PT Lentera Emas Raya, for Rp10bn in 2018 and Rp7.5bn in 2019. The bank found the fraud when it checked the work order for the Jakarta block, which named army headquarters as the client: neither the site nor the army knew of any such project. The collateral was seven land certificates held only as photocopies. The Semarang corruption court jailed the former branch head, Rudatin Pamungkas, for 13 years, finding that he had enriched Ubaydillah Rouf of PT Gading Mas Properti and Teguh Kristiono of PT Lentera Emas Raya.
cite: Antara Jateng, 15 March 2022 (hearing: the two fictitious projects, the companies, photocopied collateral); VOI (Semarang corruption court: 13 years, Rp650m fine, the two directors enriched, Rp115bn loss)
inside: Two housing developers got province-owned Bank Jateng's Blora branch head to fund buildings that did not exist, and the court found he had enriched them.

n: Two property firms paid BTN's president director Rp4.5bn for credit
org_label: PT Pelangi Putera Mandiri and PT Titanium Property
rank: President director, Bank Tabungan Negara
d: Bank Tabungan Negara (BTN) is Indonesia's state housing bank. On 4 August 2021 the Jakarta corruption court found that its former president director, Maryono, had taken Rp4.506bn from two property companies through his son-in-law, Widi Kusuma Purwanto. The court tied part of it to PT Pelangi Putera Mandiri's application for a credit facility, which Maryono approved, and Rp870m paid in instalments by Ichsan Hassan, a commissioner of PT Titanium Property, whose credit application went to BTN's central directors. Maryono was jailed for three years and fined Rp250m; his son-in-law, Yunan Anwar of Pelangi Putera Mandiri and Ichsan Hassan were each given the same. He was acquitted of money laundering, the court reasoning that the state loss had not been calculated.
cite: Detik, 4 August 2021 (verdict, the Rp4.506bn, the two companies, co-defendants, money-laundering acquittal)
inside: Two property companies paid the state housing bank's own chief executive, through his son-in-law, and he approved the credit facility one of them had applied for.

n: A developer paid a state bank's risk officer to pass fake mortgages
rank: Retail risk officer of a state-owned bank
d: Prosecutors in Karawang, West Java, allege that PT Bumi Arta Sedayu, part of the Citra Swarna group, drew mortgages from a state-owned bank for its Citra Swarna Grande and Kartika Residence estates at Klari between 2021 and 2024 through a team it set up to handle mortgage applications, using borrowed names, manipulated borrower data and forged documents.
