A state audit calculation puts the loss at Rp237,078,338,982 across 445 borrowers. Three of the developer's leaders, named as VY, OH and HH, were detained on 4 September 2026. On 8 September prosecutors named a fifth suspect, DMP, a retail risk officer at the bank, said to have taken Rp1.45bn from HJ of the developer to get the applications through. Bank Tabungan Negara has responded publicly as the lender.
cite: Antara Megapolitan, 4 September 2026 (three developer suspects, scheme, Rp237bn audit figure, 445 borrowers); AFU.id, 8 September 2026 (fifth suspect DMP, retail risk officer, Rp1.45bn from HJ); Kontan, 24 May 2026 (BTN as lender, its statement, forged employment letters and nominee borrowers)
inside: Prosecutors say the developer paid the state bank's own risk officer Rp1.45bn, so mortgages in borrowed names and on forged papers cleared its credit checks.

n: A finance firm's owner's son got Bank Jambi to buy Rp310bn of its notes
rank: Marketing director, later president director, Bank Jambi
d: Medium term notes are corporate debt securities. In 2017 and 2018 Bank Jambi, owned by Jambi province, bought notes issued by the consumer finance company PT Sunprima Nusantara Pembiayaan (SNP), whose accounts prosecutors say had been dressed up to look healthy. Prosecutors allege that an unofficial fee of three per cent, was partly used to give benefits to certain parties at Bank Jambi, among them a house, money, cars and foreign travel, and that the bank then bought the notes outside its own procedures. Jambi's high prosecutors put the loss at Rp310,118,271,000 and in May 2023 detained the bank's president director, Yunsak El Halcon. On 14 February 2025 the Jambi court jailed Leo Darwin, son of SNP's owner, for 16 years.
cite: Antara Jambi, 9 May 2023 (Kejati Jambi: scheme, the alleged 3% fee and benefits at Bank Jambi, Rp310bn, four suspects); PN Jambi 46/Pid.Sus-TPK/2024 (Leo Darwin: 16 years, Rp204.82bn restitution, decided 14 February 2025)
inside: Prosecutors say part of a hidden fee went as houses, cars and travel to people inside province-owned Bank Jambi, which then bought the finance firm's notes outside its own rules.

n: Contractors and BPD Sulsel's Pasangkayu branch heads took Rp41bn
rank: Branch head and credit division head, BPD Sulsel Pasangkayu
d: BPD Sulsel is the development bank owned by South Sulawesi province. On 12 May 2008 the Mamuju District Court convicted ten people over about Rp41bn taken from its Pasangkayu branch, in what is now West Sulawesi. The branch's head, Tahir Karim, was jailed for eight years, and its credit division head, Arman Laode Hasan, for six, with 159 credit-guarantee certificates seized from him. Seven contractors were jailed for four to six years, among them Hj Ani, who was ordered to repay Rp5.4bn, and a former public works equipment chief, Rismadi Candra, was given ten years. The defendants said they would appeal, and about ten more suspects were still being questioned. The report does not set out how the money moved.
cite: Antara, 12 May 2008 (Mamuju District Court verdicts, roles, sentences, Rp41bn)
inside: Seven contractors were convicted alongside the province-owned bank branch's head and credit chief over about Rp41bn drawn out of that branch.

n: A businessman and a BRI officer ran 252 fictitious KUR borrowers
rank: Field loan officer, BRI Unit Sudirman, Ciamis
d: Between 2021 and 2023 subsidised KUR and village credit loans were issued to 252 borrowers at the Sudirman unit of the state-owned bank BRI in Ciamis, West Java, which prosecutors say were fictitious. The unit's field loan officer, Fandu Eka Resi, was jailed in 2024 for eight years, fined Rp500m and ordered to repay Rp5.6bn; prosecutors say he began the scheme and handed out the loans, while a self-employed businessman named only as AJ found the false customer data that made the borrowers look real, and gained about Rp4.1bn. The West Java High Prosecutor's Office puts the loss at about Rp9.1bn. AJ had been on the run for nearly two years, reportedly including time in Cambodia, and was arrested in Jakarta on 25 June 2025 and detained at Bandung.
cite: Antara, June 2025 (Kejati Jabar: the two suspects, 252 fictitious borrowers, the field officer's 2024 sentence, Rp9.1bn loss, AJ's arrest)
inside: An outside businessman supplied the false borrower data and state-owned BRI's own field officer issued the loans, so 252 fictitious borrowers drew subsidised credit.

n: A broker, a bank unit head and a village clerk staged KUR in Malang
rank: Unit head and credit officer of a state-owned bank, Kepanjen
d: In 2024 the Malang district prosecutors in East Java detained three people over fictitious KUR lending at the Kepanjen branch of a state-owned bank: a former unit head, a credit officer and a third-party broker, who are said to have used the names of dozens of borrowers. The Surabaya corruption court has ruled on that case. On 20 December 2025 prosecutors detained a village official from Jenggolo, named only as S, who they say made 52 fictitious certificates of business, the document needed to apply for KUR, at the request of the people already sentenced, without the village head's knowledge. Prosecutors put his own gain at about Rp220m. An accounting firm put the loss on the lending, made between 2021 and 2024, at Rp4,040,000,000.
cite: JatimTimes, 20 December 2025 (Kejari Malang: the village official's arrest, the 52 fictitious certificates, Rp4.04bn loss, the three convicted in the 2024 case)
inside: A broker outside the bank worked with its unit head and credit officer, and a village clerk forged the business certificates, so dozens of names became subsidised loans.

n: A fake works order got Bank BJB Indramayu to pay out a works loan
rank: Employee, Bank BJB Indramayu
d: Bank BJB is the development bank owned by the West Java and Banten provinces. An official of Indramayu's culture and tourism office, Abdul Rohmat, issued a construction work order for work that did not exist; two private men, Toriq and Azmi, took it and passed it to Prima Kurnia, an employee of Bank BJB in Indramayu, who used it to process the payout of a construction working-capital credit. Police put the loss at nearly Rp600m. On 20 September 2021 the Bandung District Court jailed Prima Kurnia for four years and fined him Rp400m; he had repaid Rp114m before the verdict. Abdul Rohmat was given six years, and Toriq and Azmi four years each.
cite: Antara Jabar, 20 September 2021 (Bandung District Court verdicts, roles, the fictitious work order, loss figure)
inside: Two private men carried a fictitious government work order to a Bank BJB employee, who used it to release province-owned bank credit for building work nobody did.

n: Dhanawibawa (Pan Arcadia) ran two funds built for Jiwasraya's money
org_label: PT Dhanawibawa Manajemen Investasi (now PT Pan Arcadia Capital)
who: Dhanawibawa Manajemen Investasi (now Pan Arcadia Capital)
d: PT Dhanawibawa Manajemen Investasi (now PT Pan Arcadia Capital), a private fund manager, was charged over money that PT Asuransi Jiwasraya, Indonesia's state-owned life insurer, placed in mutual funds the firm ran. Jiwasraya held two of its funds. Prosecutors said the defendants told the manager which shares to buy, at what price and through which broker, and that those shares were risky or hard to sell. Prosecutors put the loss through this manager at Rp2.02 trillion, part of over Rp12 trillion found by the state audit board. Thirteen fund managers were named corporate suspects in June 2020, after the insurer's 2019 collapse left it unable to pay maturing policies; on 16 August 2021 the corruption court struck out their joint indictment as void, over how the cases had been joined.
inside: A private fund manager built funds to hold the state insurer's money and let its officers and favoured investors pick the shares, so Jiwasraya's investment decisions served them.
rank: Jiwasraya investment portfolio
cite: Kontan, 26 June 2020 (indictment of Jiwasraya president director Hendrisman Rahim, naming the 13 investment managers and the per-manager loss figures); Kontan, 18 August 2021 (Central Jakarta corruption court voids the joint indictment)

n: OSO Manajemen Investasi set up two Jiwasraya-only equity funds
d: PT OSO Manajemen Investasi, a private fund manager, was charged over money that PT Asuransi Jiwasraya, Indonesia's state-owned life insurer, placed in mutual funds the firm ran. Prosecutors said the insurer and the firm agreed to create two funds for the purpose, the OSO Flores and OSO Moluccas equity funds. Prosecutors put the loss through this manager at Rp521 billion, part of over Rp12 trillion found by the state audit board. The case followed the insurer's 2019 collapse, when it could not pay maturing policies. Thirteen fund managers were named corporate suspects in June 2020; on 16 August 2021 the corruption court struck out their joint indictment as void, over how the cases had been joined rather than its contents.

d: PT Pinnacle Persada Investama, a private fund manager, was charged over money that PT Asuransi Jiwasraya, Indonesia's state-owned life insurer, placed in mutual funds the firm ran. Prosecutors said one of its funds, Pinnacle Dana Prima, was created to hold the insurer's money and was controlled by Joko Hartono Tirto, a businessman linked to two investors. Prosecutors put the loss through this manager at Rp1.8 trillion, part of over Rp12 trillion found by the state audit board. d: PT Millenium Capital Management, a private fund manager, was charged over money that PT Asuransi Jiwasraya, Indonesia's state-owned life insurer, placed in mutual funds the firm ran. n: Maybank Asset Management convicted over Jiwasraya's fund money
d: PT Maybank Asset Management, a private fund manager, was convicted of corruption on 11 April 2022 by the Jakarta corruption court over money the state life insurer PT Asuransi Jiwasraya placed in a mutual fund it ran. Prosecutors said the firm agreed to and carried out buying and selling of the instruments underlying Jiwasraya's funds, and that those trades were controlled by the investors Heru Hidayat and Benny Tjokrosaputro through two intermediaries. The court fined it Rp1 billion and ordered Rp5.7 billion in restitution, suspended it from investment work for five months and revoked a fund licence. It was cleared of money laundering. The Jakarta High Court kept the penalty in October 2022.
inside: A private fund manager let two outside investors control the trades inside the state insurer's mutual fund, so Jiwasraya's money bought what those investors wanted.
cite: Detik, 12 April 2022 (verdicts of 11 April 2022); Bisnis, 24 October 2022 (appeal)
rank: Jiwasraya investment portfolio

n: Prospera Asset Management convicted over Jiwasraya's fund money
d: PT Prospera Asset Management, a private fund manager, was convicted of corruption on 11 April 2022 by the Jakarta corruption court. The state life insurer PT Asuransi Jiwasraya held two Prospera funds, Dana Berkembang and Syariah Saham, which prosecutors said were not offered to anyone outside the insurer. Prosecutors said the firm carried out trades in the instruments behind those funds under the control of the investors Heru Hidayat and Benny Tjokrosaputro, acting through two intermediaries. The court fined it Rp1.2 billion and ordered restitution of Rp11.5 billion, the management fees it had received, suspended its investment work for five months and revoked two fund licences. It was cleared of money laundering.
inside: A fund manager ran funds sold only to the state insurer and took trading orders from outside investors, so Jiwasraya's money served them and earned the firm fees.
cite: Detik, 12 April 2022 (verdicts of 11 April 2022); Kontan, 26 June 2020 (the two Prospera funds)
rank: Jiwasraya investment portfolio

n: Sinarmas Asset Management acquitted, then convicted on cassation
d: PT Sinarmas Asset Management, a private fund manager, ran the SimasSaham Ultima fund, which prosecutors said was dedicated to holding money from the state life insurer PT Asuransi Jiwasraya, with a loss to the state of Rp77 billion. The Central Jakarta corruption court convicted the company and fined it Rp1 billion. The Jakarta High Court acquitted it, reasoning that the firm had never been found in breach of the rules or sanctioned by the stock exchange or the financial regulator, and questioning a loss figure based on potential rather than actual loss; two of its judges dissented. On 2 May 2023 the Supreme Court granted the prosecutors' cassation, annulled the acquittal and restored the conviction and the fine.
inside: A fund manager ran a mutual fund made to hold the state insurer's money, and the Supreme Court held that this placement of Jiwasraya's funds was unlawful.
cite: Detik, 4 May 2023 (Supreme Court cassation dated 2 May 2023); Kontan, 20 October 2022 (High Court acquittal); Kontan, 26 June 2020 (the fund and the loss figure)
rank: Jiwasraya investment portfolio

n: OSO Manajemen Investasi charged over Asabri's fund money
rank: Asabri investment portfolio
d: PT OSO Manajemen Investasi, a private fund manager, is one of ten companies put on trial at the Central Jakarta corruption court on 29 August 2025 over money belonging to PT Asabri, the social insurance company for Indonesia's armed forces and police, between 2012 and 2019. Prosecutors say the firms supplied Asabri with mutual funds without proper analysis and moved underperforming shares into them so the trades looked profitable, taking management fees they were not entitled to. Prosecutors cited this firm as their example: Rp300 billion placed in one of its funds. The indictment puts the loss through this firm at Rp300 billion, out of Rp7.87 trillion. On 4 November 2026 prosecutors asked for a Rp4 billion fine, seizure of Rp9.83 billion and a two-year freeze on its activities.
inside: Prosecutors say a private fund manager supplied the armed forces' insurer with mutual funds that absorbed poor shares, so Asabri's money served the firms' fees rather than the fund.

n: A land broker and two Indoport firms drew on Pelindo's pension fund
org_label: Ahmad Adhi Aristo, PT Indoport Utama and PT Indoport Prima
who: a land broker and two Indoport companies
rank: Dapen Pelindo (DP4) board and investment unit
d: The attorney general's office named six suspects on 10 May 2023 over DP4, the pension fund of the state port operator Pelindo's port and dredging arm, with an indicated loss of about Rp148 billion. Five were the fund's own officers, including its president director Edi Winoto; the sixth was Ahmad Adhi Aristo, a private land broker said to have taken unlawful fees on land the fund bought in Depok and Palembang. Prosecutors said Winoto approved land purchases outside normal procedure and capital injections into PT Indoport Utama and PT Indoport Prima, where he was a commissioner, and that the money paid out was never accounted for. He was sentenced to six years; on 13 June 2024 the Jakarta High Court raised it to ten years, with Rp75 billion in restitution.
inside: A private land broker and two companies a fund director sat on reached inside a state pension fund, so its land buying and capital injections paid them.
cite: Infobank News, 10 May 2023 (six suspects, roles and mechanism); Bloomberg Technoz (allegations against each suspect); Bisnis, 18 June 2024 (Jakarta High Court appeal of 13 June 2024)

n: A fund manager and a broker emptied Bukit Asam's pension fund
org_label: PT Millenium Capital Management, PT Strategic Management Services and brokers
who: Millenium Capital Management and three other outside parties
rank: Dana Pensiun Bukit Asam board
d: Jakarta prosecutors named five suspects on 24 April 2024 over the pension fund of PT Bukit Asam, the state coal miner, putting the loss at Rp234.5 billion on a state audit. They said that between 2013 and 2018 the fund's president director Zulheri and its investment director placed members' money in two Millenium mutual funds under an arrangement with Angie Christina, who owned PT Millenium Capital Management, and in two listed stocks through the broker Sutedy Alwan Anis and Romi Hafnur, a consultant to PT Ratu Prabu Energy. The deals promised buy-backs returning 12 to 25 per cent, which were never paid. All six were convicted on 10 February 2025; Zulheri got nine years, and on appeal the Jakarta High Court raised Danny Boestamy's sentence to thirteen years.
inside: An outside fund manager, a broker and two consultants struck return promises with a state miner's pension fund directors, so members' money bought what those outsiders were selling.
cite: CNN Indonesia, 24 April 2024 (five suspects, mechanism, Rp234.5bn); Katadata, 10 February 2025 (verdicts); Dandapala, 11 April 2025 (Jakarta High Court appeal of 10 April 2025)

n: Piter Rasiman steered Jiwasraya's fund trades for two investors
org_label: Piter Rasiman and PT Himalaya Energi Perkasa
rank: Jiwasraya investment portfolio
d: Piter Rasiman, president director of the private firm PT Himalaya Energi Perkasa, was one of the intermediaries through whom two investors steered the money of PT Asuransi Jiwasraya, the state-owned life insurer. When the Jakarta corruption court convicted two of the fund managers on 11 April 2022, it recorded the prosecutors' case that the buying and selling behind Jiwasraya's mutual funds was controlled by Heru Hidayat and Benny Tjokrosaputro through Joko Hartono Tirto and Rasiman, in breach of the capital markets law. Rasiman was prosecuted separately in the Jiwasraya case and sentenced to 20 years in prison and a Rp1 billion fine, with six months' detention in default.
inside: An outside businessman acted as the channel through which two investors controlled what the state insurer's mutual funds bought, so Jiwasraya's money served them.
cite: Detik, 12 April 2022 (verdicts of 11 April 2022, naming Rasiman as one of the intermediaries); CNN Indonesia, 8 February 2025 (his post and his 20-year sentence and Rp1 billion fine)

n: Police suspect kickbacks reached the prosecutor who ran the Asabri case
org_label: unidentified payers and a detained private co-accused
rank: Deputy Attorney General for Special Crimes
d: Indonesia's national police named Febrie Adriansyah, the former Deputy Attorney General for Special Crimes and the country's most senior anti-corruption prosecutor, a suspect on 11 July 2026. He had led the prosecution of PT Asabri, the armed forces' social insurance company, over losses put at about Rp22.7 trillion. Police say the case concerns the handling of the Asabri matter and other corruption files, and suspect kickbacks were paid between 2020 and 2025 to compromise follow-up investigations or the recovery of state assets tied to the fund. They have not said who paid. A private co-accused, identified only as DR, is detained on money laundering charges. Police found cash and gold bullion at his house; he said the wealth belonged to a third party he would not name.
inside: Police suspect outside money reached the prosecutor in charge of the Asabri case, so the state's own follow-up inquiries and asset recovery were held back.
cite: JawaPos, 11-12 July 2026 (suspect designation, charges, searches); Investor Trust, 11 July 2026 (the Asabri link, the 2020-2025 period, the detained co-accused, the seized cash and gold)

n: Mitra Bina Selaras billed state insurer Jasindo for work never done
rank: retail operations director, PT Jasindo
d: On 29 April 2025 the Jakarta corruption court convicted Sahata Lumban Tobing, retail operations director of PT Jasindo, the state-owned general insurer, of corruption carried out together with the private firm PT Mitra Bina Selaras. The court found the two had run fictitious activities, costing the state Rp38 billion. Tobing was sentenced to three years and six months and fined Rp150 million, with the Rp525 million he had already returned counted towards his restitution. The company's owner, Toras Sotarduga Panggabean, was sentenced separately to two years and four months and the same fine. The ruling does not set out how the money reached the company beyond the fictitious activities.
inside: A private company and a state insurer's own director billed for activity that never happened, so Jasindo's spending went to the outside firm.
cite: CNN Indonesia, 29 April 2025 (verdict of 29 April 2025, Jakarta corruption court)

n: A company's HR head used BPJS claim verifiers to fake 391 accident claims
org_label: Renu Arianthi Sani, PT Mitra Adi Perkasa and PT Empat Enam Sejahtera
rank: claim verifiers, BPJS Ketenagakerjaan
d: BPJS Ketenagakerjaan is the public body that runs Indonesia's workers' social security, successor to PT Jamsostek. Prosecutors told the Jakarta corruption court on 9 July 2026 that Renu Arianthi Sani, head of human resources at PT Mitra Adi Perkasa, worked with two of the body's own claim verifiers, Sri Listiani and Sayoko Adi Nugroho. After one of her claims was refused because the accident happened outside working hours, the indictment says Listiani told her to alter attendance records and inflate a hospital receipt, later lending her a genuine paid claim file as a template; about 391 work-accident claims were faked between 2014 and 2024. On 8 October 2026 the court convicted all three; Sani got seven years.
inside: An outside company's HR head got the social security fund's own claim verifiers to pass fabricated accident claims, so public money paid out to her.
cite: EmitenNews, 10 July 2026 (indictment read 9 July 2026, defendants' posts and mechanism); Dandapala, verdict of 8 October 2026 at the Central Jakarta corruption court (sentences, fines, restitution, Rp24.54bn loss)

n: CBI: Canara Bank manager in Patna opened mule accounts for cyber fraudsters
org_label: an organised cyber-fraud network using mule bank accounts
rank: assistant manager, Canara Bank branch, Patna
d: India's Central Bureau of Investigation arrested Shalini Sinha, then an assistant manager at a Canara Bank branch in Patna, on 24 December 2025, alleging she helped cyber criminals open and operate mule accounts and guided them through the transfers. A mule account is one set up with falsified identity papers and used to move money stolen from victims. The agency says it gathered evidence that the bankers arrested received a quid pro quo for helping the fraudsters, and that they advised them how to avoid the bank's system-generated red flags. She was arrested in Varanasi and was to be produced in court after transit remand. The CBI had already searched 61 locations, arrested 13 people and filed charge sheets under the Prevention of Corruption Act.
inside: A cyber-fraud network allegedly paid a Canara Bank manager to open accounts for it, so the bank's own identity checks let stolen money through.
cite: PTI via NewsDrum, 24 December 2025; CBI press release of 24 December 2025 reproduced by TaxGuru, 25 December 2025

n: CBI: Axis Bank associate in Patna helped open and run mule accounts
org_label: an organised cyber-fraud network using mule bank accounts
rank: business development associate, Axis Bank branch, Patna
d: India's Central Bureau of Investigation arrested Abhishek Kumar, a former business development associate at an Axis Bank branch in Patna, on 24 December 2025, alleging he conspired with cyber criminals to open mule accounts and helped them move funds. Mule accounts are opened with falsified identity documents and used to siphon off money taken from victims. The agency says there is evidence the bankers arrested received a quid pro quo, and that they told the fraudsters how to avoid the bank's system-generated red flags. He was arrested at Betia in Bihar, in the same case in which a Canara Bank manager was held the same day. The CBI says the role of other bank officials is still being investigated.
inside: A cyber-fraud network allegedly paid an Axis Bank associate to open accounts for it, defeating the bank's identity checks so stolen money could be moved.
cite: PTI via NewsDrum, 24 December 2025; CBI press release of 24 December 2025 reproduced by TaxGuru, 25 December 2025

n: Three IndusInd Bank staff in Ahmedabad held over mule accounts
org_label: a cyber-fraud ring running a fake stock and IPO trading app
rank: branch manager and two other officers, IndusInd Bank, Chandkheda and Gota branches, Ahmedabad
d: Ahmedabad's cyber crime cell arrested five people in February 2026, among them three IndusInd Bank staff: Pooja Priyat, manager of the Chandkheda branch, Heena Darji, an ECBD manager at the same branch, and Mahesh Tarani, a key account manager at the Gota branch. Police say they helped open mule accounts for a ring that took Rs 1.54 crore from a local businessman through a fake stock and IPO trading app, and that registered mobile numbers and email addresses were altered without the account holders' knowledge so the ring controlled the accounts. One tranche of Rs 10 lakh went into an account named 'Mahadev Enterprise' and was spent on gold. Police said it was the first time senior bank officials had been arrested in the city for this.
inside: An online investment fraud ring reached IndusInd Bank through its own branch officers, who allegedly opened and altered accounts so the ring could collect and hide victims' money.
cite: DeshGujarat, 25 February 2026

n: Rajkot: bankers held over 85 fake-firm accounts used for cyber fraud money
org_label: a mule-account network moving cyber-fraud proceeds
rank: bank manager and two personal bankers, Yes Bank, Axis Bank and HDFC Bank, Rajkot district
d: Rajkot Rural Police arrested three bankers in April 2026 in an inquiry they call Operation Mule Hunt: Kalpesh Dangariya, a bank manager now with Axis Bank and formerly at Yes Bank branches in Jamkandorna, Movia and Padadhari; Maulik Kamani, a personal banker at Yes Bank; and Anurag Baldha, a former Yes Bank personal banker now with HDFC Bank. Police say at least 85 accounts, mainly at Yes Bank, Axis Bank and ICICI Bank, were opened in the names of unsuspecting people as proprietors of fake firms, using forged letters from the Rajkot and Gondal agricultural produce market committees so the accounts would be classed as agricultural. Investigators estimate more than Rs 2,500 crore passed through them, and 1,930 complaints report Rs 74 crore of cyber fraud.
inside: A mule-account network reached three private banks through their own staff, who allegedly let forged papers past account-opening checks so cyber-fraud money could be moved.
cite: DeshGujarat, April 2026

n: Hyderabad police held 32 bank staff of ten banks over mule accounts
org_label: cyber-fraud syndicates sourcing mule accounts through bank staff
rank: managers, relationship managers, KYC approvers, field officers and clerks at ten banks
d: Hyderabad city police arrested 52 people in a week-long operation reported on 20 April 2026, which they called Operation Octopus 2.0, using 16 teams across nine states. Thirty-two of those held were bank staff, from banks including IndusInd Bank, Bandhan Bank, Bank of Baroda, Federal Bank, IDFC First Bank, Karnataka Bank, Karur Vysya Bank, AU Small Finance Bank, Equitas Small Finance Bank and HDFC Bank, and ranged from managers and relationship managers to KYC approvers, field officers and clerks. Police say they opened mule accounts by bypassing due diligence and know-your-customer rules, so illicit funds could be routed and layered. The city's cybercrime police station had traced about 350 accounts linked to nearly 850 complaints and transactions of close to Rs 150 crore. None of those arrested was named.
inside: Cyber-fraud syndicates reached ten banks through their own staff, including the officers who approve identity checks, so accounts for laundering money were opened past those checks.
cite: Moneylife, 20 April 2026

n: Agribank Branch 7's director ordered prosecuted over a borrower's house
org_label: a borrower in the Agribank Branch 7 lending case
rank: director, Agribank Branch 7, Ho Chi Minh City
d: On 21 December 2015 the Ho Chi Minh City People's Court sentenced Pham Van Cu, former director of Branch 7 of Agribank, Vietnam's state-owned agriculture bank, to 20 years for breaking lending rules in a case costing 601 billion dong; two branch staff, Kieu Dinh Tho and Do Thi Thu Ha, were given 16 and nine years. Announcing the verdict, the panel issued a decision to prosecute Cu for giving and receiving bribes, saying his conduct over a house at 421 Nguyen Oanh in Go Vap district showed signs of bribery: he had gone in on the house with a party to the case, Thang, without actually contributing capital, and it was registered as co-owned with his wife. No report of that prosecution's outcome could be found.
inside: A borrower is alleged to have given the state bank branch director who approved its lending a stake in a house he paid nothing for, and the court ordered him prosecuted for bribery.
cite: Bao Dau Thau, 22 December 2015

n: Viet A's commissions reached Tien Giang's disease control centre
rank: director, Tien Giang Centre for Disease Control
d: The Covid test kit maker Viet A had the purchasing papers of Tien Giang province's Centre for Disease Control written after the event so that it would win, then paid the centre's staff a commission of over 2 billion dong. On the afternoon of 25 April 2024 the Tien Giang Provincial People's Court heard that the centre's director Nguyen Ngoc Chon told staff to ask for an advance of test kits, after which they assembled the bidding file so Viet A would be the winner. The centre paid Viet A over 11 billion dong, and the state lost over 7 billion. All four were convicted of breaking the bidding rules but exempted from punishment; the commissions were confiscated.
inside: Viet A had a provincial disease control centre's tender file written around its own kits after delivery, and paid its officers over 2 billion dong in commission.
cite: Tuoi Tre, 25 April 2024

n: Viet A's percentages bought the leaders of Ha Giang's disease centre
rank: director and testing head, Ha Giang Centre for Disease Control
d: Viet A, the Hanoi company that made Vietnam's Covid test reagents, paid the senior staff of Ha Giang province's Centre for Disease Control percentages of its contracts, and in return the centre took its reagents without a proper tender. The Ha Giang Provincial People's Court tried the case on 10 and 11 August 2023, separately from the national Viet A trial. The centre took reagents on advance payment, then signed contracts worth over 7.839 billion dong. Defendants took 1.49 billion dong in percentages inside and outside the contracts; the testing head Phan Thi Nga took 825 million and the director Nguyen Tran Tuan 250 million. The state lost over 5.06 billion dong. Nga was given 16 years six months and Tuan 11 years, with four others convicted.
inside: Viet A paid percentages to the director, testing head and chief accountant of a provincial disease control centre, which then bought its reagents outside the bidding rules.
cite: Bao Phap luat Viet Nam, 11 August 2023

n: Viet A's staff and Dak Lak's disease centre took the centre's kit money
rank: Dak Lak Centre for Disease Control
d: Viet A's own staff worked with the officers of Dak Lak province's Centre for Disease Control to lend the centre Covid test supplies first and paper over the bidding afterwards, and money was taken out of the centre's funds. The Dak Lak Provincial People's Court gave its verdict on 18 June 2026, a separate trial from the national Viet A case. Viet A's chairman Phan Quoc Viet was given seven years, bringing his total to 30 under an earlier military court appeal judgment; two Viet A sales staff, Dinh Le Le Na and Tran Thi Nguyen Hang, were given seven years each. Seven defendants, among them the former centre director Trinh Quang Tri, were exempted from punishment. The state lost over 1.5 billion dong.
inside: Viet A's sales staff worked inside a provincial disease control centre's purchasing, delivering kits before any tender and taking money from the centre's funds.
cite: Nhan Dan, 18 June 2026

n: Viet A's thank-you money reached Thua Thien Hue's disease centre
rank: chief accountant, Thua Thien Hue Centre for Disease Control
d: Viet A sold its Covid test kits to Thua Thien Hue province's Centre for Disease Control through a direct appointment that skipped the proper approvals, then paid the centre's chief accountant money it called thanks. The People's Court of Hue Regional Area 1 tried the accountant, Ha Thuc Nhat, on 9 June 2026, separately from the national Viet A case. Under the then director Hoang Van Duc, Nhat prepared a shortened direct-appointment file to buy kits routed through a provincial medical equipment company; the centre approved its own purchasing plan although that power belonged to the provincial People's Committee chairman. The state lost over 1.749 billion dong. Nhat was convicted but exempted from punishment; Duc's case was suspended.
inside: Viet A paid the chief accountant of a provincial disease control centre, which bought its kits by a direct appointment it had no power to approve.
cite: VietnamPlus, 9 June 2026

n: AIC rigged the tender for Bac Lieu's water monitoring stations
rank: director, Bac Lieu Department of Natural Resources and Environment
d: AIC, a Hanoi equipment supplier, had the Bac Lieu provincial environment department's tender for surface-water monitoring stations shaped to suit it from inside, and won it above market price. The Ca Mau Provincial People's Court convicted eight people on 12 August 2026 of breaking the bidding rules. The court heard that AIC's chairwoman Nguyen Thi Thanh Nhan set up a group of companies in AIC's own group to bid as cover, had her deputies advise the department's director Pham Quoc Nam on the equipment before the project was even drafted. The state lost over 4.4 billion dong. Nhan, a fugitive tried in absentia, was given 10 years and Nam four.
inside: AIC wrote the equipment list and the prices for a provincial environment department's tender through its own staff and a tame valuer, then won it above market price.
cite: Tien Phong, 12 August 2026

n: Viet A's promised commissions reached Dong Thap's health purchasers
rank: director, Dong Thap Centre for Disease Control
d: Viet A's sales staff arranged with the officers who bought for Dong Thap province's disease control centre and general hospital that the company would show its gratitude if it won, then had the paperwork built around goods it had already delivered. The Dong Thap Provincial People's Court heard the case on 22 May 2024, apart from the national Viet A trial. Between May and September 2021 six packages of Covid kits and reagents were bought by direct appointment; five had goods borrowed from Viet A before any contract was signed, and Viet A wrote the quotation sheets for all six. The kits cost 143,461 dong each to make; the state lost over 79 billion dong. All three were given suspended sentences.
inside: Viet A's staff agreed commissions with the officials buying for a province's hospital and disease centre, wrote the quotations, and delivered before any contract existed.
cite: Tuoi Tre, 22 May 2024

n: A Viet A saleswoman drove the rigged packages at Lam Dong's disease centre
rank: director, Lam Dong Centre for Disease Control
d: A Viet A employee, Dinh Le Le Na, proposed and carried out the unlawful steps in the Covid purchasing of Lam Dong province's Centre for Disease Control, which in 2020 and 2021 was the investor for seven packages of test kits, chemicals and medical supplies. Three of those packages were found seriously flawed. The Lam Dong Provincial People's Court convicted four people on 24 April 2025, a separate trial from the national Viet A case. The former centre director Nguyen Quoc Minh went from five years to three years suspended. The state lost more than 7.2 billion dong.
inside: A test kit company's own saleswoman shaped a provincial disease centre's Covid purchasing from inside, and three of its seven packages were rigged in her employer's favour.
cite: VOH Online, 24 February 2026

n: A medical technology supplier's director was convicted with Khanh Hoa's CDC
org_label: VNDAT (Viet Nam Phat trien Cong nghe Ung dung)
rank: director, Khanh Hoa Centre for Disease Control
d: The general director of VNDAT, a medical technology supplier, was convicted alongside four officers of Khanh Hoa province's Centre for Disease Control over the centre's Covid purchasing. On 15 April 2024 the Khanh Hoa Provincial Court found six people guilty of breaking the bidding rules in the centre's 2020 and 2021 tenders for equipment and Covid test kits. The centre's former director Huynh Van Dong was given three years six months, VNDAT's former general director Nguyen Truong Giang was given 18 months, and the owner of a household business a suspended term. Nearly 16 billion dong of state money was lost. Dong paid back 2 billion dong, which the court confiscated. The report does not set out how the rules were broken.
inside: A supplier's general director was convicted with the senior officers of a provincial disease control centre over the centre's own Covid equipment and test kit tenders.
cite: RFA Vietnamese, 15 April 2024

n: NSJ's chairwoman set the price Can Tho's health department then paid
rank: director, Can Tho Department of Health
d: Hoang Thi Thuy Nga, who chaired the founding council of the medical equipment group NSJ, agreed prices with the leaders of Can Tho's health department and then supplied both the winning bids and the losing ones. On 17 February 2023 the Ho Chi Minh City People's Court convicted 20 people of breaking the bidding rules. The court heard that in 2017 Nga was introduced to the department's director Bui Thi Le Phi by the chairman of the city People's Committee; after Phi and her deputy Cao Minh Chu agreed, Nga had her staff prepare bids for NSJ and Binh An and cover bids for two other firms, while Phi and Chu had subordinates write the funding requests and tender plans to match.
inside: An equipment group's chairwoman fixed prices with a city health department's leaders and wrote both the winning and the losing bids, so her firms took four public tenders.
cite: VietnamPlus, 17 February 2023

n: NSJ's gifts won Tay Ninh's health department a direct-appointed scanner
rank: director, Tay Ninh Department of Health
d: NSJ, the Vietnamese distributor for Siemens Healthcare, had Tay Ninh's health department ask the provincial People's Committee to buy its scanner by direct appointment, and its chairwoman later gave the department's director gifts totalling 1 billion dong. On 29 December 2023 the Ho Chi Minh City People's Court sentenced 14 defendants. In 2017 Hoang Thi Thuy Nga offered the director Hoa Cong Hau a 128-slice Siemens CT scanner for the provincial general hospital, worth 28 billion dong. Between 2018 and 2020 Hau took gifts totalling 1 billion dong and the deputy 600 million; both repaid them. The state lost over 13 billion dong. Hau was given four years and Nga six.
inside: An equipment distributor had a provincial health department write the specification for its own scanner and appoint it directly, and paid the department's director 1 billion dong.
cite: Sai Gon Giai Phong, 29 December 2023

n: NSJ paid Quang Ninh's education officials 30bn dong for equipment deals
rank: director, Quang Ninh Department of Education and Training
d: Hoang Thi Thuy Nga, who chaired the founding council of the equipment group NSJ, had her companies helped to win Quang Ninh province's school equipment purchases and then paid more than 30 billion dong to three officials of the provincial education department. The Quang Ninh Provincial People's Court gave its verdict on the afternoon of 17 October 2023. The department's former director Vu Lien Oanh took 14 billion dong and was given 15 years; her planning and finance head Ngo Vui took 14.8 billion and was given 11 years; his deputy Ha Huy Long took about 1.9 billion and was given six years. Thirteen staff of NSJ and two other firms were also convicted. Over 80 billion dong is to be paid back to the provincial People's Committee.
inside: An equipment group's chairwoman paid a provincial education department's director and finance officials over 30 billion dong, and her companies took the department's purchases.
cite: VOH Online, 17 October 2023

n: Nam Phong and Viet A's kits went through Thu Duc City Hospital on commission
who: Viet A Technology and Nam Phong Company
rank: director, Thu Duc City Hospital
d: Nam Phong Company carried the Viet A Covid test kits sold to Thu Duc City Hospital, a public hospital in Ho Chi Minh City, and paid the hospital's medical supplies officer a commission for pushing the purchase through. On 18 June 2024 the Ho Chi Minh City People's Court found that the hospital's director Nguyen Minh Quan signed decisions approving bidding plans that picked Viet A and Nam Phong before their bid files were checked, and that the supplies officer Truong Thi Bao Tran completed direct-appointment paperwork against the rules and took over 997 million dong in commission from Nam Phong. On 9 October 2024 the High People's Court in Ho Chi Minh City cut Quan's term in this case from 11 years to eight, and reduced the others.
inside: A supplier of Viet A's kits paid a public hospital's supplies officer a commission, and the hospital's directors approved the purchase before checking the bids.
cite: Sai Gon Giai Phong, 18 June 2024 and 9 October 2024

n: AIC's cover bidders took VNCERT's internet monitoring contract
rank: director, Vietnam Computer Emergency Response Team (VNCERT)
d: AIC had the bid evaluation of VNCERT, the computer emergency response centre of Vietnam's information ministry, shaped so that only its own equipment fitted, and put up companies from its own group to bid against itself. On 21 March 2025 the Hanoi People's Court convicted 13 people of breaking the bidding rules over a contract to buy equipment and services to monitor attacks on some international internet links. The state lost over 17.2 billion dong, of which AIC's chairwoman Nguyen Thi Thanh Nhan and the firm must repay over 16 billion. Nhan, a fugitive tried in absentia, was given 10 years, bringing her total to 30; VNCERT's former director Nguyen Trong Duong was given seven years.
inside: AIC had the specification written into a state cyber-response centre's tender and bid against itself with its own group companies, so the contract went to it.
cite: Bao Dau tu, 21 March 2025

n: Viet A's 680m dong in kickbacks reached Binh Phuoc's disease centre
rank: director, Binh Phuoc Centre for Disease Control
d: Viet A agreed directly with the director of Binh Phuoc province's Centre for Disease Control that the centre would take its Covid test kits and reagents, delivered the goods before any tender, and paid three of the centre's staff 680 million dong. On 20 March 2024 the Binh Phuoc Provincial People's Court heard that the director Nguyen Van Sau settled the purchase with Viet A's general director Phan Quoc Viet, then told a pharmacy officer and a testing specialist to backdate the paperwork for three packages worth over 41.5 billion dong; the centre paid Viet A over 7.1 billion for the first batch. The state lost over 5.1 billion dong. Sau was given three years and the other two, who returned the money, were convicted but exempted from punishment.
inside: A test kit maker settled a provincial disease centre's purchase with its director, delivered before any tender, and paid 680 million dong to its staff.
cite: VOH Online, 20 March 2024; Phap luat TP.HCM, 20 March 2024

n: Ninh Thuan's disease centre fixed quotes so Viet A took its kit contracts
rank: pharmacy department head, Ninh Thuan Centre for Disease Control
d: Ninh Thuan province's Centre for Disease Control borrowed Covid test kits from Viet A before buying them, then gathered price quotes arranged so that Viet A's was the lowest and it could be appointed directly. The Ninh Thuan Provincial People's Court tried two of the centre's pharmacy staff on 22 March 2024, separately from the national Viet A case. The centre signed five contracts at 470,000 to 525,000 dong a kit; investigators put Viet A's actual price at about 144,000 dong. The former pharmacy head Duong Ba Thanh Dan and a pharmacy officer were each given three years suspended for breaking the bidding rules. The report does not say either man took money, and puts the loss only at billions of dong.
inside: A test kit maker supplied a provincial disease centre before any contract, and its officers arranged the quotes so the company could be appointed directly at over three times cost.
cite: RFA Vietnamese, 22 March 2024

n: Viet A's percentage went to Nam Dinh's disease centre chief accountant
rank: director and chief accountant, Nam Dinh Centre for Disease Control
d: Viet A's deputy director agreed with the chief accountant of Nam Dinh province's Centre for Disease Control that the company would return a percentage of each contract to the centre and to him personally, and the centre bought its kits by direct appointment. The Nam Dinh Provincial People's Court sentenced eight people on 29 November 2023, separately from the national Viet A case. Between August 2020 and November 2021 the director Do Duc Luu had five contracts signed with Viet A, four of them direct appointments for 46,756 kits paid at about 21.33 billion dong. The accountant Vu Ngoc Tuyen took over 3.1 billion dong and kept a 4 per cent personal share. The state lost over 14.6 billion dong. Tuyen was given 18 years.
inside: A test kit company paid a provincial disease centre's chief accountant a percentage of every contract, and the centre appointed it directly after taking its kits on loan.
cite: Bao Dai Doan Ket, 30 November 2023

n: A supplier had five Ha Tinh district hospitals buy washers at six times cost
org_label: Ha Tinh Medical Equipment Investment JSC
who: Ha Tinh Medical Equipment Investment JSC
rank: directors of five district general hospitals
d: The director of Ha Tinh Medical Equipment Investment arranged, through her husband, for the directors of five public district general hospitals to buy a Korean washer-dryer set at 3 billion dong each when it sold for about 520 to 560 million. On 31 May 2022, after five days of trial, the Ha Tinh Provincial People's Court convicted the group of breaking the bidding rules. The company's director Mai Thi Hoa guided the hospitals to ask the province for about 3.5 billion dong each in support, and the province approved 2.5 to 3 billion apiece. The state lost over 9.4 billion dong. Hoa was given 11 years, four hospital directors three years each.
inside: An equipment supplier set the price and the paperwork for five public hospitals' purchases through their own directors, and sold them a machine at about six times its market price.
cite: Tap chi Toa an nhan dan, 31 May 2022

n: Equipment firms wrote and shared Ha Tinh's school supply tenders
org_label: Hong Ha Trading, Van Xuan and Phuong Anh equipment companies
who: Hong Ha Trading and Van Xuan
rank: director, Ha Tinh provincial public finance centre
d: School equipment suppliers took bid documents before they were issued, put up companies of their own to lose on purpose, and routed goods through intermediaries so the price nearly doubled before the Ha Tinh education department received them. The Ha Tinh Provincial People's Court sentenced 11 people on the afternoon of 30 September 2024 for breaking the bidding rules; one also for tax evasion. The state lost 5,824,031,450 dong. The firm Hong Ha's sales director was given five years and the former director of the provincial public finance centre, which invited the bids, four. A claim by one defendant that 1.5 billion dong had been paid to officials to win approval was retracted at trial and not charged.
inside: Suppliers obtained a provincial tender's documents early, filled the field with their own losing bidders, and marked the goods up through firms owned by their own relatives.
cite: Tap chi Toa an nhan dan, 3 October 2024

n: A school supplier paid Dien Bien's education director 600m dong
org_label: Dien Bien Books and School Equipment JSC
who: Dien Bien Books and School Equipment JSC
rank: director, Dien Bien Department of Education and Training
d: The director of Dien Bien Books and School Equipment went to see the provincial education director, asked to be given two teaching equipment contracts for the province's secondary schools, won both, and afterwards brought 600 million dong to the director's office. The Dien Bien Provincial People's Court sentenced eight people on the morning of 2 March 2023 for breaking the bidding rules; the conduct ran from 2019 to 2020. The department's former director Nguyen Van Kien and the company's director Dinh Van Huu were given five years each. They had already paid back 5.9 billion dong during the investigation. The report does not set out how the two tenders were rigged.
inside: A school equipment company asked a provincial education director for two contracts, won both, and then handed him 600 million dong in his own office.
cite: Nhan Dan, 2 March 2023

n: Tuan An Group's bribes won 25 supply deals at Binh Thuan Power
rank: director, Binh Thuan Power Company
d: Tuan An Group, an electrical equipment maker, agreed with two successive directors of the state-owned Binh Thuan Power Company that it would be allowed to win the company's supply tenders, and paid over 9 billion dong to people inside it. On the morning of 26 September 2025 the People's Court of Lam Dong province, branch 1, sentenced 27 people. Between 2017 and 2023 the directors told staff to work with Tuan An's people against the bidding rules, and the group took 25 packages for materials and equipment, costing state assets over 49 billion dong. An was given nine years in all, and the former director Nguyen Thanh Ngon seven years for taking bribes.
inside: An equipment group paid over 9 billion dong inside a state-owned power company, whose directors then had staff rig 25 of its own supply tenders for the group.
cite: Nhan Dan, 26 September 2025

n: A book company paid Thanh Hoa's education officials 6.2bn dong
org_label: Thanh Hoa Books and School Equipment JSC
who: Thanh Hoa Books and School Equipment JSC
rank: director, Thanh Hoa Department of Education and Training
d: The director of the Thanh Hoa book and school equipment company supplied the equipment lists and prices used to set the budgets for the province's first-grade teaching materials, agreed the outcome with the education department's officials, and paid them 6.2 billion dong after each package. On 18 August 2023, after three days of trial, the Thanh Hoa Provincial People's Court convicted 12 people of breaking the bidding rules. The department's director Pham Thi Hang directed subordinates to let the company win and signed proposals knowing the selection was not fair. The 2020 tenders were worth over 119 billion dong and the state lost over 20.8 billion. Hang and the company's director were given four years each.
inside: A school equipment company wrote the prices into a provincial education department's tenders and paid its officials 6.2 billion dong once it had won them.
cite: Bao Van hoa, 18 August 2023; Bao Phap luat Viet Nam, 19 August 2023

n: Contractors paid 11.1bn dong to Dak Lak's road project board leaders
org_label: Sai Gon and An Nguyen construction companies
who: Sai Gon and An Nguyen companies
rank: director, Dak Lak provincial transport project management board
d: Two construction companies had the experience requirements in a Dak Lak province road tender changed so their joint ventures could win, and paid the project board's director and deputy 11.1 billion dong. The Hanoi People's Court gave its verdict on the morning of 9 January 2026 over packages three and four of the eastern bypass of Buon Ma Thuot. The payments were agreed in advance as 3 per cent of the contract advance for the board's director Pham Van Ha and 9 billion dong for his deputy Bui Van Tu. Both were given eight years each and fined 180 million dong; the two company directors were given 30 and 18 months.
inside: Construction firms had a provincial project board rewrite its tender criteria for them and paid its director and deputy 11.1 billion dong for the two road packages.
cite: Nhan Dan, 9 January 2026

n: Trung Hau 68's payments won An Giang's sand mining permits
rank: chairman of the An Giang People's Committee and director of its environment department
d: The chairman of Trung Hau 68 paid An Giang province's officials to get sand exploration and mining permits and then to raise the volume he was allowed to take. On 2 April 2025 the Ho Chi Minh City People's Court sentenced 44 defendants. The court heard that between 2020 and 2023 Le Quang Binh paid officials who acted against their duties for his benefit: the province's environment department director Nguyen Viet Tri took 3 billion dong and a vice-chairman of the provincial People's Committee, Tran Anh Thu, 961 million. He was given 30 years in all for bribery, breaking the mining rules and money laundering, and must repay over 293 billion dong; the former provincial chairman Nguyen Thanh Binh was given eight years six months and Tri nine.
inside: A sand company paid a provincial environment director and a vice-chairman of the province, who then granted and enlarged its mining permits against their own duties.
cite: Sai Gon Giai Phong, 2 April 2025

n: Lilama's 5bn dong to Lao Cai's party chief got it land over an apatite seam
org_label: Lilama Construction and Trading (Nguyen Manh Thua)
rank: secretary of the Lao Cai provincial party committee
d: The director of the building firm Lilama paid Lao Cai's provincial party secretary 5 billion dong, and the province granted his company a land certificate over ground the leaders knew held apatite ore. The Lao Cai Provincial People's Court sentenced 17 people on the afternoon of 29 May 2024. A 2009 certificate for a hotel project had been revoked because the land overlapped an approved apatite mining area and given to the state-owned Apatit Vietnam; in May 2012, two months after Lilama had already mined over 167,000 tonnes during site clearing, provincial leaders approved a fresh certificate anyway. The state lost over 312 billion dong.
inside: A construction firm paid a provincial party secretary 5 billion dong, and the province re-granted it land over an apatite seam that it then mined and sold.
cite: Bao Dau tu, 29 May 2024

n: Viet A's 2.3bn dong commission reached Vinh Long's general hospital
rank: director, Vinh Long General Hospital
d: The director of Vinh Long province's public general hospital had Viet A's Covid test reagents taken on credit and the paperwork written so the company could be appointed directly, and Viet A paid him and two staff over 2.3 billion dong. The Vinh Long Provincial People's Court gave its verdict on 4 July 2024, separately from the national Viet A case. Between April and September 2021 the former director Doan Van Hung told the hospital's chief biochemistry technician and deputy pharmacy head to borrow the reagents on a pay-later basis. The state lost over 12.3 billion dong. All three returned the commission money and were given suspended sentences of three years, two years and one year.
inside: A test kit company supplied a provincial hospital on credit, had its direct appointment papered over by the hospital's own staff, and paid them 2.3 billion dong.
cite: VOH Online, 4 July 2024

n: Hoang Dan paid 40bn dong to win four reservoir contract packages
rank: deputy minister of agriculture and directors of irrigation project boards
d: The director of Hoang Dan Investment and Construction paid over 40.2 billion dong to officials of the irrigation project boards of Vietnam's former agriculture ministry to win four reservoir construction packages. On the afternoon of 7 April 2026 the Hanoi People's Court sentenced 23 people. The packages were at the Krong Pach Thuong reservoir in Dak Lak, Ban Mong in Nghe An, Ban Lai in Lang Son and Canh Tang in Hoa Binh. The former deputy minister Hoang Van Thang was given four years for taking bribes and a former project board director 13 years. The company's director Nguyen Van Dan was given 14 years in all and must repay over 269 billion dong. The court put the total loss at over 350 billion dong.
inside: A construction company paid over 40 billion dong to a deputy minister and the directors of the ministry's project boards, which then awarded it four reservoir packages.
cite: VnEconomy, 7 April 2026

n: Saigon Dai Ninh's bribes reversed the order to take back its land
org_label: Saigon Dai Ninh Company (Nguyen Cao Tri)
rank: Government Inspectorate, and Lam Dong's party secretary and provincial chairman
d: The general director of Saigon Dai Ninh paid about 7.5 billion dong to officials of Vietnam's Government Inspectorate, the Lam Dong provincial party committee and the provincial People's Committee, and an inspection conclusion that had ordered his company's project stopped and its land taken back was replaced with one allowing it to continue. The Hanoi People's Court sentenced ten people on the afternoon of 20 January 2025. Nguyen Cao Tri was given three years for paying the bribes; Lam Dong's former party secretary Tran Duc Quan five years six months and its former chairman Tran Van Hiep six years six months for taking them.
inside: A property company paid inspectors and a province's two most senior officials, who replaced the order to recover its land with one letting the project go on.
cite: VnEconomy, 20 January 2025

n: GOL paid a Brazilian legislator's firms over an airline payroll tax change
rank: a member of the Brazilian legislature; a former Brasilia official
d: GOL Linhas Aereas Inteligentes, a Brazilian airline, paid companies controlled by a member of the Brazilian legislature so that air transport would be written into a new payroll tax law. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's 2022 order says GOL paid the approximate equivalent of $1.14 million to the official from October 2012 through November 2013, and that the legislature expanded the new law to include the air transport industry, saving GOL about $39.7 million. A further $552,400 went from June to August 2013 to a company associated with a former Brasilia official, and Brasilia lowered its aviation fuel tax to 12% on or about 26 May 2013, worth about $12.24 million. The order names neither individual. GOL was ordered to pay $24,500,000 and an $87,000,000 criminal fine.
inside: An airline's money reached a sitting Brazilian legislator's companies, and the legislature then wrote air transport into a payroll tax law that cut the airline's costs.
cite: SEC cease-and-desist order 34-95800, In the Matter of GOL Linhas Aereas Inteligentes S.A., 2022

n: Consultant bribed an EBRD banker who referred the bank's clients to him
rank: official and senior banker, European Bank for Reconstruction and Development
d: Dmitrij Harder, owner of the Pennsylvania-based Chestnut Consulting Group, paid a banker inside the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development to push his clients' applications for finance. The EBRD is a development bank in London owned by more than 60 countries. Prosecutors said Harder paid about $3.5 million between 2007 and 2009 through Channel Islands accounts held by the banker's sister, and that the EBRD then approved an $85 million investment and a 90 million euro loan for one client and a $40 million investment for another, earning Chestnut about $8 million in fees. Harder pleaded guilty in April 2016 and was sentenced in July 2017 to 60 months. A British jury convicted the banker, Andrej Ryjenko, and his sister in June 2017; he was jailed for six years.
inside: A consultancy bought a senior banker inside a development bank owned by 60 governments, so the bank's lending decisions followed the consultancy's paying clients.
cite: DOJ press releases, 20 April 2016 and 18 July 2017

n: Alcatel paid Taiwanese officials to win a Taiwan Railway axle counter deal
rank: officials in the government of Taiwan; Taiwan Railway Administration contract
d: Alcatel-Lucent, a French telecommunications equipment maker, paid officials in the government of Taiwan to win a contract to supply railway axle counters to the Taiwan Railway Administration, the state body that ran the island's railways. Axle counters are the trackside devices that detect where trains are. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's 2010 settlement covered bribes paid between December 2001 and June 2006 totalling more than $8 million across several countries, and does not break out the Taiwan figure or name any official. Alcatel-Lucent paid the SEC more than $45 million, including $45.372 million in disgorgement, accepted a three-year independent monitor, and paid the Justice Department $92 million, without admitting or denying the allegations.
inside: A supplier's money reached Taiwanese officials, and the state railway administration then bought its train detection equipment.
cite: SEC press release 2010-258, 27 December 2010

n: Innospec paid Iraq's oil ministry officials for fuel additive contracts
rank: officials of the Iraqi Ministry of Oil and its refineries
d: Innospec, a fuel additive maker, paid kickbacks and gave travel and entertainment to officials of the Iraqi Ministry of Oil and its refineries to sell the anti-knock additive TEL. The US Securities and Exchange Commission said the company paid or promised more than $9.2 million in bribes between 2000 and 2007, with kickbacks of 10% of contract value on three United Nations Oil for Food contracts and more paid to keep Iraqi business after the programme ended. One ministry official was given a seven-day honeymoon. Contracts worth about $176 million were obtained. Innospec settled for $40.2 million in total: $11.2 million in SEC disgorgement, a $14.1 million US criminal fine, a 12.7 million UK Serious Fraud Office fine and $2.2 million to OFAC.
inside: A chemical firm's kickbacks and gifts reached officials inside Iraq's oil ministry, which then kept buying its fuel additive.
cite: SEC press release 2010-40, 18 March 2010

n: Innospec paid a BP Migas official to keep leaded fuel selling in Indonesia
rank: senior official of BP Migas, Indonesia's oil and gas body
d: Innospec, a fuel additive maker, paid a senior official of BP Migas, the Indonesian state oil and gas body, every year so that Indonesia would keep buying its leaded-petrol additive TEL while the country was planning to move to unleaded fuel. The US Securities and Exchange Commission said more than $2.8 million was funnelled through an Indonesian agent, and that further payments ensured the failure of a 2006 field test of MMT, a rival additive. Across Iraq and Indonesia Innospec paid or promised more than $9.2 million between 2000 and 2007. The 2010 global settlement came to $40.2 million, including $11.2 million in SEC disgorgement, a $14.1 million US criminal fine and a 12.7 million UK Serious Fraud Office fine.
inside: A chemical firm paid a senior official inside Indonesia's oil and gas body, which then kept its leaded additive in the fuel supply and failed a rival's test.
cite: SEC press release 2010-40, 18 March 2010

n: Wabtec's Indian unit paid Indian Railway Board staff to approve its prices
org_label: Westinghouse Air Brake Technologies (Wabtec) / Pioneer Friction
rank: employees of the Indian Railway Board and Zonal Railways
d: Wabtec, an American rail equipment maker, used its Indian subsidiary Pioneer Friction to pay cash to employees of the Indian Railway Board, the operating arm of India's Ministry of Railroads, and of its sixteen Zonal Railways. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's 2008 order says the payments were made so that the board would approve Pioneer's contract price, consider its bids, and let it sell extra quantities at the awarded price without a fresh tender. About $85,000 in cash went to railway staff between 2001 and 2004 and $21,217 in 2005, with further ordering payments of about $25,000 and $6,250. In 2005 the board awarded Pioneer the primary contract, producing $259,000 in profits. Wabtec paid $288,351 in disgorgement and interest and an $87,000 penalty.
inside: A brake maker's cash reached staff inside India's national railway board, which then approved its prices and awarded it the contract.
cite: SEC administrative order 34-57333, In the Matter of Westinghouse Air Brake Technologies Corporation, 14 February 2008

n: Con-way's Manila agent paid Philippine customs officials to bend the rules
rank: officials of the Philippines Bureau of Customs and the Philippine Economic Zone Area
d: Con-way, an American freight company, controlled Emery Transnational, a Manila air freight business that paid officials of the Philippines Bureau of Customs and the Philippine Economic Zone Area. The US Securities and Exchange Commission said about $417,000 in improper payments were made between 2000 and 2003, of which roughly $244,000 went to customs and economic zone officials to induce them to violate customs regulations, settle customs disputes, and reduce or not enforce fines for administrative violations. A further $173,000 went to officials of fourteen state-owned airlines, which the release does not name, to reserve cargo space, under-weigh shipments and consolidate shipments to cut charges. Con-way paid a $300,000 civil penalty and accepted a cease-and-desist order, without admitting or denying the allegations.
inside: A freight firm's payments reached officials inside the Philippine customs bureau and economic zone authority, which then bent import rules and cut its fines.
cite: SEC litigation release 20690, 27 August 2008

n: United Industrial paid a retired Egyptian Air Force general for F-16 work
rank: retired Egyptian Air Force general acting as agent; active EAF officials
d: United Industrial Corporation, an American defence firm, paid a retired Egyptian Air Force general as its agent on the Egyptian F-16 Depot Project, work carried out for the Egyptian Air Force at Helwan Air Force Base in Cairo. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's 2009 order says the air force directed how money was spent on the project and submitted a sole-source request for the subsidiary's services, and that about $564,000 was paid to the agent between 1997 and 2002 as consulting or marketing fees without meaningful records, including monthly payments that rose from $4,000 to $20,000. The order describes military officials who could influence contract awards but does not show money reaching them. The contract brought about $5.3 million in revenue. UIC paid $337,679.42 in disgorgement and interest.
inside: A defence contractor put a retired air force general on its payroll to work on officials who could steer Egyptian Air Force contracts, and it won the award sole-source.
cite: SEC administrative order 34-60005, In the Matter of United Industrial Corporation, 29 May 2009

n: Helmerich & Payne paid Argentine customs officials to move banned equipment
rank: Argentine customs officials
d: Helmerich & Payne, an American drilling contractor, paid Argentine customs officials, directly and through customs brokers, so that its drilling equipment and materials could cross the border. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's 2009 order says about $166,000 went to officials of the Argentine customs service between 2004 and 2008, obtaining permission to import and export equipment without required certifications, faster clearance, and the import of materials Argentine law did not allow. The company's own internal investigation found fifty such payments across Argentina and Venezuela. Argentina's share of avoided costs was put at more than an estimated $186,000. The company paid $320,604 in disgorgement and $55,077.22 in interest and accepted a cease-and-desist order, without admitting or denying the findings.
inside: A drilling firm's payments reached officials inside Argentina's customs service, which then cleared imports the law did not allow.
cite: SEC administrative order 34-60400, In the Matter of Helmerich & Payne, Inc., 30 July 2009

n: Helmerich & Payne paid Venezuelan customs officials to cut inspections
rank: Venezuelan customs officials
d: Helmerich & Payne, an American drilling contractor, paid officials of the Venezuelan customs service, directly and through customs brokers, so that its equipment could move across the border. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's 2009 order says about $19,673 went to Venezuelan customs officials between 2003 and 2008, buying permission to import and export equipment and materials that did not comply with Venezuelan regulations, or a partial inspection in place of a full one. Venezuela's share of the avoided costs was put at more than an estimated $134,000. The company's internal investigation found fifty such payments across Venezuela and Argentina. It paid $320,604 in disgorgement and $55,077.22 in prejudgment interest and accepted a cease-and-desist order, without admitting or denying the findings.
inside: A drilling firm's payments reached officials inside Venezuela's customs service, which then waived inspections and let non-compliant equipment through.
cite: SEC administrative order 34-60400, In the Matter of Helmerich & Payne, Inc., 30 July 2009

n: Diageo paid Indian military canteen staff and state liquor store workers
rank: employees of the Canteen Stores Department of the Indian military and of government liquor stores
d: Diageo, the British drinks group, paid employees of the Canteen Stores Department of the Indian military and of government liquor stores in the New Delhi area to push its spirits. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's 2011 order says more than 900 liquor store employees received about $792,310 in cash plus $186,299 in cash service fees between 2003 and June 2009, buying larger government sales orders and better product placement. About $530,955 was reimbursed to Canteen Stores Department employees between 2003 and 2009, with $79,364 more planned, obtaining canteen listings, label registrations, price revision approvals, favourable factory inspection reports and the release of seized shipments. Diageo paid $11,306,081 in disgorgement, $2,067,739 in interest and a $3 million penalty.
inside: A drinks company's cash reached staff inside the Indian military's canteen service and state liquor stores, which then listed, approved and ordered its brands.
cite: SEC administrative order 34-64978, In the Matter of Diageo plc, 27 July 2011

n: Diageo paid a Thai official in the prime minister's office over tax disputes
rank: Deputy Secretary to the Prime Minister; Advisor to the Deputy Prime Minister
d: Diageo, the British drinks group, paid a Thai government and political party official about $12,000 a month through a consulting firm while he served as Deputy Secretary to the Prime Minister, Advisor to the Deputy Prime Minister and Advisor to the Ministry of Agriculture and Cooperatives. He also sat on a committee of the Thai Rak Thai party and on state-owned or state-controlled industrial and utility boards. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's 2011 order says 49 payments totalling $599,322 were made between April 2004 and July 2008 for lobbying on multi-million dollar tax and customs disputes, after which the Thai government accepted aspects of Diageo's transfer pricing method and released over $7 million in bank guarantees. Diageo paid $11,306,081 in disgorgement, $2,067,739 in interest and a $3 million penalty.
inside: A drinks company put a serving aide in Thailand's prime ministerial office on a monthly retainer, and the government then settled its tax and customs disputes in its favour.
cite: SEC administrative order 34-64978, In the Matter of Diageo plc, 27 July 2011

n: Diageo paid a Korean customs official after a transfer pricing rebate
rank: Korean Customs Service official; South Korean military officers
d: Diageo, the British drinks group, paid a Korean Customs Service official 100 million won, about $86,339, in July 2004 as a reward for his role in transfer pricing negotiations that had produced a rebate of about $50 million for the company in April 2004. The US Securities and Exchange Commission's 2011 order also records $109,253 in travel and entertainment for Korean customs and other government officials in 2003 and 2004, including a trip to Scotland with side trips to Prague and Budapest, and about 400 'rice cake' payments totalling $64,184 to South Korean military officers between 2002 and 2006, with $165,287 in further gifts of which $106,051 aimed to influence purchasing decisions. Diageo paid $11,306,081 in disgorgement, $2,067,739 in interest and a $3 million penalty.
inside: A drinks company rewarded an official inside South Korea's customs service for the ruling that cut its tax bill, and paid military officers who bought its liquor.
cite: SEC administrative order 34-64978, In the Matter of Diageo plc, 27 July 2011

n: Novo Nordisk paid 10% kickbacks to Iraq's state drug importer Kimadia
rank: import manager and officials of Kimadia, Iraq's state drug importer
d: Novo Nordisk, the Danish insulin maker, paid kickbacks to Kimadia, the Iraq State Company for the Importation and Distribution of Drugs and Medical Appliances, to win United Nations Oil for Food contracts. The US Securities and Exchange Commission said a Kimadia import manager told the company's Jordan-based agent in late 2000 or early 2001 that Kimadia required a ten percent kickback, and that $1,437,946 was paid through the agent on eleven contracts between 2000 and 2003, with about $1,315,454 more agreed as after-sales service fees on two further contracts for which no services were performed. A senior vice-president authorised the payments after another officer refused. Novo Nordisk paid $4,321,523 in disgorgement, $1,683,556 in interest, a $3,025,066 civil penalty and a $9 million criminal fine.
inside: A drug maker's kickbacks reached the buying officials of Iraq's state medicines importer, which then awarded it eleven supply contracts.
cite: SEC litigation release 21033, 11 May 2009

n: Two tobacco firms paid Thailand Tobacco Monopoly officials for leaf contracts
org_label: Universal Corporation; Alliance One International (Dimon and Standard Commercial)
who: Universal Corporation and Alliance One International
rank: officials of the Thailand Tobacco Monopoly
d: Universal Corporation and Alliance One International, two American leaf tobacco dealers, paid officials of the Thailand Tobacco Monopoly, the government-owned cigarette maker, to win its tobacco purchase contracts. The US Securities and Exchange Commission said in 2010 that Universal paid about $800,000 for roughly $11.5 million in contracts for its Brazilian and European subsidiaries, and that Dimon and Standard Commercial, the firms that merged to form Alliance One, paid more than $1.2 million for more than $18.3 million in contracts. The Thailand payments ran from 2000 to 2004. Universal paid more than $4.5 million in disgorgement and a $4.4 million criminal fine; Alliance One paid $10 million in disgorgement and a $9.45 million fine. Both accepted three-year independent monitors.
inside: Two leaf dealers' money reached the buying officials of Thailand's state tobacco monopoly, which then awarded them its purchase contracts.
cite: SEC press release 2010-144, 6 August 2010

n: ABB bribed officials of Mexico's state power utilities CFE and Luz y Fuerza
rank: officials of the Comision Federal de Electricidad and Luz y Fuerza del Centro
d: ABB, the Swiss-Swedish engineering group, bribed officials of two Mexican government-owned electric utilities, the Comision Federal de Electricidad and Luz y Fuerza del Centro, to win their business. The US Securities and Exchange Commission said in 2010 that at least $2.7 million in illicit payments were made, that the Mexican scheme ran from 1999 to 2004, and that recipients were given cash and a Mediterranean cruise for officials and their wives, with cheques and wire transfers also going to officials' relatives. The Mexican contracts produced more than $90 million in revenue and $13 million in profit. ABB paid the SEC more than $39.3 million, including $17,141,474 in disgorgement and a $16,510,000 penalty, and $19 million in criminal penalties.
inside: An engineering group's cash and gifts reached buying officials inside Mexico's two state electricity utilities, which then awarded it more than $90 million in work.
cite: SEC press release 2010-175, 29 September 2010

n: GE units' kickbacks won Iraqi health and oil ministry equipment contracts
rank: officials of the Iraqi Health Ministry and the Iraqi Oil Ministry
d: Four subsidiaries of General Electric, Ionics and Amersham paid kickbacks through an Iraqi agent to win United Nations Oil for Food contracts from Iraqi ministries. The US Securities and Exchange Commission said in 2010 that between about 2000 and 2003 Marquette-Hellige paid roughly $1.2 million in goods and services for two Iraqi Health Ministry contracts, that OEC-Medical made an in-kind payment of about $870,000 on a $2.1 million contract, that Ionics Italba paid $795,000 in kickbacks on five Iraqi Oil Ministry water treatment contracts, and that Nycomed paid about $750,000 across nine contracts with Iraqi ministries. The kickbacks were paid in cash, computer equipment, medical supplies and services. GE paid $18,397,949 in disgorgement, $4,080,665 in interest and a $1 million penalty.
inside: An industrial group's kickbacks reached buying officials in Iraq's health and oil ministries, which then awarded its units medical and water treatment contracts.
cite: SEC press release 2010-133, 27 July 2010

n: Och-Ziff's bribes drew Libya's sovereign wealth fund into its own funds
rank: Libyan Investment Authority investment decisions
d: Och-Ziff Capital Management, a large American hedge fund manager, paid bribes that drew the Libyan Investment Authority, Libya's sovereign wealth fund, into investing in funds Och-Ziff managed. A sovereign wealth fund invests a country's own money. The US Securities and Exchange Commission said in September 2016 that illicit payments went to high-level government officials in Libya, Chad, Niger, Guinea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo to win special access, deals and profits, and that investor money was used to pay them. The SEC named no official. Och-Ziff and OZ Management paid $173,186,178 in disgorgement and $25,858,989 in interest; its chief executive Daniel Och paid about $2.2 million; and the firm faced a criminal penalty of $213 million with a subsidiary guilty plea.
inside: A hedge fund's payments to senior officials turned the decisions of Libya's state investment fund, so the country's own money went into the fund manager's products.
cite: SEC press release 2016-203, 29 September 2016

n: Avery Dennison paid staff of a Wuxi police research institute for contracts
rank: officials of the Traffic Management Research Institute, Ministry of Public Security
d: Avery Dennison's reflective materials division in China gave gifts, trips and a job to officials of the Traffic Management Research Institute under the Ministry of Public Security in Wuxi, Jiangsu Province, a body the US Securities and Exchange Commission said could play an important role in awarding government contracts.
