A second officer, Friendy Jean-Baptiste, supplied the gang with firearms and ammunition and told Chale about police operations aimed at the Tokyo district and Saint-Martin street.
inside: Serving police officers told a gang where the checkpoints were, sold it rifles and warned it of raids, so the force's own operations became the gang's early warning system.
undone: No prosecution or verdict is recorded. The findings are the UN Panel of Experts' account of investigations by the Haitian National Police, drawing in part on a confidential report, and the Panel sets them out at annex rather than as a judicial finding, which is why this record is coded probable. The kidnappings it describes run from 11 March 2025, when two people taken in Delmas 31 were freed for ransoms of 400,000 and 465,000 gourdes, through 4 April and 7 July 2025. None of the officers named is reported to have been charged.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, final report pursuant to Security Council resolution 2653 (2022), S/2026/714, 8 September 2026, annex on collusion between gangs and police, footnotes 182-184

n: Arkenu diverted $3bn of Libyan oil revenue through a shadow hold on the NOC
rank: National Oil Corporation board and contracting
d: Arkenu Oil Company was set up in 2023 as Libya's first private oil company and is indirectly controlled by Saddam Haftar through proxies, chiefly Rafat al-Abbar. The UN Panel of Experts found that al-Abbar exercised de facto control over decision-making inside the National Oil Corporation, the state oil company, by building a shadow governance structure, obstructing oversight and applying pressure at several institutional levels. The contract between Arkenu and the corporation was not made in accordance with Libyan law. Arkenu then diverted more than $3 billion of oil revenue to accounts outside Libya, paid no tax to the state, invested only a fraction of the $1 billion it owed on the Sarir and Mesla fields, and exported at least 42.1 million barrels.
inside: An armed group's proxy ran a shadow structure inside the state oil company, and the private firm it favoured moved more than three billion dollars of oil revenue out of the country.
undone: No trial. The Panel sets this out as its own finding in a report to the Security Council, not as a judicial determination, which is why it is coded probable. It records that Libyan authorities opened investigations and that the Attorney General issued an arrest warrant in a related strand, and that the person concerned has lived outside Libya since, travelling to Benghazi but avoiding the west of the country. The Panel calls Arkenu a prototype for similar arrangements, a Trojan horse presenting armed-group exports as private investment, and links its operations to a rise in the military capability of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report pursuant to Security Council resolution 1973 (2011), S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, paras. 104-105 (p. 31) and annex 9 section C (p. 66)

n: A fuel smuggling network used Libya's foreign ministry to free its tanker
rank: foreign ministry officials; embassy staff
d: The UN Panel of Experts identified a fuel smuggling network led by Maeen Ali Sharfeddin, a Libyan-Turkish dual national running companies in Turkiye and the United Arab Emirates with no real commercial activity. It worked with Ali Al-Mashai and the top command of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces, whose control of Benghazi old harbour let vessels enter and leave without interference from law enforcement. When one of its tankers was held, a network member travelled to Panama and forged papers to feign a change of ownership, and Sharfeddin went to Cameroon in November 2025 to meet a senior official. The Libyan embassy in Cameroon requested that meeting by note verbale.
inside: A smuggling network got Libya's own embassy to arrange a meeting that would free its detained tanker, and tried to bribe officials in two countries with more than a million dollars.
undone: No prosecution is recorded. The Panel states that the network's ability to mobilise Libyan foreign ministry officials affiliated with the Libyan Arab Armed Forces is what the embassy's involvement demonstrates, and that beyond lobbying it attempted to bribe officials in Panama and Cameroon with sums above $1 million. The Panel classified a related incident, in which the tanker MT Anhona was made to transfer about 20,700 tonnes of cargo at Benghazi anchorage under duress in May 2024, as piracy under article 101 of the Law of the Sea Convention. Table 9.2 of the report names thirteen members of the network and their roles.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, para. 118 (p. 34), annex 9 paras. 51 and 55 (pp. 72-73) and table 9.2

n: Subul al-Salam battalion opened Libya's southern border to Sudan's RSF
rank: battalion of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces
d: Subul al-Salam is a battalion within the Libyan Arab Armed Forces, drawing its strength from tribal ties to the Tubu population of the Kufrah area in Libya's south-east. The UN Panel of Experts found that it escorted factions affiliated with Sudan's Rapid Support Forces across Libyan territory and gave them fuel and spare vehicle parts, and that these actions culminated in the Rapid Support Forces advancing into the Uwaynat area. The Panel found that the battalion thereby weakened border security in southern Libya, facilitating cross-border illicit activity and strengthening non-state armed actors in the Fazzan region. As of December 2025 it held Kufrah airport.
inside: A unit inside Libya's own armed forces escorted a foreign paramilitary across the border it was meant to hold, and ran the airport at the crossing point.
undone: No proceeding is recorded. The Panel reports that the Libyan Arab Armed Forces reinforced Kufrah airport with elements of 166 brigade and 87 battalion, which it reads as Saddam Haftar's attempt to contain Subul al-Salam's growing influence and stop it developing operational autonomy, so the parent force treats the unit as a problem of its own. The Panel also records that arms originally destined for the Rapid Support Forces were diverted and resold to people involved in gold trafficking in Niger and linked to Da'esh.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, paras. 33-34 (p. 11) and the Kufrah passage at para. 11

n: Fighters recruited for a Tripoli offensive were folded into Libya's ministries
rank: Ministry of Defence and Ministry of the Interior
d: Ibrahim Al Dabiba is the nephew of Libya's prime minister and serves as national security adviser in the prime minister's office. The UN Panel of Experts found that he directly sponsored a recruitment campaign launched in Misratah to raise fighters for the May 2025 offensive against the Deterrence Apparatus for Combating Organized Crime and Terrorism, paying between 700 and 5,000 Libyan dinars a week, about $129 to $921, depending on whether a recruit brought a vehicle or weapons. Some of those recruits were later based in the Andalus district of Tripoli where he lives, and work was under way to bring some of them under the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior.
inside: Fighters hired by the week for one faction's offensive were then being written onto the payrolls of the defence and interior ministries.
undone: No proceeding is recorded. The Panel notes that control over the newly recruited forces remained volatile at the time of writing, so the integration it describes was in progress rather than complete. The same report records that the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence of the Government of National Unity, together with the rival Government of National Stability, refused to cooperate with a Central Bank project to pay public sector salaries directly against unique identification numbers, and that the Panel assessed their stated data protection grounds to be irrelevant because national identity cards are issued by the state.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, para. 14 (p. 7), paras. 17-19 (p. 8) and annex 7 (p. 62)

n: Artibonite police unit officers sold gangs the ammunition they were issued
who: Artibonite gangs, Gran Grif and Kokorat San Ras
rank: officers of the Departmental Law Enforcement Unit, Haitian National Police
d: The UN Panel of Experts investigated a network of officers of the Departmental Law Enforcement Unit of the Haitian National Police in the Artibonite department, operating mainly out of the Pat-Chawal commissariat in Saint-Marc commune. The Panel found they siphoned off boxes of twenty rounds of 5.56x45mm ammunition a few at a time and sold them for about 10,000 Haitian gourdes, roughly $75, and sold semi-automatic rifles the force had itself seized for between $5,000 and $8,000. They sold to the Gran Grif and Kokorat San Ras gangs and to armed men involved in seizing land, and the Panel also recorded them supporting that land seizure and colluding with gang members.
inside: Officers of a police riot unit sold their own issued ammunition by the box and resold the rifles their force had confiscated, arming the gangs they were deployed against.
undone: The Haitian National Police Inspectorate General is investigating; no charge or verdict is recorded. The Panel measured the effect on the gangs' arsenals: of 336 rounds of 7.62x51mm ammunition it documented from seizures from the Jamesley and Krache Dife gangs in 2026, 70 per cent had been diverted from police stockpiles, and firearms issued to the police are regularly recovered from gang members. The Panel distinguishes this theft from battlefield losses after police casualties, which account for part of the same flow. On 3 August 2025 a motorcyclist carrying diverted materiel was stopped by members of the Jean Denis Coalition, a self-defence group.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, final report pursuant to Security Council resolution 2794 (2025), S/2026/714, 3 September 2026, paras. 85, 110-111 (pp. 19, 25) and annex 19 (p. 88)

n: Haitian customs officers cleared a party leader's baby-eel smuggling route
rank: customs officers; Ministry of Agriculture licensing
d: Elvers, or baby eels, are among Haiti's most valuable natural resources and the trade is barely regulated, Haiti not being party to the convention on trade in endangered species. The UN Panel of Experts reported that a network holds influence over the industry by controlling who receives licences from the Ministry of Agriculture, Natural Resources and Rural Development, with bribery and smuggling widespread. The sector is dominated by Jean-Charles Moise, a businessman from the North Department, secretary-general of the Pitit Dessalines party and a former senator and presidential candidate. When flights from Port-au-Prince to the United States were suspended in the 2024/25 season, the Panel's sources say he moved the eels through a smuggling network instead.
inside: A party leader who dominates Haiti's baby-eel trade moved his catch out through customs officers who waved it past, in a sector where the ministry's licences are controlled by the same network.
undone: No proceeding is recorded and this is the weakest-sourced of the Panel's findings used here, which is why it is coded possible. The account of the smuggling route comes from interviews the Panel conducted with one of Moise's former elvers suppliers, a lessor of boats and an eels trader in the Dominican Republic, all of them interested parties, and it names no customs officer. The Panel states that the operation involved some Haitian customs officials who facilitated tax evasion and some Dominican owners of private boats who provided the transport. On 30 March 2026 the government issued a decree in Le Moniteur regulating the mining sector, and signed a separate decree in March on mineral concessions.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2026/714, 3 September 2026, paras. 151-157 (pp. 31-33); interim report S/2026/241, 27 March 2026, summary and paras. 58-66

n: Haitian police moved 130kg of a cocaine load through Port-de-Paix
rank: officers of the Haitian National Police
d: In August 2024 authorities in the North-West department of Haiti found that police officers had moved 130 kilograms of cocaine, part of an alleged shipment of about 250 kilograms that was being taken from a locality in Port-de-Paix to Tortuga Island and on to the Bahamas. Several officers of the Haitian National Police were implicated by the investigations. The UN Panel of Experts reported that the involvement of police officers in the trafficking network has contributed to stalled investigations and impunity, and that the absence of clear progress in this investigation itself suggests the complicity of local authorities with trafficking networks.
inside: Officers of the national police carried a third of a cocaine shipment themselves, and the Panel reads the investigation going nowhere as a sign of how far the complicity reaches.
undone: No charge or verdict is recorded and the Panel names no officer. The same report describes the force's limited capacity to act against trafficking at all: vehicles of the North department's anti-narcotics brigade were out of service at the time of writing, and the Haitian Coast Guard became operational only recently with two newly provided vessels, having previously relied on one low-capacity boat. The unit has made seizures, including 425.9 kilograms of cannabis with three arrests at Madeline, Cap-Haitien, on 28 July 2025, which the Panel says are likely to represent a fraction of the volume moving through the region.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, report pursuant to Security Council resolution 2752 (2024), S/2025/597, 2025, paras. 109-110 (p. 27)

n: AFC/M23 replaced Congo's state insurer and took its utilities' accounts
rank: state utility boards; the national insurer
d: The UN Group of Experts found that the Alliance Fleuve Congo and M23 extended their control over public utilities, insurance and financial services in the territory they hold in eastern Congo. The national water and electricity companies, REGIDESO and SNEL, were placed under the administrative authority of the governor the alliance appointed and under the financial oversight of its own finance department. In the insurance sector it facilitated the replacement of the national insurance company SONAS with Imperial Assur, a private entity that began operating in mid-2025, and by March 2026 Imperial Assur held a monopoly over much of the sector, with enforcement supported by the alliance.
inside: An armed movement put the state water and power companies under a governor it appointed and its own finance department, then swapped the national insurer for a private firm it could enforce for.
undone: No proceeding. The Group obtained copies of official notices issued by the alliance making third-party liability insurance compulsory for all vehicles and transport operators, which is how the monopoly was enforced. Payments in the territory were made through the alliance's own iteration of CADECO, a state savings institution. The Group separately documented unlicensed financial service providers emerging after Congolese authorities suspended banking operations and payment systems, among them Acces Finance S.A., which offered deposit, transfer and account services in Goma and Rubaya with planned expansion to Bukavu.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, S/2026/466, 2026, para. 93 (p. 20) and annexes 31-33 (pp. 123-126)

n: Houthi-run education ministry used Yemen's schools to recruit children
rank: Ministry of Education and Scientific Research; General Mobilization Authority
d: The Houthi movement, the armed group holding northern Yemen, runs the education ministry in Sana'a and has used it to recruit children. The UN Panel of Experts published ministry papers: a circular of 2 August 2024 calling for recruitment on the grounds of the war in Gaza; and a letter of 7 December 2024, stamped with the logo of the General Mobilization Authority, starting a programme for secondary pupils that included basic combat training. A circular of 12 April 2025 told schools and universities to give their staff and resources to a summer camps committee. The Panel reported that child recruitment is carried out through a structured, multilayered system under the leadership of the General Mobilization Authority of the Ministry of Defence, a system that includes the education ministry.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2025/650, annex 99 (pp. 218-221) and para. 151
inside: The armed movement's own appointees run the education ministry, and its circulars turned state schools into a recruiting and indoctrination channel for the movement's fighters.

n: Yemen transport ministry staff given weapons training by the Houthis
rank: Ministry of Transport and Public Works, Sana'a
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen reproduced a report that the Houthi movement ran military training courses for employees of the Ministry of Transport under its control in Sana'a, focusing on military training and the use of weapons. According to the informed sources quoted, staff were urged to spend part of their salaries on buying rifles, and objected that they had not been paid for a long time; they were promised a fuller training camp at al-Sabahah, west of Sana'a, and asked to fill in forms with detailed personal information. The Panel published the registration form and the course paper, headed 'Ministry of Transport and Public Works - Questions on Operation Al-Aqsa Storm Training Course', which asks pupils to justify armed jihad from the movement's leader's lectures.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2025/650, annex 15 (pp. 65-68), reproducing Al Masdar Online, 21 December 2024
inside: The armed movement used a ministry it controls as a recruiting pool, putting its own staff through weapons training and registering them as recruits.

n: Houthi-appointed trade ministry moved trademarks to Houthi-linked firms
rank: Ministry of Industry and Trade, Sana'a
d: A trademark is the registered name under which a company trades. The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen reported that, to increase their financial gains, the Houthis adopted what it called an arbitrary and illegal policy of withdrawing trademarks from legitimate commercial entities and transferring them to entities under their control. It said several lawsuits had been filed in the Commercial Court of First Instance in Sana'a against the Houthi-appointed Ministry of Industry and Trade for alleged violations of intellectual property rights and the revocation of trademarks registered in the companies' names, and that there had been reports of registrations of specific companies being cancelled and some subsequently transferred to others affiliated to the Houthis. The Panel said it held some documents and was still investigating.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2024/731, annex 175 (pp. 451-452)
inside: The movement's appointees hold the ministry that registers trade names, and the Panel reports it stripped firms of their marks and passed them to businesses tied to the movement.

n: Houthi loyalists lead Yemen's communications ministry and its revenues
rank: Ministry of Communications; Public Telecommunications Corporation
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen reported that all official structures in Sana'a, such as the Ministry of Communications and the Public Telecommunications Corporation, are led by Houthi loyalists, ensuring the armed movement's operational and financial control, and that those structures in turn control private operators. The Panel said telecommunications companies that moved their head offices to Aden left infrastructure in Houthi-held areas that is now run by identically named entities under new, Houthi-appointed management, and that the Houthis control the '.ye' internet domain. It put monthly revenue from international calls collected by Houthi-controlled companies at about $20 million, and said text messages were still being used to seek 100-rial contributions for the movement's missile force and drone air force.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2025/650, paras. 116-120
inside: The movement's loyalists head the communications ministry and the state telecoms corporation, which gives it control of the sector's money and of the networks it depends on.

n: Houthi transport minister's circulars warned tankers off Yemeni oil ports
rank: Minister of Transport; Maritime Affairs Authority
d: On 1 October 2022 the Houthi-appointed Minister of Transport, Abdul-Wahab Yahya al-Durra, issued a statement threatening tankers that lifted oil from ports or terminals held by the internationally recognised Government of Yemen from 1800 hours the next day. Separate circulars went out on 2 October from the ministry and from the Maritime Affairs Authority to international energy companies and shipping agents. The UN Panel of Experts published both circulars and recorded that threatening messages had been sent to flag states, shipping companies and shipmasters from the addresses ycg@yemen.net.ye, identifying as the Yemen Coast Guards, and operations@maa.gov.ye, identifying as the ministry's Maritime Affairs Authority. The Houthis then attacked oil tankers at Dubbah in Hadramawt and at Balhaf and Qana' in Shabwah.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2023/130, paras. 23-24 and annex 6 (pp. 69-72)
inside: The movement's own transport minister used the ministry's and the maritime authority's official channels to threaten shipping, and its forces then attacked the tankers that kept loading.

n: Militia family's interior minister reopened a Libyan trafficking prison
rank: Minister of the Interior, Government of National Stability
d: The Stability Support Apparatus is a Libyan militia turned state body. The detention centre at Mayah was under the direct command and control of the 55 Brigade and ran inside the Apparatus-controlled Department for Combating Settlement and Illegal Immigration, in parallel with the government's own migrant detention system. The Panel found it central to the Zawiyah smuggling network's business of holding trafficked people for profit; by March 2023 it held 3,500 to 4,000 migrants. On 2 February 2023 the Apparatus's commander ordered it closed. On 8 March 2023 Major General Issam Busriba, Minister of the Interior in the Sirte-based Government of National Stability and a family member of Hassan Busriba, the Apparatus's deputy commander in charge of its Zawiyah command, signed Decision No. 57 of 2023 establishing a migrant shelter in the Mayah area. The Panel said this gave the facility a semblance of legitimacy. It remained open.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2023/673, para. 15 and annex 19, paras. 6 and 9 with figure 19.4 (pp. 97-108)
inside: A militia commander's relative held the interior ministry and signed the decision that reopened his family's detention centre, so the trafficking network kept its prison under state cover.

n: Libyan brigade commander made defence undersecretary took the army payroll
rank: Undersecretary of the Ministry of Defence
d: Abdulsalam al-Zobi commands the 111 Brigade, an armed group whose members hold the southern part of Tripoli. In July 2024 Prime Minister Abdulhamid al-Dabiba appointed him undersecretary of the Ministry of Defence and promoted him to colonel. The UN Panel of Experts found that, despite his lack of a military background, he could approve military operations in western Libya and decide assignments, appointments and promotions in the Libyan Army, and that he administered the military salary system directly. One of his first acts was to move almost 1,000 soldiers into a directorate under his brigade's command and shift all their salary payments to the brigade's administration, which the Panel said gave the armed group direct control of salary disbursement and bypassed the Chief of the General Staff.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224, paras. 16-21; S/2024/914, para. 17
inside: An armed group's commander was given the defence ministry's top official post and moved the army's salary payments onto his own brigade's books.

n: Libya's interior minister put a militia commander over the Tunisian border
who: Imad Trabelsi and allied armed groups
rank: Acting Minister of the Interior
d: The UN Panel of Experts describes Imad Trabelsi, Libya's acting interior minister, as an armed group leader who exercised de facto control over the Ministry of the Interior; it does not name his group. On 15 November 2023 he appointed Abdulsalam al-Zobi, commander of the 111 Brigade, to head a force securing Libya's western borders with Tunisia, two weeks after the prime minister had made al-Zobi head of a joint operations room covering the west and south-west. The next day Trabelsi appointed Khairi Chengarou to head the force controlling the Ras El-Jdir crossing, one of Libya's busiest. Municipal councils in Zuwara and the Nafusa mountains declared an emergency; the Presidential Council ordered units not to move west, and the operations room withdrew on 19 November.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2024/914, annex 16, table 16.1 (pp. 91-92); S/2026/224, para. 20
inside: An armed group leader holding the interior ministry handed control of Libya's main border crossing and the western border force to a fellow militia commander.

n: Haftar's agent used Libya's oil ministry post to run the state oil firm
who: Saddam Haftar and the Libyan Arab armed forces network
rank: Undersecretary of Oil and Gas
d: Refat al-Abbar began his career as a mid-level manager at the Arabian Gulf Oil Company in Benghazi. The UN Panel of Experts found that political arrangements around the formation of the Government of National Unity led to his appointment as Undersecretary of Oil and Gas in 2021, and that he used the post to learn the oil sector's structure and position himself to become the agent of Saddam Haftar, commander of the eastern armed forces, inside it. Although formally only an adviser to the National Oil Corporation's chairman, he acted as its shadow chairman and in practice the principal decision-maker in key negotiations. The Panel found he coerced the corporation into validating inflated contracts, including daily drilling rig rates of $24,000. Al-Abbar told the Panel he played no role in the oil sector beyond advising the corporation's chairman and representing its business interests to a Member State; the Panel found his claims not credible.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224, annex 9, appendix 9.A, paras. 1-3 (p. 74), and paras. 104-106
inside: An armed force's commander placed his man in the oil ministry's senior official post, and from there he steered the state oil company's contracts to favoured operators.

n: Libya's defence ministry took in the brigade that ran a migrant prison
rank: Libyan Ministry of Defence military structures
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya found that Prison 55, in a military compound at al-Zahra in Wershafana, was one of two facilities at the heart of the Zawiyah smuggling network's method of holding trafficked and smuggled people for profit. The compound served as the military quarters of the 55 Brigade until November 2022, and rooms in its main building were used to hold migrants. The Panel recorded that the brigade may now appear under the name of the 55 Infantry Battalion, integrated into the military structures of the Libyan Ministry of Defence on 28 November 2022 by Ministry of Defence Decision No. 32 of 2022. The Panel documented unlawful and arbitrary detention, torture and other ill-treatment, and forced labour by people under the brigade's control.'s control.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2023/673, annex 19, paras. 7-9 and footnote 186 (pp. 97-99)
inside: A ministry decision folded into the Libyan armed forces a brigade that was running a prison for a trafficking network, putting its men on the state's books.

n: Sanctioned militia leader sat as a CAR minister on a disarmament body
org_label: Front populaire pour la renaissance de la Centrafrique (FPRC), Hissene branch
rank: Minister Counsellor; government technical committee for the integration of ex-combatants
d: Abdoulaye Hissene led a branch of the Front populaire pour la renaissance de la Centrafrique, an armed group; he is subject to a UN travel ban and asset freeze. He broke away from the group's main body in 2022 and became close to the government. The UN Panel of Experts recorded that on 31 March 2023 he took part in a meeting of the government's technical committee for the integration of ex-combatants in his capacity as Minister Counsellor, the body that decides how fighters are brought into state structures. The Panel wrote to the government to ask whether any salary or per diem had been paid to him, which would breach the asset freeze. In September 2023 Hissene was arrested on a Special Criminal Court warrant.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, S/2023/360, para. 91; S/2024/444, para. 14 and footnote 3
inside: A sanctioned militia leader held a ministerial post and sat on the committee deciding how fighters like his own are taken into the state's forces and paid.

n: Central African livestock minister led the UPC faction that seized M'boki
org_label: Unite pour la paix en Centrafrique (UPC), pro-government wing
rank: Minister for Livestock and Animal Health
d: Hassan Bouba is the Central African Republic's Minister for Livestock and Animal Health. The UN Panel of Experts reported that the pro-government wing of the armed group Unite pour la paix en Centrafrique is under his leadership, and that on 25 January 2023 it took the town of M'boki. In March 2023 fighters of that wing set up a checkpoint at Banagui and taxed road users, taking 7,000 CFA francs from motorcycles hired by Zemio hospital to carry medicines. As minister, Bouba headed a delegation to Birao on 28 December 2022; the Panel noted its official programme was supposedly about peaceful transhumance, but that at Am Dafok he also spoke about security force deployments. A later Panel report called that trip his first meeting with Sudan's Rapid Support Forces.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, S/2023/360, paras. 60-61 and annex 10 (p. 52); S/2024/444, para. 16
inside: An armed group's leader holds a ministry, and his official missions to the border doubled as contacts that served his faction while it seized a town and taxed roads.

n: Two Central African militia chiefs held ministries, one over the peace deal
org_label: RPRC and MLCJ, Central African Republic
who: RPRC and Mouvement des liberateurs centrafricains pour la justice
rank: Minister for Transport and Civil Aviation; Minister delegate for the peace agreement
d: The UN Panel of Experts recorded that two of the Central African Republic's serving ministers led armed groups. The Rassemblement patriotique pour le renouveau de la Centrafrique, which the Panel called pro-government and dominant around Gordil, was led by the Minister for Transport and Civil Aviation, Djono Ahaba. The Mouvement des liberateurs centrafricains pour la justice was led by Gilbert Toumou Deya, the minister delegate in charge of monitoring implementation of the Political Agreement for Peace and Reconciliation, so one group's leader held the post overseeing the process meant to wind such groups up. After the government met factions of 11 armed groups in September 2022, four, including both, announced their dissolution on 4 December 2022. The Panel found the RPRC's dissolution had had no effect on the ground.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, S/2023/87, para. 13; S/2023/360, paras. 7-9 and footnote 6
inside: Two armed groups' own leaders held ministries, one of them the post monitoring the peace deal, and the dissolutions declared under it left his ally's group intact.

n: Libyan armed groups ran local councils and fielded their own election lists
rank: Municipal councils; High National Elections Commission offices
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya found that armed groups were directly or heavily involved in the day-to-day running of local authorities, including by having their own candidates and lists, while also providing the security for the municipal council elections. It identified 16 incidents before the second round, held in stages from August 2025, all involving armed actors or security bodies under their de facto authority: election centres closed, voter cards and ballot boxes confiscated, and offices of the High National Elections Commission attacked, including arson at Zawiya and Sahel al-Gharbi on 15 August 2025 that burned ballot material. In at least six cases - four in the west, two in the east - candidates and their families faced threats, judicial harassment, unlawful detention, enforced disappearance and torture, forcing them to withdraw or relocate; in one case the armed group was backing the opposing list, in another it wanted its own local candidates to win.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224, paras. 45-47 and annex 14 (pp. 121-122)
inside: Armed groups ran Libyan town councils, stood their own candidates and drove rival candidates out, so local government decisions were made by and for the men with guns.

n: Darfur movement member made deputy governor helped the RSF take El Geneina
who: Rapid Support Forces and allied Arab militias
rank: Deputy Governor, then de facto Wali, of West Darfur
d: Tijani Karshoum, of the Mahamid community and a member of the Gathering of Sudan Liberation Forces, an armed movement that signed Sudan's Juba peace agreement, was made deputy governor of West Darfur in July 2022. The UN Panel of Experts found that he was among the leaders who facilitated and coordinated the Rapid Support Forces' attack on El Geneina, and that he and another local leader helped recruit militias to fight alongside the RSF, whose leaders met the RSF leadership in Khartoum in January 2023 and recruited their communities for money. After the governor of West Darfur was killed on 14 June 2023 and the RSF took the city, Karshoum became de facto governor, running an administration whose aid deliveries the Panel said went mainly to local Arab communities.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Sudan, S/2024/65, paras. 77-78 and 82, and timeline (pp. 19-23)
inside: A member of an armed movement was given West Darfur's deputy governorship and used that standing to help the RSF and its militias take and then run the province.

n: AFC/M23 installed its own governors and mayors in eastern Congo
who: Alliance Fleuve Congo / Mouvement du 23 mars
rank: Provincial governorships, mayoralties and territorial administrations, North and South Kivu
d: The UN Group of Experts found that, to formalise its control, the armed group AFC/M23 designated Joseph Bahati Musanga and Emmanuel Birato Rwihimbwa as governors of North and South Kivu, and made further appointments of deputy governors, territorial administrators, mayors, bourgmestres, mine delegates and other local authorities. Those appointees then took decisions over land and revenue: on 19 June 2025 the North Kivu governor authorised land registry and property title divisions to resume and ordered property registry offices reopened, interfering with land taxation and property registration, and the head of the property division in Rutshuru territory told the Group the governor approved 60 civil servants per land administration district; on 25 July the South Kivu governor issued land management rules. The group also turned villages into communes, abolishing customary rights, and ordered universities to cut ties with the education ministry in Kinshasa.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, S/2025/446, para. 26; S/2025/858, annex 13 (pp. 62-63)
inside: The armed group put its own people into Congo's provincial and municipal offices, and those officials then ran land registration and taxation to the group's benefit.

n: AFC/M23 governor made its recruitment chief deputy mayor of Goma
who: Alliance Fleuve Congo / Mouvement du 23 mars
rank: Mayoralties of Goma and Kirumba; Lubero territorial administration
d: On 9 April 2026 the governor of North Kivu appointed by the armed group AFC/M23, Bahati Musanga Joseph, signed a provincial order reorganising senior administrative posts, which it justified by the need to improve the efficiency of the public administration. The UN Group of Experts obtained the order. Among the moves, the man previously in charge of the group's mobilisation and recruitment, Nshimimana Juvenal, was appointed deputy mayor of Goma, the main city of eastern Congo; the mayor of Goma was sent to administer Lubero territory and his deputy promoted in his place, and other mayors and territorial administrators were reshuffled. The order shows the group filling the Congolese state's municipal offices from its own ranks rather than only taking over the officials it found there.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, S/2026/466, annex 27 (pp. 117)
inside: The armed group's own recruitment chief was made deputy mayor of Goma by its installed governor, putting a movement officer in charge of a city administration.

n: Spanish court found ETA controlled the party running Basque town halls
rank: Basque municipal councils and mayoralties held by Batasuna
d: On 27 March 2003 Spain's Supreme Court dissolved Herri Batasuna and Batasuna, finding that behind three parties of substantially identical ideology there was a single real subject, the terrorist organisation ETA, and a clear hierarchical subordination of the parties to it. Part of the evidence concerned the municipal institutions the parties ran. Town halls administered by Batasuna hung banners supporting terrorism on their facades on 12 and 14 August 2002; municipalities governed by the parties made apology for terrorist activities and made two ETA members honorary citizens; municipalities run by Batasuna used the emblem of Gestoras Pro-Amnistia, which the European Union had listed as a terrorist organisation; and Batasuna's municipal representatives in Vitoria and Lasarte-Oria harassed non-nationalist representatives.
cite: European Court of Human Rights, Herri Batasuna and Batasuna v. Spain, nos. 25803/04 and 25817/04, judgment of 30 June 2009, paras. 30-34
inside: An armed separatist movement controlled the party that held Basque mayoralties and council seats, and those councils used their standing to honour and back the movement.

n: Bellocco clan paid 120,000 euros to a judge to free three 'Ndrangheta men
rank: Judge of the Tribunale del Riesame, Reggio Calabria
d: Prosecutors said the judge Giancarlo Giusti, then on Reggio Calabria's review tribunal, which reviews custody orders, took 120,000 euros, 40,000 from each man, to annul custody orders obtained in August 2009 in operation 'Rosarno e nostra 2' against Rocco and Domenico Bellocco of the Bellocco clan of Rosarno and Rocco Gaetano Gallo. On 25 February 2022 a Catanzaro judge gave Armando Veneto, a lawyer and former UDEUR member of the European Parliament, six years as the go-between, but on 1 March 2024 the Catanzaro appeal court acquitted him of external participation in a mafia association and of corruption in judicial acts aggravated by mafia methods. It cut the clan side's sentences, Domenico Bellocco's from six years to five years four months. Giusti killed himself on 15 March 2015, under house arrest and never tried.
inside: A Calabrian mafia clan's money reached the judge reviewing its members' detention, prosecutors say, and the custody orders against three of them were quashed.
cite: ANSA via Espansione TV, 1 March 2024, on the Catanzaro appeal judgment (www.espansionetv.it/2024/03/01/lavvocato-armando-veneto-assolto-in-appello-da-concorso-esterno/); Il Fatto Quotidiano, 25 February 2022, on the Catanzaro first-instance verdict (www.ilfattoquotidiano.it/2022/02/25/soldi-a-un-giudice-per-far-scarcerare-tre-boss-condannato-a-sei-anni-un-avvocato-ex-eurodeputato/6507999/)
undone: Veneto's first-instance conviction of 25 February 2022 was reversed on appeal: the Catanzaro Court of Appeal acquitted him on 1 March 2024 'per non avere commesso il fatto'. The appeal court also re-determined the other sentences - Domenico Bellocco five years four months (six at first instance), Giuseppe Consiglio four years eight months (six), Vincenzo Albanese one year eight months (two) - and acquitted Rosario Marcellino, given four years at first instance, because the act is not a crime. No Court of Cassation outcome was found. Giusti was never tried, having killed himself on 15 March 2015 while under house arrest.

n: Drug defendants' families paid a Baguio judge for acquittals
rank: Presiding judge, Regional Trial Court Branch 61, Baguio City
d: The Supreme Court of the Philippines found the allegation corroborated that Antonio C. Reyes, who heard most of the drug cases in Baguio City, demanded money through go-betweens for acquittals or dismissals, and held him liable for gross misconduct, saying there was evident presence of corruption. Sworn statements from 2007 and 2008 described 50,000 to 300,000 pesos handed to a collector, Norma Domingo, for particular acquittals, and anonymous accounts of two decisions being prepared, one acquitting and one convicting, with payment deciding which was issued. A judicial audit found an acquittal granted on a second motion for reconsideration, which the rules forbid, and dismissals made before the prosecution had rested. He denied everything. On 10 November 2020 the court forfeited his retirement benefits and barred him from public office.
inside: Drug defendants' families paid collectors for the judge trying them, the Supreme Court found, so acquittals and dismissals in Baguio served the accused who paid.
cite: Supreme Court of the Philippines En Banc, A.M. No. RTJ-17-2506, Office of the Court Administrator v. Judge Antonio C. Reyes, 10 November 2020; Manila Bulletin, 28 January 2021
undone: Reyes had retired compulsorily in November 2017, so the court could not dismiss him and ordered forfeiture of benefits except accrued leave credits, with perpetual disqualification from public office. The ruling is administrative; the page records no criminal conviction.

n: US says a Mexico City judge took $2m to release a cocaine network's deputy
rank: Federal district judge, Mexico City
d: A United States indictment filed in the Central District of California alleges that Luis Benitez Alcantara, the Mexican federal district judge handling the extradition of Andrew Clark, was promised about two million dollars by Clark's side. Clark is described as the second in command of a cocaine trafficking organisation led by the former Canadian Olympic snowboarder Ryan James Wedding. Prosecutors say about 2.75 million dollars was moved through intermediaries in split payments between November 2024 and February 2025, and that on 24 February 2025, the day the judge allegedly received the money, he granted bail and ordered Clark released. Clark was re-arrested days later and sent to the United States. Benitez Alcantara was arrested in Colombia in early November 2026.
inside: Prosecutors allege a trafficking network's money reached the judge deciding its deputy's extradition, and he then ordered that man released on bail.
cite: La Cronica de Hoy (Mexico City), 5 November 2026, on the indictment in the Central District of California
undone: These are allegations and he is presumed innocent. He faces nine counts of acting as an accessory after the fact, each carrying up to fifteen years. He was detained in Colombia and the United States says it will formally request his extradition; the report does not say whether extradition has been granted.

n: Bucharest judge took gang bribes through a fortune teller; case timed out
org_label: Vica clan of Chitila and a second Bucharest gang
who: Vica clan and a second gang
rank: Judge, Bucharest Tribunal
d: Romanian prosecutors said Elena Burlan-Puscas, a judge of the Bucharest Tribunal, took 63,000 euros from members of two gangs, carried to her home and to the court by a fortune teller she was close to. In 2009 members of the Vica clan from Chitila, charged with attempted aggravated murder and blackmail, allegedly paid 10,000 euros to have detention replaced by a travel ban and 30,000 for suspended sentences for all nine. In the summer of 2010 five men charged after a bat attack allegedly paid for the same, and the one whose father did not pay received a prison term. She was sentenced in July 2020 to three and a half years, but on 16 March 2023 the High Court annulled that and ended the case as time-barred.
inside: Two Bucharest gangs' money reached the judge trying their members, prosecutors said, and detention was lifted and sentences suspended for those who paid.
cite: Agerpres, 16 March 2023, on the High Court of Cassation and Justice ruling; Radio Free Europe Romania, 2020, on the first-instance sentence
undone: She was not acquitted on the facts: the High Court annulled the 2020 conviction and ended the proceedings because criminal liability had lapsed, relying on Constitutional Court decisions 297/2018 and 358/2022. The 10,000 euro bribe was confiscated, and the report says she will receive her outstanding salaries.

n: Kruja judge signed conditional releases, Albanian prosecutors say
org_label: Convicted men seeking conditional release, and their lawyer
rank: Judge and court secretary, Kruja District Court
d: SPAK, Albania's special anti-corruption and organised crime prosecutor, says judges at the Kruja District Court took money for their decisions, mainly conditional releases for well-known convicts. On 11 February 2021 the judge Enkelejda Hoxha was arrested at the court with the Kruja lawyer Aldo Tabaku; the court's secretary Manuela Mallakuci, a forensic psychiatric expert and six other men were ordered into detention the same week on charges of passive and active corruption of justice officials and undue influence. The shqiptarja report of 2 June 2020 says Hoxha's decisions released Genc Tafili, convicted of killing the police commissioner Arben Zylyftari; the former number two of the Durres gang, Endrit Dokle, whose life sentence she extinguished; and Ilir Paja, who had just over a year left to serve.
inside: Prosecutors say convicted men and their lawyer paid a judge and a court secretary in Kruja, and the court then released the men who paid.
cite: Shqiptarja, 2 June 2020, on the releases (https://shqiptarja.com/lajm/liroi-shume-te-denuar-perjete-mes-tyre-dhe-endrit-doklen-ild-nis-hetim-ndaj-gjyqtares-u-denoncua-nga-gjonaj); Shqiptarja, 11 February 2021, on detention decision no. 14 of 10 February 2021 of the Special Court of First Instance for Corruption and Organised Crime (https://shqiptarja.com/lajm/bastisja-e-gjykates-se-krujes-report-tv-zbardh-emrat-e-10-te-arrestuarve-akuzohen-per-korrupsion); Balkanweb, 11 February 2021
undone: These are allegations and no verdict was found. The reports do not name the payers of any particular bribe or give amounts; the charge labels show three men accused of active corruption of justice officials and three of undue influence on public officials.

n: Trafficker 'el Mellizo' paid a Colombian peace-court magistrate $50,000
org_label: Miguel Angel Mejia Munera ('el Mellizo') through his lawyer
rank: Magistrate, Justice and Peace Chamber, Bogota High Court
d: The Justice and Peace Chamber is the Colombian court that handles the cases of demobilised fighters and traffickers. Colombia's Supreme Court convicted one of its Bogota magistrates, Eduardo Castellanos Roso, at first instance on 4 October 2022 of bribery in criminal proceedings. The prosecution service said that between 2013 and 2016 Marco Tulio Quintero Cano, the lawyer for the trafficker Miguel Angel Mejia Munera, known as 'el Mellizo', gave Castellanos 50,000 US dollars and other favours, so that reserved information from the chamber was passed out and Mejia's legal position eased. A charge of revealing secrets was dropped because the complaint period had expired.
inside: A trafficker's lawyer paid a magistrate of the court handling his case, prosecutors say, who then passed out the chamber's confidential information to help him.
cite: El Tiempo (Bogota), 4 October 2022, on the Supreme Court's first-instance conviction
undone: First instance only, and the report does not give the prison term, which the court said it would set later. Castellanos remained free: he had been released in late 2020 when custody time limits expired, and the court did not order his re-arrest because he kept attending summonses. No appeal outcome was found.

n: Santo Domingo investigating judge released cocaine defendants on bail
org_label: Cocaine and laundering defendants before the Fifth Investigating Court
rank: Judge, Fifth Investigating Court, Santo Domingo province
d: The Dominican attorney general's office reported to the Judicial Power Council that Jose Dionicio Duverge Mejia, judge of the Fifth Investigating Court in Santo Domingo province, had manipulated decisions in favour of people linked to drug trafficking, rejecting the prosecution's evidence in a malicious manner. It listed releases on bonds of 100,000 pesos for four men caught with 340 packages of cocaine and for a man whose van carried liquid cocaine at Haina port, and the release of a man held with 493,000 dollars in cash, and said the judge's political nephew acted as intermediary in one case. He was suspended and sent to a disciplinary trial in November 2015; in July 2016 the council dismissed him and two appeal judges as part of a network of judges.
inside: Drug defendants reached the judge deciding whether they stayed in custody, the attorney general's office said, and the court let them out on small bonds.
cite: Acento (Santo Domingo), 19 November 2015, on the Procuraduria General report to the Consejo del Poder Judicial; Acento, 24 July 2016, on the dismissals
undone: No criminal conviction was found. The attorney general of the day, Francisco Dominguez Brito, objected that the matter belonged in the criminal courts rather than in a disciplinary hearing, and the November 2015 report gives no final disciplinary ruling; the July 2016 report records the dismissal. The 2016 report names no particular ruling made for Arias Valera.

n: Costa Rican judge jailed for taking $15,000 to change a drug detention
rank: Judge, Tribunal Penal de Limon
d: A judge of the criminal court in Limon, on Costa Rica's Caribbean coast, named in the report only by the surnames Sandi Chaverri, admitted taking 15,000 dollars from Tony Pena Russell to change the pre-trial detention of a man linked to Pena Russell who was facing a drug-trafficking trial. The specialised organised crime prosecution service of the Ministerio Publico ordered his detention on 11 December 2024. He accepted the charges under the abbreviated procedure, which shortens the trial in return for a lower sentence, and the criminal court in San Jose sentenced him to 14 years and eight months, the prosecution statement listing misuse of public property, possession of child pornography, procuring impunity and money laundering, where prosecutors had asked for 25.
inside: A trafficking group's money reached the judge deciding whether a man linked to it stayed in custody, and he moved to change that detention for payment.
cite: Diario Extra (Costa Rica), report on the sentence of the Tribunal Penal de San Jose and the Fiscalia Especializada en Delincuencia Organizada
undone: The report does not say the man was in fact released, only that the judge received money in exchange for changing his precautionary measure, and it does not date the payment. It gives the sentence both as 14 years and as 14 years and eight months, and its charge list differs between the headline passage and the quoted prosecution statement.

n: Drug defendant's friend paid an Imus court sheriff 115,000 pesos for bail
org_label: A drug defendant and the friend who paid for him
rank: Sheriff IV, Regional Trial Court Branch 121, Imus City
d: A sheriff is the court officer who serves its orders and carries out its writs. Antolyn Dones Gonzales told the Supreme Court of the Philippines that Dwight Aldwin S. Geronimo, Sheriff IV at Branch 121 of the Imus City Regional Trial Court in Cavite, demanded 200,000 pesos to get her friend Monib Saadoning Amatonding's drug case resolved and bail granted, and that she paid him 115,000, with the rest due once the case was settled. Bail was later denied. In a decision of 9 July 2025 the court en banc dismissed Geronimo from the service, forfeited his retirement benefits and barred him permanently from government employment, saying that accepting money from someone with a pending case is prohibited and treating his explanation that it was a personal loan as irrelevant.
inside: A drug defendant's friend paid an officer of the court hearing his case to get him bail, so court money changed hands over a pending prosecution.
cite: Supreme Court of the Philippines En Banc decision of 9 July 2025, reported by Malaya Business Insight, 11 September 2025
undone: The money did not buy the result: bail was later denied. The ruling is administrative and the report records no criminal conviction, and it does not give the date of the payment.

n: Houthi-appointed court in Sana'a froze and seized two drug makers' assets
rank: Head of the Specialised Criminal Court and Prosecution Office, Sana'a
d: The United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen describes the Specialised Criminal Court in Sana'a, which handles state security cases, as Houthi-appointed, and names Abdullah Muhammad Zahara as head of both that court and the city's Specialised Criminal Prosecution Office. On 10 June 2024 the court sent a memorandum to the Central Bank of Yemen in Sana'a directing banks and exchange houses to freeze all the accounts and transfers of the Modern Pharmaceutical Company and the International Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Company and of their directors and staff. Houthi forces took over one factory the day before. The Panel says business owners who resist Houthi demands face detention, asset freezes, death sentences and confiscation through this court, and that these measures have become a significant source of revenue for the group.
inside: An armed movement appointed the head of a state security court in Sana'a, and its orders froze and confiscated private firms that would not submit to the movement.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2024/731, para. 120 and annexes 181 and 192; S/2025/650, paras. 140-142 and annexes 94 and 95
undone: The Panel reports this from its own sources and documents, not from any court ruling about the Houthis, and the takeover figure of 300 to 400 million dollars a year is reported to the Panel rather than established. Annex 192 records death sentences issued by the same court, including three confirmed in late July 2024 after nine years, in cases the Panel says followed prolonged arbitrary detention.

n: Indictment: two Istanbul judges freed 63 detainees on Gulen's instruction
rank: Judges of Istanbul courts; 25 former judges and prosecutors charged
d: An Istanbul indictment of April 2017, 227 pages and covering 25 former judges and prosecutors, says the Gulen movement, a religious network Turkey calls FETO, ran a structure inside the courts. It alleges that the judges Mustafa Baser and Metin Ozcelik ordered 63 detained suspects released on an encrypted instruction issued by Fethullah Gulen on 19 April 2015, that candidates for the judge and prosecutor examinations were given answer booklets already marked, that the Justice Academy was used as a profiling centre to report on candidates, and that members who had completed their internships were instructed through the Bylock application to vote in the election to the judicial board, in some cases on irregular documents. The charge is membership of an armed terrorist organisation, with up to fifteen years sought.
inside: Prosecutors say a religious movement had judges of its own inside Turkey's courts, and that two of them ordered 63 detainees released when the movement's leader told them to.
cite: Sozcu, 7 April 2017, on the indictment prepared by prosecutor Isa Dalgic and sent to Istanbul's 24th Heavy Penal Court
undone: These are allegations in an indictment, and the page carries no verdict for any of the 25 defendants. It also records that the prosecutors asked for the file to be joined to the Selam Tevhid case then before the Court of Cassation's 16th Criminal Chamber.

n: SPAK says Vlora's chief prosecutor eased a cash-smuggling case
org_label: Defendants in the Toyota Yaris cash case and Suel Cela
rank: Head of the Vlora Prosecutor's Office
d: SPAK, Albania's special anti-corruption and organised crime prosecutor, says Aurel Zarka, head of the Vlora prosecution service, used a Serious Crimes judicial police officer, Eriona Daupaj, to ease the legal position of the cousins Elvis and Alfred Vladi and of Alban Mollaymeri. Their case began in June 2018, when 3.4 million euros was found hidden in two Toyota Yaris cars at Durres port; everyone arrested was freed, and Elvis Vladi was sentenced in absentia to one year and six months for undeclared cash at the border. SPAK says Zarka also influenced asset proceedings against Suel Cela, opened on 19 February 2020, and lists eight files in all. He was ordered arrested on 29 July 2024 and charged with active and passive corruption of justice officials and with unlawful influence.
inside: Prosecutors say defendants reached the chief prosecutor of Vlora through a police officer, and the cash-smuggling case against them ended with all of them free.
cite: Bold News Albania, 30 July 2024, on the SPAK arrest orders and the files listed in them
undone: These are allegations and no verdict was found; SPAK said its preliminary investigation was continuing and might cover other facts and people. Only Zarka was taken into custody: Daupaj, the lawyer Radovan Cela and a fourth person named only as A.V. were still wanted. SPAK's case rests partly on Belgian case files and on messages from the encrypted Sky ECC service.

n: Trafficker Washo's relatives and firms got inside Durán's city government
rank: mayor's office and municipal agencies, Duran
d: Washington Aquiles Sellán Hati, a businessman in Durán known as Washo, was described by InSight Crime as the orchestrator of a sort of pax mafiosa among the city gangs. Relatives and associates were placed in the mayor's office, the transit authority, the fire department, the water and sewage company and the land planning department. A vehicle retention centre contract went to a firm in which he held shares and whose legal representative was his daughter; a 2022 contract worth $158,491 went to a company he had incorporated in 2019. Police seized nearly two tons of cocaine when they arrested him in July 2021; his detention order was lifted that October after his defence cited serious health problems; the report does not say whether he was ever convicted. He was shot dead in May 2023.
inside: A cocaine trafficker's relatives, associates and companies filled posts and won contracts in Durán's municipal bodies, so city decisions served his network.
cite: InSight Crime, 'The Rise and Fall of Washo, Duran's Criminal Puppetmaster'

n: Chone Killers sought Durán contracts and jobs for backing a mayoral run
rank: mayor's office, Duran
d: On 30 June 2025 an Ecuadorean court convicted Julio Martínez Alcívar, known as Negro Tulio, the leader of the Chone Killers gang, and 16 others of running a criminal operation in Durán, a city next to Guayaquil. The ruling relied on wiretaps and audio recordings in which the name of the mayor, Luis Chonillo, came up repeatedly. Evidence at the trial showed that Negro Tulio demanded money, contracts and government jobs from city officials in exchange for supporting Chonillo's mayoral campaign. Ecuador's Prosecutor General is investigating the mayor for possible involvement in organised crime. Chonillo has denied any links to crime and has worked remotely since August 2024, after surviving an attempt on his life. Negro Tulio was captured in Panama in May 2024.
inside: A convicted gang leader asked Durán's officials for contracts and council jobs in return for supporting the mayor's campaign; prosecutors are investigating the mayor.
cite: The Rio Times, 3 July 2025, reporting a 30 June 2025 court ruling

n: Jamaica's government lobbied Washington to drop don Coke's extradition
rank: Jamaica Labour Party and the government it formed
d: Christopher 'Dudus' Coke controlled Tivoli Gardens, the Kingston garrison district on whose votes the governing Labour Party depended to hold power's safest seat, and the party depended on its votes. After the United States asked for his extradition in August 2009, the foreign ministry, the justice ministry, the attorney general's office and the solicitor general's office allegedly ran a government-wide effort to delay it. In September 2009 a party consultant, Harold Brady, advised Prime Minister Bruce Golding to seek American legal help, and in October signed a contract on the government's behalf with the Washington firm Manatt, Phelps and Phillips, which lobbied for months; the source of the initial $50,000 payment was never revealed. The government said Brady acted for the party. The extradition order was signed in May 2010.
inside: A crime boss who delivered the ruling party's votes had its government machinery working for months to stop his own extradition.
cite: InSight Crime, 'How Jamaica Tried to Stall Dudus Coke's Extradition'

n: Jamaica inquiry urged an end to state and party money going to dons
rank: members of parliament and the Constituency Development Fund
d: The West Kingston Commission of Enquiry, appointed after the 2010 security operation in Tivoli Gardens, reported in May 2016. Dons are the strongmen who run Jamaica's garrison communities, districts that vote almost wholly for one party. The commissioners recommended that political leaders commit to 'ending the allocation of the Government's and the political party's resources to dons', and said state constituency money such as the Constituency Development Fund 'should be administered by a representative board rather than at the direction of a member of parliament'. They said political patronage and violence are two of the hallmarks of a garrison constituency, described Tivoli Gardens as an advanced-stage garrison community, and said they remained concerned about criminal organisations based in such communities.
inside: An official inquiry found public and party money reaching garrison crime bosses through members of parliament, and asked that the practice stop.
cite: Jamaica Gleaner, 30 June 2016, on the West Kingston Commission of Enquiry report

n: Cachiros traffickers agreed to fund Libre's 2013 Honduran campaign
rank: Libre party; later secretary of Congress
d: A video filmed in November 2013, weeks before Xiomara Castro's failed presidential bid, shows Carlos Zelaya, her brother-in-law and later the powerful secretary of Honduras's Congress, meeting traffickers including Devis and Javier Rivera, the leaders of the Cachiros trafficking group. InSight Crime, which published the video in 2024, reports that the traffickers agreed to give about $650,000 to support the Libre party's campaign, half of it meant for Mel Zelaya. Libre figures Adán Fúnez, the mayor of Tocoa, and Carlos Muñoz were also present. Carlos Zelaya resigned from Congress on 31 August 2024, said he had acted on his own and said there had never been any money delivered, 'at least not to me'. The report does not say whether he has been charged.
inside: A trafficking group put campaign money into the party that went on to govern, and its Congress secretary attended the meeting where the sum was agreed.
cite: InSight Crime, 'Narco Video Shows Traffickers Discussing Bribes With Honduras President's Brother-in-Law'; InSight Crime, 29 May 2025

n: 'Los Dinámicos del Centro' licence money allegedly funded Perú Libre
rank: Junín regional transport directorate; Perú Libre party
d: Prosecutors in the Peruvian region of Junín allege that Los Dinámicos del Centro, a criminal organisation they say had operated there since 2012, sold driving licences through the regional government's transport and communications directorate and turned the fees into campaign money for the Perú Libre party. The anti-corruption prosecutor Bonnie Bautista said the aim was to finance the campaign of the party in office in the 2019-2022 term, basing this on statements by people seeking to become cooperating witnesses. Prosecutors say officials recruited applicants and placed people in posts tied to licence issuance, and they name the regional transport director Eduardo Bendezú Gutarra and Perú Libre's organisation secretary Arturo Cárdenas Tovar. The charges have not been proven in court.
inside: Prosecutors say a licence-selling criminal network inside a regional government funded a party's campaign, so public office paid for the politics that protected it.
cite: Gestión (Peru), reporting the Junín anti-corruption prosecutor's hearing submissions

n: Businessmen and ex-mayor charged as a group over Molino road tenders
who: alleged criminal organisation around the former mayor
rank: district municipality of Molino, Pachitea
d: Peru's special anti-corruption team EFICCOP obtained 30 months of pre-trial detention against what it calls a criminal organisation led by Jean Sumarán Lino, the former mayor of the Molino district in Pachitea province, together with the businessmen Jhon Aquino Jara and César Eugenio Orizano. The judge Margarita Salcedo Guevara ordered the measure after two weeks of hearings, and the municipality's former manager, Milayda Valderrama Ortega, was placed under restricted release for the same period. The charges are criminal organisation, aggravated collusion and money laundering. They concern the budget allocated to the works project registered as CUI 2217835 and the municipality's 2022 public tender and simplified award for roads and pavements. None of this has been proven in court.
inside: Prosecutors say outside contractors and the district's own former mayor formed one organisation that took the municipality's road tenders and the budget behind them.
cite: Ministerio Público del Perú, weekly official bulletin (EFICCOP, Molino case)

n: PCC-linked firms rigged labour tenders in twelve São Paulo councils
rank: twelve municipal governments and city councils in São Paulo state
d: On 16 April 2024 the organised-crime unit of São Paulo state's public prosecution service, the Gaeco, launched Operação Muditia against a scheme that rigged tenders for outsourced labour in municipal governments and city councils. Investigators say the companies simulated competition between partner firms or firms in the same group, and prosecutors said some contracts served the interest of the PCC, Brazil's largest crime group, which influenced which bidders won. Public contracts of more than 200 million reais were signed by the councils of Guarulhos, São Paulo, Ferraz de Vasconcelos, Cubatão, Arujá, Santa Isabel, Poá, Jaguariúna, Guarujá, Sorocaba, Buri and Itatiba. Fifteen arrest warrants were issued, three of them for councillors in Arujá, Cubatão and Ferraz de Vasconcelos, along with 42 search warrants.
inside: Prosecutors say Brazil's largest crime group shaped who won municipal labour contracts, with councillors and officials arrested as part of the scheme.
cite: Jovem Pan, 16 April 2024, on Operação Muditia by the Gaeco of the São Paulo public prosecution service

n: Senator said to run the BLTS gang placed two heads of Haiti's aid office
rank: Senate seat for Nippes; appointments at the Bureau de monétisation
d: The UN Security Council's panel of experts on Haiti reported in September 2026 that Nenel Cassy, a senator for the Nippes Department in 2006-2012 and 2016-2020, has supported various armed actors to advance his own interests, and that he controls the BLTS criminal group in Miragoâne commune, which it says specialises in illegal firearms, murder, kidnapping for ransom and armed robbery. During his 2016-2020 term, the panel says, he used his influence to secure the appointment of the two heads of the Office for the Monetization of Development Assistance Programmes, including Patrick Noramé. He was arrested on 2 August 2025 for conspiracy against state security, financing of criminal groups, attempted murder and association with criminals, and released on 19 August 2025; officials say the case is being re-examined, but sources close to the investigation told the panel it had been dropped.
inside: A UN panel says a senator who controls an armed criminal group used his seat to choose who ran the state office that handles development aid money.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2026/714, paras. 52-58

n: Bondholders' receivership took over Liberia's customs service
org_label: 1912 refunding loan bankers and their receivership
rank: General Receiver of Customs and three Receivers of Customs
d: On 26 November 1912 Reed Paige Clark, General Receiver of Customs, took control of Liberia's customs service, and President Daniel E. Howard proclaimed the refunding loan agreement in force the same day. The proclamation named the bankers as J. P. Morgan and Company, Kuhn, Loeb and Company, the National City Bank of New York and the First National Bank of New York. Three further Receivers of Customs, Gustav Lange, Emile Frederic Wolf and Richard Sharpe, took office, and the receivers met formally on 28 November. Clark said he would remit all sums received for the loan's service to the London City and Midland Bank. The loan was about US$1.7 million. Customs duties from that date were to be held intact, subject only to the order of the General Receiver.
inside: The lenders' own officials ran Liberia's customs service, collecting the state's main revenue and sending it abroad to pay the bankers who had lent the money.
cite: US Foreign Relations of the United States 1912, document 887 (dispatch from Monrovia, 29 November 1912); Liberia Past and Present, 'President Arthur Barclay (1904-1912)'; Library of Congress country study, 'Liberia in receivership'

n: Fake-refugee racket got a forged report inside Nepal's home ministry
rank: Deputy prime minister, home minister and home secretary
d: A network that sold fake Bhutanese refugee registrations to Nepalis hoping to be resettled in the United States worked through the home ministry. A task force formed on 13 June 2019 by then home minister Ram Bahadur Thapa reported that October that only 429 people should be registered; a forged version of its report, kept at the ministry, added schedules making 875 appear eligible. Police filed cases against 31 people in August 2024. On 14 July 2026 the Kathmandu District Court jailed former deputy prime minister Top Bahadur Rayamajhi and former home secretary Tek Narayan Pandey for four years and former home minister Bal Krishna Khand for two as an accomplice. The court did not establish who forged the report.
inside: Private brokers reached inside Nepal's home ministry, where a forged official report and counterfeit refugee cards let them sell fake refugee status to paying buyers.
cite: Kathmandu District Court judgment as reported by The Kathmandu Post, 12 October 2026; Accountability Lab Nepal governance bulletin 215, July 2026

n: Warlords in Afghanistan's parliament passed their own amnesty law
org_label: Afghan armed factions' commanders in parliament
rank: Members of the National Assembly
d: Human Rights Watch says Afghanistan's parliament passed the National Stability and Reconciliation Law in 2007, backed by a coalition of powerful warlords and their supporters; it names none of them. The law says anyone engaged in armed conflict before the interim administration was formed in December 2001 shall not be prosecuted, and gives immunity to those fighting now if they reconcile with the government, which Human Rights Watch says extends amnesty to future crimes. The law was published in the official gazette without announcement, despite President Hamid Karzai's repeated promises not to let it take effect. The gazette is dated December 2008; some accounts say printed copies reached monitoring groups only in January 2010, and Human Rights Watch says it is not clear when this happened. A presidential spokesman said transitional justice was not the government's responsibility.
inside: Commanders of Afghanistan's armed factions held seats in parliament and used them to pass a law barring prosecution for the war crimes of their own past.
cite: Human Rights Watch, 'Afghanistan: Repeal Amnesty Law', 10 March 2010

n: Ex-rebels' party in Aceh's legislature made GAM's banner the flag
org_label: Free Aceh Movement (GAM) and Partai Aceh
rank: Aceh provincial legislature (DPRA)
d: Partai Aceh was set up in 2008 by former leaders of the Free Aceh Movement, the separatist force that fought Indonesia until the 2005 Helsinki agreement, and is run by a small GAM elite. It holds 42 of the 69 seats in Aceh's provincial legislature. On 25 March 2013 that legislature adopted Qanun 3/2013 by acclamation, making GAM's former banner, red with black and white stripes and a crescent and star, the flag of Aceh. Governor Zaini Abdullah, GAM's former foreign minister, signed it at once. Home affairs minister Gamawan Fauzi said the flag breached a 2007 regulation barring flags resembling those of separatist movements and on 4 April 2013 asked for thirteen parts of the law to be changed; GAM's leaders refused.
inside: The separatist movement's own party holds most seats in Aceh's legislature and used them to adopt the movement's wartime banner as the province's official flag.
cite: International Crisis Group, 'Indonesia: Tensions over Aceh's Flag', Asia Briefing, 2013

n: Aceh bylaw made a post that GAM's former leader was installed in
org_label: Free Aceh Movement (GAM) and Partai Aceh
rank: Wali Nanggroe of Aceh
d: Aceh Qanun 8/2012 governs the office of the Wali Nanggroe, which the 2006 Aceh Administration Law describes as a customary leadership to unite the people, with authority over customary institutions, titles and ceremonies on renewable seven-year terms. On 16 December 2013 Malik Mahmud Al Haytar, the Free Aceh Movement's former self-styled prime minister, was installed in it, with the governor and a serving national minister present. The home affairs ministry had not ratified the appointment and had asked Aceh's legislature to clarify 21 items in the bylaw. The International Crisis Group said Partai Aceh, the party set up by the former rebels, already controlled the province's executive and legislature, was influencing the civil service and local election commission, and controlled a new bureaucracy set up to safeguard Acehnese culture.
inside: The former rebel movement's party controls Aceh's legislature; a bylaw passed there created a provincial office that the movement's own former prime minister then filled.
cite: The Jakarta Post, 17 December 2013; International Crisis Group as reported by the Jakarta Globe, 8 May 2013

n: Gold syndicate used Biman staff to move 124kg through Dhaka airport
rank: Biman engineering, security and inspection staff
d: On 24 July 2013 customs officers at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka seized 1,064 gold bars, about 124kg, left abandoned in the luggage chamber of a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight from Dubai. The detective branch of Dhaka Metropolitan Police charged 18 people in March 2017, among them eight Biman employees: a junior security officer, a senior inspection officer, an engineering officer, two aircraft mechanics, an assistant mechanic, a sweeping supervisor and one staff member whose post the charge sheet does not give. Also charged were Gourango Rosan, a Nepalese national alleged to own the gold, the chairman of SS Cargo, an agent and seven accomplices. The investigating officer said all the accused were members of an organised gold smuggling syndicate that moved gold through different airports. Five accused, Rosan among them, were fugitives.
inside: A smuggling syndicate had the national airline's own mechanics, inspectors and security staff on its side, so its gold could pass through Dhaka airport unnoticed.
cite: The Daily Star, 6 March 2017, on the charge sheet filed at Dhaka Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court

n: Intelligence report put 272 Biman staff inside gold smuggling rings
rank: Pilots, cabin crew, pursers and ground staff
d: An intelligence report submitted to Bangladesh's Prime Minister's Office, reported in February 2015, said at least 272 officials and staff of Biman Bangladesh Airlines, the national flag carrier, were involved in gold smuggling, among them five pilots, four co-pilots, 25 cabin crew, 15 flight stewards and five chief pursers, together with several Civil Aviation Authority staff. It said Biman officials were paid Tk 1,000 to 1,500 for each ten-tola bar passed through the airports, that 30 syndicates were active, and that the rackets were backed by political leaders and some senior police and Border Guard officers. After five arrests on 18 November 2014 the report said 44 officials left the country; Biman's public relations manager denied any had fled.
inside: Smuggling rings paid staff throughout the state airline, from pilots to ground crew, so that their gold could travel on its aircraft.
cite: The Daily Star, 'Smugglers within', 2 February 2015, citing an intelligence report to the Prime Minister's Office; Customs Today, 4 February 2015

n: Smuggling gang's gold hidden by Biman catering men; four jailed
rank: Biman Flight Catering Centre pantry men
d: On 15 March 2018 Dhaka Customs House officers acting on a tip-off recovered 9.28kg of gold, worth Tk46.4 million, from an aircraft toilet at Shahjalal International Airport. Case documents said two pantry men of the Biman Flight Catering Centre, Khandaker Ruhul Amin and Shahinur Islam, had put the bars in a tissue box in the toilet of flight BG-236 from Jeddah to Dhaka while on duty. A Criminal Investigation Department inspector pressed charges on 8 July 2019 and the tribunal framed charges on 13 December 2020. In January 2022 Metropolitan Special Tribunal-3, under judge Bilkis Akter, jailed the two men and two members of the smuggling gang, Iftarul Alam Sarker and Riaj alias Amjad, for twelve years each with fines of Tk40,000.
inside: A smuggling gang used two of the airline's own catering staff to hide its gold on board a flight, and a court jailed all four.
cite: The Financial Express (Dhaka), 12 January 2022

n: Ivory network's containers cleared by Mombasa port and revenue men
rank: Kenya Revenue Authority officer and Kenya Ports Authority employee
d: In 2013 more than three tonnes of ivory were seized at Mombasa and more than a tonne in Hong Kong, in shipments linked to the network of Moazu Kromah, a trafficker later prosecuted in the United States. In March 2022 a Kenyan court convicted James Ngala Kassiwa, an officer of the Kenya Revenue Authority, and the clearing agent Fredrick Sababu Mungule of facilitating the shipments, sentencing each to two years. A Kenya Ports Authority employee, Gideon Natali Onsinyo Nyangau, was charged with them and was among those convicted. All three had earlier been acquitted in a separate case over a Singapore-bound shipment seized in January 2013, the court ruling that the prosecution had not proved a prima facie case; the account gives no year for that acquittal. The reports read do not say what the two state employees were paid.
