inside: A trafficking network's ivory left Mombasa because a revenue officer and a port authority employee cleared its containers; a court convicted them years later.
cite: Daniel Stiles, 'Open and not shut: ivory trafficking court cases in East Africa linked to the Kromah network', 2022; Daily Maverick, 22 June 2022

n: Madagascar's ministries gave 13 rosewood traders export quotas
rank: Inter-ministerial order; Forestry Administration
d: Inter-ministerial Order 38409/2009, made on 5 October 2009, gave each of 13 traders listed in an earlier order a non-transferable quota to export twenty-five 20-foot containers of precious wood within 60 days, by 30 November 2009, although the order's own text referred to the illegal nature of the products. A note from the prime minister's office on 31 December 2009 then let all traders meeting the conditions of another order load their wood, with no conditions or timetable, and a further note of 11 May 2010 permitted the export of 79 impounded containers, shipped the following month. A mission in the SAVA region organised by Malagasy forestry bodies reported possible collusion of Forestry Administration and law enforcement officials with traffickers, and a capture of state authorities by the Antalaha traders.
inside: A small group of timber traders had enough hold inside Madagascar's forestry and other ministries that official orders licensed the export of illegally cut rosewood.
cite: Global Witness and Environmental Investigation Agency, investigation into the illegal felling, transport and export of precious wood from the SAVA region, Madagascar, October 2010

n: Ti Bwa gang's network reached a serving Haitian judicial police officer
rank: Officer of the judicial police, Haitian National Police
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Haiti reported that in October 2023 a police officer named Cleevens Degazon, alias "My Man", was arrested for his association with the Ti Bwa gang, led by Christ-Roi Chery, alias "Chrisla". Although Degazon had been dismissed from the police in August 2023, the Panel found he was colluding with Ryvelor Domond, an active officer of the judicial police. Domond was in frequent communication with Chrisla and had contacts with influential Ti Bwa members, including four further police officers the Panel names. A Haitian news site reported the arrest at Cap-Haitien airport on 1 October 2023, as Degazon was booked on a flight to Miami. The sources read do not say what became of the case.
inside: The gang kept a serving judicial police officer in its network, in frequent contact with its leader, giving it reach inside the force meant to investigate it.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2026/714, annex 9; IciHaiti, 2 October 2023

n: Haitian police officers alerted gangs to kidnap targets and let them pass
rank: Officers of the Haitian National Police
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Haiti reported in 2026 that some officers of the Haitian National Police look aside during patrols to allow gangs to escape with kidnapping victims, and alert gangs to where likely victims are and how they move. The Panel described the inter-dependence between gangs, government staff and some police officers as not new, and said gangs are tipped off by police insiders about coming security operations. Its account came from interviews with an anti-kidnapping official, a gang analyst and two police officers in June 2026. Kidnapping had become a main source of gang revenue after operations cleared road checkpoints, with 143 cases recorded countrywide in January and February 2026 alone.
inside: Gangs have officers inside the police who warn them of raids and wave kidnappers through, so patrols serve the gangs' takings instead of stopping them.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2026/714, annex 21 and paras. 134 and 137

n: Gran Grif drew police ammunition through a UDMO officer's security firm
rank: Senior officer in charge of logistics and ammunition, Departmental Law Enforcement Unit, Artibonite
d: On 3 August 2025 a motorcyclist was stopped by members of the Jean Denis self-defence coalition in the lower Artibonite while carrying nine boxes of ammunition for the Gran Grif gang. The UN Panel of Experts on Haiti reported that the ammunition had been supplied by Edouens Elan, a cousin of the gang's leader Luckson Elan, and matched rounds used by the Haitian National Police, some of them donated by an international partner. Edouens Elan worked for a local private security company, not registered with the Ministry of the Interior, whose co-owner is the senior officer responsible for logistics and ammunition in the force's Departmental Law Enforcement Unit for the Artibonite. The Panel says he is a central figure of the network and used his position to divert ammunition.
inside: The gang's own relative drew on a police unit's ammunition through a security firm part-owned by the officer who controlled it, arming the gang from state stocks.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2026/714, annex 19 and paras. 85 and 110

n: Haitian police unit resold rifles it had seized to gangs in the Artibonite
org_label: Gran Grif and Kokorat San Ras gangs
rank: Officers of the Departmental Law Enforcement Unit, Pat-Chawal commissariat
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Haiti investigated a network of officers of the Departmental Law Enforcement Unit, operating mainly out of the Pat-Chawal commissariat in Saint-Marc commune, who sold ammunition to gangs and to armed individuals involved in land seizures. The Panel set out the method: officers gradually syphoned boxes of twenty rounds of 5.56mm ammunition and sold each box for 10,000 Haitian gourdes, about 75 US dollars, and also sold semi-automatic rifles the force had itself seized for between 5,000 and 8,000 US dollars. Nationally, the police seized 356 firearms in 2025 and, with no central process for managing seizures, many are unaccounted for. The force's Inspectorate General is investigating the unit's officers.
inside: Officers of a police unit sold guns the force had confiscated back to the gangs it had taken them from, turning seizures into a supply line for them.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2026/714, annex 19 and paras. 85, 110 and 114

n: Montrouis gang leader bought police rifle ammunition from a UDMO officer
rank: Officer of the Departmental Law Enforcement Unit, Artibonite
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Haiti reported that boxes of 7.62x51mm ammunition from Haitian National Police stockpiles were identified in photographs of the arsenal of Destin Wilgens, known as "Tibab", the late gang leader of Montrouis commune in the Artibonite, and that the ammunition had been purchased from an officer of the force's Departmental Law Enforcement Unit. The Panel's finding rests on confidential sources interviewed in 2026 and photographs held by the Panel; it does not name the officer. Diversions of this kind are persistent: of 336 rounds of the same calibre seized from two other gangs in 2026, 70 per cent had come from police stockpiles.
inside: A gang leader bought a police unit's own rifle ammunition from one of its officers, so state stocks armed the gang that unit was meant to fight.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2026/714, annex 19 and para. 111

n: Protected-areas brigade agents joined north Haiti gangs in seizing land
org_label: North Department gangs, some linked to Viv Ansanm
rank: Agents of the Protected Areas Security Brigade, North Department
d: The Protected Areas Security Brigade is a Haitian state force set up to guard protected land. The UN Panel of Experts on Haiti reported in 2026 that in the North Department local gangs, some of them linked to the Viv Ansanm alliance, and certain agents of the brigade, under the leadership of Alex Jean-Pierre, have been involved in land spoliation. The Panel's earlier report that year described the group seizing land, often from owners living abroad, dividing it into plots and selling it, and using the proceeds to buy weapons and uniforms and to build houses and hotels. Brigade agents also set up an illegal checkpoint at Bois d'Anse, in Limonade commune, to charge transit fees.
inside: Gangs worked with agents of a state conservation force, so a brigade meant to guard protected land helped seize and sell it and taxed the road beside it.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2026/714, para. 39; S/2026/241, para. 26

n: AFC/M23 installed its own intelligence chief in Congo's ANR office, Goma
rank: Chief of intelligence, Agence nationale de renseignements office, Goma
d: After the armed alliance AFC/M23 took Goma in January 2025, it installed a man known as Baziramwabo, alias Baz, as chief of intelligence (ANR) in the city. The Agence nationale de renseignements is Congo's national intelligence service, and the UN Group of Experts recorded that the office Baziramwabo used was the Congolese government's own ANR office. Bari and Hermann Bahinzi were put in charge of all ANR administration, and Bonane Bujakera was attached to Baziramwabo's office. The same announcements named an AFC/M23 governor of North Kivu, a mayor of Goma and appointees down to commune level. The Group treats these appointments as part of a parallel administration imposed in conquered territory.
inside: AFC/M23, an armed movement, placed its own appointee over the national intelligence office in Goma, so intelligence work in the city served the movement.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, final report S/2025/446, annex 16 (para. 26)

n: AFC/M23 put its own staff in Congo's migration and customs posts at Goma
rank: Officials of the Directorate-General of Migration and the Directorate-General of Customs and Excise
d: AFC/M23 replaced the officials of Congo's state migration police, the Directorate-General of Migration, and of the customs authority, the Directorate-General of Customs and Excise, with people it appointed itself. The UN Group of Experts reported that these appointees were instructed not to screen goods transiting at Grande Barriere, the main border crossing between Goma and Gisenyi in Rwanda, and to leave border control for transiting goods to the Rwandan authorities instead. The Group also recorded that AFC/M23 appointed officers of the police forces and of intelligence networks in the areas it held. Its sources were Goma residents, journalists, civil society and researchers.
inside: An armed movement replaced Congo's border and customs officers with its own appointees, who then waved transiting goods through to Rwanda as the movement wanted.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, final report S/2025/446, paras. 26 and 30

n: FDLR kept liaison officers inside Congo's army, one flying on its aircraft
org_label: Forces democratiques de liberation du Rwanda-Forces combattantes abacunguzi (FDLR-FOCA)
rank: FDLR liaison officers to FARDC; FARDC-appointed liaison colonel
d: FDLR is a Rwandan Hutu armed group under UN sanctions that operates in eastern Congo. The UN Group of Experts reported that in 2026 the Congolese armed forces (FARDC) and government authorities used FDLR liaison officers to coordinate joint action. Fidel Sebagenzi, the FDLR-FOCA liaison officer primarily based in Kinshasa, travelled regularly to North Kivu aboard FARDC military aircraft, and FDLR-FPP and FDLR-RUD liaison officers based in Beni and Kasindi were in regular contact with Colonel Cyprien Sekololo, the FARDC-appointed liaison with the Wazalendo militias. In January 2026 the FARDC chief of staff banned any collaboration with FDLR, yet officials in Kinshasa and officers on the ground reassured FDLR that the planned neutralisation operations would not be genuine.
inside: A sanctioned armed group kept its own liaison officers working inside the army's command arrangements, which went on supplying and tasking the group after being ordered to stop.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, final report S/2026/466, paras. 134-138

n: FDLR's liaison reached North Kivu's military governor as the army armed it
org_label: Forces democratiques de liberation du Rwanda-Forces combattantes abacunguzi (FDLR-FOCA)
rank: Governor of North Kivu, Major General Cirimwami
d: On 21 November 2023, under diplomatic pressure, the FARDC chief of staff, Lieutenant General Christian Tshiwewe, issued instructions banning cooperation between the Congolese army and FDLR, a Rwandan armed group under UN sanctions. The UN Group of Experts reported that FDLR-FOCA nonetheless stayed part of the coalition supporting the army and remained at front-line positions, including at the army's request. The FDLR commander Fidel Sebagenzi acted as liaison between FDLR-FOCA and the government's Wazalendo militias, and between the sanctioned FDLR-FOCA military commander Ntawunguka Pacifique, alias Omega Israel, and the governor of North Kivu, Major General Cirimwami. The army provided military equipment and financing to FDLR-FOCA in return for fighting M23, in violation of the arms embargo.
inside: The armed group's own liaison officer dealt directly with the province's military governor, and the army's equipment and money then went to the group despite an order forbidding it.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, final report S/2024/432, paras. 70-72

n: ADF ran its prison network through bribed Congolese prison and spy staff
rank: Penitentiary, judicial and intelligence authorities, including prison directors
d: The Allied Democratic Forces is an armed group in eastern Congo affiliated to Islamic State. The UN Group of Experts found that ADF detainees had set up an organised system in each prison holding them, with a leader and deputy designated by the sanctioned ADF leader Musa Baluku, who communicated with them directly or through intermediaries. Key ADF detainees had been moved to Kinshasa after the October 2020 Kangbayi jailbreak. Most kept access to telephones and other facilities, the Group reported, often with the complicity of penitentiary, judicial and intelligence authorities whom they bribed or who were in direct contact with ADF leadership in the bush. Detainees said authorities at Makala, Beni and Bunia prisons, including at director level, benefited from the corruption.
inside: An armed group's money reached prison, judicial and intelligence staff, who let its jailed members keep phones, cash and contact with the group's leadership.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, final report S/2024/432, paras. 16-17 and annexes 6 and 8

n: ADF freed a commander from a state safehouse with help from soldiers
rank: Prison guard at Makala; FARDC elements who helped him escape a FARDC/National Security Council safehouse
d: Hamuli Balume Guylain, alias Kanane, one of the few Congolese ADF commanders and a close adviser to the group's leader, was arrested at Bunia in March 2020 and transferred to Makala prison in Kinshasa. ADF leadership sent him forged documents through a prison guard, which he did not use. In 2022 the Congolese army and the National Security Council moved him out of prison into a safehouse, and a few months later he escaped from it with the help of some army elements and returned to the bush. The UN Group of Experts reported that the ADF figure known as Amigo used connections at the highest levels of the army in both attempts, possibly including the sanctioned officer Muhindo Akili Mundos.
inside: The armed group reached a prison guard and then soldiers guarding a state safehouse, who let one of its commanders walk out and rejoin it.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, final report S/2024/432, annex 7 (para. 17)

n: AFC/M23 paid Congolese army officers to bring their units over
rank: Serving FARDC officers and Wazalendo militia leaders
d: The UN Group of Experts documented concerted efforts by AFC/M23 to bribe serving officers of the Congolese armed forces, and leaders of the government's Wazalendo militias, in order to trigger mass defections to the alliance. The Group's sources were AFC/M23 members and intelligence sources. The report notes that AFC/M23 was itself losing people at a high rate, mainly among forcibly recruited former Congolese soldiers. The Group does not name the officers approached or say how many accepted.
inside: An armed movement offered money to serving army officers so that they and their units would come over to it, which is the movement buying people inside the national army.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, final report S/2026/466, para. 67

n: Wazalendo militias took over border posts and police work in South Kivu
org_label: Volontaires pour la defense de la patrie/Wazalendo (VDP/Wazalendo)
rank: Border posts, taxation and police functions in Uvira, Fizi and Mwenga territories
d: The Wazalendo are militias that the Congolese government uses as a proxy force against AFC/M23 and Rwandan troops. The UN Group of Experts reported that before AFC/M23 took Uvira in December 2025 they operated as a loose coalition of about a dozen competing coordinations which increasingly encroached on state prerogatives, including the control of border posts, taxation and police functions, and preyed on civilians. The government funded them: $300,000 a month through the office of the governor of North Kivu, with army Colonel Sekololo as liaison and army helicopter rotations delivering uniforms, weapons, ammunition and food. In Uvira, Fizi and Mwenga their roadblocks forced civilians to pay heavy fees, with extortion, abuse, sexual violence and summary executions reported.
inside: State-funded militias came to run border posts, taxation and policing in government-held South Kivu, so those state functions were worked for the militias' own benefit.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, final report S/2026/466, para. 110; final report S/2025/858, paras. 75 and 82

n: Militia units inside South Sudan's army answered to their own commanders
org_label: Murle 'Cobra' faction and allied community militias
rank: SSPDF units including 'Brigade 23', 'Agrab Battalion', '188 Battalion' and 'Special Brigade'
d: The UN Panel of Experts reported that community militias had been taken into South Sudan's army, the SSPDF, while keeping their own chains of command. The Murle-dominated Cobra faction under David Yau Yau was formally integrated, and others, such as Joshua Konyi, a former government official and by then SSPDF commander in Pibor, took command of local military units through political appointment. Few of these units joined the formal unification process, they appear to mobilise as necessary, and they go by names including Brigade 23, the Agrab Battalion, the 188 Battalion and the Special Brigade, typically bypassing the military hierarchy and reporting straight to SSPDF headquarters. The Panel said this generated confusion about the forces' loyalties and deepened Anyuak feelings of marginalisation.
inside: Militias entered the national army as whole units under their own commanders, so army formations in Pibor took orders from the militias rather than the ordinary chain of command.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan, final report S/2023/922, paras. 62-64

n: South Sudan's army handed its operations to militias with their own feuds
org_label: Shilluk Agwelek, Dinka Padang and Azande forces
who: Agwelek, Dinka Padang and Azande militias
rank: SSPDF operational command in Upper Nile and Jonglei States
d: The UN Panel of Experts reported that competition between elites in Juba and years of neglect had fragmented and weakened South Sudan's army, the SSPDF, which became increasingly reliant on local militia forces and defectors only recently and loosely integrated into its ranks. The Panel named Shilluk Agwelek and Dinka Padang forces in Upper Nile and Jonglei States and Azande forces under the command of James Nando in Western Equatoria State. In Upper Nile and northern Jonglei, where the opposition SPLM/A-IO and the White Army held significant territory, the army entrusted many of its operations to the recently integrated Agwelek forces and Dinka militias, which have their own historic disputes with local Nuer communities.
inside: Militias taken loosely into the national army were handed its operations, so state military force was used to pursue the militias' own disputes with neighbouring communities.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan, interim report S/2025/768, paras. 25 and 28

n: Agwelek militia led South Sudan's Jonglei campaign with police behind it
org_label: Shilluk Agwelek forces under Johnson Olony
rank: SSPDF formations, national police, military intelligence and National Security Service reinforcements
d: Johnson Olony leads the predominantly Shilluk Agwelek forces, loosely integrated into South Sudan's army after he left the opposition SPLM/A-IO in 2021, and he was appointed an SSPDF deputy chief of defence forces in 2025. For the 2025-2026 campaign in Upper Nile and Jonglei States, the UN Panel of Experts reported that his Agwelek forces were reinforced with troops from Juba, Divisions 3, 11 and 12, and with forces from the national police, military intelligence and the National Security Service. Agwelek paraded vehicle-mounted ZU-23-2 anti-aircraft guns, a 122mm howitzer and mortar systems, which sources said played a key part in army ground operations, and appeared to have received a significant transfer of new weapons and equipment.
inside: A militia inside the army was given police, military intelligence and security service units and new heavy weapons, so national forces fought under the militia's command.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan, final report S/2026/340, paras. 48, 51, 60 and 85

n: Defected commander's own force in Unity State got new army vehicles
rank: SSPDF-allied force in Mayom, Unity State
d: The UN Panel of Experts documented a large import of military vehicles by South Sudan's army, unarmed at the point of import but in several cases later fitted with weapons. Photographs obtained by the Panel indicate that forces under the command of Tito Biel Wich in Mayom, Unity State, also received vehicles. He is a former SPLA-IO commander who defected to the army in February 2022 and, the Panel reported, then controlled a semi-autonomous army-allied force that has repeatedly clashed with SPLA-IO forces, including at Nyuelnyuel. The Panel noted that in at least one case vehicles went to army and proxy forces fighting SPLA-IO units, and argued that distributing them to non-unified forces may be inconsistent with the peace agreement.
inside: A commander who brought his own force into the army kept control of it and drew the state's new military vehicles for his fight with his former movement.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan, final report S/2024/343, paras. 131-133

n: Opposition commanders took army supplies and turned on their old force
rank: SSPDF commanders in Unity State
d: In October 2023 the SPLA-IO commanders Lieutenant General Simon Maguek Gai and Major General Samuel Dok Wanjang, with several officers from Leer County, announced their defection to South Sudan's army in what became known as the Thonyoor declaration. The UN Panel of Experts reported that the defection was coordinated by senior SPLM figures in Juba and Unity State, including the state governor, Joseph Monytuil, that the commanders were given weapons, food and supplies and were immediately taken into the SPLM party. Some of the defecting officers subsequently detained dozens of civilians and at least two dozen SPLA-IO soldiers in Koch County, Unity State, allegedly for refusing also to defect, and on 28 November 2023 their forces joined the army in attacking an SPLA-IO base and civilian locations in Leer County.
inside: Opposition commanders brought their own units into the national army, were armed and supplied by it, and used that backing to jail and attack their former movement's forces.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan, final report S/2024/343, paras. 81-84

n: SPLA-IO split Adok port fees with South Sudan's army and SPLM officials
org_label: Sudan People's Liberation Movement/Army in Opposition (SPLM/A-IO)
rank: SSPDF soldiers and SPLM officials at the port of Adok, Unity State
d: River ports in South Sudan have become centres of illicit taxation, with charges described as port fees running from 200,000 to one million South Sudanese pounds depending on the location and the vessel. At the port of Adok in Unity State, the UN Panel of Experts reported, local government officials and SPLA-IO forces had until recently agreed to share the takings, with 60 per cent going to the SPLM/A-IO and 40 per cent to SPLM officials and the army. After fighting resumed, SPLA-IO forces went back to keeping all the revenue they collected. The Panel's information came from interviews with SPLM/A-IO representatives in February 2026.
inside: The armed opposition paid soldiers and officials a share of the fees it levied at a state river port, and they let the movement go on collecting there.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan, final report S/2026/340, para. 142

n: Libya's coastal security took in a militia's boat units
rank: General Administration for Coastal Security, Ministry of the Interior
d: The Stability Support Apparatus, a Tripoli armed group that holds the status of a state apparatus, had its maritime units formally brought into the General Administration for Coastal Security under Libya's Ministry of the Interior, the UN Panel of Experts reported in 2023. The Panel also found that private trafficking networks running migrant camps around Zawiyah tipped off the location of migrant boats to men of the expanded Zawiyah Network who belonged to the Libyan Coast Guard and to the Apparatus's maritime units stationed along the Zawiyah and al-Mayah coast. The Panel noted separately that the Apparatus is not among the forces declared to be under government control, so the transfer of one patrol boat to it was, in the Panel's assessment, a violation of the arms embargo.
inside: An armed group's boat crews became part of the state coastal security service, which then served the smuggling network they belonged to.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report S/2023/673 (2023), para. 79, annexes 18 and 19, and annex 26

n: Militia commander held Libya's judicial police post and Mitiga prison
who: Deterrence Apparatus for Combating Crime and Terrorism (Radaa)
rank: Commander, Judicial Police Operations Department; deputy director of the Judicial Police
d: The Deterrence Apparatus for Combating Crime and Terrorism, a Tripoli armed group known as Radaa, ran detentions through posts inside the state's own police and prosecution services. The UN Panel of Experts identified Osama Najim, one of its commanders, as commander of the Judicial Police Operations Department and deputy director of the Judicial Police, and as responsible for administering unlawful arrests and the mistreatment of detainees at the Mitiga detention facility; staff at the Military Attorney General's office issued the paperwork used to justify the arrests. The Apparatus told the Panel it had no responsibility for detention inside Mitiga. The ICC issued a warrant for him on 18 January 2025; Italy arrested him in Turin, released him days later and returned him to Libya, and the Panel reported in 2026 that victims and witnesses continued to identify him as responsible.
inside: An armed group's commander also held the state judicial police command, so state police powers and a state prison were used for the group's purposes.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2024/914 (2024), para. 42 and annex 20; S/2026/224 (2026), para. 51 and annex 14; International Criminal Court press release, 22 January 2025

n: Haftar's forces held the eastern branch of Libya's security agency
rank: Internal Security Agency, eastern branch
d: Libya's Internal Security Agency, the domestic intelligence service, runs in two branches. In its table of Libyan bodies working on counter-terrorism, the UN Panel of Experts recorded the western branch, headed by Lotfi Al-Harari, as attached to the Office of the Prime Minister, and the eastern branch, headed by Osama Al-Darsi, as attached to the Libyan Arab armed forces, the armed coalition led by Khalifa Haftar. The Panel had earlier reported that civilians unlawfully deprived of liberty by Haftar-affiliated units were held at the agency's premises in Ajdabiya and Benghazi before being transferred to detention facilities controlled by the Tariq Bin Ziyad brigade.
inside: An armed coalition holds the eastern half of the state intelligence service, whose cells were used to hold civilians its own units had seized.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2024/914 (2024), annex 13, table 13.1; S/2023/673 (2023), annex 16, para. 3

n: Haftar brigade kept its own wing inside a Libyan state prison
rank: detention section inside the Gernada detention facility
d: The Tariq Bin Ziyad brigade, a unit affiliated with Khalifa Haftar's forces, held civilians in two unofficial places of detention: one at its military base in Sidi Faraj in Benghazi, and one a detention section inside the Gernada detention facility in Bayda'. The UN Panel of Experts documented nine incidents of unlawful confinement, enforced disappearance, torture and other ill-treatment there between October 2020 and August 2022. The LAAF command told the Panel the facility and all its sections fall exclusively under the authority of the interior ministry and that the brigade commands no wing there, and Mohamed al-Tagouri said he was a military policeman guarding the facility with no command function. In 2026 the Panel still placed both facilities under LAAF control.
inside: An armed group held a wing inside a state prison and cells on its own base, keeping civilians outside the reach of any court.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2023/673 (2023), paras. 45 and 51 and annexes 16-17; S/2026/224 (2026), para. 53

n: Zawiyah group given command of Libya's Stability Support Apparatus
rank: Commander, Stability Support Apparatus
d: On 1 June 2025, weeks after the killing of the Stability Support Apparatus chief Abdelghani Al-Kikli, Presidential Council President Mohammed el-Menfi appointed Hassan Busriba as commander of the Apparatus in Tripoli. Busriba, from Zawiyah, had commanded the Apparatus there in relative autonomy and leads a Zawiyah armed group; his brother Ali sits in the House of Representatives. On 24 June 2025 Busriba and forces under his command entered Tripoli and took control of the Apparatus headquarters in Janzour. The UN Panel of Experts recorded this as the first time a Zawiyah-based armed group established a presence in Tripoli, and said it was widely read as an attempt to undermine Prime Minister Dbeibah's hold on the capital's security structure.
inside: A local armed group's leader was handed command of a state security apparatus and took its headquarters with his own fighters.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224 (2026), annex 8 and para. 55; S/2023/673 (2023), para. 15

n: Smuggling-linked battalion made Libya's half of a joint border force
rank: Libyan component of the Libya-Chad joint border force
d: On 13 November 2025 the Libyan Arab armed forces and the Chadian National Army announced a joint force to secure the Libya-Chad border, and the Libyan component was drawn from Subul al-Salam, a battalion based in Kufrah. The UN Panel of Experts assessed that this placed the battalion in charge of the very routes it had been using to supply Sudan's Rapid Support Forces through Libya and Chad, largely across territory under the effective control of Tubu communities. The Panel called the arrangement an inter-State-like security arrangement operationalised by the armed forces through local armed proxies, and part of a wider trend in which those forces strike security agreements with states in order to present themselves as a legitimate security actor.
inside: A battalion that ran the border for a foreign armed force was given the state's own border-security role on the same routes.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224 (2026), paras. 33, 36 and 37, and annex 12

n: RSF men collected arms at Libya's border through a Haftar battalion
rank: 128 battalion of the Libyan Arab armed forces; Kufrah airport
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya received confirmation that members of the Libyan Arab armed forces at the least facilitated the transfer of military materiel from Kufrah airport to the Sudanese border using Sudanese fighters affiliated with 128 battalion, a unit of those forces. The Panel determined that a captain of Sudan's Rapid Support Forces was instructed by his command to move from El Geneina in West Darfur to the Libyan border to collect materiel, and that the timing of his movement matched the delivery. The supplies were destined for units fighting for Merowe airport in Sudan. The Panel added that it found no evidence the armed forces as an organisation moved materiel out of Libya and could not confirm an arms embargo violation.
inside: A Sudanese paramilitary used fighters attached to a Libyan army battalion, and an airport it controlled, to collect weapons at the border.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2023/673 (2023), paras. 27-28 and 31

n: Libyan armed groups imported 240 vehicles on state paperwork
org_label: Al-Katiba 55 and the Border Guards and Critical Facilities Directorate
rank: end-user certificate of the Ministry of Defence's border guards directorate
d: An end-user certificate dated 6 May 2025 named the Border Guards and Critical Facilities Directorate as recipient of 154 vehicles for the exclusive use of Libya's Ministry of Defence. The UN Panel of Experts found the directorate was under the effective control of Abdelsalam al-Zobi and was not among the forces declared to be under government control, and that the shipment in fact covered at least 240 vehicles, 86 of them armoured, moved through a transport channel controlled by the banker Ahmed Alushibe. Six vehicles left off the certificate were intended for Al-Katiba 55, an armed group the Panel had previously reported for violations of international human rights law. The Panel assessed the transfer as an arms embargo violation.
inside: An armed group and a militia-run directorate used defence ministry paperwork to bring in armoured vehicles the state could not lawfully receive.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224 (2026), paras. 73 and 76, and annex 22, paras. 29-37

n: Ex-rebel movement inside Sudan's army recruited 4,000 fighters for it
rank: Sudanese Armed Forces 16th Division; major-general's rank
d: JEM/Dabajo, a former Darfur rebel group that signed the Doha Document for Peace in Darfur in 2013 and was afterwards integrated into the Sudanese Armed Forces, was used by the army to recruit from the Zaghawa community as it tried to match the Rapid Support Forces' surge in Darfur. After the movement's head, Bakhit Dabajo, himself an army major-general, travelled to Port Sudan and met General al-Burhan early in September 2023, the army's 16th Division in El Fasher recruited and graduated some 4,000 fighters, many of them through JEM/Dabajo networks, according to sources in the group. The army lost El Fasher to the Rapid Support Forces in late October 2025.
inside: A former rebel movement folded into the army kept its own networks inside it, and the army raised a division's new fighters through them.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Sudan, S/2024/65 (2024), paras. 22 and 25; FDD's Long War Journal, 30 October 2025, on the fall of El Fasher

n: Musa Hilal's border guards militia absorbed into Sudan's RSF
rank: Rapid Support Forces; later army training centres in Darfur
d: Musa Hilal's border guards force, a Darfur militia since dissolved, had been integrated into the Rapid Support Forces, Sudan's state paramilitary, in 2017. The UN Panel of Experts on the Sudan reported that as tensions between the army and the Rapid Support Forces rose before the April 2023 war, the army sought to recruit the force's former members and considered re-forming the border guards, and that meetings were held between Hilal and army leaders including General Hassan Bilal, deputy director of military intelligence. Using former border guard officers such as Hilal's nephew Musa Omer Hilal, the army assembled several hundred fighters near El Fasher and Nyala in March 2023 for military training; a few hundred then fought for it in North Darfur. The Panel said Hilal's recruitment efforts were thwarted by the army's limited financial resources, according to sources in his own group.
inside: A Darfur militia's fighters were taken into the state paramilitary, and the army later built its own units from the same militia's officers and clan.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Sudan, S/2024/65 (2024), para. 22

n: Darfur movements joined the army's command and ran arrests in El Fasher
org_label: SAF-aligned joint force of Darfurian armed movements
rank: integrated command-and-control structure with the Sudanese Armed Forces
d: By mid-April 2024 field commanders of the Darfurian armed movements that had signed the Juba Peace Agreement, who had until then stayed neutral, declared their allegiance to the Sudanese Armed Forces and formed a joint force which from May operated under an integrated command-and-control structure and took the buffer zone in El Fasher. The UN Panel of Experts named Juma Haggar, Abdallah Janna, Lieutenant General Aboud Adam Khater and Tijani Duhaib among its commanders, and recorded that army and joint force movements were coordinated mainly through Haggar and the army's General Mohamed Ahmed Alzafir. From mid-May the joint force carried out widespread arbitrary arrests of civilians, holding detainees in shipping containers at the former UNAMID compound for up to two weeks.
inside: Armed movements' commanders entered the army's own command structure, and then used state military authority to arrest and hold civilians.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Sudan, S/2025/239 (2025), paras. 20, 36, 41 and 42

n: Houthi women's security wing sits inside Yemen's police and intelligence
rank: women's unit in the Security and Intelligence Service and the police security and intelligence sector
d: The Zaynabiyat, which the UN Panel of Experts describes as the female security wing of the Houthi movement, form a women's unit inside both the Security and Intelligence Service and the police security and intelligence sector of the interior ministry the Houthis have appointed in Sanaa. The Panel reported that the unit supports policing and intelligence operations, prison management and child recruitment, that its members are trained in intelligence and surveillance, and that they use electric shock devices against women at demonstrations and in places of detention. Fatima al-Houthi, sister of Ali Hussein al-Houthi, who heads a new police intelligence unit, and Fatima al-Hamran are reportedly leading its operations. Confidential sources told the Panel that members delivered women held in detention to Houthi affiliates to be raped.
inside: A movement's own women's force staffs units inside the state police and intelligence service, and polices, jails and recruits for the movement.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2025/650 (2025), paras. 38-39 and 146; S/2024/731 (2024), para. 146 and footnote 54

n: Southern council's Security Belt Forces hold Aden's arrests and a prison
rank: state security force in Aden; Bi'r Ahmad prison
d: The Security Belt Forces are among the armed groups the UN Panel of Experts describes as affiliated with the Southern Transitional Council, the southern Yemeni separatist movement, and they act as state security forces in Aden. The Panel reported that, according to a local advocacy group, many civilians abducted or disappeared by state security forces, some as far back as 2016, remain missing or detained, including 118 taken by the Security Belt Forces, 18 by government security services and seven by the Joint Forces. The Panel was investigating the case of the journalist Ahmed Maher, allegedly seized from his home in Aden on 6 August 2022 and held at Bi'r Ahmad prison, where he was allegedly ill-treated and forced under threat of death to confess to terrorism offences.
inside: A separatist movement's brigades act as the state's security force in Aden, making most of its arrests and running the prison the detainees go to.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2023/130 (2023), paras. 107-108; S/2023/833 (2023), para. 46

n: Gioia Tauro port border police officer tipped off the Grasso 'ndrina
rank: Sovrintendente, border police post, port of Gioia Tauro
d: Gianluca Castagna was a sovrintendente of the Polizia di Stato at the border police post inside the port of Gioia Tauro, Italy's largest container port. Prosecutors at the Reggio Calabria anti-mafia directorate say he worked for Rosario Grasso of the Grasso 'ndrangheta family. On 8 July 2018 he texted a warning about "Ares", a Carabinieri operation against mafia families in Rosarno; Grasso and six other suspects then hid for months. The custody order says he repeatedly let Grasso enter the port secretly to collect cocaine from containers, supplied information from police computer systems on container movements and ships, and once staged a false explosives alert elsewhere in the port so a boss's container would not be inspected. He was arrested in October 2020. The report read gives no verdict.
inside: The clan had an officer inside the port's border police, so police databases and port access served its cocaine imports instead of the state's controls.
cite: Il Fatto Quotidiano, 14 October 2020 (custody order, DDA Reggio Calabria)

n: Siderno police sergeant passed files to the Scali 'ndrangheta locale
rank: Sovrintendente, Siderno police commissariato
d: On 25 July 2023 the Reggio Calabria mobile squad arrested twelve people in operation "Malea", an inquiry by the city's anti-mafia directorate into the cosca led by Rodolfo Scali, the 'ndrangheta cell based at Mammola in Calabria. Among them was Domenico Sita, a sovrintendente, or police sergeant, posted to the police commissariato at Siderno, placed under house arrest on a charge of external complicity in a mafia-type association. Investigators called him 'una divisa infedele', and Il Fatto Quotidiano reported that he allegedly passed confidential information to Rodolfo Scali, head of the Mammola locale, in exchange for gifts, and more recently did the same for a person under investigation by the Turin anti-mafia prosecutors. The Interior Ministry's DIA report records the same finding.
inside: The cosca had a serving police sergeant feeding it confidential information, so what the station knew about investigations reached the clan it was watching.
cite: Il Fatto Quotidiano, 25 July 2023; DIA, Relazione semestrale al Parlamento, 2 semestre 2023, p. 29

n: Two carabinieri fed secrets to a Rome 'ndrangheta group
rank: Two carabinieri at a barracks on the Roman coast
d: On 17 February 2022 Rome's anti-mafia directorate had 65 people arrested in an inquiry into an 'ndrangheta criminal group in the city. Two of them were carabinieri working at one of the barracks on the Roman coast. Prosecutors say the two obtained and distributed confidential information, revealed to help the 'ndrangheta group targeted in the raid. Both are suspected of revealing and using official secrets, and one is also charged with external complicity in a mafia-type association. One was sent to prison, the other placed under house arrest. Other suspects face mafia association and international drug trafficking aggravated by the mafia method. Carabinieri also searched the municipal offices of Anzio and Nettuno. The report read names no clan and no verdict.
inside: Prosecutors say the group had two serving carabinieri supplying it with police information, so what the force knew reached the people it was investigating.
cite: Open, 17 February 2022 (DDA Rome, deputy prosecutors Michele Prestipino and Ilaria Calo)

n: Pagliarelli prison officers let phones and drugs in for cash
org_label: Detainee-run drug and mobile phone network at Pagliarelli prison
who: Detainee drug and phone network at Pagliarelli
rank: Polizia penitenziaria officers, Pagliarelli prison
d: Palermo's anti-mafia directorate investigated the Pagliarelli prison between September 2023 and April 2025 with the Carabinieri and the prison police's own investigative unit. On 23 May 2025 twelve people were placed under a precautionary order. Investigators found a group of detainees bringing drugs and mobile phones into the jail through relatives at visits, inmates allowed out to work, and officers who took money. Items seized during the inquiry included 56 micro-phones, 25 smartphones, 20 SIM cards and more than a kilogram of drugs. On 10 June 2026 a Palermo preliminary-hearing judge convicted eight people in an abbreviated trial, among them two prison officers; Francesco Paolo Cardinale, a former officer, was given four years and four months. The criminal association charge did not stand.
inside: A drug and phone ring run by inmates paid prison officers, so the staff guarding the wing helped move the goods it was meant to keep out.
cite: LaPresse, 23 May 2025 (https://www.lapresse.it/cronaca/2025/05/23/palermo-droga-e-telefoni-in-carcere-con-complicita-agenti-12-arresti/); LiveSicilia, 10 June 2026 (DDA Palermo)

n: Giarre prison officer accused of hiding a Laudani clan phone
rank: Prison officer, Giarre prison (also deputy mayor of Itala)
d: On 9 October 2024 the Catania anti-mafia directorate had Carmelo Palo, a prison officer at Giarre prison in Sicily and also deputy mayor of the town of Itala, placed in pre-trial custody. The report gives his rank as assistente capo in one passage and ispettore capo in another. Prosecutors allege he helped Antonino Di Grazia, 43, son of Orazio Di Grazia, named as head of the Picanello group of the Laudani clan: hiding a phone the detainee held, delaying entry of a disciplinary report into the databases so an imminent leave permit would not be lost, warning him of cell searches, and letting him use the prison registry telephone. In return he was allegedly promised betting arrangements and cash kept at his home. The charge carries a mafia-method aggravating circumstance.
inside: Prosecutors say a clan family had an officer inside the prison, so searches, records and phone access were handled to suit a detainee rather than the jail.
cite: LiveSicilia, 9 October 2024 (DDA Catania)

n: Carabinieri captain at the DIA accused of serving the Lo Giudice clan
rank: Carabinieri captain, Direzione Investigativa Antimafia, Reggio Calabria
d: Saverio Spadaro Tracuzzi was a Carabinieri captain who until a few weeks before his arrest served at the Reggio Calabria office of the Direzione Investigativa Antimafia, Italy's dedicated anti-mafia investigative agency. The ROS arrested him in Livorno in December 2010 on a charge of external complicity in a mafia-type association. Investigators say he gave the Lo Giudice brothers, Luciano and Nino, confidential information on live investigations, including arrest plans and when checks on fugitives would be stepped up, and agreed for money to use his position to block inquiries into clan members. In return he allegedly received money, paid travel and hotel costs, designer clothes and a Porsche registered in his name. The report read gives no verdict.
inside: Investigators say the clan had an officer inside the agency built to fight it, so its own arrest plans reached the family they were aimed at.
cite: Il Fatto Quotidiano, 19 December 2010 (DDA Reggio Calabria, prosecutor Beatrice Ronchi)

n: Naples detainees' ombudsman accused of carrying phones into Poggioreale
org_label: Poggioreale prison phone and drug ring
who: Poggioreale prison phone and drug ring
rank: Garante dei detenuti, Comune di Napoli
d: On 18 October 2022 Carabinieri arrested Pietro Ioia, the Naples city council's garante dei detenuti, an ombudsman for prisoners whose office gave him free access to jails, on a custody order from the Naples court covering eight people. Investigators say he used that access to bring mobile phones and drugs into Poggioreale prison for payment, charging between 500 and 850 euros for handing phones to detainees drop 'and handing them over in the visiting room'; he was filmed passing an object to a detainee. Recorded conversations mention hashish worth up to 10,000 euros and cocaine that detainees resold inside. The judge called him the pivot of the group's activity and said his post was the means necessary for access. Mayor Gaetano Manfredi said revocation measures were being prepared.
inside: Prosecutors say a prison smuggling ring used the official with free access to jails, so the prisoners' own watchdog office carried its goods inside.
cite: Dire, 18 October 2022 (Procura di Napoli; GIP Valentina Giovanniello)

n: Carinola prison officers sold phones and drugs to jailed Casalesi
rank: Two polizia penitenziaria officers, Carinola prison
d: On 17 March 2012 two prison police officers on duty at Carinola prison, in the Caserta area, were among eight people placed under a custody order in a Casalesi clan case. The report says they built up relationships with detained clan members and sold them drugs, mobile phones, perfumes, watches and other prohibited goods. The same order covered two killings committed between late 2003 and early 2004 in the feud between the Tavoletta-Ucciero and Bidognetti groups for control of crime in Villa Literno. The charges listed were homicide, corruption and supplying narcotics. Carabinieri in Caserta carried out the arrests with the prison police's central investigative unit, and the anti-mafia directorate led the murder inquiry. The report words the officers' conduct as an allegation.
inside: The clan had two officers inside the prison selling its jailed members phones and drugs, so the wing's own staff supplied what it was meant to stop.
cite: Blitzquotidiano, 17 March 2012

n: Carabiniere in 'Revolvo' shielded 'ndrangheta-linked builders
rank: Carabiniere, Reggio Calabria
d: In the "Revolvo" investigation by the Reggio Calabria anti-mafia directorate, reported on 15 December 2022, four people were placed under house arrest: three entrepreneurs from one family group described as close to the 'ndrangheta, and one carabiniere. The report says the carabiniere let one suspect under house arrest systematically ignore the conditions of his restrictions, and supplied equipment and technical means so that some suspects could sweep for and evade wiretaps. Ten other people were investigated, including officials of Reggio Calabria city council. The charges were external complicity in a mafia-type association, corruption and rigging of tender procedures, with the aggravating circumstance of facilitating the mafia. Eleven construction firms worth over 10 million euros were seized. The report gives no verdict.
inside: Prosecutors say the group had a carabiniere inside the force, so house-arrest checks and wiretaps worked for the builders rather than against them.
cite: Italpress, 15 December 2022 (DDA Reggio Calabria)

n: Prison officer carried a Lo Russo boss's notes out of L'Aquila jail
rank: Polizia penitenziaria officer, L'Aquila prison
d: Luigi Cossentino, a prison police officer whom the report places on duty at L'Aquila at the time, though elsewhere it says he served at Spoleto prison, was placed under house arrest in January 2020 on a charge of continued corruption aggravated by the mafia method. Prosecutors say that in 2014, after the Camorra boss Antonio Lo Russo was captured in Nice and held at L'Aquila under Italy's 41-bis hard-prison regime, the officer made himself available as Lo Russo's postman and carried coded notes out of the jail. The notes gave instructions on collecting a 600,000 euro debt and on restarting drug dealing to retake the via Valente market in Naples. Each of the two notes was allegedly paid for with 3,000 euros. The case rests on statements by cooperating witnesses, and Lo Russo identified the officer from photographs.
inside: Prosecutors say the clan paid an officer inside the prison, so a boss held in isolation could still send orders to the men running his drug market.
cite: Il Fatto Quotidiano, 22 January 2020 (Naples GIP Emilia Di Palma)

n: Trapani prison officers took money to let phones and drugs reach detainees
rank: Polizia penitenziaria officers, Trapani prison
d: In operation "Alcatraz", reported on 13 April 2023, Carabinieri of the Trapani provincial command and the prison police's regional investigative unit served 24 precautionary measures across Puglia, Campania and Sicily. Thirty people were under investigation; 17 were sent to prison and five to house arrest. The inquiry by the Trapani prosecutors, running from October 2019, found that drugs and mobile phones were entering Trapani prison, and that some prison officers allegedly accepted money or other benefits to let them reach detainees, in one case sexual favours from a detainee's partner. Where officers were unavailable, phones and doses were hidden in shoes or body cavities after family visits, or flown in by drone. Charges include corruption and abuse of office. The report names no clan.
inside: A smuggling network reached detainees by paying prison officers, so staff on the wing let through the phones and drugs they were there to stop.
cite: Open, 13 April 2023 (Procura di Trapani)

n: Serbian police inspector Stolic convicted of leaking to the Belivuk clan
rank: Inspector, police organised-crime unit (SBPOK)
d: Bozidar Stolic was an inspector in SBPOK, the Serbian police unit that investigates organised crime. A court in Belgrade found him guilty of a prolonged offence of abuse of office for passing information to the criminal group led by Veljko Belivuk and Marko Miljkovic. He was sentenced to a year and a half in prison and barred from interior ministry employment for five years. The material against him was gathered during the investigation into Belivuk's group. An appellate court had earlier annulled a first conviction, from 2022, of two years and ordered a retrial; the Sky ECC messages and photographs were the key evidence, and his lawyers argued they had been unlawfully obtained. He was acquitted of criminal conspiracy. The reports read do not give the year of the conduct.
inside: The Belivuk cocaine group had an inspector inside the police unit investigating it, who passed the group information that unit was meant to keep from it.
cite: Vreme, 23 July 2024; Human Rights Action (HRA), 18 February 2025

n: Ukrainian border unit chief charged over a cigarette route into Romania
rank: Head of a department, 31st border detachment
d: The Chernivtsi regional prosecutor's office, working with the SBU security service, charged the head of one of the departments of Ukraine's 31st border detachment with accepting a bribe. Prosecutors say a woman already held in another criminal case approached him at the end of April 2026, and that he agreed to pass on the locations of patrols and photo-traps, pick safe routes and times, move his subordinates elsewhere, and himself drive tobacco through a stationary checkpoint, so cigarettes could be taken into Romania away from official crossings. They say he was to be paid for each box smuggled, with the money transferred after he moved to another post. He is in custody, with bail set at more than 180,000 hryvnia, and has been suspended.
inside: Prosecutors say smugglers recruited the officer running a border unit, so Ukraine's border guard moved its own patrols aside for their cigarette loads.
cite: Chernivtsi Regional Prosecutor's Office, reported by UNN, 8 July 2026

n: Moldovan migration bureau employee charged as part of a smuggling group
rank: Regional employee, Bureau for Migration
d: Moldova's Prosecutor's Office for Combating Organised Crime and Special Cases charged a regional employee of the Bureau for Migration with organising the illegal transit of two Ukrainians through Moldova, saying the official was part of a criminal group. The group charged 2,000 euro to help a person cross and a further 350 euro for an official entry stamp's own staff could supply. The crossings concerned took place in October 2022. Two members of the group were convicted in November 2023. Prosecutors sought confiscation of illegal income of more than 100,000 lei. The report read does not give an outcome for the official.
inside: A people-smuggling group had an official inside Moldova's migration bureau who could put a genuine entry stamp in the papers of those it moved.
cite: Moldova, Prosecutor's Office for Combating Organised Crime and Special Cases, reported by Moldova Live

n: Ankara police chiefs arrested over the Ayhan Bora Kaplan crime network
rank: Deputy provincial police chief for organised crime, and organised-crime branch managers
d: Ankara's chief public prosecutor's office arrested seven suspects, among them two senior police chiefs and a commissioner, in its investigation into the criminal organisation led by Ayhan Bora Kaplan. Those detained included Murat Celik, the deputy provincial police chief in charge of combating organised crime, Sevket Demircan, deputy head of the organised crime branch, and Kerem Gokay Oner, a branch manager overseeing organised crime investigations, who was later released. The investigation covers attempts to influence witnesses, revealing job-related secrets and favouritism within the network, alongside charges of establishing a criminal network, intentional injury and deprivation of liberty. The allegations were first made by Serdar Sertcelik, a fugitive defendant linked to the group.
inside: Prosecutors say the Kaplan network reached the very police officers tasked with organised crime in Ankara, who are accused of revealing secrets and favouring it.
cite: Hurriyet Daily News, 20 May 2024

n: Bulgarian border policemen at Shabla charged as part of a smuggling group
rank: Border policemen running the radio-location station at Shabla
d: Milen Dimov and Nachko Tashkov were border policemen who also managed the radio-location station at Shabla, on Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, the installation used to watch shipping off that stretch of border. They were arrested in the autumn of 2006 along with 23 other people, and prosecutors said they were part of a crime group together with two men from the nearby resort of Kranevo, Raiko Kristov and Anton Klashnikov. In April 2007 prosecutors asked for the maximum sentences. The investigation of Bulgarian smuggling that reported the case records no verdict against them.
inside: A smuggling group took in the border policemen who ran the radar station watching that coast, the post best placed to see or miss a boat.
cite: OCCRP, Bulgarian Smuggling investigation

n: Eight Bobrowniki customs officers on trial over Belarusian cigarette route
org_label: cigarette-smuggling group in Podlaskie and Mazowieckie
rank: Customs officers at the Bobrowniki road border crossing
d: Nine people are on trial at the district court in Bialystok, eight of them former customs officers from the Bobrowniki road crossing on Poland's border with Belarus, dismissed after the investigation began. Prosecutors say the group ran from November 2018 to April 2020 in the Podlaskie and Mazowieckie regions, distributing Belarusian cigarettes brought in through Bobrowniki, and that the officers failed to perform their duties and allowed vehicles carrying cigarettes to pass through the border. They put the quantity at about 29.4 million packs, the loss to the state at no less than 498 million zlotys in unpaid excise, duty and VAT, and the bribes at 4.9 million zlotys. The first hearing was in March 2026 and no verdict has been reported; one defendant has reached an agreement with prosecutors and the others have accepted the principal penalty but not the claim for damages.
inside: Prosecutors say smugglers paid the customs officers manning a Polish border crossing, so loaded lorries were waved through the lane they controlled.
cite: Reform.news, 10 April 2026; Nasha Niva interview with a former Bobrowniki customs officer

n: Lithuanian border guard fined for telling smugglers where patrols were
rank: Junior specialist, Vilnius border guard unit
d: The Panevezys regional court convicted six people of smuggling cigarettes from Belarus and handling them illegally as an organised group. One was a 42-year-old junior specialist from the Vilnius border guard unit, charged also with abuse of office, who was said to have told the smugglers about the movements of his fellow officers; he was dismissed from the service. Four men were detained near Lake Prutas in the Ignalina district, two carrying cigarette boxes by boat and two loading them into a minibus, and 90,000 packs with Belarusian excise stamps worth nearly 384,000 euro were seized. Fines came to nearly 100,000 euro, of which the former border guard was fined 14,700 euro. All those convicted fully admitted guilt. The verdict took effect on 7 May 2026.
inside: A cigarette-smuggling group had a border guard inside the Vilnius unit telling it where his colleagues were patrolling on the nights it crossed.
cite: Reform.news, 8 May 2026

n: Two Lithuanian customs officers convicted in a 10m euro tobacco scheme
org_label: tobacco-smuggling scheme prosecuted by the EPPO
rank: Customs officers, Lithuanian customs
d: The European Public Prosecutor's Office, the European Union body that prosecutes crimes against the EU budget, secured four convictions at the Vilnius regional court on 23 January 2025 in a cigarette smuggling scheme that evaded nearly 10 million euro in import, customs and excise taxes. Two of the four were former Lithuanian customs officers, convicted of smuggling large quantities of cigarettes, illegally disposing of excise goods and abuse of office. The goods entered the EU through a customs post on the Belarusian-Lithuanian border. The two officers were barred from civil service posts, one for three years, the other for five. The defendants together were ordered to pay almost 10 million euro in damages and fined nearly 300,000 euro, with a further 42,000 euro confiscated. The announcement does not name them.
inside: Smugglers had two serving customs officers in the scheme, so cigarettes crossed into the European Union through the service meant to stop them.
cite: European Public Prosecutor's Office, 28 January 2025

n: Albanian special-force police officer held over leaks to a cocaine group
org_label: cocaine trafficking group operating in Albania and Italy
rank: Judicial police officer, Directorate of the Special Operational Force, State Police
d: Igli Haxhiaj was a judicial police officer in the Directorate of the Special Operational Force of Albania's General Directorate of the State Police, responsible for investigative and procedural steps in a case against a cocaine trafficking group. SPAK, Albania's special prosecution office for corruption and organised crime, says he disclosed to the suspects data from procedural acts that constituted an investigative secret, and sought irregular monetary benefits in exchange. The group is said to have moved cocaine from South America into Europe through EU ports and stored it at six logistics bases in Italy. SPAK identified the officer by analysing Sky ECC communications. He was arrested on 27 November 2025 and charged with abuse of office, disclosure of secret acts or data, and passive corruption.
inside: Prosecutors say the cocaine group bought the officer handling the case against it, so Albania's own investigation file reached the people it targeted.
cite: SPAK, reported by Shteg, November 2025

n: Five Bulgarian border police at Elhovo charged over migrant crossings
org_label: migrant-smuggling groups on the Turkish border
rank: Border police at the Elhovo checkpoint, three of them high-ranking officials
d: Bulgarian prosecutors charged five border police, three of them high-ranking officials, with being part of an organised crime group and with accepting bribes. They said the officers took money from migrant smugglers to let dozens of migrants cross illegally from Turkey at the Elhovo checkpoint in the south-east of the country, on their way to western Europe, and that the scheme ran from about July 2015, when migrant numbers rose sharply. Groups led by rival traffickers who had not paid the officers were arrested as well. Prosecutors said it remained to establish how many people managed to cross the border through the corruption scheme. The charges were announced on 9 February 2016, the day after the arrests, and the report read gives no trial or verdict.
inside: Smuggling groups paid serving border police at a crossing from Turkey, so the officers controlling that checkpoint let their clients through.
cite: Bulgarian prosecutors, reported by PTI, 9 February 2016

n: Bulgarian border police deputy director accused of warning smugglers
org_label: cigarette-smuggling ring moving goods from Turkiye
rank: Deputy director, Border Police
d: The Bulgarian anti-corruption group BOEC released WhatsApp screenshots which it said showed that superiors told six police officers to abandon a raid on a contraband cigarette operation in Plovdiv in November 2024, with the message "Colleagues, withdraw". BOEC alleged that Kalin Litov, the deputy director of Bulgaria's border police, telephoned the smugglers directly to warn them and ordered the officers to stand down. The officers went ahead anyway, but the suspects appeared to have been warned and tried to flee, and the officers later received disciplinary punishments. The interior minister, Daniel Mitov, said on 3 April 2025 that Litov had been dismissed. He rejected calls to resign himself, saying he would not allow speculation to tarnish the ministry's work. The report records no criminal charges.
inside: An anti-corruption group alleges the deputy head of the border police tipped off a cigarette ring and called off the raid on it, so the smugglers were served inside.
cite: Brussels Signal, 8 April 2025, reporting claims by BOEC

n: Ex-police colonel recruited serving Ecuadorian officers for a Los Lobos route
rank: National Police officers on active service
d: Julio Cesar Mino, a former colonel of Ecuador's National Police and former head of the Guayas judicial police, was charged in December 2024 as part of a network that packed cocaine into export containers leaving Guayaquil for Europe, mainly Spain. Prosecutors say he had two jobs in the structure: recruiting police officers still on active service, and coordinating the security of the organisation and the transport of the drugs. In Ecuador the network was linked to Los Lobos, which provided its security; Spanish authorities are examining a possible Albanian mafia connection. Eight people were charged with organised crime, among them the alleged head, Carlos Zambrano. Prosecutors say they are still identifying serving officers who passed Mino information.
inside: A cocaine export network tied to Los Lobos used an ex-colonel to recruit serving police officers, so police information and protection worked for the traffickers.
cite: Primicias (Ecuador), 10 January 2025, on the Fiscalia's charges in the case

n: Ecuadorian navy captain fed naval operation details to a cocaine network
rank: Captain, Ecuadorian Navy
d: Galo Manuel Litardo Garcia, described by Primicias as a captain of Ecuador's navy, was charged in December 2024 alongside a former police colonel in the same cocaine export network, which moved drugs out of Guayaquil in containers. Prosecutors say he handed over information on naval operations, warned the group about raids, and helped distract other officers with false alerts. The report says the public prosecutor presented no direct evidence that he took part in the trafficking itself, but did produce records of calls with the group's leaders. He was not held in custody because he cares for a minor child, and the article says he remained a serving member of the navy. The case was at the investigation stage.
inside: A cocaine network tied to Los Lobos had a serving navy captain who, prosecutors say, passed it naval operation details so its shipments were not intercepted.
cite: Primicias (Ecuador), 10 January 2025

n: Albanian network's $300,000 offer for an Ecuadorian military informant's name
rank: military intelligence agents
d: Prosecutors in Ecuador alleged that an Albanian trafficking network sought the identity of the armed forces' informant behind a seizure of 22 tonnes of cocaine at Vinces, in Los Rios province, on 21 January 2024. In a recorded call, Hector Castillo, then working in the military intelligence department of Los Rios, told an active-duty intelligence agent that "los duros de la mafia albanesa" would be paying USD 300,000 for the information; the money was said to be meant for two serving agents; a defence lawyer said they had not been prosecuted. Castillo and two retired servicemen were arrested in northern Quito in February 2024 with about USD 100,000. Charges were filed on 10 January 2025, but on 25 January Judge Maria Fernanda Castro dismissed the case. The prosecutor appealed.
inside: Prosecutors say an Albanian trafficking network offered money to serving military intelligence agents to name the informant behind a cocaine seizure; a judge dismissed the case.
cite: Primicias (Ecuador), on the charges of prosecutor Santiago Requelme and the dismissal by Judge Maria Fernanda Castro

n: Caso Depuracion Azul: police sold ammunition to two Guayaquil gangs
rank: Storage Department, National Logistics Directorate, National Police
d: Eight people, six of them police officers, were charged in July 2025 over the sale of police service ammunition taken from the storage department of the National Police's National Logistics Directorate. Five of the officers were on active duty and one in passive service. Primicias reports that the buyers were the criminal organisations Mafia 18 and Freddy Krueger, with the ammunition going towards Guayas, and that what was sold included 5.56 millimetre rifle rounds and 9 millimetre pistol rounds. The corporal said to have headed the department is identified in reports only as Francisco P. The preliminary investigation opened on 13 January 2025 and raids followed on 3 July in four provinces. Seven of the accused were ordered into pretrial detention the next day.
inside: Two Guayaquil gangs bought their ammunition from the police unit that stores it, so the force's own stock armed the groups it was meant to fight.
cite: Primicias (Ecuador) and Teleamazonas on the Fiscalia's case Depuracion Azul, July-August 2025

n: Ecuadorian anti-narcotics officers sold 321kg of seized cocaine to Los Lobos
org_label: Los Lobos and other transnational traffickers
rank: anti-narcotics police officers
d: InSight Crime reported that two officers of Ecuador's anti-narcotics police stole 321 kilogrammes of seized cocaine, valued at about USD 400,000, from an official police warehouse in Guayaquil in February 2024, and sold it to transnational traffickers, among them the Lobos. The theft was revealed by an Ecuavisa investigation published on 15 May. The report does not name the officers and does not say what stage any prosecution had reached. It set the case beside others from the same weeks, and quoted Guillermo Palacios, a former head of the anti-narcotics police, saying that organised crime had strategically penetrated the country's most sensitive logistical areas.
inside: Traffickers including Los Lobos bought seized cocaine back out of the police warehouse holding it, through the officers guarding the state's own evidence.
cite: InSight Crime, on new security force corruption cases in Ecuador, citing an Ecuavisa investigation of 15 May

n: Ecuadorian army sub-lieutenant leaked an arms-trafficking operation
rank: sub-lieutenant, Ecuadorian Army
d: InSight Crime reported that an Ecuadorian army sub-lieutenant was arrested on 20 May, in a run of security-force cases it gathered in 2025, for leaking information about an operation against an arms trafficking network. The operation ended with no arrests. The report does not name the officer, the unit or the network, and does not say how the leak was traced. It placed the case alongside others in the same weeks: the theft and sale of 321 kilogrammes of seized cocaine by two anti-narcotics officers in Guayaquil, two serving officers arrested over a kidnapping, and the revocation of United States visas for at least three senior police officials the US believed were linked to organised crime.
inside: An arms trafficking network got warning of the operation against it from a serving army officer, so the raid it should have faced produced no arrests.
cite: InSight Crime, on new security force corruption cases in Ecuador, 2025

n: Los Lobos cell recruited a serving Ecuadorian soldier and a transit agent
org_label: Los Lobos cell 'La Resiliencia - La Hermandad'
rank: serving soldier; agent of the Comision de Transito del Ecuador
d: On 16 October 2026 Ecuador's interior minister, John Reimberg, announced Operation Fenix 578, a simultaneous action in seven provinces in which 24 people were detained. Among them were a soldier on active service and an agent of the Comision de Transito del Ecuador, the national transit body. Investigators say the cell, which calls itself La Resiliencia - La Hermandad, is part of Los Lobos and has also recruited other members of the army. It worked mainly in Babahoyo and Montalvo, in Los Rios province, and extorted businesses and transport operators for sums ranging from USD 50 a week to USD 20,000 a month. Both men are accused of unlawful association. Primicias does not name them or state what each did.
inside: A Los Lobos cell recruited a serving soldier and a transit agent, investigators say, putting state uniforms behind its extortion of businesses and transport firms.
cite: Primicias (Ecuador), 16 October 2026, on Operation Fenix 578

n: Two serving Ecuadorian police charged in a Choneros-linked laundering network
org_label: network linked to Los Choneros' leadership
rank: police major; officer on active service
d: In the case Ecuador's prosecutors call Emporio Presidiario, nine people were charged with money laundering after raids in Guayas, Los Rios and Pichincha on 20 March 2026. Two are police officers. Hans Estuardo Tipan Caiza, a police major, held accounts that Primicias reports handled about USD 3.4 million with direct transactions with the companies under investigation, and was found with USD 37,000 in cash. Pedro Alvaro Reyes Franco, an officer on active service, allegedly received transfers from workers of those firms and sent USD 4,000 to the partner of a man described as a former associate of "Fito" in Los Choneros' leadership. The government first said the network moved USD 1,700 million; in court prosecutors traced about USD 110 million. Judge Sebastian Cornejo ordered all nine held.
inside: Prosecutors say a laundering network tied to Los Choneros' leadership moved money through two serving police officers' accounts, putting the force inside the gang's finances.
cite: Primicias (Ecuador), 24 March 2026, on the Emporio Presidiario charges

n: Traffickers paid Peru's Loreto anti-drug police to pass cocaine to Brazil
org_label: trafficking organisations of the Peru-Colombia-Brazil triple frontier
rank: head of the Anti-Drug Manoeuvres Division, Iquitos
d: El Comercio reported that prosecutors are investigating whether trafficking organisations paid the police division that fights drug trafficking in Loreto, Peru's Amazon region. A cooperating witness said in August 2021 that Jose Tello Tantalean, known as "Payuchi", gathered money from trafficking organisations and paid Colonel Vic Cardenas del Pino, head of the Anti-Drug Manoeuvres Division in Iquitos, through the chiefs of individual anti-drug units, so that drugs could be moved to Brazil. The police said six units had been infiltrated, without naming them; Cardenas had 160 officers under him across five anti-drug detachments and two tactical operations departments. Besides the colonel the paper names a major, three sub-officers and a technician among those investigated. It reports no amounts and no convictions, and says most of the officers remain in service.
inside: Prosecutors say traffickers' money reached the chief of Loreto's anti-drug police division through unit commanders, so the squad meant to stop cocaine let it cross to Brazil.
cite: El Comercio (Peru), investigative unit, on the Loreto anti-drug police inquiry

n: Rio police station accused of selling the closing of a Comando Vermelho case
rank: titular delegate, 44th Police Station (Inhauma), Rio de Janeiro civil police
d: On 6 March 2026 Justice Alexandre de Moraes of Brazil's Supreme Federal Court ordered the preventive detention of fifteen people in inquiry 5020, made public on 11 March. Among them were Marcus Henrique de Oliveira Alves, titular delegate of Rio de Janeiro's 44th police station in Inhauma, his brother Franklin Jose de Oliveira Alves, a police commissioner, and a notary clerk of the civil police. The Federal Police allege that officers demanded 1.5 million reais from the trafficker Gabriel Dias de Oliveira, known as "Indio do Lixao", to close an investigation at that station, with Franklin leading the negotiations. Investigators describe the money as bribes for omitting official acts. The court removed the officials from office and froze assets of up to 36.3 million reais.
inside: A Comando Vermelho trafficker's money went into the police station investigating him, prosecutors say, so the inquiry into him would be dropped.
cite: Supreme Federal Court of Brazil, news release on INQ 5020, 11 March 2026; CNN Brasil, 10 March 2026

n: Rio military police guarded a Comando Vermelho trafficker day to day
rank: military police officers, Rio de Janeiro
d: In the same Supreme Federal Court order of 6 March 2026, seven military police officers of Rio de Janeiro were among the fifteen people whose preventive detention Justice Alexandre de Moraes granted at the Federal Police's request in inquiry 5020. The court's notice says they are accused of providing security and logistics to the Comando Vermelho trafficker Gabriel Dias de Oliveira, "Indio do Lixao": daily protection, escorts to medical visits and to funerals, and security for his guests. The notice describes those detained as the faction's armed and political arms. The officers were removed from their posts, and the order also covered search warrants and the lifting of telephone and data secrecy. These are allegations, and the case is at the inquiry stage.
inside: A Comando Vermelho boss had serving military police as his personal guard, prosecutors say, so the force meant to police him protected him instead.
cite: Supreme Federal Court of Brazil, news release on INQ 5020, 11 March 2026

n: Federal Police delegate paid over a jailed Dutch trafficker's case in Rio
rank: Federal Police delegate; prison police officer
d: Operation Anomalia, run by Brazil's Federal Police on 9 March 2026, targeted a group accused of using public posts to help Gerel Lusiano Palm, a Dutch trafficker wanted by Interpol and held in prison in Rio de Janeiro for five years.
