Among those whose detention the Supreme Federal Court ordered were Fabrizio Romano, a Federal Police delegate from the agency's social security crimes unit, Luciano Pinheiro, a prison police officer previously convicted over drug trafficking links, and Alessandro Pitombeira Carracena, a lawyer and former Rio state secretary, who the court says coordinated the favours. One negotiation concerned Palm's refugee application. Romano is said to have offered influence inside the Federal Police. Four arrest warrants were carried out.
inside: A jailed Dutch trafficker's money bought influence inside the Federal Police and the prison service, prosecutors say, so decisions on his own case went his way.
cite: Supreme Federal Court of Brazil, news release on INQ 5020, 11 March 2026; InfoMoney, 10 March 2026, on Operation Anomalia

n: Nineteen Rio officers charged as a gambling boss's armed security unit
org_label: Rogerio de Andrade's illegal gambling organisation
rank: military and prison police officers, Rio de Janeiro
d: On 10 March 2026 Gaeco, the organised crime unit of Rio de Janeiro's public prosecutor's office, charged nineteen officers: eighteen military and prison police, serving and in the reserve, and one retired civil police officer. Prosecutors say they formed the armed security unit for illegal gambling points run by the bicheiro Rogerio de Andrade in the Bangu area of the city, the bicho being Brazil's long-established illegal numbers game. The charges are armed criminal organisation and active and passive corruption, with aggravating factors, and prosecutors say the group used bribery to avoid police action against the betting shops. A court issued twenty preventive arrest warrants, one of them for Andrade. These are allegations.
inside: An illegal gambling boss hired serving police as his armed guard and, prosecutors say, paid officers to keep the force away from his betting shops.
cite: InfoMoney, 10 March 2026, on the Gaeco charges in Rio de Janeiro

n: Rio police sergeants leaked operation plans to the Comando Vermelho
rank: sergeants, Rio de Janeiro military police; a member of the Brazilian Navy
d: Operation Tredo, run by Brazil's Federal Police on 8 December 2025, targeted public officials accused of passing confidential information about police operations to the leadership of the Comando Vermelho, so that the faction could get ahead of the security forces in the favelas it controls. Two sergeants of Rio de Janeiro's military police were arrested; a Bope sergeant who assigned the teams for incursions is among those under investigation. SBT News reports that a member of the Brazilian Navy is accused of supplying drones and training faction members to fly them. The 3rd specialised court for criminal organisations issued eleven temporary arrest warrants and six search warrants. Investigators said they were still looking for other faction infiltrators inside the state apparatus. No one is named.
inside: The Comando Vermelho had serving police and a navy member feeding it the timing of raids, prosecutors say, so its areas were warned before the state arrived.
cite: Jovem Pan and SBT News, 8 December 2025, on the Federal Police's Operation Tredo

n: Los Patrones paid Guatemalan police to move its drug loads
rank: officers of the National Civil Police
d: Guatemalan prosecutors said the trafficking group Los Patrones, which worked across the south and west of the country, operated with the support of local officers of the National Civil Police. The attorney general's office said the police "facilitated the transportation of the illicit substances in exchange for economic benefit". Fifteen members of the group were captured in an operation of thirty raids in Guatemala, San Marcos, Huehuetenango and Escuintla, reported on 31 March 2019. Those named as leaders were Miguel Antonio Solan Solis, known as "El Patron", and Sonia Haydee Lainez Aguilar de Salan, "La Patrona"; Donil Vinicio Orozco Lopez, "El Mas Chingon", is said to have headed the network of police collaborators. The report records no charges or convictions against the officers.
inside: A trafficking group paid local police to carry its drug loads, so officers of the national force became part of its transport chain.
cite: Q Costa Rica, 31 March 2019, on the Guatemalan attorney general's statement

n: Santa Fe prison guards charged with opening a cell for an inmate killing
rank: guards and head of surveillance, Santa Fe prison service, Unit 11 Pinero
d: Agustin de la Encina Capelletti, who prosecutors say worked for Esteban Alvarado's drug gang and had been blamed for the loss of a 32-kilogramme cocaine shipment, was killed on 13 January 2025 in wing 6 of Unit 11 at Pinero, in Argentina's Santa Fe province. Two guards of the provincial prison service, Julian Aguirre and Gustavo Raimondi, were charged with aggravated homicide as primary participants and with abuse of office for facilitating the killing; the wing's head of surveillance, named in reports as Hernan P., allegedly ordered them to open the cell door. Nine inmates were charged on 20 November 2025, among them the wing delegate as instigator. The two guards were later released on bail.
inside: Prisoners got the guards of their own wing to open a cell door, prosecutors say, so the prison service's control was used to carry out a killing inside it.
cite: La Capital (Rosario), 20 November 2025, on the charges before Judge Carlos Sosa

n: Casalesi clan held a monopoly on Caserta hospital's contracts
rank: director general and contracts of the Sant'Anna e San Sebastiano hospital
d: Investigators said the Casalesi, a camorra clan of the Caserta area whose Zagaria faction is based at Casapesenna, controlled who won work at Caserta's public hospital, the Azienda Ospedaliera Sant'Anna e San Sebastiano. Prosecutors said the jailed boss Michele Zagaria, held under the strict 41-bis prison regime, 'riusciva a controllare e a gestire, in regime di assoluto monopolio, lavori e concessione di appalti o servizi'. Firms tied to him won tenders for painting, lift maintenance and the bar and vending machines. Reported on 21 January 2015, after an inquiry of more than two years, 24 people were placed under precautionary measures, ten in prison, among them the hospital's former director general Francesco Bottino and the boss's sister Elvira Zagaria. Charges included mafia association, corruption and bid rigging. The sources read do not report the outcome.
inside: A camorra clan reached a public hospital through its former director general and its tender process, so contracts went to firms the clan controlled.
cite: Quotidiano Sanita, "'Gomorra' al Sant'Anna e San Sebastiano: 24 indagati", 21 January 2015; LiveSicilia, 'Blitz contro i Casalesi, scattano 24 arresti', 21 January 2015 (https://livesicilia.it/?p=267988)

n: Cimmino-Caiazzo clan rigged tenders at three Naples public hospitals
rank: officials of the Cardarelli, Azienda dei Colli and Nuovo Policlinico hospitals
d: Naples prosecutors asked for 48 people to be sent for trial over what they called a 'sistema corruttivo per favorire la camorra' inside three of the city's public hospitals: the Cardarelli, the Azienda dei Colli and the Nuovo Policlinico, all named as injured parties. The clan said to be behind it is the Cimmino-Caiazzo group, run in turn by the Alleanza di Secondigliano and led by Luigi Cimmino of the Vomero quarter. Officials of the hospitals and former union representatives are among the defendants; investigators said officials 'apparecchiato gare d'appalto, cucite su misura' for firms close to the clan, and that pressure reached patient transport, funeral services, building work, cleaning, catering and vending machines. The report is dated 1 April 2022.
inside: A camorra clan had hospital officials write tenders to fit firms it was close to, so three public hospitals' contracts served the clan's businesses.
cite: Fanpage, 'Clan e appalti negli ospedali a Napoli, chiesto processo per 48 indagati', 1 April 2022

n: Veneruso clan reached Campania's buying agency Soresa through its chairman
rank: chairman of Soresa spa, the Campania Region's purchasing company
d: Soresa spa buys goods and services for the health system of Italy's Campania Region. On 10 November 2026 Naples anti-mafia prosecutors obtained 13 precautionary measures, nine in prison and four under house arrest, in an inquiry into the Veneruso camorra clan of Volla, Casalnuovo and eastern Naples. Among those remanded was Tommaso Casillo, Soresa's chairman, a former senator and former undersecretary in the Prodi government. Prosecutors allege a 100,000-euro bribe, handed over in a sealed envelope, to help the firm M.L. Sanity win a Soresa tender worth about 23.8 million euros to rent out stretchers to Campanian health facilities. The director general of Asl Napoli 3 Sud, Giuseppe Russo, is under investigation. One account puts the alleged conduct between 2020 and 2025. La Notizia also reports a second alleged bribe, 20,000 euros, over a 29.6-million-euro waste collection tender at Somma Vesuviana. Charges include mafia association, corruption and bid rigging.
inside: Prosecutors say a camorra clan paid the chairman of the region's health-buying company, so a public tender worth millions went to a firm the clan backed.
cite: AGI, 'Appalti rifiuti, 13 misure per il clan Veneruso', 10 November 2026 (https://www.agi.it/cronaca/news/2026-11-10/appalti-rifiuti-clan-veneruso-39962979/); Il Sole 24 Ore (English), 'Camorra and public contracts: 13 arrests in Naples and the surrounding area', 10 November 2026; La Notizia, 11 November 2026 (https://www.lanotiziagiornale.it/?p=431903)

n: Misratah force stormed Libya's oil corporation to win supplier contracts
rank: National Oil Corporation headquarters, Tripoli
d: On 28 May 2025, fighters of the Joint Operation Force, a Misratah-based armed group set up by a prime-ministerial decree in 2013 and kept funded by the Government of National Unity, forced their way into the headquarters of the National Oil Corporation, Libya's state oil company, in Tripoli. The UN Panel of Experts on Libya found that the purpose was to pressure officials into awarding supplier contracts to companies controlled by or associated with the group. In the same May 2025 fighting the force also took two Libyan Intelligence Service sites. The Panel said the authorities, including the corporation's own leadership, played the incident down, which it read as a sign of the impunity armed groups have when they target state institutions.
inside: A Misratah armed group forced its way into the state oil company's head office to make officials give supplier contracts to firms it controls.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, para. 10 and annex 6, para. 2

n: Militia chief al-Kikli's pick ran Libya's state electricity company
org_label: Stability Support Apparatus (Abdel Ghani al-Kikli) and 111 Brigade
rank: Chairman, General Electric Company of Libya
d: The General Electric Company of Libya is the state company that generates and distributes the country's electricity. The UN Panel of Experts found that Mohamed Omar Hassan Al-Mashay, who had no prior experience in energy, was made its chairman in July 2022 as one of the conditions for Abdel Ghani al-Kikli, commander of the Tripoli militia turned state agency the Stability Support Apparatus, to back Abdulhamid Dbeibah as prime minister. The Panel found Al-Mashay then managed the company under the direct instruction of al-Kikli and Colonel Abdulsalam Al-Zobi of 111 Brigade, took al-Kikli's instructions on where transmission lines went, and blocked audits; armed men turned auditors away from the headquarters in 2022 and 2023. Al-Kikli denied any connection with the company or the appointment.
inside: A militia made the chairmanship of the state power company part of its price for backing a prime minister, then gave the chairman his instructions.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2024/914, 2 December 2024, paras. 12-16; UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, annex 9, paras. 25-26

n: Arkenu's designer chaired the committee meant to police its NOC contract
org_label: Saddam Haftar's network and Arkenu Oil Company
rank: Chairman of the NOC-Arkenu management committee
d: The contract signed in March 2023 between Libya's National Oil Corporation and Arkenu Oil Company set up a joint management committee as the forum where both sides would check that contract obligations were being met. The UN Panel of Experts found that Belqacem Shengeer was made chairman of that committee as the corporation's own representative, with the support of Rafat al-Abbar, who acts as a proxy for Saddam Haftar. Shengeer is a former corporation board member and, the Panel says, the technical architect behind the creation of Arkenu. He filed no report of the committee's activities, so no oversight was possible, and the Panel found he directly represented the interests of Saddam Haftar and the Libyan Arab armed forces top command. He lives in Benghazi.
inside: The man who designed the private oil firm also sat as the state company's representative on the committee meant to check it, and filed no reports.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, annex 9, paras. 16-17

n: Houthi-run assembly put an outsider on the board of Kamaran company
rank: Board of Directors, Kamaran Industry and Investment Company
d: Kamaran Industry and Investment Company makes cigarettes in Yemen and counts the government and the Yemen Bank for Reconstruction and Development among its shareholders. The UN Panel of Experts recorded that an external individual was appointed to its board of directors contrary to the company's own rules, in a move aimed at controlling the company's assets. The company's board, which sits in Aden, said in a statement of 1 October 2024 that a meeting called in Sana'a on 30 September 2024 lacked a quorum, that representatives of the government, of Tabouh International and of the bank were absent, and that people who were not shareholders were appointed to the board in order to seize the firm's decision-making, assets and funds. It said it does not recognise the outcome.
inside: An armed movement's side of the country held a shareholders' meeting of its own and put its appointee on a part-state company's board to control its assets.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2025/650, August 2025, para. 124(c) and annex 86

n: AFC/M23 named its own mining coordinator on SAKIMA's Rubaya permit
org_label: Alliance Fleuve Congo / Mouvement du 23 mars (AFC/M23)
rank: AFC/M23-appointed coordinator for artisanal mining, Rubaya
d: Rubaya, in Masisi territory in eastern Congo, holds most of North Kivu's coltan production. The hill where the mining happens lies inside exploitation permit PE16159, which the mining registry records as attributed to the Societe aurifere du Kivu et du Maniema (SAKIMA). The UN Group of Experts found that the armed movement AFC/M23, which took the area in April 2024, appointed Bazimazika Kabano Bazinga as its coordinator for artisanal mining in Rubaya, and that he was also one of the main local traders buying the minerals. AFC/M23 taxed production at the point of sale, $4 a kilogram for coltan and $2 for cassiterite, approved the transporters and had the tax paid into a bank account held by its provincial financial coordinator.
inside: An armed movement appointed the man coordinating mining on the permit the registry attributes to SAKIMA, and he also traded the ore the movement taxed.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, S/2026/466, 2026, paras. 213-217 and annex 67

n: Iraq's state broadcaster board put under three designated movements
org_label: Kataib Hezbollah and two other US-designated movements
rank: Board of the Iraq Media Network
d: The Iraq Media Network is the state-run broadcaster, funded from the national budget. Michael Knights of the Washington Institute wrote in CTC Sentinel in November 2025 that on 28 February 2024 the Iraqi cabinet placed the network's board under the majority control of three movements designated as terrorist organisations by the United States. He names Awsam Majid Ghanem Hassan al-Mohammedawi, a media operator of Kataib Hezbollah, among the figures linked to the network. Change the cite from footnote 39 to footnote 't'., an Iran-backed armed group that also holds brigades inside Iraq's state security forces. The source is an analytical article resting on the author's own profile of the network rather than a court or parliamentary finding, and it does not say what the board has since decided.
inside: Armed movements were given most of the seats on the state broadcaster's board, so the decisions of Iraq's public media now rest with them.
cite: Michael Knights, 'Rise of the E-Militias: Designated Terrorist Groups Infest Iraq's Digital Economy', CTC Sentinel, 20 November 2025, and its footnote 39

n: Asaib Ahl al-Haq's spokesman appointed to Iraq's media regulator board
org_label: Asaib Ahl al-Haq and the Badr Organization
rank: Board of the Communications and Media Commission
d: The Communications and Media Commission is the Iraqi state authority that licenses and regulates broadcasters and telecommunications. Michael Knights wrote in CTC Sentinel in November 2025 that under Prime Minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani its board came to be dominated by the Coordination Framework parties, and that Mahmoud al-Rubaie was appointed to it after serving as spokesman for the political office of Asaib Ahl al-Haq, an Iran-backed armed group designated as a terrorist organisation by the United States. Another member is described as a former Badr Organization representative on the Basra provincial council. The article says all six members come from Shia Islamist parties, but its own footnote names one member as not drawn from those factions.
inside: An armed movement's spokesman was appointed to the board of the authority that licenses Iraq's broadcasters, putting the movement inside its own regulator.
cite: Michael Knights, 'Rise of the E-Militias: Designated Terrorist Groups Infest Iraq's Digital Economy', CTC Sentinel, 20 November 2025, and its footnotes 38 and s

n: Smuggling network's commander held the Zawiya refinery's fuel supply
org_label: the Zawiya trafficking and smuggling network
rank: Commander, Petroleum Facilities Guard in Zawiya
d: The UN Panel of Experts reported in 2023 that the Zawiya refinery, west of Tripoli, was held by Mohamed Al Amin Al-Arabi Kashlaf, commander of the Petroleum Facilities Guard in Zawiya and a man the Security Council listed in 2018. The Panel found he does not answer to the guard's hierarchy in Tripoli, oversees the fuel supply from the refinery, and that this makes him a key figure in western Libya's fuel smuggling; with the local coast guard commander he runs a large smuggling network. Uncrewed aircraft strikes authorised by the prime minister picked targets mainly to weaken his hold on the refinery, but no ground operation followed and it stayed with him. Later Panel reports read for this record do not say whether he still holds the post.
inside: A smuggling network's commander controls the state refinery's fuel supply through the guard unit posted there, and the fuel feeds his own trade.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2023/673, 15 September 2023, paras. 13 and 60, and para. 142

n: Fuel network exported from Tubruq on state oil contracts and false papers
rank: Arabian Gulf Oil Company contracts and Tubruq Chamber of Commerce certificates
d: Only the National Oil Corporation may export refined fuel from Libya. The UN Panel of Experts found that tankers calling at Tubruq port in 2025 were loading to schedules set by contracts between the Arabian Gulf Oil Company, a subsidiary of the corporation, or Benghazi-based oil companies and foreign petroleum traders, and that their certificates of origin were issued by the Tubruq Chamber of Commerce, a body not authorised to issue them, which made the paperwork fraudulent and invalid. The Panel estimated close to one million metric tons of refined product left eastern Libyan ports, and traced cargoes to Greece, Belgium, Egypt, Germany, Malta and Spain. It assessed that most carriers were either complicit in or indifferent to their part in illicit exports.
inside: A smuggling network's cargoes left on contracts with a state oil subsidiary and on origin certificates from a public chamber with no power to issue them.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, annex 9, paras. 30-36

n: Gabon's forests minister signed export papers for banned kevazingo
rank: Minister of Forests
d: Gabon outlawed the cutting of kevazingo, a slow-growing hardwood, in March 2018. In February 2019 the authorities seized 392 containers of it at Owendo port, worth an estimated US$252 million, at the depots of two Chinese-owned companies. ENACT, the organised-crime programme of the Institute for Security Studies, reported that the forestry minister Guy-Bertrand Mapangou's signature was found on documents authorising the containers' export; he said the documents were fake. He was dismissed along with the vice-president, with his successor appointed in June 2019, though the president did not link either dismissal to the scandal. In April 2019, 353 of the containers disappeared while in Ministry of Justice custody; about 200 were recovered and 153 were unaccounted for. Several public servants were suspended. Investigations into kevazingo smuggling were reported as ongoing; the article does not say whether anyone has been charged.
inside: A timber trafficking network's banned kevazingo left Gabon under export papers carrying the forests minister's signature, which he says were forged.
cite: ENACT, Institute for Security Studies, 22 January 2020

n: Guinea's CITES chief sold wildlife export permits to animal dealers
rank: Head of Guinea's CITES Management Authority
d: CITES is the treaty that controls trade in endangered species, and each country has an office issuing its export permits. Ansoumane Doumbouya headed Guinea's from 2008 to 2013 and, according to the Project to End Great Ape Slavery, sold fraudulent permits recording wild-caught animals as captive-bred, the code that allows trade. It reported that China used this route between 2007 and 2012 to import more than 130 chimpanzees and possibly ten gorillas for commercial zoos and safari parks, a chimpanzee permit earning up to US$3,000. CITES suspended commercial trade with Guinea in 2013. He kept signing retained blank permits after losing the authority to do so, was arrested in August 2015 and sentenced to 18 months, then pardoned by President Alpha Conde while his appeal was pending.
inside: Animal dealers bought export permits from the official who issued them, so Guinea's own paperwork certified wild-caught apes as captive-bred and legal to ship.
cite: PEGAS/freetheapes.org, 29 January 2017; EAGLE Network, 20 August 2015

n: Indonesia's mining chief signed quotas for an unlawful nickel operation
rank: Director General of Minerals and Coal, energy ministry
d: Ridwan Djamaluddin was director general of minerals and coal at Indonesia's Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources, the post that approves miners' annual work plans and budgets, known as RKAB. On 25 April 2024 the Jakarta corruption court sentenced him to three years and six months and a fine of Rp200 million over nickel ore mining in the Mandiodo block in North Konawe, Southeast Sulawesi. Prosecutors said he approved RKAB documents that conflicted with a ministerial decree, and that the approvals benefited Windu Aji Sutanto, owner of PT Kara Nusantara Investama, and two other men. Eight defendants were convicted; Sutanto received eight years and Rp135.8 billion in restitution. Auditors put state losses at Rp2.3 trillion. Kabar24 reported that on 2 July 2024 the Jakarta High Court upheld the sentence on appeal. On his arrest in August 2023 Reuters reported a loss figure of 5.7 trillion rupiah.
inside: Men mining nickel outside the rules obtained the energy ministry's quota approvals, and those decisions let their ore be sold as if it were lawful.
cite: Hukumonline, 26 April 2024; Bisnis/Kabar24, 26 April 2024; Kabar24/Bisnis, 3 July 2024, on the appeal (https://kabar24.bisnis.com/read/20240703/16/1779005/eks-pejabat-esdm-tetap-dihukum-35-tahun-di-kasus-korupsi-nikel); Reuters via The Star, 10 August 2023

n: Haiti's eel export permits shaped by Moise's smuggling syndicate
rank: Ministry of Agriculture permit office
d: Elvers are baby eels, worth $3,000 to $5,000 a kilogram abroad while Haitian fishers are paid $0.34 to $1.70. In its 2026 final report the UN Panel of Experts on Haiti said the trade is dominated by Jean-Charles Moise, a businessman, former senator and secretary-general of the Pitit Dessalines party. According to the Panel's sources his network decides who works in the office that issues elvers export permits, and he influences the Ministry of Agriculture, Natural Resources and Rural Development, through which the licences are issued, as well as customs officials, so that they act in his favour. Former associates refused permits became his rivals. The Panel said he runs a syndicate of illicit exporters linked to a wider regional criminal network.
inside: A smuggling syndicate picked the staff of the ministry office that issues eel export permits, so licences went to its own people and rivals were refused.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2026/714, paras. 152-158

n: Libyan interior ministry men ran trafficking ventures with foreign networks
rank: Individuals of the Ministry of Interior
d: In its final report of December 2024 the UN Panel of Experts on Libya identified four illicit enterprises built on collaboration between international trafficking and smuggling networks and Libyan armed actors controlling key areas in Benghazi, Musa'id, Ra's Judayr, Tubruq and Zuwarah. It said those actors, including individuals of the Ministry of Interior of Libya and of the Haftar-affiliated forces, made money by taking a leading role in coordinating trafficking and smuggling operations, or by permitting criminal networks to operate on the territory they controlled in return for revenue and the use of migrants for forced labour. The Panel named seven members of the Al-Habouni Network and six of the Al-Katani Network, with hubs in Musaid and Tubruq, as directly responsible for running the operations.
inside: International smuggling networks paid people inside Libya's interior ministry for the run of the territory they policed, and the ministry's own men helped run the trade.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2024/914, paras. 48-49

n: Rwandan mines ministry agents signed off smuggled Congolese ore
org_label: cross-border tin and tantalum smuggling network
rank: Geology and Mines Department, Ministry of Mines
d: Tin, tantalum and tungsten ore from eastern Congo is traced by numbered tags that are supposed to prove which mine it came from. The UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo documented that in 2014 and 2015 cassiterite from South Kivu, including areas held by the Raia Mutomboki armed group, was smuggled into Rwanda and sold as Rwandan, and that the tags were misused and sold on the black market with the complicity of Rwandan companies and of tagging agents of the Geology and Mines Department of Rwanda's Ministry of Mines, who signed the mine site logbooks. In June, July and August 2015 the Group documented the sale of 12 tags with logbook copies, ministerial orders granting research licences and transport papers by three Rwandan companies.
inside: Smugglers bought the ministry's tags and its agents' logbook signatures, so ore mined under an armed group in Congo entered the legal market as Rwandan.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the DRC, S/2024/969, annex case 2, citing S/2015/797, paras. 53-60

n: Gang leader's family bribed Yunnan high court to cut his death sentence
rank: Officials of the Yunnan High People's Court, including its president
d: Sun Xiaoguo, whom China Daily calls a high-profile gang leader, was sentenced to death by the Kunming Intermediate People's Court in 1998 for rape, intentional injury and disturbing public order. China Daily reported that between June 2005 and 2008 his mother, a former policewoman, and his stepfather, then head of a district urban management bureau in Kunming, approached officials of the Yunnan High People's Court and the provincial government several times with bribes to win a lenient penalty at a retrial. His sentence became 20 years and he was freed in April 2010. On 15 December 2019 nineteen defendants were jailed: his mother for 20 years, his stepfather for 19, and seventeen staff of the provincial court, police and prison systems for two to twelve years. On 23 December 2019 the Yunnan High People's Court retried the 1998 case and restored the death sentence.
inside: A gang leader's family paid officials of the provincial high court that reviewed his case, and the court cut his death sentence to 20 years.
cite: China Daily, 16 December 2019, on the sentencing of the 19; China Daily, 23 December 2019, on the retrial and his gang-related offences
undone: The 16 December report names only his mother, who received 20 years, and his stepfather, who received 19; the other 17 are unnamed and are described only as having worked for the provincial court, public security and prison systems. Zhao Shijie, the high court's former president, was placed on one year of party probation for demanding that judges pervert the law at the hearing that reduced the sentence, which is party discipline and not a criminal conviction. On 23 December 2019 the Yunnan High People's Court retried the 1998 case, restored the death sentence and ordered his property confiscated.

n: Chone Killers part-owner's firm won Buena Fe municipal works contracts
rank: contracting of the Buena Fe municipal government (GAD)
d: The Chone Killers are an Ecuadorian criminal group led, Primicias says, by Julio Martinez Alcivar, alias Negro Tulio. Primicias found that the municipal government of Buena Fe, in Los Rios province, awarded about 801,000 US dollars of infrastructure work in the closing months of 2023 to Constructora & Consultora Oscimaq S.A.S. Half of that company was held by Carlos Cabrera Baidal. In a separate case concerning the municipality of Duran, prosecutors charged Cabrera as the person who influenced public contracting processes in favour of the Chone Killers; Primicias does not say the Buena Fe contracts were part of that charge. The reporting traced the same pattern across several Ecuadorian municipalities, which buy works and services from firms owned by people named as gang figures.
inside: Buena Fe council bought works from a company half-owned by a man whom prosecutors, in a separate Duran case, charge with steering public contracting for the Chone Killers.
cite: Primicias (Ecuador), investigation into Ecuadorian municipalities contracting works and services with companies linked to organised crime

n: Faction toll and voter coercion alleged behind three Sobral councillors
org_label: criminal factions in Sobral (not named in the source)
rank: three seats on the Camara Municipal de Sobral
d: Brazilian electoral prosecutors charged three sitting councillors of Sobral, in Ceara, and a lawyer on 11 November 2026 over alleged links to criminal factions at the 2024 municipal election. The complaint says a group demanded a toll of 60,000 reais so that candidates could campaign in certain Sobral districts, and lists extortion, coercion of voters, embezzlement, obstruction of electoral propaganda and financing or joining a criminal organisation. The accused are Mario Vicktor Linhares Cavalcante, Raimundo Nonato do Nascimento and Carlos Evanilson Oliveira Vasconcelos, with the lawyer Lintor Jose Linhares Torquato. Prosecutors asked for loss of the three mandates and an eight-year ban from office. All four deny the accusations. No ruling has been given.
inside: Prosecutors say factions taxed and coerced the vote in Sobral's districts, so three councillors reached the city council on terms set by the groups.
cite: O Povo, 12 November 2026, on the Ministerio Publico Eleitoral complaint of 11 November 2026 (Operacao Omerta)

n: Rio state deputy investigated over delay to TCP boss's resort demolition
rank: member of the Rio de Janeiro state assembly (Alerj)
d: The Terceiro Comando Puro is a Rio de Janeiro drug trafficking faction. In June 2026 prosecutors at the Ministerio Publico do Rio de Janeiro served fourteen search warrants, among them one at the Alerj office of the state deputy Roosevelt Barreto Barcelos, known as Val Ceasa, over suspected action in favour of the faction. Reporting on the case says the demolition of a resort in Cidade Alta attributed to the faction's chief, Alvaro Malaquias Santa Rosa, known as Peixao, was put off for about fifteen months after political dealings, and that a separate demolition in Parada de Lucas was postponed. Messages cited date from 16 January 2025. Val Ceasa had earlier denied any link to criminal organisations.
inside: Prosecutors suspect a faction used a state deputy's standing to hold off demolition of its chief's resort, so a state decision served the traffickers.
cite: Tribuna do Sertao, 18 June 2026, on the MPRJ operation and the earlier Federal Police investigation

n: TSE removes Cabedelo mayor over Comando Vermelho arm's hold on city hall
who: Tropa do Amigao, an arm of Comando Vermelho
rank: mayor, deputy mayor and a councillor of Cabedelo
d: Brazil's superior electoral court removed the mayor and deputy mayor of Cabedelo, in Paraiba, for abuse of political and economic power at the 2024 municipal election. The court found that city hall appointed people linked to the Tropa do Amigao, described as an arm of the Comando Vermelho drug faction, to commissioned posts and outsourced jobs on the recommendation of trafficking leaders; the adoptive daughter of one leader was among those hired. Food parcels, goods and cash of 80 to 300 reais were offered for votes, with 42 voting receipts and payment keys found on seized phones. Andre Luis Almeida Coutinho and Camila Lucena lost office on 7 April 2026; the councillor Marcio Alexandre de Melo e Silva lost his mandate and was barred for eight years.
inside: A drug faction's recommendations decided who city hall hired, so Cabedelo's own payroll and jobs went to people the traffickers put forward.
cite: Ministerio Publico Federal / MP Eleitoral release on the TSE judgment of 7 April 2026 upholding the TRE-PB decision

n: Operation Hereditas: PCC leader's firm among Guaruja tender beneficiaries
rank: city council and city government of Guaruja
d: Gaeco, the organised crime unit of Sao Paulo state's prosecution service, ran Operation Hereditas with the civil police in Guaruja, in the Baixada Santista, serving 26 search warrants on the city council and the city government. Prosecutors allege bid-rigging in public tenders with bribes paid to officials to make the scheme work, and said one company that benefited belonged to a notorious leader of the Primeiro Comando da Capital, the prison-born faction known as the PCC, who was shot dead in March 2024. The reporting does not name him. Three councillors were among the targets. The businessman Claudio Fernando de Aguiar, then a mayoral candidate, said he had nothing to hide and that his firm won a council contract on the lowest price.
inside: Prosecutors say bribes to Guaruja officials steered the town's tenders, and that one of the winning firms belonged to a PCC leader.
cite: ABC do ABC, 1 October 2024, on the Gaeco and Policia Civil operation Hereditas in Guaruja

n: Belford Roxo mayor made two militia leaders city secretaries, says MP
rank: two municipal secretariats of Belford Roxo
d: Brazil's electoral prosecution service asked the superior electoral court to bar the candidacy of Marcio Canella, elected a Rio de Janeiro state deputy in 2026, over ties to armed criminal groups. Its filing says that as mayor of Belford Roxo in 2025 he appointed two militia leaders to run municipal secretariats: one had already been convicted of forming a militia, the other faced charges of extortion and unlawful possession of firearms and was later convicted. Both had worked on his campaign. Militias in Rio are armed groups, often led by serving or former police, that control neighbourhoods and their trades. Canella was arrested in the eighth phase of a money-laundering investigation; the regional court had earlier cleared his candidacy without the sealed evidence.
inside: Prosecutors say the mayor handed two armed militia leaders charge of city departments, putting the groups in control of Belford Roxo's own services.
cite: Ministerio Publico Federal / MP Eleitoral release on case RO-El 0601451-66.2026.6.19.0000 before the TSE

n: Customs officers at Cap-Haitien were paid to clear an arms container
org_label: Arms trafficking ring led by a former Haitian police officer
rank: senior customs officer and officers of the Cap-Haïtien customs office
d: On 5 April 2024 Haitian authorities seized 26 firearms, 34 magazines and 999 rounds in a container that reached Cap-Haitien from Port Everglades, Florida. It was the largest seizure since the UN arms embargo on Haiti began in October 2022. The UN Panel of Experts found that customs officers at Cap-Haitien had been paid to let the goods pass. One senior customs officer had already put a concealed box into his vehicle to take it out of the port; when weapons were found in a second box he returned the first and left. Local officers were reluctant to arrest him, but he was detained days later and removed from his post; the Panel records that he was released without trial in July 2025, reportedly after pressure from powerful figures. One officer was suspended for four months, two were cautioned, and the Panel says more are implicated.
inside: Arms traffickers had paid officers inside Haiti's customs service at Cap-Haitien, so the port cleared a weapons shipment instead of stopping it.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2024/704, annex 23 and para. 56; S/2025/597, para. 83

n: Celestin's smuggling network paid Haitian customs and border agents
org_label: Rony Célestin's cross-border network with the 400 Mawozo gang
rank: customs officials and border security agents at the Belladère crossing
d: Rony Celestin, a businessman and former Haitian senator, financed the 400 Mawozo gang and ran a cross-border network that the UN Panel of Experts says is made up of businesspeople, informal traders, transporters, corrupt border security and customs agents, local smugglers and gang members. The Panel spoke to 18 confidential sources in Haiti and the Dominican Republic, some of them part of the network. Five described how cargo trucks of contraband pass through the Belladere crossing, at times with arms and ammunition concealed for the gang, with his knowledge. Sources said he pays the gang, his designated customs officials and other members 3,000 to 5,000 dollars a truck so that cargo is not inspected and duties are not paid. Canada has sanctioned him for economic crimes.
inside: A smuggling network paid officers inside Haiti's customs and border services, so trucks of contraband and gang ammunition passed uninspected and untaxed.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2024/704, paras. 167-172 and annex 44

n: Gangs paid Kenscoff police to hold back as they took the commune
rank: Haitian National Police officers serving in Kenscoff commune
d: From January 2025 gangs attacked Kenscoff, a hillside commune above Port-au-Prince, destroying infrastructure, killing residents, raping women and burning homes in order to take land for politicians and businesspeople, the UN Panel of Experts reported. Part of that scheme, the Panel says, involved corrupting police officers so that security operations were hampered and the gangs could set up bases in the commune. The attacks left hundreds of victims and, according to the Panel, were reportedly instigated by politicians who wanted to expose the police's inability to protect one of the capital's most residential areas. Haiti's Central Directorate of Judicial Police has made several arrests in connection with the attacks. Gangs still hold parts of Kenscoff.
inside: Gangs paid serving police officers in Kenscoff, so the force held back while the gangs built bases and cleared land for their political backers.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2025/597, para. 49; S/2026/714, paras. 48-51

n: Haiti's G9 gang coalition had police officers in Solino acting for it
org_label: G9 Family and Allies gang coalition
rank: Haitian National Police officers based in and living in Solino
d: Jimmy Cherizier, a former Haitian police officer known as Barbeque who leads the G9 coalition of gangs, kept working relations with serving officers after he left the force, the UN Panel of Experts reported in 2024. The Panel says some policemen living in the Solino neighbourhood of Port-au-Prince were his allies in the fight against gangs, and that when G9 began to fracture he reportedly asked certain officers to stop the Chyen Mechan gang attacking other G9 gangs. He also accused some officers on social media of trafficking weapons with him. The arrangement broke down as the Viv Ansanm alliance attacked police premises; G9 then joined its former rival to attack Solino and Delmas 24, and at least 128 people were killed or injured there from March 2024.
inside: A gang coalition's leader had serving police officers in Solino act on his requests, so police action followed one gang's interests against its rivals.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2024/704, annex 10

n: Drug networks in southern Haiti kept police and judicial cases blocked
rank: police officers and the coast guard detachment for the South, Grand'Anse and South-East
d: The UN Panel of Experts visited Les Cayes and Jacmel in southern Haiti in 2025 and found the area badly exposed to drug trafficking, in part because of entrenched criminal networks made up of influential private actors, corrupt police officers and government officials, alongside little state oversight. The coast guard detachment covering the South, Grand'Anse and South-East departments sits opposite Ile-a-Vache, an island about 10 km off Les Cayes used as a waypoint for the drugs-for-guns trade, but its patrol boats are not working. Despite several reported seizures, the Panel says complicity has obstructed deeper police and judicial processes, letting key actors operate with impunity. It names no officer.
inside: Drug networks in southern Haiti counted police officers among their members, so investigations into seizures went no further and the traffickers kept working.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2025/597, paras. 103, 116

n: Operation Pandora: Dominican police armoury chiefs sold its ammunition
org_label: Ammunition trafficking network run through the Dominican National Police armoury
rank: head of the Intendencia de Armas and head of the arms and ammunition depot, National Police
d: On 17 November 2024 Dominican prosecutors launched Operation Pandora against a network they say stole more than 900,000 projectiles from the National Police armoury and sold them on. Those held include Colonel Narciso Antonio Feliz Romero, head of the Intendencia de Armas, which has custody of police weapons and ammunition, Captain Nelson Valdez, who ran the arms depot, an auditor accused of altering audit results to hide the losses, and Miguelina Bello Segura, who prosecutors say received dozens of boxes of ammunition and resold them clandestinely to Haitian nationals at 5,200 to 6,000 pesos a box. The inquiry followed a UN panel tracing 5,000 rounds seized in Mirebalais, Haiti, to the stockpile; the Dominican police inventory put the loss at 908,001 items, mostly ammunition. Detention was ratified in March 2026. Bello Segura admitted the facts and was sentenced in October 2026 to three years, half suspended, with eighteen months under house arrest; Feliz Romero, Valdez and the other accused were sent for full trial.
inside: Ammunition traffickers worked through the police officers guarding the armoury, so the force's own stockpile supplied buyers, prosecutors say including Haitians.
cite: Dominican Ministerio Publico/Policia Nacional release on Operacion Pandora, 17 November 2024 (https://www.policianacional.gob.do/ministerio-publico-pone-en-marcha-la-operacion-pandora-contra-red-criminal-integrada-por-policias/); De Ultimo Minuto, 19 November 2024, on the resale to Haitian nationals and the prices (https://deultimominuto.com/nacionales/justicia/imputada-en-operacion-pandora-vendia-municiones-de-la-policia-a-haitianos-segun-mp/); Acento, 25 March 2026, on the ratification of detention; Revista Mercado, 26 October 2026, on the sentence and the opening of the full trial (https://revistamercado.do/actualidad/condenan-a-tres-anos-a-una-mujer-que-vendia-a-haitianos-municiones-robadas-a-la-policia-dominicana/); UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2025/597, annex 25, on the 908,001 items and the Mirebalais tracing (https://docs.un.org/en/S/2025/597)

n: Cocaine convoy moved in a Niger mayor's car under military escort
rank: military escort for the convoy and the car of the mayor of Fachi
d: On 6 January 2022 police in the Niger seized 214 kg of cocaine that had come in from Gao in Mali and was bound for Libya and then Europe, the largest cocaine seizure recorded in the country, valued by its authorities at 16.8 million euros. Reporting on the Niger's investigation, the UN Panel of Experts on Mali says the load travelled by road from Gao to Niamey and on to Agadez hidden in a refrigerated container, and that in Agadez it was repacked into the car of the mayor of Fachi and sent to Dirkou with a military escort for the convoy. Two citizens of the Niger ran the two legs. The Panel was still checking whether those named were linked to sanctioned individuals.
inside: A cocaine network moved its load in a Niger mayor's car under military escort, so a local official's car and the army's protection served the traffickers.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Mali, S/2023/578, paras. 92-94; S/2022/595, para. 68

n: Officers' own posts used to run guns over Haiti's Belladere border
org_label: Dominican-Haitian arms and ammunition trafficking networks
rank: police officers, civil servants and relatives of local authorities at border crossings
d: Haitian gangs, the 400 Mawozo above all, buy firearms and ammunition from Dominican traffickers across the 392 km land border. In its 2023 report the UN Panel of Experts says that in several cases it investigated, officials, including police officers, civil servants and relatives of local authorities, used their own positions to move materiel across, and that most of the trafficking it recorded went through the Belladere crossing, the main point of entry for goods from the Dominican Republic. The Panel also found that economic and political actors contest control of the crossings through bribes and by influencing who is appointed to key customs and police posts, and that armed men from Croix-de-Fer were being used to intimidate customs and police officers at Belladere.
inside: Arms traffickers used serving police officers and local officials at Haiti's main border crossing, so their own posts carried the weapons through.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2023/674, para. 104 and annex 31

n: Carabinieri colonel Naselli passed case secrets to an 'ndrangheta go-between
rank: Lieutenant colonel, former head of the Carabinieri investigative unit, Catanzaro
d: Giorgio Naselli, a Carabinieri lieutenant colonel who had commanded the force's investigative unit in Catanzaro, Calabria, passed information about live investigations to Giancarlo Pittelli, a lawyer and former senator whom prosecutors treated as a go-between for 'ndrangheta clans. Prosecutors cited a September 2018 exchange about a waste company tied to a man they placed in the Piromalli and Mole clans, which they said let him avoid fresh preventive measures, and an August 2019 warning, repeated three times, that a man Pittelli should avoid had the financial police on him. In the Rinascita-Scott appeal reported on 20 December 2025 Naselli was given two years for disclosure of official secrets, with the mafia aggravating circumstance dropped.
inside: A lawyer acting as the clans' go-between drew live investigation secrets from a senior Carabinieri officer, so police knowledge served the 'ndrangheta figures he dealt with.
cite: Il Fatto Quotidiano, 19 December 2019, on the Catanzaro post, the September 2018 waste-company exchange and the August 2019 warning; L'Indipendente, 20 December 2025, on the appeal sentence (https://www.lindipendente.online/2025/12/20/maxiprocesso-rinascita-scott-in-appello-condanne-al-ribasso-per-istituzioni-e-ndranghetisti/)

n: Carabiniere Ventura convicted of aiding a mafia group from the Vibo unit
rank: Carabiniere, investigative unit, Vibo Valentia
d: Antonio Ventura, a carabiniere serving at the force's investigative unit in Vibo Valentia, Calabria, was convicted of aggravated aiding and abetting carried out to benefit a mafia association. The case formed part of Rinascita-Scott, the mass prosecution of the Mancuso 'ndrangheta clan and its contacts, whose first arrests were made on 19 December 2019. The appeal court, in a ruling reported on 20 December 2025, confirmed his first-instance conviction and his sentence of five years and eight months, while cutting many other sentences in the same trial. The reports read do not give the period of his conduct or say what he passed.
inside: An 'ndrangheta clan had a serving carabiniere in the unit investigating it, and a court found his help was given to benefit the association.
cite: L'Indipendente, 20 December 2025; Il Fatto Quotidiano, 19 December 2019

n: DIA marshal Marinaro's leak charge in Rinascita-Scott ruled time-barred
rank: Former marshal, Direzione Investigativa Antimafia, Catanzaro
d: Michele Marinaro, a former marshal of the Direzione Investigativa Antimafia, Italy's specialist anti-mafia police directorate, at its Catanzaro office, was prosecuted in Rinascita-Scott, the mass case against the Mancuso 'ndrangheta clan and its contacts whose first arrests came on 19 December 2019. He had been charged with external complicity in a mafia association. On appeal, in a ruling reported on 20 December 2025, the court reclassified the charge as disclosure of official secrets and then found it time-barred, so no finding on the merits stands against him. The report read does not say what he was alleged to have disclosed, or to whom.
inside: Prosecutors alleged an 'ndrangheta clan had a marshal of the anti-mafia directorate leaking to it; the charge lapsed before any court ruled on it.
cite: L'Indipendente, 20 December 2025

n: Bicocca prison commander Cardamone served the Laudani clan for cash
rank: Commander of the prison police, Bicocca prison, Catania
d: Giuliano Gerardo Cardamone commanded the prison police at Bicocca prison in Catania, Sicily. Investigators described a paid-favours system in which officers took 200 to 300 euros a parcel to let detainees receive banned food, alcohol, perfume, mobile phones, computer media, cocaine and cannabis, and in some cases, investigators allege, meetings between jailed bosses were arranged, along with calls home beyond the permitted number and the carrying of bosses' messages out. The anti-mafia prosecutors' inquiry began with the arrest in November 2012 of a man caught with such a parcel. Cardamone favoured detainees tied to the Laudani clan for money and was found to have been wholly at the family's service. His ten-year sentence for corruption and external complicity in a mafia association became final after the trial closed in December 2025.
inside: A Catania mafia family paid the officer who commanded a prison's guards, so the prison's own rules were bent to keep its jailed members supplied and in contact.
cite: La Sicilia, 16 April 2026; LiveUnict, 15 April 2026; LiveSicilia, 18 April 2026 (https://livesicilia.it/ex-agente-penitenziario-arrestato-il-legale-trasferitelo-al-carcere-militare/), for Cardamone's detention at Agrigento and his lawyer's request for transfer to the military prison
undone: Cardamone went on the run in January 2026 and was arrested in a flat in Librino, Catania, in April 2026. He is serving the ten years at the prison in Agrigento. On 18 April 2026 his lawyer, Giuseppe Lipera, applied to the justice and interior ministers, Nordio and Piantedosi, and to the prison administration (DAP) to have him moved to the military prison at Santa Maria Capua Vetere, arguing that he is not safe at Agrigento and that his more than ten years' service as commander of the maximum-security prison at Catania Bicocca entitle him to the transfer.

n: Carabinieri at an intelligence agency and the ROS aided the Rinzivillo clan
rank: Carabinieri serving in an intelligence agency and in the ROS special operations group
d: In a blitz on 5 October 2017 against the Rinzivillo clan of Gela, a Cosa Nostra family long allied to the Madonia and the Corleonesi, prosecutors in Rome and Caltanissetta charged two carabinieri. Marco Lazzari served, at the time of the alleged conduct, in one of Italy's intelligence agencies; Cristiano Petrone served in the ROS, the force's special operations group. Prosecutors said the pair supplied the clan's acting head with information about extortion victims and their businesses, and that Lazzari also handled contacts with clan members, including one in Germany. Lazzari was charged with external complicity in a mafia association, and both men with unlawful access to computer systems. The sources read give no verdict.
inside: A Cosa Nostra family had two carabinieri, one inside an intelligence agency, feeding it police data on the people it was extorting, so state files served the clan's rackets.
cite: Gazzetta del Sud, 5 October 2017; La Notizia, 17 January 2019

n: Trani boss told parliament he paid Foggia prison guards for phone and gun
rank: Custody officers, Foggia prison
d: Salvatore Annacondia, who led a mafia group around Trani in Puglia before turning state witness, told Italy's parliamentary anti-mafia commission on 30 July 1993 that he had paid officers at Foggia prison. Asked who brought him contraband, he answered that it was the custody officers, and said he paid the man who brought him a mobile phone two to two and a half million lire each time, which he described as paying him a salary. He said he also kept a 6.35 calibre pistol in his cell, along with cocaine, hashish, perfume and money, and that each prisoner of standing had his own guards. He said he had already given names to magistrates.
inside: A Puglia mafia boss paid prison officers so that inside the jail he had a phone, a gun and drugs, leaving the prison's own staff working to his orders.
cite: Fabio Iadeluca, 'La criminalita organizzata in Puglia e Basilicata', vol. XIX, Pontificia Academia Mariana Internationalis, Appendice 1: extract from the parliamentary hearing of Salvatore Annacondia, 30 July 1993 (reprinted from the Camera dei Deputati and Senato della Repubblica verbatim record of that date)

n: Milan police inspector tried as a mole for traffickers, then acquitted
rank: Inspector, state police, Comasina station, Milan
d: Tommaso Saladino, an inspector of Italy's state police at the Comasina station in Milan, was accused of acting as the mole for drug traffickers whom a Sicilian investigation placed under the auspices of Cosa Nostra. Prosecutors said that in 2013, after 240 kilograms of hashish were seized at Paderno Dugnano, he repeatedly queried the interior ministry's SdiWeb database about three men under investigation. He was charged with unlawful access to a computer system and disclosure of official secrets, and convicted at first instance to three years and nine months. Milan's appeal court acquitted him of all charges, in a ruling reported on 2 December 2022, on the ground that the facts did not exist. A Guardia di Finanza marshal charged with the same offence was also acquitted.
inside: Prosecutors alleged traffickers backed by Cosa Nostra had a police inspector searching the interior ministry's database for them; the appeal court found it had not happened.
cite: Il Giorno, 2 December 2022

n: Licata carabinieri officer accused of taking a capomafia's money
rank: Luogotenente, Carabinieri investigative unit, Licata
d: Gianfranco Antonuccio, a luogotenente of the Carabinieri at the investigative unit in Licata, Sicily, was arrested by the ROS on the orders of the Palermo anti-mafia prosecutors in an operation reported on 4 July 2022. He had been given the job of checking that Giancarlo Buggea, described as a capomafia, was keeping to the terms of his house arrest. Prosecutors alleged that he turned a blind eye in exchange for money; a former lawyer described as a main intermediary for leading Sicilian bosses told them he had asked Buggea for 1,500 euros. He was charged with inducing the handing over of money, trafficking in counterfeit coins and disclosure of official secrets. The report read names no clan and gives no verdict.
inside: Prosecutors allege a mafia boss paid the Carabinieri officer assigned to police his house arrest, so the check on him was not carried out.
cite: Fanpage, 4 July 2022

n: Carabinieri leaked a wiretap on Messina Denaro's possible hideout
rank: Carabinieri lieutenant colonel at the DIA, Caltanissetta, and a corporal at the Castelvetrano company
d: Two carabinieri were arrested in April 2019 in an investigation by the Palermo prosecutors over a leak from the hunt for the fugitive Cosa Nostra boss Matteo Messina Denaro. Prosecutors said Giuseppe Barcellona, a corporal at the Castelvetrano company in Sicily who handled wiretap transcription, accessed the system without authorisation and photographed a transcript of a recorded conversation about the Castelvetrano mafia family and a possible hideout of the boss. In March 2017 he sent it to Marco Zappala, a lieutenant colonel at the anti-mafia directorate in Caltanissetta, who emailed it to Antonio Vaccarino, a former mayor of Castelvetrano. The next day, prosecutors said, Vaccarino met a mafioso and drug trafficker and revealed part of it. The sources read give no verdict.
inside: Prosecutors allege two carabinieri working on the hunt for a Cosa Nostra boss moved a secret wiretap out of the force, and it reached a mafioso named in it.
cite: BlogSicilia, 16 April 2019; Open, 16 April 2019

n: Judge found Trani prison officers were on the detainees' payroll
org_label: Trani prison detainees, one a nephew of the Parisi clan boss
rank: Officers of the prison police corps, Trani prison
d: Prison officers at Trani prison in Puglia were accused of selling favours to detainees. The investigating judge, in an order reported on 26 November 2021, called them public officials on the payroll and described an alarming picture of a criminal system resting on stable illicit relationships between members of the prison police corps and prisoners rather than isolated episodes. Two officers were arrested, with 29 people under suspicion in all, among them five further officers, six inmates and relatives; one of those held was a nephew of the Japigia boss Savinuccio Parisi. The alleged conduct covered 17 episodes between May and October 2020. The report read does not say the officers acted for a clan, and gives no verdict.
inside: Detainees, one of them a mafia boss's nephew, allegedly had prison officers on a retainer, so the jail's own rules were applied to suit the prisoners paying.
cite: L'Unione Sarda, 26 November 2021

n: Two Bari municipal police officers sacked over turning to the Parisi clan
rank: Officers of the municipal police, Bari
d: Rosalinda Biallo and Anna Losacco, officers of the municipal police in Bari, Puglia, were dismissed by the municipality, on the order of the local police command, after a disciplinary case built on papers from the district anti-mafia prosecutors, reported on 27 March 2024. Police said the two had turned to Fabio Fiore, alleged to be an associate of the Parisi clan, after a motorist they had ticketed for running a red light insulted them; the clan punished him by stealing his car, which was found the next day. One officer was said to have boasted of her friendship with the clan boss's son, to have put Fiore, whose licence had expired, in touch with a colleague who usually handled the paperwork, and to have named a clerk for an identity card renewal. Both are under investigation for failing to report a crime.
inside: Two municipal police officers allegedly used a Bari clan to settle a grievance and handled its associate's paperwork, so the clan's man was served by the force policing him.
cite: La Repubblica, 27 March 2024

n: Palermo policeman tipped off the Brancaccio clan about raids
rank: Officer of the state police, Palermo
d: Vincenzo Di Blasi, a former officer of Italy's state police in Palermo, was described by investigators as the linchpin of a system that leaked police information to the Brancaccio clan of Cosa Nostra and its boss Stefano Marino. Reporting on his re-arrest on 19 June 2020 set out that he had tipped Marino off about an imminent raid in 2006, alerted him in 2009 before the Old Bridge operation, supplied police tabards and signalling paddles to clan associates, and in September 2018 warned him about two cars rented for surveillance. He had already been convicted once and sentenced to six years, finishing that sentence in 2013. Investigators also said a retired carabiniere in his network was in touch with a serving colleague who supplied the plates of cars rented by plain-clothes officers.
inside: A Palermo mafia clan had a police officer warning it of raids and surveillance, so the force's own operations against it were known to the boss in advance.
cite: LiveSicilia, 20 June 2020

n: Prosecutors say timber smugglers' interests ran Brazil's environment ministry
rank: Minister of the Environment
d: Brazil's prosecutors say illegal timber exporters had their interests served inside the environment ministry. Ricardo Salles was Minister of the Environment from 2019 until he resigned in June 2021. Prosecutors say he appointed political staff inside the ministry to secure the illegitimate interests of timber companies, pushed through rule changes giving a veneer of legality to exports that broke the rules, and had the forestry agency Ibama issue certificates releasing timber seized in the United States. A federal court in Para accepted the charges on 28 August 2023; the Supreme Court release names 22 accused. On 1 September 2025 the case moved to the Supreme Court, where Salles, now a federal deputy, faces counts of criminal association, facilitating the smuggling of forest products and obstructing environmental inspection. Salles called the accusation absurd.
inside: Prosecutors say timber exporters' interests were served by staff the environment minister placed inside his own ministry, which then issued papers legitimising illegal timber.
cite: Jornal de Brasilia, 28-29 August 2023, on the Federal Court in Para accepting the prosecution's complaint, the rule changes, the Ibama certificates and Salles's response; Brazilian Supreme Court (STF) news release, 1 September 2025, on Acao Penal 2705 and the 22 accused (https://noticias.stf.jus.br/postsnoticias/stf-vai-julgar-ricardo-salles-por-suposto-esquema-de-facilitacao-de-contrabando-de-produtos-florestais/)

n: Passport syndicate had a South African home affairs official issue 192 passports
org_label: passport syndicate operating through Home Affairs officials
rank: official, Department of Home Affairs
d: A syndicate selling South African passports to foreign nationals who did not qualify for them worked through staff inside the Department of Home Affairs, the ministry that issues the country's passports. Judy Zuma, a Home Affairs official, processed 192 passports between 28 May and 12 June 2021 and was paid 4,000 rand for each. She was caught in a sting after offering a Home Affairs counter-corruption officer 10,000 rand, left the department in December 2021 and, the Daily Dispatch reported, pleaded guilty and was convicted on 1,159 counts of fraud, corruption and contravention of the Immigration Act and the Identification Act. The Durban Commercial Crime Court gave her 12 years, with another 24 suspended, reported on 4 August 2024. It is alleged that a former official, Zima Shange, recruited her; he was sentenced to an effective ten years in October 2023.
inside: A syndicate selling passports put an official inside the home affairs department on its payroll, and she issued the documents the buyers could not lawfully get.
cite: SAnews (South African Government News Agency), 4 August 2024, 'Former DHA official sentenced to 12 years imprisonment'; Daily Dispatch, 7 March 2024, on her guilty plea and the 1,159 counts (https://www.dispatchlive.co.za/news/2024-03-07-durban-home-affairs-employee-and-foreigners-convicted-for-passport-fraud-scam/)

n: A gendarmerie colonel led a CMA militia of serving Malian officers
rank: Colonel of the Malian Gendarmerie commanding an Imouchagh militia
d: In December 2019 a colonel of the Malian Gendarmerie, Guichma Ag Hakeily, led a 76-strong armed mission to Inchinanane in the Ménaka region under a mission order issued by the Coordination des mouvements de l'Azawad (CMA), the coalition of Tuareg-led armed movements that signed Mali's 2015 peace agreement. The UN Panel of Experts recorded that the convoy included four Malian armed forces vehicles, and that Colonel Guichma leads a group of between 20 and 30 Imouchagh members of the Malian army, National Guard, Gendarmerie, customs and police. One of them, the gendarme Alkadi Ag Tankana, was killed in the fighting. The remainder of the column were HCUA fighters.
inside: An armed coalition issued the order for a column led by a serving gendarmerie colonel whose militia was made up of serving soldiers, gendarmes, customs and police officers.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Mali, S/2020/158, paras. 14-16

n: GATIA's area commander sat inside a Malian army tactical group
org_label: Groupe autodéfense touareg Imghad et alliés (GATIA)
rank: Officer affiliated with the eighth combined arms tactical group (GTIA), Malian armed forces
d: Moussa Tiliche, in charge of operations in the Gourma area for GATIA, a Tuareg Imghad militia that signed Mali's 2015 peace agreement, is affiliated with the eighth combined arms tactical group of the Malian armed forces and has influence over GATIA combatants integrated into the reconstituted Malian army, the UN Panel of Experts reported in 2021. The reconstituted army is the force being built by folding the signatory movements' fighters into army units. The Panel also obtained evidence of cooperation between Tiliche and a trafficking network in moving several hundred parcels of hashish from Mali into the Niger in February 2021; Tiliche denied conducting drug deals with that network. On 29 April 2021 he attended an army integration ceremony for 422 former combatants at Ségou.
inside: A militia's area commander holds a place in an army tactical group and sways the movement's fighters now in army uniform, so army units answer partly to the militia.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Mali, final report S/2021/714, paras. 81-83

n: A national guard sergeant and a gendarmerie captain commanded Mali's CJA
org_label: Congrès pour la justice dans l'Azawad (CJA)-Gargando
rank: Sergeant of the national guard; captain of the gendarmerie
d: The two military commanders of CJA-Gargando, an armed group made up predominantly of Kel Antessar Tuareg from Gargando, in the Goundam area of Timbuktu region, hold serving posts in Mali's own security forces. The UN Panel of Experts recorded that Mohamed Ousmane Ag Hama, known as Mourou, is a sergeant of the national guard and that his brother Ahmad is a captain in the gendarmerie. At the legislative elections of April 2020 the group used that standing against the state: CJA elements commanded by Mourou faced Malian armed forces units protecting voting operations at Echel and kept voters from the polling station, and, according to a confidential report, the army had to fire into the air to stop CJA and CMA fighters breaking into the mayor's office at Tonka to seize ballot boxes.
inside: Two men holding ranks in Mali's national guard and gendarmerie are the military commanders of an armed group whose fighters then faced down army units at the polls.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Mali, final report S/2021/714, paras. 52-54 and footnote 46

n: A CMA force held the guard on Mali's governor's office in Kidal
org_label: Coordination des mouvements de l'Azawad (CMA) and MNLA
rank: Guard force at the governorate of Kidal
d: The compound of Mali's governor in Kidal was guarded not by the state's forces but by the Commission sécuritaire mixte de l'Azawad (CSMAK), described by the UN Panel of Experts as a local CMA force headed by and constituted mostly of elements from the Mouvement national de libération de l'Azawad (MNLA). CMA is the coalition of Tuareg-led movements that signed Mali's 2015 peace agreement. On 22 February 2021, while that force held the guard, a group of men in vehicles and on motorbikes entered the compound, removed the Malian flag that had been raised there on 11 February and put up the MNLA flag in its place. CMA officials told the Panel the men justified the act by the President's declaration that the agreement would be revised.
inside: An armed movement's own force provided the security of the state governor's compound, and the national flag came down there while it stood guard.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Mali, final report S/2021/714, para. 28

n: Two Somali soldiers convicted of moving al-Shabaab car bombs through checkpoints
rank: Soldiers of the Somali National Army manning Mogadishu checkpoints
d: Two former soldiers of the Somali National Army, Mohamed Abdulle Nur Abkow and Sharif Mohamed Barkhadle, were convicted in late December 2022 and early January 2023 for their role in facilitating the transportation of Al-Shabaab vehicle-borne improvised explosive devices, that is car and lorry bombs, through checkpoints in Mogadishu. Garowe Online reported in December 2022 that Abkow, who had served more than a decade, was sentenced to death by a military court for using his name and identity card to help the bombs pass. The same UN Panel report records that in January 2023 the Prime Minister announced investigations into the role security personnel played in facilitating Al-Shabaab access to attack the Villa Rays hotel in Mogadishu on 28 November 2022.
inside: Soldiers posted on the state's own checkpoints worked for Al-Shabaab, waving its car bombs through the cordon they were there to hold.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Somalia, S/2023/724, paras. 19-20 and footnote 25; Garowe Online, 15 December 2022

n: Known anti-balaka fighters recruited into CAR's presidential guard
rank: Members of the Groupement spécial chargé de la protection républicaine (presidential guard)
d: The UN Panel of Experts found that recruitment into the presidential guard, the Groupement spécial chargé de la protection républicaine, was handled discreetly rather than through an open process, centred on young people from the President's Bangui neighbourhood of Boy Rabe, his church and his ethnic group, and included known anti-balaka elements. Anti-balaka are the militias formed from 2013 against the Séléka rebellion. The named example is Thierry Lébéné, alias Colonel 12 Puissances, a former anti-balaka fighter under Patrice-Édouard Ngaïssona's command, whom anti-balaka members and guard members confirmed as a member of the unit. The guard's Director General, General Alfred Service, denied the involvement of armed group members in its operations. The 2017 national defence plan did not provide for the unit at all.
inside: A militia's fighters were taken into the unit that guards the president, so men who had answered to armed-group commanders now hold the state's weapons and uniforms.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, final report S/2021/569, paras. 100-102; S/2023/360, para. 115

n: Ex-militia 'requins' in CAR's presidential guard emptied police cells
org_label: les requins, drawn from former anti-balaka elements
rank: Vigilante roster operating within the ranks of the presidential guard
d: Les requins, the sharks, began in 2019 as an online group spreading false information and threatening the political opposition, and re-emerged at the end of 2020 drawing, in the UN Panel's words, on a roster of vigilantes, primarily former anti-balaka elements, operating within the ranks of the presidential guard. From December 2020 they ran extrajudicial operations at night under the government curfew. Their most common practice was to take people from their homes, or remove them from police or gendarmerie custody, and bring them to an office in Camp de Roux, the base housing both army and presidential guard headquarters. Orders were given by a group of presidential advisers. The guard's Director General said he was not aware of any such involvement by his unit's elements.
inside: Former militia fighters wearing presidential-guard uniform pulled detainees out of police and gendarmerie cells, so the state's custody served whoever was tasking them.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, final report S/2021/569, paras. 103-106

n: PK5 self-defence fighters given CAR gendarmerie uniforms and vehicles
rank: Fighters issued gendarmerie uniforms and vehicles, promised enrolment in the gendarmerie
d: From mid-January 2021, under the direct supervision of the Minister of the Interior and Public Security, Henri Wanzet-Linguissara, 58 fighters of the PK5 neighbourhood self-defence groups, which had fought the internal security forces and the UN mission since 2013, were recruited outside the official disarmament programme and fought alongside the army, the internal security forces and Russian instructors. Their leader Mahamat Rahama, known as LT, negotiated the recruitment with the minister. Each of the three groups was given weapons, gendarmerie uniforms and one gendarmerie vehicle, the vehicles having been donated by UNDP with United States funding. Recruits were paid per diems and allowances in cash and were promised enrolment in the gendarmerie, but received no document or mission order. The Panel wrote to the minister and had received no reply.
inside: A neighbourhood militia's fighters were put into gendarmerie uniforms and vehicles and paid in cash, operating as police while still answering to their own leader.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, final report S/2021/569, paras. 107-111

n: CAR army units in Grimari armed and tasked a wanted anti-balaka faction
rank: De facto auxiliary of the Armed Forces of the Central African Republic (FACA)
d: The UN Panel of Experts collected evidence that army units based in Grimari gave weapons and uniforms to the local anti-balaka faction of Dmitri Ayoloma, a group known to have committed human rights and humanitarian law violations across Ouaka prefecture, and that collaboration evolved into direct tasking, with Ayoloma and his elements working in coordination with the army. On 12 March 2021, after soldiers and Russian instructors had moved through Bangao village, Ayoloma arrived and burned houses belonging to Muslims and a mosque; sources said the complicity emboldened another anti-balaka group nearby to similar acts. Throughout, local judicial authorities confirmed that Ayoloma remained the subject of an arrest warrant issued in 2020 for killing a peacekeeper. The Panel found no evidence that army leadership in Bangui endorsed the strategy.
inside: A militia whose leader was wanted for killing a peacekeeper was armed, uniformed and given tasks by local army units, then used that backing against Muslim civilians.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, final report S/2021/569, paras. 113-117

n: Armed movements' fighters placed inside CAR's joint security units
rank: Elements of the Unités spéciales mixtes de sécurité; special adviser to the Prime Minister on those units
d: The 2019 peace agreement created joint security units, Unités spéciales mixtes de sécurité, combining the national defence and security forces with fighters from the armed groups. The UN Panel of Experts found that army leadership did not have full control over those elements, that mistrust and divisions were evident between the army, the internal security forces and the armed group elements, and that rules of engagement and weapons control had not been settled before deployment. The leader of the 3R movement, Abbas Sidiki, was special adviser to the Prime Minister on the units. He abandoned that post days after the graduation ceremony at Bouar in May 2020, around 38 former 3R members of the units deserted back to 3R, and on 9 June 3R combatants reportedly attacked the Bouar camp.
inside: Armed movements' fighters were placed inside state security units while their own leaders kept a hand on them, and some took their state training back to the movement.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, S/2020/662, paras. 64-69; S/2021/87, annex 5.4

n: CAR put armed group men in new army battalions and used them as proxies
org_label: anti-balaka, UPC and other Central African armed groups
rank: Elements integrated into territorial infantry battalions; army proxies
d: After human rights vetting with the UN mission ended in 2021, eight further army battalions were trained by Russian instructors at Berengo, taking the army to between 14,000 and 15,000 personnel against a defence plan ceiling of 9,800. The UN Panel of Experts found that these battalions were formed without a transparent recruitment or integration process, and that for each one approximately 20 loyalist armed group members from the provinces were transferred to Berengo to be integrated. The Ministry of Defence recognised the integration of certain armed group elements but rejected the use of proxies; army and gendarmerie officers in Bria told the Panel that 52 men demobilised at Sam-Ouandja served as proxies. Anti-balaka proxies acting with the army killed eight civilians at Bokolobo on 9 May 2022.
inside: Armed groups' fighters were put into new army battalions without vetting and used as proxies on operations, so part of the army's fighting was done by the movements' men.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, final report S/2023/360, paras. 115-121

n: Azande militia folded into CAR's army as auxiliaries at Obo
rank: Auxiliaries in the ranks of the Armed Forces of the Central African Republic (FACA)
d: The prefect of Haut-Mbomou and the local army commander told the UN Panel of Experts in March 2024 that Russian instructors arriving in Obo would reinforce the army in controlling the armed activities of AAKG, an Azande armed group that emerged in 2023. The Panel was also informed of weapons-handling training sessions run by the instructors for 120 AAKG elements, and that army elements working with the instructors were not under the command of the local army commander. On 26 March a UN mission vehicle heading for the training area was forced by soldiers to turn back without explanation.
