The Panel wrote that the scenario of the integration of AAKG elements as auxiliaries in the ranks of the army appears to have overtaken the disarmament programmes under way in the prefecture.
inside: An armed group's fighters were being trained and folded into the army as auxiliaries outside the official process, with the units involved outside the local commander's control.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, S/2024/444, paras. 79-82

n: Mai-Mai militias supplied by the Congolese brigade commander at Minembwe
rank: Commander of the 12th Rapid Reaction Brigade, FARDC, Minembwe
d: The UN Group of Experts reported that General Dieudonné Batenchi Muhima, commander of the Congolese army's 12th Rapid Reaction Brigade at Minembwe since March 2020, regularly supplied Mai-Mai groups with ammunition, and that army officers who opposed this were threatened or moved out of the zone of operations. Mai-Mai are local militias of the Hauts-Plateaux of South Kivu fighting Banyamulenge self-defence groups. Soldiers based at Kipupu cooperated with Mai-Mai attacks on neighbouring villages, and on 21 December 2020 army members and Mai-Mai combatants jointly attacked Twirwaneho fighters at Kamombo. The Group cited six army sources, including several senior officers, and could not reach Muhima. It treated the collusion as a violation of the sanctions regime.
inside: Militias had the army's own brigade commander arming them, and soldiers under his command fought beside them against their enemies in South Kivu.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, final report S/2021/560, paras. 144-145 and annex 107

n: Resistance brigades inside Yemen's army at Ta'izz kept their own units
org_label: Ta'izz resistance groups, including the Abu al-Abbas brigade
rank: Brigades of the Government of Yemen armed forces at Ta'izz
d: Resistance groups that had fought the Houthis at Ta'izz were integrated into the Government of Yemen armed forces, Hamoud al-Mikhlafi's fighters among them in 2017, and the Ta'izz military leadership told the Panel the schools they had occupied were given back to the Ministry of Education, though armed elements remained in some buildings. The UN Panel of Experts was told that cohesion in the Ta'izz military had deteriorated partly because it was unable to control some elements from the original resistance forces, who still operated as distinct units under the different brigades. One of these was the Abu al-Abbas brigade, some of whose elements left their locations in Ta'izz for al-Mukha after fighting the Ta'izz military. With salaries unpaid for months, the Panel also recorded army members from Ta'izz joining the better-funded Tareq Saleh forces.
inside: Militia brigades were given army ranks at Ta'izz but kept their own units and commanders, so parts of the state's army went on answering to the movements.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2021/79, annex 5, section II (paras. 8-11) and table 5.2; annex 9, para. 1, on al-Mikhlafi's fighters; annex 10, para. 2, on the schools

n: Vibo Valentia health authority commissioned over 'ndrangheta conditioning
who: 'Ndrangheta clans of the Vibo Valentia area
rank: Azienda Sanitaria Provinciale di Vibo Valentia (provincial health authority), its management and governing bodies
d: The Azienda Sanitaria Provinciale of Vibo Valentia, the public body that runs hospitals and health services for the province, was handed to a government-appointed commission by presidential decree on 30 September 2024 after inspectors found 'ndrangheta clans shaping its decisions. The prefect's report, quoted in the anti-mafia investigative directorate's half-yearly report to parliament, said the conditioning ran through staffing, professional appointments, property, public works, supplies and contracted care, and that the procedures for awarding public contracts took concrete form “in favouring companies and professionals actually adjacent to local 'Ndrangheta cosche”. Rents on the authority's own buildings were set below the tax agency's minimum or not collected at all, in favour of people close to local criminals, a loss put at over 545,000 euros.
inside: Clans reached the managers of a public health authority, so its contracts, jobs and rents were handed to firms and people tied to the clans.
cite: Direzione Investigativa Antimafia, Relazione semestrale al Parlamento, 2024 (English edition, at the link), Calabria section (quoting the prefect's report and DPR 30 September 2024); Il Fatto Quotidiano, 10 May 2023, on the underlying Maestrale-Carthago inquiry into the same authority

n: Clans' 'official doctor' alleged inside Vibo Valentia's health authority
rank: head of the prevention department, Azienda Sanitaria Provinciale di Vibo Valentia
d: In the Maestrale-Carthago investigation, made public on 10 May 2023 with 167 suspects and 61 people held, prosecutors in Catanzaro accuse Cesare Pasqua, former head of the prevention department of the Vibo Valentia provincial health authority and a former town councillor, of acting as the mafia organisation's doctor inside the body. Prosecutors say he was not a settled member of the group but made a concrete contribution, helping the Mancuso and Fiare clans influence the authority's decisions, stepping in over bureaucratic problems in its procedures and over inspections and seizures against firms the clans had an interest in, and that in return he obtained mafia protection for his own problems and, when his son Vincenzo stood for election, the backing of the clans he had favoured. The catering contracts at the Vibo Valentia, Serra San Bruno and Tropea hospitals are attributed to the Mileto locale and Fiare clan interests generally. The case was reported as an investigation; Il Fatto Quotidiano records no verdict.
inside: Prosecutors say clans had a senior doctor inside the public health authority who bent its decisions and contracts to suit the two clans.
cite: Il Fatto Quotidiano, 10 May 2023 (Lucio Musolino)

n: Quinta bolgia: clan monopoly over Catanzaro health authority's ambulances
rank: Azienda Sanitaria Provinciale di Catanzaro: director general, administrative director, head of the Suem 118 ambulance service
d: In the Quinta bolgia operation of 12 November 2018 the Guardia di Finanza arrested 24 people and seized ten million euros of assets, alleging that the Iannazzo-Cannizzaro-Daponte cosca held an absolute monopoly over services bought by the Catanzaro provincial health authority: stand-in ambulances, funeral services, medical supplies and blood transport. Prosecutors said the clan's Putrino group won the stand-in 118 ambulance contract in 2009 and kept it from 2010 to 2017 through repeated extensions obtained by privileged ties with the authority's leadership. The former MP Giuseppe Galati, put under house arrest, was described by prosecutors as the link between the 'ndrangheta and some of the authority's directors; its director general until that August, its administrative director until October 2017 and its former head of the 118 service were charged with abuse of office. The sources read give no verdict.
inside: Prosecutors say a clan's firms took the health authority's ambulance and supply work through its own directors, who kept extending the contracts without tender.
cite: LaPresse, 12 November 2018

n: Italy dissolves Catanzaro's health authority over criminal conditioning
who: local criminal organisations, unnamed in the decision
rank: Azienda Sanitaria Provinciale di Catanzaro, whole management
d: The Council of Ministers, on a proposal from the interior minister, dissolved the management of the Catanzaro provincial health authority for 18 months and put it under an extraordinary commission, citing established conditioning by local criminal organisations. The Interior Ministry's report to Parliament for 2020 records the decree as a presidential decree of 13 September 2019; the same report records the Reggio Calabria provincial health authority dissolved by decree of 11 March 2019, and before that the Locri local health authority in 2006 and the No. 5 authority of Reggio Calabria in 2008. The health minister, Roberto Speranza, said the health situation in Calabria was very serious and that strict respect for the rule of law would be essential. Neither the decision as reported nor the article names a clan or an official, so this record names none.
inside: The government found criminal groups bending a public health authority's management, and removed the whole management, putting state commissioners in its place.
cite: Quotidiano Sanita, 'Calabria, Cdm scioglie Asp di Catanzaro per infiltrazioni mafiose'; Ministero dell'Interno, Relazione sull'attivita svolta dalle commissioni per la gestione straordinaria degli enti sciolti per infiltrazione e condizionamenti di tipo mafioso, Anno 2020 (Camera dei Deputati, Doc. LXXXVIII n. 4, transmitted 18 May 2021), pp. on the ASP of Catanzaro and Reggio Calabria, at documenti.camera.it/_dati/leg18/lavori/documentiparlamentari/indiceetesti/088/004_RS/INTERO_COM.pdf

n: Locri health authority commissioned after 'ndrangheta found in its staff
who: 'Ndrangheta clans of the Ionian side of Reggio Calabria province
rank: Azienda Sanitaria Locale n. 9 di Locri, whole management
d: The local health authority of Locri, on the Ionian coast of Calabria, was put under commissioners after an access commission found what the parliamentary anti-mafia committee's report describes as a real infiltration of the body: staff, doctors and non-medical employees with close family ties to local criminal figures, and irregularities in spending and public funds. The decree cited the established interference of organised crime in the authority's running. The extract published by Editoriale Domani names no clan and no individual. Of 306 names appearing in the access commission's report and in a Reggio Calabria custody order, 17 were on masonic lodge lists seized by the committee in 2017 or by prosecutors in Palmi in 1993 and 1994. The Interior Ministry's report to Parliament dates the dissolution to 2006.
inside: Inspectors found mafia families' relatives working inside a public health authority and its spending bent accordingly, so the state replaced its management.
cite: Editoriale Domani, extract from the Parliamentary Anti-Mafia Commission report, XVII Legislature (Bindi committee), published 1 April 2023; Ministero dell'Interno, Relazione sull'attivita svolta dalle commissioni per la gestione straordinaria degli enti sciolti per infiltrazione e condizionamenti di tipo mafioso, Anno 2020 (Camera dei Deputati, Doc. LXXXVIII n. 4), for the year of the dissolution ('l'A.S.L. n. 9 di Locri, gia sciolta nel 2006 per infiltrazioni della criminalita organizzata'), at documenti.camera.it/_dati/leg18/lavori/documentiparlamentari/indiceetesti/088/004_RS/INTERO_COM.pdf

n: D'Alessandro clan ran emergency transport inside Castellammare's hospital
rank: San Leonardo public hospital, Castellammare di Stabia: the hospital's ambulance service
d: A Carabinieri operation in November 2025 broke up what investigators describe as the D'Alessandro clan's hold on emergency transport at the San Leonardo public hospital in Castellammare di Stabia, near Naples. The clan's business was run through the ambulance firm New Life, which had replaced an earlier company covered by a 2021 inquiry. Investigators allege that people inside the hospital told clan-linked ambulances when patients were being discharged or had died, so that the journey could be arranged in them for a fee, and that doctors signed false certificates so that dead patients could be sent home. Antonio Rossetti is described as running the ambulance service and as the clan's exclusive contact inside the hospital. A cooperating witness, Pasquale Rapicano, said of the hospital's emergency department that there were never problems there “because the doctors are with the D'Alessandro”. These are allegations; Libero Quotidiano reports no verdict.
inside: Prosecutors say a camorra clan had staff inside a public hospital feeding it work, so its ambulance firm took the hospital's transport business.
cite: Libero Quotidiano, 15 November 2025

n: Lo Russo clan and bribed officials rigged Santobono hospital cleaning deals
rank: public officials employed by the Azienda ospedaliera Santobono-Pausilipon
d: On 14 June 2016 the Naples flying squad arrested 12 people over camorra infiltration of cleaning contracts at hospitals and other public bodies in Naples. Among those investigated were leaders of the Lo Russo clan, known as the Capitoni, which operates in the north of the city; administrators and consultants of Kuadra Spa, a cleaning company with offices in Naples, Rome and Genoa and many public and private clients; and public officials employed by the Santobono-Pausilipon hospital trust, a leading children's hospital. Police said the Santobono officials favoured Kuadra in return for bribes, with the clan's hidden interest behind it. The charges were mafia-type association, corruption, rigging of tenders, drug possession and extortion, and Kuadra's business, shares and assets were seized.
inside: A camorra clan's interest sat behind a cleaning firm, and bribed hospital officials steered the children's hospital's contracts to that firm.
cite: Polizia di Stato press release, 14 June 2016

n: Vibo Valentia's health authority dissolved in 2010 for mafia infiltration
who: 'Ndrangheta, including the Lo Bianco clan linked to the Mancuso family
rank: Azienda Sanitaria Provinciale di Vibo Valentia, whole management
d: On 17 December 2010 the Council of Ministers dissolved the Vibo Valentia provincial health authority for mafia infiltration. A commission of access installed by the prefect, Luisa Latella, in January 2010 finished work in October and sent its report to anti-mafia prosecutors in Catanzaro. The commission took up a Guardia di Finanza report, adopted by the anti-mafia committee in February 2008, which had found organised-crime figures among the staff of firms winning contracts and managers who had favoured awards to firms linked directly or indirectly to prominent local crime figures. A 2007 operation had arrested about twenty alleged members of the Lo Bianco clan, linked to the Mancuso family, some of whom worked at the hospital.
inside: The state found clans holding the health authority's contracts through managers who favoured them, and removed the authority's whole management.
cite: Blitz Quotidiano, 17 December 2010, citing ANSA

n: GDE faction money funded Morada Nova councillors, who gave it posts
rank: president, board secretary and three members of the Morada Nova city council
d: The Guardioes do Estado (GDE) is a criminal faction in the Brazilian state of Ceara. In Operacao Traditori on 12 March 2026 the Federal Police detained five councillors of Morada Nova, among them the council president Hilmar Sergio and the board secretary Gleide Rabelo. Investigators say money from drug and arms trafficking was laundered and then lent or paid to campaigns at the 2024 municipal elections, including those of the five, and that in return councillors appointed GDE members to commissioned posts in public bodies, including the council's own. The police describe three linked tiers: faction leadership, financial operators and politicians, with loan-sharking and debt collection on the faction's orders. A court ordered the five held in preventive detention. Hilmar Sergio and Gleide Rabelo deny any link to organised crime.
cite: Diario do Nordeste, 'Comando financeiro e politico: como funcionava esquema entre faccao e vereadores em Morada Nova (CE)', Mar 2026; O Povo, 14 Mar 2026
inside: Police say a faction's laundered cash paid for council campaigns and the elected councillors then put faction members on the public payroll, including inside the council.

n: Belford Roxo barricade clearance handed territory back to Comando Vermelho
rank: mayoralty of Belford Roxo
d: Belford Roxo is a city in the Baixada Fluminense, the belt of towns around Rio de Janeiro. Brazil's electoral prosecution service told the superior electoral court that there were indications that, during Marcio Canella's time running the city, which he took over in 2025, the municipal operation called Barricada Zero involved informal agreements with the Comando Vermelho faction. Under them, according to the filing, access to communities was opened temporarily so that public works could be done and videos filmed, and territorial control was then handed back to the faction. The same filing says he gave a commissioned post in his state assembly office to the wife of a militia leader until 2023 and that, on taking over Belford Roxo in 2025, he made two local militia leaders heads of municipal secretariats, one of them already convicted of forming a militia. The service asked the court to bar Canella, elected a Rio de Janeiro state deputy in 2026, from taking the seat. The opinion was filed on 23 October 2026 and the court had not ruled. These are the prosecution's allegations.
cite: Ministerio Publico Federal, PGR, 'MP Eleitoral pede que TSE barre candidatura de deputado eleito no RJ por vinculo com o crime organizado', Oct 2026
inside: Prosecutors say the city's own barricade-clearing operation was run by deal with the faction, which got its territory back once the works and filming were done.

n: Rio councillor allegedly traded kiosks for Comando Vermelho's permission
rank: member of the Rio de Janeiro city council
d: Salvino Oliveira is a Rio de Janeiro city councillor who was the city's youth secretary under mayor Eduardo Paes from 2021 to 2024. He was arrested on 11 March 2026. According to the investigation, which covers money laundering and logistical support to the Comando Vermelho drug faction, he negotiated with traffickers in the Gardenia Azul district for permission to campaign there in exchange for installing kiosks in the area the faction controls. The state governor, Claudio Castro, called him the faction's right-hand man inside Rio city hall. Paes said the operation might have been used for political ends. Salvino's office denied the accusations, said the governor was using the police to intimidate rivals and said his lawyers were taking action against him.
cite: Diario do Rio, 'Prisao de vereador aliado de Paes acirra disputa com Castro...', Mar 2026
inside: Investigators say a sitting councillor bought the faction's permission to campaign in its district by putting municipal kiosks where it wanted them.

n: Sao Joao de Meriti councillor held over barricades built for the TCP
rank: member of the Sao Joao de Meriti city council
d: The Terceiro Comando Puro, or TCP, is a drug trafficking faction in Rio de Janeiro. On 25 November 2025 police arrested Ernane Aleixo, a councillor of Sao Joao de Meriti in the Baixada Fluminense, in Operacao Muro de Favores, part of the state's wider Barricada Zero drive against road blockages. Police say audio recordings and messages suggest he offered logistical support for building barricades on the roads into communities, and that those barricades hindered the security forces and public services. He was also cited for alleged collaboration with members of the group. Eight arrest warrants and 36 search warrants were issued. The city council said it was following the case and awaiting formal notification from the courts. CNN Brasil said it was trying to reach his defence.
cite: CNN Brasil, 'Vereador e preso em operacao contra o TCP na Baixada Fluminense', 25 Nov 2025
inside: Police say a sitting councillor supplied the help a drug faction needed to wall off its streets, keeping police and public services out of them.

n: Cuautla town hall officers held as Sinaloa Cartel's protection network
rank: council secretary, oficial mayor and treasurer of Cuautla; the mayor
d: Mexico's federal prosecution service is investigating whether the Sinaloa Cartel built protection networks in at least eight municipalities of Morelos state, financing the campaigns of candidates who then took office, striking deals with public servants and intimidating rivals. In arrests under Operacion Enjambre, reported on 21 May 2026, three officers of the Cuautla town hall were detained: Horacio N, the secretary of the council, Pablo Adrian N, the oficial mayor, and Jonathan N, the treasurer. Cuautla's mayor, Jesus N, was named a target and had not been captured. A federal judge in Sonora issued the warrants for organised crime offences linked to crimes against health, and the authorities also cite probable extortion and arms trafficking. The financial intelligence unit was to freeze 22 people and ten companies.
cite: La Razon, 'El Cartel de Sinaloa se infiltro en municipios de Morelos, caen ediles', 21 May 2026
inside: Prosecutors say the cartel paid for campaigns and dealt with officials so that the town hall's own senior officers shielded its extortion and drug business.

n: Atlatlahucan mayor detained in the Morelos Sinaloa Cartel inquiry
rank: mayor of Atlatlahucan; a state councillor of the Morena party
d: Atlatlahucan is a municipality in the Mexican state of Morelos. Its mayor, named by the authorities as Agustin N and elected on a PAN-PRI-PRD and RSP ticket, was detained in May 2026 in the arrests under Operacion Enjambre that followed a federal inquiry into the Sinaloa Cartel in Morelos. Also detained were Arisbel Rubi N, a former candidate for the same mayoralty and a state councillor of the Morena party, and Irving N, a former mayor of Yecapixtla. The federal prosecution service says the cartel financed the campaigns of candidates who went on to hold office and made deals with public servants, and a 2025 video is said to show local officials, among them two detained mayors, meeting the cartel's regional leader. The warrants were for organised crime offences.
cite: La Razon, 'El Cartel de Sinaloa se infiltro en municipios de Morelos, caen ediles', 21 May 2026
inside: Prosecutors say the cartel paid for the campaigns that put these local office-holders in place in Morelos and then dealt with them once they held office.

n: Urbina Soto clan ran Yoro's town hall for the Cachiros traffickers
who: Urbina Soto clan and Los Cachiros
rank: mayor of Yoro and municipal treasury and budget officers
d: Arnaldo Urbina Soto was elected mayor of Yoro, in central Honduras, in 2009 and re-elected in 2013. InSight Crime reported that prosecutors called his family network the Urbina Soto Gang and said it worked with the larger trafficking group Los Cachiros. They say the municipality rented heavy machinery from a relative who cashed the cheques and passed the money on, up to 5 million lempiras reaching the mayor or his associates. Government investigators told InSight Crime that the mayor's office supplied a 20-officer police unit with fuel so the officers would watch over the group's operations, and that he personally chose the local head of the national forestry institute, which let the clan control logging licences. He was convicted of money laundering in February 2017 and sentenced to 36 years. Two brothers were acquitted.
cite: InSight Crime, 'Honduras Political Clan, Criminal Fiefdom', Mar 2017
inside: A trafficking family held the mayoralty of Yoro, so municipal machinery hire, police fuel and forestry appointments all worked for its cocaine and logging business.

n: Apopa mayor accused of paying gangs with municipal jobs and budget money
org_label: MS-13 and the Revolucionarios faction of Barrio 18
rank: mayor of Apopa and municipal employees
d: Apopa is a municipality in the San Salvador area. In June 2016 El Salvador's attorney general announced the arrest of its mayor, Jose Elias Hernandez, alleging that he headed a criminal structure that offered goods and employment to gang members. According to the report, the gangs received goods and jobs paid for with public funds, reportedly in exchange for votes and promises to reduce violence: municipal street-cleaning jobs and the post of head of the local slaughterhouse, mobile phones, vehicles and fuel that supported their extortion, the use of a municipal garage to service their vehicles, and reportedly several thousand dollars a month from the municipal budget. Police sources said Barrio 18's Revolucionarios faction was the main beneficiary. Fifteen municipal employees and 14 gang members were arrested. Hernandez denied wrongdoing. On 1 February 2018 the specialised sentencing judge Godofredo Salazar convicted him of illicit associations and sentenced him to 12 years, finding that the municipality had hired gang members and had handed the gang fuel, telephone lines and paid for repairs to its vehicles out of municipal funds; he was acquitted of the murder of a municipal worker who belonged to the rival Mara Salvatrucha, the judge finding the witness evidence inconsistent.
cite: InSight Crime via Q Costa Rica, 'El Salvador Mayor's Arrest Highlights Gangs' Political Clout', 2016; InSight Crime, 'El Salvador Convicts First Mayor for Ties to Gangs', 2 February 2018; Revista Estrategia y Negocios (Diario El Mundo), 'El Salvador: Condenan a exalcalde por vinculos con pandillas', 2 February 2018
inside: Prosecutors say the mayor put gang members on the municipal payroll and gave them vehicles, fuel and budget money, so the town hall financed their extortion.

n: Taraza council vice-president accused of leaking to a Clan del Golfo front
rank: vice-president of the Taraza municipal council
d: Taraza lies in the Bajo Cauca sub-region of Antioquia, in Colombia, where the Clan del Golfo trafficking group has long been present. El Colombiano, setting out a list of Antioquia office-holders drawn into the group's political dealings, reported that in 2018 Mario Eliecer Sierra Correa, the vice-president of Taraza's municipal council, was captured for conspiracy to commit crime and accused of leaking confidential information to the group's Julio Vargas front, which operates in the Bajo Cauca, and of being part of its political arm. The same list records that in 2018 Jose Berrio Berrio, the mayor of Caceres, was jailed over alleged ties to the same front. The paper presents these as allegations and does not give the later outcome of either case.
cite: El Colombiano, 'Asi va la lista de corrupcion politica del Clan de Golfo', 5 December 2022
inside: Prosecutors say the council's second officer passed confidential material to the trafficking group's local front, so the council became a source of intelligence for it.

n: Necocli and Carepa ex-mayors charged over a trafficker's contracts
rank: mayors of Necocli and Carepa and a municipal planning secretary
d: El Colombiano reported a case against four officials who held posts between 2016 and 2019, three of them in Antioquia, Colombia, and one in Quindio: Jaime Lopez Pacheco, former mayor of Necocli, Ovidio Ardila Rodas, former mayor of Carepa, Alex Lozano Lozano, Carepa's former planning secretary, and Dario Ospina Marin, a former adviser to Quindio's governorship. They are alleged to have taken campaign money, or bribes, to award contracts to companies linked to a Clan del Golfo figure known as Messi, in the Uraba region and the coffee belt. Twenty people from his network have been captured. The paper says he has been in La Picota prison in Bogota since 2021, serving an 11-year sentence, and awaits extradition to the United States. The paper presents the allegations as presumptions.
cite: El Colombiano, 'Asi va la lista de corrupcion politica del Clan de Golfo', 5 December 2022
inside: Prosecutors allege two mayoralties awarded municipal contracts to companies tied to a trafficking boss, whose money had helped pay for the mayors' campaigns.

n: CAR army west sector commander accused of working for the CPC rebels
org_label: Coalition des patriotes pour le changement (CPC)
rank: Sector West Commander, Armed Forces of the Central African Republic (FACA), Bouar
d: The Coalition des patriotes pour le changement, or CPC, was the rebel coalition that tried to seize Bangui in January 2021. The UN Panel of Experts reported that a disciplinary council had been set up to decide how to punish soldiers who abandoned their posts and then came back to work, and that 39 cases had been sent to the military justice prosecution service, including that of Colonel Yabanga, the former Sector West Commander of the Armed Forces of the Central African Republic in Bouar. He was accused of sharing intelligence with the CPC and of orchestrating a fake ambush in which he planned to defect to the coalition with a large amount of weapons, ammunition and vehicles. Investigations remained ongoing.
inside: A rebel coalition is accused of having the army's own western sector commander, feeding it intelligence and preparing to hand it weapons and vehicles.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, final report S/2021/569, para. 63 and annex 3.1 (Security crisis: desertions, defections, abandonments of post and associated loss of government stocks of weapons, ammunition and equipment)

n: Anti-balaka leader held a CAR police command before joining the CPC revolt
rank: Police commander; Minister for disarmament, demobilization, repatriation and reintegration
d: The anti-balaka are the militias formed from 2013 against the Séléka rebellion. The Director General of the Police told the UN Panel of Experts that at least three police officers had defected to the CPC rebel coalition and been struck off the police register, including one police commander and anti-balaka leader Maxime Mokom, who also lost his ministerial position after defecting; the Panel elsewhere records him as Minister for disarmament, demobilization, repatriation and reintegration. The Deputy Director of the Gendarmerie reported that approximately five or six gendarmes defected. Mokom was surrendered to the International Criminal Court on 14 March 2022; its prosecutor withdrew the charges in October 2023, saying there was no reasonable prospect of conviction at trial, and the pre-trial chamber terminated the proceedings on 17 October 2023.
inside: A militia leader sat inside the police as a serving commander and in the cabinet, and went over to the armed coalition when it rose against the government.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, S/2021/569, annex 3.1 (Security crisis: desertions, defections, abandonments of post and associated loss of government stocks of weapons, ammunition and equipment); S/2021/87, annex 2.13; S/2023/360, para. 39; International Criminal Court, Mokom case page (Situation in the Central African Republic II), icc-cpi.int/carII/mokom

n: Weapons seized by CAR's army in Birao reportedly sold to the MLCJ militia
org_label: Mouvement des liberateurs centrafricains pour la justice (MLCJ)
rank: Armed Forces of the Central African Republic camp, Birao
d: On 16 February 2020, during fighting in Birao between the FPRC and the MLCJ armed groups, an FPRC gun truck was disabled and the vehicle and its contents were taken to the army camp in Birao. The UN Panel of Experts obtained pictures of the captured materiel, which included the gun truck, a mortar tube, base plate and mortar bomb, one rocket and launcher, three machine guns and a considerable amount of ammunition. The Panel confirmed that by 22 April the materiel was no longer at the camp. Local sources reported that the weapons and ammunition had been sold to MLCJ elements and Kara youth and the vehicle given to the Sultan of Birao. Army commanders said it had gone to Bangui on rotation; the Panel found no such record.
inside: Weapons captured from one armed group and held inside an army camp reportedly reached a second armed group, which the army was supposed to be disarming.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, S/2020/662, paras. 44-46 and annex 3.7 (Photographs of vehicle, weapons and ammunition recovered following fighting in Birao on 16 February 2020)

n: CAR army units paid and armed a Vakaga militia raised by armed group chiefs
org_label: MLCJ and RPRC commanders and the Vakaga youth militia
rank: Army elements at Ndélé and Birao; militia promised integration into the army or internal security forces
d: After the CPC coalition's failed coup attempt of January 2021, politicians from Vakaga prefecture organised, funded and deployed a militia of armed local young people. The UN Panel of Experts named the Minister of Transport and Civil Aviation, Arnaud Djoubaye Abazene, as its leader; he denied involvement and described it to the Panel as a spontaneous initiative of Vakaga youth. On 7 February a plane rented by his ministry flew the MLCJ zone commander of Birao from Bangui, after he had reportedly been given eight million CFA francs, collected on the airstrip by the MLCJ chief of staff; an RPRC general moved fighters by truck. Army elements at Ndélé reportedly received ten million CFA francs in February as part of a similar recruitment drive in the neighbouring prefecture of Bamingui-Bangoran. In total 112 were recruited, and the recruits the Panel met said that their weapons were their own but that they got ammunition from army elements at Ndélé and Birao, and that they had been promised future integration. The Panel noted that, according to sources, the army's involvement in providing payment and ammunition to the Vakaga youth militia stemmed from decisions which bypassed the army's leadership, who were not aware of the actions of elements on the ground.
inside: Armed group commanders drew state money, a ministry's aircraft and army ammunition for a militia the army's own leadership had not approved, and their men were promised state posts.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, final report S/2021/569, para. 112 and annex 4.4 (Militia in Vakaga created by Bangui-based politicians)

n: More than 300 ex-UPC men disarmed at Bambari reported used as army proxies
org_label: Unité pour la paix en Centrafrique (UPC) and anti-balaka
rank: Ex-combatants used as proxies for the national defence and security forces
d: The UN Panel of Experts called the group disarmed at Bambari in June 2022, with the involvement of the Minister for Livestock, Mr Bouba, the most problematic caseload of ex-combatants, many of whom are reported to have been used as proxies in recent months. The group numbered more than 300 individuals, mostly former UPC and some anti-balaka. Their weapons, needed to determine eligibility for socioeconomic integration or for integration into the national defence and security forces, had been handed to the army rather than to the UN mission or the government's disarmament unit. When that unit came to Bambari in April 2023 to process 150 of them, the army handed over only 66 weapons, six of them used by more than one combatant, which let the unit process 80 of the ex-combatants. The whereabouts of the remaining combatants is not known.
inside: An armed group's disarmed fighters and their weapons passed into army hands outside the official programme, and many of the men are reported to have then been used as the army's proxies.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, final report S/2023/360, paras. 121-122

n: Anti-balaka men put into CAR's seventh army battalion without vetting
rank: Recruits of the seventh territorial infantry battalion (BIT-7)
d: The government announced the creation of a new army battalion, BIT-7, on 30 January 2021. On 3 February the presidential security adviser Valery Zakharov posted that the PK5 neighbourhood self-defence groups would form the basis of its elements; senior army sources denied this and told the UN Panel of Experts that the battalion had been formed from recent recruits who completed their initial training with the European Union mission in 2020. Senior sources informed the Panel that the new recruits in BIT-7, who come from Bangui, were not subjected to an appropriate vetting procedure in coordination with the UN mission, despite assurances to the contrary, while recruits from outside Bangui did undergo it. A later Panel report records selected anti-balaka elements among those integrated.
inside: Fighters from a militia were taken into a new army battalion without the human rights vetting that was meant to screen armed group men out of the army.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, S/2021/569, annex 3.7 (FACA training and recruitment); S/2023/360, para. 115

n: Honduran national judge took money to put trafficker 'Moncho' under house arrest
rank: Judge of the Juzgado de Letras de lo Penal with national jurisdiction
d: Wendy Vanessa Caballero Reyes was a judge of Honduras's Juzgado de Letras de lo Penal with national jurisdiction, a bench whose jurisdiction runs across the whole country rather than one judicial district. In December 2013 she ordered house arrest for Alexander Montes Aguilar, alias 'Moncho', reported as the alleged leader of the 18th Street gang and a drug trafficker, on a private doctor's report rather than the opinion of the Forensic Medicine service that prosecutors said was needed; the ground given was colon surgery and the lack of care in prison. Intercepted calls recorded her secretary negotiating with Montes's lawyers; prosecutors said she asked for $45,000 and received $39,000 and a truck, handed to her brother in three bags. She was arrested at San Pedro Sula airport on her return from the United States and Montes was charged with paying. In May 2016 she and her brother were each sentenced to five and a half years for bribery and Montes to five years; La Prensa reported in September 2017 that she was still in prison.
inside: An alleged trafficker and gang leader paid the judge hearing his case, so a court built to try organised crime sent him home instead of to prison.
cite: La Prensa (Honduras), 'Honduras: Recapturan a supuesto narco y envian a jueza a la carcel', 21 December 2013 (her bench, the arrest at San Pedro Sula airport, the private doctor's report and the missing Forensic Medicine opinion); La Prensa, 'Escuchas hunden a exjueza Wendy Caballero', 25 November 2015 (the sums asked and received); La Prensa, 'Exjueza Wendy Caballero es absuelta por el delito de abuso de autoridad', 1 September 2017 (the May 2016 sentences)

n: Tren de Aragua leader allegedly paid a Venezuelan prosecutor $360,000
rank: Prosecutor, Public Ministry
d: Prosecutor Renny Amundarain Duran, of Venezuela's Public Ministry, and public defender Adys Salcedo were accused of accepting $360,000 from a leader of Tren de Aragua, the prison-born gang that now operates across several countries. Authorities said the money was for favourable treatment of imprisoned members of the leader's family and the return of seized assets. The payer was not confirmed officially, but was widely reported to be Hector Rusthenford Guerrero Flores, alias 'Nino Guerrero'. The case came to light when the leader, said to have got nothing for his money, posted recordings of the calls to the Attorney General's Office. Attorney General Tarek William Saab ordered the pair arrested at the end of January 2024 on charges including obstruction of the administration of justice and criminal association.
inside: A gang leader's money reached a serving prosecutor, who was accused of trading easier treatment for his jailed relatives and the return of seized assets.
cite: InSight Crime, 19 February 2024

n: Witness said he paid two Salvadoran judges to drop a cocaine case
rank: Judges of the San Salvador and San Juan Opico courts; case prosecutor
d: A protected witness called 'Omega' testified that in 2011 he had bribed two Salvadoran judges to obtain his own release. He said he paid $5,000 to San Salvador judge Ana Lorena Rodriguez, $10,000 to San Juan Opico judge David Amael Moran Ascencio and $5,000 to the case prosecutor. His charges were lowered in San Salvador from drug trafficking to possession, and were then dropped altogether at San Juan Opico. Omega had been arrested in 2011 trying to sell a kilo of cocaine said to belong to Jorge Ulloa Sibrian, alias 'Repollo', accused of trafficking close to ten tonnes of cocaine. In February 2013 an appeals court overturned the dismissal and sentenced Omega to three years for possession; he then began cooperating in the Repollo case and his prison term was changed to community service and a fine. The two judges denied the claims, though the prosecutor Moran said he had been offered money.
inside: A courier for a cocaine network said he paid the judges hearing his own case, and the charges against him were cut and then dropped.
cite: InSight Crime, 8 May 2013, citing La Prensa Grafica

n: Paraguay's anti-drug prosecutor in Salto del Guaira fed a marijuana ring
rank: Assistant prosecutor, anti-drug unit, Attorney General's Office
d: Wilson Gauto Campuzano, an assistant prosecutor in the anti-drug unit of Paraguay's Attorney General's Office at Salto del Guaira, was arrested for allegedly accepting bribes to pass intelligence to a marijuana trafficking network. Prosecutors described a protection system around the group that also took in serving and former soldiers, customs officials and police, several of whom were dismissed. Officials were said to have taken money for turning a blind eye to shipments and for alerting the network to investigations and raids. Nine alleged members were arrested on 1 August 2018 after a year-long investigation, among them the alleged leader Flaviano Gimenez and his son; nearly 16 tonnes of marijuana was seized, with handwritten records of bribe payments.
inside: A marijuana network allegedly paid the prosecutor who was supposed to investigate it, and got warning of the raids aimed at its shipments.
cite: InSight Crime, 10 August 2018

n: Jailed Costa Rican trafficker and his lawyer convicted of offering a judge money
rank: Judge due to testify in a criminal trial
d: Darwin Gonzalez Hernandez, known as 'Pancho Villa' and already serving a sentence for drug trafficking, was convicted of plotting from prison to pay a judge, Hazel Murillo Beita, for testimony favouring his side at a criminal hearing. The aim, prosecutors said, was to support a claim of defective procedure that would bring the case down. The lawyer Gracel Maria Arguedas Gonzalez, a university friend of the judge, was contacted through an intermediary to make the approach; Raul Paniagua Paniagua was the intermediary. The coordination took place between January and February 2024; Arguedas was arrested on 21 March 2024 and Paniagua on 6 August 2024. The criminal court at Goicoechea sentenced Gonzalez to six years on top of his existing term and Arguedas to five. The report gives no amount and does not say the judge accepted anything.
inside: A convicted trafficker tried to buy a judge's evidence so his own case would collapse; the attempt was prosecuted and the judge is not said to have taken it.
cite: CRHoy (Costa Rica), Jose Adelio Murillo, 19 November 2025

n: Court: Guerini's waste firms infiltrated Bouches-du-Rhone's institutions
rank: President of the Bouches-du-Rhone departmental council; director of urban cleanliness at the MPM intercommunality
d: Alexandre Guerini, a waste-industry businessman, was convicted over the influence he built inside the public bodies that bought waste services in and around Marseille. His brother Jean-Noel Guerini was president of the Bouches-du-Rhone departmental council, the elected authority for the area, and a senator. In March 2022 the Aix-en-Provence appeal court confirmed Alexandre's six-year prison sentence, punishing what it called his strategy of influence and infiltration of public institutions, for the benefit of his companies. The Cour de cassation closed the case on 13 March 2024, making Jean-Noel Guerini's conviction for unlawfully taking an interest final and costing him his Senate seat. Michel Karabadjakian, who ran street cleaning at the MPM intercommunality, was also convicted; the investigation showed he had been informing Alexandre.
cite: Marsactu, 31 March 2022 (Aix-en-Provence appeal court ruling); Marsactu, 14 March 2024 (Cour de cassation); Marsactu, 15 September 2022 (metropole disciplinary case against Michel Karabadjakian)
inside: A waste businessman got influence and an informant inside the Marseille-area public bodies that bought waste services, and their workings served his firms.

n: Firms paid the Bouches-du-Rhone council's works director for contracts
rank: Former service director, Bouches-du-Rhone departmental council
d: Renaud Chervet, a former service director at the Bouches-du-Rhone departmental council in Marseille, was sentenced to five years in prison on 2 December 2022 for corruption. From 2011 to 2016 he gave a group of company bosses privileged access to the council's works contracts in exchange for gratuities, gifts, restaurant meals, foreign trips and numerous payments, in cash or by transfer, routed through the account of his accomplice Jerome Disdier, a project-management assistant at the authority. Several of the businessmen, and Disdier, were found guilty of active corruption, the offence of paying an official. Judgment was delivered by Celine Ballerini, president of the sixth chamber, who read it with the defendants gathered at the back of the courtroom.
cite: Marsactu, 2 December 2022 ('Affaire Chervet : prison ferme pour le petit cercle de la corruption au departement')
inside: Company bosses paid a department's service director, with his deputy handling the money, and the council's works contracts went to the payers.

n: Prosecutors raid El Eslabon town hall over a S/7.5m road contract
org_label: contractor Yvan Guevara and a bidding consortium
rank: Mayor and three officials of the El Eslabon district municipality
d: Peru's specialised anti-corruption prosecutors for San Martin searched the El Eslabon district council, in Huallaga province, in February 2026, as part of an investigation into aggravated collusion, the offence of an official secretly agreeing with a bidder. The mayor, Luis Mundaca, is being investigated together with three municipal officials, relatives and a contractor, after signs were found of an unlawful pact to favour a consortium in the tender for a road scheme valued at S/7,497,583.32. Preliminary enquiries indicate, the prosecution service says, that the mayor allegedly favoured the businessman Yvan Guevara with the works contract in exchange for a high-end pickup truck and a projected financial benefit of three million soles. Prosecutors seized phones and computers and lifted the secrecy of the communications of the mayor and the others investigated.
cite: Ministerio Publico (Peru), Boletin Oficial no. 6, 2026, pp. 2-3
inside: Prosecutors allege a contractor's pickup truck and promised millions bought the mayor's decision, so a district council's road tender went his consortium's way.

n: Prosecutors say Estre's proxy ran Bauru's R$5.2bn waste concession
rank: Municipal environment secretary and deputy secretary, and legal affairs secretary, Bauru city hall
d: On 9 September 2026 Gaeco, the Sao Paulo state prosecution service's organised crime unit, ran Operation Cavalo de Troia in Bauru, Sorocaba and Sao Paulo over a suspected rigged tender for Bauru's integrated solid waste concession, estimated at R$5.2bn and lasting 30 years. Prosecutors say the tender was steered from the drafting of the technical studies onward, and are also examining possible payments of undue advantages. A judge of the regional guarantees court ordered the preventive detention of six people, among them the city's former environment secretary Cilene Chabuh Bordezan and the Estre Ambiental executive Hamilton Liborio Agle. Gaeco says Bordezan acted as Estre's private proxy inside the administration. The state audit court suspended the tender notice. Estre said it reaffirms its commitment to ethics. On 28 September 2026 the prosecutors charged the six with corruption and unlawful contracting, saying in a 317-page indictment that they had made Bauru city hall a stage for a criminal organisation.
cite: Tribunal de Justica de Sao Paulo, news release, 9 September 2026; JuriNews, 21 September 2026 (Vara Regional das Garantias detention ruling); Diario do Grande ABC, 28 September 2026 (www.dgabc.com.br/Noticia/4349549)
inside: Prosecutors say a waste company's proxy held the city's environment post and steered Bauru's 30-year rubbish concession towards the company.

n: Habitasul's owner bought Florianopolis permits for protected-area building
rank: Staff of Florianopolis's environment foundation (Floram) and its urbanism and public services secretariat (Susp)
d: On 21 June 2017 Marcelo Kras Borges, judge of the sixth federal environmental court in Florianopolis, convicted 16 people of corruption over a scheme to clear building work in a permanent preservation area at Jurere Internacional, an affluent district of the city. The scheme, revealed in 2007, was led by the businessman Pericles de Freitas Druck of the company Habitasul, who kept contacts with staff of bodies including the municipal environment foundation Floram and the urbanism and public services secretariat Susp. Those staff granted the unlawful building authorisations and in return obtained stays in Habitasul hotels and bribes. Druck was sentenced to 28 years in closed regime, and the judge ordered the beach clubs demolished. A lawyer for defendants linked to Habitasul said he would appeal.
cite: ((o))eco, 22 June 2017 ('Justica condena acusados de compra e venda de licencas ambientais')
inside: A property company's bribes and free hotel nights reached city environment and planning staff, who then issued the permits its buildings needed in a protected area.

n: Farmers' money allegedly sped licences at Bahia's environment institute
org_label: west Bahia farm businesses and licensing consultants
rank: Former director-general and staff of Inema, Bahia's institute for the environment and water resources
d: Bahia's state prosecution service charged eight people in August 2025 over an alleged criminal scheme inside Inema, the state institute for the environment and water resources, which carries out policy and inspection work to protect biodiversity, water and the climate. The investigation covers consultants and farmers, a former parliamentary secretary, the former coordinator of the institute's outpost at Guanambi and Inema's former director-general, Marcia Cristina Telles de Araujo Lima, the last on suspicion of illicit enrichment. The case states that from 2018 to 2024 the group allegedly moved at least R$16.5 million in bribes to speed up and loosen environmental licensing for large rural enterprises in the west of the state. The prosecutors say the money reduced the rigour of technical analysis and eased deforestation authorisations. Inema told news outlets that the frauds charged happened before the current management, and said it had joined the state's public integrity programme and taken measures on ethics, corruption prevention and institutional transparency.
cite: ((o))eco, 15 August 2025 ('Denunciado suposto esquema milionario de corrupcao e desmate no governo da Bahia'), reporting the Ministerio Publico da Bahia charges
inside: Farm businesses and their consultants allegedly paid officials of Bahia's environment institute, whose licences then came faster and cleared more land.

n: Loggers paid the Ibama staff who were meant to inspect them in Para
rank: Staff of Ibama, Brazil's federal environment agency, in Para
d: Three staff of Ibama, Brazil's federal environment agency, were arrested in the state of Para on 31 October 2017, accused of taking bribes from the loggers they were supposed to inspect. Operation Concisor was run by the federal police with Ibama's own support and covered the towns of Maraba, Parauapebas, Breu Branco, Canaa dos Carajas and Eldorado dos Carajas; four people were arrested in all. According to the federal police, the accused staff passed on privileged information about inspection operations in exchange for bribes. Fifteen court orders were carried out, including four arrest warrants, five search warrants and orders removing staff from public duty. Those investigated were to answer for passive and active corruption and extortion by an official. Ibama said all the accused staff would face internal disciplinary proceedings.
cite: ((o))eco, 31 October 2017 ('Por conluio com madeireiras, tres servidores do Ibama sao presos'), reporting the Policia Federal and Ibama
inside: Loggers paid staff of the federal agency that polices logging, and those staff passed them advance warning of inspections, the federal police said.

n: Prosecutors: PT Ceria Nugraha paid energy ministry staff for export papers
rank: Director of Mineral Business Development at the Directorate General of Mineral and Coal and the former secretary-general, Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources; head of the minerals and coal division of the South East Sulawesi provincial energy office
d: Indonesia's Attorney General's Office named four people and one company as suspects in September 2026 over alleged corruption in nickel governance in South East Sulawesi between 2017 and 2020, put at Rp401 billion in state losses. The company suspect is PT Ceria Nugraha Indotama, which holds a production mining licence in Kolaka district and exported nickel without completing its domestic market obligation. Prosecutors say the firm unlawfully had the Sucofindo unit in Kendari issue nickel grade test documents not matching reality, then sought an export recommendation from the energy and mineral resources ministry, which a serving director and the former secretary-general passed although the firm lacked the required work plan approval. The office says the documents came with payments from the company to the officials involved.
cite: Justisio, 25 September 2026, reporting the Kejaksaan Agung announcement by Anang Supriatna, head of its legal information centre
inside: Prosecutors say a nickel miner paid officials of the energy ministry and a provincial office, which then issued the export and work-plan approvals it did not qualify for.

n: World Bank debars firm over payments to Iraq's electricity ministry unit
org_label: contractor debarred by the World Bank (not named in the decision)
who: a debarred contractor and its joint venture partner
rank: Officials of the project implementation unit run by the Ministry of Electricity
d: On 9 March 2026 the World Bank Group's Sanctions Board declared a contractor ineligible for Bank-financed work for at least one year and three months, for related corrupt and fraudulent practices on the Iraq Emergency Operation for Development Project. Iraq's Ministry of Electricity was the designated project implementation unit for the relevant parts. The Board found it more likely than not that offers or payments were directed at officials of that unit, and that the firm's chief executive understood public officials were the intended targets of what the companies called commissions. The joint venture partner recorded 2 per cent of the contract value as envisaged expenses, later discussed as 3 per cent. The venture signed a US$9,785,978 contract for ten mobile substations in November 2016. The firm denied any bribery.
cite: World Bank Group Sanctions Board Decision No. 146 (Sanctions Case No. 779), 9 March 2026, paras. 6-8, 29-39
inside: A contractor's payments were aimed at officials of the unit inside Iraq's electricity ministry that ran the tender, and its joint venture took the contract.

n: Supplier paid the Liberian finance ministry's data centre manager
org_label: energy systems distribution company debarred by the World Bank (not named in the decision)
rank: Data centre manager, and at times acting director, Ministry of Finance and Development Planning
d: On 22 September 2022 the World Bank Group's Sanctions Board sanctioned a supplier and an official over contracts under two public financial management projects run by one unit inside Liberia's Ministry of Finance and Development Planning. The official was the ministry's data centre manager from 2013 to 2019 under Bank-financed consultant contracts. The Board found that he took US$2,000 in or around October 2015 and US$1,000 in May 2016 from an energy systems distribution company and, in exchange, influenced the procurement or execution of five contracts, including by ensuring deliveries were accepted, getting invoices processed and inducing the single-sourcing of orders in the company's favour. He argued he had no final say over procurement; the Board was not persuaded. He was debarred for at least two years and ten months.
cite: World Bank Group Sanctions Board Decision No. 138 (Sanctions Case No. 693), 22 September 2022, paras. 5-12; Sanctions Board Decision No. 139 (Sanctions Case No. 724), 22 September 2022, paras. 7-11, 45-49
inside: A supplier paid the finance ministry manager who oversaw its contracts, and the ministry then accepted its deliveries and gave it orders without competition.

n: SPAK: Albania's minister fixed a tunnel tender for two Turkish builders
rank: Minister of Infrastructure and Energy, later deputy prime minister; director of the Albanian Road Authority; ministry secretary-general
d: Albania's Special Prosecution Office, SPAK, announced on 16 November 2026 that it had closed its investigation and was sending the former deputy prime minister Belinda Balluku for trial, adding corruption, concealment of assets and money laundering to an existing charge of breaching equality in tenders. Twenty-five other people and two companies are also to be tried over ten procurement procedures. SPAK says Balluku, who headed the Ministry of Infrastructure and Energy, continuously directed the Llogara tunnel procurement although she had formally delegated it to the ministry's secretary-general, with the aim of predetermining as winner the joint venture of the Turkish companies Intekar Yapi and Asl Insaat, and that she obtained two villas on the Himara coast whose ownership was hidden through a former footballer. Balluku denies the charges.
cite: Reporter.al (BIRN Albania), 16 November 2026, reporting the SPAK press conference by Klodian Braho, Dorina Bejko and Dritan Prenci
inside: Prosecutors say two Turkish builders' tender was decided inside the infrastructure ministry by the minister herself, who allegedly received two coastal villas.

n: Nepal charges a supplier with health officials over mammography machines
rank: Additional secretary, Ministry of Health and Population; directors of the Department of Health Services and of its management and supply divisions
d: Nepal's Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority filed a corruption case in the Special Court on 19 October 2025 against 15 people over the purchase of mammography machines for the Department of Health Services. They include Sangita Kaushal Mishra, who had just left the post of additional secretary at the Ministry of Health and Population and had earlier been the department's director general, the directors of the management and supply divisions, accountants, a legal officer, engineers and the chief of the supplier Maxim Incorporation Traders. The commission says the defendants colluded with contractors while costs were being estimated and released payment although the supplier had not delivered everything the contract required, using a falsified post-shipment inspection report, fake delivery papers and fabricated invoices. The Special Court has since acquitted Mishra and seven other defendants, saying the charges against them were not substantiated by evidence, and convicted five others, among them the department's then director of the management division, giving them four months each and ordering them to pay Rs3,834,723 between them in compensation.
cite: Kathmandu Post, 19 October 2025 (CIAA charge sheet, Special Court); HimalPress, 19 October 2025 (CIAA statement on the mammography procurement); HimalPress, 'Dr Sangita Mishra, seven others acquitted in corruption case' (en.himalpress.com/dr-sangita-mishra-seven-others-acquitted-in-corruption-case)
inside: A medical equipment supplier allegedly worked with health ministry and department officials on the costings and paperwork, and was paid for machines not fully delivered.

n: Houthi education minister had Yemen's school textbooks replaced
rank: Houthi-appointed Minister of Education
d: The Houthi movement, the armed group holding northern Yemen, appoints the education ministry in Sana'a. The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen reported that the Houthis had recently introduced changes in school textbooks, starting with primary levels, in areas under their control, and that the changes reflect their ideology and political views, influenced by Shia religious beliefs. In November 2022 the Houthi-appointed Minister of Education, Yahia Bader Al-Din Al-Houthi, presided over a first national conference on developing curricula, and told Al-Masirah television that what was required was not an amendment but a complete renewal of the textbooks. The Panel added that teachers' strikes had resulted in education staff being replaced with Houthi-appointed personnel, and considered the content of the revised textbooks it saw of great concern.
inside: The armed movement appoints Yemen's education ministry, which rewrote the state school textbooks around the movement's own ideology and replaced striking teachers with its own people.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2023/833, annex 85 ('Houthi revision of textbooks in primary and secondary schools, including summer camps'), pp. 241-242

n: Houthi-appointed education office made Sana'a schools pay for drones
rank: Houthi-appointed education office, Sana'a
d: The Houthi movement appoints the education administration in Sana'a, the capital it holds. The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen said it had learned from its sources that the Houthi-appointed education office in Sana'a regularly compels schools in Houthi-controlled areas to make payments for uncrewed aerial vehicles, the drones the group flies. The Panel received a copy of a receipt evidencing the collection of 20,956,250 Yemeni rials by the Houthis, and reproduced it, with an unofficial translation, in an annex headed 'Receipt of payment from schools for Drones (UAVs)'. It said the matter was under investigation. The same section of the report sets out other Houthi fundraising from the public, including a mass text-message campaign for the group's uncrewed aerial vehicle 'air force', with donations collected in accounts the Houthis designated at the Central Bank of Yemen in Sana'a.
inside: The movement's own appointees run the Sana'a education office, and it required state schools to hand over money that went to the movement's drones.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2024/731, 11 October 2024, paras. 105-106, case study 10 and annex 174 (pp. 449-450)

n: Sadr-held Iraqi ministries' guard forces paid and employed the Mahdi Army
rank: Ministries of Health, Agriculture and Transportation; Facilities Protection Service
d: Every Iraqi ministry had its own armed unit, the Facilities Protection Service, ostensibly to guard the ministry's infrastructure; together these units came to roughly 145,000 uniformed Iraqis under arms. The Iraq Study Group, the panel co-chaired by James A. Baker III and Lee H. Hamilton, reported in December 2006 that in the ministries of Health, Agriculture and Transportation, which it described as controlled by Moqtada al-Sadr, the Facilities Protection Service was a source of funding and jobs for the Mahdi Army, Sadr's militia, which the report said might number as many as 60,000 fighters. A senior United States official called the service incompetent, dysfunctional or subversive, and the report said several Iraqis simply referred to the units as militias.
inside: A militia leader's movement controlled three Iraqi ministries, and the armed guard units those ministries paid for became wages and jobs for his fighters.
cite: The Iraq Study Group Report, December 2006, Assessment section, pp. 9-10 (Facilities Protection Services), p. 5 (Mahdi Army) and p. 14 (Sadr)

n: Gang backer placed her pick atop Haiti's social assistance fund
who: Haitian gang leaders and their backers
rank: Director General, Social Assistance Fund
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Haiti found that Rosemila Petit Frere, a businesswoman and former mayor of Arcahaie, used her political connections with former government officials to have people of her choice appointed to strategic positions in government, with the aim of those appointees embezzling funds on her behalf. A confidential report and accounts from investigators showed that she regularly exchanged information with Prophane Victor, sanctioned for supporting and arming gangs, and with Magalie Habitant, described as a key intermediary between gangs and their economic backers and financiers. Its example is a former Director General of the Social Assistance Fund, whom she put forward for the appointment in 2021. That person was later charged with embezzling funds from the Fund, and the Panel says the trail led to Petit Frere as the main recipient. She passed part of the money to Jean Gardy, leader of the Krache Dife gang, part of the Viv Ansanm alliance. Petit Frere denied the Panel's findings when given the chance to reply; the Panel stands by them.
inside: A gang backer had her own candidate appointed to run a state welfare fund, and prosecutors say its money was embezzled to her, with part going to a gang leader.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, final report S/2026/714, 3 September 2026, paras. 146-150 (pp. 30-31)
undone: Petit Frere denied the Panel's findings. The Panel reviewed the information she shared, shared it with the Committee and stands by its findings. No court finding on her role is recorded; the Panel says the appointee was later charged with embezzling the Fund's money.

n: Bondholders' receivership collected all Dominican customs duties
org_label: Dominican Republic bondholders and the United States customs receivership
rank: General Receiver of Dominican Customs and assistant receivers
d: Creditors had claims of over $30 million against the Dominican Republic, settled down to about $17 million and refinanced with $20 million of new 5 per cent bonds. Under a convention signed at Santo Domingo on 8 February 1907 and proclaimed by President Theodore Roosevelt on 25 July 1907, the President of the United States appointed a general receiver of Dominican customs who, with assistant receivers and other employees appointed by the President, collected all the customs duties accruing at the several customs houses of the republic until the bonds were paid off. The receiver paid the receivership's expenses, then bond interest, then amortisation, and only the remainder to the Dominican government. The republic could not increase its public debt or change import duties without United States agreement.
inside: The creditors' arrangement placed a foreign-appointed receiver and his staff inside every Dominican customs house, and the duties they collected paid the bondholders before the government.
cite: Convention between the United States and the Dominican Republic providing for the assistance of the United States in the collection and application of the customs revenues of the Dominican Republic, signed 8 February 1907, proclaimed 25 July 1907; Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States 1907, Part I, document 263

n: Manaus city hall adviser held in Comando Vermelho infiltration inquiry
who: Comando Vermelho's operational arm in Manaus
rank: technical adviser seconded to the municipal Casa Civil, Manaus
d: Amazonas civil police arrested at least 13 people on 20 February 2026 in Operation Erga Omnes, a Comando Vermelho drug-trafficking scheme that police say involved holders of public posts in the executive, legislature and judiciary. Investigators say the suspects moved around R$70 million since 2018 through front companies. One target was Anabela Cardoso Freitas, a police investigator seconded to Manaus's municipal Casa Civil as a technical adviser and a former chief of staff to the mayor, David Almeida, who is not a target. Police said the public servants gave logistical support, eased access to the public administration or passed confidential information. Prosecutors charged 16 people in May 2026, calling the group the faction's operational arm in Manaus; Freitas was not among them and was released on habeas corpus.
inside: Police say a Comando Vermelho arm had public servants inside, one of them seconded into Manaus city hall, easing the group's access to the state.
cite: Agência Brasil / O Povo, 20 Feb 2026 (https://www.opovo.com.br/noticias/brasil/2026/02/20/am-policia-detem-agentes-publicos-suspeitos-de-colaborar-com-faccao.html); A Crítica, 15 May 2026 (https://www.acritica.com/manaus/mp-denuncia-16-investigados-por-esquema-ligado-ao-comando-vermelho-no-am/)

n: Sao Paulo council ex-president made a defendant over a PCC bus scheme
rank: former president of the Câmara Municipal de São Paulo
d: A São Paulo court accepted the prosecution's charges and made Milton Leite and 13 others defendants over suspected links to the Primeiro Comando da Capital, the faction known as the PCC. Leite is a former councillor and former president of the city council of São Paulo. He was jailed in September 2026 after a police and prosecution operation examining the PCC's role in the capital's public transport, and when the decision was made public on 12 November 2026 his detention became preventive. The charge says the group worked "to infiltrate and perpetuate the faction in the exploitation of public transport, in procurement proceedings and in public power", and that Leite promoted its interests through his political influence and as de facto owner of the bus concessionaire Transwolff.
inside: Prosecutors say the PCC worked through a former city council president and a bus concession to keep its hold on São Paulo's transport and tenders.
cite: O Imparcial (São Luís), 13 Nov 2026

n: Cabedelo mayor removed two days after election over faction labour deals
who: Tropa do Amigão, a Comando Vermelho arm in Paraíba
rank: mayor and former president of the Cabedelo city council
d: Edvaldo Neto was removed as mayor of Cabedelo, near João Pessoa, two days after winning a supplementary election, as one of 13 targets of the Federal Police's Operation Cítrico in April 2026, which examines alleged tender fraud, diversion of public money, laundering and possible financing of a criminal faction. Police said the scheme included the fraudulent contracting of labour-supply firms tied to Tropa do Amigão, a Comando Vermelho arm in Paraíba, with contracts that could reach R$270 million, and described a "consortium between political agents of the municipality's top leadership, businessmen and members of a criminal organisation". Neto had been president of the city council. The interim mayor later announced the cancellation of the city's contract with Lemon Terceirização e Serviços, through which more than 700 people worked.
inside: Police say a Comando Vermelho arm supplied Cabedelo's outsourced municipal workforce through contracted firms, so city contracts served the faction.
cite: Jornal de Brasília, 'Cabedelo (PB) tem segundo prefeito afastado por suspeita de ligação com o Comando Vermelho'; PB Agora, 12 May 2026 (https://www.pbagora.com.br/noticia/politica/jose-pereira-anuncia-fim-de-contrato-com-terceirizada-investigada-na-operacao-citrico-em-cabedelo-ja-iniciamos-um-processo-de-cancelamento/)

n: Paterno council dissolved; mayor on trial over clan votes traded for jobs
rank: mayor, a former assessore and the council of Paternò
d: On 20 November 2025 Italy's Council of Ministers dissolved the council of Paternò, near Catania, and handed the comune to a special commission for 18 months because of mafia infiltration, after the carabinieri's Athena operation of April 2024 and a report by the anti-mafia access commission appointed by the prefect. In the resulting case the mayor Nino Naso, the former assessore Turi Comis and the administrator Pietro Cirino are defendants for mafia-political vote exchange, with Vincenzo Morabito, said to be a regent linked to the Laudani clan. The prosecution says votes at the 2022 municipal election were traded for fixed-term jobs at Dusty, the firm that collects Paternò's waste, for two people close to the clan. Naso said the administration had always observed the law.
inside: Prosecutors say a Catania clan delivered votes to Paternò's administration and was repaid with jobs at the firm that collects the town's waste.
cite: BlogSicilia, 20 Nov 2025

n: Francofonte comune put under commissioners over mafia conditioning
rank: mayor, council and technical and financial services of Francofonte
d: On 10 June 2026 Italy's Council of Ministers, on the interior ministry's proposal, placed the comune of Francofonte, in Syracuse province, under a special commission for 18 months for mafia infiltration. BlogSicilia reported that the measure closed an inspection which had confirmed the conditioning of organised crime over the management of public affairs. A prefectural commission had been installed on 21 August 2025 after suspicion attached to a member of the municipal administration said to be close to a company traceable to his own family and suspected of links to Cosa Nostra; investigators consider the area to be under the influence of the Nardo clan. The commission examined the council's acts and procedures, concentrating on technical and financial services.
inside: Italy's government found organised crime shaping how Francofonte's comune was run and replaced the elected administration with state commissioners.
cite: BlogSicilia, 10 Jun 2026

n: Corigliano Rossano councillor accused of trading a job for cosca votes
rank: member of the Corigliano-Rossano city council
d: On 28 October 2026 the Catanzaro anti-mafia prosecutors' Ginestra inquiry led to 41 precautionary measures in the Sibaritide area of Calabria. Among those held were Pietro Lucisano, elected to the Corigliano-Rossano city council in June 2024, and Antonio Mingrone, whom investigators consider close to the Rossano cosca; both were put under house arrest with an electronic tag, and the investigating judge found serious indications of mafia-political vote exchange. Officers recorded the pair at Lucisano's campaign office on 20 May 2024 discussing votes, polling-station monitors and a job, and the judge's order says Lucisano handed Mingrone a sum of money that is not quantified. On 2 October 2024 Mingrone was hired on a permanent contract as a building labourer, which the judge treats as support for the alleged exchange.
inside: Prosecutors say a cosca-linked vote broker helped win a council seat and the new councillor then pursued the permanent job he had been promised.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 28 Oct 2026

n: Massaro clan took Santa Maria a Vico's votes, then its kiosk and works
rank: mayor, deputy mayor, a majority councillor and a former assessore of Santa Maria a Vico
d: In October 2025 the Guardia di Finanza of Caserta, on a Naples investigating judge's order, placed under house arrest the mayor of Santa Maria a Vico, Andrea Pirozzi, the deputy mayor Veronica Biondo, the majority councillor Giuseppe Nuzzo and the former assessore Marcantonio Ferrara, and sent to prison two senior figures of the Massaro camorra clan. The charges include mafia-political vote exchange. Investigators say the clan planned the distribution of votes at the 2020 municipal election and in return demanded works, contracts and jobs: a cremation plant beside the municipal cemetery, to be run by a company in which an affiliate was a hidden partner; and the municipal concession for a kiosk-bar at San Marco, obtained without paying any fee although the kiosk was due for demolition.
inside: Prosecutors say the Massaro clan delivered the votes that elected Santa Maria a Vico's administration and was repaid in municipal concessions, works and hirings.
cite: Anteprima24, 22 Oct 2025

n: Clan Russo swayed two Naples-area council votes and taxed planning files
rank: municipal councils of Cicciano and Casamarciano; municipal technical staff at Nola
d: On 17 November 2025 carabinieri carried out 44 precautionary measures, 34 in prison and ten under house arrest, ordered by a Naples investigating judge in an inquiry by the city's anti-mafia prosecutors covering 2022 to 2024. Investigators say the Russo clan controlled, directly and indirectly, all economic activity in the three Naples-area comuni of Nola, Cicciano and Casamarciano, above all in property, demanding payment on sales, on design work and on the progress of the related applications at the comune, and they documented extortions against municipal technical officers, designers and builders. The charges include mafia-type association, extortion and mafia-political vote exchange. Prosecutors say the clan also conditioned the municipal elections at Cicciano in May 2023 and at Casamarciano in June 2022, using intermediaries.
inside: Prosecutors say a camorra clan shaped two councils' elections and charged a fee on planning applications inside the comune, extorting municipal staff.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 17 Nov 2025

n: Appeal court confirms Calabrian councillor paid San Luca cosca for votes
who: the San Luca cosca and the Pelle-Gambazza family
rank: member of the Calabrian regional council, previously mayor of Bagnara Calabra
d: On 2 July 2026 the Court of Appeal of Reggio Calabria confirmed in full the convictions in the political strand of the Reale 6 inquiry, after the Court of Cassation quashed that part in 2021 and sent it back: four years and three months for the former regional councillor Santi Zappalà and four years each for Giuseppe Antonio Mesiani Mazzacuva and Antonio Pelle, for mafia-political vote exchange. The prosecution case is that Zappalà, then mayor of Bagnara Calabra, sought and obtained the electoral backing of the San Luca cosca before the 2010 regional elections in exchange for about 400,000 euros, of which investigators say 100,000 reached the Pelle-Gambazza family through ten circular cheques. Zappalà was elected to the regional council and arrested in December 2010.
inside: A Calabrian mafia family sold the electoral backing that put a regional councillor in office and was paid hundreds of thousands of euros for delivering it.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 2 Jul 2026

n: Mallardo clan votes for Giugliano's mayor, repaid with jobs and permits
rank: former mayor and sitting city councillor of Giugliano in Campania, a former assessore and a department head
d: In February 2025 carabinieri arrested 25 people over episodes of mafia-political vote exchange at the 2020 municipal elections in Giugliano in Campania. Among them was the former mayor Antonio Poziello, by then a city councillor, for whom the investigating judge ordered prison. Prosecutors accuse him of several corruption episodes and of accepting the Mallardo clan's help to obtain votes at the vote of 20 and 21 September 2020, paying 10,000 euros to a senior clan figure and promising further favours and contracts to firms traceable to the organisation if elected. One alleged episode concerns a refused building permit for a fast-food complex, with money, votes and an Audi Q3 offered so that the refusal would not become final; that operation was never completed.
inside: Prosecutors say a camorra clan supplied votes to Giugliano's mayor and was promised municipal contracts, jobs and a building permit in return.
cite: Anteprima24, 3 Feb 2025
