Galarza served at the Barboncito police station in the San Martín de Porres district of Lima, and his role was to persuade people who came in to report threats to pay the extortionists instead, who belonged to the criminal organisation known as the Tren de Aragua. The original sentence was handed down in January 2025 against Galarza and two others; his appeal was rejected. He is held at Lurigancho prison.
inside: A gang's extortion reached the counter where victims report it: a police officer talked complainants into paying the gang instead.
cite: Caretas, 7 October 2025, citing the Seventh Superior Criminal Prosecutor's Office of Lima

n: Police officer and Interpol official charged over Carrasco cocaine flight
org_label: an unnamed cocaine trafficking network using Carrasco airport
rank: Police officer and an official of Uruguay's Interpol bureau
d: Repeated allegations of weak security and customs checks at Uruguay's main international airport, Carrasco in Montevideo, followed a series of cocaine seizures in 2019. The biggest came in May 2019, when more than 600 kilograms of cocaine were found at Mulhouse in France on a private jet that had taken off from Carrasco. Uruguay's anti-drug directorate opened an investigation into how the airport's checks had failed to detect it. Europol suspected that a network of Uruguayan officials may have been bribed to help the drugs through, and one police officer and one Interpol official have been charged on suspicion of taking bribes to let the drugs past security. Uruguay's customs director Enrique Canon defended the system on 1 August and resigned the next day.
inside: Traffickers allegedly paid a police officer and an Interpol official to let a cocaine load pass the checks they were posted to run.
cite: InSight Crime, 13 April 2020, citing El País, Subrayado and El Observador

n: Brazilian trafficker Felicio had 21 Paraguayan police on the Amambay border
rank: Police officers at posts in Amambay department, including high-ranking officers
d: Twenty-one Paraguayan police officers arrested on 28 October 2019 are alleged to have taken bribes to let the suspected trafficker Levi Adriani Felicio move drugs into neighbouring Brazil, and to have passed him classified information. All had been stationed in Amambay department on the Brazilian border, at police posts close to marijuana plantations. The Attorney General's Office set out how he used police contacts to learn when and where raids would happen, and relied on high-ranking officers to transfer cooperative officers to posts near the plantations, release detained associates and seized loads, and have any officer getting too close moved elsewhere. Authorities said he had operated in Amambay since 2014 and kept contacts with the PCC and the Comando Vermelho; he was arrested in Asuncion on 14 October 2019 and has since been extradited to Brazil.
inside: A trafficker's monthly payments bought him the postings, raid warnings and releases he needed from the border police meant to stop him.
cite: InSight Crime, 4 November 2019, citing ABC Color and Paraguay's Attorney General's Office

n: Montes Bobadilla clan's police paid men killed Honduras' anti-drugs chief
org_label: the Montes Bobadilla clan and other criminal groups
rank: Police officials, Honduran National Police headquarters
d: In 2009 the Montes Bobadilla family, a trafficking clan on Honduras' Caribbean coast, helped finance the murder of the country's top police official and anti-drugs chief, Julián Arístides González. Years after the killing, leaked video footage confirmed that the assassins who carried out the hit were police officials on the payroll of multiple criminal groups, and that the execution was planned inside the Honduran National Police headquarters. The case illustrates how, as their power grew, the clan and its associates increasingly corrupted the security forces. The organisation has since been indicted in the United States, and in 2024 Honduran military forces found two artificial canals cut from the sea to an inland warehouse that the group allegedly used to store drug shipments.
inside: Traffickers' money reached officers inside Honduras' national police, who then planned and carried out the killing of the state's own anti-drugs chief.
cite: InSight Crime, Montes Bobadilla profile, 25 February 2025

n: Costa Rican OIJ agents tracked cocaine loads for trafficker 'Pancho Villa'
org_label: Darwin González Hernández's cocaine theft ring
rank: Agents, Judicial Investigation Department (Organismo de Investigación Judicial)
d: At least two agents of Costa Rica's Judicial Investigation Department, the country's main investigative police body, have been charged with working for the accused trafficker Darwin González Hernández, alias "Pancho Villa". According to the department's director, Walter Espinoza, the agents used police operating systems to track cocaine shipments that were then intercepted and stolen by the gang. Their part came to light after a ton of cocaine was seized in October 2020 from a lorry stopped in Garabito, Puntarenas province; investigators later found the cocaine had been stolen from another group and that the agents had directed the lorry to a property on the Pacific coast.
inside: A theft ring used agents inside Costa Rica's investigative police to look up rivals' cocaine loads in police systems and route them to its own hands.
cite: InSight Crime, 13 April 2021, citing CRHoy, La Nación and OIJ director Walter Espinoza

n: Bufalo NK network paid Dominican drug agency and navy for safe landings
rank: Agents of the National Drug Control Directorate (DNCD) and of the Dominican Navy
d: The Dominican public prosecution service's indictment in the Búfalo NK case states that members of the trafficking structure made recurring payments, in the form of bribes, to agents of the National Drug Control Directorate (DNCD) and of the Dominican Navy to guarantee that drug consignments could enter the country and be unloaded safely. The prosecution says the scheme was coordinated by Isidoro Rotestán Clase, alias "El Men", who acted as financier and as the link with local holders of power, and that by penetrating those institutions he made it possible for the organisation to move cocaine on to warehouses in La Vega and the east of the country, from where shipments were organised to Puerto Rico, Miami and Barcelona. Operation Búfalo NK was carried out in September 2024.
inside: Prosecutors say a cocaine network paid agents of the Dominican drug agency and navy so its consignments could enter and be unloaded undisturbed.
cite: El Día, 16 November 2025, citing the indictment of the Dominican Public Prosecution Service in the Búfalo NK case

n: Two Rosario police convicted of feeding a Los Monos faction police secrets
org_label: a faction of the Los Monos gang
rank: Officers of the Criminal Investigation Agency (now PDI) and of Regional Unit II, Santa Fe police
d: On 2 February 2024 a court in Rosario sentenced the Santa Fe police officers David Luciano Arellano and Marcos Barúa to three years' effective imprisonment under a plea agreement, in which they accepted having reported confidential information to men linked to a faction of the Los Monos gang. Prosecutor José Luis Caterina argued that Arellano's position in the homicide brigade gave him access to confidential information he used to help the barra brava Guillermo Sosa stay out of the reach of the courts, knowing that his contact, the expelled officer Juan José Raffo, had been convicted in 2018 as a member of Los Monos. Prosecutors attributed to Barúa the supply of police contacts and information to Sosa, but that participation was not proven.
inside: A gang faction got its warnings from inside the homicide brigade, so police files helped a wanted man stay out of the courts' reach.
cite: La Capital (Rosario), 3 February 2024, citing prosecutor José Luis Caterina and the plea agreement approved by judge Rodrigo Santana

n: Rosario officers took a dealer's money and framed her rivals
org_label: a retail drug-selling group in Parque Casas, Rosario
who: a retail drug seller and her group
rank: Officers of the Motorised Brigade and command of the 10th precinct, Santa Fe police, Rosario
d: On 22 July 2026 two officers of the Santa Fe police Motorised Brigade in Rosario, Marcelo Borovachi and Ricardo Font, accepted sentences of three years' imprisonment and six years' disqualification for a series of false operations over the previous two years. Six officers of the brigade had been detained in March 2025 for fabricating cases and taking bribes in the Parque Casas neighbourhood, where prosecutors say they were protecting one retail drug seller and going after a competitor. The practices came to light when Sandra Álvarez, a seller, was arrested; her phone showed close contact with brigade officers who had guarded her house after a shooting. The convictions cover unlawful detentions, false statements in records, threats and unlawful entry. In one operation cocaine was planted at the scene.
inside: A drug seller's payments bought police protection, and the same officers fabricated cases against the rival selling point nearby.
cite: La Capital (Rosario), 22 July 2026, citing the sentence handed down by judge Facundo Becerra and prosecutors Pablo Socca and Karina Bartocci

n: Twelve Chilean prison officers charged over an Alto Hospicio drug ring
org_label: a criminal organisation trafficking drugs inside Chilean prisons
rank: Serving officers of Gendarmería de Chile, the prison service
d: Chile's public prosecution service and the investigative police carried out a national operation in which nineteen people were detained, twelve of them serving officers of Gendarmería, the prison service, accused of belonging to a network that brought drugs into prisons and sold them there. The investigation, led by the regional prosecutor's office in Tarapacá, found that the officers allegedly acted together with inmates and private individuals outside, taking payments in exchange for allowing in illicit substances, phones and other prohibited items. The organisation's centre of operations was the Alto Hospicio prison, where irregular money movements were detected between prison officers and inmates' relatives. The charges cover drug trafficking, bribery and money laundering at prisons in four regions. Gendarmería said it had cooperated with the investigation.
inside: A drug ring paid prison officers to carry its goods through the gates, so the service guarding the prisons supplied the trade inside them.
cite: Diario Constitucional (Chile), 5 November 2025, citing the Public Prosecution Service and the Tarapacá Regional Prosecutor's Office

n: Syrian faction chiefs took army divisions made of their own fighters
org_label: Syrian National Army factions (Sultan Suleiman Shah, Hamzat, Sultan Murad)
rank: Senior Ministry of Defence posts; commanders of the 62nd, 76th and 86th Divisions
d: After Bashar al-Assad's government fell in December 2024, the new authorities merged dozens of armed factions into a fledgling Ministry of Defence. Human Rights Watch found that integration was nominal and that many groups retained their structures and loyalties, allowing previously unaccountable units to rebrand as state forces; Turkish-backed factions including Sultan Suleiman Shah, Hamzat and Sultan Murad were integrated and their leaders appointed to senior positions despite the factions' abusive records. Mohammed al-Jassem (Abu Amsha), sanctioned by the United States in August 2023 over abuses attributed to his brigade, took command of the army's 62nd Division, formed from his own faction; Ahmed al-Hayes (Abu Hatem Shaqra) took the 86th Division and Sayf Boulad the 76th. In August 2026 the three were reassigned to administrative posts away from their former areas of command.
inside: Armed factions folded into Syria's defence ministry kept their own commands while their leaders took senior army posts, so state units answered to faction chiefs.
cite: Human Rights Watch, 'Are You Alawi?', 23 September 2025; The National, 'Syria removes three civil war-era commanders in army shake-up', 7 August 2026 (www.thenationalnews.com/news/mena/2026/08/07/syria-removes-three-civil-war-era-commanders-in-army-shake-up/)

n: US says Hezbollah drew intelligence from inside Lebanon's army and security service
rank: Chief of the National Security Department, General Directorate for General Security; chief of the Dahiyah branch, Lebanese Armed Forces Intelligence Directorate
d: On 21 May 2026 the US Treasury designated nine people in Lebanon for obstructing the peace process and impeding Hezbollah's disarmament, describing them as Hezbollah-aligned officials embedded across Lebanon's parliament, military and security sectors. Treasury said that Brigadier General Khattar Nasser Eldin, chief of the National Security Department of the General Directorate for General Security, and Colonel Samir Hamadi, chief of the Dahiyah branch of the Lebanese Armed Forces Intelligence Directorate, had shared important intelligence with Hezbollah during the conflict over the past year. It was the first time Lebanese officers had been sanctioned by the United States. The army said its members' loyalty was solely to the institution and the nation and that it had not been informed beforehand; Hezbollah condemned the sanctions.
inside: Treasury says two serving officers of Lebanon's army intelligence and state security passed information to Hezbollah, so state secrets served the armed movement.
cite: US Treasury press release sb0505, 'Treasury Targets Hizballah-Aligned Officials Obstructing Peace and Disarmament', 21 May 2026; OFAC recent actions, 21 May 2026; Asharq Al-Awsat English / AFP, 22 May 2026, 'Lebanon Army Says Soldiers Loyal after US Sanctions One over Alleged Hezbollah Links', same text at naharnet.com/stories/en/320292

n: Southern council leader heads Yemen's new state Counter-Terrorism Unit in Aden
rank: Head of the Counter-Terrorism Unit, Aden; head of the unit's Aden office
d: Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council directed several security and intelligence agencies to merge into a Central Agency for State Security. Under that directive, the UN Panel of Experts on Yemen recorded, a specialised agency, the Counter-Terrorism Unit, was set up, headquartered in Aden and headed by a prominent leader of the Southern Transitional Council, a southern secessionist movement with its own armed forces. The Panel also reported that the Council remained reluctant to place its forces under one unified command. Yusran al-Maqtari, head of the Aden office of the Council-supported unit, was accused over the kidnapping of a Yemeni army officer; the Supreme Security Committee, headed by the Minister of Defence, decided to suspend and arrest him. The Panel said many suspects were arrested but the main suspect was not.
inside: A secessionist movement's leader heads a new national counter-terrorism agency, so a state security body sits under the movement's own command.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2024/731, paras. 48 and 50 and footnote 29

n: Council-backed Elite Forces kept another Yemeni state force out of Mukalla
rank: Hadramawt Elite Forces within the armed forces of the Government of Yemen
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen recorded competition over influence in the south that led to an incident in Hadramawt between two armed groups of the Government of Yemen. The Elite Forces, supported by the Southern Transitional Council, a southern secessionist movement, prevented the National Shield Forces from entering Mukalla city. The Council then issued a statement suggesting that it would be preferable for the National Shield Forces to protect the valley and the desert in the region, while leaving coastal areas to the Elite Forces, which it said had historically safeguarded them. Government officials told the Panel the issue was easily resolved and that the newly established Joint Forces Command, which comprised representatives of all the forces, would not allow such situations to be repeated.
inside: A secessionist movement's units inside Yemen's own armed forces blocked a rival state force from a city, so state troops enforced the movement's territorial claim.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2024/731, para. 49

n: Karen splinter army became a state Border Guard Force and kept its command
who: Democratic Karen Buddhist Army / Karen Border Guard Force
rank: Border Guard Force battalions under the Myanmar military's Directorate of People's Militia and Territorial Forces
d: The Democratic Karen Buddhist Army, a splinter from the Karen National Union, was transformed in 2010 into a Border Guard Force under the Myanmar military's Directorate of People's Militia and Territorial Forces, Justice For Myanmar reported. Its leader San Myint, who uses the name Saw Chit Thu, kept command; the force had four military regions and 13 battalions, each holding shares in the military conglomerate Myanma Economic Holdings, as a leaked 2010-11 shareholder report showed. Justice For Myanmar found that, in exchange for integrating into the military's command, Saw Chit Thu and his family gained material support from the army and space to build businesses. The US Treasury designated the group, renamed the Karen National Army in March 2024, and Saw Chit Thu on 5 May 2025.
inside: An armed Karen splinter group was made a state border guard force under army command while keeping its own leaders, who used that status for their businesses.
cite: Justice For Myanmar, 'The Karen Border Guard Force/Karen National Army criminal business network exposed'; US Treasury press release sb0129, 5 May 2025 (home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0129)

n: Ampatuan clan's private army held Philippine police and militia commissions
rank: Civilian Volunteer Organization, Police Auxiliary Unit, CAFGU and Special CAFGU Active Auxiliary members, plus serving police and military
d: Human Rights Watch reported in November 2010 that, according to individuals with knowledge of the Ampatuans' force structure, most members of the Maguindanao ruling family's private army were also members of state-sanctioned paramilitary forces: the Civilian Volunteer Organization, the Police Auxiliary Unit, the Citizen Armed Force Geographical Unit or the Special CAFGU Active Auxiliary. Their forces also included regular members of the police and military. Militia members swore allegiance to the family and operated without the police or military supervision required by law. Fifty-eight people were killed in Maguindanao on 23 November 2009. On 19 December 2019 the court convicted 28 of the more than 107 who stood trial of murder, giving them 40-year terms less ten years for time served, and found 15 more guilty as accessories; Andal Ampatuan Jr and his brother Zaldy were sentenced to life without parole, 55 defendants were acquitted and 80 suspects remained at large.
inside: A ruling family's private army held the state's militia and police commissions, so police powers and state weapons served the clan rather than the public.
cite: Human Rights Watch, 'They Own the People: The Ampatuans, State-Backed Militias, and Killings in the Southern Philippines', 16 November 2010; Human Rights Watch, 'Masterminds Guilty in Philippines Massacre', 19 December 2019 (www.hrw.org/news/2019/12/19/masterminds-guilty-philippines-massacre)

n: Taliban infiltrator in the Kandahar governor's guard killed the police chief
rank: Member of the Kandahar governor's bodyguard
d: On the afternoon of 18 October 2018 gunfire broke out at the governor's compound in Kandahar, after a high-ranking meeting about election security had ended. Spokesmen for the ministries of defence and interior said at a press conference that a member of Kandahar governor Toryalai Wisa's bodyguard opened fire, and identified him as Gulbuddin. The Taliban claimed responsibility and said he was an infiltrator called Abu Dujana. According to the ministries' statement, General Abdul Razeq, the Kandahar police chief and the strongest figure in southern Afghanistan, was killed along with the provincial intelligence chief, Abdul Momen Hussainkhel, while Governor Wisa and the police chief of the southern zone, General Nabi Elham, were injured. The killings came two days before parliamentary elections and left provincial security forces leaderless.
inside: The Taliban had a man inside the provincial governor's protection detail, and he used that access to kill the province's police and intelligence chiefs.
cite: Afghanistan Analysts Network, 'The Killing of Razeq: Removing the Taleban's strongest foe in Kandahar, an indirect hit at elections', October 2018

n: Police constable accused of taking the bomber into Peshawar's police lines
org_label: Jamaatul Ahrar, a faction of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan
rank: Police constable, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police
d: A suicide bombing at a mosque inside the Peshawar Police Lines on 30 January 2023 claimed 84 lives. On 12 November 2024 the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Inspector General of Police, Akhtar Hayat Khan Gandapur, told a press briefing in Peshawar that the facilitator arrested the day before was 'our own policeman', police constable Muhammad Wali. He said Wali dropped the suicide bomber, known as Qari, at the Pir Zakori bridge and then reported the attack's success to his handler by Telegram, and that he allegedly received Rs200,000 through the hundi-hawala system. The inspector general said the constable had acted on the orders of the banned Jamaatul Ahrar, a faction of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan; the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan had claimed responsibility for the bombing and later distanced itself from it.
inside: Police say a serving constable worked for a banned Taliban faction and brought its bomber into a police compound, where 84 people died.
cite: Dawn, 'Arrested facilitator of 2023 Peshawar Police Lines blast was our own policeman: KP IG', 12 November 2024

n: Karuna group cadres said to man Sri Lankan army and police checkpoints
org_label: Karuna group / Tamil Makkal Viduthalai Pulikal (TMVP)
rank: Army and police checkpoints in the eastern districts; police and Special Task Force guard on the group's offices
d: Human Rights Watch reported in January 2007 that Tamils in Ampara, Batticaloa and Trincomalee districts said they had seen members of the Karuna group working with the army and police at checkpoints, an allegation the military denied, and that armed cadres walked freely through government-controlled areas, sometimes wearing Sri Lankan army uniforms. The Karuna group broke away from the Tamil Tigers; its political party was the Tamil Makkal Viduthalai Pulikal. Human Rights Watch observed in October 2006 that the party's Batticaloa office, where parents said they had seen abducted children, was guarded on three sides by the police; the Akkaraipattu office was guarded by the police Special Task Force and the Trincomalee office by the navy. The military and the defence spokesman denied any state involvement with the group; the group's leader, V. Muralitharan (Colonel Karuna), denied any involvement in child abductions or forced recruitment.
inside: Residents said a breakaway Tiger faction's cadres worked at state checkpoints while police guarded its offices, so state security served the group's operations.
cite: Human Rights Watch, 'Complicit in Crime: State Collusion in Abductions and Child Recruitment by the Karuna Group', January 2007, chapters IV and V

n: Casalesi-linked group won Italian state railway contracts via its managers
rank: Head of the purchasing directorate and other managers of Rete Ferroviaria Italiana
inside: A business group held to be close to a camorra clan paid and promoted managers inside the state railway company, which then awarded its contracts to the group's firms.
d: Rete Ferroviaria Italiana is the company that owns and runs Italy's railway network. In April 2019 Carabinieri searched RFI offices in via Gianturco in Naples and the homes of three of its managers, among them Massimo Iorani, head of the purchasing directorate, over contracts allegedly won illicitly by a business group investigators consider close to the Schiavone faction of the Casalesi camorra clan. Prosecutors say the businessman Nicola Schiavone, a close friend of the clan's boss, also helped those managers' careers inside RFI. Thirty-five people were arrested in May 2022 and a trial of 59 defendants opened at Santa Maria Capua Vetere in December 2023. Of the nine who chose summary trial, eight were convicted in October 2023, among them Dante Apicella, held to be a leading Casalesi figure, who was given sixteen years five months and ten days; Luigi Russo was acquitted. Nicola Schiavone had been discharged in June 2023 of laundering and fictitious ownership.
cite: Stylo24, 28 October 2023 (www.stylo24.it/appalti-rfi-al-clan-dei-casalesi-raffica-di-condanne-in-abbreviato/); Stylo24, 3 April 2019 (www.stylo24.it/clan-dei-casalesi-appalti-rfi/); Anteprima24, 25 October 2023; Stylo24, 30 March 2024

n: Moccia clan's firms took railway contracts with two RFI officials paid off
rank: Two officials of the Napoli Est territorial unit, Rete Ferroviaria Italiana
inside: A camorra clan used firms it was linked to and two paid railway officials, so the state rail company's contracts went to the clan's businesses.
d: On 20 April 2022 Carabinieri of the ROS and finance police served 59 custody measures and seized 150 million euros of assets in an inquiry into the Moccia clan of Afragola, near Naples, which prosecutors say reinvested criminal money in waste disposal and in large railway and high-speed rail contracts. All the offences charged carry the aggravating circumstance of helping the clan. For the contracts of Rete Ferroviaria Italiana, the state company that runs Italy's rail network, the clan allegedly used entrepreneurs whose firms held proper anti-mafia certificates. Two officials of the Napoli Est territorial unit, Salvatore Maisto and Stefano Deodato, were placed under house arrest for corruption, accused of pocketing 29,000 euros. The contracts included maintenance at Afragola high-speed station.
cite: Anteprima24, 20 April 2022; Stylo24, 20 April 2022

n: Contini clan men ran the booking desk inside a Naples public hospital
rank: Centro unico di prenotazione (central booking service), San Giovanni Bosco hospital
inside: Relatives of a camorra boss ran a public hospital's appointment booking with staff help, so the clan's people and friends jumped the queue for care.
d: In June 2019 police arrested 126 alleged members of the Alleanza di Secondigliano, the pact of the Contini, Mallardo and Licciardi camorra clans in Naples. The custody order signed by the investigating judge Roberto D'Auria describes the central booking service of the San Giovanni Bosco public hospital being run by men of the Contini clan, named as Angelo Botta, brother of the boss Salvatore, and his nephew Vincenzo Botta, with the complicity of people working there. Intercepted calls show relatives and associates getting tests and specialist appointments at once, bypassing the ordinary booking and payment routine; the judge wrote that access to specialist care was following privileged, non-institutional channels. The order also covers clan management of hospital staffing and catering.
cite: Cronache della Campania, 27 June 2019; Libero Quotidiano, 15 November 2025

n: Lucca ring with Casalesi ties bought an ASL Napoli 3 Sud official
who: ring of businessmen close to the Casalesi clan
rank: Senior official handling contracts, ASL Napoli 3 Sud local health authority
inside: A criminal group paid an official of a local health authority, which then awarded and paid for building works its firms never carried out.
d: ASL Napoli 3 Sud is the public health authority for the area south of Naples, with its seat at Torre del Greco. In March 2018 the finance police of Lucca, in operation Ghost Tender, served five custody measures and carried out 50 searches against businessmen described as close to the Casalesi camorra clan, their companies, front men and a public official. Investigators say that through cartel agreements the group, based in the province of Lucca, obtained more than 50 emergency and direct-award jobs from the health authority, and kept up corrupt relations with an official there who awarded the contracts and let the group be paid although the works were largely never done. More than 6 million euros was taken this way and laundered through the group's property business.
cite: Stylo24, 26 March 2018 (Guardia di Finanza statement)

n: 'Ndrangheta-linked health director rigged a Milan hospital's nursing tender
rank: Health director of the ASL of Pavia and the administrative director of the San Paolo hospital, Milan
inside: A health manager convicted of helping 'ndrangheta clans rigged a public hospital's tender from inside, so the award served the firms behind the bribes.
d: The former health director of the local health authority of Pavia was arrested in July 2010 in part of Infinito, the large inquiry into the 'ndrangheta in Lombardy, and was finally jailed to 12 years for external participation in a mafia association. In August 2024 the Lombardy section of the Court of Auditors, which hears claims for loss caused to public bodies, ordered him and the former administrative director of Milan's San Paolo hospital jointly to pay 40,000 euros for damage to the body's standing. The criminal case concerned a nursing services tender for Milan's Opera prison, run by the San Paolo hospital and provisionally awarded to the Fatebenefratelli consortium. The administrative director agreed a plea; the health director's conviction was two years and one month, with some counts time-barred.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 29 August 2024, reporting ANSA on the Lombardy Court of Auditors judgment

n: Heroin ring hired PIA staff to load drugs on flights to London
rank: Traffic supervisor, engineer, driver, shuttle operators and sanitation staff of Pakistan International Airlines
inside: A smuggling ring hired staff of the national airline, who used their access to planes and hangars to put heroin aboard its London flights.
d: On 24 June 2017 Pakistan's Anti-Narcotics Force director general, Maj Gen Mussarat Nawaz Malik, said at least 14 people had been arrested over a ring that smuggled heroin on Pakistan International Airlines flights from Islamabad's Benazir Bhutto International Airport to London Heathrow. Most of those held were PIA employees, identified with the help of surveillance footage, and over 100 PIA staff were put under surveillance. Malik named a traffic supervisor who took drugs from a dealer and delivered them to the plane, shuttle operators who hid drugs in lockers, an engineer, a driver, sanitation workers and an airport IT staffer who allegedly said when a plane would reach the hangar. The suspected ringleader, Arif Badshah, was arrested in Karachi and, Malik said, confessed to hiring people and supplying heroin.
cite: Dawn, 24 June 2017; Dawn, 1 August 2016 (13 PIA employees held, Lahore)

n: Bari clan boss put on the city waste company's payroll in 2013
rank: Staff of Amiu, Bari's municipal refuse collection company
inside: A clan boss was taken onto the payroll of the city's own refuse company through a hiring clause that should not have covered him.
d: Amiu is the municipal company that collects and handles household refuse in Bari. On 30 October 2013, a day before a private firm's contract for cleaning public toilets in the Carrassi district ran out, the city council asked Amiu to take over the service and take on its 56 workers temporarily, there being no time for a new tender. The agreement signed the next day between Amiu and the unions contained a social clause obliging the company to absorb workers with at least four months' service. All met that condition except one, the clan boss Francesco Diomede. Amiu's president told prosecutors the unions had assured him a derogation existed for Diomede; it is cited in the agreement but nobody has produced it. The anti-mafia prosecutor's file was open in 2016.
cite: Borderline24, 29 February 2016

n: Cosenza clan placed a member in a firm collecting ten towns' refuse
rank: Job inside E-Log srl, holder of municipal refuse contracts in ten Calabrian towns
inside: A clan had one of its men hired, through a union official, by the company that collects refuse for ten towns, so the clan got a place inside it.
d: In the Reset operation of 2022 the anti-mafia prosecutors of Catanzaro set out how Massimo Bertoldi, whom they consider a member of the D'Ambrosio group among Cosenza's confederated clans, was taken on by E-Log srl through the intermediation of Gianluca Campolongo, an official of the Fit-Cisl transport union, who was placed under house arrest on the day of the raid over an alleged extortion. The prosecutors' application for custody measures says Campolongo thereby showed that he answered to instructions given by Massimo D'Ambrosio, and links him to two attempts, the first successful, to secure jobs for clan men in waste firms. E-Log holds municipal refuse contracts in ten towns in the province of Cosenza and had already been served with anti-mafia interdiction orders in 2016 and 2019.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 19 September 2022, quoting the DDA Catanzaro custody application

n: Inquiry told a Transnet insider steered a cocaine ship's berth at Durban
org_label: cocaine trafficking syndicate shipping from Brazil
rank: Unnamed employee inside Transnet, the state ports and rail company
inside: A trafficking syndicate had someone inside the state port company who could choose where a ship berthed, so its people could reach the containers.
d: On 9 July 2021 South African police seized 715.86 kilograms of cocaine, worth about 300 million rand, at Aeroton south of Johannesburg; portions later went missing in police custody and nobody had been arrested five years on. A Hawks officer, Colonel Francois Steyn, told the Madlanga judicial commission in May 2026 that the cargo had entered the country through Durban harbour and travelled by truck, hidden among legitimate freight. In June 2026 Lieutenant-Colonel Joseph Sebola told the same commission that someone within Transnet, the state-owned ports and rail company, had worked with corrupt officers to give access to the cocaine shipped from Brazil, and agreed with the commissioner's reading that this person decided where the ship should berth and could manipulate where it landed.
cite: SABC News, 8 June 2026 (www.sabcnews.com/sabcnews/transnet-employee-implicated-in-2021-aeroton-cocaine-bust/); The Citizen, 11 May 2026 (www.citizen.co.za/news/madlanga-commission-aeroton-cocaine-bust-arrests/)

n: Militia chief's brother ran a firm on Libya's power and oil contracts
rank: contracts of the General Electric Company of Libya and the National Oil Corporation
d: The UN Panel of Experts found that the North Africa Development and Investment Holding Company, managed by Fathi Al-Kikli, brother of Abdel Ghani al-Kikli, commander of the Tripoli armed group the Stability Support Apparatus, held contracts with both the state-owned General Electric Company of Libya and the National Oil Corporation, and that these contracts were deliberately kept outside Libyan oversight. On 16 March 2023 al-Kikli and other commanders came to the Libyan Audit Bureau with over 20 armed vehicles to force it into approving a contract worth over $200 million for electricity meters; the holding company was then granted subcontracts to install and maintain them, which it barely executed. Al-Kikli denied any connection with the electricity company. The Panel records his killing in Tripoli on 12 May 2025.
inside: A militia commander's brother ran the firm holding the state power and oil companies' equipment contracts, which were kept away from Libyan oversight bodies.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2024/914, 2 December 2024, paras. 15 and 17, with al-Kikli's denial at para. 16; UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, annex 16 'Violations of international human rights law committed in the context of the May 2025 events', para. 2

n: Haftar asked for 96 Libyan state projects to go under his authority
rank: Military Investment and Public Works Authority of the armed forces General Command
d: The Military Investment and Public Works Authority belongs to the General Command of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces, the eastern force led by Khalifa Haftar. The UN Panel of Experts published his letter of 5 December 2017 asking the prime minister of the Libyan interim government, which the Panel describes as based in Al Baida, to issue a decision bringing 96 listed public projects under the authority, saying some of their managers had requested it so that the projects could be protected and revitalised 'in the service of the military efforts' of his forces. The list runs from farms and cattle projects to hotels, markets, shipping and engineering companies, factories and presses. The Panel said at least 30 per cent of these businesses had been taken over by the authority.
inside: An armed force asked the government to put dozens of public companies and projects under its own authority, and took over at least 30 per cent of them.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2021/229, 8 March 2021, para. 24 and annex 12 'Funding sources for the LNA's Military Investment Authority', appendix C 'A list of targeted businesses for confiscation', with the Al Baida-based government at para. 111

n: Haftar's investment authority told Libya's ports company to load scrap
rank: Director, Libyan Ports Company, and the director-general of the Sea Port of Tubruq
d: The UN Panel of Experts published a letter of 12 June 2018 from Major General Muhammad al-Madani Abdulhafiz al-Fakhiri, head of the Military Investment Authority of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces General Command, addressed to the director-general of the Sea Port of Tubruq, the port's security director and customs office head, the director of the Libyan Ports Company and the chief of the Tubruq naval base. It asked them to authorise the shipping contractor Awa'il to complete entry procedures and load the ship Al-Nur with 5,000 tons of scrap. The Panel said the documents demonstrated the authority's illegal takeover of the scrap metal export business in eastern Libya, one of the activities through which it brought in revenue for Haftar's forces and their senior leadership.
inside: An armed force's business arm instructed the state ports company and the port's own officers to clear a scrap cargo it was exporting for its own revenue.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2021/229, 8 March 2021, para. 24 and annex 12 'Funding sources for the LNA's Military Investment Authority', appendix A 'Illegal export of scrap metal', figures 12.A.3 and 12.A.4

n: Houthis installed a director at Yemen's Amran cement factory
rank: Director of the Amran cement factory
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen received information from sources indicating that the Houthis had taken control of the management and assets of Yemen's largest cement production company, Amran. It reports that Abdul Fattah Ismail Al-Ashmouri, the newly appointed director of the factory, appointed by the Houthis, allegedly dismissed 30 employees in July 2023 and appointed Houthi loyalists, and that Houthi leaders are accused of obtaining large loans in the company's name and embezzling substantial funds. It is alleged that cement was given free of charge, disguised as humanitarian aid, to the Ministry of Defence and other Houthi-affiliated entities for construction projects. The company reportedly borrowed 40 billion rials at high interest, ran up debts above 60 billion and halted production. The Panel is investigating the matter.
inside: An armed movement appointed the director of the country's biggest cement works, which then shed staff, hired loyalists and supplied its ministries free of charge.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2024/731, 2024, annex 177 'Misappropriation of the assets of Amran cement factory'; an earlier Panel report lists the state Public Corporation for the Industry and Marketing of Cement, with factories including one rendered 'Omran', among Yemen's state-owned enterprises (S/2021/79, annex 25 'Case Study: Analysis of the Houthi State Budget', para. 5(a))

n: Houthi custodian's brother made managing director of Sabafon
rank: Managing director and chairman, Sabafon (Sana'a)
d: Sabafon is one of Yemen's main mobile operators, owned by the Al Ahmar family and others. The UN Panel of Experts listed it among the entities appropriated by Major General Saleh Mesfer Alshaer, whom a specialised criminal court under Houthi control designated judicial custodian of funds and assets taken from the movement's opponents, and recorded his brother Abdullah Mesfer Saleh Alshaer as a director. The Panel was later informed that Abdullah Mesfer Al-Shaer was appointed managing director and chairman of Sabafon in Sana'a on 29 July 2019 and that he then appointed the board's vice-chairman, the executive general manager and the financial manager. The Panel said he had been instrumental in taking control of Sabafon's management, and that telecommunications revenue has been a major source of funds for the Houthis.
inside: The movement's asset custodian put his own brother in charge of a national mobile operator, and he then chose the rest of its senior management.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2020/326, 2020, annex 26 'Unlawful appropriation by major general Saleh Mesfer Alshaer network', tables 26.1 and 26.2; UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2022/50, 2022, para. 84 and annex 29 'Telecom Sector in Yemen', paras. 2 and 7

n: Houthi custodian's brother made director of the seized firm Yemen Armored
rank: Director, Yemen Armored
d: Yemen Armored is a Yemeni company whose owner the UN Panel of Experts names as Ahmed Saleh Ali Arrahbi. The Panel listed it among the entities appropriated by Major General Saleh Mesfer Alshaer, designated judicial custodian of funds and assets taken from the Houthis' opponents by a specialised criminal court under their control, and identified Alshaer's brother Abdullah Mesfer Saleh Alshaer as its director, with his nephew Raed and another man recorded as beneficiaries of the company's accounts. The Panel noted that the owner had emailed United Nations personnel on 14 July 2019 saying he had been tortured and that his company had been appropriated by the Houthis. The Panel treated the custodian's confiscations of companies, bank accounts and real estate as unlawful appropriation.
inside: The movement's asset custodian took a company from its owner and installed his own brother as its director, with relatives drawing on its bank accounts.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2020/326, 2020, annex 26 'Unlawful appropriation by major general Saleh Mesfer Alshaer network', tables 26.1 and 26.2 and footnote 121; UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2021/79, 2021, annex 27 'Illegal Seizure of Assets by the Judicial Custodian and the Specialised Criminal Court', table 27.2

n: Houthi custodian put a ministry undersecretary over eight seized firms
rank: legal representative and manager of InTime Corporation and seven other companies
d: The UN Panel of Experts compiled the companies whose assets had been confiscated by the Houthis' judicial custodian, Saleh Mosfer Alshaer, over the three years to its January 2021 report. Alshaer appointed Osama Sari, the undersecretary of the ministry of youth and sports, as his representative for InTime Corporation, and the Panel recorded Sari as managing Ed Simo Corporation, FlexTrack Corporation, Agrayss Corporation, Almaz Corporation, Aram Radio FM, Tocast Company and Minar Vaz Company. The Panel said Alshaer had set up an extensive network of collaborators to help him seize assets, that a specialised criminal court in Sana'a had designated him judicial custodian, and that the court used its powers to add the appearance of legality to appropriation for his benefit.
inside: The movement's custodian handed eight confiscated companies to a serving ministry official of his own side, who ran them as his representative.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2021/79, 2021, annex 27 'Illegal Seizure of Assets by the Judicial Custodian and the Specialised Criminal Court', table 27.2 and paras. 3-4

n: Houthis seized Yemen's Kamaran tobacco firm and named its chief executive
rank: Chief executive, Kamaran Industry and Investment Company
d: Kamaran Industry and Investment Company is a public joint stock tobacco company in Yemen, 27.81 per cent government-owned, which the UN Panel of Experts calls one of the largest financial contributors to the government. The Panel found that Kamaran was seized by the Houthis in 2017 and that they appointed Ahmad Al-Sadiq as its chief executive, and that by taking control of its administrative and financial functions they could dictate how the company spent its cash. The central bank in Sana'a froze its accounts in November 2017 and the ministry of finance asked it to transfer 38 billion rials, about $152 million, more than its treasury held. The Panel obtained documents showing payments to loyalists and militia leaders, and contributions to Houthi-affiliated foundations.
inside: An armed movement seized a part-state tobacco company, appointed its chief executive and then decided where the company's cash went.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2021/79, 2021, annex 26 'Case Study of Houthi Mismanagement & Diversion of Public Funds: The Kamaran Industry and Investment Company', paras. 1-5 and figure 26.1

n: Iraq's state telecoms company signed a satellite contract for the PMF
rank: General manager, Al-Salam State Company of the Ministry of Communications
d: Al-Salam State Company is the Iraqi Ministry of Communications' telecommunications company, and it is responsible for approving the licensing of devices that could affect frequency management, including satellite terminals. Michael Knights wrote in CTC Sentinel in November 2025 that on 28 November 2024 the US-sanctioned Falah al-Fayyadh signed a contract for the supply of strategic satellite communications systems for the Popular Mobilization Committee, worth 1.09 billion Iraqi dinars or $832,000, countersigned by Nabeel Abdal-Baqi, then the company's general manager, with the price annex listing United States-made Kymeta satellite terminals. The article describes militia control of the prime minister's office, the Ministry of Communications and its subsidiary operators. It rests on the author's own documents rather than an official finding.
inside: A state telecoms company, which the author says militias control through the ministry, signed over strategic satellite systems to the militia umbrella's headquarters.
cite: Michael Knights, 'Rise of the E-Militias: Designated Terrorist Groups Infest Iraq's Digital Economy', CTC Sentinel, 20 November 2025, and its footnote ah

n: Appeal judge freed a PCC boss in Mato Grosso do Sul; bribery alleged
rank: Desembargador, Court of Justice of Mato Grosso do Sul
d: Divoncir Schreiner Maran, an appeal judge at the Court of Justice of Mato Grosso do Sul, granted house arrest on his duty shift of 21 April 2020 to Gerson Palermo, 'Pigmeu', the local chief of the Primeiro Comando da Capital prison gang, serving 126 years for drug trafficking. Palermo broke his electronic tag and fled hours later and has never been found; a colleague revoked the order next day. A federal police inquiry holds that Maran laundered bribe money by buying cattle, and a Superior Court of Justice judge, Maria Isabel Gallotti, pointed to evidence that he had committed himself in advance to granting it. On 10 February 2026 the National Council of Justice unanimously imposed compulsory retirement. His lawyers would not comment, citing the file's secrecy.
inside: A federal police inquiry says gang bribe money reached an appeal judge, whose release order let the PCC's local boss walk out and disappear.
cite: Estadao report republished by viva.com.br, 11 February 2026 (viva.com.br/noticias/cnj-afasta-de-vez-desembargador-que-soltou-chefao-do-pcc-condenado-a-126-anos.html); O Povo, 8 May 2024, on the Federal Police report and the STJ decision (www.opovo.com.br/noticias/politica/2024/05/08/pf-ve-indicios-de-que-desembargador-soltou-pigmeu-do-pcc-em-troca-de-propinas.html)

n: PCC's lawyers' network reached a public defender in Campo Grande
rank: Public defender, Public Defender's Office of Mato Grosso do Sul
d: Helkis Clark Ghizzi, a public defender in Campo Grande, was arrested on 14 March 2023 in a case covering criminal association and corruption involving lawyers, officials and the Primeiro Comando da Capital, a prison-based crime group. Gaeco, the state prosecution's organised-crime unit, says he used confidential passwords to run searches in police and judicial systems in the names of people who might be targets of an attack, among them a civil police detective. He had been removed from his post on 1 March in Operation Maitre. His son Bruno Ghizzi had been held since the previous year in the same group, described as central to inquiries into the PCC branch known as the 'Sintonia dos Gravatas'.
inside: A prison gang's network of lawyers reached a state public defender, who used his official passwords to look up people the gang might attack.
cite: O Jacare, Campo Grande, 14 March 2023, citing Gaeco and the Public Defender's Office

n: 'Ndrangheta's Lampada clan paid a Calabrian judge in escorts and hotels
rank: Judge of real-estate executions at Reggio Calabria, later investigating judge at the Palmi tribunal
d: Giancarlo Giusti was a judge of real-estate executions at Reggio Calabria from 2001 and an investigating judge at the Palmi tribunal from 2010. Milan's anti-mafia prosecutors had him arrested in March 2012 in their inquiry into the Lampada family, part of the Calabrian mafia known as the 'Ndrangheta. The accusation was that he worked for the clan in the property auctions he himself handled and in other judicial matters, receiving business opportunities and luxury stays in the company of prostitutes. At his custody hearing he recognised 'the errors committed with regard to the trips, the dinners paid for and the escorts' but denied having been corrupted. On 27 September 2012 Milan's preliminary hearing judge sentenced him to four years for corruption aggravated by mafia purpose. He tried to kill himself in Opera prison the day after the sentence and was later moved to house arrest on psychological grounds; he killed himself at home on 15 March 2015, aged 48, while still under house arrest.
inside: A mafia family bought a serving judge, so that decisions in the property auctions he ran, and in other cases, went the clan's way.
cite: Blitzquotidiano, 27 September 2012 on the Milan sentence (archivio.blitzquotidiano.it/cronaca-italia/giancarlo-giusti-ndrangheta-processo-sesso-1353829); Blitzquotidiano, 30 March 2012 on the custody hearing (archivio.blitzquotidiano.it/cronaca-italia/ndrangheta-giancarlo-giusti-ho-sbagliato-ma-non-sono-corrotto-1175517/); Blitzquotidiano on his death (archivio.blitzquotidiano.it/cronaca-italia/giancarlo-giusti-suicida-il-giudice-ai-domiciliari-per-rapporti-con-ndrangheta-2131081/); ANSA via Espansione TV, 1 March 2024

n: Men close to the 'Ndrangheta paid the president of the Imperia court
who: men described as close to the 'Ndrangheta
rank: President of the Tribunale di Imperia
d: Gianfranco Boccalatte, 67, president of the court of Imperia in north-west Italy, was placed under house arrest in May 2011 on a charge of corruption in judicial acts. Prosecutors in Turin, who handle cases against Ligurian magistrates, said he had taken payments from men close to the 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, and in exchange had worked to lighten the detention of people under the shadow of the clans. His driver, Giuseppe Fasolo, a justice ministry employee, had been arrested in January as the go-between. Two men with previous convictions, Nicola Sansalone and Leonardo Michele Andreacchio, were also placed under measures; prosecutors said Andreacchio promised Boccalatte money if he adopted a favourable surveillance ruling. The judicial council had already transferred Boccalatte to the Florence appeal court on 14 April 2011, at the request of the prosecutor general at the Court of Cassation.
inside: Clan-linked men paid the head of a court through his driver, and prosecutors say his rulings then eased detention for people tied to the mafia.
cite: Il Fatto Quotidiano, 19 May 2011, on the Turin prosecutor's statement

n: Trader close to the Mancuso clan got a Vibo Valentia judge's ruling
rank: Section president, Tribunale di Vibo Valentia
d: Patrizia Serena Pasquin, a section president at the court of Vibo Valentia in Calabria, was arrested in November 2006 with fifteen others in an inquiry by Salerno's anti-mafia prosecutors named 'Dynasty 2 - do ut des'. Prosecutors said that she had, among other things, 'fixed' a bankruptcy proceeding to help Antonio Ventura, a trader regarded as close to the Mancuso clan of Limbadi, which controls 'Ndrangheta business across the province; Ventura was arrested too. Two magistrates who sat with her on the panel that adopted that ruling, Michele Sirgiovanni and Francesca Romano, were investigated for complicity in corruption in judicial acts. Her name had already surfaced in a 2003 Catanzaro inquiry, in which the boss Diego Mancuso and his nephew Domenico, discussing a seizure of assets, called the judge 'contactable'.
inside: A mafia-linked trader reached a court's section president, whose panel then gave the bankruptcy ruling he wanted, prosecutors say.
cite: Il Giornale, 11 November 2006, on the investigating judge's custody order

n: Judge charged with taking $3.5m to free Iranian drug baron Zindasti
rank: Judge, Istanbul 5th Criminal Judgeship of Peace
d: Naci Serifi Zindasti, an Iranian drug trafficker seized in an operation in Istanbul's Kucukcekmece district on 6 April 2018, was held for six months on charges including murder, incitement to murder and membership of the Gulen movement. He and three of his men were released on 19 October 2018 by a midnight decision of Cevdet Ozcan, judge at Istanbul's 5th Criminal Judgeship of Peace. Prosecutor Melih Yildirim has since charged Ozcan with abuse of office and bribery, seeking up to fifteen years. The indictment, filed at Bakirkoy's 20th Heavy Penal Court, says he took a $3.5 million bribe through a jeweller in the Kapalicarsi bazaar for the release order, issued it after hours at 20.15, and himself thought it was not right.
inside: A drug network's money allegedly reached a duty judge, whose evening order released its leader and three of his men from custody.
cite: Cumhuriyet, 18 March 2021, reporting Sozcu's account of the indictment

n: Drug defendant's money alleged behind a Gaziantep acquittal and release
rank: President and a member judge of the Gaziantep 14th Heavy Penal Court, and a Gaziantep public prosecutor
d: Turkey's Council of Judges and Prosecutors suspended three members of the judiciary in Gaziantep for three months after an allegation that a defendant on trial for drug trafficking was acquitted and released in return for material benefit. WhatsApp messages found on a phone seized in a separate drug operation, and the sudden bringing forward of a hearing date, set off an inspection. The suspended officials, named by initials, are Gorkem B., president of the Gaziantep 14th Heavy Penal Court, Mesuda Y., a member judge of the same court, and Taner B., a Gaziantep public prosecutor. One message relays the judge as saying that a named lawyer should file a release petition, which he would approve and act on as soon as he arrived. The report does not date the acquittal.
inside: A drug defendant is alleged to have paid for his own acquittal, and the court that tried him freed him; three of its officials are suspended.
cite: GZT, 16 August 2026, reporting Sabah and the Council of Judges and Prosecutors' decision

n: Judges freed the Turkish head of a Dutch cocaine network, inspectors say
rank: President and two member judges, Istanbul 15th Heavy Penal Court
d: Fifty-one suspects were prosecuted in Istanbul, facing up to 82 years, over a network that the Dutch 'Cherokee' investigation found was led by the Dutch drug baron Joseph Johannes Leijdekkers, with Abdullah Alp Ustun running its Turkish arm. At the first hearing, on 5 July 2024, the trial prosecutor asked for all the defendants to stay in custody; the court president, named by initials as Oktay A., released fifteen of them, Ustun among them. The chief prosecutor's office objected and the 16th Heavy Penal Court accepted the objection. Ustun, placed under an order not to leave his home, absconded, and of those for whom arrest warrants were then issued only Aziz Demir was caught. Inspectors for the Council of Judges and Prosecutors reported an emailed tip that the panel had agreed $750,000 with relatives of the defendants, and sought the dismissal of all three judges. The council suspended them.
inside: An emailed tip says a cocaine network's side agreed $750,000 with a court panel, which then freed fifteen defendants including its Turkish chief.
cite: Haberturk, 8 August 2024, on the judicial inspectors' report

n: Fuel-smuggling defendant paid an Adana judge 500m lira, inquiry says
rank: Judge at the Adana courthouse
d: Turkey's Council of Judges and Prosecutors authorised an investigation into Gul A., a judge at the Adana courthouse, after a complaint by a former partner who said he was being threatened over videos of their relationship. In the inquiry it emerged, according to the reporting, that she had taken 500 million lira from a man tried for fuel smuggling at the Osmaniye Criminal Court of First Instance in return for an acquittal. She is said to have told him that a prosecutor with whom she had served in Edirne would deliver an acquittal opinion at the hearing, and to have taken the money by hand. The prosecutor did ask for acquittal, but at the next session another prosecutor asked for conviction and the man was sentenced.
inside: A smuggling defendant allegedly bought his own acquittal from a judge, who arranged for a prosecutor to ask the court to clear him.
cite: Serbestiyet, 19 June 2024, reporting Halit Turan's account in Sabah of the HSK file

n: Bogota judge held over a habeas corpus freeing a Dutch drug suspect
org_label: Dutch citizen sought in extradition on drug-trafficking charges
rank: Control-of-guarantees judge, Bogota
d: Myriam Alcira Martinez, a control-of-guarantees judge in Bogota, was arrested in an investigation by Colombia's attorney general's office into her decision ordering the release of a Dutch citizen wanted in extradition for offences connected with drug trafficking. The prosecutors say an agreement of 1,200 million pesos lay behind the habeas corpus ruling, of which 600 million was handed over in cash. Among the material gathered are images of bundles of 100,000-peso notes said to have been photographed by the Dutch citizen himself before a handover to his lawyer. That lawyer, Emperatriz Herrera Cuenca, and Waldo Garavito Mejia, an official of Bogota's judicial services centre, were arrested as well, and prosecutors asked for all three to be held in prison.
inside: Prosecutors say a drug suspect's money reached a judge and a court-services official, and a habeas corpus ruling then let him out of extradition custody.
cite: Portafolio, 30 October 2026, on the Fiscalia's case and Semana's reporting

n: Kukes prosecutor took 2,000 euros to close a drug-trafficking case
org_label: Four men arrested for drug trafficking in Kukes
rank: Prosecutor, Kukes Prosecution Office
d: Edmond Karriqi, a prosecutor in Kukes in northern Albania, was arrested in July 2021 after investigators gathered what they said was proof that he had met and taken a bribe for dropping the case against four people arrested for drug trafficking. Albania's special court for corruption and organised crime, the GJKKO, ordered him held in prison, and imposed the same measure in absentia on a secretary at the Kavaje prosecution office who had acted as the go-between. Intercepts carried by the press record the arrangement - 'on Monday we send the money, on Wednesday you have it at home' - and put the sum at 2,000 euros. Investigators had opened the file in 2019.
inside: Men arrested for drug trafficking paid the prosecutor handling them, who then shut their case down, Albanian investigators say.
cite: Shqiptarja.com, 3 July 2021, on the GJKKO decision and the intercepts

n: Korce appeal judge took 6,000 euros to bail a people-smuggling suspect
org_label: Nejton Bali, Klaudjo Zhilla and Skender Demiraj
rank: Judge, Korce Court of Appeal
d: On 15 December 2022 Albania's special court for corruption and organised crime, the GJKKO, convicted Mimoza Margjeka, a judge of the Korce Court of Appeal, of passive corruption and sentenced her to four years and six months, converted into probation. According to the special prosecution, SPAK, Nejton Bali, Klaudjo Zhilla and Skender Demiraj gave her 6,000 euros through her husband, Arben Cara, so that the detention of Orion Bali would be replaced by a property guarantee. Bali had been arrested by the Pogradec prosecution for assisting illegal border crossings under article 298/3 of the criminal code. The Korce appeal court did change the measure and he left his cell. The three men who paid were convicted too. Margjeka said after the verdict that she no longer trusted the institutions.
inside: Associates of a people-smuggling suspect paid an appeal judge through her husband, and the court then swapped his detention for bail.
cite: Shqiptarja.com, 15 December 2022, on the GJKKO sentence and SPAK's case

n: Houthi-directed Sanaa court confiscated President Hadi's bank funds
rank: President of the al Amana specialized criminal court, Sanaa
d: On 27 June 2021 the president of the al Amana specialized criminal court in Sanaa sent a memorandum to Tadhamon Bank stating that frozen funds in three accounts held in the name of Abdrabuh Mansour Hadi, then president of Yemen, had been confiscated by the court on his conviction on charges including 'compromising the independence of the Republic of Yemen'. The court directed the bank to transfer the money to accounts at the central bank of Yemen in Sanaa, managed under the public prosecutor's supervision. The United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen said it believed that, given the political nature of the case, the court was acting under the control or direction of Abdulmalik al-Houthi, the Houthi leader, who is under UN sanctions.
inside: An armed political movement directed a criminal court, which confiscated the funds of the president it was fighting and sent them to the bank it controls.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2022/50, paras. 80-81 and footnote 89

n: Glencore's cash bought crude cargoes for its South Sudan venture
rank: Government officials who could influence the allocation of crude oil cargoes; Ministry of Petroleum tender process
d: Glencore Energy UK Ltd pleaded guilty on 21 June 2022 to seven United Kingdom Bribery Act counts, one of them failing to prevent the bribery of officials in South Sudan. Its 2011 joint venture with the state oil company Nilepet, Petronile, was soon in trouble: the Ministry of Petroleum meant to sell the country's crude through its own competitive marketing. Court documents say Glencore hired a South Sudanese intermediary because it "had access to government ministers, the President and his assistant", and that $800,000 flown to Juba on 2 August 2011 was used "to pay bribes to government officials who could influence the allocation of crude oil cargoes". Petronile was awarded 2 million barrels on 10 August, and 600,000 more in November after a further $275,000 withdrawal.
inside: A commodity trader's cash, carried by a local middleman, reached officials deciding who got oil cargoes, and its own venture then won them.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan, S/2023/294, annex 36 'Glencore pleads guilty to South Sudan bribery in UK Court', pp. 122; citing Rex v Glencore Energy UK Limited, Case Summary T20227145, 2 November 2022

n: Malawi's lands minister charged over a Mercedes from Sattar's agent
rank: Minister of Lands and Urban Development
d: Malawi's Anti-Corruption Bureau arrested Kezzie Msukwa, then Minister of Lands and Urban Development, in December 2021. It alleged he had received an advantage in the form of a Mercedes-Benz C-Class and money from the businessman Zuneth Sattar, purportedly to be allocated land in Lilongwe and Salima through Ashok Nair, said to be Sattar's agent. Sattar had been arrested in Britain by the National Crime Agency in October 2021 over alleged corrupt dealings involving his firms' Malawian government contracts. Msukwa said the plot had been sold to Sattar by the ministry before he became a minister. He sought judicial review; High Court judge Redson Kapindu dismissed it with costs, Msukwa appealed in 2022, and by May 2024 the Supreme Court had set no hearing date.
inside: A businessman's car and cash allegedly reached the minister who controls land allocation, so that land in two districts would go his way.
cite: Nyasa Times, 'Three years of no movement, should Malawians forget about Zuneth Sattar cases?', 13 May 2024; Nyasa Times, 'Msukwa claims sale of plot to Sattar was made before he became Minister', 3 January 2022

n: Zambian builder's director paid the ministry engineer certifying its dam
rank: Engineering assistant and site engineer, Ministry of Energy and Water Development, Konkola Dam project
d: Zambia's Anti-Corruption Commission announced in March 2024 that the Choma Subordinate Court had convicted Titus Mukwamba, an engineer at the Ministry of Water Development and Sanitation, on five counts of corrupt practices by a public officer, and Oliver Mulimo, director of Kalomo Construction Company of Livingstone, on three counts of corrupt practices with a public officer. The charges describe Mukwamba as an engineering assistant at the then Ministry of Energy and Water Development and site engineer on the Konkola Dam project. The payments, made in Choma District between 2011 and 2012, were to induce him to issue completion certificates; the release puts the total at K14,150 corruptly obtained by Mukwamba across his counts and K6,350 corruptly given by Mulimo across his. Each man was jailed for 12 months with hard labour.
inside: A contractor's director paid the ministry engineer who signs off its dam work, so the certificates releasing payment would come from inside.
cite: Anti-Corruption Commission of Zambia, press release 'Engineer at Ministry of Water Development Convicted for Corruption', 4 March 2024

n: Alko Impex paid for an Albanian minister's villa, then won her tender
rank: Minister of Infrastructure and Energy, later Deputy Prime Minister
d: Albania's special prosecution against corruption and organised crime, SPAK, accuses the former infrastructure minister and deputy prime minister Belinda Balluku of obtaining a second luxury villa in the Green Coast resort at Palase in exchange for a tender on Tirana's Big Ring road. A Special Court seizure decision puts the cost of the features she asked for, from an infinity pool to hydromassage baths, at about 290,000 to 410,000 euros, paid by the company Alko Impex General Construction, which was at the same time being rewarded with a 2.2 billion lek tender, about 23.9 million euros, for the Big Ring. The charges include violating equality in tenders, concealing assets, passive corruption of high state officials and money laundering. Balluku has denied them.
inside: A road contractor allegedly paid for the minister's seaside villa, and the ministry's tender for Tirana's ring road went to that contractor.
cite: Reporter.al (BIRN Albania), 'Nje vile ne kembim te tenderit, SPAK: Si e fshehu Balluku pronen e dyte ne Palase', 11 September 2026

n: Dricons' bribe to Albania's health ministry won a supervision tender
rank: Secretary General of the Ministry of Health and Social Protection
d: On 13 November 2023 Albania's Special Court of First Instance for Corruption and Organised Crime found Joana Duro, Secretary General of the Ministry of Health, guilty of passive corruption by a high state official. She was given four years, reduced to two years and eight months under abbreviated trial, for receiving a bribe of 330,000 lek to favour the company Dricons sh.p.k. in a procurement with a limit fund of 805,000 lek. The tender was for supervising health centre reconstruction in the Tirana and Durres regions, and six of eight bidders were disqualified before Dricons won. Its administrator Vladimir Topi, its engineer Silvi Shehi and the intermediary Laura Shteto each got a year, reduced to eight months. Shteto and Topi admitted guilt.
inside: A construction supervision firm's money reached the health ministry's most senior official, and its tender was awarded to that firm.
cite: Reporter.al (BIRN Albania), 'Zyrtarja e larte e Ministrise se Shendetesise denohet me 2.8 vjet burg', 13 November 2023; Reporter.al, 'Prokuroria arreston biznesmenin dhe inxhinierin per ryshfetin te Shendetesia', 4 June 2023

n: Incinerator firm paid the Albanian environment ministry adviser
rank: External adviser to the Minister of Environment; Ministry of Environment as contracting authority
d: Albania's special prosecution, SPAK, sent twelve people for trial in July 2026 over the Tirana incinerator concession, alleging a group led by the fugitive businessmen Mirel Mertiri and Klodian Zoto diverted tens of millions of euros. The 2017 concession was presented as an unsolicited proposal by Energy Recuperator, Paul Wurth Italia and Integrated Technology Services, the last owned by Zoto. SPAK found the concession documents were drawn up by public officials paid both by the state and by Zoto's company. Vladimir Bezhani has accepted that, as external adviser to environment minister Lefter Koka, he was paid by Zoto's company and used the ministry's email address to deal with it; SPAK's evidence is that he himself wrote the "Letter of Interest" submitted as the company's unsolicited proposal. Mertiri's lawyer says SPAK attributes no concrete act to him.
inside: A waste company paid the environment ministry's own adviser, who then drafted the proposal the ministry accepted as the company's unsolicited offer.
cite: Reporter.al (BIRN Albania), 'Si u bene tym milionat e djegesit fantazme te mbetjeve ne Tirane', 13 August 2026

n: Dominican army ammunition reached Haitian gangs through its own officers
rank: Dominican Armed Forces (ERD) stockpiles; a second lieutenant of the army
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Haiti documented several types of ammunition that appear to have been diverted from Dominican national stockpiles, in use by the 400 Mawozo gang established near the Dominican border. Multiple security sources in both countries indicated that corrupt officers within the Dominican police and armed forces were involved in the diversion, including sales in border areas for onward transfer to Haiti. Inspecting seized materiel in February 2026, the Panel found rounds marked ERD, for the Dominican army; Colombian authorities confirmed they came from two 2022 contracts with the army and the defence ministry. The Dominican authorities said a second lieutenant was arrested in December 2025 carrying 1,516 rounds on a motorbike with a Haitian national. The prosecution is ongoing.
inside: Haitian gangs buying ammunition reached officers inside the Dominican army and police, whose diversions put state stockpiles at the gangs' disposal.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2026/714, paras. 105-106 and annex 18 ('Dominican ammunition in use by Haitian gangs')

n: Gold network had Burundian police wave its mules through Gatumba
org_label: Congo-Burundi gold smuggling network around Celestin Nduwimana
rank: Burundian police officers and an agent at the Gatumba border post
d: The UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo confirmed that on at least six occasions between December 2022 and March 2023 Celestin Nduwimana moved 11 kg of gold from Congo into Burundi, in transactions worth the equivalent of $455,000, promising smugglers protection by the Burundian authorities once they crossed. Three carriers said they were stopped at two police checkpoints on the Bujumbura-Muyinga road but passed without difficulty once the driver mentioned a Burundian general's name, and that the police had been told of their passage in advance. Two others said a search at the Gatumba border post was aborted after Nduwimana telephoned a police agent. Burundi's authorities told the Group the individuals were unknown to them.
inside: A gold smuggling network had Burundian police officers warned in advance and a border search called off, so the force that was meant to stop the gold let it through.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, final report S/2023/431, paras. 178-185

n: Banned timber convoys paid $160 a truck at a Congolese army checkpoint
org_label: Wooden-plank transporters and wholesalers on the Goma-Rutshuru road
rank: State agents manning the 'OPRP' checkpoint: army (FARDC), ANR intelligence, border police and the North Kivu tax agency
d: An order of 24 May 2022 by the Governor of North Kivu barred trucks from the Goma-Rutshuru road. The UN Group of Experts found that an estimated two to three trucks carrying wooden planks still passed daily, with the complicity of state agents operating the checkpoint known as OPRP at Kanyaruchinya, in Nyiragongo territory, transporters paying $160 on arrival at night. In the first quarter of 2024 the agents collected $25,000 to $37,000 from plank transporters, an average of $100,000 to $150,000 a year, and issued no proof of payment. The Group recorded that those manning the checkpoint came from the provincial tax agency, the ANR intelligence service, the army, the border police, the forestry fund and the chieftaincy.
inside: Traders moving timber banned from the road paid the soldiers, spies and border police on the checkpoint, so the state's own barrier worked as their toll gate.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, final report S/2024/432, para. 137 and annex 80 ('Illegal taxes paid by road users at OPRP check point in Kanyaruchinya')

n: Zawiyah's drug market ran under the interior ministry's anti-drug unit head
rank: Head of the Anti-Drug Unit of the Ministry of the Interior in Zawiyah
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya reported that the main actors behind the criminal networks dominating fuel smuggling, migrant smuggling, trafficking in persons and drug trafficking along the coast west of Tripoli are armed groups that have gained a semblance of legitimacy through security mandates from the state, which lets them operate with impunity, and that the entanglement between security forces and criminal activity in Zawiyah has steadily increased since 2020. As an illustration it recorded a narcotics market listed on Google Maps as 'Sifaw for the sale of hashish and Bafra rolling papers', with which the head of the ministry's Anti-Drug Unit in Zawiyah, Mohamed Sifaw, is openly associated. The Panel received confirmation from multiple sources that ministry vehicles trade in narcotics under a bridge at the site.
inside: Smuggling networks in Zawiyah held state security mandates, and the interior ministry unit meant to fight drugs was headed by a man openly tied to a drug market.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2023/673, para. 10 and annex 7 ('Narcotics Marketplace in Zawiyah')

n: Tubruq trafficking networks used military posts to dodge police raids
rank: Military positions in, and ties to personnel of, the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF)
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya identified seven members of the Al-Habouni Network and six of the Al-Katani Network as directly responsible for running international trafficking and smuggling operations, with hubs at Musaid and Tubruq and cooperatives active in five countries, moving large groups of migrants through secret detention facilities from Tubruq to Greece; in those facilities 49 migrants endured beatings and floggings under armed guard. The Panel found that key figures of the two networks used their military positions or their ties to personnel of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces to operate without disruption: those connections helped coordinate movements between secret facilities, alerted the networks to law enforcement raids and secured free passage for trafficking vessels. The LAAF command said it had taken disciplinary measures.
inside: Trafficking network leaders held posts in or ties to Libya's eastern armed forces, which warned them of raids and let their boats of migrants leave unchecked.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2024/914, paras. 49-50 and annex 24 ('Operation centres of private human trafficking and migrant smuggling networks in Libya')

n: Gangs 'bought the wing' from guards at Ecuador's Litoral prison
org_label: Tiguerones, Netas and other Litoral prison gangs
rank: Prison guards and their superiors, Litoral Penitentiary
d: InSight Crime reported that at Ecuador's Litoral Penitentiary each wing was held by a different gang and that, in the words of a local leader of the Netas gang, 'in every wing there was a different gang, and the guards would go and collect their daily dues from them'. If a wing's boss wanted to intimidate the guards, the guards would talk to their superiors, 'who would order a change in the leaders', and the wing would be taken over by someone else with resources; the practice was called 'buying the wing'. The man known as Negro Willy began as a prison guard in 2012 and got his job back at Litoral after his release in May 2018, working with wing leaders across the prison.
inside: Prison gangs paid the guards a daily cut and, through their superiors, had wing bosses swapped, so the prison's own chain of command allocated territory for them.
cite: InSight Crime, 'The Rise and Fall of Negro Willy, Ecuador's Prison Guard Mafia Boss', 28 November 2024

n: Scan images at Ghana's Tema Port let a 3.9-tonne cocaine export through
org_label: Exporters of four cocaine containers from Tema Port
rank: Contract staff member of the Ghana Revenue Authority and three co-accused
d: Four people charged with abetment of crime in Ghana's 3.9-tonne cocaine case are alleged to have failed to properly analyse abnormal scan images of four containers, thereby facilitating the attempted exportation of the suspected narcotic substances. The Ghana News Agency names them as Togbe Agbeti, Andrews Tetteh Amponsah, Daniel Laryea and Helena Akua Denkyi, and describes Denkyi as a contract staff member of the Ghana Revenue Authority, the body whose customs division scans cargo; it gives no employer for the others. The substances were intercepted at Tema Port on 12 August 2026, in containers being exported to the Netherlands without a licence from the Minister of Health. The case is before the Kwabenya Circuit Court, presided over by Prince Osei Owusu, and was adjourned to 5 November 2026.
inside: Prosecutors say the exporters' containers passed because people inside the revenue authority's scanning process did not act on the abnormal images they saw.
cite: Ghana News Agency, 'Accused seeks removal from 3.9 tonne cocaine trial', 21 October 2026

n: Bonavota clan's jailed men got compliant reports from a Vibo prison doctor
