rank: Forensic doctor and health director of the Vibo Valentia prison
d: In the Maestrale-Carthago operation, carried out by the carabinieri on 10 May 2023 for the Catanzaro district anti-mafia directorate, 167 people were placed under investigation and 61 were made subject to detention orders. Among them is Alfonso Luciano, a forensic doctor and the health director of the prison at Vibo Valentia. Prosecutors accuse him of issuing compliant expert reports in favour of detained clan members and of revealing confidential information about ongoing investigations and imminent arrests, receiving in return goods, sums of money, protection from extortion demands and electoral support; Il Fatto Quotidiano reports that he sought the backing of the Bonavota cosca at the 2004 elections. A cosca is a clan of the 'ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia. These are allegations made as the arrests were carried out.
inside: Prosecutors say a clan obtained favourable medical reports for its jailed members, and warnings of coming arrests, from the doctor running the prison's health service.
cite: Il Fatto Quotidiano, 10 May 2023

n: SBU official took $68,000 to clear two men off a draft wanted list
org_label: Two men paying to escape mobilisation
who: Two men buying their own deferrals
rank: Official of the Security Service of Ukraine for Kyiv city and Kyiv region
d: Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau records in its report for the first half of 2026 that, for $68,000, an official of the Security Service of Ukraine in the city of Kyiv and Kyiv region promised two citizens to settle the question of removing them from the wanted list of the Territorial Centres for Recruitment and Social Support and then to arrange a deferral from mobilisation. Under the scheme the deferrals were to be issued on the basis of knowingly false documents stating that each of them had three minor children, and the price also covered their not being prosecuted for arranging a fictitious deferral. The Territorial Centres are the bodies that call men up for military service. The report gives no court outcome.
inside: Two men's money reached an officer of the state security service, who used his position to lift their call-up status and shield them from prosecution for it.
cite: National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine, report for the first half of 2026, section on corruption in the law enforcement system and the prosecutor's office

n: Smuggling group paid Moldovan border police for secret crossings
org_label: Cross-border cigarette smuggling group of 15 people
rank: Employees of Moldova's Border Police
d: Moldova's Security and Intelligence Service announced on 5 May 2022 that its officers, with Border Police employees, the Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office and Romanian authorities, had dismantled a cross-border organised criminal group of 15 people specialising in smuggling. Over six months investigators documented five controlled deliveries of cigarettes across the state's 'green' border, meaning sections away from the legal checkpoints, and detained people in the act. The service said the documented persons corrupted employees of the Border Police, who were reportedly paid between 4,000 and 7,000 euros for organising each clandestine crossing. Twelve searches were carried out in several localities in northern Moldova and four people were detained. The service notes that the suspects are presumed innocent.
inside: A smuggling group bought border police staff, who then arranged the unguarded crossings its cigarette loads needed, turning the frontier guard into part of the route.
cite: Security and Intelligence Service of the Republic of Moldova, 'Cigarette Smuggling Chain - Dismantled', 5 May 2022

n: Rosario's former intelligence chief prosecuted over tips to traffickers
org_label: People linked to drug trafficking in Rosario
rank: Former head of the SIDE state intelligence service in Rosario
d: Ivan Jokanovich, a 53-year-old criminal lawyer and former head of the SIDE state intelligence service in Rosario, has been prosecuted for having supplied key information to people linked to drug trafficking so that they could avoid criminal prosecution, in a scheme detected by prosecutors of Argentina's federal anti-drug office, Procunar. La Politica Online reports that what is attributed to him is using restricted information in a pending case to warn a provincial prosecutor that there were suspicions against him, because Juan Jose Raffo, a police officer convicted as a member of the Los Monos gang, was using a vehicle registered in the prosecutor's name. Federal judge Marcelo Bailaque prosecuted him in 2024, and the National Criminal Cassation Chamber confirmed his detention on 29 May.
inside: Prosecutors say the man who had run the state intelligence office in Rosario passed restricted information to people in the drug trade so they could stay ahead of prosecution.
cite: La Politica Online, 'Un ex jefe de la Side de Rosario quedo detenido por sus conexiones con el mundo narco', 3 June 2025

n: Mombasa port's verification head charged over an ivory container release
org_label: Ivory trafficking networks shipping through Mombasa
rank: Former head of verification, Kenya Revenue Authority, Mombasa Port
d: Reviewing the prosecutions connected to the network of the wildlife trafficker Moazu Kromah, the Daily Maverick reported that James Njagi, former Kenya Revenue Authority head of verification at Mombasa Port, was implicated in two separate prosecutions. He was charged in relation to a 2014 seizure made in Mombasa, and a witness testified that Njagi's identity document was used when releasing the container holding the ivory for shipment. In relation to a 2011 Mombasa seizure his name was identified on a verification form for the shipment found to contain ivory, which Njagi argued was a forgery. The Kenya Revenue Authority is the body whose officers verify and clear cargo. The article records long delays in these cases and gives no outcome for Njagi.
inside: Ivory shippers had their container released on the authority of the revenue officer who headed verification at the port, so the check meant to stop the cargo cleared it.
cite: Daily Maverick, 'The long road to prosecuting wildlife trafficking kingpin Moazu Kromah', 22 June 2022

n: Prison officer warned a Caltagirone mafia heir of an imminent raid
rank: Assistant of the prison police corps (polizia penitenziaria)
d: Angelo Allegra, an assistant in Italy's prison police corps, was arrested on charges of aiding an offender and revealing official secrets, aggravated by having favoured Cosa nostra in the Caltagirone area. Two days before the Agora operation, Gianfranco La Rocca, son of Caltagirone's deceased godfather and regarded as his heir in running the local family, was warned of it. The carabinieri ROS special operations group intercepted a conversation on 14 June in which Allegra described the imminent operation, due the next evening and involving at least 50 people in the province of Catania. Investigators said they could establish the officer's 'full availability and subservience' to the boss, and that on occasions he acted as an intermediary. La Rocca was located four days after the order was executed.
inside: A clan heir had a serving prison officer who told him when a police operation was coming, which is how he stayed out of reach when the arrests were made.
cite: LiveSicilia, 'Mafia: avviso La Rocca jr del blitz, arrestato agente penitenziario', 8 September 2022

n: Siracusa prison officer arrested over paid favours for detainees
org_label: Detainees at Siracusa prison and their relatives
rank: Officer of the prison police (polizia penitenziaria), Siracusa prison
d: Paolo Zagarella, 55, an officer of the prison police serving at Siracusa, was arrested on charges of corruption for acts contrary to his official duties, embezzlement and false attestations. According to investigators he had done 'favours for detainees or their relatives, procuring goods or conveying information both from outside the prison and into it, so allowing the restrictions provided for detainees to be evaded'. The inquiry was coordinated by the Siracusa public prosecutor Fabio Scavone, and the arrest was carried out by the carabinieri and the prison police. Zagarella was held in the Piazza Lanza prison in Catania. The report read gives no outcome.
inside: Detainees and their families paid an officer inside the prison, who then carried goods and messages past the restrictions he was employed to enforce.
cite: LiveSicilia, 'Agente penitenziario arrestato: Ha fatto favori ai detenuti', 18 June 2019

n: Two Palermo flying-squad officers held over protection sold to dealers
org_label: Palermo drug-dealing group around Ignazio Carollo
rank: Two deputy superintendents (vice sovrintendenti) of the Palermo squadra mobile
d: Fabrizio Spedale and Salvatore Graziano, both deputy superintendents of the Palermo squadra mobile, the city police force's flying squad, were taken into custody on allegations that they had offered protection to drug pushers in exchange for money and four motorcycles. The judge for preliminary investigations, Cristina Lo Bue, ordered the same measure for Ignazio Carollo, 42, the man they are said to have favoured. LiveSicilia reports that the tip-offs concerned ongoing investigations and searches, and that drugs kept in police warehouses went missing. The Palermo prosecutor's office had had bugs installed for another inquiry and contacts with the officers emerged; in the recorded conversations Spedale was referred to as 'Mirko' and described as warning of who was being investigated.
inside: Dealers paid two serving officers of the city's flying squad, who sold them warnings of the searches and investigations that squad was running.
cite: LiveSicilia, 'Palermo, le microspie e i poliziotti infedeli', 4 October 2023

n: Finance police lieutenant suspended over tips to a mafia-linked builder
who: Cosa Nostra through the businessman Giovanni Palazzolo
rank: Luogotenente of the Guardia di Finanza, Palermo
d: Umberto Frecentese, 61, a lieutenant of the Guardia di Finanza in Palermo, Italy's financial police, was suspended from duty by the judge for preliminary investigations, Alfredo Montalto, who had deferred the decision until the suspect had been questioned. He is alleged to have revealed confidential information about ongoing investigations to Giovanni Palazzolo, a businessman from Carini arrested for mafia offences weeks earlier. Palazzolo, founder of the Carini firm Gls, is said to have learned from him that Guardia di Finanza colleagues in Modena had asked their Palermo counterparts about him after he applied for one of his companies to be put on a prefecture's white list. He is said to have returned the favour with job offers for the officer's relatives.
inside: A businessman described as the bosses' arm in Carini's town hall got a serving finance police officer to tell him what investigators were asking about him.
cite: LiveSicilia, "L'imprenditore Palazzolo, la mafia e le soffiate: sospeso un finanziere", 13 May 2024

n: Carabinieri lieutenant accused of taking camorra money for two decades
who: Camorra clans running a usury ring
rank: Luogotenente of the carabinieri, Bagnoli company, Naples
d: Giuseppe Bucolo, 56, a carabinieri lieutenant originally from Catania and serving with the Bagnoli company in Naples, was placed under house arrest by his own colleagues in an investigation into a usury ring run by the camorra, and is accused of corruption. LiveSicilia reports that the custody order describes a public official who is said to have pocketed camorra money, clan after clan, for almost two decades. A collaborator with justice, Gennaro Carra, also linked him to the wounding of the police superintendent Nicola Barbato, shot on 24 September 2015 during an anti-racket operation by an affiliate, Raffaele Rende, who was later arrested and convicted: Carra said Rende took the pistol to Antonio Volpe, later killed, and that Volpe called Bucolo to make it disappear.
inside: Prosecutors say camorra clans kept a serving carabinieri officer on their money for years, and used him to make a weapon used against a policeman disappear.
cite: LiveSicilia, 'Giro di usura a Napoli: il carabiniere arrestato e catanese', 25 October 2022

n: Border police at Cayenne airport ran cocaine mules past their own checks
org_label: Cocaine trafficking network between French Guiana and Orly
rank: Eleven former adjunct officers of the border police, Felix-Eboue airport, Cayenne
d: Former border police officers at Cayenne's Felix-Eboue airport in French Guiana were sentenced by the Creteil criminal court to up to eight years' firm imprisonment over a large cocaine trafficking network to mainland France, with fines of up to 80,000 euros, temporary bans from airports and permanent bans from public-service employment. Twenty people were tried, including eleven former adjunct officers of the airport. Mules carried cocaine hidden in rum containers, the drug diluted in the liquid, which the officers placed in the false ceilings of the airport toilets, then swapped for containers bought in the duty-free shop. The officers made sure coloured stickers exempting passengers from pre-boarding checks were on the mules' passports, getting round the '100% passenger control' regime set up at Cayenne in October 2022.
inside: A trafficking network worked through the airport's own border police, who used their control of boarding checks to send its couriers through unsearched.
cite: Outremers360, 'Trafic de cocaine depuis la Guyane: jusqu'a 8 ans de prison ferme pour d'anciens policiers', 14 March 2025

n: Guardia Civil lieutenant jailed for selling police data to traffickers
rank: Lieutenant, Unidad de Seguridad Ciudadana of the Guardia Civil, Seville
d: The provincial court of Seville sentenced a Guardia Civil lieutenant to eight years and ten months after a jury found him guilty of continuous bribery, attempted drug trafficking and two attempted thefts; he was acquitted of revealing secrets. The jury found that the officer, posted in 2019 and 2020 to Seville's Unidad de Seguridad Ciudadana, learned through a second defendant of that man's contacts with people in the drug trade and, to get inside the organisations and obtain money, agreed to supply the police information asked of him, searching the databases his post reached and trying to draw in an undercover officer who could reach the CITCO organised-crime database. On 7 August 2020 the three took 29 bales of hashish from the Guardia Civil's Seville headquarters.
inside: Traffickers paid a serving Guardia Civil lieutenant, who searched police databases for them and tried to recruit a colleague with access to the national organised-crime files.
cite: General Council of the Judiciary (CGPJ), press note of the TSJ of Andalucia, Ceuta and Melilla, 25 March 2024, on the Audiencia Provincial de Sevilla judgment of 14 March 2024

n: Guardia Civil sergeant opened Donana park to hashish landings for pay
org_label: Hashish trafficking organisations landing on the Donana coast
rank: Sergeant of the Guardia Civil's SEPRONA detachment in Donana National Park
d: The provincial court of Huelva sentenced a sergeant of the Guardia Civil's SEPRONA environmental unit detachment in Donana National Park to three years and three months and barred him from the force, in a judgment agreed by the parties in March before the trial, with two fines of 23,500 euros, for trafficking in drugs not causing grave harm, bribery, membership of a criminal group and revelation of secrets. The court found that from at least 2016 until his arrest in May 2018 he was a fundamental link for organisations landing hashish in his policing area: he told them which days a landing could be made safely, had the park gate opened for the vehicles, intercepted Guardia Civil radio traffic and supplied patrol rosters.
inside: Hashish organisations paid the sergeant who policed Donana, and he used that control of the park and its patrol information to time and cover their landings.
cite: LegalToday (Aranzadi LA LEY), citing Europa Press, 3 April 2025, on the Audiencia Provincial de Huelva judgment

n: Whole Phagwara police crime team held over a bribe to free a smuggler
org_label: A drug smuggler known as Hani
who: A drug smuggler buying his own release
rank: Crime Investigation Agency team, Phagwara, Punjab Police: in-charge sub-inspector, two assistant sub-inspectors and a constable
d: The entire team of the Crime Investigation Agency of Phagwara, in Punjab's Kapurthala district, was arrested on Friday 23 May 2025 for allegedly taking a bribe of 2.5 lakh rupees to release a notorious drug smuggler, Hani, who was in their custody. The Free Press Journal names the arrested officials as the unit's in-charge, sub-inspector Bisman Singh Mahi, assistant sub-inspectors Nirmal Kumar and Jaswinder Singh, and constable Jagrup Singh. The Crime Investigation Agency is a state police investigation unit. According to media reports there had been several complaints about the officers' conduct, after which senior officers watched them, and they were caught red-handed on accepting the money. The Jalandhar range deputy inspector general, Naveen Singla, confirmed the arrests and said the department has zero tolerance for corruption.
inside: A smuggler's money reached the whole police unit holding him, which was about to use its own custody powers to let him go.
cite: The Free Press Journal, 'Punjab News: Entire Phagwara CIA Team Held For Taking Rs 2.5 Lakh Bribe To Free Drug Smuggler', 23 May 2025

n: Customs zone chief passed a cartel's drug couriers without scrutiny
org_label: Drug cartel operated from Thailand and the United States
who: A Thailand- and US-based drug cartel
rank: Customs superintendent heading the western zone; two Navi Mumbai police constables
d: Navi Mumbai police arrested ten people in a drug network supplied by air courier from the United States and Thailand, among them Prashant Gaur, 40, the customs superintendent heading the western zone. Deputy commissioner Amit Kale said couriers reached Indian Postal, which sent those addressed to Maharashtra to the zonal customs office Gaur headed, and that Gaur was given the consignment numbers in advance and passed them without raising any alarm; he was allegedly paid one lakh rupees for every kilogram. Two constables, Sachin Bhalerao of Kharghar police station and Sanjay Phulkar of the Anti Narcotics Unit, were also arrested; police sources say they were tasked with protecting the cartel from cases and arrests and had been paid about ten lakh rupees in total.
inside: Prosecutors say the cartel bought the customs officer who screened its parcels and two police officers to keep cases away, so the state cleared and guarded its imports.
cite: The Free Press Journal, 'Navi Mumbai Drug Racket: Customs Superintendent, 2 Cops Among 10 Held', 30 April 2025

n: Haitian gangs placed informants inside remittance houses and taxed payouts
rank: Agents working in remittance houses (money-transfer outlets)
d: The United Nations Panel of Experts on Haiti reported that gangs have recruited agents working in some of Haiti's remittance houses as informants. Remittance houses are the outlets where Haitians collect money sent by relatives abroad, and the Panel notes that more than 70 per cent of those transfers come from the United States. According to four victims of gang extortion interviewed by the Panel, the recruited agents identify recipients of significant amounts of cash and pass the information to gang members, who then waylay those people away from the collection points. One victim from Kenscoff said that on 15 February 2025 an agent deducted a mandatory US$30 “facilitation” fee and made him sign two registers, one official and one untitled register belonging to the gang controlling the area.
inside: A UN panel reports that gangs recruited staff inside money-transfer firms as informants and fee collectors, so the outlets' counters worked for the gangs.
cite: United Nations Panel of Experts on Haiti, final report S/2026/241, paras. 53–54 and annex 15 (“The dynamics of gang revenue collection”)

n: Exam-fixing ring paid at least €81,000 inside Romania's road authority
org_label: Organised criminal group of a company administrator and a driver-training centre owner
rank: Director general and examination commission members, Autoritatea Rutieră Română (A.R.R.)
d: Romania's National Anticorruption Directorate sent to trial, in preventive detention, Anton Cristian, director general of the Autoritatea Rutieră Română, the state body that examines and certifies professional transport drivers. Prosecutors allege that in the second half of 2024 he formed an organised criminal group with R.B.A., the administrator of a commercial company, and D.D.R.I., who held a vocational training centre, to rig the authority's certificate examinations. The indictment says Anton Cristian allegedly received at least €81,000 from R.B.A. over examinations in Bucharest and Arad county, where people from R.B.A.'s circle sat the computer test for favoured candidates and answer sheets were handed over in the examination room, passing at least 149 candidates; a further €34,000 allegedly bought the appointment of compliant examiners for at least 117 more.
inside: Prosecutors say an outside businessman's money reached the head of Romania's road authority, so its examination commissions passed candidates who had paid rather than qualified.
cite: Direcția Națională Anticorupție (Romania), press release no. 580/I-36, 20 August 2026

n: Clan men inside a Catania port terminal firm moved cocaine containers
rank: Employees with operational roles in the port area, Europea Servizi Terminalistici Srl
d: The court in Catania placed Europea Servizi Terminalistici Srl under judicial administration for one year in March 2026. The firm, registered in Palermo, handles container and cargo movement at five Sicilian ports. Judicial administration does not seize a company; it temporarily replaces its managers with court-appointed administrators. Catania's prosecutor, Francesco Curcio, said members of the Pillera-Puntina clan operating in the port area had allegedly helped cocaine arriving on South American cargo ships in and then out again, for 30 to 40 per cent of each load. Investigators pointed to Angelo Sanfilippo, a long-serving employee, and three of his sons, all working in the port for the firm. Six custody orders were issued in the first months of 2025, and at least three imports totalling 215 kilograms were established.
inside: A Catania clan's men allegedly held operational jobs inside a port terminal company, and the court found the firm's structures were used to bring cocaine through.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 5 March 2026, reporting the Tribunale di Catania prevention measure and Catania prosecutor Francesco Curcio

n: PCC money built up São Paulo bus firm Transunião to qualify for city tenders
rank: Informal financial management and command group, Transunião Transportes
d: São Paulo state prosecutors from the Gaeco organised-crime group allege that about 50 million reais belonging to the PCC criminal faction was hidden inside the bus company Transunião Transportes as capital contributions and profit distributions, and used to build up the firm's capital so that it would qualify economically for the city's urban public transport tender. In a 291-page filing the prosecutors say city councillor Senival Moura, though holding no formal directorship, controlled the company's financial management and decisions on how it ran, alongside its director Lourival de França Monário. A technical report records that between 10 October 2018 and 23 July 2020 eleven company bank accounts took in 545.47 million reais. Moura was arrested in June 2026 and again in October; his defence stated its disagreement with the order.
inside: Prosecutors say the PCC's drug money was put into a bus company and its people ran the firm's finances, so the company bid for city routes on the faction's capital.
cite: Diario de Pernambuco / Estadão Conteúdo, 28 October 2026, on the Ministério Público de São Paulo (Gaeco) filing in the second phase of Operação Última Parada

n: Zagreb airport employee indicted with a cocaine ring using private jets
org_label: Cocaine trafficking ring led by Miroslav Anicic
who: Cocaine trafficking ring led by Miroslav Anicic
rank: Employee of Zagreb airport
d: Croatia's Bureau for Combating Corruption and Organized Crime, USKOK, indicted nine members of an international cocaine smuggling ring in April 2012 over trafficking from the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic to Europe between the autumn of 2010 and April 2011, using rented private jets. OCCRP reported that among the defendants was an employee of Zagreb airport who worked with the gang, together with employees at the Salzburg and Stuttgart airports who helped circumvent the cargo control for the flights carrying the cocaine. According to the indictment the group bought 74 kilograms of cocaine in January 2011 and flew it by private jet to Zagreb, where at least 59 kilograms were then sold in Croatia and Slovenia. The defendants were indicted at the Zagreb County Court.
inside: According to the indictment a trafficking ring had an airport employee on its side, so cargo checks let its cocaine flights through for the gang.
cite: OCCRP, “Nine International Drug Smugglers Indicted in Croatia”, 16 April 2012, reporting the USKOK indictment

n: Cocaine network used Tocumen airport's staff and facilities for baggage swaps
org_label: Cocaine trafficking network behind operations Eros and Colibrí
who: Trafficking network in operations Eros and Colibrí
rank: Staff of Tocumen International Airport
d: Panama's Superior Appeals Court for the First Judicial District confirmed on 17 December 2025 the provisional detention of thirty-two people over drug offences that prosecutors say were committed using the facilities and personnel of Tocumen International Airport, the state-owned airport company serving Panama City. The detainees were arrested in operations Eros and Colibrí, run by the specialised drugs prosecution service with the national police at several points around the country, and the case rests on investigative work carried out by the Public Ministry since 2023. The method under investigation is the “colillaje” of suitcases, in which baggage tags are switched. The thirty-two are charged with conspiracy to commit drug offences and with international drug trafficking, and were represented by twenty private lawyers.
inside: Prosecutors say a trafficking network worked through the airport company's own staff, so baggage handling at Tocumen sent the network's cocaine abroad.
cite: TVN Panamá, 18 December 2025, on the ruling of the Tribunal Superior de Apelaciones del Primer Distrito Judicial de Panamá

n: Mafia convict's firm accredited by Messina's health authority after pressure
org_label: Carmelo Vetro, convicted mafia boss of Favara, and businessman Giovanni Aveni
who: Carmelo Vetro and businessman Giovanni Aveni
rank: Director general and administrative director, Azienda Sanitaria Provinciale di Messina
d: Palermo prosecutors are investigating Salvatore Iacolino, head of strategic planning at Sicily's regional health department and later director general of the Messina Policlinico, for external complicity in a mafia association and aggravated corruption. They allege he pressed the director general and administrative director of the Azienda Sanitaria Provinciale di Messina, the provincial health authority, to accredit Arcobaleno srl of Milazzo, a company tied to the businessman Giovanni Aveni, through whom Carmelo Vetro is said to have moved his interests to Messina. Vetro has served a heavy sentence as mafia boss of Favara. The accreditation came through the previous October. Iacolino resigned when he learned of the investigation; his lawyers say the procedure was regular, no money passed, no accreditation was revoked and Vetro's intercepted claims were boasting.
inside: Prosecutors say a convicted mafia boss's associate reached a provincial health authority through a senior health official, who pressed its directors to accredit the associate's firm.
cite: LiveSicilia, 16 March 2026 and 30 March 2026, on the Palermo prosecutors' investigation and the defence filing at the Tribunale del riesame

n: Fourteen Gioia Tauro port workers cleared cocaine containers with fake seals
who: 'Ndrangheta Bruzzaniti group and a Naples group (Imperiale and Carbone)
rank: Teams of port operators handling containers at Gioia Tauro
d: The Tre Croci investigation by the anti-mafia prosecutors in Reggio Calabria led to the arrest of 36 people accused of mafia association and international drug trafficking. Prosecutors describe an alliance between a Naples group, around Raffaele Imperiale and Bruno Carbone, and an 'ndrangheta group linked to the Bruzzaniti family, importing South American cocaine through Gioia Tauro. Inside the port the organisation had teams of port operators who recovered the cocaine from transiting ships and moved it out. Fourteen corrupted port workers are accused of running a fraudulent handling of containers so as to evade customs checks, by fitting counterfeit seals in place of the seals meant to guarantee the cargo. In January 2024 prosecutors asked for sentences of between six and twenty years in the abbreviated trial.
inside: Prosecutors say two crime groups had paid port workers inside the container terminal, so the port's own handling and seals passed their cocaine through customs.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 17 January 2024, on the abbreviated trial arising from the DDA Reggio Calabria “Tre Croci” investigation

n: Bank of America banker opened 36 accounts for a cartel-linked drug network
org_label: Drug trafficking organisation with ties to a Mexican drug cartel
who: Drug trafficking organisation tied to a Mexican cartel
rank: Personal banker, Bank of America
d: Presiliano Garcia, a personal banker at Bank of America, was convicted of misprision of a felony and sentenced to three years' probation. Prosecutors said that between 2012 and March 2016 he opened about 36 bank accounts used by his co-defendants to structure deposits and funnel money from places around the United States, including Buffalo, to accounts in California. A total of $8,359,223 arrived in roughly 1,092 cash deposits, mostly structured between $8,000 and $9,990, made in fifteen states. Bank of America identified about 205 suspect customers potentially linked to him. Garcia knew a structuring felony was being committed but filed no suspicious activity reports. He was one of seven defendants in a narcotics operation stretching from Sinaloa, Mexico to western New York; all seven were convicted.
inside: A drug network's money was moved through accounts a bank's own employee opened for it, and he kept the bank's reporting system quiet for them.
cite: United States Attorney's Office, Western District of New York, press release, 19 June 2019

n: Trafficker paid a JetBlue flight attendant to carry cocaine past crew checks
rank: Flight attendant, JetBlue Airways
d: Gaston Brown, a Jamaican national, was sentenced in July 2022 to 165 months in federal prison for supplying a JetBlue flight attendant with nearly 60 pounds of cocaine. A jury convicted him in February 2018 on all charges. On six occasions between October 2015 and March 2016 Brown paid the flight attendant, Marsha Gay Reynolds, to carry cocaine and drug money in suitcases through “known crewmember” checkpoints at Los Angeles International Airport and New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport, where crew were subject to much lighter screening. On 18 March 2016 Brown supplied her with about 27 kilograms of cocaine; selected for extra screening at LAX, she dropped her luggage and fled. Reynolds pleaded guilty in December 2016.
inside: A cocaine supplier paid an airline's cabin crew member, so her staff pass and lighter crew screening carried his drugs and cash across the country.
cite: United States Attorney's Office, Central District of California, press release, 7 July 2022

n: Delta ramp staff at Atlanta airport took in a drug bag from Mexico City
org_label: Drug importing group around Luis Marroquin
rank: Ramp shift performance leader and ramp employees, Delta Air Lines
d: Three former Delta Air Lines employees were sentenced in March 2013 for conspiring to possess methamphetamine and heroin with intent to distribute. On 13 January 2012 a Delta agent found an unclaimed suitcase at a baggage carousel in Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport, tagged for flight 364 from Mexico City; Customs and Border Protection officers found packages of suspected narcotics inside, later valued at more than $614,000. Carlos Springer led the shift of ramp employees who unloaded that flight, and agents found coded text messages between him and Luis Marroquin around the time it landed. Kelvin Rondon was filmed unloading the flight while off duty and without authorisation to work it. Prosecutors said Marroquin recruited Rondon, who was to be paid $500 per package.
inside: A drug importing group recruited airline ramp staff, so the men unloading an international flight were working to take its drug bag off for them.
cite: United States Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia, press release, 6 March 2013

n: Traffickers recruited an airline worker to walk cocaine past Las Vegas security
rank: Airline employee at McCarran International Airport
d: Bryan M. Bledsoe, an airline employee working at McCarran International Airport in Las Vegas, was sentenced in February 2016 to 36 months in prison after pleading guilty to conspiring to distribute cocaine. Prosecutors said conspirators recruited him to help them bypass security with cocaine: they handed him bags holding multiple kilograms, and he used his airport employee credentials to carry them in without screening, then returned the unscanned bags to co-conspirators inside the secure area. Bledsoe admitted involvement in shipments of between five and fifteen kilograms. The conspiracy began as early as 2012 and ran until June 2014, moving cocaine to Anchorage and more than one million dollars in cash proceeds back out of Alaska.
inside: A trafficking group recruited an airline employee at the airport, so his staff credentials took their cocaine round the security screening it was meant to pass.
cite: United States Attorney's Office, District of Alaska, press release, 2 February 2016

n: Cape Air worker used his airport clearance to pass four kilos of cocaine
org_label: Cocaine smuggling pair including Roy Hodge III
rank: Employee of Cape Air at Cyril E. King Airport
d: Wayne Fahie, an employee of the airline Cape Air, pleaded guilty in the District Court of the Virgin Islands in February 2018 to conspiracy to possess cocaine with intent to distribute. According to the plea agreement, on 30 July 2017 Fahie and his co-defendant Roy Hodge III tried to smuggle four kilograms of cocaine through Cyril E. King Airport on St Thomas. Fahie used his security clearance to reach the men's lavatory in the airport departure lounge, where he met Hodge and the cocaine changed hands. Officers watching saw Hodge stay inside for about 33 minutes while Fahie went in and out three times, each time with a bulge in his pocket. Hodge pleaded guilty on 1 February 2018 and sentencing was set for 7 June 2018.
inside: A smuggler used an airline employee's security clearance to reach a sealed part of the airport, so the airline's own pass moved his cocaine.
cite: United States Attorney's Office, District of the Virgin Islands, press release, 6 February 2018

n: Airport services staff in San Juan cleared 20 tons of cocaine for traffickers
org_label: Drug trafficking organisations using Luis Muñoz Marín airport
who: Drug trafficking organisations shipping through San Juan
rank: Baggage handler and ramp employee of Airport Aviation Services; employee of the airport security company
d: A federal grand jury in Puerto Rico indicted twelve defendants in February 2017 for conspiracy to possess cocaine with intent to distribute. Prosecutors said that from 1998 through 2016 they helped smuggle approximately 20 tons of cocaine through Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in suitcases each holding at least 8 to 15 kilograms, sometimes using as many as five couriers on a single flight. Javier Ortiz, a baggage handler and ramp employee of Airport Aviation Services, collected suitcases he knew held cocaine from couriers at the check-in counter, put them through the X-ray machines watched by the indicted screeners, then took them to their flights. Another defendant, who worked for the airport security company, was a source of supply of cocaine to the organisation.
inside: Prosecutors say trafficking organisations had paid staff inside the airport's handling and security firms, so baggage screening and loading at San Juan served the shipments.
cite: United States Attorney's Office, District of Puerto Rico, press release, 13 February 2017

n: Lead baggage handler took cocaine off flights at Newark Liberty airport
org_label: Multi-year cocaine smuggling conspiracy at Newark Liberty airport
rank: Lead baggage handler for a commercial airline, Newark Liberty International Airport
d: Tyrone Woolaston, a lead baggage handler for a commercial airline at Newark Liberty International Airport, was sentenced in December 2020 to 180 months in prison. A jury convicted him in February 2019 of conspiring to distribute more than five kilograms of cocaine and of using a firearm in furtherance of cocaine trafficking. Prosecutors said that from about 2013 through February 2018 he abused his secure access to restricted areas to take suitcases holding multiple kilograms of cocaine off international flights and carry them through the airport for distribution in New York City. In an undercover operation a confidential source arranged a shipment with him, and on 10 February 2018 he carried a suitcase of sham cocaine off a flight from the Cayman Islands, evading customs screening.
inside: A smuggling conspiracy had its man inside the airport workforce, so his secure access lifted cocaine off international flights past customs for them.
cite: United States Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York, press release, 11 December 2020

n: American Airlines worker crossed DFW security with bags for a drug group
org_label: Drug distribution group around Moniteveti Katoa
rank: Employee of American Airlines at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport
d: Janelle Isaacs, a former American Airlines employee, was sentenced in December 2016 to 72 months in federal prison after pleading guilty to conspiring to distribute at least five kilograms of cocaine. Court documents say four defendants used their jobs at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, or contacted people who held such jobs, to bypass security and carry kilogram quantities of a substance represented to be cocaine onto commercial flights, in what they did not know was an undercover operation. The conspiracy ran from about 18 April 2013 to 14 July 2015. Isaacs admits she suspected her husband, Moniteveti Katoa, was moving a controlled substance, performed at least one dry run, and on 8 December 2014 took a backpack past security for him. He was sentenced to 188 months.
inside: A drug distribution group used airline staff jobs at the airport, so an employee's pass carried its bags round the security screening and onto flights.
cite: United States Attorney's Office, Northern District of Texas, press release, 2 December 2016

n: 'Ndrangheta ran a hidden bank through companies it controlled near Milan
rank: Shell companies Solution Srl (formerly CM Costruzioni), PG Service and Easytech, run from the offices of Ge.Ma. at Pero
d: Milan's anti-mafia prosecutors allege a so-called hidden bank of the 'ndrangheta: an organisation that supplied illegal financial services to people linked to organised crime through shell companies, Italian and foreign accounts and cryptocurrency wallets, run from an organised structure inside the offices of the firm Ge.Ma. at Pero, just outside Milan. The custody order signed by investigating judge Luca Milani describes companies held at the organisation's disposal, among them Solution Srl, formerly CM Costruzioni, PG Service and Easytech. Investigators traced at least €27,182,458 moving from those companies to the Canadian blockchain infrastructure firm ALT 5 Sigma between 23 October 2024 and 17 July 2025, including from a Lithuanian Revolut account in Solution Srl's name, and then converted into cryptocurrency.
inside: Prosecutors allege a mafia-linked group held companies at its disposal and ran a clandestine banking service from inside a firm's offices, moving criminal money abroad.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 16 November 2026, on the custody order of investigating judge Luca Milani in the Milan DDA “banca occulta” investigation

n: Three mafia families secretly controlled New York waste-hauling companies
who: Genovese, Gambino and Luchese crime families
rank: Waste disposal businesses held through nominee owners, New York metropolitan area and New Jersey
d: Federal prosecutors in Manhattan unsealed charges against 32 people in January 2013 over what they called the Waste Disposal Enterprise, in which members and associates of three Cosa Nostra families, the Genovese, Gambino and Luchese, worked together to control waste disposal businesses in the New York City area and several New Jersey counties. Because the men were either banned from the industry or unlikely to be licensed, they concealed themselves behind firms officially owned by people with no known mafia links, whom the indictment calls Controlled Owners. They then dictated which rubbish collection stops a hauling company could use, extorted protection payments, and settled at sit-downs which faction controlled which company and on what terms control passed between them. Twenty-one of the 32 defendants had been convicted by May 2014.
inside: Three mafia families owned waste companies through front owners, so the firms' routes, prices and transfers were decided by the families, not their nominal owners.
cite: United States Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York, press releases of 16 January 2013 and 13 May 2014 (https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdny/pr/two-members-genovese-crime-family-sentenced-manhattan-federal-court-loansharking)

n: Fraud ring recruited four Wells Fargo staff to sell it customer account data
org_label: Bank fraud ring led by Ronald Reed
who: Bank fraud ring led by Ronald Reed
rank: Four Wells Fargo Bank employees
d: A federal grand jury in Los Angeles indicted eight people in late September 2015 over a scheme that prosecutors say caused Wells Fargo losses of about $1.4 million. According to the indictments, Ronald Reed recruited four bank employees in 2013 and 2014, asked them to look up the bank's computer records, and bought personal identifying information belonging to customers, including dates of birth, account numbers, driving licence numbers and social security numbers. Unidentified “runners” then used fake identity documents to impersonate those customers and withdraw substantial sums in cash at branches across southern California and in Minnesota and Nevada, in some cases also depositing worthless cheques to get cash back. Three defendants had not been identified when the charges were announced. Wells Fargo cooperated with the investigation.
inside: The indictments allege a fraud ring paid bank employees to open the bank's own customer records to it, so its impostors could draw money out.
cite: United States Attorney's Office, Central District of California, press release, 6 October 2015

n: International fraudsters had 26 Western Union agents convicted of working for them
rank: Western Union agents in the United States and Canada
d: Western Union, a money transfer business based in Englewood, Colorado, agreed in January 2017 to forfeit $586 million and admitted criminal violations including aiding and abetting wire fraud. Announcing the settlement, the United States Attorney for the Middle District of Pennsylvania said that since 2001 his office had charged and convicted 26 Western Union agents in the United States and Canada who conspired with international fraudsters to defraud tens of thousands of American residents through mass marketing schemes. A separate prosecution had a Western Union agent plead guilty to structuring transactions, conduct the prosecutor said the company knew about for at least five years; company documents indicated its employees fought to keep that agent and other high-volume independent agents in New York.
inside: Fraud networks worked through the money transfer company's own agents, who took in and paid out victims' money, and the company kept the busiest of them on.
cite: United States Department of Justice, press release, 19 January 2017 (deferred prosecution agreement with The Western Union Company)

n: Mass-marketing fraudsters ran a group of corrupt MoneyGram agents in Toronto
rank: MoneyGram agents in the Toronto area
d: James E. Ugoh of Toronto was resentenced in January 2014 to 151 months in prison as the former leader of a group of corrupt Canadian MoneyGram agents who helped defraud thousands of Americans of $4 million between January 2004 and April 2009. Prosecutors said Canadian mass-marketing fraudsters sent thousands of letters and counterfeit cheques to Americans, falsely promising cash prizes, loans and commissions; recipients were tricked into depositing the worthless cheques and then sending money for supposed taxes and fees through MoneyGram. Ugoh led a corrupt group of agents who conspired with the fraudsters to intercept, launder and distribute those transfers. He and three other Toronto-area agents were indicted in October 2009, extradited to Harrisburg, Pennsylvania and pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit mail fraud, wire fraud and money laundering.
inside: Fraud networks had the money transfer company's own Toronto agents collecting victims' payments for them inside the firm's payout system.
cite: United States Attorney's Office, Middle District of Pennsylvania, press release, 29 January 2014

n: Piromalli clan supplied and staffed Reggio Calabria's health authority
who: Piromalli clan, through the Tripodi family
rank: Medical and paramedical staff handling supply requests, and district directors, Azienda Sanitaria Provinciale di Reggio Calabria
d: Reggio Calabria's anti-mafia prosecutors closed their inquiry, named Chirone, into the Piromalli clan's infiltration of the provincial health authority through the Tripodi family, notifying 17 suspects. In March 2021 the investigation had led to 13 arrests, among them doctors and managers of the authority, and the seizure of companies valued at €8 million. Prosecutors say the clan won supply contracts at the authority through firms linked to the Tripodi family, Minerva srl, Mct Distribution & Service srl and Lewis Medica srl, using direct awards and a tested system of corrupting the staff who requested supplies, with kickbacks of 2.5 to 5 per cent and gifts such as designer handbags. The chief prosecutor said the clans altered or even imposed the appointment of district directors. The facts date to 2018.
inside: Prosecutors say a mafia clan sold supplies to a public health authority through its own firms, with corrupted staff and imposed managers deciding inside what was ordered.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 12 October 2021 and 23 March 2021, on the DDA Reggio Calabria “Chirone” investigation (https://www.corrieredellacalabria.it/2021/03/23/bombardieri-nomine-dei-dirigenti-dellasp-imposte-dai-piromalli/)

n: 'Ndrangheta cartel got its man made captain of an MSC container ship
who: Cartel of the Piromalli, Alvaro, Crea and Reggio Ionian families
rank: Captain of the MSC vessel Poh Lin
d: Operation Vulcano, run by the anti-mafia prosecutors in Reggio Calabria, uncovered a network set up by clans of the Piana di Gioia Tauro to import cocaine from Latin America. The Guardia di Finanza found that one of the main nodes was a ship's captain, Gabriello Salvarese, who, although long retired, had obtained from the shipping company MSC the command of the vessel Poh Lin on the California Express route, which calls at Cristóbal and Balboa in Panama. Prosecutors said the Piromalli, Alvaro and Crea clans and some Reggio Ionian families had formed a single cartel to buy large quantities of cocaine, and planned to take the load off onto a fishing boat at the edge of territorial waters, a manoeuvre only the captain could authorise.
inside: Prosecutors say a cartel of mafia families had its own man given command of a shipping line's vessel, so cocaine could be handed over at sea.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 14 July 2016, on operation Vulcano of the DDA Reggio Calabria and the Guardia di finanza

n: Casalesi-backed firm held the ambulance monopoly at Aversa's hospital
rank: Croce Aversana, the ambulance firm carrying patients to and from the Moscati hospital
d: In May 2018 the court in Naples ordered the arrest of Luigi Belfiore, owner of the ambulance firm Croce Aversana, and of Augusto Bianco, a businessman the local news site InterNapoli described as a camorrista tied to the Schiavone clan of Casal di Principe. Investigators said the Casalesi clan had favoured the Croce Aversana's monopoly, so that patients reached the Moscati hospital in Aversa only in ambulances owned by Belfiore, while competing firms were left with nothing. Belfiore, then 62, was said to be protected and promoted by Bianco, whose father Cesare was a trusted man of the boss Francesco Schiavone. The charges ranged from unfair competition to camorra association with the aggravating circumstance of intimidation. Both men were held in the high-security prison at Santa Maria Capua Vetere.
inside: Investigators say a camorra clan backed one ambulance firm and squeezed out rivals, so emergency transport to a public hospital ran through a company it protected.
cite: InterNapoli.it, 14 May 2018, on the Naples anti-mafia prosecutors' investigation and the arrest order of the Tribunale di Napoli

n: Chase banker sold customer account data used to loot the accounts
org_label: Buyers of stolen bank customer data
who: Buyers of stolen bank customer data
rank: Personal banker, JP Morgan Chase Bank
d: Peter Persaud, a former personal banker at JP Morgan Chase Bank, was sentenced in August 2018 to 48 months in prison for aggravated identity theft in connection with access device fraud, having pleaded guilty in March 2017. According to the publicly filed documents and the facts presented at sentencing, from 2011 to 2015 he sold personal identifying information and account information belonging to bank customers to others, or used it himself, in order to make unauthorised withdrawals from the accounts. The scheme was exposed when he sold the information to a confidential informant in 2014 and to an undercover law enforcement officer in 2015. He told the undercover officer he had to “take it easy” because Chase might notice he had accessed all the accounts that “got hit”.
inside: Outside buyers paid a bank's own personal banker for its customer records, and money was then taken from those customers' accounts without their authority.
cite: United States Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York, press release, 10 August 2018

n: Haitian prosecutor freed the handlers of an ammunition shipment
rank: General Prosecutor, Port-de-Paix
d: On 1 July 2022 Haitian customs officers found 120,000 rounds of ammunition in a container landed at the Port-de-Paix wharf from the United States. One man was arrested as he tried to collect the cargo for a second man who would distribute it. Sources close to the investigation told the UN Panel of Experts that police did not obtain from the Port-de-Paix General Prosecutor the papers they needed to search the ship, and that firearms hidden on board were taken off that night. Two days after the arrest the prosecutor released the second man and the ship's owner ‘against all odds’. He was later arrested on suspicion of corruption and illicit firearms trafficking, and said two Ministry of Justice officials had asked him to free the suspects.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2023/674, annex 30, ‘Case 2: Miss Lili One – Seizure in Port-de-Paix’ (October 2023)
inside: Arms traffickers' interests reached the prosecutor's office at Port-de-Paix, which released two suspects and did not supply the papers police needed to search their ship.

n: Bolivian prosecutors freed trafficker Marset and returned seized goods
rank: Departmental prosecutor for Santa Cruz, Ministerio Público
d: In October 2026 the Bolivian government said former officials of the Ministerio Público, the prosecution service, had been detained over what it called a covert network inside the Fiscalía. It justified acting directly on the ground that the offence was a continuing one, and cited as a precedent of impunity the prompt release of the cocaine trafficker Sebastián Marset in 2023 and the return of goods seized from him, when Roger Mariaca was departmental prosecutor for Santa Cruz. Mariaca is among those held. Fourteen people were detained, all in the custody of the counter-narcotics force FELCN awaiting hearings, and the government said they would be tried in Bolivia's ordinary courts.
cite: Correo del Sur (Bolivia), 1 October 2026
inside: A cocaine network's interests reached the Santa Cruz prosecution office, which the government says a covert ring inside the Fiscalía used to free Marset and hand back his property.

n: Bari judge De Benedictis sold releases to mafia-linked defendants
rank: Investigating judge (gip), Tribunale di Bari
d: Giuseppe De Benedictis, an investigating judge at the court in Bari, was arrested on 24 April 2021 with the Bari criminal lawyer Giancarlo Chiariello, who is accused of paying him for liberty rulings favouring his clients. Those clients included people belonging to local mafia clans or otherwise linked to organised crime in Bari and Foggia. In a wiretapped conversation Danilo Della Malva, a convicted member of the ‘mala garganica’, said he had spent thirty thousand euros and ‘bought the judge in Bari’; he was moved to house arrest in April 2020. Investigators found 58,000 euros at the judge's home. De Benedictis resigned and confessed to taking bribes; prosecutors allege four episodes.
cite: Il Giornale, 25 April 2021; Il Sussidiario (arrest report); La Notizia, 5 April 2024 (confession and committal)
inside: A criminal lawyer's money reached a Bari investigating judge, who granted release and house arrest to clients belonging to or linked with local mafia clans.

n: Bacolod court clerk dismissed for selling favours to litigants
org_label: Litigants in criminal cases, including a drug defendant's family
rank: Clerk, Regional Trial Court, Bacolod City
d: The Supreme Court of the Philippines, sitting en banc, dismissed Bee Pee G. Viñas, a clerk at the Regional Trial Court in Bacolod City, in a per curiam decision dated 3 June 2026. It found gross misconduct, citing her admission that she had told a respondent in an estafa, or fraud, case that a warrant had been issued against that person, and evidence that she solicited money from litigants. An elderly woman identified Viñas as the person who demanded money to speed up the release of her grandchild, who faced drug charges. An accused said a female court employee had offered to halve his bail for cash. She denied trading in favourable orders.
cite: Daily Tribune (Philippines), 17 November 2026, reporting the Supreme Court per curiam decision of 3 June 2026
inside: Money from people with cases in court reached a Bacolod court clerk, who the Supreme Court found tipped off a wanted litigant and solicited payments.

n: Milan court driver held in a mafia 'hidden bank' laundering case
rank: Driver handling seized assets, investigating judge's office, Milan
d: On 21 October 2026 the Guardia di Finanza of Milan and Monza Brianza said it had dismantled a ‘banca occulta’, a hidden bank, run for organised crime, and was carrying out 30 arrests on a measure requested in a note signed by the Milan prosecutor Marcello Viola. The charge is criminal association aggravated by the mafia method and by assisting the mafia, the aggravating element concerning the ‘Ndrangheta and the Foggia groups known as the ‘fourth mafia’. Among those arrested and placed under house arrest is Domenico Bruno, a driver in Milan's investigating judge's office who dealt with assets under seizure, accused of unauthorised access to a computer system.
cite: Open (open.online), 21 October 2026
inside: A mafia-linked laundering network had a man inside the Milan court office that handles seized assets; he is accused of unlawfully entering its computer system.

n: Rome court mole bought secret wiretap and case information
org_label: People under investigation who paid for secret court information
rank: Official of the wiretap office, Rome public prosecutor's office
d: Camilla Marianera, a trainee lawyer in Rome, and her partner Jacopo De Vivo were arrested on 14 February 2023. Prosecutors alleged that an official in the wiretap office of the Rome public prosecutor's office, whose identity the custody order left unknown, was paid to reveal the existence of criminal proceedings covered by secrecy and of telephone, environmental and electronic interceptions, at about 300 euros a request; the buyers were people willing to pay to learn what the prosecutor's office was doing. She rejected the accusations when questioned. The eighth section of the court in Rome later sentenced her to six years for corruption in judicial acts; De Vivo had already been given five years.
cite: Il Post, 22 February 2023; La Notizia, 5 April 2024 (sentences)
inside: Money from people under investigation reached an official in the Rome prosecutor's wiretap office, who told them of secret cases and interceptions concerning them.

n: Libya's foreign ministry mobilised for the Sharfeddin fuel network
org_label: Maeen Ali Sharfeddin fuel smuggling network
rank: Officials of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; Libyan Embassy to Cameroon
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya found that a fuel smuggling network led by Maeen Ali Sharfeddin, a Libyan-Turkish dual national, operated in close coordination with the Libyan Arab Armed Forces and could call on officials of Libya's Ministry of Foreign Affairs affiliated with that force. After Panama stopped the network's tanker MT Nobel from transiting the canal in July 2025, forged papers were presented in Panama and in Cameroon, the vessel's flag state. Sharfeddin travelled to Cameroon in November 2025 to try to meet a senior government official, and the Libyan Embassy there requested the meeting by note verbale. The Panel said this showed the network's capacity to mobilise ministry officials.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224, paras. 118–120 and annex 9, section H, ‘Maeen Ali Sharfeddin and the criminal network’ (paras. 44–51)
inside: A fuel smuggling network could move Libya's foreign ministry, whose embassy asked a foreign government for a meeting to help free the network's tanker.

n: Favara mafia boss reached Sicily's regional infrastructure department
rank: Senior manager, regional infrastructure department, Regione Siciliana
d: Gazzetta del Sud reported that Teresi, an engineer who for years held top posts in the Sicilian Region's infrastructure department, was jailed on a charge of corruption aggravated by having favoured Cosa Nostra, together with Carmelo Vetro, the boss of Favara, in an inquiry into infiltration of the regional administration. Investigators say the strategic role he held inside that administration allowed the Favara boss to get into some public works. A regional decree of 31 December 2024 had postponed his retirement. On 18 March 2025 Vetro went to his office with an envelope of cash, and on 20 August 2025 he is alleged to have collected a payment tied to the works.
cite: Gazzetta del Sud, 11 March 2026 (full-text reprint)
inside: A mafia boss's cash reached a senior manager of Sicily's regional infrastructure department, whose position let the boss into regional public works.

n: South Africa's visas and permits sold inside the Home Affairs department
rank: Adjudicators and officials, permit section and Refugee Reception Offices, Department of Home Affairs
d: The Special Investigating Unit, a state body that investigates corruption under presidential proclamation, said at a briefing in February 2026 that officials of South Africa's Department of Home Affairs had been selling visas and permits, and that the immigration system had been treated as a commodity. It said gains exceeding 181 million rand were linked to fraudulent visa applications; that officials were paid between about 300 and 5,000 rand a document, through eWallet transfers, spouses' accounts or in kind; and that four officials earning under 25,000 rand a month had received 16 million rand in deposits. It raided five refugee reception offices.
cite: GroundUp, 23 February 2026 (SIU press briefing); The African Mirror (SIU findings, R181m and R16,313,327)
inside: People buying immigration status paid Home Affairs officials, so the department granted permits and visas to applicants who did not qualify for them.

n: Passport syndicate bribed officials at Krugersdorp Home Affairs
rank: Officials of the Krugersdorp office, Department of Home Affairs
d: Arfan Ahmed, a Pakistani national, was convicted of corruption and of bribing Department of Home Affairs officials at the Krugersdorp Home Affairs office with 45,000 rand, after a sting operation at that office in March 2022 led to his arrest. He is serving eight years for the bribery, and the Krugersdorp Regional Court later sentenced him to a further ten years as the person the department called the kingpin of a passport photo swap, bringing the total to 18 years. Home Affairs said the syndicate aimed to obtain South African passports fraudulently for Pakistani nationals who had no legal right to them. Twelve officials who enabled the scheme were dismissed.
cite: ProtectionWeb, 19 June 2024, reporting the Department of Home Affairs and the Krugersdorp Regional Court
inside: A passport syndicate's cash reached Home Affairs staff at Krugersdorp, who put South African passports into the hands of people with no right to them.

n: Passport syndicate ran two Home Affairs clerks in Queenstown and Durban
rank: Administration clerks, Department of Home Affairs
d: Anda Ngozi and Nomthandazo Eunice Mboyana, administration clerks of the Department of Home Affairs stationed in Queenstown who also worked at Home Affairs offices in Commercial Road, Durban, and in Prospecton, were convicted of more than 300 counts, including fraud and contravening the Immigration Act. Passports were issued to foreign nationals whose identities are unknown to the state, using the details of South African citizens. A syndicate issued the fake passports to foreign nationals for 3,000 to 5,000 rand each and provided the two clerks with accommodation and transport; Mboyana received 125,000 rand. Both pleaded guilty. The Durban Magistrate's Court sentenced Ngozi to 26 years, of which 10 are effective, and Mboyana to 22 years, of which 8 are effective. Mboyana faces another case.
cite: Daily News (IOL), 21 September 2023, reporting the Durban Magistrate's Court
inside: A passport syndicate paid and housed two Home Affairs clerks, who put South African passports in the names of citizens into foreign nationals' hands.

n: Home Affairs clerk swapped passport photos for 1,000 to 5,000 rand each
rank: Department of Home Affairs employee, White River office
d: Nhlanhla Mathebula, 39, a Department of Home Affairs employee stationed at White River in Mpumalanga, was convicted at the Nelspruit Commercial Crimes Court of 12 counts of corruption and 13 counts of contravening the Immigration Act. He processed passport applications for people the report describes as illegal immigrants, swapping the photographs of South African citizens for those of foreign nationals, and was paid between 1,000 and 5,000 rand an application. The report says he went into the office while on leave to do it, and names May 2021. He was given an effective ten years' direct imprisonment, the court ordered that the money he received be recovered from his pension funds, and the passports were forfeited to the state.
cite: Business Report (IOL), 12 October 2023, reporting the Nelspruit Commercial Crimes Court
inside: Applicants without legal residence paid a Home Affairs clerk, who put their photographs on passport applications in South African citizens' names.

n: Home Affairs immigration officer sold work permits to 11 foreign nationals
org_label: Work permit buyers and their intermediary
rank: Immigration officer, Department of Home Affairs
d: Robert Reginald Booth, 53, described by the paper as a former immigration officer at Home Affairs, and Barry Victor Welgemoed, 35, described as an ordinary member of the public, pleaded guilty to corruption over the selling of fraudulent work permits. The National Prosecuting Authority spokesperson Monica Nyuswa said the pair were selling the permits to 11 foreign nationals at 5,500 rand each. The arrest followed events of 16 March 2022 at a farm near Karino, outside Nelspruit. The Nelspruit Specialised Commercial Crimes Court sentenced them to eight years, half of it suspended for five years. The report does not say over what period the permits were sold.
cite: Sunday World, 24 August 2022, reporting the National Prosecuting Authority and the Nelspruit Specialised Commercial Crimes Court
inside: Foreign nationals paid 5,500 rand each through an intermediary to a Home Affairs immigration officer, who supplied them with fraudulent work permits.

n: Home Affairs official at Malamulele sold birth certificates to foreigners
org_label: Paying foreign nationals seeking South African documents
rank: Home Affairs official, Malamulele office
d: Amos Ngwenyama, a Home Affairs official based at Malamulele in Limpopo, was arrested after a joint investigation by the Department of Home Affairs counter-corruption unit and the Hawks, the police's priority crimes unit, in Limpopo in 2023. The department said he had issued birth certificates to undeserving foreigners in exchange for money. He was sentenced on two counts of fraud and corruption to eight years and six years, to run concurrently; the minister, Aaron Motsoaledi, announced the sentence in April 2024. The report does not name the court, does not say how much was paid or by whom, and gives only the year of his arrest, so the period of the conduct is not established.
cite: The Citizen (South Africa), 22 April 2024, reporting the Minister of Home Affairs
inside: Foreign nationals' money reached a Home Affairs official at Malamulele, who issued them South African birth certificates they did not qualify for.

n: Appeal court confirms 12 years for Sicilian deputy who helped the mafia
rank: deputy in the Sicilian regional assembly
d: Paolo Ruggirello, a Trapani politician who sat as a deputy in Sicily's regional assembly, was convicted of concorso esterno in associazione mafiosa, a charge used for outsiders who help a mafia group without belonging to it. The Palermo appeal court confirmed his 12-year sentence in January 2025, while the prosecution general had asked for 15 years for mafia association. He is accused of having favoured the Trapani mafia over public contracts and of having sought the clans' electoral backing. He had admitted that before the 2017 regional elections Pietro Virga, son of the jailed boss Vincenzo Virga, asked him for 50,000 euros in exchange for a thousand votes, saying he accepted only to end the conversation. The case came from the 2019 Carabinieri operation 'Scrigno'.
inside: Mafia clans traded electoral support with a regional deputy, and the courts found he used his position to favour their interests in public contracts.
cite: Giornale di Sicilia, 25 January 2025 (full-text reprint in the Messina Antiusura newspaper archive)

n: Camorra pact at Sant'Antimo: 21 convicted, two ex-councillors among them
rank: two former municipal councillors of Sant'Antimo and a family active in business and politics
d: A trial in Naples ended in May 2024 with 21 convictions in a case built by the Carabinieri's ROS on alleged political-mafia agreements in the comune of Sant'Antimo and an alleged pact of mutual convenience between the Puca camorra clan and a powerful family active in business and politics. Antimo Cesaro received 11 years for concorso esterno in associazione mafiosa and vote-buying, and Aniello and Raffaele Cesaro ten years and six months each. Two former Sant'Antimo councillors, Francesco Di Lorenzo and Nello Cappuccio, were given 16 years and seven months and 11 years and five months. Corrado Chiariello was acquitted and the brothers' lawyers said they would appeal. Their brother, former senator Luigi Cesaro, is tried separately; his electoral-corruption count is dated to the 2015 Campania regional elections.
inside: Prosecutors said a camorra clan and a political family struck a pact over one town's politics, and a court convicted 21 people, two of them former councillors.
cite: La Repubblica, 10 May 2024 (reprint in the Messina Antiusura archive); Anteprima24, 14 October 2022

n: Casalesi-linked waste contractor sat as a Campania regional councillor
who: Clan dei Casalesi, Schiavone and Bidognetti factions
rank: member of the Campania Regional Council
d: A waste-treatment businessman from Casal di Principe, who had been a member of the Campania Regional Council, was convicted by the Naples appeal court of concorso esterno in associazione mafiosa, the judgment becoming final on 16 April 2015. In October 2020 police and the Guardia di Finanza confiscated more than four million euros of assets linked to him, among them the 834,226.46 euros he had drawn in council allowances and his councillor's pension. The criminal judge found him a colluding businessman and politician from at least 2000, and in any case before his election to the council in 2005, with the heads of the Casalesi clan's Schiavone and Bidognetti factions, subordinating both his business and his political work to their aims in return for electoral support.
inside: A camorra clan's electoral support put a waste contractor on a regional council, and he acted as its go-between with local administrators to channel public contracts to it.
cite: Polizia di Stato press release, 8 October 2020

n: Catania clans and Trecastagni's technical office in a refuse-tender case
org_label: Cappello and Laudani clans of Catania
rank: head of the technical office and the public works and environmental services director, Comune di Trecastagni
d: In November 2017 the anti-mafia investigation directorate in Catania executed a custody order issued by the city's preliminary-investigations judge against leading members of the Cappello and Laudani clans and against businessmen and administrative officials of the Comune di Trecastagni who ran the procedures awarding refuse-collection services. Gabriele Antonio Maria Astuto, head of the comune's technical office, and Domenico Sgarlato, at the time head of its public works and environmental services office, were charged with aggravated interference with the choice of contractor and with corruption. Vincenzo Guglielmino, sole administrator of the winning firm E.F. Servizi Ecologici, was charged with mafia association; the judge found he belonged to the Cappello clan and paid it regular sums.
inside: Clan-linked waste firms paid the officials who ran a town's refuse tenders, prosecutors allege, so the awards went to companies tied to Catania's mafia clans.
cite: InterNapoli, 27 November 2017, on operation 'Gorgoni'

n: Camorra group took Caivano's contract secrets from town administrators
rank: public administrators of the town of Caivano
d: Italian police arrested 18 people on 1 November 2023 in an investigation into suspected camorra clan infiltration at Caivano, a town in the Naples area. Judicial sources said this latest alleged infiltration related particularly to the management of public works contracts. Police said the criminal organisation was able to obtain confidential information from public administrators about the awarding of contracts, so that it could address extortion demands to the winners. Caivano's town council had already been dissolved for mafia-related offences on 16 October. The report names no clan, no official and no prosecuting office. The town had drawn national attention after the gang rape of two cousins aged 10 and 12 the previous summer, which prompted a government decree.
inside: A camorra group had administrators inside a town hall passing it the contract decisions, police say, and it used them to extort the firms that won the work.
cite: ANSA English, 1 November 2023

n: Fezza-De Vivo clan's cooperative took Pagani's cemetery and cleaning work
rank: administrative structure of the Comune di Pagani; a former councillor and environment assessore
d: Carabinieri from Nocera Inferiore executed a custody order from the Salerno preliminary-investigations judge in November 2024 against eight people, three sent to prison and five to house arrest, for offences against the public administration aggravated by the aim of helping a mafia group. The investigation concerned the Fezza-De Vivo camorra clan's conditioning of the administrative activity of the Comune di Pagani in order to obtain public supplies. Investigators allege the clan worked through the businessman Alfonso Marrazzo and the PE.DE.MA. cooperative he chaired, which obtained municipal contracts including running the cemetery, street sweeping and pandemic sanitisation. Marrazzo was a Pagani councillor for about twenty years and environment assessore until 2016.
inside: A camorra clan worked through a cooperative run by a long-serving councillor to bend a town hall's awards, prosecutors say, winning its cemetery and cleaning contracts.
cite: Anteprima24, 8 November 2024

n: Ring linked to a cosca ran Reggio Calabria's public housing allocations
who: Franco-Murina cosca, federated with the Tegano-De Stefano clan
rank: a former Aterp housing manager and employees of the Comune di Reggio Calabria, including its municipal police
d: The 'Case popolari' investigation by anti-mafia prosecutors in Reggio Calabria led in February 2024 to nine arrests, two in prison and seven under house arrest, over an association formed to manage the illegal allocation of public housing and to commit extortion. Among those arrested was Carmelo Consolato Murina, described by investigators as the organiser and regent of the Franco-Murina cosca, federated with the Tegano-De Stefano clan. The group relied on people inside the public administration, among them a former manager at the Reggio Calabria office of Aterp, the public housing agency, said to be able to steer allocations, a council employee who handed over keys for money and prepared false residence papers, and a municipal police employee who falsified documents.
inside: A clan-linked ring had a housing manager and council staff at its disposal, so flats went to people it chose rather than to those on the official waiting list.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 15 February 2024

n: Chone Killers leader's wife's firm won a Duran park contract
rank: officials of the Municipality of Duran, its fire service and the canton's transit authority
d: On 15 August 2024 police mounted a large operation in Duran, one of the centres of criminal violence in Ecuador, detaining 23 people said to belong to a criminal organisation headed by Julio Martinez Alcivar, alias 'Negro Tulio', leader of the Chone Killers. Police said the organisation had the direct participation of officials of the Municipality of Duran, the fire service and the canton's transit authority, and would have served to launder money through public contracting. At a press conference police pointed to a contract worth 190,000 US dollars awarded to the construction firm Arkhe Proyectos y Construcciones, owned by Martinez's wife Alexandra Estrada Aquino, who is prosecuted for alleged terrorism and organised crime. The contract, to regenerate a park, was signed in May 2024.
inside: Police say a gang had officials inside a city government and its agencies, and public works money then went to a firm owned by the gang leader's wife.
cite: Primicias with CONNECTAS, 19 November 2024

n: Trafficker's family firm was sole bidder for Duran's vehicle pound
org_label: Washington Sellan ('Washo') and the Latin Kings
rank: Autoridad de Transito de Duran (ATD), the canton's transit authority
d: In 2019 Washington Sellan Hati, alias 'Washo', worked as a data clerk at Duran's transit authority and then placed close friends and relatives in jobs in the companies of that same mayoralty while operating for the Latin Kings, according to an InSight Crime investigation cited by Primicias. He was caught in the act for drug trafficking in July 2021 but freed three months later on a habeas corpus, and prosecutors then declined to charge him. In mid-2023 a firm he held with one of his daughters, Transporsellcar, took a contract worth 992,395 US dollars from the transit authority to build the canton's vehicle pound. It was the only bidder. Duran's current mayor says the works show no progress so far and the city is moving to terminate it.
inside: A trafficker put his own people inside a city transit authority, which later awarded his family firm a million-dollar works contract with no competing bid.
cite: Primicias with CONNECTAS, 19 November 2024

n: Gang leader demanded a senior Carrefour post for a close associate
org_label: Chrisla's gang, part of the Viv Ansanm coalition
who: the gang leader known as Chrisla
rank: a senior public position in the commune of Carrefour
d: The United Nations Panel of Experts on Haiti reported that on 11 May 2026 the gang leader known as Chrisla renewed his calls on the government to appoint a close associate of his to a senior public position in the commune of Carrefour, while threatening to paralyse municipal institutions if his demand was not met. The Panel wrote that the demand reflects further efforts to entrench influence within formal governance structures and secure political leverage. It described Carrefour as a haven for Viv Ansanm, where behind an apparent normalcy lies a parallel system of gang governance that replaced public authority. The Panel does not say whether the appointment was made.
inside: A gang leader pressed the government to place his associate in a senior commune post, threatening to shut the commune's institutions if it refused.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, S/2026/714, annex 7 ('Gang presence in southern Haiti amid security operations')

n: Developer's money reached Navodari's chief architect over building permits
who: Aqua Force S.R.L. and another local developer
rank: chief architect of the town of Navodari
d: Romania's National Anticorruption Directorate sent to trial in January 2025 the chief architect of the town of Navodari, Giorgiana Cotigi, on two counts of taking a bribe and one of using her office to favour others, together with the company Aqua Force S.R.L., its administrator and a second businessman, each for giving a bribe.
