d: Sources told the UN Panel of Experts on Yemen that Major General Muhammad Ahmad al-Talibi, director of procurement at the Houthi-appointed ministry of defence and attached to the Houthis' office in Tehran, is in charge of the illicit shipment of materiel to the Houthis through a network of individuals and entities, and that he also arranges for Houthi combatants to be trained in Iran. In a case study the Panel said that, according to confidential sources, in 2022 al-Talibi ordered a Yemeni customs broker who was clearing smuggled materiel for the Houthis to move to Djibouti. The broker was exposed after Yemeni customs seized 52 Dehlavieh anti-tank missiles at the Shihan border post on 10 March 2022, and he was reportedly arrested in Djibouti in February 2024.
inside: The movement's man held the procurement post in the ministry of defence it had appointed, and used it to bring in weapons for the movement.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2024/731 (26 September 2024), para. 77 and case study 6

n: Houthi committee ran a prison inside Sana'a's Central Security Camp
who: Houthi National Committee for Prisoners' Affairs
rank: The so-called Exchange House prison, Central Security Camp, Sana'a
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen reported that the Central Security Camp in Sana'a includes several buildings, among them the so-called Exchange House prison, which is operated by the Houthi National Committee for Prisoners' Affairs under the leadership of Abdulqader Al-Murtada. The prison holds mostly civilians, including political prisoners, journalists and prisoners of war from the battle of Jabara Valley of 2019, some of whom have been there for years. The Panel said prisoners are systematically tortured and otherwise ill-treated by the prison's staff and that, on multiple reports it received, members of the prison's management including Al-Murtada were and still are torturing prisoners. It also gathered evidence that prisoners and their families are made to pay to make brief phone calls or to meet.
inside: A committee of the armed movement runs a prison inside a state security camp, where the Panel says the staff systematically torture mostly civilian detainees.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2023/833 (6 November 2023), annex 80 ('The Central Security Camp in Sana'a and the so-called Exchange House prison'), paras. 1-4

n: Houthi leader's nephew made interior undersecretary over a new spy unit
rank: Undersecretary of the de facto Ministry of the Interior and head of the new police intelligence unit
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen said the Houthis used a range of repressive measures and heightened surveillance of people to prevent any opposition, and that the creation of a new police intelligence unit was proof of the intensification of those measures. Ali Hussein al-Houthi, a nephew of the Houthi leader Abdulmalik al-Houthi, is the head of the new unit. An annex reproduces a report of 21 April 2025 by the Yemeni state news agency Saba describing him as a major general and undersecretary of the Ministry of the Interior, meeting the head of the Security and Intelligence Service, Major General Abdulhakim al-Khaiwani, to discuss carrying out the directives of the president of the Houthi-appointed Supreme Political Council on countering espionage and surveillance networks, including referring suspects to the judiciary.
inside: The movement's leading family holds the interior ministry post running a new police intelligence unit the Panel calls proof of intensified measures against opposition.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2025/650 (17 September 2025), paras. 38-39 and annex 23 ('Creation of a new police intelligence unit under the lead of Ali Hussein al-Houthi to counter espionage and surveillance'), p. 78

n: Warrap governor armed a militia with South Sudan's unified-forces kit
rank: Mixed force of soldiers and civilian militias paraded by the Governor of Warrap
d: On 8 March 2021 the Governor of Warrap State, Aleu Ayieny Aleu, in military fatigues, paraded a mixed force of soldiers and civilian militias known as 'Tuek Tuek' in Kirik, in Tonj North County. The UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan worked from a video of the parade and verified it independently. Aleu said he had been mandated by President Salva Kiir to arm the force, and called it 'Mathiang Anyoor Two' after a militia that committed crimes against civilians in the conflict from 2013 on. Army sources told the Panel the weapons and uniforms in the video had originally been procured for the necessary unified forces, and that Aleu promised the militiamen places in the regular armed forces. The Panel said this breached the peace agreement.
inside: Civilian militias were paraded alongside soldiers with state weapons and uniforms, and promised places in the army, by the governor who armed them.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan, S/2021/365 (15 April 2021), paras. 69-71

n: Peace funds bought rebel commanders posts in South Sudan's police and army
rank: Paid positions in the Police and the South Sudan People's Defence Forces
d: The UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan reported that, as the National Salvation Front faced logistical and resource problems, it became easier for the Government to encourage its commanders to defect. Several were enticed by the promise of a paid position within the Police or the South Sudan People's Defence Forces, and some had already been integrated into army units in Mundri East and Morobo counties. The Panel said it was also alleged that a substantial portion of funds allocated for implementing the peace agreement, but diverted to the Ministry of Cabinet Affairs, had been used to encourage defections. Summoned by parliament, the Minister for Cabinet Affairs, Martin Elia Lomuro, confirmed an irregular withdrawal of $1,050,000 in April 2024 to facilitate 'peace implementation' with NAS commanders.
inside: Commanders of an armed opposition movement were given paid police and army posts, and the state then used their forces against their old movement.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan, S/2024/855 (29 November 2024), paras. 26-29 and annex 16 ('Partial Integration List of Kennedy Kenyi "Warrior" Abdu Lopiong's forces into the SSPDF, 2 February 2024')

n: AFC/M23 left men inside Uvira's police units after pulling out
rank: Local 'police' units in Uvira
d: The UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo reported that AFC/M23 and Rwandan troops withdrew from Uvira in South Kivu on 18 January 2026 after sustained international diplomatic pressure, having held the town for more than a month, forced the Burundian army out, captured large Congolese army bases and set up a parallel administration. In an annex on the withdrawal announcements the Group found that, despite public claims of withdrawal, only a partial, staged withdrawal took place, and that AFC/M23 and the Rwanda Defence Force maintained a covert presence within Uvira, including through combatants dressed in civilian attire or their integration into local 'police' units. The Group said the town remained effectively under AFC/M23 and Rwandan control until January.
inside: As the armed movement withdrew from the town it placed fighters inside the local police units, keeping its hold on policing without uniforms.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, S/2026/466 (June 2026), para. 77 and annex 24 ('Announcements of withdrawal from Uvira'), pp. 105-106

n: Libyan armed group used military prosecutors to paper over its arrests
org_label: Deterrence Apparatus for Combating Crime and Terrorism (DACOT)
who: Deterrence Apparatus for Combating Crime and Terrorism
rank: Individuals working at the Military Attorney General's office
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya identified eight cases of unlawful detention, enforced disappearance and torture committed by members of the Deterrence Apparatus for Combating Crime and Terrorism and of the Judicial Police Operations Department acting under its effective control. The Panel called the Apparatus and the Internal Security Agency in Tripoli two armed entities, and found the violations were administered through a coercive quasi-judicial system the Apparatus's command enforced to keep detainees outside the Libyan judicial system's protection. One component the Panel set out was individuals working at the Military Attorney General's office, responsible for issuing the prosecutorial documentation required to justify the arrests and the proceedings against the detainees. Victims were selected in an organised manner, among other grounds for social engagements that challenged the Apparatus's authority.
inside: An armed group holding state security powers had people in the military prosecutor's office issuing the paperwork that made its own arrests look lawful.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2024/914 (3 December 2024), annex 20, paras. 1-2, and appendix A ('Violations of IHL and IHRL committed in places of detention under the control of DACOT'), paras. 1-2, pp. 102-103

n: Court said to be Houthi-run declared a mobile firm bankrupt in Sana'a
rank: A commercial court in Sana'a
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen reported that, according to a media report, the Houthis allegedly took over the mobile telecommunications company Y after arranging to declare it 'bankrupt by a court under their control'. The media report, which quoted sources in the Sana'a-based ministry of communications and information technology, said Houthi leaders, named as Muhammad Ali al-Houthi, Abu Ali al-Hakem and others, were seeking to take over the company after declaring it bankrupt, and that a commercial court subject to the control of the Houthi militias in Sana'a announced the bankruptcy of 'Y' mobile company in an official notice in the Al-Thawra newspaper on 11 March 2020. The Panel wrote to Y Telecom for confirmation and its response was awaited.
inside: A court said to be under the movement's control declared a mobile company bankrupt while the movement's leaders were trying to take the company over.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2022/50 (25 January 2022), para. 84 and annex 29 ('Telecom Sector in Yemen'), para. 5 and footnotes 271-272

n: Armed group chiefs held Libya's interior and defence ministries
org_label: Imad Trabelsi's and Abdulsalam Al-Zobi's armed groups
rank: Ministry of the Interior and Ministry of Defence, Government of National Unity
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya found that the armed group leaders Imad Trabelsi and Abdulsalam Al-Zobi exercised de facto control over the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence of the Government of National Unity. In late August 2025 the finance ministry and the Central Bank of Libya began paying public sector salaries directly, linking each employee to one identification number, to control spending and remove ghost employees; salaries are about 65 per cent of the national budget. Both ministries refused to cooperate, citing their workers' privacy, which the Panel assessed as irrelevant because identity cards are state-issued. The Panel said the two leaders engaged in coordinated pressure, including threats, with the aim of keeping their administrations outside the new system.
inside: Two Libyan armed group leaders controlled the interior and defence ministries and used them to keep their payrolls outside a state system that would expose them.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, paras. 17-21

n: Premier's nephew drove out Libya's oil minister to clear the Arkenu deal
org_label: Ibrahim Al Dabiba's armed group network
rank: Minister of Oil and Gas
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya found that Ibrahim Al Dabiba, nephew of Prime Minister Abdulhamid Al Dabiba, became a kingmaker on the strength of his alliances with armed group leaders. He and Saddam Haftar, whose forces hold the areas where most Libyan oil fields lie, struck a deal creating Arkenu Oil Company as a structure for reaching crude oil revenues, with the Libyan Arab armed forces as the first beneficiary. The Panel found that he then exerted pressure on officials in the oil sector and played a central role in the suspension of the Minister of Oil and Gas in March 2024, with the aim of installing a replacement amenable to implementing the Arkenu deal.
inside: An armed group financier had Libya's oil minister suspended so that a more willing replacement would carry through an oil deal paying his allies.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, paras. 15 and 98

n: Libyan ministries gave al-Nawasi Brigade men diplomatic posts abroad
rank: Consular Attaché, Libyan Embassy in Tunis; health attaché, Libyan Consulate in Istanbul
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya reported the continued infiltration of Libyan state institutions by armed groups, in particular the Nawasi Brigade, and said a common method was to use recordings as blackmail to obtain coveted government positions. Two al-Nawasi affiliates, Al-Tahir Urwah and Mohamed Bu Dara', named in an earlier annex over a reported 2019 attack on the Minister of Finance, had reportedly been appointed as attachés to Libyan posts abroad and presumably receive diplomatic immunity. The Panel confirmed that Urwah is a Consular Attaché at the Libyan Embassy in Tunis. It said Abu Dara' is a police officer whom the interior ministry suspended and placed on a no-fly list in April 2020, yet whom the foreign ministry reportedly appointed as a health attaché in Istanbul.
inside: A Tripoli militia obtained state diplomatic posts for two of its men, which the Panel said presumably carry the immunity that shields them from Libyan proceedings.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report S/2021/229, 8 March 2021, para. 8 and annex 6 ('Continued encroachment of armed groups on state institutions'), para. 4

n: Central African transport minister led a militia funded via his ministry
org_label: RPRC, MLCJ and FPRC networks in Vakaga
rank: Minister of Transport and Civil Aviation
d: The UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic found that after the Coalition des patriotes pour le changement failed to take Bangui in January 2021, politicians originally from Vakaga Prefecture organised, funded and deployed a militia of armed local youth under the leadership of Arnaud Djoubaye Abazene, the Minister of Transport and Civil Aviation and a close associate of the former Seleka leader Michel Djotodia. On 7 February a small plane rented by the minister flew the MLCJ zone commander of Birao from Bangui; confidential sources said he was reportedly given eight million CFA francs ($14,632), collected on arrival by the MLCJ chief of staff. The Panel obtained the plane's rental receipt addressed to the ministry. Abazene denied involvement, calling it a spontaneous youth initiative.
inside: Politicians tied to Central African armed groups used a ministry's own aircraft and cash to raise a militia, and the groups' commanders took the money and the recruits.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, final report S/2021/569, 25 June 2021, para. 112 and annex 4.4 ('Militia in Vakaga created by Bangui-based politicians')

n: Central African energy minister was in the armed group behind an attack
org_label: Rassemblement patriotique pour le renouveau de la Centrafrique (RPRC)
rank: Minister for Energy and Hydrocarbon
d: The UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic found that the Parti du rassemblement pour la nation centrafricaine continued to be used as a cover for military operations by the leadership of the Rassemblement patriotique pour le renouveau de la Centrafrique, an armed group: Zakaria Damane and his nephew Djono Ahaba, at that time the Minister for Energy and Hydrocarbon. The Panel said the front group's official leader, Nourd Gregaza, served only as a figurehead, and that according to members the decision to attack Ndele on 11 March 2020 was taken and prepared by Damane, who directly instructed Azor Kalite to conduct it. The leadership hoped to claim the three north-eastern prefectures to secure political gains after the elections, in particular a Goula prime minister.
inside: A sitting Central African minister was part of the armed group's leadership, which used a front group for attacks aimed at winning it more posts in government.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, final report S/2020/662, 7 July 2020, para. 32

n: Mali made four armed group men ministers; one gave the groups border work
org_label: Coordination des mouvements de l'Azawad and the Plateforme
rank: Four ministers in a 25-member transition government, including the Minister of Malians Abroad and African Integration
d: On 5 October 2020 Mali's President of the Transition, Bah N'Daw, appointed a 25-minister government that for the first time included representatives of armed groups. The UN Panel of Experts named four: Harouna Toureh of the Plateforme, Alhamdou Ag Ilyene for its GATIA-Gamou component, and Mossa Ag Attaher and Mohamed Ould Mahmoud for the Coordination des mouvements de l'Azawad. Others got non-ministerial government posts, including in the Office of the President. The Panel later reported that Ag Ilyene, as Minister of Malians Abroad, conceived a project to stem migrant smuggling by strengthening local border control and signed a declaration on it with Italy. It noted that compliant armed groups had recovered 251 migrants in March 2021, though no concrete actions had yet been undertaken under the project.
inside: Malian armed movements took four ministries and posts in the presidency, and one of their ministers designed a border project that gave the groups themselves a state role.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Mali, final report S/2021/151, 15 February 2021, para. 18 and footnote 4; interim report S/2021/714, 6 August 2021, paras. 93-95

n: US says Iraq's deputy oil minister diverted oil for an Iran-backed militia
rank: Deputy Minister of Oil; head of the licensing and contracts office; acting Minister of Oil
d: On 7 May 2026 the US Treasury designated Ali Maarij Al-Bahadly, Iraq's Deputy Minister of Oil, saying he abuses his position to facilitate the diversion of oil sold for the benefit of the Iranian regime and its proxy militias in Iraq. The release says that since 2018 he has held several posts in the Ministry of Oil and that in those capacities he enriched the oil smuggler Salim Ahmed Said, the militia Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq and Iran by granting export rights to Said's companies, authorising the trucking of oil from the Qayarah field to VS Oil at Khor Zubayr, and falsifying documents on the oil's provenance. Treasury says Said bribed complicit officials and reportedly installed him in his post.
inside: The US Treasury says a smuggler put the man into Iraq's oil ministry who then signed away export rights and papers that enriched him and an armed militia.
cite: US Department of the Treasury, Office of Foreign Assets Control, 'Economic Fury Targets Iraqi Oil Official, Iran-Backed Terrorist Militias in Iraq', 7 May 2026

n: Iraq's communications ministry waived bidding for a PMF firm's fibre contracts
who: Popular Mobilization Forces and Kata'ib Hezbollah
rank: Minister of Communications; Council of Ministers
d: On 23 April 2024 Iraq's Minister of Communications, Hiyam al-Yassiri, sent a letter marked 'extremely urgent' to the cabinet secretariat asking that two fibre optic contracts be exempted from contracting rules: one to rehabilitate the existing national network, the other to build an alternate one. Michael Knights, writing in CTC Sentinel, says no reason was given for the sudden urgency, that both were added to the same day's cabinet agenda with no notice and approved as non-competed awards that day, and that cabinet consideration of them was left out of the published minutes. The awardee of both was the Muhandis General Company, a construction arm of the Popular Mobilization Forces, which the US Treasury designated in October 2025 as controlled by Kata'ib Hezbollah.
inside: A militia's own construction company got two national fibre contracts after the minister and the cabinet set competition aside in a single day.
cite: Michael Knights, 'Rise of the E-Militias: Designated Terrorist Groups Infest Iraq's Digital Economy', CTC Sentinel, November/December 2025, pp. 67-69; US Department of the Treasury, 'Treasury Takes Aim at Iran-Backed Militia Groups Threatening the Safety of Americans', 9 October 2025 (https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0277)

n: Militia-linked deputy minister placed in Iraq's communications ministry
org_label: Popular Mobilization Forces network around Falah al-Fayyadh
rank: Deputy Minister for technical affairs and head of media relations, Ministry of Communications
d: Michael Knights, writing in CTC Sentinel, reports that within the Iraqi Ministry of Communications formed after 2022 the minister, Hiyam al-Yassiri, appointed a deputy minister for technical affairs, Buraq Abdal-Qader Abdal-Karim, from the inner circle of Khamis Khanjar, a politician the United States designated for corrupt activities in favour of Iran-backed militias. She also appointed as head of media relations Omar Abdal-Razaq Muhsib, previously the personal photographer of Falah al-Fayyadh in the Popular Mobilization Forces leadership office. Al-Fayyadh was designated by the United States over the killing and abduction of unarmed protesters in the 2019 Tishreen uprising. Knights assesses that the minister, the prime minister and the sector's regulator worked to place the central fibre optic backbone under the control of US-designated entities.
inside: A militia network's people filled senior posts in Iraq's communications ministry, and the author says the ministry then steered the national fibre network towards designated groups.
cite: Michael Knights, 'Rise of the E-Militias: Designated Terrorist Groups Infest Iraq's Digital Economy', CTC Sentinel, November/December 2025, pp. 66-67

n: Houthi defence ministry's buying chief ran the movement's arms shipments
rank: Director of procurement, Houthi-appointed Ministry of Defence
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen reported that sources had informed it that Major General Muhammad Ahmad al-Talibi, director of procurement at the Houthi-appointed ministry of defence and attached to the Houthis' office in Tehran, is in charge of the illicit shipment of materiel to the Houthis through a network of individuals and entities, and also makes arrangements for Houthi combatants to be trained in Iran. An earlier Panel annex had already listed him as director of procurement at the ministry of defence and an assistant to Saleh Mosfer Alshaer, the Houthis' judicial custodian of seized assets. The Panel has reported that all official structures in Sana'a are led by Houthi loyalists.
inside: The movement's own man held the defence ministry's buying job in Sana'a and used it, the Panel's sources say, to bring in weapons for the movement itself.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2024/731, 10 October 2024, paras. 75-77; S/2021/79, 22 January 2021, annex 27 ('Illegal Seizure of Assets by the Judicial Custodian and the Specialised Criminal Court'), list of collaborators; S/2025/650, para. 117

n: Haftar-backed chairman reshaped Libya's oil corporation for armed groups
who: Libyan Arab armed forces and allied armed group actors
rank: Chairman of the National Oil Corporation
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya found that Farhat Bengdara, made chairman of the state National Oil Corporation in July 2022 with the backing of the Haftar family, colluded with armed group actors to allocate oil service contracts to newly established entities tied to them and to divert oil and gas revenue. He pressed subsidiary chairmen to bank with Al-Masraf, set up a 'Strategic Planning' department outside the corporation's formal structure to negotiate contracts outside the legal framework, and created a crude marketing post bypassing existing procedures. He resigned on 16 January 2025 and the Attorney General issued an arrest warrant. Bengdara told the Panel he had no oversight of the Al-Masraf funds and played a peripheral role in the Arkenu contracts; the Panel found his claims not credible.
inside: Armed groups put a man of their own in the chair of Libya's state oil company, who rebuilt its structure so their firms won its contracts and its revenue.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, paras. 101-103 and annex 9 ('Armed groups' footprint on the oil sector'), section B, paras. 4-12; S/2024/914, para. 96

n: Libya's power company kept diverting fuel for armed groups after exposure
org_label: Libyan armed group actors in western and eastern Libya
rank: Chairman, General Electricity Company of Libya
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya had found that the chairman of the state General Electricity Company of Libya, Mohamed al-Mashay, ran the company's operations and assets under the direct instruction of Tripoli armed group leaders. In 2026 the Panel said that despite public criticism and an announced Attorney General investigation he kept access to state resources and continued to collude with armed group actors in western and eastern Libya. He went on facilitating the unchecked diversion of fuel allocated to the company, feeding public fund misappropriation and the financing of armed groups. The Panel established a direct relationship between him and the Libyan Arab armed forces' top command, and said the company operated outside the Libyan legal framework because of its chairman's relationship with armed group actors.
inside: Armed groups' chosen chairman stayed in charge of Libya's state power company and kept its subsidised fuel flowing to the groups rather than to power stations.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, annex 9 ('Armed groups' footprint on the oil sector'), section D, paras. 24-26; S/2024/914, paras. 12-15

n: Broker sold Libyan crude $8 under the state price for armed group owners
who: Saddam Haftar's and Ibrahim Al Dabiba's networks
rank: Crude export access of the National Oil Corporation; sales representation for Arkenu Oil Company
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya found that Arkenu Oil Company, indirectly controlled by Saddam Haftar, relied on newly created broker companies in Libya so that other top commanders of the Libyan Arab armed forces could benefit from oil exports without any contractual relationship with the state National Oil Corporation. Al-Gandal, registered in early 2023 with front individuals listed as its owners, acted as Arkenu's sales representative, advertising and negotiating sales exclusively below the corporation's market price through social media messaging applications. The Panel reviewed a sample Al-Gandal contract for two million barrels a month for a year, priced at $8 below the corporation's international market rate. It found this compelled the corporation to grant companies controlled by armed group actors access to international petroleum markets.
inside: Front companies owned for armed commanders were fitted into the state oil corporation's export chain, forcing it to sell their crude abroad below its own price.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, annex 9 ('Armed groups' footprint on the oil sector'), paras. 20 and 22

n: Houthi asset custodian's nephew made director of a seized Yemeni university
rank: Director, University of Technology Twintech
d: In its April 2020 report the UN Panel of Experts on Yemen named businesses and institutions unlawfully appropriated by Major General Saleh Mesfer Saleh Alshaer, the custodian appointed by a Sana'a special criminal court over the property of Houthi opponents, and managed by members of his family who were made the authorised signatories of the entities' bank accounts. Among them was the University of Technology Twintech, taken from Khaled Rashad Al Raed Alimi, where Alshaer's nephew Raed Hassan Mesfer Alshaer was made director; the Panel's list of associates also names Wael Abdelmoghni al Aghbari as its finance director. The Panel said it was investigating whether the appropriation of social foundations and education institutions was aimed at reaching funds from international donors and at disguising outside financial support.
inside: The movement's asset custodian handed a seized Yemeni university to his own nephew, who then ran it and signed for its money on the movement's behalf.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2020/326, 28 April 2020, annex 26 ('Unlawful appropriation by major general Saleh Mesfer Alshaer network'), paras. 1-4 and table 26.1; S/2021/79, annex 27, table 27.2

n: Houthi-run ministry renamed a seized foundation and changed its signatories
rank: Al Saleh Foundation board and bank signatories
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen found that the Al Saleh Foundation, whose original owner was Ahmed Ali Abdullah Saleh, a man under UN sanctions, was appropriated by the network of Major General Saleh Mesfer Alshaer, the Houthis' judicial custodian of opponents' property. The Panel said it was renamed the al Shaab foundation on 24 July 2018 by the ministry of social affairs and labour under Houthi control, after its appropriation and without the approval of its legal board of directors, and that new authorised signatories were put on its accounts. The Panel's list of associates names Ahmed Mohamed Alkabsi as president of the foundation's accounts and Akram Yahya Baker as its director. The Panel was investigating whether taking over social foundations was aimed at reaching international donor funds.
inside: A ministry under the movement's control renamed a charitable foundation it had seized and installed new signatories over its accounts, putting its money at the movement's disposal.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2020/326, 28 April 2020, annex 26 ('Unlawful appropriation by major general Saleh Mesfer Alshaer network'), table 26.1, footnote 119 and table 26.2; S/2021/79, annex 27, table 27.2

n: Houthi judicial guard took a Yemeni media group, campuses and a hospital
rank: Shibam Holding Company; University of Science and Technology; Azal University; Hospital of Science and Technology
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen published in January 2021 a list of entities whose assets had been confiscated by the Houthis' 'judicial guard', headed by Saleh Mosfer Alshaer, over the previous three years. It included Shibam Holding Company, which ran the Al-Yaman Al-Youm television channel and newspaper, the University of Science and Technology, Azal University and the Hospital of Science and Technology. The Panel said the custodian had been aggressively confiscating companies, bank accounts and real estate of people the Houthis consider enemies, and that the group used a body called the specialised criminal court, which designated Alshaer as judicial custodian, to lend the seizures legality. That court ordered the provisional seizure of the assets of 75 military leaders, 35 parliamentarians and at least 100 political leaders.
inside: The movement's custodian and its own court took ownership of a Yemeni media group, two universities and a hospital, and ran them for the movement.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2021/79, 22 January 2021, annex 27 ('Illegal Seizure of Assets by the Judicial Custodian and the Specialised Criminal Court'), paras. 1-5 and table 27.2

n: Iraq's new 5G company and its contractors tied to militia-linked figures
org_label: Popular Mobilization Forces-linked networks and Coordination Framework parties
rank: National Mobile Telecommunications Company; its 5G contractors
d: In March 2025 Iraq's Ministry of Communications and its state-owned Informatics and Telecommunications Public Company began forming the National Mobile Telecommunications Company to run 5G. Michael Knights, writing in CTC Sentinel, assesses that the deal was pockmarked by irregularities: the regulator told existing operators the new company could use their towers, and none of them was able to bid for the 5G contract. An Iraqi specialist security judge put a hold on the contract in October 2025. Knights writes that Nokia was directed by the ministry to use the local firms Enkidu and Atlas, and that a major shareholder in Atlas Information Systems, one of a chain of Atlas-named companies, is the brother of the US-sanctioned Popular Mobilization Forces chairman.
inside: Militia-linked investors and firms were written into the state company set up to run Iraq's 5G, and the regulator cleared the ground by shutting rivals out.
cite: Michael Knights, 'Rise of the E-Militias: Designated Terrorist Groups Infest Iraq's Digital Economy', CTC Sentinel, November/December 2025, pp. 69-70

n: Alvaro clan's dockers deleted cocaine containers from Gioia Tauro's check list
rank: Port workers inside the Gioia Tauro container terminal
d: A custody order signed by investigating judge Elsie Clemente at the Reggio Calabria court describes a team of port workers at Gioia Tauro, Italy's largest container port, allegedly working for a group tied to the Alvaro cosca of Sinopoli. Prosecutors say Filippo Gallo worked outside the terminal and his brother-in-law Antonio Reitano inside. On 12 January 2020 Francesco Alvaro told an accomplice they had found a tested contact: if a container was put on the customs black list, the workers could delete it. The price was four of thirty-one packages, which Alvaro thought too high. Reitano allegedly told South American suppliers to hide cocaine in a container's structural cavities rather than refrigerated units. Carabinieri placed 35 people under custody orders in July 2026.
inside: A mafia clan had dockers inside the container port who could allegedly erase a container from the customs check list, so cargo it had bought passed uninspected.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 24 July 2026 and 23 July 2026, reporting the GIP custody order (Tribunale di Reggio Calabria, DDA Reggio Calabria)

n: Rossano cosca boss pressed a security firm into hiring his son at an Enel plant
rank: Gatehouse and security staff, Cosmopol Vigilanza, at Enel's Rossano power station
d: Operation Ginestra, run by the Catanzaro anti-mafia prosecutors, devotes a chapter of the custody order signed by judge Fabiana Giacchetti to interference in hiring at Enel's thermoelectric power station at Rossano in Calabria. Investigators hold Salvatore Galluzzi, born 1976, to be head of the local 'ndrangheta cosca. On 5 May 2022 a union official, Marco Pacenza of Uiltec Calabria, was recorded relaying Galluzzi's words about his son Antonio's delayed gatehouse job: he might go and speak to the plant's managers himself, and they would be frightened. Antonio Galluzzi was then hired by Cosmopol Vigilanza, the firm contracted for gatehouse and security work at the site. On 26 October 2022 the plant manager, Filippo Lo Nigro, went to the carabinieri of his own accord to report what had happened.
inside: A mafia boss's intimidation allegedly got his son a job guarding the gate of a power station, putting the clan's family inside the firm controlling access.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 29 October 2026, on the Operation Ginestra custody order (DDA Catanzaro)

n: Mannolo clan put 22 people on a Cutro holiday village's payroll
rank: 22 imposed employees of Alberghi del Mediterraneo, owner of the Porto Kaleo village
d: Alberghi del Mediterraneo owns and runs the Porto Kaleo holiday village on the coast at Cutro in Calabria. Its owner, Giovanni Notarianni, reported the local 'ndrangheta group to the Catanzaro anti-mafia prosecutors in 2018 and became a witness against it. An economic report written for him by Professor Giuseppe Fabbrini puts his losses between 2001 and 2018 at almost eight million euros. Extortion accounted for 752,000 euros. The larger part, 2,937,340.74 euros, came from hirings imposed by the clan, half of it, 1,468,670.37 euros, with no real value, because the 22 people imposed on the payroll did not keep to shifts or do the work they were paid for. When Notarianni refused a hiring, the report says, property was damaged.
inside: A mafia group placed twenty-two of its relatives and allies on a holiday village's payroll, so the firm paid wages to the clan's people for work not done.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 11 October 2020, on the expert report filed for Giovanni Notarianni in the trial of the Cutro cosche

n: Robin Hood: clan-linked staff on the books of Vibo Valentia's health authority
who: 'Ndrangheta (Vibo Valentia cosche, including Fiarè, Lo Bianco and Fiarè-Razionale-Gasparro)
rank: Staff of the Azienda sanitaria provinciale di Vibo Valentia and of the provincial industrial development consortium
d: The Robin Hood investigation by the carabinieri ROS traced jobs at the provincial health authority of Vibo Valentia, which runs the area's hospitals, and at the provincial industrial development consortium. The turncoat boss Andrea Mantella told prosecutors of an arrangement of votes for jobs, and named men of the Fiarè and Lo Bianco families posted to the Porto Salvo water treatment plant who, he said, were hired on paper and only collected their money at the end of the month. He said one Lo Bianco got a hospital job as a lift attendant on a bogus certificate. The order says the collaborator's statements on the hirings were fully corroborated: eight men allegedly tied to organised crime, three at the health authority since 1994.
inside: Mafia families allegedly got their men onto the payrolls of a public health authority and an industrial consortium, which paid wages to clan associates for little or no work.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 7 February 2017, on the Operation Robin Hood custody order (DDA Catanzaro, carabinieri ROS)

n: San Francisco money transfer teller charged with wiring a trafficker's cash
org_label: Unnamed San Francisco Bay Area drug trafficker
rank: Teller at a money services business in the Tenderloin district, San Francisco
d: Federal prosecutors in San Francisco charged Yessenia Margarita Barrientos-Lainez, 42, of Daly City, with conspiring to launder drug money. A money services business is a shop that wires cash abroad for customers. According to the criminal complaint she worked as a teller at one in the Tenderloin district until mid-May 2023 and used the job for an unnamed co-conspirator whom drug agents knew as a Bay Area trafficker. The complaint alleges that on 1 May 2023 she texted him that her boss had gone, so he could bring cash; within about two hours she wired thousands of dollars to three names and accounts he had sent her by photograph, two of them in Sinaloa. It alleges she charged an under-the-table fee and structured each wire to evade reporting rules.
inside: Prosecutors say a trafficker used a teller inside a cash transfer shop, so the shop's own counter wired his drug money abroad below reporting limits.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Northern District of California, press release, 1 November 2023 (criminal complaint)

n: Buda-Imerti cosca men kept on the payroll of the Strait of Messina ferry firm
rank: Ticket office and quay staff, Caronte & Tourist Spa
d: Caronte & Tourist Spa runs the ferries across the Strait of Messina. In January 2021, in Operation Scilla e Cariddi, the Reggio Calabria court placed the firm under judicial administration, holding that people and companies tied to the Buda-Imerti cosca were the instruments of mafia infiltration. Domenico Passalacqua, convicted of mafia association in the Meta trial, had been a ticket clerk since 1990; collaborators said the ticket office served as a front office for clan members. After his release in October 2015 managers took him back, formalised on 14 March 2016, creating a shift for him rather than dismissing him, and later proposed paying him without work. Massimo Buda, son of a cosca figure, was head yard man at Messina's Norimberga quay.
inside: A mafia clan had its convicted men inside the ferry company's ticket office and quays, and managers kept them on, giving the clan a post in the firm.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 3 and 5 February 2021 and 18 August 2022, on the Scilla e Cariddi judicial administration decrees (Tribunale di Reggio Calabria, DDA Reggio Calabria and DIA)

n: 'Ndrangheta families took over Spumador's transport contracts by subduing its managers
rank: Managers and employees handling third-party transport contracts, Spumador Spa
d: Spumador Spa, a fizzy drinks maker near Como with turnover above 200 million euros, was placed under judicial administration in June 2022 by the Milan court after a Guardia di Finanza investigation. Investigators described an alleged scheme to win total control of the company's transport contracts through repeated extortion using mafia methods against its managers and staff, who were in practice subjected to the will of the 'ndranghetisti. The judges found serious mafia infiltration lasting from 2018 onwards. Attilio and Antonio Salerni, arrested in November 2021, allegedly used violence and threats to take the haulage work through their firm Sea Trasporti. In November 2022 the court revoked the measure, saying the company, not under investigation, had cooperated and built strong checks.
inside: Mafia families allegedly frightened a drinks company's managers into handing them its haulage work, so the firm's own contracting decisions served the clans.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 20 June 2022 and 29 November 2022, on the Milan court's judicial administration decree and its revocation (DDA Milan, Guardia di Finanza Como)

n: Eurospin Sicilia's Calabria development manager accused of steering work to clan firms
who: 'Ndrangheta (De Stefano and Araniti cosche, through businessman Gangemi)
rank: Head of development for Calabria, Eurospin Sicilia Spa
d: In the Planning investigation, prosecutors in Reggio Calabria placed Gianluca Taverniti, head of development for Calabria at the supermarket company Eurospin Sicilia Spa, under investigation for external complicity in mafia association. The court decree putting the Catania-based company under judicial administration says its expansion in the Reggio area was strongly conditioned by mafia interference through Gangemi, a businessman close to the De Stefano cosca, and points to subcontracts on the Gallico building site. Investigators say a company in which Taverniti is sole shareholder was used to channel money to him from firms suspected of mafia ties, for helping them monopolise the building of new stores. A turncoat said an Araniti cosca figure had frightened a Eurospin manager into his hands.
inside: Prosecutors say clan-linked builders had the supermarket chain's own development manager, so its building subcontracts in Calabria went to firms tied to the cosche.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 16 March 2023, on the Operation Planning judicial administration decree (DDA Reggio Calabria, DIA and Guardia di Finanza)

n: Mancuso-linked haulier got inside Schenker Italiana's transport subcontracts
rank: Transport subcontracts and managers with decision-making power, Schenker Italiana
d: Schenker Italiana, the Italian arm of the German logistics group owned by Deutsche Bahn, was placed under judicial administration in May 2022 by the Milan court. The case began with the seizure of about 30 kilograms of cocaine at the port of Dover on 15 March 2020, hidden in a lorry loaded two days earlier at the firm's Guanzate branch near Como. The lorry also carried pallets collected for Schenker by Fiuto Autotrasporti, registered to the wife of Nicola Bevilacqua, 70, said to belong to the Mancuso clan; prosecutors say he used it to get into Schenker's subcontracts. The judges found seriously negligent failure to check by some managers. Neither the company nor its staff are under investigation.
inside: A convicted mafioso allegedly ran a haulage firm in his wife's name to win subcontracts inside a global logistics company, whose lorries then carried his cocaine.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 17 May 2022, on the Milan court's 38-page judicial administration decree (DDA Milan, Guardia di Finanza GICO)

n: Iaconis clan's hidden partner held Euroscatola's paper processing contract
rank: Processing contracts, suppliers and hiring, Euroscatola Spa
d: Euroscatola Spa, a paper and cardboard processor at Cantù near Como, was placed under judicial administration in July 2026 by the Milan court, after work following the 2021 Cavalli di Razza operation against the clans. Milan's chief prosecutor, Marcello Viola, said the inquiry established that from 2019 the company had continuous dealings with a firm in Lomazzo attributable to a leading figure of the Fino Mornasco 'ndrangheta locale, already definitively convicted of fraudulently transferring assets with mafia facilitation. The judges held the mafia nature of Valcart, a firm created in Euroscatola's orbit, to be beyond dispute, and said Alessandro Tagliente, right hand of the boss Bartolomeo Iaconis, was the hidden partner holding its processing contract.
inside: A mafia clan's hidden partner held the processing contract of a paper company whose management stayed inert, so its work and suppliers served the clan.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 21 July 2026, on the Milan court's judicial administration decree and the Milan prosecutor's statement

n: Court found the Tegano clan colonised Reggio Calabria's Multiservizi company
rank: Shareholding of the private partner in Multiservizi S.p.A.
d: Multiservizi S.p.A. was a mixed public and private company paid by Reggio Calabria's local authority to maintain its buildings. In the Archi-Astrea trial the court, presided over by judge Giuseppe Campagna, convicted the defendants and held it proved that from its foundation the company was the Tegano clan's own. The judgment says the clan's leaders, in substance co-owners of the building firm Com.edil formally registered only to the Rechichi brothers, colonised Multiservizi by placing their most trusted people in the shareholding of its private partner, so as to take the profits agreed with the local authority. The court rejected an appeal ruling that had blamed only the former operating director.
inside: A mafia clan put its trusted men into the shareholding of a council services company's private partner, so public maintenance money went to the clan.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 29 January 2015, on the Archi-Astrea judgment (Tribunale di Reggio Calabria, judge Giuseppe Campagna presiding)

n: D'Alessandro clan held Juve Stabia's tickets, security, coaches and cleaning
who: Camorra (D'Alessandro clan of Castellammare di Stabia)
rank: Security, ticketing, refreshment, cleaning, health and team transport contractors of Juve Stabia
d: On 13 October 2025 the Naples court's prevention measures section placed the Serie B football club Juve Stabia under judicial administration, on a joint proposal by the national anti-mafia prosecutor Giovanni Melillo, the Naples prosecutor Nicola Gratteri and the Naples police chief. Investigators found that services around the team's matches had been entrusted to firms and people close to the D'Alessandro clan: security, ticketing, refreshments, cleaning, health services, and until 2024 the first team's transport. At the Juve Stabia-Bari match of 9 February 2025 police found a banned supporter filtering spectators at the turnstiles beside the stewards. Tickets issued with altered personal details let banned men close to the clan in.
inside: A camorra clan supplied the football club's own security, ticketing and transport services, so the firm's contracts and its stadium gates served the clan.
cite: InterNapoli, 21 October 2025, on the Naples court's judicial administration decree of 13 October 2025 and the prosecutors' press conference

n: Palermo detergent chain employed mafia bosses' relatives across ten shops
who: Cosa Nostra (Pagliarelli, Uditore and Santa Maria di Gesù families)
rank: Staff and premises of Serena Distribuzione and Bagnasco, ten detergent outlets
d: The Palermo court placed Serena Distribuzione and Bagnasco, which run ten wholesale and retail detergent shops valued at about 18 million euros, under judicial administration for a year in November 2022, appointing an administrator alongside the owners, brothers Giorgio and Francesco Bagnasco. The court said these are not mafia businesses but that a barrier was needed against contact with Cosa Nostra. Prosecutors said the brothers were extortion victims in the early 2000s and did not report it, and that the position developed into a constant readiness to employ relatives of important bosses and to take shop premises owned by known mafiosi. Financial police found the wife and cousin of the Pagliarelli regent Giuseppe Calvaruso worked there.
inside: A retail chain kept mafia bosses' relatives on its payroll and rented mafia-owned premises, so its hiring and its shops served Cosa Nostra families.
cite: LiveSicilia, 8 November 2022, on the Palermo court's judicial administration decree (Guardia di Finanza, Nucleo di polizia economico-finanziaria)

n: Four flight attendants used crew security lanes to fly fentanyl cash to the Dominican Republic
org_label: Fentanyl trafficking and money laundering network (unnamed)
rank: Flight attendants on commercial New York to Dominican Republic routes
d: Four flight attendants working commercial routes between New York and the Dominican Republic, Charlie Hernández, Sarah Valerio Pujols, Emmanuel Torres and Jarol Fabio, were arrested on 7 May 2024. United States investigators say they regularly carried cash in their suitcases, proceeds of the fentanyl trade, from the United States to the Dominican Republic. The case began with a tip to Homeland Security Investigations from others in the scheme; agents then handed the attendants cash they were told came from drug trafficking and was to be delivered to other members of the organisation. Their known crewmember status let them use a special security lane at John F. Kennedy airport.
inside: A trafficking network used airline cabin crew, whose crew security passes let them carry its drug cash through airports without the usual screening.
cite: InSight Crime, 16 May 2024, citing the US prosecution and Homeland Security Investigations

n: Gold and diamond smugglers passed Cameroon's eastern customs posts
org_label: Gold and diamond smuggling networks on the Central African Republic border
rank: Customs agents based at Kenzou and Garoua-Boulai; a border police officer at Gbiti
d: Gold and diamonds mined illegally in the Central African Republic were carried into eastern Cameroon and sold there. The UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic investigated how smugglers crossed without being stopped, and reported that smugglers said they could also count on the indulgence of Cameroonian customs agents, especially those carrying small quantities. Two customs agents based at Kenzou and Garoua-Boulai and a border police officer at Gbiti told the Panel they paid more attention to drugs and weapons than to gold. The same two agents said they had been asked by their hierarchy to send large carriers to the mining office, but that this was impossible because carriers were often accompanied by other customs officers.
inside: Smuggling networks had Cameroonian customs officers escorting their carriers past the border controls those officers were posted to enforce.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, final report S/2021/569, paras. 158-159

n: Fuel smuggling network ran Benghazi's old harbour through a commander
org_label: Maeen Ali Sharfeddin petroleum smuggling network
rank: Ali Al-Mashai, commander with control over military personnel stationed at Benghazi port
d: A criminal network led by Maeen Ali Sharfeddin, a Libyan-Turkish dual national based in Turkiye, exported petroleum illicitly from eastern Libya through at least 24 tanker vessels held by single-purpose shell companies. The UN Panel of Experts on Libya found that Sharfeddin worked in close coordination with Ali Al-Mashai and the top command of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces, and that Al-Mashai's command and control over military personnel stationed at Benghazi port, and over the old harbour's resources, were decisive in turning that harbour into a fuel smuggling hub. The Panel listed Al-Mashai's role in the network as enabling it to operate in ports under LAAF control. It recorded no investigation by Libyan authorities into the network's armed robbery and piracy at sea.
inside: A fuel smuggling network worked through the commander of the troops guarding Benghazi port, so the harbour's military control served the network's exports.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, paras. 117-119 and annex 9 (criminal network growing through illicit export of petroleum), paras. 43-46

n: Traffickers paid Libyan forces for migrants' entry stamps at Benina airport
org_label: Private trafficking and smuggling networks in eastern Libya
rank: Individuals belonging to the Haftar Armed Forces controlling arrivals at Benina airport
d: Migrants flown into eastern Libya on trafficking routes landed at Benina airport outside Benghazi. The UN Panel of Experts on Libya found that individuals belonging to the Haftar Armed Forces held the migrants' visa papers and confiscated their passports until elements of the trafficking network based in Benghazi paid an unspecified sum, after which the documents were returned with a Libyan entry stamp and the network could move the migrants on. The Panel holds samples of the entry stamps produced by those forces. The LAAF general command contested the Panel's findings on its units' involvement in trafficking and said migrants were the interior ministry's responsibility, but supplied no supporting evidence; the Panel relied on 24 victims and eyewitnesses and over 20 documents.
inside: Trafficking networks paid the armed force controlling arrivals at Benina airport, which then stamped their migrants into Libya on demand.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report S/2023/673, annex 21 (trafficking and smuggling of persons in eastern Libya), paras. 6 and 12-13

n: Libyan coastguard and group 20/20 took boat fees from migrant smugglers
org_label: Private trafficking and smuggling networks in Tobruk and Musaid
rank: Individuals of the Libyan Coast Guard East and the group 20/20 maritime units; the TBZ brigade
d: Private networks ran migrant boats to Europe from the coast at Tobruk and Musaid in eastern Libya. The UN Panel of Experts on Libya found that, before departure, individuals of the Haftar Armed Forces' coastguard were paid around $100 per migrant for free passage into international waters on condition that no more than 250 people were carried, with an additional fee when that limit was broken, and that individuals of the group 20/20 maritime units demanded around $80,000 to provide security for larger fishing boats. Boats whose organisers had not paid were interdicted and returned to Tobruk, and the migrants held on shore until the smugglers paid about $4,500 for their release. The LAAF general command contested these findings without supplying evidence.
inside: Smuggling networks bought the eastern coastguard's own patrol decisions, so the force that was meant to stop the boats escorted the paying ones out.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report S/2023/673, annex 21 (trafficking and smuggling of persons in eastern Libya), paras. 9-13

n: Trafficking rings paid Libya's 20-20 battalion commander $500 a migrant
org_label: International human trafficking and migrant smuggling rings
rank: Ali Al Mashai, commander of the 20-20 battalion; TBZ brigade personnel at Benghazi port
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya identified Ali Al Mashai, commander of the 20-20 battalion, as a key operative in an international trafficking and smuggling scheme carried out with international trafficking rings since at least 2023. The Panel found he allowed migrant boats safe passage through eastern Libyan territorial waters in return for $500 per person as a protection racket, collected from a separate Libya-based criminal network. To run the scheme he controlled an unofficial detention site in Benghazi port, a hangar holding between 650 and 1,000 migrants, some for over a year, used as forced labour for LAAF ranks. After one partner network refused a stopover, the Panel found he ordered TBZ personnel to detain and torture five of its migrants.
inside: International trafficking rings paid a Libyan battalion commander a fee per migrant, and his troops and vessels then waved their boats through.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report S/2024/914, annex 25 (Ali Al Mashai), paras. 1-8

n: Gang leader's family bribed Yunnan prison officials for three term cuts
org_label: Sun Xiaoguo's criminal gang and his family
rank: Officials of the justice bureau and of the prison holding him; staff of the provincial court, public security and prison systems
d: Sun Xiaoguo was sentenced to death by the Kunming Intermediate People's Court in 1998 for rape, intentional injury and disturbance of public order. From 2004 to 2009 his parents visited officials at the justice bureau and at the prison where he was held, asking them to give him special care in return for bribes. He later received a falsified patent that helped him qualify for commutation, and his sentence was illegally cut three times; at the end of 2008 his parents had him transferred to another prison so it could be cut again. He was released in April 2010 after 12 years and five months. In December 2019 Yunnan courts sentenced 19 people, his mother to 20 years and his stepfather to 19.
inside: A gang leader's family paid prison and justice officials, who then handed him illegal sentence cuts and a transfer that let him walk out early.
cite: China Daily, 16 December 2019, '19 sentenced for helping death row man cut jail time'

n: Kunming police took bribes and bailed a gang leader after an assault case
org_label: Sun Xiaoguo's criminal gang and his family
rank: Police officials who handled his detention; officials of the public security and judicial systems
d: In July 2018 Sun Xiaoguo, who had been released early from a Yunnan prison and had built up bars and company holdings, was caught by the Kunming Public Security Bureau on suspicion of intentionally injuring another man. Under the law he should have been detained, but he was released on bail a month later after police officials received bribes from his stepfather Li Qiaozhong and a friend, according to the statement issued by the provincial authorities. Even after media reports exposed his record, Li offered further bribes to officials in the public security and judicial systems. In November 2019 a court sentenced Sun as the ringleader of a 13-member gang to 25 years in prison.
inside: A gang leader's family paid police officials, who then released him on bail instead of holding him as the law required.
cite: China Daily, 16 December 2019, '19 sentenced for helping death row man cut jail time'

n: Ivory syndicate used Dar es Salaam airport security men to move tusks
org_label: Ivory smuggling syndicate exporting through Julius Nyerere International Airport
rank: Two Tanzania People's Defence Forces soldiers seconded to the airport and two Tanzania Airports Authority security officers
d: Four security officers at Julius Nyerere International Airport in Dar es Salaam were charged in September 2015 with aiding ivory smuggling. They were two soldiers of the Tanzania People's Defence Forces seconded to the airport, Salum Mnyonesi and Albadil Mshana, and two Tanzania Airports Authority security officers, Clemence Mbaruck and Emmanuel Nsanganiye. Prosecutors alleged that between 2 and 6 July, as public officials working as security officers, they went against their duties and furthered the intentions of a criminal racket, facilitating the export of 150 kg of tusks, 21 lion teeth and 35 lion claws valued at $127,334. The Kisutu court remanded them, and prosecutors said investigations were continuing.
inside: A smuggling racket had the soldiers and security officers who screened the airport's cargo clearing its ivory through instead of stopping it.
cite: The Citizen (Tanzania), 15 September 2015, 'JNIA security men charged over ivory'

n: Traffickers had Bolivia's anti-narcotics chief guarding their cocaine
org_label: Cocaine trafficking network shipping from Bolivia to New York
rank: Director of the Fuerza Especial de Lucha Contra el Narcotrafico (FELCN), Bolivia's chief anti-narcotics agency
d: Maximiliano Davila Perez was director of FELCN, the force that leads Bolivia's drug enforcement. The US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York said that between about February 2019 and November 2019, while he held that post, he used his office and his law-enforcement connections to help large-scale cocaine trafficking: he diverted investigators away from favoured traffickers and supplied heavily armed FELCN personnel as security for cocaine shipments leaving Bolivian airports. On recorded calls he said he would run an operation elsewhere to take out everyone who might interfere, and authorised a 10 kg sample delivered in Lima. He was extradited in December 2024, convicted on 23 October 2025 and sentenced on 19 March 2026 to 25 years.
inside: Traffickers obtained the head of Bolivia's drug-fighting agency, whose armed officers then guarded their cocaine and whose investigators were steered away.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York, press release 26-071, 19 March 2026

n: Czech policeman convicted of selling operation details to a dealer
rank: Officer of the Czech police, since dismissed from the force
d: A Prague court gave Miroslav Tolar, a police officer who had been dismissed from the force, a one-year suspended sentence. Radio Prague reported in August 2004 that he was found guilty of repeatedly giving information about police operations to an Albanian drug dealer, whom the report calls a crime boss. The report does not say which unit Tolar served in, what he was paid, or over how long the information passed, and it gives no further detail of the operations concerned. What the court convicted him of is the transfer itself: a serving officer handing a trafficker information about the operations of the force he belonged to.
inside: A drug dealer bought a serving Czech police officer, who then told him what police operations were coming so he could avoid them.
cite: Radio Prague International, 20 August 2004, 'Former policeman gets suspended sentence for aiding drug boss'

n: Gangs paid guards wing by wing inside Ecuador's biggest prison
who: Los Choneros and allied prison gangs
rank: Prison guards and their superiors at the Litoral penitentiary, Guayaquil
d: William Joffre Alcivar Bautista, known as El Negro Willy, took a job as a prison guard in 2012, first at La Regional and then at Litoral, Ecuador's biggest prison. A leader of the Netas gang told InSight Crime that each wing held a different gang and that guards collected their daily dues from them, and that if a wing boss wanted to intimidate the guards, the guards would talk to their superiors, who would order a change in the wing's leaders. Alcivar began smuggling in phones, chargers, SIM cards and then guns, working with wing leaders, and was taken up by Choneros leader Jorge Luis Zambrano. Prosecutors also alleged guards paid inmates up to $75 a bag to swallow cocaine and carry it back after court hearings.
inside: Prison gangs paid Litoral's guards a daily cut, and one of those guards became a trafficker who later founded his own gang.
cite: InSight Crime, 28 November 2024, 'The Rise and Fall of El Negro Willy, Ecuador's Prison-Guard Mafia Boss'

n: Two Ecuadorian navy personnel worked as a Choneros leader's bodyguards
rank: Two serving personnel of the Ecuadorian Navy
d: InSight Crime reported in January 2023 that an investigation into Junior Roldan, alias JR, a leader of the Choneros gang, had found in January of the previous year that two navy personnel had been working as his bodyguards. The report sets this among a run of cases tying Ecuador's navy to criminal groups, including navy officers said to have sold information to Colombian armed groups. A journalist who read the intelligence reports told InSight Crime that most cocaine now leaves by sea, and that the navy is in the ports, decides about permits and crews the ships. The item does not name the two personnel, their unit or the outcome of the investigation.
inside: A drug gang had serving navy personnel guarding its leader, putting the force's own people at the service of the men it was meant to pursue.
cite: InSight Crime, 26 January 2023, 'Ecuador's Navy Grappling With Mounting Evidence of Criminal Collusion'

n: Vibo prison health director accused of compliant reports for clan men
who: 'Ndrangheta clans of the Vibo Valentia area
rank: Forensic doctor and health director of the Vibo Valentia prison
d: The Catanzaro district anti-mafia directorate's Maestrale-Carthago investigation, made public in May 2023, listed 167 suspects and set out how clans around Vibo Valentia reached public administration. Among them is Alfonso Luciano, a forensic doctor and health director of the Vibo prison. Prosecutors accuse him of issuing compliant expert medical reports in favour of affiliated detainees. Investigators say he also interceded with other doctors and staff of the local health authority to cancel or lighten administrative penalties, and passed on confidential news including about investigations under way and imminent arrests, receiving goods, sums of money, protection from extortion demands and electoral support, as at the 2004 elections when he sought the Bonavota clan's backing.
inside: Prosecutors say clans got the doctor who ran a prison's health service, whose medical reports and leaks then served their jailed members.
cite: Il Fatto Quotidiano, 10 May 2023, on the Maestrale-Carthago investigation, DDA Catanzaro

n: Caltagirone prison officer warned a mafia heir of a raid two days ahead
rank: Assistant of the prison police corps (polizia penitenziaria)
d: Two days before the Agora operation, Gianfranco La Rocca, son of the dead Caltagirone boss Ciccio La Rocca and regarded as his heir, was warned by an assistant of the prison police. The ROS intercepted a conversation on 14 June in which the officer, Angelo Allegra, described the raid due the following evening, which would involve at least 50 people in the province of Catania. La Rocca then behaved in ways designed to avoid arrest and was located only four days after the order was executed. Allegra was arrested on charges of aiding an offender and revealing official secrets, aggravated by having favoured Cosa nostra. Investigators recorded his full availability and subservience to the boss, and said he also acted as an intermediary.
inside: A mafia heir had a serving prison officer inside the police, who told him the date of the raid meant to arrest him.
cite: LiveSicilia, 8 September 2022

n: Palermo flying-squad officers accused of selling protection to drug dealers
org_label: Palermo drug-dealing group around Ignazio Carollo
rank: Two vice sovrintendenti of the squadra mobile, Palermo police headquarters
d: Fabrizio Spedale and Salvatore Graziano, both deputy superintendents of the Palermo flying squad, were jailed in October 2023 on corruption charges. Prosecutors allege they offered protection to drug dealers in exchange for money and four motorcycles, tipping them off about investigations under way and about searches; the article also refers to the unexplained disappearance of drugs held in police stores. The same custody measure was ordered for the man they are said to have favoured, Ignazio Carollo. The Palermo prosecutor's office found the contacts after bugs were placed for a separate inquiry; in intercepted talk the officer was referred to by the cover name Mirko, and the dealers discussed whether their phones were being monitored.
inside: Dealers paid two serving officers of Palermo's flying squad, who then told them which investigations and searches were coming.
cite: LiveSicilia, 4 October 2023

n: Foggia prison officers held over phones and drugs sold to inmates
org_label: Inmates and outside intermediaries running phone and drug supply at Foggia prison
rank: Two officers of the prison police corps serving at Foggia prison
d: Two officers of the prison police serving at Foggia prison were placed under precautionary measures in October 2025 in an investigation into illegal traffic in mobile phones and drugs inside the jail. One is accused of bringing in the handsets and SIM cards and also drugs then sold on to inmates for money; he was taken into custody, while his colleague was barred from the profession for a year. Six other people, five inmates and a professional, were reported at liberty for unlawful access to communication devices. The investigation was run by the Guardia di Finanza provincial command in Foggia with prison police staff, and uncovered a system of favours that let detainees reach the outside world.
inside: Inmates and their outside suppliers paid two serving prison officers, whose own hands carried the phones and drugs past the prison's checks.
cite: Antenna Sud, 6 October 2025, 'Foggia, droga e sim in carcere: un agente arrestato, uno sospeso'

n: Nuoro prison officer accused of helping a mafia boss escape over the wall
org_label: Marco Raduano's Gargano mafia clan and its network of helpers
rank: Officer of the prison police serving at the Badu 'e Carros prison, Nuoro
d: Marco Raduano, a boss of the Gargano mafia, escaped from the Badu 'e Carros prison near Nuoro on 24 February 2023 and was arrested in Corsica on 1 February 2024. In December 2024 a second custody order, sought by the Cagliari district anti-mafia directorate, led to 14 arrests including an officer of the prison police serving at Badu 'e Carros, accused of having helped the escape by supplying him with material of various kinds. Raduano had mobile phones, duplicate keys to the building, and a hook taken from the prison workshops that let him get over the perimeter wall on knotted sheets. Seven more people were arrested on the Bari directorate's request for aiding an offender.
inside: A mafia boss reached an officer inside the prison holding him, who is accused of supplying the kit he used to get over the wall.
cite: Antenna Sud, 5 December 2024, 'Fuga boss Raduano, un poliziotto penitenziario tra gli arrestati'

n: Taranto prison officer paid by an inmate drug ring fed by drones
org_label: Inmate-run drug ring at Taranto's Magli prison and its outside logistics network
who: inmate-run drug ring at Taranto prison
rank: Officer of the prison police, second section, Magli prison, Taranto
d: From May 2024 prosecutors in Taranto investigated a trade in hashish and cocaine for inmates of the Magli prison, run mainly by three medium-security detainees who used an outside logistics network of relatives, friends and recruited drone operators to fly packages to cell windows. The investigation documented the involvement of an officer of the prison police serving there who, in exchange for sums of money, made himself available to assist the group. That officer, Domenico Matera, had already been arrested in October 2024 with about 900 grammes of hashish, 12 grammes of cocaine and a miniature phone hidden in his car inside the prison perimeter and at his home. Eleven people were placed under precautionary measures in May 2026.
inside: An inmate drug ring paid a serving prison officer, who then carried its hashish, cocaine and phones through the gate for it.
cite: Antenna Sud, 22 September 2024 and 28 May 2026

n: Prison Dealer: Augusta inmates' drug market ran through an officer
org_label: Criminal association supplying drugs and phones to Augusta prison inmates
who: Catania-Augusta drug and phone supply group
rank: Superintendent of the prison police serving at the Augusta-Brucoli prison
d: In April 2021 the Guardia di Finanza in Catania executed a custody order against 16 people in the Prison Dealer inquiry, 15 of them sent to jail. Prosecutors say a criminal organisation active between Catania and Augusta had two purposes: to obtain and sell drugs, from cocaine to skunk, among inmates of the Augusta-Brucoli prison, and to deliver mobile phones to them. The business was allegedly directed from inside by two detainees who gave instructions by phone to associates outside. The charges include criminal association for drug trafficking, association to procure phones for detainees, and corruption of public officials for acts against their duties. The group is said to have got past every check thanks to a superintendent of the prison police serving there.
inside: An inmate-run drug business reached a prison police superintendent, whose cooperation let its drugs and phones pass every check at the gate.
cite: LiveSicilia, 14 April 2021, on the Guardia di Finanza 'Prison Dealer' operation, Procura di Catania

n: Foggia municipal police officer dealt heroin in a clan-linked network
org_label: Societa Foggiana-linked trafficking and stolen-vehicle group
rank: Officer of the local police of the comune of Foggia
d: Carabinieri in Foggia arrested five people in October 2019 after an investigation by the Foggia prosecutor's office into attempted extortion, handling stolen goods, money laundering, theft and drug dealing. The group's largest profits came from selling vehicles whose identifying data had been altered by swapping chassis onto stolen cars. The prosecutor's office said that in the drug side of the business there also operated an officer of the local police of the comune of Foggia, who was moreover a relative of a prominent figure of the Societa Foggiana arrested in the Decima Azione operation. The officer, Antonio Spiritoso, dealt in heroin and cocaine, including from his home, where drugs and precision scales were found.
inside: A clan-linked trafficking group counted a serving municipal police officer among the people running its heroin and cocaine business.
cite: l'Immediato (Foggia), 16 October 2019, on the Procura di Foggia operation

n: Naples carabiniere allegedly set a roadblock for a clan's ambush
rank: Carabiniere identified in the custody order only as Giuseppe B.
d: A custody order of October 2022 against the Baratto-Volpe clan sets out two collaborators' statements about a carabiniere named only as Giuseppe B. Davide Leone, formerly senior in the Puccinelli camorra group, says the officer parked outside his house while he was under house arrest so other forces would not check on him, and that on 15 May 2007 he told the officer where he had hidden the two pistols used in a shooting that day, so the officer searched the basement himself and the guns did not come out. Leone also says the officer warned him of a bug in a power socket and agreed to mount a roadblock so his group could locate a man they planned to kill; that ambush was never carried out.
inside: Prosecutors say camorra groups had a serving carabiniere whose own searches, warnings and roadblocks were run for them, not against them.
cite: Stylo24, 15 and 17 November 2022, on the October 2022 custody order against the Baratto-Volpe clan

n: Fuel-fraud clans reached finance police and a carabiniere in Taranto
rank: Two men of the Guardia di Finanza provincial command in Taranto; a carabiniere
d: In April 2021 the Potenza and Lecce anti-mafia directorates' Febbre dell'oro nero inquiry into fuel-trade fraud sent 26 people to jail and 11 to house arrest. It set out links between separate but connected criminal organisations in Lecce, Potenza, the Vallo di Diano and the province of Taranto, all turning around mafia families traceable to the Casalesi clan and to Taranto groups. Among those jailed was a carabiniere accused of revealing official secrets, who investigators say passed valuable information to other suspects and was rewarded for it. Two men of the Guardia di Finanza provincial command in Taranto were suspended for six months on the same charge. Prosecutors said suspects applied many pressures on police, which in almost all cases came to nothing.
inside: Fuel-fraud clans reached officers of the finance police and the carabinieri, who are accused of selling them what the investigations held.
cite: Stylo24, 12 April 2021, on the 'Febbre dell'oro nero' operation, DDA Potenza and Lecce

n: Naples carabiniere kept a clan boss out of the police database
rank: Carabiniere of the Bagnoli company, Naples
d: Mario Cinque, a carabiniere of the Bagnoli company in Naples, was one of two officers of the force arrested in August 2021, accused of having favoured the activities of the Cutolo clan of Rione Traiano. Gennaro Carra, then the clan's boss in the district and now a collaborator with prosecutors, told them that in 2015, during a stop, Cinque said he needed a stolen Mercedes SLK; Carra obtained a black one about a month later and, on Cinque's instructions, left it unlocked with the keys under the sun visor outside a restaurant in Pozzuoli, and was never paid. Carra said that in most cases Cinque did not enter him in the police database, so he was not checked at all. The presumption of innocence applies.
inside: A camorra boss says he supplied a carabiniere with a stolen car, and the officer in return kept him off the police database and out of checks.
cite: Stylo24, 5 August 2021, on the custody order executed the previous day

n: Catanzaro prison officer accused of being the clan's sentinel inside
who: Rom clan of Catanzaro and 'ndrangheta groups
rank: Officer of the prison police, Catanzaro prison
d: Domenico Sacco, a prison officer, was arrested in April 2023 in the Catanzaro anti-mafia directorate's investigation into the rise of the city's Rom clan. The judge's view was that he systematically let himself be corrupted to help detainees belonging to criminal organisations, giving the group privileged information, carrying messages between bosses and members, and putting pressure on some to stop them cooperating with prosecutors. Collaborator Santo Mirarchi said in March 2016 that while he was held in Catanzaro prison Sacco brought him a mobile phone for 200 euros. Collaborator Annamaria Cerminara said Sacco told her former partner which detainees meant to turn, warned detainees that visiting rooms were bugged, and asked for a car and a job for his wife.
inside: Clans had a serving officer inside Catanzaro prison who moved their messages, warned of bugs and pressed detainees not to testify.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 19 April 2023, on the DDA Catanzaro custody order

n: Cosenza prison officers charged with selling comfort to clan bosses
rank: Officers of the prison police, Cosenza prison in via Popilia
d: The Catanzaro anti-mafia directorate obtained the imprisonment in June 2019 of two prison officers at Cosenza's jail in via Popilia, Luigi Frassanito and Giovanni Porco, on charges of external complicity in a mafia association; a third, now retired, was investigated at liberty. Prosecutors say they made prison life more comfortable for the heads and members of the Cosenza cosche, from the Lanzino-Rua and Rango-Zingari groups to the Perna group and the Bruni family, with the comforts reserved for those with criminal standing. Adolfo Foggetti, a former member of the Rango-Zingari cosca, told prosecutors the officers were at their disposal and were paid with sums of money drawn from the cosca's pot, and that he also gave perfumes.
