inside: Clans paid officers inside Cosenza prison, who then ran the wing's privileges for their bosses and carried their messages out.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 19 June 2019, on the DDA Catanzaro investigation

n: Volla's mayor and officials took Langella cash, with a cut for clan Veneruso
who: Clan Veneruso and the Langella business group
rank: Mayor of Volla, a former public works assessore, a municipal official and an Ecology Office employee
d: A Guardia di Finanza inquiry coordinated by the Naples anti-mafia directorate brought thirteen custody measures and 54 suspects in November 2026. Investigators allege the Veneruso clan lent its intimidation to the Langella family's waste and health firms, which in return funded the organisation, and that awards at the comuni of Volla, Casoria, Somma Vesuviana and Cercola were examined. At Volla, prosecutors allege a system of illicit payments, cash wrapped in newspaper and handed over in a car, to municipal officials; the mayor, Giuliano Di Costanzo, is accused of corruption for an act contrary to his duties, allegedly chasing payment of the firms' invoices. Part of the money allegedly went to the clan. The mafia aggravation is excluded for the mayor.
inside: Prosecutors say a camorra clan's allied contractors paid Volla's mayor, an ex-assessore and officials, so municipal refuse awards and payments served the firms and the clan.
cite: Anteprima24, 10 November 2026, on the Naples GIP's custody order (pm Woodcock and Colonna Romano)

n: Cerva's mayor won on a 'ndrina's votes, then bent his office for it
who: The 'ndrangheta locale at Cerva and Petrona
rank: Mayor of Cerva, a majority councillor, an assessore-councillor for public works and a municipal employee
d: In operation Karpanthos, carabinieri in Catanzaro arrested members of an 'ndrangheta locale that prosecutors say dominated the comuni of Cerva and Petrona and also controlled Cerva's municipal administration. Mayor Fabrizio Rizzuti was put under house arrest for political-mafia vote exchange: in 2017 he and two candidates allegedly asked Tommaso 'Masino' Scalzi, already convicted of mafia association, for electoral help through the mayor's brother, a municipal employee, promising money and a percentage of the comune's public contracts. Their list won 436 votes to 416 and seven of ten council seats. The investigating judge wrote that Rizzuti was ready to bend his public function to clan members' interests, citing a falsely certified wedding. Rizzuti denied ever having had dealings with one of them; the judge held the charge incontrovertibly proved.
inside: A Calabrian mafia cell delivered votes that made Rizzuti mayor of Cerva, and prosecutors say he then used his office for its members' private requests.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 22 September 2023, quoting the Catanzaro GIP's custody order

n: Amantea council dissolved after favours to firms tied to the local cosca
rank: Mayor, electoral lists, polling scrutineers and departmental staff of the comune of Amantea
d: A commission of access appointed by the prefect of Cosenza found concrete, unambiguous and significant evidence of direct and indirect links between Amantea's administrators and organised crime, and the interior minister's report said the distorted use of public office had taken the form of favouring people or firms connected to criminal circles. Signatories of two of the three lists at the 2017 municipal elections, and polling scrutineers named by the municipal electoral commission, included people close to or related to the Gentile-Africano-Besaldo cosca. Just over 57 per cent of payments under a home-care project went to a firm barred under anti-mafia rules, and a day centre's operator kept receiving municipal money despite a ban. Amantea's council was dissolved.
inside: A Calabrian cosca's people stood among Amantea's candidate lists and polling staff, and the comune kept paying firms the state had barred for mafia links.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 3 March 2020, quoting the Cosenza prefecture's report and the interior minister's dissolution report

n: Mileto's former assessore steered the comune's refuse contract for a 'ndrina
rank: Former city councillor, assessore and deputy mayor of the comune of Mileto
d: After the two Maestrale-Carthago operations run by the Catanzaro anti-mafia directorate, the prefect of Vibo Valentia sent a commission of access into the comune of Mileto in December 2023 to check for conditioning by local organised crime. Prosecutors allege that several men who had held municipal office at Mileto for years, as councillor, assessore and deputy mayor, were active members of the town's 'ndrangheta locale. They say Vincenzo Nicolaci, known as 'the assessore', used his political contacts to steer the urban refuse contract covering Briatico, Mileto and Rizziconi, and that he and another suspect collected the contractor's profits and handed them to clan figures. The sitting mayor and administration are not under investigation.
inside: Prosecutors say men who had held Mileto's council seats belonged to the local mafia cell and used their contacts to direct the comune's refuse contract to it.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 11 December 2023, on the Maestrale-Carthago files and the prefect's decision

n: Catanzaro appeal judge Petrini paid for rulings; a cosca's family tried too
who: Gallace-Gallelli-Saraco cosca and a brokering network
rank: Section president, Catanzaro Court of Appeal, and president of the provincial tax commission
d: The Salerno anti-mafia directorate, which handles crimes involving Calabrian magistrates, had seven people arrested in January 2020. Among them was Marco Petrini, a section president of the Catanzaro Court of Appeal. Prosecutors allege suspects repeatedly promised and handed him cash, valuables and sexual services for rulings favourable to themselves or to others, in some cases to undo first-instance convictions, preventive measures or anti-mafia asset seizures; a retired health official allegedly paid him 1,500 euros a month. One strand concerns a Locri lawyer whose father the judges hold to belong to the 'ndrangheta cosca Gallace-Gallelli-Saraco: a 100,000-euro cheque was shown to reach the presiding judge through her husband. That attempt failed, and the appeal court confirmed the convictions on 17 July 2019.
inside: Prosecutors say money and favours bought a senior appeal judge's rulings, and a mafia family's relatives tried to buy the bench that was judging them.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 15 January 2020, two reports on the Salerno prosecutors' custody order

n: Istanbul prosecutor accused of tipping off the group around the city's mayor
org_label: The network prosecutors call the Imamoglu criminal organisation
who: A group prosecutors describe as a criminal organisation
rank: Public prosecutor at the Istanbul Courthouse
d: Turkiye's Board of Judges and Prosecutors opened an investigation into a prosecutor at the Istanbul Courthouse, named only by the initials S.C.S., over claims that she met the lawyer of the then Istanbul mayor Ekrem Imamoglu before the corruption operation that led to his arrest in March 2025, and that she indirectly threatened a prosecutor handling his case. The claim first came from the jailed former driver of a businessman in the same case, who is seeking leniency; inspectors reviewed hotel footage, phone and cell-tower records, which they said put her and the lawyer at the same hotel. She denied all the allegations and said the witness statements were inaccurate. She was reportedly suspended and moved to the Sanliurfa chief prosecutor's office.
inside: Prosecutors allege a group around Istanbul's mayor had a prosecutor inside the courthouse warning it of raids, which would turn the court's own secrecy to its use.
cite: Daily Sabah, 1 December 2025, reporting the Sabah newspaper and the HSK investigation

n: Istanbul enforcement judge jailed over a case decided for an MP
org_label: An alleged criminal organisation led by a suspect named as M.S.
who: An alleged bribery organisation reaching Istanbul's courthouses
rank: Judge of the Istanbul 4th Enforcement Court; five judges and prosecutors suspended
d: The Bakirkoy chief public prosecutor's office is investigating a bribery network reaching across Istanbul's courthouses. Five judges and prosecutors were removed from duty, and inquiries were opened into a retired prosecutor and a judge who had resigned. The former judge of the Istanbul 4th Enforcement Court, named as B.K., was jailed for bribery on 3 October 2026. Investigators say evidence indicates that a case at that court, in which a member of parliament for Kocaeli was a party, was concluded in the member's favour through an alleged crime group leader and a man who has fled abroad, and that material benefit was given to the judge; part was allegedly paid into his bank account as a deposit. A lawyer was also jailed.
inside: Prosecutors say an organised bribery ring reached judges inside Istanbul's courts and had one enforcement case decided for the party who paid.
cite: Isci Haber, 18 November 2026, citing Hurriyet, on the Bakirkoy prosecutors' investigation

n: Palermo prosecution usher became the criminal circuit's check on its own files
rank: Judicial usher, Public Prosecutor's Office of Palermo
d: Police arrested a judicial usher serving at the Palermo prosecutor's office in November 2023 on a custody order for continued and aggravated assistance to offenders. His job was carrying case files from prosecutors' secretariats to other court offices. Prosecutors allege he consulted proceedings without authority, photographed and circulated documents covered by secrecy, took files out of the building and told the people concerned about investigations and wiretaps under way, seriously damaging several inquiries. The chief prosecutor, Maurizio de Lucia, said in a note that the usher appeared to have become the point of reference for figures in the Palermo criminal circuit who wanted to check whether investigations existed against them, and that the operation was part of wider work to find such moles.
inside: A clerk inside Palermo's prosecution service allegedly sold criminal suspects advance word of the inquiries and wiretaps aimed at them.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 7 November 2023, quoting the note of Palermo prosecutor Maurizio de Lucia

n: Catanzaro prosecution official accused of feeding the Cutro 'ndrina case news
who: Martino 'ndrina of Cutro, linked to the Grande Aracri family
rank: Judicial official, Public Prosecutor's Office of Catanzaro
d: Operation Sahel, run by the Catanzaro anti-mafia directorate, struck a 'ndrangheta association working at Cutro and a drug-trafficking group subordinate to it, with 31 cautionary measures. When the inquiry was formally closed in February 2025 the list of 54 suspects included Renato Guarnieri, a judicial official serving at the Catanzaro prosecutor's office. Prosecutors allege that, without belonging to it, he assisted the Cutro mafia association from outside, and in particular the Martino 'ndrina linked to the Grande Aracri family, with the task of supplying confidential information about criminal proceedings under way that concerned that family. Investigators also say a brother-in-law of the 'ndrina's head disclosed that an investigation existed which could have led to arrests.
inside: Prosecutors say an official inside the Catanzaro prosecution service passed a mafia family confidential news of the criminal cases against it.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 6 February 2025, on the closure of the Sahel investigation

n: Businessman's 1,500 lei sped an invoice at CFR Calatori's Timisoara branch
org_label: A buildings-repair contractor of SRTFC Timisoara
rank: Director of the Timisoara regional branch, Societatea Nationala CFR Calatori SA
d: CFR Calatori is Romania's state passenger rail operator, and it runs its work through regional branches. In July 2022 anticorruption prosecutors sent for trial Florin Blagaila, at the time director of the Timisoara regional branch, for bribe-taking, together with a businessman charged with giving a bribe and the businessman's son charged as an accomplice. The prosecutors allege that on 17 March 2022 Blagaila received 1,500 lei from the businessman to speed up payment of an invoice worth 33,724 lei, issued by the businessman's company under a contract with the Timisoara regional branch for the repair and maintenance of buildings on the Deva lot. The file went to the Timis Tribunal; all are presumed innocent.
inside: A rail contractor paid the branch director who controlled its payments, so the state operator settled that firm's bill ahead of others.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press bulletin no. 598/VIII/3, 4 July 2022, item 2

n: Festive-lighting firm's no-notice contract at Ploiesti's city company
rank: Director general and deputy director general, SC Servicii de Gospodarire Urbana Ploiesti SRL
d: Servicii de Gospodarire Urbana Ploiesti is a company owned entirely by the city of Ploiesti through its local council. In June 2021 prosecutors sent its director general Donald-Nicolae Constantin, deputy director general Ovidiu Negulescu and a company administrator for trial. Prosecutors allege that in 2013 the two directors, by prior agreement with the businessman, awarded his firm a contract to rent decorative festive lighting without publishing a participation notice, a route open only for extreme urgency caused by unforeseeable events. The day before being invited to negotiate, his firm had rented the same equipment from another company. Against an initial rental price of 491,700 lei the public company paid him 1,090,767 lei. On 14 January 2026 the Ploiesti Court of Appeal ended the case as time-barred and ordered damages.
inside: A supplier's prior deal with the two directors of a city-owned company got it a no-notice contract, and the company paid twice the going rate.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 592/VIII/3, 17 June 2021, with the update of 14 January 2026 on the Ploiesti Court of Appeal decision

n: Supplier set the prices for Piatra Neamt hospital's paediatrics refit
org_label: A medical equipment supplier in a bidding consortium
rank: Manager and head of the procurement service, Piatra Neamt County Emergency Hospital
d: In November 2021 anticorruption prosecutors sent for trial Ioan Lazar, manager of the Piatra Neamt county emergency hospital, Oana-Dana Murariu, head of its procurement service, and a company administrator charged as an accomplice. Prosecutors allege that in 2015 the businessman supplied the list of medical and non-medical equipment and its prices before the hospital drew up the tender papers for refitting the paediatrics ward, so that the estimate was inflated and only one bidder took part. The estimated contract value was set at 11,858,855 lei without VAT, of which 5,014,294 lei, about 42 per cent, was the overvalued equipment. The works were still unfinished, but the equipment was delivered and paid for between December 2015 and December 2017. All are presumed innocent.
inside: A supplier wrote the price list and specifications the hospital then tendered on, so the hospital bought his equipment at his own inflated figures.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 952/VIII/3, 18 November 2021

n: Businessman's firm wired into a Romanian water company's treatment plant
org_label: A company connected to the Pucioasa treatment plant supply
rank: Director general, SC Compania de Apa Targoviste - Dambovita SA
d: Compania de Apa Targoviste - Dambovita is the county water and sewerage company in southern Romania. In November 2021 prosecutors sent its director general Adrian Dumitru for trial on two counts of abuse of office, one with benefits obtained for another, together with a company administrator charged as an accomplice. Prosecutors allege that in November 2017 Dumitru ordered the businessman's company connected illegally to the electricity network of the Pucioasa treatment plant, which the water company ran, with no documents setting out supply, invoicing or payment. The water company lost 79,517 lei in unpaid electricity and the businessman's firm gained the same amount. Prosecutors also allege that on 1 March 2021 Dumitru abusively ended the employment of a subordinate who had reported the arrangement.
inside: A firm got free power from a county water company because its director ordered the connection, and the employee who reported it was dismissed.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 958/VIII/3, 19 November 2021

n: Software firm's 164,505 lei won two Hidroelectrica monitoring contracts
org_label: A monitoring software company held by a Hidroelectrica engineer
rank: Deputy technical director, Curtea de Arges hydropower branch, Hidroelectrica SA
d: Hidroelectrica is Romania's state hydropower producer, and it runs its plants through branches. In August 2015 prosecutors sent for trial Octavian Florian Oprea, deputy technical director of the Curtea de Arges hydropower branch. Prosecutors allege he accepted a promise and received 164,505.99 lei in 2011 from Stefan Vulparu, an engineer in the branch's technical service who was also a partner in a commercial company, so that Vulparu's company would be given two contracts, awarded preferentially, to install monitoring and diagnostic software systems at the Noaptes hydroelectric plant. On 25 April 2024 the Pitesti Court of Appeal ended the case against eight defendants, Vulparu among them, as time-barred, and ended it against Oprea because he had died.
inside: A company part-owned by a branch engineer paid the deputy technical director who awarded its contracts, so the state producer bought its software without competition.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 1370/VIII/3, 14 August 2015, with the update of 25 April 2024 on the Pitesti Court of Appeal decision

n: A fifth of each invoice went to Ploiesti county hospital's manager
org_label: A services contractor of the Ploiesti county hospital
rank: Manager, Ploiesti County Emergency Hospital
d: In September 2015 anticorruption prosecutors sent Ion Alexandru Baloi, manager of the Ploiesti county emergency hospital, for trial in pre-trial detention. Prosecutors allege that between April 2014 and July 2015 he repeatedly took sums from a businessman, who reported him, amounting to about 20 per cent of the value of the invoices the businessman's firm issued under a services contract with the hospital. According to the prosecutors Baloi delayed those payments in order to make the firm's representatives hand over the agreed commission. The release says the evidence showed the benefits were handed over, and the file went to court; Baloi was presumed innocent at that stage.
inside: A hospital contractor paid its manager a fifth of every invoice because he controlled when the hospital paid, and payment followed the commission.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 1490/VIII/3, 22 September 2015

n: Bill-payment firm placed between Posta Romana and the terminal network
org_label: SC Super Total Services SRL, later SC Smart Telecom Solutions SRL
rank: Director general and a deputy director general, CN Posta Romana SA
d: CN Posta Romana is Romania's state postal company. In November 2015 prosecutors sent several people for trial over its electronic bill-payment service. They alleged that on 27 July 2006 the company signed a disadvantageous joint-venture contract with SC Super Total Services SRL, later Smart Telecom Solutions SRL, which placed itself between Posta Romana and the firm owning the card terminals and took part of the state company's profit, costing it 1,437,139.24 euros; the then director general Dan Mihai Toader was said to have pushed subordinates to sign after an understanding with Emmanouil Sorillos. On 7 February 2025 the Bucharest Court of Appeal ended the case against three defendants as time-barred and acquitted Toader, Sorillos, Marian Constantinof and Smart Telecom Solutions, finding the acts were not offences in criminal law.
inside: A middleman firm was written into the state post's bill-payment service and took a cut, and a politician later installed his own man over the commercial directorate.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 1814/VIII/3, 19 November 2015, with the update of 7 February 2025 on the Bucharest Court of Appeal decision

n: Phone-card firm's contract rewritten by a Loteria Romana employee
rank: Director general and the acting head of the purchasing service, CN Loteria Romana SA
d: Loteria Romana is Romania's state lottery, selling through its own loto agencies. In December 2015 prosecutors sent director general Gheorghe Benea and others for trial. They say that on 5 December 2008 Loteria Romana signed a commission contract with SC Form Trade SRL, run in fact by Ionut Marius Marinescu, under which the state company kept a commission on phone cards sold through its agencies, put up no money of its own and carried no risk if the cards did not sell. On 30 April 2009 Ovidiu Ripanu, an employee delegated only to run the purchasing service, signed in the director general's place and without authority; the two then turned the commission contract into a purchase contract, so the state company took on loss-making obligations and commercial risk.
inside: A supplier had a Loteria Romana employee sign in the director general's name, turning a risk-free commission deal into one that put the state company's money at risk.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 2076/VIII/3, 30 December 2015

n: Contractor's 10,000 euros unblocked invoices at Tecuci's municipal hospital
org_label: A contractor on an EU-funded hospital contract
rank: Manager, Anton Cincu Municipal Hospital, Tecuci
d: In June 2016 anticorruption prosecutors sent Teodor Negru, manager of the Anton Cincu municipal hospital in Tecuci, eastern Romania, for trial. Prosecutors allege that between 2014 and 2016 he demanded and received 10,000 euros from the administrator of a commercial company, who reported him, in exchange for the smooth running of a contract signed in 2014 and for releasing for payment invoices the company had issued to the hospital. The contract, financed from European funds, was signed on 21 July 2014 after the company won a public tender. The file went to court and Negru was presumed innocent at that stage.
inside: A contractor paid the hospital manager who controlled its invoices, and the hospital then released the payments that had been held up.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 762/VIII/3, 6 June 2016

n: Garage doors and free work for the head of the Harlau forest district
org_label: A works contractor of the Harlau forest district
rank: Head of the Harlau forest district, Iasi Forestry Directorate
d: Romania's state forests are run through forestry directorates and local forest districts, which buy in works. In April 2016 prosecutors sent for trial Ioan Amariei, head of the Harlau forest district in Iasi county and the purchaser's representative for the Iasi Forestry Directorate. Prosecutors allege that between June and August 2014 he demanded and received benefits from a businessman who reported him: three garage doors worth 7,000 lei, fitted to an outbuilding of the forest district, and the non-payment of 7,000 lei of work the businessman had carried out at Amariei's own house. According to prosecutors he obtained them either by threatening that the firm would not be put forward for further works contracts in the district, or in connection with contracts it already held.
inside: The forest district head took work and goods from a contractor whose future contracts he controlled, so the district kept using that firm.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 602/VIII/3, 28 April 2016

n: Coal supplier's 5 per cent for the finance director of CET Bacau
org_label: A coal supply and transport company
rank: Economic director, SC CET SA Bacau
d: CET Bacau is the municipal combined heat and power company in eastern Romania. In October 2015 anticorruption prosecutors sent for trial its economic director Gabriela Mazilu and her husband Ovidiu Mazilu. Prosecutors allege that at the start of 2010 she demanded, through her husband, 5 per cent of the value of a contract for the supply and transport of energy coal, worth 12,705,000 lei without VAT, from the administrator of the supplying company. In exchange she is said to have promised that CET Bacau would pay the company's invoices on time. The file went to court and both were presumed innocent at that stage.
inside: A coal supplier paid the heat company's finance director a share of its contract, and in return its invoices were paid on time.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 1592/VIII/3, 12 October 2015

n: Four phones for a SMART SA director to release a supplier's invoice
org_label: A supplier of SMART SA's Constanta branch
rank: Director of the maintenance and development directorate, SC SMART SA
d: SMART SA is a Romanian state-owned company in the electricity sector. In December 2015 anticorruption prosecutors sent for trial Liviu Petrache, director of its maintenance and development directorate, and Marius Merfu, charged with buying influence. Prosecutors allege that between 20 and 30 April 2015 Petrache demanded and received, for himself and others, four mobile telephones worth about 16,000 lei from Merfu, in exchange for intervening with the decision-makers at the state company's Constanta branch so that an invoice would be paid to the influence-buyer's firm. The file went to court and both were presumed innocent at that stage.
inside: A supplier gave phones to a state company director who leaned on its branch, so the branch paid that firm's invoice.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 1964/VIII/3, 14 December 2015

n: Valve distributors' congress money reached Catania's cardiology chiefs
org_label: Local distributors of multinational heart-valve makers
rank: Professors heading cardiology units, including at the university Policlinico of Catania
d: On 5 July 2024 four professors of cardiology were placed under house arrest in Catania, among them Corrado Tamburino, who headed one of the largest units in eastern Sicily at the university Policlinico, a public hospital trust. Guardia di Finanza investigators describe a mechanism involving the four, all members of the scientific committee of a project called the Sicilian cardiovascular academy, and the representatives of local distributors of multinational manufacturers. The investigators say the distributors used the organisation of training events as a screen to promise and then pay large sums in order to win the favour of the unit heads. Aortic valves were paid for at up to 20 per cent more than the same products awarded under a national Consip framework agreement.
inside: Valve distributors paid the doctors who chose the valves, through sponsored congresses, and Sicilian hospitals then paid a fifth more than the national price.
cite: LiveSicilia, 5 July 2024, on the Guardia di Finanza investigation and the house arrests

n: Med Line's cash and gifts bought supply orders at Palermo's Civico hospital
org_label: Med Line, a medical supplies company
rank: Heads of clinical units, ARNAS Civico hospital, Palermo
d: ARNAS Civico is a public hospital trust in Palermo. Giuseppe Castorina, administrator of the supplies company Med Line, was arrested and then co-operated, describing payments he had made to secure orders there. In 2009 he admitted in a plea bargain handing bribes to two unit heads, Mario Re and Giustino Strano, and got three years; on 21 May 2015 he was given a further six months. The judge found the corruption of Re time-barred; that count concerned supplies worth 381,000 euros up to 2007, rewarded with campaign money, season tickets, two cars and flights. Castorina was convicted over the payments to Strano, up to 2008, to secure supplies worth 342,000 euros; Strano was to receive 10 per cent of the contract value, plus dinners, flights, hotel stays and watches.
inside: A medical supplier paid the hospital unit heads who ordered its products, in cash, cars and trips, and the orders kept coming to it.
cite: LiveSicilia, 21 May 2015, on the new sentence and the earlier 2009 plea bargain

n: 100,000 lei released a contractor's flood-works money at Apele Romane
org_label: A works company holding three Mures water basin contracts
rank: Deputy director general, National Administration Apele Romane
d: Administratia Nationala Apele Romane manages Romania's rivers, dams and flood works through regional water basin administrations. On 2 July 2020 prosecutors sent for trial Cristian Bratanovici, at the time its deputy director general, for bribe-taking, and two businessmen, administrators of a commercial company, for giving a bribe. The indictment says that on 8 November 2019, in Targu Mures, Bratanovici received 100,000 lei from one of the two in connection with his duty to secure financing so that the company would be paid for work under three contracts with the Mures Water Basin Administration, covering flood and river works in three counties. On 11 January 2023 the Targu Mures Court of Appeal convicted him, three years suspended, and convicted the two payers.
inside: A contractor paid the deputy head of the state water body to find the money for its contracts, and the funding for its flood works was released.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 386/VIII/3, 2 July 2020, and the conviction notice on Targu Mures Court of Appeal decision 7 of 11 January 2023

n: 7 per cent of a Baia Mare hospital works contract reached its manager
org_label: A company holding the operating-block works contract
rank: Manager, Dr Constantin Opris County Emergency Hospital, Baia Mare
d: Sorina Pintea was manager of the Dr Constantin Opris county emergency hospital in Baia Mare, northern Romania, and its authorising officer for spending. Prosecutors said that between November 2019 and 28 February 2020 she demanded and received, through an intermediary, 10,000 euros on 20 December 2019 and 120,000 lei on 28 February 2020 from the representatives of a commercial company. The sums came to 7 per cent of the value of a public procurement contract signed by the hospital in 2019 for the design and execution of works on its operating block and cardiovascular surgery theatre. She was caught in the act in her hospital office. On 6 June 2025 the Cluj Court of Appeal convicted her of bribe-taking in continued form, three years and six months in prison, final.
inside: A works company paid the hospital manager who signed off its contract a share of its value, and she was the official who could keep the money moving.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press releases no. 98/VIII/3 of 29 February 2020 and no. 262/VIII/3 of 30 April 2020, and the conviction notice on Cluj Court of Appeal decision 993 of 6 June 2025

n: Chantel Sante's 25,000 euros and a 949,620 lei robot for Brasov's hospital
rank: Management of the Clinical Hospital of Infectious Diseases, Brasov
d: In December 2020 anticorruption prosecutors detained twelve suspects over the alleged fraudulent award of public procurement contracts at hospitals in the Brasov and Harghita counties of Romania, among them Ramona Delia Ionescu, at the time manager of the Brasov hospital of infectious diseases. Prosecutors say that between October 2019 and September 2020 Marius Andrei Kadas Iluna received 5,000 euros directly and 20,000 euros through an intermediary from a businessman who controlled SC Chantel Sante SRL, a pharmaceutical wholesaler, to use influence he claimed over the hospital's decision-makers. According to the prosecutors the influence proved real: on 18 February 2020 the hospital bought an ultraviolet disinfection robot from the firm for 949,620 lei with VAT, when its market value lay between 285,000 and 380,000 lei. All are presumed innocent.
inside: A medical supplier paid intermediaries with influence over a public hospital's management, and the hospital then bought its robot at nearly three times market value.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 830/VIII/3, 4 December 2020

n: 850 lei fire hoses for the Rovinari mine of Complexul Energetic Oltenia
org_label: SC Ratetalav SRL and a second supplier
rank: Economic director, Rovinari open-cast mine, SC Complexul Energetic Oltenia SA
d: Complexul Energetic Oltenia is Romania's state lignite mining and power group in the south-west, and its Rovinari open-cast mine is one of its operations. In December 2020 prosecutors sent for trial Vasile Ghimis, at the time the mine's economic director, together with a businessman and SC Ratetalav SRL. Prosecutors allege that between September and December 2012 Ghimis ordered firefighting materials and first-aid kits bought at inflated prices, splitting the purchase so it could be made directly, from two firms including Ratetalav, which the businessman controlled, after agreeing the prices with him beforehand. A fire hose was bought at 850 lei each against a market price of about 120 lei. The mine lost 169,234 lei. On 12 July 2023 the Craiova Court of Appeal ended the case as time-barred.
inside: A supplier agreed the prices in advance with the mine's economic director, who split the purchase to award it directly, and the state mine paid several times the market rate.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press bulletin no. 16/VIII/3, 8 January 2021, item 1, with the update of 12 July 2023 on the Craiova Court of Appeal decision

n: 4.83m lei bought a contractor's funding from Apele Romane's director general
org_label: A works company contracting with Apele Romane
rank: Director general, National Administration Apele Romane
d: Administratia Nationala Apele Romane is the Romanian state body that manages the country's rivers, dams and flood defences and holds the contracts for work on them. On 5 October 2020 anticorruption prosecutors sent its former director general Victor Sandu for trial in pre-trial detention for bribe-taking, together with a businessman charged with giving a bribe and two others charged as accomplices. The indictment says that while Sandu was director general, between 17 May 2017 and 6 May 2019, he demanded sums of money and received a total of 4,830,464 lei from the businessman, who in fact ran a commercial company, as a bribe for allocating the funds needed to carry out contracts the company had with Apele Romane. All are presumed innocent.
inside: A contractor paid the head of the state water body millions of lei, and the funds its own contracts depended on were allocated.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press releases no. 472/VIII/3 of 4 August 2020 and no. 652/VIII/3 of 5 October 2020

n: Mozigres Construct's 49,200 lei at Romania's air navigation authority
rank: Investments service expert, central administration of ROMATSA RA
d: ROMATSA is Romania's state-owned air traffic services administration, and its central administration in Bucharest approves the invoices of its regional directorates. In May 2017 anticorruption prosecutors sent for trial Vasile Pop and Mihai Vasile Pop, administrators of SC Mozigres Construct SRL of Baia Mare. The indictment says that between 2013 and 2014 they handed a total of 49,200 lei to Petre Gabriel Dragomirescu, at the time an expert in the investments service of ROMATSA's technical directorate. He is said to have demanded and received the money in exchange for awarding their firm renovation and interior fitting works in premises of the Baia Mare air navigation services directorate, for the smooth running of those contracts, and for accepting for payment statements of work that had not been done.
inside: A building firm paid the official in the air navigation authority's investments service, which got it the works and had unperformed work accepted for payment.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press releases no. 260/VIII/3 of 20 March 2017 and no. 476/VIII/3 of 12 May 2017

n: Two businessmen's firms supplied an army unit at Budieni at inflated prices
org_label: Companies of two businessmen supplying U.M. 01541 Budieni
who: Two suppliers to an army unit
rank: Commander and logistics staff, Military Unit 01541 Budieni, Gorj county
d: On 3 January 2022 military prosecutors of Romania's anticorruption directorate sent for trial Colonel Marin Bran, at the time commander of Military Unit 01541 at Budieni in Gorj county, six other servicemen of the unit, and two individuals who were administrators of commercial companies. The indictment says that between October 2011 and July 2015 Bran breached his duties under the public finance law by buying goods from the companies of one of the two businessmen at overvalued prices, including building and electrical materials, and by ordering payment to the other for services that were never carried out. The other servicemen are said to have supplied the paperwork, some of it falsified. The unit lost 918,910 lei and the two men's companies gained the same.
inside: Two suppliers' firms, with the unit's commander and logistics staff, got army money for overpriced goods and work never done.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 2/VIII/3, 3 January 2022

n: A luxury watch and overpriced cars for the chief of Calarasi county police
org_label: Businessmen with cases and petitions before Calarasi police
rank: Chief inspector, Calarasi County Police Inspectorate
d: In July 2022 anticorruption prosecutors sent for trial Marian Iorga, at the time chief inspector of the Calarasi county police inspectorate in southern Romania, for bribe-taking and influence peddling in continued form. The indictment says that on 29 April 2017 he received a luxury watch worth 4,350 lei from a businessman in connection with the favourable resolution of a complaint the man had earlier made. It also says that between February 2017 and August 2018 Iorga required businessmen to buy, at inflated prices, cars he owned or was about to buy, promising in return to use his influence over subordinates handling criminal cases or petitions concerning them, so that these were resolved favourably or speeded up. Three such transactions brought him 4,000 euros.
inside: Businessmen bought the county police chief's cars above their worth, and he leaned on the officers handling their own cases.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 626/VIII/3, 6 July 2022

n: A customs inspector's 5,500 lei loan from the firm he was checking
org_label: A company undergoing a customs inspection
rank: Customs inspector, Ploiesti Regional Customs Directorate
d: In November 2015 anticorruption prosecutors sent Ion Caramidaru for trial in pre-trial detention. He was a customs inspector, graded senior adviser, in the Ploiesti regional customs directorate within the Ploiesti regional directorate of public finance. The indictment says that between 18 and 29 July 2015 he asked for and received 5,500 lei, in several instalments and described as a loan, from a businessman whose company he had been assigned to inspect, and who reported him. Prosecutors say the money was sought in connection with the inspection he was carrying out, so that he would conduct it contrary to his duties and in a way favourable to the firm being checked. The file went to court and he was presumed innocent at that stage.
inside: The company being inspected lent money to the customs inspector assigned to it, so the inspection was run in its favour.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 1708/VIII/3, 5 November 2015

n: A petroleum trading certificate bought at Bihor's excise and customs office
org_label: Companies controlled by a fuel businessman
rank: Coordinating director, Bihor County Directorate for Excise and Customs Operations
d: In February 2016 anticorruption prosecutors sent Dorel Patcas for trial. He had been coordinating director of the Bihor county directorate for excise and customs operations in western Romania, the office that licensed fuel trading. The indictment says that between November and December 2009 he demanded and received from the administrator of several firms 5,000 lei and food and non-food goods worth 6,000 lei, in exchange for issuing a certificate to trade petroleum products to one of the companies the businessman controlled. The file went to court and he was presumed innocent at that stage.
inside: A fuel trader paid the customs director who issued trading certificates, and his company got the licence it needed.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 194/VIII/3, 26 February 2016

n: 80,000 lei bought real protection from Romania's organised crime directorate
org_label: A fruit and vegetable trading businessman
rank: Head of service, Directorate for Combating Organised Crime
d: In July 2016 anticorruption prosecutors sent Constantin Bolbosanu for trial in pre-trial detention. He had been a police officer and head of a service in Romania's directorate for combating organised crime. The indictment says that during 2007 he received, through an intermediary, 80,000 lei as a bribe from a businessman, to secure him protection from criminal investigators and favourable outcomes in the cases in which he was being investigated. Part of the money paid for building work on a property belonging to Bolbosanu. The prosecutors state that the protection promised was real: the businessman was not troubled by any body with powers in the field although he was trading in fruit and vegetables, and the checks carried out on him were purely formal.
inside: A trader paid a senior organised-crime police officer, and the inspections and cases that should have reached his business became formalities.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 962/VIII/3, 5 July 2016

n: 8,000 lei handed to two Bucharest economic-crime officers in a firm's office
rank: Deputy commissioners, economic crime investigation service, Sector 6 Police, Bucharest
d: In March 2016 anticorruption prosecutors sent for trial Nicos Colesca and Daniel Mihai Chivu, deputy commissioners of police in the economic crime investigation service of Sector 6 Police in Bucharest. The indictment says that on 14 October 2015, while on duty inside a firm's premises in a commercial complex in Ilfov county, the two demanded 10,000 lei from the company's administrator and actually received 8,000 lei. In exchange they promised the administrator that they would help him obtain a favourable outcome in a criminal case concerning him. Both were placed under house arrest and the file went to court; they were presumed innocent at that stage.
inside: A company administrator paid the two economic-crime officers investigating him, buying the outcome of his own case from inside the police.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 234/VIII/3, 4 March 2016

n: A fuel firm's cash and cisterns for Prahova's own anticorruption chief
org_label: A petroleum products trading company and two other firms
rank: Head of the Prahova County Anticorruption Service, General Anticorruption Directorate
d: The General Anticorruption Directorate is the Romanian interior ministry's own anticorruption police. In December 2016 prosecutors sent for trial Constantin Ispas, who had headed its Prahova county service. The indictment says that in April 2010 he demanded, and between April 2010 and February 2011 received, two instalments of 10,000 euros from a person who reported him, plus financial help for a commercial company, in order to steer an officer of the organised crime brigade in Ploiesti to handle a criminal case in a way that favoured him. It also says that between 2010 and 2013 Ispas used his position to make the administrators of two firms create advantages for a petroleum products trading company, receiving 1,500 lei for each of 72 cisterns of fuel delivered, 108,000 lei in all.
inside: A fuel trader and other firms paid the police anticorruption chief in cash and cargo, and the cases and contracts around them were steered their way.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press releases no. 1376/VIII/3 of 18 August 2015 and no. 1566/VIII/3 of 22 December 2016

n: Car importer's group drew in the chief of Timis county police
org_label: Two car import companies run by the businessman Iulian Bot
rank: Chief inspector and head of the economic crime investigation service, Timis County Police Inspectorate
d: In February 2016 anticorruption prosecutors charged Petru Sorin Muntean, chief inspector of the Timis county police inspectorate in western Romania, Dumitru Pavel, head of its economic crime investigation service, and the businessman Iulian Bot. Prosecutors say that between 2011 and 2013 Bot and others ran a group importing cars from the European market and reselling them off the books, avoiding taxes and costing the state budget over 2 million lei through two companies held via nominees. According to the prosecutors the group's activity enjoyed the support and protection of the two officers, who were drawn into its sphere of influence and kept loyal by the periodic offering of material advantages and sums of money; the two then recruited other police officers into the group.
inside: A car importer's money made the county police chief and his economic-crime head part of the group, and they recruited other officers to bury his case.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 88/VIII/3, 2 February 2016

n: Timber businessmen's complaints moved two officers off their trail in Alba
org_label: Businessmen in timber exploitation in Alba county
rank: Chief inspector of the Alba County Police Inspectorate and the head of its Campeni rural police section
d: In June 2024 anticorruption prosecutors charged Florin Constantin Dogaru, chief commissioner and head of the Alba county police inspectorate in central Romania, with abuse of office, and Dan Toma, at the time head of its Campeni rural police section 9, with bribe-taking and other offences. Prosecutors are investigating how, in 2021 and 2022, the officers protected the interests of the other defendants, most of whom were then in timber exploitation, by exercising their duties defectively against two police officers whose work had interfered with the businessmen. At the businessmen's insistence, or following the offering of undue benefits in Toma's case, the officers are said to have pressed repeatedly to move those agents and to have passed the businessmen one agent's work roster.
inside: Timber businessmen reached the county police chief and a section head, who then moved against the two officers checking their logging.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 596/VIII/3, 20 June 2024

n: A transport firm's electronics kept its drivers unsanctioned at Roman
rank: Police commissioner, traffic bureau, Roman municipal police
d: In June 2020 anticorruption prosecutors sent for trial Ioan-Iulian Closca, at the time a police commissioner in the traffic bureau of the Roman municipal police in eastern Romania, for bribe-taking. The indictment says that between November and December 2019 he demanded several electronic products from the administrator of a passenger transport company, so that he would not record and sanction any offences, or would apply lighter penalties, against the drivers working for the businessman's firm. It says that on 28 December 2019, in Roman, he received one of the products he had asked for, worth 1,549 lei. Prosecutors had earlier concluded guilty-plea agreements with two individuals in the same case, for giving a bribe and for false testimony.
inside: A bus company paid the traffic officer in goods, and its drivers were left unpenalised on his patch.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press bulletin no. 398/VIII/3, 7 July 2020, item 1

n: A businessman's 25,000 lei steered a Bucharest fraud squad file
org_label: A businessman who had brought the complaint
rank: Judicial police officer, Fraud Investigation Service, Bucharest municipal police
d: In August 2020 anticorruption prosecutors charged Gabriel Necsulescu, a judicial police officer in the fraud investigation service of the Bucharest municipal police. Prosecutors say he demanded 15,000 euros directly from a businessman as a bribe and received 25,000 lei of it through an intermediary on 5 March 2010, so that he would handle in line with the businessman's interests a criminal file opened on the businessman's own complaint. They say that later, for the same purpose, he demanded and received from the same man, again through an intermediary, various goods worth about 6,500 lei. Asset measures were ordered to secure confiscation. He is presumed innocent.
inside: A complainant paid the fraud officer handling his file, so the police investigation ran the way he wanted it to.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 494/VIII/3, 21 August 2020

n: A restaurant's catering bought its drivers cover from Iasi traffic police
org_label: A restaurant whose management agreed the arrangement
rank: Police officer, traffic bureau, Iasi municipal police
d: In August 2020 anticorruption prosecutors charged Nicolae Robert Barabas, a police officer in the Iasi traffic bureau in eastern Romania. Prosecutors say that between 22 June 2019 and 7 March 2020, under a tacit understanding that existed between the Iasi traffic police and the management of a restaurant, he demanded and received through intermediaries, with the restaurant director's agreement, catering food products worth 2,650 lei. The purpose, according to the prosecutors, was to protect the restaurant's drivers by not recording and sanctioning the offences they had committed or might commit, or by applying lighter penalties. He is presumed innocent.
inside: A restaurant fed the traffic bureau under a standing arrangement, and its own drivers were shielded from penalties.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 498/VIII/3, 27 August 2020

n: 27,000 euros for a classification proposal from a Bucharest police officer
org_label: A businessman and his firm under criminal investigation
rank: Judicial police officer, economic crime investigation service, Bucharest General Police Directorate
d: In July 2022 anticorruption prosecutors sent Andrei Iulian Stancu for trial in pre-trial detention. He was a judicial police officer in the economic crime investigation service of the Bucharest general police directorate. Prosecutors say that between February and April 2022 he demanded and received undue benefits from people who were subjects of criminal files he was handling, promising to steer the inquiries to an outcome that favoured them. In particular he is said to have demanded and received 27,000 euros, of which 20,000 euros for himself, from a businessman, in exchange for the favourable resolution of a criminal file concerning the man and his firm, undertaking to draw up a report proposing that the case be closed.
inside: A businessman paid the officer running his own case, who undertook to write the report proposing the file be closed.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press releases no. 566/VIII/3 of 28 June 2022 and no. 688/VIII/3 of 15 July 2022

n: Importers' 41,000 euros opened the Varsand border crossing into Romania
rank: Police commissioner and officers, Varsand border police sector, Oradea Territorial Border Police Inspectorate
d: The Oradea territorial border police inspectorate covers Romania's western frontier, including the Varsand sector in Arad county. In March 2017 anticorruption prosecutors sent eighteen defendants for trial. The indictment says that between 17 August and 6 December 2016 Florin Avram, a police commissioner in the Varsand sector, demanded and received from two businessmen sums ranging from 150 to 41,000 euros and other goods, so that products without supporting documents could be brought into Romania. In some instances he sought the benefits in order to influence border police and customs officers on the Serbian and Hungarian frontiers so that lorries carrying contraband cigarettes and used tyres would be let in. On 19 January 2018 the Timisoara Court of Appeal convicted him, two years and six months suspended, final.
inside: Importers paid a commissioner and officers of the border police sector, and their undocumented loads and contraband lorries were waved into Romania.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, press release no. 214/VIII/3, 7 March 2017, and the conviction notice on Timisoara Court of Appeal decision 81 of 19 January 2018

n: Pakistani applicants' cash moved passports through Bothaville Home Affairs
org_label: Pakistani nationals who paid for the passports
rank: Administration clerks, Department of Home Affairs, Bothaville office
d: Two clerks of South Africa's Department of Home Affairs, the ministry that issues identity documents and passports, are accused of putting South African passports into the hands of people with no right to them. The Hawks, the police unit for serious corruption, say that between January and March 2022 two administration clerks based in Bothaville in the Free State assisted about ten Pakistani nationals with passport applications made in the names of South African citizens, and that the passports were issued carrying the Pakistani applicants' photographs. The officials allegedly received 10,000 rand in gratification from the Pakistani nationals. Larrick Tirick Steward, Kamohelo Gordon Sebatane and Thabiso Meshark Seutlwadi appeared at the Bothaville Magistrate's Court in October 2026 on charges of fraud, corruption and breaches of the Identification and Immigration Acts,
inside: People buying South African identity paid clerks inside the passport office, so the state issued passports in other citizens' names to foreign applicants.
cite: Sunday World, 28 October 2026, reporting the Hawks' Free State spokesperson Warrant Officer Fikiswa Matoti and the Bothaville Magistrate's Court

n: Marriage syndicate ran a clandestine Home Affairs office in Durban
rank: Official of the Durban office, Department of Home Affairs
d: South African police say a syndicate ran an unofficial Home Affairs operation out of a block of flats on Matthews Meyiwa Road in Greyville, Durban, which was apparently used to arrange illegal marriages and spousal visas. The provincial police spokesperson, Colonel Robert Netshiunda, said the suspects would obtain the identity documents of South African women and marry them to strangers, especially undocumented foreign nationals, so that the fake husbands would gain South African citizenship. Preliminary investigations identified a Department of Home Affairs official, attached to the department's Durban office, who had been working with the suspects; the official could not be named before appearing in court, and was due at the Durban magistrate's court with co-accused on charges of fraud and defeating the ends of justice.
inside: A syndicate selling citizenship through sham marriages had a Home Affairs official working with it, so the department recognised marriages and visas it should have refused.
cite: Sunday World, 29 October 2024, reporting KwaZulu-Natal police spokesperson Colonel Robert Netshiunda

n: Passport syndicate held keys to two Durban Home Affairs offices
rank: Former official of the Prospecton office and a municipal project volunteer at the Commercial Road office, Department of Home Affairs
d: A Home Affairs-led operation supported by the Hawks arrested five people in June 2025 over a syndicate committing passport fraud at the uMngeni and Commercial Road offices of South Africa's Department of Home Affairs in Durban. The departmental spokesperson, Siya Qoza, said those arrested were a former Home Affairs official from the Prospecton office, a municipal project volunteer working at the Commercial Road office, and three members of the public. One of the three was found with 226 passports recently stolen from the uMngeni office. Another suspect was found with keys to the Commercial Road and Prospecton offices and with copies of enabling documents that did not belong to him. Two further suspects were still being sought.
inside: A passport syndicate had people and keys inside Durban's Home Affairs offices, so blank passports and the documents behind them passed into its hands.
cite: Sunday World, 16 June 2025, reporting Department of Home Affairs spokesperson Siya Qoza

n: Licence-fraud syndicate said to have bought transport officials' NaTIS logins
rank: NaTIS users and officials of the national Department of Transport (alleged)
d: South Africa's National Traffic Information System, NaTIS, is the state register used to licence vehicles and drivers. In July 2026 a man was arrested at a private house in Parys in the Free State where, authorities were told, he was allegedly operating NaTIS and fraudulently helping motorists renew vehicle licences. Officers found a computer showing the NaTIS login screen with a user number and password already entered, along with documents holding vehicle registration numbers, identity numbers and what were believed to be NaTIS user credentials. The suspect, an information technology specialist, allegedly told investigators that the operation involved former transport department officials, current NaTIS users in several provinces and individuals linked to the national Department of Transport, and that credentials were bought from officials and passed on memory sticks.
inside: A licensing fraud ring allegedly bought the log-ins of transport department staff, so the state's own vehicle register issued licences for its paying customers.
cite: Sunday World, 29 July 2026, reporting the Road Traffic Management Corporation's National Anti-Corruption Unit, SAPS Crime Intelligence and the Hawks

n: Criminal group inside a Polish labour office cleared 12,500 work entries
org_label: organised criminal group selling seasonal-work certificates
rank: Two senior officials of a district labour office in Masovia
d: Polish district labour offices issue the certificates behind a seasonal-work visa. Border guards detained three people in April 2025, among them two officials described as high-ranking who worked at a district labour office in Masovia, the province containing Warsaw. Prosecutors in Grojec charged them with taking part in an organised criminal group, organising illegal crossings of the Polish border, abusing their powers and failing to meet their obligations, in conduct the border guard spokeswoman Dagmara Bielec said was connected with the issuing of certificates of entry for seasonal work. Between 2018 and 2024 almost 12,500 foreigners obtained the documents needed to apply for visas to Poland and the Schengen area. The officials allegedly entered false information that Polish employers, some of them entirely fictitious, intended to employ them.
inside: An organised group worked through senior staff of a Polish labour office, so the office certified fictitious jobs that opened Schengen visas for its clients.
cite: Notes from Poland, 9 April 2025, reporting Border Guard spokeswoman Dagmara Bielec and the Grojec prosecutors

n: Tyson paid Mexico's state plant vets who inspected its chicken factories
rank: Government-employed inspection veterinarians, inspection programme supervised by the Mexican Department of Agriculture
d: Any company exporting meat from Mexico must take part in an inspection programme supervised by the Mexican Department of Agriculture, and the programme at each plant is run by an on-site veterinarian employed by the government of Mexico to check that exports meet Mexican health and safety law. Tyson Foods acknowledged responsibility for improper payments by its subsidiary Tyson de Mexico to two such publicly employed veterinarians who inspected its two chicken processing plants at Gomez Palacio. About $90,000 was paid between 2004 and 2006, directly and through the veterinarians' wives, who were listed on the payroll although neither performed any services. The court documents say the payments were made to keep the veterinarians from disrupting the plants' operations, and produced profits of about $880,000.
inside: A meat company paid the state vets posted inside its own plants, so the officials who certified its exports were on its payroll rather than the public's.
cite: US Department of Justice, 10 February 2011, deferred prosecution agreement and criminal information, District of Columbia; related SEC settlement of more than $1.2m in disgorgement

n: Magyar Telekom's secret protocol delayed a Macedonian mobile licence
rank: High-ranking Macedonian government officials, and officials of the ruling parties
d: In early 2005 the Macedonian government moved to open up the telecommunications market in a way the Hungarian operator Magyar Telekom judged harmful to its Macedonian subsidiary, Makedonski Telekomunikacii. Magyar Telekom then entered a secret agreement, a so-called protocol of cooperation, in which high-ranking Macedonian government officials agreed to delay the entry of a third mobile licence into the market and to grant other regulatory benefits. Two copies were signed with high-ranking officials of the different ruling parties, and the only executed copies were kept outside company records. To secure those benefits the company used sham consultancy contracts with entities controlled by a Greek intermediary to pay 4.875 million euros, about 6 million dollars, knowing all or part would be passed to Macedonian officials.
inside: A telecoms company's hidden payments bought a written deal with Macedonian officials, so the state held back a rival mobile licence to protect the company's market.
cite: US Department of Justice, 29 December 2011, criminal information and deferred prosecution agreement, Eastern District of Virginia

n: Air equipment maker's sham deal bought a UK defence ministry official
rank: Official of the United Kingdom Ministry of Defence handling Royal Air Force equipment contracts
d: Pacific Consolidated Industries, a private firm in Santa Ana, California, made oxygen and nitrogen generating equipment for aircraft support and military hospitals. Its former director of sales and marketing, Leo Winston Smith, pleaded guilty in 2009 to conspiring to bribe an official of the United Kingdom Ministry of Defence to win and keep equipment contracts with the Royal Air Force. Smith and the company's president created a sham marketing agreement between the firm and a relative of the official, through which more than $70,000 was paid. Smith admitted the company obtained ministry contracts in return. The official pleaded guilty in Britain to accepting more than $300,000 in bribes and was sentenced to two years. The release gives no dates for the payments.
inside: A military equipment supplier paid a defence ministry official through his relative, so the ministry's purchasing decisions went the supplier's way.
cite: US Department of Justice, 3 September 2009, guilty plea in the US District Court at Santa Ana, California

n: Turkish power firm's bribes reached Ghana's Minister of Power
rank: Minister of Power and his senior adviser; five Ghanaian officials
d: Asante Kwaku Berko, a dual American and Ghanaian citizen and a former executive director at Goldman Sachs, was convicted by a federal jury in Brooklyn in 2026 of bribing Ghanaian government officials over a power plant. From December 2014 he handled a deal between Ghana and Aksa Enerji Uretim, a Turkish energy company and Goldman client, to build and finance a plant during a national energy crisis. Prosecutors proved he conspired to pay more than $1m to officials at numerous levels of government so Aksa won the bid. In April 2015 he and his co-conspirators discussed paying $1m to the Minister of Power, responsible for securing key approvals, and $250,000 to his senior adviser. Bribes were paid to five officials on an all-expenses-paid trip to Turkey.
inside: A Turkish energy company's money, moved by a Goldman banker, reached the minister who signed off its power plant, so the approvals served the bidder.
cite: US Department of Justice, Eastern District of New York, jury verdict 2026; nine-day trial before Judge Diane Gujarati

n: Teva kept a Ukrainian health ministry official as its registration consultant
rank: Senior official within the Ukrainian Ministry of Health
d: A medicine cannot be sold in Ukraine until the state registers it. Teva Pharmaceutical Industries, the world's largest maker of generic medicines, admitted paying bribes to a senior official within the Ukrainian Ministry of Health to influence the Ukrainian government's approval of its drug registrations. Between 2001 and 2011 Teva engaged the official as the company's registration consultant, paid him a monthly fee and gave him travel and other things of value worth about $200,000. In exchange, the official used his official position and influence within the Ukrainian government to influence the registration of Teva products, including the multiple sclerosis drug Copaxone and insulins. The admission came in a deferred prosecution agreement covering Russia, Ukraine and Mexico, with a criminal penalty of $283,177,348.
inside: A drug company put a serving health ministry official on its own payroll as a consultant, so the ministry registered its medicines for sale.
cite: US Department of Justice, 22 December 2016, deferred prosecution agreement and criminal information, Southern District of Florida

n: Engineering firm's golf membership and cash bought a US procurement officer
rank: Employee of the General Services Administration able to recommend contractors for GSA-managed contracts
d: The General Services Administration manages United States federal buildings and buys goods and services for other agencies. Francisco L. Bituin, owner of the engineering firm FLBE of Herndon, Virginia, which had received over $30m in government contracts since 2003, pleaded guilty in 2014 to bribing a GSA employee who was in a position to recommend his firm for contracts the agency managed. The bribes he admitted included a $3,750 golf club membership and $2,000 in cash handed over during lunch at a restaurant in Tysons Corner, Virginia. On another occasion he offered the employee access to a retirement home in Las Vegas, the down payment on a home in Virginia and five per cent of the equity in his firm. He was due to be sentenced in November 2014.
inside: A contractor paid the federal official who recommended firms for work, so the agency's buying decisions were steered to the man paying him.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Virginia, guilty plea 2014, statement of facts filed with the plea agreement

n: Libyan cabinet decree turned revolutionary brigades into a state security authority
rank: National Support Forces Authority, subsidiary to the Cabinet, Tripoli
d: On 22 May 2023 Libya's Government of National Unity cabinet issued Decision No. 313, which the UN Panel of Experts reproduces in full. It created a National Support Forces Authority under the cabinet, with legal personality, a share of the state budget, bank accounts, a Tripoli headquarters and a chief nominated by the prime minister. Article 2 brings together the 17 February Revolutionaries' Brigades, the armed groups formed in the 2011 uprising, to restructure them and regulate their vehicles and weapons. The Panel said the new force's composition, mandate and capabilities remained vague and that it operates directly under Prime Minister Abdulhamid Al Dabiba. Four days later the High Council of State's president accused Al Dabiba of building up security forces under his own office for his political ambitions.
inside: Brigades from the 2011 uprising were given a state authority with a budget and legal powers, answering to the prime minister who created it.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report S/2023/673, para. 16 and annex 9 ('Decree establishing the National Force Support Authority'), reproducing Cabinet Decision No. 313 (2023) of 22 May 2023; annex 8

n: Haftar-allied brigade commander given a new Libyan army force in the south
who: 116 brigade, a Haftar-allied armed group in Sabha
rank: Commander, Counter-Terrorism and Organized Crime Force in the Libyan south
d: On 17 June 2021 Libya's Presidency Council, acting as commander-in-chief of the Libyan army, created a Counter-Terrorism and Organized Crime Force for southern Libya by Decision No. 7, and by Decision No. 9 appointed Masoud Abdallah Masoud Abdeljallil, known as Masoud Jeddi, as its commander. The UN Panel of Experts, which reproduces both decisions, describes him as the then commander of 116 brigade and the main military ally of the Haftar Armed Forces in Sabha. The decree built the new force out of the first company of that same brigade and gave it powers to arrest armed gangs and investigate terrorism. Khalifa Haftar responded with a decree of 11 September 2021 disbanding the 116 brigade, although most of its men stayed with his forces.
inside: A militia allied to one armed faction was rebadged by decree as a state counter-terrorism force under its own commander, with arrest powers across southern Libya.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report S/2022/427, para. 17 and annex 10 (Commander-in-Chief Decisions No. 7 and No. 9 of 2021, 17 June 2021), and annex 11

n: Militia deputy made head of Libya's Presidential Guard as the price of support
who: Stability Support Apparatus and the Tripoli Revolutionary Brigade
rank: Head of the Presidential Guard
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya records that Ayub Aburas, from the Tripoli Revolutionary Brigade and one of the deputies of Abdel Ghani Khalifa, the Stability Support Apparatus leader better known as al-Kikli or Ghenewa, was appointed head of Libya's Presidential Guard. The Panel gives the appointment as an illustration of the competing efforts of the rival prime ministers Fathi Bashagha and Abdulhamid Al Dabiba to win the Apparatus's backing, and of how much weight the Apparatus had gained since the Presidency Council created it on 11 January 2021. The Panel reports the appointment in a footnote without giving its date, alongside a widely publicised visit by Al Dabiba to Abu Slim prison on 7 March 2022. The guard protects Libya's presidency.
inside: A Tripoli militia's deputy commander was handed the force guarding Libya's presidency, as the prime minister bid for that militia's political support.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report S/2022/427, para. 14 and footnote 24

n: Houthis took over two Sana'a pharmaceutical companies and their management
rank: Management of two of Yemen's largest pharmaceutical companies, Sana'a
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen found that the Houthis took over two of Yemen's largest pharmaceutical companies in Sana'a, which its 2025 annex calls Modern Pharma and Global Pharma. The companies' leaders had agreed to share profits with the movement but refused to give up running them. On 9 June 2024, after an IT employee was detained in a failed attempt to recover removed cloud data, Houthi forces entered the factory and assumed total control. Eight senior staff were detained; seven were released after signing coerced pledges to cooperate with the Houthis. On the day of the takeover the Houthis told the central bank the owner was no longer the manager. The takeover reportedly brings the movement 300 to 400 million dollars a year.
inside: The armed movement seized two drug companies, removed the owner as manager and bound the surviving staff by written pledges to work with it.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2025/650, annex 95 ('Private business overtaken by the Houthis after a judgement by the Specialised Criminal Court in Sana'a'), section (a); UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2024/731, para. 120 and annex 181, which name the Modern Pharmaceutical Company and the International Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Company

n: Houthi prosecutors put their own interim director over the firm Prodigy
rank: Interim director of Prodigy, appointed by the Houthi district attorney's office
d: Prodigy, a Yemeni monitoring and evaluation company, was confiscated by Houthi authorities. Its director was detained on 15 April 2023 by the Security and Intelligence Service, denied a lawyer and held without formal charges for about seven months; ten other staff were detained and released over three months. The service refused to obey a formal order from the attorney general to reopen the company. After the director rejected a partnership, the Houthis set up a parallel organisation that reportedly took over Prodigy's contracts, and a district attorney decision appointed an interim director bound to consult that office on financial decisions. The director was sentenced to death on 5 December 2024, commuted on appeal to 15 years on 12 May 2025, with all confiscated property transferred to the state.
inside: The movement's prosecutors installed a director inside a private company who had to clear decisions with them, and a parallel body took its contracts.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2025/650, annex 95 ('Private business overtaken by the Houthis after a judgement by the Specialised Criminal Court in Sana'a'), section (b) and the notes to figures 95.3-95.6

n: Houthi authority used Sana'a air traffic control to charge airlines overflight fees
rank: Houthi-appointed authority holding the air traffic control centre at Sana'a airport
d: Yemen's General Authority for Civil Aviation and Meteorology moved to Aden, and the recognised government notified airlines to redirect their overflight fees to the authority there, but the air traffic control centre at Sana'a airport stayed in Houthi hands, and the UN Panel of Experts found that the Houthi-appointed authority in Sana'a used it to collect fees from airlines flying over Yemen. About 150 aircraft cross Yemeni airspace daily, each paying around 600 dollars, which the Panel estimated at roughly 32.85 million dollars a year, a collection the recognised government calls unlawful. Airline officials told the Panel they were reluctant to stop paying for fear of attacks on their aircraft. The same authority also took landing, take-off, passenger and freight charges.
inside: The movement's appointees held a national air-navigation function and billed foreign airlines for it, with the money going to the movement rather than the state.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2024/731, 10 October 2024, annex 175 ('Houthi revenue from customs, taxes, fees, and other illegal fees'), section 'Collection of illegal fees from civil aviation sector', pp. 452-453; UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2025/650, para. 122 (a); UN document page https://docs.un.org/en/S/2024/731
undone: The Panel's next report said overflight collection had been suspended since April 2025.

n: Houthis seized the Yemen Digital Media Company and its assets
rank: Ownership and assets of the Yemen Digital Media Company
d: In August 2024 the Yemen Digital Media Company, a privately owned media business, was forcibly seized by Houthi authorities. The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen records the confiscation of company assets, including real estate, and the freezing of accounts totalling about 815,000 dollars. Attempts by outsiders to help the owner were met with threats from the Houthi Preventive Security Service, and one of his brothers was detained and coerced into signing pledges renouncing any connection with him. The owner was sentenced to death on 24 September 2024 and his appeal was rejected. The Panel describes an excerpt of the judgement ordering the confiscation of his and the company's assets in favour of the Houthi authorities.
inside: The armed movement took a media company's assets into its own hands through its courts, after jailing and condemning the man who owned it.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2025/650, annex 95 ('Private business overtaken by the Houthis after a judgement by the Specialised Criminal Court in Sana'a'), section (c) and the note to figure 95.7

n: Iraq's new state mobile company and its 5G licence steered to militia-linked men
org_label: Popular Mobilization Forces leadership network around Falah al-Fayyadh and Coordination Framework parties
who: Popular Mobilization Forces leadership network and Coordination Framework parties
rank: National Mobile Telecommunications Company; Communications and Media Commission
d: From March 2025 Iraq's communications ministry and its Informatics and Telecommunications Public Company set up a National Mobile Telecommunications Company, funded by the State Employees' Pension Fund, the Trade Bank of Iraq and the ministry's Al-Salam General Company, to hold the country's 5G licence. Michael Knights of the Washington Institute, writing in CTC Sentinel, reports that the consortium behind it was assembled at meetings in Oman in 2024 attended by the communications minister Hiyam al-Yassiri, Qais Saeed al-Ameri, then Iraq's charge d'affaires there and a brother-in-law of Popular Mobilization Forces chairman Falah al-Fayyadh, and Ahmed Mutawa al-Saeedi, a business agent of Coordination Framework parties and another al-Fayyadh in-law. The regulator told existing operators the new company could use their towers, and none of them could bid.
inside: Relatives and agents of the militia force's chairman shaped a new state mobile company, which was then given the 5G licence that private operators could not bid for.
cite: Michael Knights, 'Rise of the E-Militias: Designated Terrorist Groups Infest Iraq's Digital Economy', CTC Sentinel (Combating Terrorism Center at West Point), November/December 2025

n: US says Hezbollah paid Marada's leader to take reformist MPs' seats
rank: Leader of the Marada Movement; parliamentary seats in Lebanese elections
d: On 18 June 2026 the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control designated Sleiman Antoine Frangie, leader of the Lebanese Marada Movement, saying he had used his alliance with Hezbollah to serve his own political ambitions. The release says Frangie accepted financial support from Hezbollah in return for supporting the group's efforts to target the parliamentary seats of reformist and independent members of parliament in Lebanese parliamentary elections. He was designated under Executive Order 13224 for materially assisting or supporting Hezbollah. The same action designated Mahmoud Qamati, deputy head of Hezbollah's political council, who Treasury says coordinates cash smuggling from Iran. The findings are Treasury's own assertions, not a court's.
inside: An armed movement's money went to another party's leader so his party would help it unseat independent and reformist members of parliament.
cite: US Department of the Treasury press release, 'Treasury Targets Hizballah-Aligned Officials and Intensifies Pressure on Global Financial Network', 18 June 2026

n: Armed-group-held eastern Libyan security agency vetted who could stand for office
who: Armed groups holding the eastern Internal Security Agency
rank: Internal Security Agency, eastern Libya; municipal election candidates
d: In the run-up to Libya's second round of municipal council elections in 2025, the Internal Security Agency in eastern Libya made every prospective candidate go through an extra layer of security clearance, filling in a detailed and intrusive form, although the central authorities in Tripoli had already cleared them.
