The UN Panel of Experts identified at least six cases of threats, judicial harassment, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearance and torture against candidates and their families, four in the west and two in the east, which forced some to withdraw or move away. Every one of the 16 incidents the Panel identified involved armed actors or security bodies under the de facto authority of armed groups.
inside: A state security agency held by armed groups decided for itself who could appear on local ballots in eastern Libya, on top of the national vetting.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report S/2026/224, paras. 46-47 and annex 15 (contents-page title: 'Acts that obstruct or undermine the successful completion of the political transition in Libya'), paras. 3 and 9, p. 122; the main report's para. 47 cites the same material as annex 14

n: Libya's oil minister suspended to clear the way for an armed groups' oil deal
org_label: Armed group networks of Ibrahim Al Dabiba and Saddam Haftar
who: Armed group networks of Ibrahim Al Dabiba and Saddam Haftar
rank: Minister of Oil and Gas
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya found that armed group actors, mainly Ibrahim Al Dabiba and Saddam Haftar, built the ability to control the National Oil Corporation at every level of its decision-making. Ibrahim Al Dabiba is the prime minister's nephew and officially serves as national security adviser in the prime minister's office. The two men struck a deal to create Arkenu Oil Company as a structure for reaching crude oil revenues, with Haftar's forces as the first beneficiary. The Panel found that Ibrahim Al Dabiba then played a central role in the suspension of the minister of oil and gas in March 2024, aiming to install a replacement willing to implement the Arkenu deal. Arkenu went on to divert more than 3 billion dollars abroad.
inside: Armed group figures had Libya's oil minister removed so that a more willing minister would let their own oil company take the state's crude revenues.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, final report S/2026/224, paras. 97-98 and 104, and annex 7 ('Ibrahim Dbeibah, a central figure in armed groups politics')

n: Houthi mobilisation put a Yemeni health office's staff through military courses
rank: Health and Environment Office, Hajjah Governorate
d: On 23 January 2025 the Houthi General Mobilization body in Hajjah Governorate and the governorate's Health and Environment Office together held a manoeuvre for 250 health staff who had graduated from the movement's open military courses, called Al-Aqsa Flood Level Two. Houthi media said the exercise used light and medium weapons and tested combat skills, accuracy of fire, storming mock enemy positions and camouflage, and that the graduates declared their readiness to fight the nation's enemies. The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen reproduced the report and found that such courses show systematic and increasing efforts to indoctrinate and recruit in support of Houthi military capability. Those mobilised included tribesmen, students, journalists and staff of various ministries.
inside: The movement's mobilisation body ran a government health office's staff through weapons training, turning public employees into a reserve for its own war.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2025/650, paras. 33-34 and annex 14 ('Mobilization and military training of staff of the Health and Environment office of Hajja Governorate')

n: Militia chairman's nominee ran Iraq's communications ministry and staffed it
org_label: Popular Mobilization Forces leadership under Falah al-Fayyadh
who: Popular Mobilization Forces leadership under Falah al-Fayyadh
rank: Minister of Communications; deputy minister for technical affairs; ministry head of media relations
d: Michael Knights of the Washington Institute reports in CTC Sentinel that Hiyam al-Yassiri, communications minister in Iraq's government formed in 2022, was a ministry adviser whose October 2022 candidacy was sponsored by Falah al-Fayyadh, chairman of the Popular Mobilization Forces. Al-Fayyadh was designated by the United States after using his authority as the force's chairman, and then as national security adviser, to orchestrate killings and abductions of unarmed protesters in the 2019 Tishreen uprising. Within the ministry after 2022, Knights writes, al-Yassiri appointed as deputy minister for technical affairs Buraq Abdal-Qader Abdal-Karim, from the circle of Khamis Khanjar, a politician the United States sanctioned for corrupt activities favouring Iran-backed militias, and as head of media relations Omar Abdal-Razaq Muhsib, previously al-Fayyadh's personal photographer in the militia force's leadership office.
inside: The militia force's chairman sponsored the minister who ran Iraq's communications ministry, and she filled senior ministry posts from militia-linked circles.
cite: Michael Knights, 'Rise of the E-Militias: Designated Terrorist Groups Infest Iraq's Digital Economy', CTC Sentinel (Combating Terrorism Center at West Point), November/December 2025

n: Houthi decree put the movement's man in as Yemen's ambassador to Iran
rank: Ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary of Yemen to Iran
d: The Houthis named Ibrahim Mohammed al-Dailami as Yemen's ambassador to Iran in August 2018, by a decree they issued themselves rather than the internationally recognised government, and on 19 November 2019 Iran's president Hassan Rouhani formally received his credentials. The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen said the move amounted to state recognition of the Houthis' authority and helped the movement build a formal international presence. The Panel reproduces an Iranian media report of 22 December 2019 in which al-Dailami, as ambassador, discussed military cooperation with Iran's defence minister Brigadier-General Amir Hatami, passing on greetings from the Houthi-appointed defence minister Mohammed al-Atifi and chief of staff Mohammed al-Ghamari. Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said it provided only consultative and ideological support.
inside: The movement filled a national embassy post by its own decree, and its ambassador then discussed military cooperation on the movement's behalf.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2024/731, para. 75 and annexes 105 and 106; UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2020/326, para. 42

n: Catering firm's cash reached Sorrento's mayor over school contracts
rank: Mayor of Sorrento
d: Massimo Coppola, then mayor of the Italian coastal town of Sorrento, was arrested in flagrante in May 2025 after a businessman handed him 6,000 euros in cash at a restaurant dinner. Prosecutors in Torre Annunziata say the money related to the town's school catering contract for 2023 to 2026, a tender with a reserve price above 4.5 million euros, and that up to the day before the arrest about 66,000 euros had reached the mayor, directly or through his collaborator Francesco Di Maio. A second strand concerns the municipal nursery service, for which the businessman allegedly paid another 50,000 euros in instalments. Di Maio was sentenced to four years and two months in June 2026 after admitting the charges.
inside: A catering contractor's cash reached the mayor who awarded the town's school and nursery services, and the contracts went the payer's way.
cite: Stylo24, 10 June 2026, 19 and 21 September 2025 and 7 September 2025

n: Drummond and Balch & Bingham paid an Alabama legislator over EPA cleanup
who: A coal company and its law firm
rank: Member of the Alabama House of Representatives, House Rules Committee
d: A federal jury convicted Balch & Bingham partner Joel Gilbert and Drummond Company's vice president for government and regulatory affairs, David Roberson, of bribing Alabama state representative Oliver Robinson. The payment was a consulting contract worth 360,000 dollars, routed through Robinson's charitable foundation between 2015 and 2016. The aim was to oppose the Environmental Protection Agency's plan to prioritise or expand a Superfund site in north Birmingham, after the agency named Drummond's ABC Coke subsidiary as potentially responsible for arsenic, lead and benzo(a)pyrene in the soil. Robinson spoke to state environmental bodies without disclosing who was paying him, and voted in the House Rules Committee to send an anti-EPA resolution Gilbert had drafted to the floor. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed both convictions in 2021.
inside: A coal company and its law firm put a secret retainer inside a state legislator's foundation, and he then voted and lobbied against the cleanup they feared.
cite: US Attorney, Northern District of Alabama, 23 July 2018, 24 October 2018 and 28 May 2021

n: A healthcare provider's payments bought an Arkansas senator's bills and audits
who: A health and behavioural services provider
rank: Arkansas state senator
d: Robin Raveendran, a former executive of Preferred Family Healthcare, pleaded guilty in June 2019 to conspiring to bribe then Arkansas state senator Jeremy Hutchinson so that he would take legislative and official action favourable to the provider and its executives. Preferred Family paid money to the Alliance for Health Care, a private association set up in early 2014 by Raveendran, Hutchinson and a lobbyist who was also a company executive. Raveendran admitted directing those funds to Hutchinson in exchange for holding up agency budgets, starting legislative audits, sponsoring, filing and voting for legislation including shell bills, and pressing other officials to act for the provider. The payments were falsely recorded as legal fees and retainers. Hutchinson was charged in a separate case.
inside: A health services provider funnelled money through a private association to a sitting state senator, who then filed bills and blocked budgets to suit it.
cite: US Attorney, Western District of Missouri, 12 June 2019

n: Dallas developer paid the council's housing chair for loans and an extension
rank: Dallas City Council member for District 7, chair of the Housing Committee
d: Devin Hall, a Dallas real estate developer, pleaded guilty in 2020 to conspiracy to bribe a member of the Dallas City Council. He admitted that between 2013 and 2015 he paid the council member for District 7, who chaired the city's Housing Committee, at least 8,000 dollars in instalments of 750 to 1,000 dollars, in cash or through an intermediary, and promised her a consulting job after her term ended. In return she voted to allocate 650,000 dollars in city forgivable loans to his Grand Park Place apartment project, then moved to extend its completion date by two years and urged colleagues to do the same. The council approved both. The council member, since deceased, was not charged over this scheme.
inside: A developer's cash reached the council member who chaired housing, and the council then funded and extended his apartment project.
cite: US Attorney, Northern District of Texas, 6 August 2020

n: Developer's gifts won Taylor's foreclosed properties from the mayor
rank: Mayor of Taylor, Michigan
d: Shady Awad, a real estate developer, was sentenced in October 2024 to a year and a day in prison for bribing Richard Sollars, then mayor of Taylor in Michigan. Between 2016 and 2018 Awad gave Sollars a steady stream of cash, improvements to his home and lake house, appliances and other items, and agreed to charge more than 19,000 dollars to his own credit cards and convert it to cash for the mayor. The goods and services came to 85,011.73 dollars. In exchange Awad was allowed to acquire tax-foreclosed properties through the city's Right of First Refusal programme, under which Taylor took such properties from Wayne County for redevelopment, and Sollars recommended that the council award Awad the vast majority of them.
inside: A developer paid the mayor in cash and home renovations, and the mayor then steered the city's stock of foreclosed land to him.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of Michigan, 24 October 2024

n: An accountant's gifts bought his acquittal from a Puerto Rico judge
who: A businessman facing his own trial
rank: Supervisory judge, Puerto Rico Superior Court, Aguadilla judicial region
d: Manuel Acevedo-Hernandez, a supervisory judge of the Puerto Rico Superior Court in the Aguadilla judicial region, was convicted by a federal jury in January 2015 of conspiracy to commit federal programs bribery and of receiving a bribe. He had presided over the case of Lutgardo Acevedo-Lopez, a certified public accountant in Aguadilla, whose car collided with another on 30 June 2012, killing the other driver, and who was charged with criminal vehicular homicide. Through an intermediary the accountant paid taxes the judge owed, paid for the construction of a garage for him, and gave him a motorcycle, clothing, cufflinks and a watch. The judge acquitted him of all charges. The judge was sentenced to ten years and the First Circuit affirmed in 2018.
inside: A businessman on trial for a fatal crash paid the judge hearing his case in cash substitutes, and the judge acquitted him of everything.
cite: US Department of Justice, 21 January 2015 and 7 August 2018

n: A law firm's payments bought rulings from a Brownsville district judge
rank: Presiding judge, 404th State District Court, Texas
d: Abel Limas, presiding judge of the 404th State District Court in Brownsville, Texas, admitted using his court as a criminal enterprise. He took money and other consideration from attorneys in civil cases before him in return for favourable pre-trial rulings, including a case over a helicopter crash at South Padre Island in February 2008. He admitted receiving 8,000 dollars in May 2008, described in calls as eight golf balls. That summer he negotiated work as an of counsel attorney with the Austin firm Rosenthal & Watson, which promised an advance of at least 100,000 dollars and a share of fees in the helicopter case. He received two 50,000 dollar cheques and, after the case settled for about 14 million dollars, a further 85,000 dollars.
inside: A law firm put a serving judge on its own payroll while its cases sat before him, and he ruled for it in exchange for cash and a share of the fees.
cite: US Attorney, Southern District of Texas, 21 August 2013

n: An attorney's cash bought bond rulings from a Hidalgo County judge
org_label: An attorney practising before the 93rd District Court
rank: Presiding judge, 93rd District Court, Hidalgo County, Texas
d: Rodolfo Delgado, a Texas state district judge, was convicted in July 2019 of conspiracy, three counts of federal program bribery, three counts of Travel Act bribery and obstruction of justice. As presiding judge of the 93rd District Court, which covers criminal and civil cases in Hidalgo County, he conspired with an attorney from January 2008 to November 2016 to accept bribes in exchange for favourable judicial consideration of criminal cases in his courtroom. During an FBI investigation he took bribes on three occasions for agreeing to release three of the attorney's clients on bond: the first two came to about 520 dollars, the third, in January 2018, to about 5,500 dollars. He then gave the attorney a false story about the payments.
inside: A defence attorney paid the judge hearing his clients' cases, and the judge released those clients on bond and tilted rulings his way.
cite: US Department of Justice, 11 July 2019

n: Market traders' bribes for licences convicted Barano d'Ischia's leaders
org_label: Traders of the municipal market and a hotel operator
who: Market traders and a hotel business
rank: Mayor and councillors of Barano d'Ischia; local police commanders
d: The first criminal section of the Naples tribunal convicted eight defendants over the running of fairs, markets and events in Barano d'Ischia, a town on the island of Ischia. Prosecutors say bribes were demanded before licences and authorisations were granted to traders in the municipal market. The case dates from 2015. Among those convicted were the former mayor Paolino Buono, four years, the sitting municipal councillor and former regional councillor Maria Grazia Di Scala, three years, two local police commanders, seven and four years, and the hotel operator Raffaele Piro, three years. A second strand concerned an attempt to acquire a hotel at Maronti, under a demolition order, for less than its market value. Several abuse-of-office counts were time-barred or dismissed.
inside: Traders needing municipal licences paid the town's elected leaders and police chiefs, and the permissions they needed were then granted.
cite: Anteprima24, 17 November 2026

n: A builder's 15,000 euros reached Sommatino's mayor over town works
rank: Mayor of Sommatino; head of the municipal technical area
d: Carabinieri in Caltanissetta say they found a network inside the town hall of Sommatino in Sicily, running from extortion of small traders to the manipulation of large public tenders. In July 2026 a judge placed the resigning mayor Salvatore Letizia and the Favara contractor Diego Caramazza under house arrest, suspended a council employee for a year, and barred an architect and two builders from contracting with the public administration for a year. The judge ordered the preventive seizure of 15,000 euros the mayor is alleged to have received from Caramazza. The technical area head is accused of asking 50,000 euros over a 981,000 euro rock-face consolidation job, refused by a contractor who found it excessive, and 5,000 euros over a nursery. Investigations ran from July 2024 to October 2025.
inside: A contractor's money is alleged to have reached the mayor and technical chief who awarded the town's works, and the awards followed.
cite: LiveSicilia, 7 July 2026

n: An 800,000 euro bribe for a hotel ran through Lampedusa's technical office
org_label: Private interests behind an unauthorised hotel
rank: Head of the technical office, municipality of Lampedusa e Linosa
d: Prosecutors alleged a system inside the town hall of Lampedusa, the Italian island off Sicily, in which public offices were used between 2008 and 2012, during Dino De Rubeis's time as mayor, to favour private interests and obtain bribes. The charges included criminal association, corruption, forgery and interference with tenders, and among them a bribe of 800,000 euros for building an unauthorised hotel. The engineer Giuseppe Gabriele, then head of the technical office, was sentenced to eight years and ten months at first instance, reduced to five years and seven months on appeal. After the Court of Cassation sent the case back, the prosecutor general asked the Palermo appeal court for four years. The other four defendants were time-barred.
inside: Builders paid the municipal official who handled permits and tenders on the island, and unauthorised building went through.
cite: LiveSicilia, 8 October 2026

n: Firms bought rulings from Salerno's tax judges and lost the state 40m euros
org_label: Companies and taxpayers appealing their tax assessments
rank: Judges and officials, Salerno section of the regional tax commission
d: Prosecutors in Salerno, in the Ground Zero investigation led by Elena Guarino, found a system of corruption inside the Salerno section of Italy's regional tax commission, the court that hears appeals against tax assessments. Investigators examined twenty second-instance judgments handed down between 2016 and May 2019, all in favour of the taxpayers who had appealed, worth about 40 million euros in tax, interest and penalties. The investigation led to arrests and final convictions. In November 2026 the Court of Auditors' prosecutors sought 13.7 million euros from five former judges and officials, naming Fernando Spano, Giuseppe De Camillis, Giuseppe Naimoli, Salvatore Sammartino and Teodoro Tascone, over 21 corruption episodes. Bribes reached 100,000 euros and the disputes ran to nine million.
inside: Companies appealing their tax bills paid the judges and clerks who decided the appeals, and their assessments were cancelled.
cite: Stylo24, 26 October 2019 and 7 November 2026

n: Bom Jesus Agropecuaria bought land rulings from Bahia's appeal court
rank: Appeal judges of the Bahia Court of Justice
d: Operation Faroeste, a federal police investigation opened in 2019, examined the sale of judicial decisions in land disputes in western Bahia. Federal prosecutors say magistrates, businessmen and lawyers negotiated decisions favourable to private interests, and that between 2017 and 2020 rulings were traded to benefit the company Bom Jesus Agropecuaria in cases over rural properties. On 4 November 2026 Brazil's Superior Court of Justice unanimously sentenced the retired appeal judge Sandra Ines Moraes Rusciolelli Azevedo to 14 years and 20 days for passive corruption and money laundering, and revoked her pension. Her son, the lawyer Vasco Rusciolelli Azevedo, received 13 years and 11 months, the businessman Nelson Jose Vigolo four years and one month, and the lawyer Vanderlei Chilante four years and 11 months.
inside: An agribusiness group paid judges of a state appeal court, and rulings then moved title to the rural land it wanted.
cite: Correio da Manha (Brazil), 5 November 2026, on Superior Court of Justice Acao Penal 953

n: Businessmen's euros allegedly eased their cases inside Albanian prosecutions
org_label: Businessmen Pando Papuci and Vasil Bakalli
rank: Head of the Sarande prosecution office; head of the Lushnje prosecution office
d: Albania's special prosecution office against corruption and organised crime, SPAK, announced on 29 January 2026 that it had closed its investigation and sent for trial the former head of the Sarande prosecution office, Kledian Llaho, another former prosecutor and two businessmen. SPAK says Llaho was one-sided in an abuse-of-office investigation into a complainant who had rented a hotel owned by Llaho's father-in-law, and asked him to repay a debt of 1.8 million lek through Vasil Bakalli so that his procedural position would be eased. It also alleges the businessman Pando Papuci handed Bakalli and Llaho 30,000 euros to lean on a prosecutor, and 25,000 euros to his lawyer Clirim Shahini, who promised to influence the judge. Llaho calls the claims fabricated.
inside: Businessmen under criminal investigation allegedly paid prosecutors and an intermediary so that the offices investigating them would go easy.
cite: BIRN Albania (Reporter.al), 29 January 2026 and 7 May 2026

n: 'Ndrangheta reached road services firm ASE through its own employees
rank: Two employees of ASE - Autostrade service - servizi al territorio spa
d: The prevention measures section of the Reggio Calabria court placed ASE - Autostrade service - servizi al territorio spa, a company with its registered office in Rome, under judicial administration in June 2020, and put Hidro Geologic Line sas of Reggio Calabria under judicial control. Carabinieri served notice of the end of the investigation on thirteen people: two employees of the Rome company for external complicity in mafia association, and eight public administrators from Reggio Calabria's comune and council, the metropolitan authority, the regional council and the comune of Taurianova, accused along with the company's managing director of pressing for the hiring of people they recommended, or of corruption to favour the company. Investigators said the firm's territorial expansion rested on its permeability to mafia interests.
inside: Clan-linked staff sat inside a road services company while officials pushed its hirings, so the firm's growth and work served 'ndrangheta interests.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 9 June 2020, reporting the Reggio Calabria court decree and the Carabinieri notice of conclusion of investigation

n: Megna cosca men ran security services inside FC Crotone's stadium
rank: Security, steward and surveillance services at the Scida stadium, FC Crotone srl
d: The Catanzaro court placed the football club FC Crotone srl under judicial administration for twelve months in September 2025. The decree held that the club's business had been subject, directly or at least indirectly, to intimidation and subjection by local 'ndrangheta clans over the previous decade. It drew on the Glicine investigation, in which the court said reference figures of the Megna cosca had, almost always covertly, managed security and surveillance services inside the stadium. Prosecutors named Gaetano Russo, considered close to the cosca and the main referent for security work in the Crotone area, whose company Big Brother ran from July 2016 to 2018. The club's lawyer said the measure was not punitive and that the court supposed no complicity by the club or its managers.
inside: A mafia cosca's men covertly held the football club's stadium security and steward work, so the club's own services were run in the clan's interest.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 16 September 2025, on the Catanzaro court's judicial administration decree and the Glicine investigation

n: Port logistics staff moved a gang's cocaine out of Hamburg's port
rank: Jobs in Hamburg port logistics firms; self-employed hauliers working in the port
d: The Hamburg regional court sentenced eleven men aged between 35 and 57 to between six and fifteen years in prison in January 2024, finding it proved that they had smuggled about eight tonnes of cocaine from Colombia through the port of Hamburg in sea freight containers, hidden under bananas, charcoal and tyre parts. The court said the men were part of an internationally operating gang. In several cases three of the accused were said to have used their jobs in port logistics firms to get the arriving containers and their loads out of the port, while two self-employed hauliers in the port organised the containers' transport. The nine deliveries were in 2020. The report does not name the firms.
inside: A smuggling gang had men in jobs at port logistics companies, and they used that access to move its cocaine containers out of Hamburg's port.
cite: dpa report, 19 January 2024, on the judgment of the Hamburg Landgericht ('Acht Tonnen Kokain geschmuggelt - Bis zu 15 Jahre Haft')

n: Freight handlers at Sydney Airport pulled 100kg of cocaine off a flight
rank: Employees with access to freight handling operations, Sydney international airport
d: On 7 October 2023 two men employed at Sydney's international airport, aged 55 and 61, used their access to freight handling operations to take five bags holding about 100 kilograms of cocaine from a container in the cargo hold of an aircraft arrived from South Africa, and carried them out of the secure airside area, the Australian Federal Police alleged. The police said the two handed the bags to a car outside an airport freight terminal, and called them trusted insiders; a Padstow man had sourced the cocaine with figures overseas and a Hillsdale man coordinated the pair. In March 2025 the Downing Centre Local Court sentenced a former airline logistics manager to three years, a second man to ten years and the collector to two years nine months.
inside: A drug syndicate used two men's airport freight jobs to take its cocaine out of a plane and through the secure area, so their work served the syndicate.
cite: Australian Federal Police media releases, 9 October 2023 ('Five men charged over plot to import 100kg of cocaine Sydney Airport') and 24 March 2025 ('Trusted insiders jailed over failed plot to import 100kg of cocaine at Sydney Airport')

n: A syndicate's insiders at Port Botany opened containers of cocaine
org_label: Criminal syndicate importing through Port Botany
who: A criminal syndicate importing drugs through Port Botany
rank: Workers inside Port Botany cargo terminals, including a forklift driver at a sea freight facility
d: In April 2025 a Multi Agency Strike Team of Australian and New South Wales agencies began investigating a criminal syndicate alleged to have members working inside Port Botany, Sydney's container port, to bring in commercial quantities of drugs. Police say the network was linked to attempts to reach more than a tonne of drugs hidden in containers between February and October 2025. On 31 August 2025 a 38-year-old forklift driver was watched moving containers at a sea freight facility to reach one that was later found to hold about 506 kilograms of cocaine, and a second man was arrested leaving that container with tools. Five alleged insiders were charged in May 2026 over that import and two more in June 2026. The charges have not been tried.
inside: A drug syndicate had workers inside a container port, and they moved and opened its containers so its cocaine could be taken out before delivery.
cite: Australian Federal Police and NSW Police Force joint media releases, 2 September 2025 ('Three alleged trusted insiders charged by the MAST following failed 506kg cocaine import') and 5 June 2026 ('MAST charges another two alleged facilitators of trusted insider network in Sydney')

n: Sydney airport worker warned a drug ring of law enforcement interest
rank: Airport worker, Sydney Airport
d: In October 2020 Australian Border Force officers intercepted a consignment of rolls of denim arriving in Sydney from India and found 127 kilograms of pure pseudoephedrine, a precursor used to make methamphetamine, in packets among the fabric. Intelligence from the encrypted platform monitored during the police operation Ironside led investigators to allege that a Sydney airport worker had used his position to alert the criminal organisation behind the import to law enforcement interest in it. He was arrested in June 2021, pleaded guilty on 18 June 2026 to supporting a criminal organisation, and on 11 August 2026 the New South Wales District Court sentenced him to two years and four months, with a non-parole period of eighteen months.
inside: A drug importing organisation had a man inside the airport whose job let him see police interest in its consignment and warn it in time.
cite: Australian Federal Police and Australian Border Force joint media release, 11 August 2026 ('Ironside: Sydney airport worker jailed over role in 127kg pseudoephedrine importation')

n: Customs team leader set rosters for a Sydney Airport drug conspiracy
org_label: Pseudoephedrine importing conspiracy at Sydney Airport
rank: Leader of the Air Border Security team, Australian Customs Service, Sydney Airport
d: Phillip Cranney had been an Australian customs officer for nearly ten years and led the Air Border Security team, whose job was to investigate airport staff suspected of crime. From 2010, at least a dozen customs officers and baggage handlers at Sydney Airport allegedly took part in a scheme to import pseudoephedrine, a methamphetamine precursor, from Vietnam in couriers' luggage, with baggage handlers separating the tainted bags and customs officers seeing them through. A jury in the New South Wales District Court found Cranney guilty of conspiring to import a commercial quantity of pseudoephedrine and of three counts of dishonestly agreeing to receive a benefit intended to influence his duties. It found he adjusted rosters, coordinated four importations and received $140,000, and sentenced him to fourteen years.
inside: A smuggling conspiracy had the officer who led airport border security, and he set the rosters so its luggage passed the checks he was paid to run.
cite: Sydney Criminal Lawyers case report, 'Customs Officer Sent to Prison for Drug Charges', on the New South Wales District Court verdict and sentence

n: Border Force officer charged with taking cash to pass a cocaine parcel
who: A man alleged to have organised crime links
rank: Employee of the Australian Border Force
d: On 12 March 2025 a 50-year-old employee of the Australian Border Force, the agency that examines goods arriving in Australia, was charged with receiving a bribe as a Commonwealth official, abuse of public office, unauthorised disclosure of information and aiding the importation of border controlled drugs. A 67-year-old Mount Pritchard man, who the Multi Agency Strike Team alleges has organised crime links, was charged with bribery of a Commonwealth official and aiding the same importation. Police allege he conspired with the Border Force employee to ensure that a parcel holding 6.9 kilograms of cocaine would bypass Border Force examination, and that the officer had received cash and high-value items in the preceding months, partly for the parcel's safe passage and partly for information about a trial consignment of cosmetics.
inside: An alleged crime figure paid a border agency employee so that the officer waved his cocaine parcel past the checks he was employed to carry out.
cite: Australian Federal Police, NSW Police Force and Australian Border Force joint media release, 12 March 2025 ('New strike team targets double dealers working for organised crime'), on charges under Operation Proctor

n: Corrections officer took money to carry an encrypted phone into a jail
org_label: Criminal network using the Ghost encrypted application
who: A criminal network using the Ghost encrypted application
rank: Serving officer, New South Wales corrective services
d: The Australian Federal Police charged a 25-year-old Sydney man in May 2025 with corruptly receiving a benefit of less than $2,000 and with committing an offence for the benefit of a criminal organisation. Police allege that, as a serving corrections officer, he smuggled a dedicated encrypted communications device into a correctional facility in return for money. He was identified after the arrest in September 2024 of several Sydney men under Operation Kraken-Kamino, who are alleged to have used the Ghost encrypted mobile application to organise drug imports and to manufacture a false terrorism plot; examination of an encrypted device held by one of them suggested a serving officer had exploited his position for a criminal organisation. The release does not name the prison. The charges have not been tried.
inside: A criminal network paid a prison officer to carry its encrypted phone inside, so the jail's own staff kept its communications running from a cell.
cite: Australian Federal Police media release, 5 August 2025 ('NSW corrections officer charged over alleged corrupt conduct')

n: Ground services staff at Sydney Airport ran a syndicate's imports
org_label: Drug importing syndicate using Sydney Airport insiders
rank: Employees of an airport ground services provider, Sydney Airport
d: The Australian Federal Police said in June 2021 that an investigation of more than two years had examined employees of an airport ground services provider allegedly involved in drug trafficking at Sydney Airport. In March 2019 the inquiry led to two arrests and the seizure of 38 kilograms of methamphetamine brought into Sydney on an Air Canada flight. Investigators then identified a man they suspected of overseeing the importation inside the airport precinct, using an encrypted device to talk to a wider syndicate. Intelligence from Operation Ironside showed that syndicate planning a further importation through the airport in late 2019, and police allege it was made up of people with trusted insider access. A Liverpool man and woman charged in June 2021 had allegedly handled about $600,000 in suspected proceeds.
inside: A drug syndicate worked through staff of the firm handling aircraft on the ground, whose airport access let its consignments move inside the airport.
cite: Australian Federal Police media release, 12 June 2021 ('IRONSIDE: Two people charged over Sydney Airport import scheme')

n: Traffickers had the master of a bulk carrier on a 320kg cocaine run
org_label: Cocaine importing enterprise using a bulk carrier's master
rank: Master of the bulk carrier Interlink Veracity
d: Australian authorities seized 320 kilograms of cocaine, worth about $128 million, at Port Hedland in Western Australia on 15 May 2022 and arrested two men they alleged had collected the plastic-wrapped drugs from the ocean off the Pilbara coast. A week later the Australian Federal Police arrested the 51-year-old master of an international bulk shipping carrier, the 179-metre Interlink Veracity, on board his vessel and charged him with importing a commercial quantity of border controlled drugs. Police said a forensic examination of a mobile device seized from him had turned up messages about the importation. The man, a Montenegrin national, appeared at South Hedland court on 24 May 2022. The charge has not been tried, and the release does not name the ship's operator.
inside: A cocaine enterprise had the man in command of a cargo ship, so the vessel itself carried and delivered its load into an Australian port.
cite: Australian Federal Police, Western Australia Police Force and Australian Border Force joint media release, 24 May 2022 ('Ship Captain charged over WA 320kg cocaine plot')

n: Two Rikers Island officers took bribes to run inmates' contraband trade
org_label: Incarcerated gang members and their outside co-conspirators
who: Incarcerated gang members and their outside co-conspirators
rank: Correction officers, New York City Department of Corrections, Rikers Island
d: Two New York City correction officers pleaded guilty to bribery in federal court in Brooklyn in 2022. Katrina Patterson admitted accepting at least $34,090 in bribes sent by co-conspirators on behalf of Michael Ross, an inmate at the Robert N. Davoren Center on Rikers Island, and smuggling contraband in for him; narcotics and phones were later found in his cell. Krystle Burrell admitted taking about $9,780 arranged by another inmate, Terrae Hinds, and smuggling at least two phones into the Anna M. Kross Center, facilitating what prosecutors called Hinds's contraband smuggling business and his sale of narcotics inside. The US attorney said the two had thrown in their lot with Bloods gang members; the Homeland Security Investigations officer in charge said they smuggled contraband to incarcerated known gang members.
inside: Jailed gang members paid two guards through outsiders, so the officers running the wings carried in the phones and drugs their trade depended on.
cite: US Department of Justice, Eastern District of New York, press release of 20 September 2022, 'Two New York City Correction Officers Plead Guilty to Accepting Bribes in Exchange for Smuggling Contraband Into Rikers Island'

n: Baltimore jail officers joined detainees' contraband racket for cash
org_label: Detainees of the Chesapeake Detention Facility and their outside facilitators
rank: Correctional officers, Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services, Chesapeake Detention Facility
d: Two correctional officers at the Chesapeake Detention Facility in Baltimore, a maximum-security jail run by Maryland's corrections department under contract to the US Marshals Service to hold federal pretrial detainees, pleaded guilty in October 2021 to a racketeering conspiracy. Their plea agreements said they had conspired with other employees, detainees and associates to bring narcotics, phones and tobacco in. Talaia Youngblood admitted that from at least November 2017 she met outside facilitators to collect contraband and bribes at the direction of detainees, one of whom she was involved with. Darren Parker admitted smuggling for a detainee from no later than 2018, taking $1,980 in four payments in early 2019 and being stopped in the jail car park in March 2019 with a bag holding a phone, charger, Suboxone and tobacco.
inside: Detainees and their helpers outside paid two officers of the jail holding them, so the staff meant to search the place carried its contraband in.
cite: US Department of Justice, District of Maryland, press release of 19 October 2021, 'Two Correctional Officers Plead Guilty to a Racketeering Conspiracy, Admit to Smuggling Contraband Into Maryland Jail'

n: Inmates' people bought Essex County jail officers a contraband market
org_label: Inmates of the Essex County Correctional Facility and their outside associates
rank: Corrections officers, Essex County Correctional Facility, Newark
d: In 2014 federal prosecutors charged two corrections officers, a lawyer and six other people over smuggling phones and marijuana into the Essex County Correctional Facility in Newark, which holds federal pretrial detainees. The US attorney said the defendants had operated a contraband marketplace inside the jail. Officer Stephon Solomon was alleged to have smuggled phones, tobacco and marijuana to the inmate Quasim Nichols on at least five occasions between October 2013 and April 2014 for cash bribes, with Nichols's friends collecting the goods outside. A separate officer, John Grosso, admitted agreeing in December 2013 to take cash bribes to help bring contraband in, and was sentenced to 24 months. Nichols was sentenced to 148 months for a carjacking and the conspiracy, and two women admitted paying officers.
inside: Inmates and relatives outside paid officers of the jail that held them, so staff carried in the phones and drugs sold on the wings.
cite: US Department of Justice, District of New Jersey, press releases: 'Corrections Officers, Lawyer, Among Nine Charged In Schemes To Smuggle Contraband Into Federal Pretrial Detention Facility'; 'Former Corrections Officer Sentenced To Two Years In Prison For Accepting Cash Bribes'; 'Essex County, New Jersey, Man Sentenced To 148 Months'; 'Two New Jersey Women Admit Roles In Plots To Bribe Corrections Officers'

n: Inmates' families paid a Georgia prison officer to carry drugs inside
org_label: Inmates of Autry State Prison and their families
rank: Correctional officer, Georgia Department of Corrections, Autry State Prison
d: A federal jury convicted Jokelra Copeland of accepting bribes to smuggle contraband, including illegal drugs, into Autry State Prison at Pelham in Georgia. Prosecutors said she began work for the Georgia Department of Corrections in 2014 on the overnight shift and, within months of being hired, conspired with inmates and other officers to bring contraband in, hiding packages of marijuana under her clothing as she passed through the prison's security entrance. Over a four-month period in mid-2015 she accepted more than $13,000 in bribes from the families of at least two inmates, and financial records showed payments sent to her on at least eleven occasions through international money transfer services. She was one of 68 Georgia corrections officers arrested by the FBI in 2016 after a long investigation.
inside: Inmates' families paid a prison officer, so the staff member searched at the gate was the one carrying their drugs past it.
cite: US Department of Justice, Northern District of Georgia, press release, 'Former Georgia Department of Corrections officer convicted of accepting bribes to smuggle contraband into state prison'

n: Medical lab's 18,000 euros reached the manager of Adjud town hospital
rank: Manager, Adjud Municipal Hospital, Vrancea county
d: Spitalul Municipal Adjud is a town hospital in Vrancea county, Romania. The National Anticorruption Directorate said that between October 2015 and 25 February 2016 its manager, Florin Padurariu, demanded and received 18,000 euros in three instalments from representatives of a medical analysis laboratory company, through a second defendant who administered a commercial company. The money was so that he would settle with those representatives the absence from the hospital's stock of an analysis machine the firm had not returned, and extend a joint-venture contract between the hospital and the laboratory. Prosecutors caught him taking the final 9,000 euros. On 19 April 2018 the Bucharest Court of Appeal convicted both men on plea agreements, giving Padurariu two years and six months, suspended.
inside: A private laboratory's money reached the manager of the public hospital it supplied, and he worked to extend its contract and clear its debt.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticorruptie, press release 474/VIII/3, 12 May 2017; DNA notice of Bucharest Court of Appeal decision 595/A of 19 April 2018

n: Three firms' gifts won refurbishment work at Romsilva's Mures directorate
org_label: SC TM GIP SA, SC Fune Serv SRL and SC Creative Art SRL
rank: Director, economic director, technical director and a forestry technician, Targu Mures Forestry Directorate, Romsilva
d: Directia Silvica Targu Mures is a county branch of Romsilva, Romania's state forestry company. In October 2007 anticorruption prosecutors sent four of its directors for trial together with the heads of three private firms, over the design, award, execution and acceptance of works to modernise the directorate's headquarters between 1999 and 2002. Prosecutors said the directors took benefits, including construction and installation work carried out for them, so that the firms obtained contracts through formal selections that ignored procurement rules, and put the loss at 219,536.27 lei. On 21 October 2014 the High Court of Cassation convicted the director Ioan Anton Dogaru and a forestry technician of bribe-taking and the economic director of abuse of office, acquitted three defendants and ended proceedings against two.
inside: Contractors' building work and cash reached the directors of a state forestry branch, which then steered its refurbishment contracts to those firms.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticorruptie, press release 245/VIII/3, 4 October 2007; DNA notice of High Court of Cassation decision 2849 of 21 October 2014

n: Regiotrans bought its train-km confirmations inside Romania's rail company
rank: Head of the transport monitoring service, CNCF CFR SA
d: CNCF CFR SA is Romania's state railway infrastructure company. The state subsidy a private passenger operator receives depends on the train-kilometres it runs, a figure CFR confirms. Anticorruption prosecutors said that between 3 June 2010 and 6 April 2015 Estrella Stefanescu, head of CFR's transport monitoring service, took money and benefits worth 24,653.67 lei from Florin Hadarean, general director of Regiotrans SRL, for confirming the company's train-kilometre volumes, which were attached to its subsidy claims. They said Regiotrans unlawfully obtained subsidies of 236,238,281 lei, about 54.5 million euros. Hadarean admitted the payments in a plea agreement in March 2018 and accepted one year and four months, suspended; Stefanescu was sent for trial.
inside: A private rail operator paid the state rail company's monitoring chief to certify the mileage figures on which its state subsidies were calculated.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticorruptie, press releases 332/VIII/3 of 19 February 2015, 278/VIII/3 of 23 March 2018 and 288/VIII/3 of 30 March 2018

n: Cluj hospital's repair work went to the contractor who paid its director
org_label: SC Relian Prod Impex SRL and SC Goodwill Eximp SRL
who: Two repair firms run by Anica Cimpan
rank: Former financial and administrative director, and a bid evaluation committee member, Adults Clinical Hospital, Cluj-Napoca
d: Spitalul Clinic de Adulti in Cluj-Napoca is a public hospital. Anticorruption prosecutors sent for trial its former financial and later administrative director, Emilia Roman, and Gheorghe Pop, a member of the committees that evaluated bids and accepted completed works. They said that between 2002 and 2004 the two awarded repair works on the hospital's wards, in breach of public procurement rules, to firms run by Anica Cimpan, administrator of Relian Prod Impex SRL and in fact of Goodwill Eximp SRL, who helped them. Both officials were charged with bribe-taking and abuse of office and Cimpan with two counts of giving a bribe. The directorate's bulletin records no outcome.
inside: A contractor's money reached a public hospital's administrative director and a bid evaluator, who then handed her two firms the hospital's repair work.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticorruptie, press bulletin 1/VIII/3, 5 January 2009, summary of cases finalised in December 2008

n: Paper supplier's man installed atop Posta Romana's stamp factory
who: Marian Constantinof and the firms he controlled
rank: Director of the Fabrica de Timbre branch, Compania Nationala Posta Romana SA
d: Compania Nationala Posta Romana is Romania's state postal operator, and its Fabrica de Timbre branch bought paper to fill orders from headquarters. In March 2017 anticorruption prosecutors sent for trial the businessman Marian Constantinof, Stefan Gheorghe, then mayor of Piatra Neamt and a party vice-president, and Cosmin Dragos Mihailescu. The indictment says that in July and August 2009 Gheorghe offered, for money, to use his influence with the company so that the branch awarded paper supply contracts to firms Constantinof controlled, and that on 8 September 2009, with Gheorghe's support, Mihailescu, a man close to Constantinof, was appointed to run the branch and tasked with controlling and manipulating the procurement procedures.
inside: A businessman's associate was put in charge of the state post's stamp factory so its paper contracts went to firms he controlled.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticorruptie, press release 206/VIII/3, 3 March 2017

n: Osiris Design's home fit-outs bought contracts at Buzau's municipal utility
rank: General director and economic director, Regia Autonoma Municipala Buzau
d: Regia Autonoma Municipala Buzau was the town's municipally owned utility company. Anticorruption prosecutors said that between 2003 and 2004 its general director, Victor Busuioc, and economic director, Florica Onel, demanded and received benefits worth 26,787 euros from Marius Negoita, administrator of Osiris Design SRL, delivered through one of his employees as fitting-out work at their homes and their families' homes. In exchange the firm was unlawfully awarded a works contract and sold the utility furniture and services worth 4,065,336.83 lei, and the directors accepted payment for work not carried out and for overvalued goods. On 9 December 2014 the High Court of Cassation convicted them and Negoita, and ordered 1,538,354.81 lei in damages to the utility.
inside: A supplier paid for building work on two municipal utility directors' homes, and the utility then awarded and overpaid his firm's contracts.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticorruptie, press release 257/VIII/3, 15 October 2008; DNA notice of High Court of Cassation decision 3113 of 9 December 2014

n: Food supplier's gifts kept deliveries flowing at Ploiesti county hospital
rank: Manager and a procurement economist, Ploiesti County Emergency Hospital
d: Spitalul Judetean de Urgenta Ploiesti is the county emergency hospital in Prahova. Anticorruption prosecutors said Adrian Rotila, administrator of ADLIV TERMO SRL, which delivered food to the hospital, gave its manager Adrian Strambeanu a lamb and a collector's sword, valued by investigators at a minimum of 299 lei, and gave Marian Emanuel Rotaru, the employee who ran the procurement procedures his firm won, a door, garden furniture and two trips to the Danube Delta, at a minimum of 2,991 lei, so that both would help his deliveries continue in breach of procurement rules. On 22 April 2024 the High Court ended the case against Rotila and Rotaru as time-barred, acquitted Strambeanu and confiscated the goods Rotaru had received.
inside: A food supplier's gifts reached a county hospital's manager and its procurement officer so its deliveries continued outside procurement rules.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticorruptie, press release 294/VIII/3, 16 February 2015, with its update of 28 May 2024 on High Court decision 13 of 22 April 2024

n: Suppliers helped write and win ASP Crotone's health tenders
org_label: medical supply firms in Crotone province
who: Medical supply firms and their intermediaries
rank: Public officials then serving at the Azienda sanitaria provinciale di Crotone
d: The Azienda sanitaria provinciale di Crotone is the provincial health authority in Calabria. In October 2026 the Crotone prosecutor's office served notices closing preliminary investigations on thirteen people, among them officials then serving at the authority, businessmen and professionals, over supply tenders worth more than three million euros called between 2019 and 2021 by the province's main health bodies. The Guardia di Finanza alleges that some firms obtained tender documents and confidential information in advance, that representatives of the firms to be favoured took part directly in drawing up the specifications, and that sums fixed as a percentage of each contract were paid, often presented as consultancy work; investigators documented more than 45,000 euros handed over in cash.
inside: Suppliers' money and their own drafting got inside a provincial health authority's tender process, which then awarded contracts to suit those firms.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 10 October 2026

n: Supply firms' payments ran back through a Catanzaro hospital's own doctor
rank: Head of the obstetrics department, Azienda ospedaliera Pugliese Ciaccio
d: The Azienda ospedaliera Pugliese Ciaccio in Catanzaro, since merged into the Renato Dulbecco hospital, buys medical equipment and supplies. In September 2023 the Catanzaro prosecutor asked for seven people to be committed for trial over corruption said to have taken place until 2017 in dealings between a doctor and firms supplying the hospital. Prosecutors say Fulvio Zullo, then head of the obstetrics department, had the hospital buy products from firms connected to him, which then paid several thousand euros into a company linked to the same doctor. Those named with him include the owner of a medical equipment firm and two sales representatives of supply companies. One asked to be tried by summary procedure.
inside: Supply firms paid a hospital department head through a company of his own, and the hospital then bought those firms' products.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 30 September 2023

n: 10,000 euros for a Palermo hospital's sterilisation tender, prosecutors say
org_label: Servizi ospedalieri spa and two businessmen
who: Servizi ospedalieri spa and two businessmen
rank: Former member of the board of auditors of the Civico hospital and of the Palermo health authority
d: ARNAS Civico-Di Cristina-Benfratelli is Palermo's main public hospital group. In November 2025 an investigating judge placed five people under house arrest in a Sicilian health corruption inquiry. Prosecutors allege that Antonio Maria Sciacchitano, a Palermo accountant and former member of the board of auditors of the Civico hospital and of the Palermo health authority, received a bribe of 10,000 euros paid by the businessmen Gaetano Di Giacomo and Massimiliano De Marco to help Servizi ospedalieri spa win the contract to supply and sterilise surgical material for the group, a tender revoked in 2023 and called again in 2024. The judge suspended the official responsible for the procedure from public office for a year.
inside: A supplier's money reached an accountant who had sat on a hospital group's audit board, to steer its sterilisation contract that company's way.
cite: LiveSicilia, 29 November 2025

n: Vendors' kickbacks ran the purchasing cards at two Florida VA hospitals
rank: Employees of the West Palm Beach and Miami VA Medical Centers
d: The Department of Veterans Affairs runs medical centres in West Palm Beach and Miami for former service members. In December 2019 federal prosecutors charged fifteen South Florida residents over a kickback scheme in which, court filings alleged, medical centre employees used government credit cards to order medical and hospital supplies from vendors who paid them cash bribes, at grossly inflated prices or with orders only partly filled or not filled at all. Prosecutors said the scheme let the corrupt vendors obtain more than 20 million dollars in purchase orders. In August 2021 the last of sixteen defendants were sentenced; the vendor Earron Starks received 30 months and was ordered to repay 2,451,000 dollars.
inside: Suppliers paid cash to the staff holding two veterans' hospitals' purchasing cards, and those staff then ordered from them at inflated prices.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida, 11 December 2019 and 19 August 2021

n: Seico Construction's cash won building jobs at Miami's Jackson North hospital
rank: Employee handling vendor contracts, Jackson North Medical Center, Jackson Health System
d: Jackson North Medical Center is part of the Jackson Health System, the public hospital system of Miami-Dade County. In January 2014 federal prosecutors filed two charging documents over bribery in the system's vendor contracts. They alleged that Douglas Denton, an employee at Jackson North, solicited and agreed to accept cash payments so that he would be influenced and rewarded in connection with contracts to provide goods and services, and that he awarded construction jobs at the medical centre to the operators of a small business called Seico Construction Co. The filings allege he received 5,000 dollars in five payments of 1,000 dollars between 2010 and 2013. The two named operators of Seico were charged with conspiring to pay him.
inside: A small builder paid a public hospital's contracts employee in cash instalments, and he then awarded the firm the hospital's construction jobs.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida, 31 January 2014

n: Euroil's 45,000 lei offered to spare its station a Braila customs fine
rank: Senior official, Braila County Directorate for Excise and Customs Operations
d: The Directia Judeteana pentru Accize si Operatiuni Vamale Braila enforced excise and customs rules in Braila county. Anticorruption prosecutors charged the company SC Euroil SRL, a fuel trader, with giving a bribe, saying that between 20 and 22 October 2010 its associate and legal representative, Ioan Marta, promised a senior official of the directorate 45,000 lei so that the official would breach his duties and not apply the penalties an inspection had found due: closing the company's fuel station, confiscating 350,000 lei and a 100,000 lei fine. The official reported the offer. Marta handed over 7,100 lei and was caught giving a second instalment of 13,000 lei. Prosecutors placed the station under seizure.
inside: A fuel retailer tried to buy the customs official inspecting it, so the penalties due against its filling station would not be applied.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticorruptie, press bulletin 455/VIII/3, 4 July 2011, summary of cases finalised in June 2011

n: Hotel firm pressed for 5,000 lei by Mures's environment commissar
org_label: the company owning a Targu Mures hotel
who: The company that owned a Targu Mures hotel
rank: Commissar, Mures County Commissariat, National Environmental Guard
d: The Garda Nationala de Mediu is Romania's environmental inspectorate, working through county commissariats. Anticorruption prosecutors sent Ioan Ciorbagiu, a commissar at its Mures county commissariat, for trial for bribe-taking in continued form. They said that on 2 September 2008, during an inspection at a hotel in Targu Mures, he demanded 5,000 lei from two of the legal representatives of the company that owned the hotel so that, having found faults in the hotel's sewerage system, he would impose a smaller fine or no more than a warning. The file went to the Mures Tribunal. The directorate's bulletin records no outcome.
inside: A hotel company's money was sought by the environmental inspector examining it, in exchange for a lighter penalty on its sewerage faults.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticorruptie, press bulletin 323/VIII/3, 3 December 2008, summary of cases finalised in November 2008

n: Firm's seaside stay bought warning of Arges labour inspections
org_label: SC Valahia 2002 SRL, later SC MGC International Investments SRL
rank: Labour inspector, Arges Territorial Labour Inspectorate
d: The Inspectoratul Teritorial de Munca is Romania's county labour inspectorate, which checks employers' compliance with labour law. Anticorruption prosecutors sent Florian Anghelina, a former labour inspector at the Arges inspectorate, for trial for bribe-taking in continued form, with Said Salah, administrator of a Topoloveni company, charged with giving a bribe. They said that during 2007 Salah gave Anghelina a free stay at a hotel on the Romanian coast so that he would breach his duties and favour Salah's firm by telling it about the inspectorate's planned checks, and that during 2008 Anghelina accepted promises of food and other goods from representatives of two further companies so that he would omit findings or announce inspections in advance.
inside: An employer paid a labour inspector with a holiday so the inspectorate would tell the firm when its compliance checks were coming.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticorruptie, press bulletin 1/VIII/3, 3 January 2012, summary of cases finalised in December 2011

n: Guard firm paid a Bucharest police officer 300 lei a month to escape fines
rank: Police officer with guard-systems duties, Section 22, Bucharest General Police Directorate
d: Section 22 is one of Bucharest's police stations, and one of its officers held duties over guard systems, which the police inspect. Anticorruption prosecutors sent Daniel-Nicusor Istratie for trial for bribe-taking in continued form, saying that between June 2015 and January 2017, across sixteen meetings, he demanded and received 5,900 lei in total from the representative of a private guard company as a protection fee of 300 lei a month, except August 2015 when he took 200 lei. On 19 January 2017 he was caught taking 1,200 lei covering October 2016 to January 2017. Prosecutors said the money was so that no penalties followed the faults found in the firm's guard arrangements, and that none were applied in that period.
inside: A private security firm paid a monthly fee to the police officer who inspected guard systems, and it faced no penalties while it paid.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticorruptie, press bulletin 140/VIII/3, 14 February 2017, summary of cases finalised in January 2017

n: Beauty salon's free treatments bought off a 9,500 lei consumer fine
rank: Two commissars, West Region Regional Commissariat for Consumer Protection
d: The Comisariatul Regional pentru Protectia Consumatorilor Regiunea Vest enforces consumer rules in western Romania. Anticorruption prosecutors sent two of its commissars, Maria Pirvulescu and Marinela Ilias, for trial in October 2019 for bribe-taking in continued form. They said that in May 2019, inspecting a beauty salon, the two proposed and demanded that the company's representatives give them a year of free hairdressing, cosmetic, manicure and pedicure treatments in exchange for not applying a 9,500 lei fine, and that between May and July 2019 the two and their relatives took treatments worth 1,773 lei, with Pirvulescu also taking a flight worth 454 lei. On 11 February 2022 the Timisoara Court of Appeal convicted both, with suspended sentences of three and two years.
inside: A salon company paid two consumer-protection inspectors in free treatments, and the fine their own inspection had found due was not applied.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticorruptie, press bulletin 884/VIII/3, 12 November 2019, summary of cases finalised in October 2019; DNA notice of Timisoara Court of Appeal decision 97 of 11 February 2022

n: AVCOM's cash and gifts bought its own FAA safety inspector
who: AVCOM, a Miami aviation repair company
rank: Aviation Safety Inspector, FAA South Florida Flight Standards District Office
d: The Federal Aviation Administration's South Florida Flight Standards District Office inspects aviation repair firms. From 2010 until June 2013 Manuel R. Fernandez worked there as an aviation safety inspector while also holding posts, including vice-president of operations, at AVCOM, a Miami aviation repair company under that office's jurisdiction. Trial evidence showed AVCOM's co-owners, Patricia and Rolando Suarez, provided more than 150,000 dollars in cash, as well as jewellery, a cruise, clothing and about 15,000 dollars funnelled to Fernandez's mother. In return he gave AVCOM advance notice of FAA inspections of the firm, disclosed financial information about its competitors and supplied improperly obtained repair manuals. A jury convicted him on twenty-one counts in June 2019; he was sentenced to 75 months.
inside: A repair company had its own vice-president sitting inside the aviation regulator that inspected it, warning it of inspections and leaking rivals' data.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida, 13 June 2019 and 5 December 2019

n: Aerochem's cash and nights out reached a Corpus Christi depot supervisor
rank: Supervisor of a paint-stripping division, Corpus Christi Army Depot
d: The Corpus Christi Army Depot strips and repairs US Army helicopter parts. Aerochem, Inc., an Oklahoma City maker of paint remover, began selling its products to the depot in 2010. Federal prosecutors charged the company's founder and president, Christopher Houston Hensley, with conspiring to bribe a public official there, saying that he and a former Aerochem officer built a relationship with Richard Balderas Jr., who supervised the depot division that stripped paint from helicopter parts, and gave him entertainment, wire transfers and more than 3,000 dollars in cash in exchange for favourable treatment of Aerochem's business at the depot. Hensley pleaded guilty in 2015, admitting he approved club outings and the purchase of a 2,600 dollar football helmet for Balderas's son's team.
inside: A paint-remover maker paid the army depot supervisor who used its product, and the depot then treated the company's business favourably.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Western District of Oklahoma, 23 June 2015

n: Housing contractor's payments to the US Army's Kuwait City housing office
org_label: a maintenance company owned by an Egyptian businessman
rank: Housing specialist, off-post housing office, US Army Area Support Group-Kuwait
d: The US Army's Area Support Group-Kuwait maintains Camp Arifjan and runs an off-post housing office in downtown Kuwait City that procures, leases and supervises housing for American personnel. William Rondell Collins worked there as a housing specialist, responsible for supervising private contractors and procuring apartment rentals. In January 2009 a company owned by an Egyptian businessman won a fixed-price United States government contract to provide maintenance for the housing Collins's office managed. Collins pleaded guilty in 2010, admitting that between July and December 2009 he solicited more than 11,000 dollars in bribes from that businessman in exchange for submitting an inflated apartment lease for approval, and that he took unlawful payments supplementing his salary.
inside: A maintenance contractor paid the army housing specialist who supervised it, and he put an inflated lease forward for the army's approval.
cite: US Department of Justice, Criminal Division, 18 February 2010 and 21 April 2010

n: Construction firm's 1,200 dollars spared it a New York stop-work fine
rank: Inspector, New York City Department of Buildings
d: The New York City Department of Buildings inspects construction sites and enforces stop-work orders. In late July 2020 its inspector Francesco Ginestri re-inspected a site in Queens that had been given a stop-work order for safety violations earlier that month, and learned that work had continued. Instead of seeking a penalty on the company, he solicited a 1,200 dollar cash bribe from one of its employees in exchange for ensuring that the department would not issue the company a 25,000 dollar fine. Ginestri was arrested on 10 February 2021 and resigned from the department the same day. In May 2021 he pleaded guilty to solicitation and receipt of a bribe.
inside: A builder's cash reached the city inspector who had caught it breaching a stop-work order, and the department's fine was never issued.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York, 10 February 2021 and 19 May 2021

n: O&U Towing's bribes let it jump Miami-Dade's police wrecker rota
rank: A police officer and a public service aide, Miami-Dade Police Department
d: Miami-Dade County runs a rotational wrecker system: tow companies contract with the county, are placed on a list and are called in turn by police when a driver cannot arrange their own tow, paying the county a fee for each referral. In 2015 federal prosecutors charged a former Miami-Dade police officer, Yuri Millan, the tow company owner Oriel Ugardes, his driver Jose Guim and a former public service aide, Elina Rodriguez. The complaint says that in 2013 an FBI task force learned Ugardes, owner of O&U Towing, was paying department employees to help his trucks get round the rota, and that investigators documented him and Guim paying Millan and Rodriguez cash to let O&U trucks tow vehicles directly from accident scenes.
inside: A towing firm paid police staff to call it instead of the company next on the county's rota, and its trucks took the work.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida, 17 November 2015

n: Two Afghan trucking firms paid the US Army's Bagram transport office
org_label: Afghan International Trucking and Afghan Trade Transportation
rank: Officials of the Transportation Operations Support Office, Bagram Airfield
d: The US Army's Transportation Operations Support Office at Bagram Airfield oversaw all trucking contracts on the base and assigned work among nine Afghan trucking companies according to their performance records. In June 2010 two of them, Afghan International Trucking and Afghan Trade Transportation, pleaded guilty in Virginia to bribery and agreed to pay 4.4 million dollars in criminal fines. Under the plea agreements, AIT made corrupt payments of more than 120,000 dollars to military officials, among them James Paul Clifton and Ana Chavez, and ATT more than 30,000 dollars to Clifton. AIT's employees began offering money in 2004; it once paid Chavez 70,000 dollars in a sweet box, and by mid-2008 was paying Clifton 20,000 dollars a month.
inside: Two haulage firms paid the army officers who allotted trucking work on the base, and the work was then assigned to suit them.
cite: US Department of Justice, Criminal Division, 25 June 2010

n: Developer's appliances for a Pittsburgh occupancy certificate
rank: Building inspector, City of Pittsburgh
d: City of Pittsburgh building inspectors inspect properties whose owners have applied for certificates of occupancy. In 2018 a developer was converting a commercial building in downtown Pittsburgh into luxury apartments and hotel rooms, and needed a temporary certificate of occupancy for one floor by the end of December 2018 to obtain a historical tax credit that formed part of the project's financing. Walter Eiseman, a city building inspector, pleaded guilty in February 2024, admitting he inspected two floors of the project that December, which resulted in a temporary certificate being issued, and that in return he accepted home appliances from the developer, delivered in early January 2019. He also admitted asking for kitchen cabinets, ordered but never delivered.
inside: A developer paid a city building inspector in household goods, and he signed off the occupancy certificate the project's tax credit depended on.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Western District of Pennsylvania, 7 February 2024

n: K&B Auto Body paid a Philadelphia police dispatcher for crash locations
org_label: K&B Auto Body and K&B Autocraft
who: A Philadelphia body shop and towing business
rank: Civilian radio dispatcher, Philadelphia Police Department
d: Philadelphia's police department employs civilian radio dispatchers who handle confidential operational information. A federal indictment unsealed in May 2014 charged the dispatcher Dorian Parsley and three men with conspiracy and bribery. It alleges that between February 2011 and December 2013 Parsley used her post to pass accident locations, the positions of police squad cars and vehicle registration details to tow truck operators who paid her cash. Stepfon Flowers, who worked for K&B Autocraft, allegedly paid her 100 to 150 dollars a week; in September 2012 he is said to have introduced William Cheeseman, an owner of K&B Auto Body, so that he could receive the information too, and in April 2013 a K&B Auto Body driver was given her contact details for the same purpose.
inside: A body shop paid a police dispatcher weekly for crash locations, and the force's own information steered the towing work to its trucks.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania, 9 May 2014

n: Supplier promised a Korean defence procurement official a post-retirement reward
org_label: Deck Won Kang's US naval supply companies
who: Deck Won Kang's two US companies
rank: procurement official, Defense Acquisition Program Administration
d: Deck Won Kang, a New Jersey man who controlled two American companies selling naval equipment and technology to South Korea, pleaded guilty in December 2020 to bribing a Korean government official to win and keep contracts with the Defense Acquisition Program Administration, the state-owned and state-controlled agency inside the Republic of Korea's Ministry of National Defense that buys its military equipment. Kang admitted that from about January 2009 he promised the official, a high-ranking Korean navy figure and a procurement official at the agency, something of value for after he left public office. In exchange the official passed Kang non-public information about the contracts. Between April 2012 and February 2013, at the official's direction after his retirement, Kang wired 100,000 dollars to an Australian account for his benefit.
inside: A supplier bought a serving defence-procurement official with a promised future payment, and the official fed it secret bid information from inside the agency.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 17 December 2020

n: LAN Airlines paid an adviser to Argentina's transport ministry secretary
rank: adviser to the Secretary of the Ministry of Transportation
d: LATAM Airlines Group admitted in July 2016 that executives at its predecessor LAN Airlines signed a fictitious 1.15 million dollar consulting agreement, in October 2006, with an adviser to the Secretary of Argentina's Ministry of Transportation. The agreement purported to require a study of Argentine airline routes; the consultant never provided any such services. He instead funnelled the money to Argentine labour union officials in exchange for the union accepting lower wages and not enforcing a costly labour rule, and LAN profited by more than 6.7 million dollars. LATAM paid a 12.75 million dollar criminal penalty under a deferred prosecution agreement and about 9.4 million dollars to the Securities and Exchange Commission. No decision by the ministry serving the airline has been identified.
inside: An airline put money in the hands of a serving adviser to the transport ministry's secretary, whose post oversees airlines, to settle a labour dispute in its favour.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 25 July 2016 (LATAM deferred prosecution agreement)

n: IT supplier's 2.08m dollars bought the head of Honduras's social security
rank: Executive Director, Honduran Institute of Social Security
d: The Honduran Institute of Social Security is the government agency that provides workers' compensation, retirement, maternity and death benefits. Mario Roberto Zelaya Rojas was its executive director from 2010 to 2014. A United States forfeiture complaint filed in January 2015 alleges that he solicited and accepted 2.08 million dollars in bribes from Compania De Servicios Multiples, an information-technology company, in exchange for prioritising and expediting payments owed to it under a 19 million dollar contract with the institute, and that he told the company to pay two members of the institute's board who were charged with overseeing that contract. The money was allegedly routed through an affiliate and laundered into New Orleans property; the United States sought nine houses worth about 1,528,000 dollars.
inside: A contractor's money reached the head of the national social-security institute and two board members supervising its contract, which was then paid first.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 13 January 2015 (civil forfeiture complaint)

n: Weatherford's kickbacks won nine contracts with Iraq's Ministry of Oil
org_label: Weatherford Oil Tools Middle East Limited
rank: Ministry of Oil and other ministries
d: Weatherford Oil Tools Middle East Limited, a subsidiary of the Swiss oil services group Weatherford International, paid about 1,470,128 dollars in kickbacks to the government of Iraq between about February and July 2002 on nine contracts with Iraq's Ministry of Oil and other ministries, to supply oil drilling and refining equipment. The money was concealed from the United Nations by inflating contract prices by ten per cent under the Oil for Food programme, and recorded in the books as ordinary costs and fees. In November 2013 three Weatherford subsidiaries agreed to plead guilty and the group entered deferred prosecution agreements, paying 252,690,606 dollars in all. The group's corrupt conduct in Africa, described in the same filings, names no country or body.
inside: An oilfield supplier paid secret ten per cent kickbacks into Iraq's government on contracts with its oil ministry, which kept awarding it equipment work.
cite: US Department of Justice press release, 26 November 2013 (Weatherford FCPA resolution)

n: Contractor's house for Boisoara's mayor followed 4.9m lei of commune contracts
org_label: SC Electrovalcea SRL and SC Marvelov SRL
who: two companies controlled by Ovidiu Eugen Ciogescu
rank: mayor of the commune of Boisoara, Valcea county
d: Between 2006 and 2010 Petre Popescu, mayor of the commune of Boisoara in Valcea county, awarded two companies controlled by the businessman Ovidiu Eugen Ciogescu public supply and works contracts worth 4,887,872.87 lei, about 1,289,676 euros, in breach of Romania's procurement rules. In 2008 Ciogescu built the mayor a two-storey house in Boisoara, put by prosecutors at 392,664 lei in materials and labour, and gave him an appliance worth 1,079.90 lei; the two signed a false works contract with one of the firms to hide it. Bucharest's appeal court convicted Popescu of taking bribes and Ciogescu of giving them on 16 February 2015, finally, with three and two years in prison and 170,581.72 lei confiscated.
inside: A contractor built the mayor a house, and the mayor's town hall kept awarding that contractor's firms the commune's supply and works contracts.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 233/VIII/3 of 12 April 2011 and conviction release on decision 254/A of 16 February 2015

n: Split invoices and a Chrysler for Calafat's mayor cost the city 403,000 euros
rank: mayor of the municipality of Calafat
d: Between 2008 and 2011 Mircea-Marinel Guta, mayor of Calafat and its principal spending officer, repeatedly bought goods and materials with city funds by direct award from companies run by the businessman Constantin Coman. Coman supplied invoices broken down into components while delivering finished goods, which kept each purchase under the legal threshold for direct awards and allowed prices above the market and the figures listed on Romania's public procurement platform. Prosecutors put the loss to Calafat's budget at 403,041.93 euros. At the end of 2008 Guta demanded and received a Chrysler car from Coman in return for using his decision-making power inside the town hall for Coman's firms. Craiova's appeal court convicted both on 23 May 2018; Guta got four years and eleven months.
inside: A supplier gave the mayor a car and split invoices, and the town hall bought from that supplier by direct award at inflated prices.
