cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 1082/VIII/3 of 18 July 2014 and conviction release on decision 777 of 23 May 2018

n: Unicarm's 59,000 lei bought a building permit from Beius's mayor
who: SC Unicarm SRL and its administrator Vasile Lucut
rank: mayor of the municipality of Beius, Bihor county
d: Romania's National Anticorruption Directorate sent Adrian Nicolae Domocos, mayor of Beius in Bihor county, to trial on 10 March 2015. Prosecutors allege that between 14 October 2010 and 26 April 2012 he demanded and received 59,000 lei in four instalments from Vasile Lucut and his company SC Unicarm SRL so that, in breach of his duties, he would unlawfully issue a building permit for a department store in Beius. Lucut and the company were charged with giving the bribe and with helping to launder it; the head of the town hall's planning department was charged with abuse of office. Domocos also faced money-laundering and numerous conflict-of-interest counts. The directorate's page records the referral to court and the presumption of innocence, and publishes no later judgment.
inside: A food company's cash reached the mayor, who then issued the building permit the company needed for its store.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 478/VIII/3 of 10 March 2015

n: Grindu's mayor took a 10 per cent cut on a commune contract he steered
org_label: a businessman's company contracting with Grindu town hall
who: a businessman bidding for commune work
rank: mayor of the commune of Grindu, Ialomita county
d: Prosecutors opened a criminal case against Costel Vieriu, mayor of the commune of Grindu in Ialomita county, and detained him on 29 November 2018. They say that during 2017 he demanded from a businessman, a witness in the case, a commission of ten per cent of the invoices to be issued under a contract the man's company meant to sign with Grindu town hall. Once he had made sure the firm won the contract, Vieriu received 41,000 lei in two instalments. In a similar context and for the same reason he asked the same person for a fifteen per cent commission and took 30,000 lei on 29 November 2018, when he was caught in the act. Bucharest's tribunal placed him under house arrest for thirty days.
inside: A contractor paid the mayor a percentage of its invoices, and the mayor made sure the commune's contract went to that contractor.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 878/VIII/3 of 3 December 2018

n: Paving and 61,554 lei from a town hall contractor reached 1 Decembrie's mayor
org_label: a company in contractual relations with 1 Decembrie town hall
who: a company contracting with the commune
rank: mayor of the commune of 1 Decembrie, Ilfov county
d: Romania's National Anticorruption Directorate placed Gheorghe Petre, mayor of the commune of 1 Decembrie in Ilfov county, under judicial control on 5 November 2019. Prosecutors say that between 29 April and 17 September 2016 he directly demanded, and then received, 61,554 lei in cash and paving worth 79,201 lei from the administrator of a company that was in contractual relations with the town hall, in connection with acts that fell within or ran against his official duties, over the course of those dealings. He was barred from entering the town hall or acting as mayor. The company administrator agreed a guilty plea to two counts of bribe-giving and was convicted of them, finally, on 9 June 2020, receiving two years suspended.
inside: A company working for the commune gave the mayor cash and paving while its contracts with his town hall ran on.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, releases 864/VIII/3 of 6 November 2019, 72/VIII/3 of 7 February 2020 and the conviction release on sentence 265 of 26 March 2020

n: Buzau county chief took 95,000 lei for two direct-award strategy contracts
org_label: Asociatia pentru Dezvoltare, Inovatie, Cultura si Antreprenoriat (ADICA) Calarasi
rank: president of the Buzau County Council
d: Marian Cristinel Bigiu, president of the Buzau County Council, asked for money and on 20 December 2013 and 6 December 2014 received 45,000 lei and 50,000 lei through intermediaries in connection with his duties: approving the direct award to the Calarasi-based Association for Development, Innovation, Culture and Entrepreneurship of two contracts to draft the first parts of Buzau county's sustainable development strategy for 2014 to 2020, and approving the payments once the work was accepted. The association's director, Gabriela Camelia Badica, paid the first 45,000 lei and was convicted of bribe-giving, finally, on 24 September 2015. Bucharest's appeal court convicted Bigiu on 16 December 2016, finally, of taking bribes, conflict of interest and attempted money laundering, with five years and two months in prison.
inside: A consultancy paid the county council's president, who approved the direct award of its two strategy contracts and then the payments for them.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 188/VIII/3 of 2 February 2015 and conviction releases on decisions 1199 of 24 September 2015 and 1883/A of 16 December 2016

n: Ghimbav's mayor bought overpriced goods from one businessman's firms
rank: mayor and chief accountant of the town of Ghimbav, Brasov county
d: Romania's National Anticorruption Directorate sent Dorel Toma, mayor of the town of Ghimbav in Brasov county, to trial on 14 August 2018. Prosecutors allege that from 2008 to 2017 he ordered purchases of goods, services and works from companies controlled by the businessman Fluture Goman and three others at overvalued prices, by direct award, splitting contracts to stay under the legal thresholds, and that the town hall's chief accountant, Ana-Alina Geogean, signed the payment orders without the required approvals or supporting documents. Between 12 September 2008 and 27 May 2010 she received 81,700 lei from Goman in five instalments, directly or through her husband. The alleged loss to Ghimbav's budget is 20,341,753 lei, with 8,462,175 lei said to have been laundered afterwards.
inside: A businessman paid the town hall's chief accountant, and Ghimbav's mayor and accountant kept buying from his firms at inflated prices.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 676/VIII/3 of 14 August 2018

n: Cracolici clan steered Cortale's tenders with a councillor's help
rank: municipal councillor and head of the technical-maintenance office, Comune di Cortale
d: Carabinieri arrested nine people at Cortale, in Calabria, on 18 June 2026 in operation Artemis. Investigators describe Domenico Cracolici as the undisputed head of the 'ndrina operating around Cortale, Maida, Jacurso and Maierato. The Catanzaro antimafia prosecutors say the clan infiltrated the comune's public contracts through unfaithful staff inside its offices, and that Cracolici influenced three forestry tenders called by Cortale from 2022 onwards, hunting for a puppet firm, threatening or dissuading rival bidders and letting the first two rounds go unfilled before a company traceable to him won. He also allegedly disturbed two school-meal auctions. Among those arrested are the municipal councillor Francesco Feroleto and Giuseppe Vinci, head of the technical-maintenance office.
inside: A Calabrian clan had a serving councillor and the comune's technical chief on hand, and the town's forestry and canteen contracts went to its front firms.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 18 June 2026, on the Catanzaro DDA's operation Artemis

n: Altomonte council dissolved over a crime-linked businessman's hold on it
rank: mayor, an assessore, a councillor and a senior employee of the Comune di Altomonte
d: On 20 November 2025 Italy's Council of Ministers dissolved the council of Altomonte, in Calabria, and put the comune under a three-member commission for eighteen months. The prefect of Cosenza reported on 10 September 2025 that there were concrete, consistent and significant elements of direct and indirect links between local administrators and mafia-type organised crime. The interior ministry's report centres on a businessman described as notoriously tied to local organised crime, already under five years of special surveillance and asset confiscation. A councillor had been his business partner until September 2023. The report also records that an assessore put forward two names for hire by the company holding a municipal service contract, both said to be tied to Altomonte's organised crime.
inside: A businessman tied to a local mafia group shaped the town hall's business, and an assessore had his associates hired by the firm holding a council contract.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 7 January 2026, on the interior ministry's report and the dissolution decree of 20 November 2025

n: Corigliano Rossano's mayor held over an alleged mafia electoral pact
rank: mayor and a city councillor of Corigliano-Rossano
d: On 28 October 2026 carabinieri carried out 41 precautionary measures ordered by Catanzaro's investigating judge against an alleged 'ndrangheta association in the Sibaritide, split between a Corigliano cosca and an Acri cosca and operating under the locale of Ciro. Among the charges is political-mafia electoral exchange between members of the criminal group active at Rossano and administrators in office at the Comune di Corigliano-Rossano, at the municipal elections of 8 and 9 June 2024. The mayor, Flavio Stasi, was placed under house arrest, as was the city councillor Piero Lucisano. The investigation began in 2021 from the statements of collaborators with justice, and the other charges include mafia association, three murders, extortion and migrant smuggling.
inside: Prosecutors allege a Calabrian clan traded votes with people running for the comune, and the mayor and a councillor took office on that pact.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 28 October 2026, on the Catanzaro DDA's operation in the Sibaritide

n: Soriano Calabro dissolved a third time over clan interference in its contracts
who: the local 'ndrangheta clan at Soriano Calabro
rank: mayor, councillors and staff of the Comune di Soriano Calabro
d: Italy's interior minister dissolved the council of Soriano Calabro, in Calabria, on 28 April 2026, the comune's third dissolution after 2007 and 2022. His report says forms of 'ndrangheta interference were found that compromised the administration's impartiality and the running of its services. It records an alleged attack on a rival candidate by local mafia figures during the 2024 campaign and the presence of such people, some not resident in the town, near polling stations. It also lists suspect awards: water-network maintenance to a firm with inadvisable family ties that appears to have used an unauthorised subcontract, a school-canteen contract funded by the recovery plan, and a confiscated asset assigned without a complete antimafia check. Mayor Antonino De Nardo, elected in June 2024, has never been investigated.
inside: A local clan is said to have pressed its weight on the 2024 vote and on the comune's awards, which went to firms tied to people around it.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 22 May 2026, on the interior ministry's report behind the dissolution of 28 April 2026

n: Scilla's beach concessions ran through the comune for clan-linked firms
rank: mayor, a councillor, assessori and technical-office staff of the Comune di Scilla
d: Italy's interior minister dissolved the council of Scilla, on the Calabrian coast, setting out why in a report published in May 2023. Seaside tourism is the local cosche's main business, and the report says they held maritime state concessions through front companies, counting on the compliance of the comune's offices and above all its technical office. Mayor Pasqualino Ciccone, who resigned on 28 September 2022 after the operation Nuova Linea, is accused of political electoral exchange for accepting the promise of votes from the local 'ndrangheta in return for guaranteeing concessions of public property. The councillor Girolamo Paladino allegedly obtained votes controlled by a cosca figure and was treated as the clans' reference administrator for concessions.
inside: A coastal clan got its votes, firms and informants inside Scilla's town hall, which handed its beach concessions to companies fronting for the cosca.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 9 May 2023, on the interior ministry's report dissolving the comune and the Nuova Linea investigation

n: Tropea's council dissolved after service contracts went to crime-linked firms
rank: mayor, administrators and employees of the Comune di Tropea
d: Italy's Council of Ministers dissolved the council of Tropea, a tourist town in Calabria, on 23 April 2024. The prefect of Vibo Valentia's proposal found alterations of the administration's work across many areas, largely to the advantage of people connected directly or indirectly with the criminal groups dominant in the area, and concrete elements linking members of the elected bodies to local organised crime. Several firms holding comune service contracts had such links and the administrators never acted to correct how the work was awarded, in a field the mayor admitted intervening in himself. Public lighting and sewerage work went out by sub-threshold direct award without the required rotation. The Council of State upheld the decree on 2 February 2026.
inside: Firms tied to the local clans held the comune's service contracts, and the administration kept awarding them directly instead of putting a stop to it.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 17 May 2024, on the prefect's dissolution proposal; and 2 February 2026 on the Council of State ruling

n: Simeri Crichi dissolved after works went to a cosca-linked family firm
rank: mayor, a tourism assessore and a sitting assessore of the Comune di Simeri Crichi
d: Two Catanzaro antimafia investigations, Basso Profilo and Coccodrillo, converged on the comune of Simeri Crichi in Calabria, and the interior ministry proposed dissolving its council in 2021. The access commission described relations between administrators and the local criminal groups, and a distorted use of public business in favour of people and firms linked directly or indirectly to criminal circles. The tourism assessore, arrested in Basso Profilo, was said to be the leading figure of a hamlet at the centre of those groups' business interests. A family business group close to the cosche took more than 730,000 euros of commune work, including road maintenance, with the technical office later approving a variance that raised the price.
inside: Clan-linked businessmen had the assessore and the technical office they needed, and the comune's road and service work went to their firms.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 2 October 2021, on the access commission's report and the interior ministry's dissolution proposal

n: Guardavalle dissolved over direct awards to a Gallace-linked businessman
rank: mayor, elected and administrative staff of the Comune di Guardavalle
d: Italy's president decreed the dissolution of the council of Guardavalle, in Calabria, in March 2021, putting it under commissioners for eighteen months. The interior minister's report, drawing on the Catanzaro prefecture's antimafia access, found the political and bureaucratic sides of the administration conditioned in the award of works, goods and services: numerous direct awards to companies in fact run by a man close to the local cosche, some going back to the current mayor's first term, artificial splitting of public commissions, and unjustified use of extreme-urgency procedures. Three of those companies were later hit with antimafia interdictions. A statue of the patron saint donated by the Gallace cosca stood outside the town hall; the mayor voiced fears for his safety about removing it.
inside: A businessman close to the Gallace cosca ran firms the comune kept awarding work to directly, with no checks and outside public tender.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 18 March 2021, on the interior minister's report and the dissolution decree

n: Stefanaconi dissolved over its mayor's ties to two convicted businessmen
who: the D'Amico cousins and the Vibo 'ndrangheta
rank: mayor of Stefanaconi and the comune's awarding offices
d: Italy dissolved the comune of Stefanaconi, in Calabria, on 25 July 2024. The interior minister's report found a direct link with organised crime and the contiguity of mayor Salvatore Solano with his businessmen cousins Giuseppe and Antonio D'Amico, sentenced to thirty and eighteen years in the Petrolmafie trial against the Vibo 'ndrangheta. Giuseppe D'Amico gave Solano explicit support at the provincial elections of 31 October 2018, and was recorded putting illicit pressure on councillors and mayors to vote for his cousin. Solano was given one year suspended for electoral corruption, the judges excluding the mafia aggravation. The report also lists 82 direct awards to firms absent from the white lists, nineteen of them with problems.
inside: A convicted 'ndrangheta businessman pressed councillors and mayors to elect his cousin, who as mayor awarded work to firms outside the antimafia white lists.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 11 September 2024, on the interior minister's report; and 27 June 2025 on the regional court ruling

n: Appeal court barred two Lamezia councillors backed by a cosca
rank: vice-president of the city council and a city councillor of Lamezia Terme
d: Lamezia Terme's council, in Calabria, was dissolved for mafia infiltration in November 2017. On 6 November 2019 Catanzaro's appeal court confirmed a ruling barring from office Giuseppe Paladino, former vice-president of the city council, and Pasqualino Ruberto, a councillor who had stood for mayor in 2015. The judges held the conditioning of the administration proved both in the shaping of electoral consent and in the impartiality of its work, citing the electoral support the Cerra-Torcasio-Gualtieri cosca gave the two candidates. They described cosche still conditioning wide sectors of the administration through administrators they trusted, and contracts going to firms of mafia reputation. The court rejected the request to bar the former mayor, Paolo Mascaro.
inside: A Lamezia cosca put its electoral weight behind two men who took council seats, and the comune's contracts circled among a few favoured firms.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 6 November 2019, on the Catanzaro appeal court ruling

n: Farm companies paid the APIA deputy director who cleared their subsidy claims
org_label: farming companies run by Traian Grigore and others
rank: deputy executive director, Tulcea county centre, Agency for Payments and Intervention in Agriculture
d: Romania's Agency for Payments and Intervention in Agriculture pays out area-based farm subsidies. Prosecutors charged Cristina Gherghisan, deputy executive director of its Tulcea county centre, with three counts of taking bribes in the autumn of 2014: 5,000 lei and later an envelope of cash from Traian Grigore, goods from Mariana Rece and a smartphone from Toader Sandu, all administrators or partners in companies. The indictment says she acted so that their firms would get the authorisations and approvals the agency had to give them to draw subsidies on the farmland they worked. Constanta's appeal court convicted her of taking bribes on 8 June 2017, finally, with three years and six months in prison, and Grigore of giving them, with two years and six months suspended. Rece and Sandu were acquitted.
inside: Farm companies paid the official inside the state subsidy agency who had to approve their claims, and the approvals came through.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 1042/VIII/3 of 11 June 2015 and the conviction release on decision 627 of 8 June 2017

n: Fertiliser for the Mures agriculture director delayed a GM soya check
org_label: a farming company run by Ioan Pop
who: a farming company run by Ioan Pop
rank: executive director, Mures County Directorate for Agriculture
d: Romania's National Anticorruption Directorate sent Liviu Timar, executive director of the Mures County Directorate for Agriculture, to trial on 11 February 2015 on five counts of taking bribes and three of receiving undue benefits. Prosecutors say that between 2012 and 2014 the directorate carried out seven checks at a company run by Ioan Pop, and that Timar received from its administrator 34,000 kilograms of fertiliser, 184 litres of pesticide and seven sacks of maize seed worth 88,366 lei in all. The goods were given for the improper exercise of his duties and to delay checks meant to establish whether the firm grew genetically modified soya, which would let Pop harvest the crop first.
inside: A farming company's fertiliser and pesticide reached the head of the county agriculture directorate, who then held back the checks on its soya crop.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 268/VIII/3 of 11 February 2015

n: Laureana di Borrello's assessore convicted as the Ferrentino-Chindamo clan's man
rank: municipal assessore of Laureana di Borrello
d: The Lex trial before the tribunal of Palmi, in Calabria, ended on 24 October 2020 with seventeen convictions and twelve acquittals. It grew out of a carabinieri operation against the Ferrentino-Chindamo and Lamari cosche of Laureana di Borrello, which had brought 40 arrests in November 2016. Alongside mafia association and drug trafficking, the charges covered the clan's relations with the comune of Laureana di Borrello, where it managed to take hold of contracts and works that were then assigned to firms traceable to the bosses. The municipal assessore Vincenzo Laina, held to be the clan's political reference, was sentenced to five years for external complicity in mafia association. This was the first-instance judgment.
inside: A clan had the town's assessore as its political reference, and the comune's contracts went to companies traceable to its bosses.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 24 October 2020, on the Palmi tribunal's judgment in the Lex trial

n: Road contractor paid a tenth of its contracts to Caras-Severin's deputy chief
org_label: a road-maintenance company holding Caras-Severin county contracts
rank: vice-president of the Caras-Severin County Council
d: Ionesie Ghiorghioni, vice-president of the Caras-Severin County Council in Romania, demanded and took 230,000 lei and 8,400 euros from a businessman between 2013 and May 2015, a ten per cent share of public utility contracts for road maintenance that the man's company held with the council. In return, prosecutors said, the firm was favoured: the contracts were awarded to it, the council's property administration directorate paid it ahead of others, and officials of the same institution accepted and signed its works estimates. A further 30,000 lei, a tenth of two December 2014 snow-clearing contracts, was handed over in two parts, the second in a sting. Timisoara's appeal court convicted both on 18 February 2016, finally.
inside: A road contractor paid the county council's deputy chief a tenth of its contracts, and the council awarded, paid and signed off its work first.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 1006/VIII/3 of June 2015 and the conviction release on decision 213 of 18 February 2016

n: Agriculture ministry chiefs demanded 40,000 euros from their events firm
org_label: the company organising the ministry's agricultural events
who: an events company holding a ministry contract
rank: secretary general and a state secretary, Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development
d: Romania's National Anticorruption Directorate opened criminal action on 8 January 2015 against Virgil-Laurentiu Gaman, secretary general of the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development, and Peter Tamas Nagy, a state secretary in the same ministry, over bribery, and against two company administrators as accomplices. Prosecutors say that in October 2014, in connection with an act within their official duties over the staging of agricultural events, the two officials demanded 40,000 euros from the management of the firm organising them. The sum was part of the 414,160 euros the firm was owed under its contract with the ministry, and was to be routed to the two men through a company they approved.
inside: Two senior officials in the agriculture ministry demanded a cut of the contract held by the firm staging the ministry's own events, routed through companies they chose.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 54/VIII/3 of January 2015

n: Home-care firms drew 20m lei from Bucharest's health insurance house
org_label: home medical care companies in Bucharest
rank: president of the National Health Insurance House and the leadership of its Bucharest house
d: Romania's National Health Insurance House pays for care under the state health insurance scheme. On 13 July 2018 the National Anticorruption Directorate sent 90 defendants to trial, among them people from the leadership of the national house and of its Bucharest house and officials of both, together with home medical care companies. Prosecutors say more than 20 million lei, about 4.5 million euros, was taken from the Bucharest house's funds through the unlawful reimbursement of fictitious home care between 2016 and August 2017. Those charged include the national house's president Marian Burcea, the head of its anti-fraud monitoring directorate, two successive presidents of the Bucharest house and the head of its home-care programmes service.
inside: Home-care companies had the insurance house's own managers and clerks signing off visits that never happened, and the fund paid them for it.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, releases 866/VIII/3 of 1 September 2017 and 598/VIII/3 of 13 July 2018

n: 2.7m euros was meant for the minister behind Romania's Microsoft deal
org_label: the D-CON.NET consortium of IT firms
who: the favoured consortium of IT licence resellers
rank: Minister of Communications and the Information Society
d: Romania's state Microsoft licensing contract was moved to the Ministry of Communications in 2008, and the earlier framework agreement with Fujitsu Siemens Computers lapsed on 26 April 2009. Prosecutors say that in the spring of 2009 the businessman Dorin Cocos, the mayor of Piatra Neamt Gheorghe Stefan and the communications minister Gabriel Sandu met over what would follow, and that Cocos then demanded 9,000,000 euros for himself, 3,996,360 euros for Gheorghe Stefan and 2,700,000 euros for the minister, so that firms backed by a businessman would win the 2009 Microsoft licensing contract. Cocos received 9,000,000 dollars through an intermediary from the account of D-CON.NET, which led the favoured group of firms.
inside: Prosecutors allege resellers' money was shared out to the communications minister and his go-betweens so his ministry would award them the state's Microsoft licences.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, releases 1512/VIII/3 of 28 October 2014 and 162/VIII/3 of 29 January 2015

n: A flat's refit for Romania's environment minister, then tender favours
org_label: SC Lescaci Com SRL and SC Azimut Com SRL
who: two contractors bidding for water works
rank: Minister of Environment and Forests
d: Romania's anti-corruption prosecutors asked, in February 2015, for the Chamber of Deputies to be approached for permission to investigate Laszlo Borbely, a sitting deputy and former Minister of Environment and Forests, over three counts of trading in influence. They allege that during 2011, as minister, he received from Ioan Ciocan, administrator of SC Lescaci Com SRL, the renovation and fitting out of a flat worth 80,952 lei, so that he would use his influence over officials of the National Administration Apele Romane, a body coordinated by his ministry, to favour that company at the tenders its basin administrations ran. The Chamber had refused an earlier request on 11 September 2012, and the High Court confirmed the reopening in 2015.
inside: Two water contractors are said to have refitted the environment minister's flat so he would lean on the state water body that ran their tenders.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 236/VIII/3 of 5 February 2015

n: Contractors paid a tenth to Romania's regional development minister
org_label: SC Termogaz Company SA, SC Consmin SA and SC Europlus Computers SRL
rank: Minister of Regional Development and Tourism, her secretary general and personal adviser
d: Prosecutors charged Elena-Gabriela Udrea, Romania's Minister of Regional Development and Tourism, on 1 April 2015 over the handling of public funds at her ministry between 2010 and 2012. They said she ran a system in which the people closest to her, her personal adviser, her personal assistant, the ministry's secretary general and the head of the National Investment Company, took money from company representatives, with her knowledge, to guarantee that works financed by the ministry were paid on time. In 2010 the brothers Adrian and Miron Gardean transferred 695,367.06 lei through fictitious contracts to a company controlled by her adviser, a tenth of the ministry's payments under the Ski for Romania programme.
inside: Builders paid a tenth of their money to the minister's circle, and the ministry released the payments on their state-funded works on time.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 748/VIII/3 of 1 April 2015 and the conviction release on High Court decision 93 of 5 June 2018

n: Nine Isola Capo Rizzuto administrators barred after the council's dissolution
who: Arena cosca and allied groups of Isola Capo Rizzuto
rank: mayor, deputy mayor, an assessore and councillors of Isola Capo Rizzuto
d: Italy's president dissolved the council of Isola Capo Rizzuto, in Calabria, on 24 November 2017, and on 23 May 2018 Crotone's civil court barred nine of its administrators from standing again. The prefect's report found the administration's impartiality compromised and local administrators easing the work of one of the 'ndrangheta's most powerful groups. Mayor Gianluca Bruno had been reported for external complicity in mafia association for making himself available to the cosca leaders Antonio Poerio, Fernando Poerio and Leonardo Sacco as the institutional figure able to secure the Misericordia confraternity control of the contracts serving the CARA migrant centre. Municipal contracts went repeatedly to the same firms by rotation, among them office cleaning awarded from July 2014 to a company run by the niece of an alleged cosca affiliate.
inside: A clan had the mayor and councillors it needed, and the comune's contracts circled among firms tied to its people.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 23 May 2018, on the Crotone tribunal's ineligibility ruling and the interior ministry's report

n: Kataib Hezbollah and Badr men hold the Iraqi PMF's command posts
who: Kataib Hezbollah and the Badr Organization
rank: PMF military commander, chief of operations, and heads of the intelligence, internal security, training and religious instruction directorates
d: The Popular Mobilization Forces are a state-funded, state-paid part of Iraq's armed forces, which the law places under the prime minister's authority. A CTC Sentinel study by Michael Knights and co-authors reports that by 2020 the PMF's civilian and military leadership and its most powerful directorates had become dominated by Kataib Hezbollah and Badr leadership figures with long ties to Iran's Revolutionary Guard, and that Badr-origin members still occupy the posts of military commander, chief of operations and head of the intelligence, internal security, training and religious instruction directorates. The authors say the PMF's military commander, Abdal-Aziz al-Mohammadawi, publicly admitted taking orders primarily from Iran's then Supreme Leader.
inside: Two armed movements hold the top command and directorate posts of Iraq's state-funded militia force, and its commander says he waits on Iran's leader.
cite: Michael Knights and co-authors, 'Standing with Iran: the integrated combat performance of Iraqi militias during Operation Epic Fury', CTC Sentinel, 2026

n: Half of Iraq's PMF brigades backed designated groups in the 2026 war
who: Iraqi muqawama militias, including Kataib Hezbollah and Badr
rank: 36 of about 65 to 70 brigades of the Popular Mobilization Forces; PMF trucking fleets and cantonments
d: The Popular Mobilization Forces are paid and housed by the Iraqi state. In the 2026 war, a CTC Sentinel study assesses that 36 PMF brigades either launched weapons at United States forces, Iraqi civilians and infrastructure, or neighbouring states, or provided material support to the groups doing so, including the US-designated Kataib Hezbollah; with about 65 to 70 brigades in existence, the authors say this means half or more have members supporting designated groups. They describe extensive use of the PMF's cantonments and compounds, and say the Badr Organization was the main land transport provider through its control of PMF trucking fleets, its key logistics unit being PMF 27.
inside: Armed movements inside Iraq's state militia force used its brigades, depots and lorry fleets for a war Iraq's government had not declared.
cite: Michael Knights and co-authors, 'Standing with Iran: the integrated combat performance of Iraqi militias during Operation Epic Fury', CTC Sentinel, 2026

n: Libya's premier put an armed group leader over a joint operations room
rank: Head of the Joint Operations Room for the defence of the western and south-western region
d: On 29 October 2023 the prime minister of Libya's Government of National Unity, Abdelhamid Dbeibah, issued a decision forming a Joint Operations Room for the defence of the western and south-western region, bringing together seven brigades, eight battalions and twelve security and military agencies to deter the groups responsible for attacks in Gharyan. The United Nations Panel of Experts on Libya records in its timeline of the Ras El-Jdir border crisis that Abdelsalam Zobi, who leads the 111 Brigade armed group, was appointed head of that operations room. Two weeks later the acting interior minister appointed him to head a related force securing the western border with Tunisia.
inside: An armed group's commander was given formal command of a state operations room over seven brigades and twelve security agencies in western Libya.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2024/914, annex 16, table 16.1 ('Ras El-Jdir border crisis timeline'), entries for 29 October and 15 November 2023

n: Libya's Presidency Council took the Radaa militia under its own command
org_label: Special Deterrence Force (Radaa), Nawasi Brigade and Ghenewa militia
who: Special Deterrence Force and allied Tripoli militias
rank: Special Deterrence Force, placed under the direct control of the Presidency Council by decree 578
d: The Presidency Council was Libya's collective head of state in Tripoli. On 1 September 2020 it brought the Special Deterrence Force, an armed group that ran its own prisons, under its direct control by decree 578. The United Nations Panel of Experts on Libya recorded increased consolidation of armed groups or their leaders under the Council's direct authority, and found that continued infiltration of state institutions by armed groups, in particular the Nawasi Brigade, Ghenewa and the Special Deterrence Force, unduly legitimises these groups and fosters competition within the security structure. The Panel also reported that a common method used by armed groups is blackmail with recordings to obtain coveted government positions.
inside: Tripoli militias were written into the state's own security structure by decree, and the Panel says some used blackmail to win the posts.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2021/229, paras. 8-9 and annex 6 ('Continued encroachment of armed groups on state institutions'), para. 3

n: Armed groups took over security at Libya's electoral commission offices
rank: High National Electoral Commission premises and municipal election security arrangements
d: The High National Electoral Commission runs Libya's elections. The United Nations Panel of Experts on Libya identified sixteen incidents before the second round of municipal elections in August 2025, all involving armed actors under the de facto authority of armed groups. It found that armed groups were directly or heavily involved in the day-to-day running of local authorities, including by fielding their own candidates and lists, while playing a key role in organising the elections by providing security arrangements. After attacks on commission premises in Zliten, Zawiya and Al-Sahel al-Gharbi, armed groups positioned themselves to provide security for those premises. The Panel concluded the commission could not function independently.
inside: Armed groups both fielded candidates and supplied the guards on the offices of Libya's election commission, which then could not act independently.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224, annex 15 ('Acts that obstruct or undermine the successful completion of the political transition in Libya'), paras. 3 and 5-8

n: Iraqi militias got use of water ministry sites and vehicles for weapons
rank: Ministry of Water Resources premises and vehicles, and municipality locations, in Baghdad, Diyala and Nineveh
d: Iraq's Ministry of Water Resources runs dams, canals and irrigation. In a CTC Sentinel study of the 2026 war, Michael Knights writes that interview data gathered across Baghdad, Diyala and Nineveh provinces repeatedly mentioned drones and missiles being stored and distributed using Ministry of Water Resources and municipality locations and vehicles, access to which the militias had obtained. The authors link this to the known practice of caching weapons at sites protected from air attack by international humanitarian law, and note video from Houthi-held Yemen showing water-tanker disguises on missile launchers. The interviews ran from 2023 to 2026 and the authors withheld exact dates, names and places at the interviewees' request.
inside: Militias obtained the use of a government ministry's yards and lorries to hide and move missiles, sheltering them behind the ministry's civilian status.
cite: Michael Knights and co-authors, 'Standing with Iran: the integrated combat performance of Iraqi militias during Operation Epic Fury', CTC Sentinel, 2026, endnote cv

n: Sana'a University journalism head replaced by a Houthi appointee
rank: Head of the journalism department, Faculty of Mass Communication, Sana'a University
d: Sana'a University is Yemen's main state university. The United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen annexed a circular published on 17 July 2023 by a Houthi-affiliated Student Forum which, the annex says, had reportedly replaced the university's Students Union. It told students of the Faculty of Mass Communication that the academic year would begin on 22 July with three days a week set aside for male students and three for female students. Students and professors objected. Reportedly, the head of the journalism department, Dr Samia Al-Aghbary, was removed from her post over her disagreement and was replaced by the Houthi-appointed Dr Ali Hussein Hassan Al-Ammar.
inside: A Houthi-run student body issued orders inside a state university, and the academic who objected was replaced by the movement's own appointee.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, S/2023/833, annex 83 ('Houthis' gender segregation policy: the case of the Faculty of Mass Communication of Sana'a University'), paras. 1-4

n: Laudani clan and an INPS official ran 500 fake farm-labour claims
rank: Official at the INPS counter in Giarre, National Social Security Institute
d: INPS is Italy's national social security institute, which pays unemployment benefit to farm labourers. In Operation Podere mafioso, announced on 29 March 2017 after two years of investigation, the Guardia di Finanza made seventeen arrests over what investigators described as a pact between men of the Catania Laudani clan and officials of public bodies to run 500 bogus agricultural hirings through ten shell companies, taking about 1.5 million euros from INPS. Investigators named Filippo Bucolo, an INPS employee at the Giarre counter, as the heart of the system, accusing him of supplying confidential information on pending claims and speeding them up for money.
inside: Prosecutors say a mafia clan paid an official inside Italy's benefits agency, who then pushed through claims for 500 labourers who did not exist.
cite: LiveSicilia, 29 March 2017 (Guardia di Finanza operation) and 28 September 2017 (review court decision on Bucolo)

n: Trucking-school brokers paid California DMV staff for lorry licences
org_label: California commercial driver's licence bribery ring
who: Truck driving school owners acting as brokers
rank: Licensing registration examiners and motor vehicle representatives, California Department of Motor Vehicles offices in Sacramento and Salinas
d: The California Department of Motor Vehicles tests and licences drivers. Federal prosecutors in Sacramento found that between June 2011 and March 2015 three owners of truck driving schools acted as brokers, taking money from people who wanted a Class A commercial licence without passing the required written and driving tests, and used it to bribe DMV employees to enter false passing results in the department's computer database, so that the DMV issued official licences to unqualified drivers. Court documents indicated the number of licences could run past 100. By November 2022 all twenty defendants charged had been convicted and sentenced, except one who died before trial; the longest sentence was 60 months.
inside: A ring of driving-school owners bought staff inside the state licensing department, which then issued lorry licences to drivers who had passed no test.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of California, 11 August 2015 and 14 November 2022

n: Recruiters paid El Cajon DMV examiners to pass untested drivers
rank: Licensing registration examiners and a supervising manager, California Department of Motor Vehicles offices in El Cajon and Rancho San Diego
d: Federal prosecutors in San Diego charged 31 people over a scheme in which recruiters collected money from licence applicants and paid bribes to employees of two California Department of Motor Vehicles offices in El Cajon, who entered false passing written and driving test scores. Bribes ran from 75 to 600 dollars a licence, and applicants paid recruiters about 400 to 500 dollars for an ordinary licence and typically 2,500 to 3,000 dollars for a commercial one. Jeffrey Bednarek, an examiner at the El Cajon office, admitted producing more than 100 fraudulent permits and licences from April 2009 and was sentenced in 2014 to three years. Thirty of the 31 defendants pleaded guilty; one was a fugitive.
inside: Licence brokers bought examiners inside two state motor vehicle offices, which then certified drivers, including lorry drivers, who had taken no test.
cite: US Attorney, Southern District of California, 11 February 2013 and 5 September 2014

n: Brokers paid Torrance DMV staff to issue licences without tests
rank: Licence registration examiner and office manager, California Department of Motor Vehicles offices in Torrance and Lincoln Park, Los Angeles
d: Federal prosecutors in Los Angeles charged brokers who, between April and October 2016, negotiated cash prices of 400 to 1,400 dollars from people ineligible for a California driving licence, then paid the scheme's ringleader, Antanacio Villegas, a licence registration examiner at the Torrance office of the Department of Motor Vehicles. Villegas recruited other DMV employees, who took cash to record in the department's database that applicants had passed tests they had never taken, after which the department issued the permits and licences. Investigators believe more than 100 licences were issued. Villegas admitted that staff took bribes several times a week and that ineligible applicants were steered to a corrupt employee's window by a signal such as a red hat.
inside: Licence brokers had a ring of paid staff inside two state motor vehicle offices, which issued real driving licences to people who had passed nothing.
cite: US Attorney, Central District of California, 19 May 2021

n: Attorneys' gifts to a DMV hearing officer set aside licence suspensions
org_label: Attorneys and law-firm staff who paid a DMV driver safety officer
who: Six attorneys and their staff or representatives
rank: Driver Safety Officer, California Driver Safety Office, Department of Motor Vehicles
d: A Driver Safety Officer at the California Department of Motor Vehicles presides over hearings that decide whether a driver charged with drink-driving loses their licence. Alva Garrido Benavidez, who had worked there since August 2000, pleaded guilty in February 2015 to conspiracy to accept bribes. She admitted that between 2005 and August 2014 she agreed with six attorneys and six of their staff or representatives to obtain favourable treatment for their clients, taking cash, meals and luxury goods worth more than 5,000 dollars. She admitted stealing arrest packets before the drink-driving records were entered, setting aside licence suspensions, and issuing unauthorised temporary licences. She retired after search warrants were executed.
inside: Law firms paid the official who decided drink-driving licence hearings, and she then set aside suspensions and handed out temporary licences for their clients.
cite: US Attorney, Southern District of California, 3 February 2015

n: Black market in Massachusetts vehicle-inspection licences ran in the RMV
org_label: Vehicle-inspection licence black market around Simon Abou Raad
who: A service-station owner running a market in inspection licences
rank: Project manager for vehicle safety and compliance services and a senior inspector, Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles
d: The Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles licenses the garages that carry out vehicle safety inspections, and with the network at capacity it was granting no new licences from its waiting list. Federal prosecutors charged the registry's project manager for vehicle safety and compliance, Mark LaFrance, a senior inspector, David Gaw, and a service-station owner, Simon Abou Raad, with conspiring to extort money under colour of official right in exchange for inspection licences. Prosecutors alleged LaFrance identified low-volume stations, Abou Raad bought their licences and equipment for about 5,000 to 6,000 dollars and resold them for 50,000 to 75,000, dressing the deals up as mergers with forged paperwork that LaFrance approved. He sold at least ten for about 657,000 dollars.
inside: A garage owner worked with the officials who approve inspection licences, so the registry signed off sham mergers and he sold the licences at a mark-up.
cite: US Attorney, District of Massachusetts, 26 June 2013

n: Ring bribed New York DMV guards to let lorry-licence tests be faked
org_label: New York commercial driver's licence cheating ring
who: A ring selling help to cheat commercial licence exams
rank: Security guards at New York State Department of Motor Vehicles offices in Queens, Long Island and Manhattan
d: New York State's Department of Motor Vehicles issues the commercial licences needed to drive buses and heavy lorries, and applicants must pass written or audio tests. Federal prosecutors in Brooklyn charged eleven people in September 2013 with a conspiracy in which defendants employed as DMV security guards, paid in cash, signalled applicants to walk out of the testing rooms with their uncompleted answer sheets, which accomplices filled in outside before the applicants returned them for marking. Another method was a pencil marked with dots and dashes giving the answers. Applicants paid about 1,500 to 2,500 dollars. The 2013 complaint said over 60 people were helped; a Brooklyn jury convicted five defendants in July 2015 on trial evidence covering over 40.
inside: A cheating ring paid the guards inside state licensing offices, so the state issued bus and lorry licences to applicants who never sat the exam.
cite: US Attorney, Eastern District of New York, 26 September 2013 and 17 July 2015

n: Identity ring had four Haymarket RMV clerks issuing real Massachusetts IDs
org_label: Identity-document ring around Bivian Brea and Angel Tejada
who: A ring selling stolen Puerto Rican identities
rank: Four clerks, Haymarket office, Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles
d: In October 2015 law enforcement received an anonymous letter alleging that a corrupt employee of the Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles was supplying licences to people using false identities. Investigators found four clerks at the registry's Haymarket office in Boston were working with two men who obtained identity documents belonging to United States citizens in Puerto Rico and sold them on, for up to 2,700 dollars an identity, to clients who included people previously deported and one who admitted facing drug charges. The clerks took hundreds of dollars in cash to issue authentic registry licences and identity cards on those identities, and further bribes to run database checks confirming the stolen identities belonged to real people. Five agreed to plead guilty.
inside: A ring selling stolen identities paid four clerks inside the state registry, which then issued genuine licences and ID cards in those stolen names.
cite: US Attorney, District of Massachusetts, 2 August 2017 and 2 October 2017

n: Reggio Calabria preventive-measures judge fed the Valle-Lampada clan
rank: President of the preventive measures section, Tribunale di Reggio Calabria
d: The preventive measures section of an Italian court decides on the seizure of assets from suspected mafia members. Vincenzo Giuseppe Giglio, a judge of the Tribunale di Reggio Calabria, was arrested in November 2011 on charges of corruption, disclosure of official secrets and aggravated aiding, for helping the Valle-Lampada clan of the Calabrian mafia. The prosecutor-general told the Milan appeal court that while he presided over that section Giglio met the clan figure Giulio Lampada several times and, through the former regional councillor Franco Morelli, gave him confidential information on current investigations, obtaining the promise of a management post for his wife at the Vibo Valentia health authority. He was convicted at first instance and sentenced to four years and seven months.
inside: A mafia clan reached the judge who ruled on seizing mafia assets, and got the court's secret information on the investigations into it.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 28 April 2014, on the prosecutor-general's submissions in the Milan appeal of the 'zona grigia' case

n: Pressure through a deputy minister got Kočner his Bratislava ruling
rank: Judge, Bratislava fifth district court; the deputy justice minister who pressed her
d: The Slovak businessman Marian Kočner forged promissory notes saying he had lent nearly 70 million euros in 2000, guaranteed by the television station TV Markíza, and sued the station in 2016. OCCRP, using court documents and messages taken from his phone, reported that he turned to Monika Jankovská, a former judge who had become deputy justice minister, exchanging over 6,000 calls and messages with her in the ten months to his arrest in June 2018. Jankovská had been the mentor and supervisor of Zuzana Maruniaková, the new judge at Bratislava's fifth district court hearing the case. Maruniaková told police she acted under Jankovská's pressure, and on 26 April 2018 ruled the notes genuine. Jankovská publicly denied knowing or communicating with Kočner; OCCRP said the messages showed otherwise.
inside: A businessman used a serving deputy justice minister to lean on the junior judge hearing his case, who then ruled his forged notes genuine.
cite: OCCRP and investigace.cz, 22 February 2021, 'Slovak Businessman Accused of Masterminding Jan Kuciak's Murder Had Judges in the Palm of His Hand'

n: Cosoleto's mayor won on a cosca's votes, then its firms took the works
rank: mayor, deputy mayor, councillors and staff of the Comune di Cosoleto
d: Cosoleto is a small town in Reggio Calabria province. On 23 November 2022 the President of the Republic dissolved its council on the interior minister's report, which drew on the prefect's own report. It says the mayor, a member of the local mafia clan and a council employee "drew up a political-mafia electoral agreement" for the 2018 municipal elections: the clan member promised votes for the mayor's list in exchange for jobs for people the group cared about. The mayor was also committed for trial over dealings with a building firm said to be aimed at steering two public works contracts, with the aggravating purpose of assisting the 'ndrangheta. The report adds that works were awarded directly to several companies whose owners, in some cases, had police records.
inside: A Calabrian mafia clan traded votes for jobs and building work, so the town's awards and hiring served the clan instead of residents.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 22 December 2022, quoting the interior ministry's report and the prefect of Reggio Calabria's report published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale

n: Anzio council dissolved after an 'ndrangheta clan's votes bought town contracts
who: local 'ndrangheta clan on the Rome coast
rank: mayor, deputy mayor, assessori, councillors and staff of the Comune di Anzio
d: Anzio is a coastal town in the province of Rome. Its council was dissolved for 'ndrangheta infiltration on the interior minister's report, published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale. The report says wiretaps from the campaign period showed the local clan gathering votes for the candidate who then won the mayoralty, especially in some polling districts of an outlying area. It also says some members of the giunta, including the deputy mayor, former assessori and council employees, had a standing relationship of interest with leading clan figures, who assured several of them electoral support in exchange for municipal contracts. Annual files for many beach concessions were incomplete and lacked the holders' anti-mafia certificates, and some sewer inspection work went directly to a company traced to a known 'ndrangheta family.
inside: A Calabrian mafia clan delivered votes to Anzio's winning list and was repaid with municipal contracts and beach concessions decided in its favour.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 21 December 2022, quoting the interior minister's report published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale

n: Nettuno dissolved a second time over an 'ndrangheta locale's electoral support
rank: mayor, assessori and councillors of the Comune di Nettuno
d: Nettuno, on the coast south of Rome, had its council dissolved for 'ndrangheta infiltration by presidential decree, the second time after 2005. The interior minister's report says the investigating commission examined the 2019 municipal elections, won by lists tied to the then mayor Alessandro Coppola, and found evidence of "genuine electoral support" from the local 'ndrina for the mayor's slate and for some councillors, including recorded phone contact between Coppola and a man held to be close to local organised crime, and bugged conversations in which councillors and assessori asked people linked to 'ndrangheta families for electoral backing. The report also records irregular free-beach concessions renewed to existing holders, many tied to local criminal groups, and urban plans over land owned by people linked to the 'ndrina.
inside: A Calabrian mafia cell supplied votes to Nettuno's winning councillors, and the town's concessions and planning decisions then favoured people tied to it.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 23 December 2022, quoting the interior minister's report published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale

n: Portigliola's awards went to a cooperative run by a man close to the local cosca
rank: mayor, deputy mayor and technical office of the Comune di Portigliola
d: Portigliola is a village in the province of Reggio Calabria. The interior ministry's report led the President of the Republic to dissolve its council in May 2022 for alleged 'ndrangheta interference, and the Lazio administrative court later rejected the former administration's appeal. The report says the comune's decisions from June 2017 showed repeated irregular awards, including no market research and single quotations, and that numerous awards for sweeping, cleaning and brush-clearing went to a cooperative chaired until five days before the inspectors arrived by a man with adverse police records, living in houses available to the mayor and the deputy mayor. The deputy mayor was said to have close family ties to members of mafia groups, and further awards went to firms later hit with anti-mafia bans.
inside: A Calabrian clan's circle supplied the firm the village paid for its cleaning work, so public money and contracts followed the clan's people.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 25 June 2022, quoting the interior ministry's report; Corriere della Calabria, 24 November 2023, on the Lazio administrative court's ruling

n: Cutro's water service ran for years on direct awards to a cosca-linked firm
rank: mayor, council and the public works, planning and enforcement offices of the Comune di Cutro
d: Cutro, in the province of Crotone, had its council dissolved on 22 July 2020, and the reasons were published as an annex to the Gazzetta Ufficiale. The prefect of Crotone's report says the commission found that between 2016 and 2019, of 39 procedures for water and sewage services, 36 were direct awards without tender and 30 went to the same operator, which took 571,182.80 euros of a total 742,852.22 euros. The firm's owner is related by marriage to a close relative of the head of the dominant cosca, and papers from the investigation called "Thomas" described the firm as entirely at the cosche's disposal. It also records people known to police and traceable to local mafia cosche at some 2016 campaign rallies of Salvatore Divuono, who was then elected mayor.
inside: A Calabrian clan's firm held the town's water service through repeated no-tender awards, so public money ran through a business the clan controlled.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 27 September 2020, quoting the dissolution reasons annexed to Gazzetta Ufficiale no. 239 and the prefect of Crotone's report

n: Cassano allo Ionio kept paying a firm four months after its anti-mafia ban
rank: mayor, giunta and council of the Comune di Cassano allo Ionio
d: Cassano allo Ionio, in Cosenza province, was dissolved for mafia infiltration in 2017. In June 2019 the Council of State rejected the appeal of former mayor Gianni Papasso and other members of the dissolved giunta and council, finding that the Cassano cosche had "penetrated, through relationships of various kinds, inside the decision-making organs of the comune". It singles out work awarded to Garofalo Group, owned by a close relative of the then council president, including a no-tender award on 9 August 2016, four months after the firm received an anti-mafia ban. It also found welfare payments handed out at will, a proportionally significant number to signatories of lists backing the mayor and at least one beneficiary linked to local cosche, and inaction over illegal building favouring leading local 'ndrangheta figures.
inside: Calabrian clans reached inside the town's decision-making, which kept paying a banned clan-linked firm and spread public money to the mayor's backers.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 17 June 2019, quoting the Council of State judgment upholding the dissolution

n: Limbadi's school meals and gardening went to firms close to the Mancuso clan
rank: mayor, giunta and administrative staff of the Comune di Limbadi
d: Limbadi, in the province of Vibo Valentia, is the Mancuso clan's stronghold. On the prefect Guido Longo's report the Council of Ministers dissolved it in 2018, finding "concrete, unambiguous and significant evidence of direct and indirect links between local administrators and mafia-type organised crime". The summary records gardening work worth more than 50,000 euros awarded without market search to a company flagged by the mayor himself, whose owners had police and criminal records; a school meals contract for 2015-16 left running for a year because the comune did not send the prefecture the papers needed for checks, which ended in an anti-mafia ban; and the next year's meals contract awarded directly to a sole trader whose owner belonged to a family carrying various offences, including associative ones.
inside: A Calabrian clan's circle supplied the firms Limbadi paid for school meals and public works, so the town's contracts kept the clan's businesses alive.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 15 May 2018, quoting the interior ministry summary sent to the Council of Ministers and the prefect of Vibo Valentia's report

n: Castellammare di Stabia dissolved again over 18m euros of direct awards
rank: mayor, council president, councillors and technical office of the Comune di Castellammare di Stabia
d: Castellammare di Stabia, in the Naples metropolitan area, had its council dissolved again for camorra infiltration in 2026. The 400-page commission report described a body "without adequate antibodies" in its most sensitive offices. It says refuse-bag distribution went to firms traced to a family with contacts in the Casalesi area; clearance of rubbish at a school went to a firm in the orbit of people close to the Cesarano clan; relatives of the D'Alessandro clan were in school catering; and work went to a company with a shareholder in business with council president Roberto Elefante. Technical office managers signed 18 million euros of direct awards. The former mayor Luigi Vicinanza has taken the dissolution to the administrative court, which has ordered the interior ministry to hand over the papers.
inside: Camorra-linked families reached the town's contracting offices, so refuse, school and building work was awarded to firms in the clans' circles.
cite: Stylo24, 23 July 2026, quoting the interior ministry commission's report; Anteprima24, 14 July 2026 and 5 November 2026

n: Marano di Napoli's building permits and contracts favoured clan-linked firms
rank: mayor, giunta, councillors and offices of the Comune di Marano di Napoli
d: Marano di Napoli, north of Naples, had its council dissolved for the fourth time in 2021. The reasons, drawn up by the prefect of Naples Marco Valentini and published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale, record concrete, unambiguous and significant evidence of direct and indirect links between administrators and organised crime. The report counts eight contracts awarded to firms whose shareholders were traced to businessmen said to be in collusion with the clans, and eleven building permits, all of them flawed, issued to people linked directly or indirectly to organised crime. Thirty-two anti-mafia bans were issued against firms working in the area while the council's offices failed to start the required checks. It also describes the comune doing nothing about an illegal garage built by a clan boss's brother on municipal land.
inside: Camorra clans reached Marano's planning and contracting offices, which then issued permits and awards to the firms and relatives the clans put forward.
cite: Stylo24, 19 July 2021, quoting the prefect of Naples' dissolution reasons published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale

n: Acquaro made 113 no-tender awards and seated an assessore by a 'reckless pact'
rank: mayor, an assessore and the technical and building offices of the Comune di Acquaro
d: Acquaro, in Vibo Valentia province, was dissolved by the Council of Ministers on 18 September 2023 "in view of the proven interference of organised crime". The prefect Paolo Giovanni Grieco's report concentrates on two councillors, one of them an assessore who also ran the private building section of the technical office and who, the prefect writes, keeps current company with a senior figure of the local criminal group and several of that man's relatives. Questioned on 25 May 2023, he gave no explanation of acts he had signed, and the prefect records the commission's view that his appointment to the giunta came of "some reckless pact". The report also counts 113 direct awards without any tender, some to firms not on the anti-mafia white list.
inside: A Calabrian criminal group's influence reached Acquaro's giunta and building office, whose signatures and no-tender awards then served interests outside the comune.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 18 October 2023, quoting the prefect of Vibo Valentia's report behind the dissolution

n: Sparanise dissolved after Casalesi-linked care co-ops won its social contracts
rank: mayor and social services of the Comune di Sparanise
d: Sparanise is a town in the province of Caserta. The interior ministry dissolved its council on 16 December 2022 for camorra infiltration, after an inquiry by the Naples anti-mafia prosecutors and the Caserta flying squad into social care and personal assistance services in the surrounding area run by cooperatives that investigators hold to be controlled by people close to the Casalesi clan. Among them is Eufrasia Del Vecchio, sister of Carlo Del Vecchio, described as the Casalesi's long-standing contact at Santa Maria Capua Vetere and in prison for years, and related to the Schiavone camorra family. The former mayor Salvatore Martiello is among those investigated, answering for corruption and bid-rigging. The prefecture of Caserta then refused anti-mafia certification to nine care firms and cooperatives in the area.
inside: Cooperatives run by people close to a camorra clan held the town's social care work, so Sparanise's welfare contracts served the clan's circle.
cite: Anteprima24, 1 March 2023, on the dissolution of the Comune di Sparanise and the prefecture of Caserta's nine anti-mafia bans

n: Crotone resort file pushed through the town hall at criminal circles' urging
who: Megna cosca of Papanice and Cutro criminal circles
rank: a former and a sitting Calabrian regional councillor, and the mayor and technical office of Crotone
d: The Catanzaro anti-mafia inquiry "Glicine-Acheronte" produced 34 precautionary measures in June 2023. In November 2023 the Catanzaro review court refused to lift the house arrest of former regional councillor Enzo Sculco, describing an organised group able to commit offences against the public administration "also thanks to the representation expressed through his daughter Flora Sculco, a sitting regional councillor". The judges wrote that Sculco and Giancarlo Devona were urged by criminal circles to speed up the paperwork at Crotone's municipal technical office for "Europaradiso", a tourist resort, although neither held office there. The circles named are Salvatore Aracri, held close to the Megna cosca of Papanice, and Domenico Grande Aracri, brother of Cutro boss Nicolino. A meeting in January 2017 brought Aracri, the two Sculcos and the mayor Ugo Pugliese together.
inside: Calabrian clan figures used two regional politicians to push a resort permit through Crotone's town hall, so the file moved at the clans' request.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 30 November 2023, quoting the Catanzaro review court's reasons in the Glicine-Acheronte case

n: Court put Scali Unipersonale under judicial administration over cosca ties
rank: Scali Unipersonale Srl, a building and road construction company
d: Scali Unipersonale Srl is a building and road construction company based at Siderno, province of Reggio Calabria. In July 2020 the anti-mafia investigative directorate served a decree of the Reggio Calabria court placing it under judicial administration under article 34 of the anti-mafia code. The court found "the company's permeability to infiltration by organised crime, as well as the stable facilitation carried out by the company in favour of several people tied to the local 'ndrangheta cosche interested in controlling the public building sector", through an objective mixing of the facilitated party's criminal activities with the firm's own lawful business. The prosecutors relied on the Martingala, Mandamento Jonico and Confine investigations. Public contracts were 95 per cent of the firm's turnover. Its sole director had already received an anti-mafia ban.
inside: Calabrian clans worked through a named building firm that held almost only public contracts, so its business steadily served the clans' hold on local works.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 13 July 2020, quoting the Reggio Calabria court's judicial administration decree reported by the DIA

n: De Stefano clan controlled Reggio Calabria's refuse company Fata Morgana
rank: Fata Morgana S.p.A., the mixed public-private company running Reggio Calabria's refuse collection
d: Fata Morgana S.p.A. was the mixed public-private company that ran refuse collection for Reggio Calabria and nearby towns for almost ten years, and also built waste treatment plants. The 2017 inquiry "Trash", coordinated by the Reggio Calabria anti-mafia prosecutors, led to arrests for mafia association and aggravated extortion of Orazio De Stefano, his nephew Paolo Rosario De Stefano and three others held to be part of or close to the De Stefano clan. Investigators said the clan effectively controlled the company, and private firms supplying and servicing its collection vehicles, by imposing large extortion payments, the choice of compliant suppliers and the hiring of staff it approved. A cousin of Orazio De Stefano who later turned state witness, Salvatore Aiello, had been the company's technical manager for 2007 to 2010.
inside: A Calabrian clan ran the city's refuse company from inside, choosing its suppliers and its staff and taking money out of a public service.
cite: Corriere della Calabria, 11 May 2017, on the Reggio Calabria anti-mafia prosecutors' Trash inquiry

n: Driving-school money ran the road tests at Brockton's motor registry
org_label: Brockton driving-school owner and a licence broker
rank: Road test examiner, Registry of Motor Vehicles service centre, Brockton, Massachusetts
d: The Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles tests and licenses drivers. Federal prosecutors in Boston charged two people with paying a road test examiner at the Brockton service centre to report that applicants had passed their road test when they had not, and in some cases had not turned up for the test at all; the Registry then posted licences to them. Estevao Semedo, who owned a driving school, paid the examiner $17,000 and was sentenced in August 2023 to six months. Neta Centio paid the same examiner over 40 separate bribes by CashApp and was sentenced in January 2024 to 15 months, a $10,000 fine and forfeiture of $19,305.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts, press releases 2 March 2023, 17 August 2023 and 18 January 2024
inside: Licence brokers paid an examiner inside the state licensing agency, so its decisions issued real driving licences to the brokers' paying customers.

n: Brockton registry manager took cash to pass learner permit tests
rank: Manager, Registry of Motor Vehicles service centre, Brockton, Massachusetts
d: Mia Cox-Johnson, then manager of the Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles service centre in Brockton, was charged in March 2023 with extortion under colour of official right and agreed to plead guilty. Prosecutors allege that between December 2018 and October 2019 she took money to mark customers as having passed the multiple-choice learner permit tests for ordinary and commercial licences whether or not they had passed. Customers were allegedly told to ask for a paper test, which she scored herself. On 28 December 2018 she allegedly accepted $1,000 in cash, passed on by a friend, for a relative who had failed the test six times; on 21 October 2019 she allegedly took $200 to pass an applicant on three commercial permit tests.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts, press release 2 March 2023
inside: Applicants' cash allegedly reached the manager running a licensing office, so the state recorded test passes that served the payers rather than road safety.

n: Idaho's contracted driving examiner sold commercial licence passes
rank: Third-party commercial driver licence skills test examiner, Idaho Transportation Department
d: To get a commercial driver's licence in Idaho an applicant must be passed by a skills test examiner, and the Idaho Transportation Department contracts third parties to run those tests. Kelly Nathaniel Goodman had been an Idaho examiner since the 1990s. Court records show that between December 2017 and May 2020 he accepted at least $38,000 in bribes for giving passing scores, without the department's knowledge or permission, and he pleaded guilty to taking a bribe on 31 August 2021 for passing one applicant. He was sentenced in June 2023 to two years in federal prison for honest services wire fraud and ordered to forfeit $38,000.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Idaho, press releases 3 April 2023 and 22 June 2023
inside: Applicants' money reached the examiner the state relies on to test lorry drivers, so official passes were recorded for people who never drove the test.

n: Meridian driver paid $500 to have Idaho licence restrictions lifted
rank: Third-party commercial driver licence skills test examiner, Idaho Transportation Department
d: Ryan Basnaw of Meridian pleaded guilty in March 2026 to federal programme bribery. Court records state that on 2 July 2025 he offered and agreed to give an Idaho commercial driver licence skills tester $500 in cash for a passing score on a test he never took, so that three restrictions could be removed from his existing commercial licence. The Idaho Transportation Department contracts third-party examiners to run these tests, and the release notes that in 2025 the department's motor vehicle division received more than $10,000 in federal funding under a commercial licence grant. Sentencing was set for June 2026.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Idaho, press release 30 March 2026
inside: A driver's cash reached the examiner acting for the state, so the licensing record was changed to suit the man who paid for it.

n: A restaurant owner's bribes ran a Louisiana lorry licence pipeline
rank: Two employees of the Office of Motor Vehicles office in Donaldsonville and state-certified skills test examiners, Louisiana Department of Public Safety and Corrections
d: All six defendants in a Louisiana commercial driver's licence scheme pleaded guilty in 2026. Mahmoud Alhattab, a restaurant owner, took about $5,000 from each applicant and bought his way past all three federally required steps. He bribed Shakera Millien and Jenay Davis, employees of the Office of Motor Vehicles branch in Donaldsonville, who sat the written knowledge tests for applicants, looking up answers on their phones, and then issued learner permits; they let Alhattab in through a side door and he sometimes worked the camera himself. Jonathan Parsons and Christopher Burns, state-certified examiners, filed false training and skills test entries at $400 to $500 each. From August 2020 to February 2024 at least 124 people obtained licences this way.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Louisiana, press releases 28 August 2025, 29 July 2026 and 10 September 2026
inside: A licence broker's payments bought staff inside a state licensing office and its certified examiners, so the state issued lorry licences to his customers.

n: Texas licensing official sold 215 lorry licences at about $1,000 each
rank: Employee overseeing commercial driver licence issuance, Texas Department of Public Safety
d: Alonzo Blackman was an employee of the Texas Department of Public Safety who oversaw the issuing of commercial driver's licences. Court documents show that from January 2017 until June 2019 he passed applicants as though he had given them the required skills test when he had not. He issued 215 fraudulent commercial licences and was paid about $1,000 for each, with the bribes paid by two co-defendants, Fernando Guardado Vazquez and Marino Maury Diaz-Leon. Of those licences 197 went to Cuban nationals. Blackman pleaded guilty in February 2020 and was sentenced in July 2022 to 24 months and a $215,000 money judgment; Diaz-Leon received 12 months and a day.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas, press release 7 July 2022
inside: Brokers paid the state employee who signed off lorry licences, so the Texas licensing system certified drivers it had never tested.

n: Cash bribes at a Hondo licence office produced Texas licences to order
rank: Customer service representative, Texas Department of Public Safety office, Hondo
d: Jose A. Ytuarte, a customer service representative at the Texas Department of Public Safety office in Hondo, admitted that from May 2013 to July 2015 he took cash bribes from a co-conspirator for entering false information into the department's computer system, recording that an applicant had been born in the United States so that a driving licence would be issued to an undocumented person. He pleaded guilty in March 2016 and was sentenced in September 2016 to 18 months. According to the indictment his co-defendant Azeez Mistry directed people who could not obtain a licence lawfully to Ytuarte and charged between $1,000 and $5,000 for each licence, paying Ytuarte part of the fee. Mistry was charged and is presumed innocent.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas, press release 8 September 2016
inside: A broker's cash reached a clerk inside the state licensing office, so its records and its licences were written to suit the broker's clients.

n: Broker's payments turned a Largo licensing counter into a document shop
rank: Two employees, Largo branch office, Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration
d: Warner Antonio Portillo of Manassas, Virginia pleaded guilty in August 2019 to conspiring with two employees of the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration's Largo branch. From at least July 2015 to March 2016 applicants who could not get a licence lawfully paid Portillo and others between $800 and $5,000 each; he supplied the employees with the applicants' details and forged supporting documents, sent the applicants to a particular workstation, and paid the employees $500 to $1,000 per licence. At least 276 Maryland licences were produced this way and his money judgment was set at $276,000. Marion Rose Payne, one of the employees, was indicted in March 2021 and the allegations against her are untested.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Maryland, press releases 13 August 2019 and 5 April 2021
inside: A document broker bought two staff inside the state licensing agency, so it issued genuine Maryland licences to people he was paid to supply.

n: Bakersfield truck school paid a DMV clerk to pass its students
rank: Motor vehicle representative, California Department of Motor Vehicles office, Bakersfield
d: Ulises Pena, a motor vehicle representative at the California Department of Motor Vehicles office in Bakersfield, pleaded guilty in September 2022 to producing commercial driver's licences in exchange for bribes. Court records state that from January 2015 through August 2016 he arranged passes for students of a truck driving school run by his co-defendant Bikramjit Singh Pannu who were having trouble passing the tests, in return for payments from Pannu. Pena reached into the students' departmental records and altered them to show passes that had not happened, which caused commercial licences to be issued to unqualified students. He agreed to cooperate against Pannu, whose charges were pending and who is presumed innocent.
