cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California, press releases 5 April 2018 and 20 September 2022
inside: A driving school's payments reached a clerk inside the state motor vehicle agency, so its records were altered and its licences served the school's customers.

n: Nashville licensing clerk took almost $70,000 from a licence broker
rank: Licensing clerk, Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security driver services centre
d: Larry Murphy, a licensing clerk employed by the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security at one of the state's driver services centres, was sentenced in February 2013 to 27 months in prison and ordered to forfeit almost $70,000 in bribes he had taken for issuing driving licences to unauthorised applicants. Anny Castillo, who brokered the transactions, was sentenced to 90 days in prison and nine months of house arrest for paying him bribes to obtain licences for applicants who had not passed the required tests, and forfeited $42,500 she had received for arranging them. The department said it began the investigation as soon as it learned of possible criminal activity by its employee.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee, press release 27 February 2013
inside: A broker's money reached a clerk inside the state licensing department, so it issued licences to applicants who had not qualified for them.

n: Hart Lane examiner sold 21 Tennessee licence permits at $250 each
rank: Licence examiner, Hart Lane station, Tennessee Department of Safety
d: Walton Michael Wand, a licence examiner employed by the Tennessee Department of Safety at the Hart Lane station in Nashville, was found guilty by a federal jury in March 2017 after a two-week trial and sentenced in June 2017 to 12 months in prison and a $7,500 fine. Prosecutors said he used his position to solicit and accept bribes for issuing driving licence permits to unqualified people, issuing at least 21 fraudulent permits and charging $250 for each; many of the applicants could not pass the written examination. Three co-defendants, Faransis Romany Faltas, Nourrdine Abidi and Youssef Aziz Abdelmalak, were sentenced for their parts in the conspiracy.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Middle District of Tennessee, press release 27 June 2017
inside: Payers reached the examiner at a state licensing station, so official learner permits went to people the state had not tested.

n: Colorado's contracted driving tester certified tests nobody sat
org_label: Little Lake Driving Academy and an identity ring
who: Identity ring and a contracted tester
rank: Third-party tester for the Division of Motor Vehicles, Colorado Department of Revenue
d: Little Lake Driving Academy in Aurora acted as a third-party tester for the Colorado Department of Revenue's Division of Motor Vehicles, authorised to run written and driving examinations on the state's behalf. According to the indictment unsealed in April 2013, from August 2009 through November 2012 the owner, Stuart Bryan King, and the academy's clerk, Griselda Trevino De Valenzuela, charged applicants roughly $130 to $420 in cash and falsely certified that they had taken and passed the written test; applicants then presented the certificates and the division posted them licences or permits. Investigators found conspirators transporting people from Missouri who had bought the identities of US citizens. The allegations were untested when the two were arraigned.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Colorado, press release 10 April 2013
inside: Cash from an identity ring's clients allegedly reached the private tester carrying out the state's licensing tests, so the state licensed people it never examined.

n: A broker bought a Revere registry clerk for immigration-barred drivers
org_label: Edwin Amaurys Parra Suarez, licence broker
rank: Clerk, Registry of Motor Vehicles office, Revere, Massachusetts
d: Edwin Amaurys Parra Suarez of Chelsea pleaded guilty in June 2015 and was sentenced in August 2015 for conspiring to produce false identification documents. From December 2012 through December 2013 he bribed a clerk at the Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles office in Revere to issue licences to people not entitled to them. Acting as a broker, he sent clients to the clerk with their paperwork, and for payments of $100 to $1,000 the clerk overlooked the fact that they lacked the immigration documents a Massachusetts licence requires. More than two dozen licences were produced. The release placed the case in a series of identity theft and corruption investigations at the registry, including clerk Alexander Brewer, sentenced in April 2014, who forfeited $60,000.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts, press release 18 August 2015
inside: A broker's payments reached a clerk inside the state registry, so it issued real licences to clients the law barred from holding them.

n: Philadelphia lorry school owner bought passes from a licence examiner
rank: Commercial driver licence examiner, Pennsylvania
d: Vladimir Tsymbalenko, the former owner of Vlad's CDL School in Philadelphia, pleaded guilty in October 2023 to bribery concerning programmes receiving federal funds and to witness tampering, and was sentenced in April 2024 to 57 months in prison and a $5,000 fine. Prosecutors said he bribed a commercial driver's licence examiner to pass students of his school who had not in fact passed the examination, and in some cases had never taken it, and that he asked a witness to lie. The case was investigated by the Department of Transportation's inspector general and the FBI, with help from the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation and the state police.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania, press release 15 April 2024
inside: A driving school's owner paid the examiner who certifies lorry drivers, so the licensing system passed students who served the school's business.

n: Thirteen Ector County jail staff charged with selling contraband inside
org_label: Federal detainees and their outside contacts
rank: Twelve guards and a food service worker, Ector County Correctional Center, Odessa, Texas
d: Federal agents arrested twelve former guards of the Ector County Correctional Center and one former food service worker in January 2013. Thirteen separate grand jury indictments, returned on 23 January 2013 and unsealed that morning, alleged that during 2011 and 2012 the correctional officers and the food service worker Barbara Garrett smuggled contraband to inmates of the federal detention facility, including mobile phones and chargers as well as tobacco and marijuana, in exchange for cash and in knowing violation of their official duties. Each defendant was charged with one count of accepting a bribe. The allegations were untested and the thirteen were presumed innocent.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Western District of Texas, press release 30 January 2013
inside: Detainees' cash allegedly bought more than a dozen staff inside one jail, so the people guarding them ran their trade in phones and drugs.

n: A San Quentin death row inmate paid a guard to bring in 25 phones
org_label: A condemned inmate and his outside associates
rank: Correctional officer, East Block (death row), San Quentin State Prison, California
d: Keith Christopher, a correctional officer in San Quentin State Prison's East Block, known as death row, admitted taking bribes to smuggle at least 25 contraband mobile phones into the prison and delivering them to a condemned inmate who sold many of them on to other inmates. From 2019 he worked with that inmate and three outside associates, Isaiah Wells, Tanisa Smith-Symes and Dustin Albini. In December 2019 ten phones were posted to Smith-Symes in Nevada and passed to Christopher for $5,000, sent by Venmo and Walmart transfers; in May 2020 he agreed to carry 15 more for $7,500, finally taking $6,500. He pleaded guilty in September 2022 and was sentenced in February 2023 to 20 months.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Northern District of California, press release 24 February 2023
inside: An inmate's money and his outside helpers reached an officer on death row, so the prison's own guard supplied the phones his business ran on.

n: Toledo jail officers charged with taking inmates' money for contraband
org_label: Inmates and their associates, Lucas County
rank: Corrections officers, Lucas County Correctional Center, Toledo, Ohio
d: Two former corrections officers at the Lucas County Correctional Center in Toledo were indicted in federal court in August 2018 for taking bribes in return for smuggling contraband to inmates, and a third was charged with providing contraband. According to the indictment Robert Hobson accepted bribes from an inmate or their associates in November 2015 and supplied synthetic cannabinoids and tobacco, and Marcus Henderson did the same in June 2016, supplying a mobile phone and tobacco; Matthew Wiegand was charged with providing contraband tobacco in May 2017. The county sheriff said his office found the problem and took it to the FBI. The indictments were allegations and the three were entitled to a trial.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Northern District of Ohio, press release 24 August 2018
inside: Inmates and their outside associates allegedly paid officers inside a county jail, so the staff supplying contraband worked for the people they held.

n: Harrisburg inmates bribed jail staff to run phones into the prison
org_label: Inmates and their outside relatives, Dauphin County Prison
rank: Corrections officers and staff, Dauphin County Prison, Harrisburg, Pennsylvania
d: A federal grand jury in Harrisburg indicted four people on 31 July 2020 over the smuggling of mobile phones and other contraband into Dauphin County Prison. The indictments allege that Danny Cruz, then an inmate there, and other inmates bribed corrections officers and staff to bring phones in, and arranged for people outside the prison to obtain the phones and hand over the bribes, with the money moved through Western Union and MoneyGram. Those outside included Aida Rosado, Lizarah Matthews, who was the girlfriend of an inmate, and, in a separate indictment covering a conspiracy in 2015, Alice Martinez, whose brother was an inmate facing federal charges. The indictments were only allegations.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Middle District of Pennsylvania, press release 4 August 2020
inside: Inmates' relatives allegedly carried the cash to prison staff, so officers inside the jail ran the communications the inmates wanted.

n: Leavenworth guard took more than $200,000 from inmates for tobacco
rank: Correctional officer, United States Penitentiary, Leavenworth, Kansas
d: Marc Buckner, a guard at the United States Penitentiary in Leavenworth, was indicted in June 2016 on a charge of accepting bribes. The indictment alleged that from 2005 to 2014, while working at the prison, he accepted more than $200,000 in bribes for smuggling tobacco to prisoners, receiving about $750 each time. He pleaded guilty to one count of a public official accepting bribes, and the office later announced that inmates paid him $750 for each can of Bugler loose tobacco and rolling papers he carried in. He was sentenced to three years in federal prison.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Kansas, press releases 9 June 2016 and subsequent plea and sentencing releases
inside: Inmates' payments bought a federal prison guard for nine years, so the officer searching for contraband was the man importing it.

n: Inmates' families paid a second Leavenworth guard $1,000 a tobacco can
org_label: Inmates with families and friends outside
rank: Correctional officer, United States Penitentiary, Leavenworth, Kansas
d: Michael Harston, a guard at the United States Penitentiary in Leavenworth, pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to accept bribes and one count of accepting bribes, and was sentenced in October 2016 to two years on probation with six months of home confinement and $4,800 in fines. In his plea he admitted accepting bribes to provide inmates with tobacco, which is contraband in a federal prison. The prosecutors said inmates coordinated with their families and friends outside the prison to pay him, and that they paid as much as $1,000 for a single six-ounce can of Bugler loose tobacco.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Kansas, press release 17 October 2016
inside: Inmates' families outside paid a serving guard, so a man employed to keep contraband out was selling it to the prisoners.

n: Inmates' relatives paid a Fort Dix officer thousands for drugs inside
rank: Corrections officer, Federal Correctional Institution Fort Dix, New Jersey
d: Paul Anton Wright, a corrections officer at the Federal Correctional Institution at Fort Dix, was arrested in April 2018 and charged by complaint with agreeing to accept and accepting bribes. According to the complaint, in 2015 he smuggled contraband including synthetic marijuana and suboxone to inmates, receiving both the contraband and cash bribes from two people outside the prison. Between February and September 2015 he allegedly took thousands of dollars in cash from the relative of an inmate and delivered the drugs to that inmate, including a $2,500 withdrawal from the relative's bank account on one day in 2015 and a $2,500 deposit into his own the next. Between October and December 2015 he allegedly took thousands more from the relative of an inmate's girlfriend.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of New Jersey, press release 12 April 2018
inside: Inmates' relatives allegedly paid a serving officer, so the federal prison's own staff carried in the drugs the inmates had ordered.

n: A Lexington inmate directed outside buying to bribe his prison officer
org_label: Inmate Keith Griffith and an outside purchaser
rank: Corrections officer, Federal Medical Center, Lexington, Kentucky
d: Four people were convicted over a contraband ring at the Federal Medical Center in Lexington, Kentucky. Between May 2015 and August 2016 Stephanie Dukes of Louisville bought items that federal inmates may not possess, at the direction of inmate Keith Griffith, and paid corrections officer James Carrington to carry them in; Carrington left them at agreed places inside, where Griffith and a second inmate, Amai Rawls, collected them for their own use and to pass to other inmates. The goods included MP3 players, tobacco, mobile phones, weight supplements and synthetic marijuana. Carrington was sentenced to 24 months, Dukes to 18 months, Griffith to four years and Rawls to five months.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Kentucky, press releases 2017 and 28 February 2018
inside: An inmate's buyer outside paid a serving officer, so the prison's own staff delivered the goods the inmate was running inside it.

n: An inmate paid a Salinas Valley prison lieutenant about $95,000
org_label: A Salinas Valley inmate and an outside helper
rank: Correctional lieutenant, Salinas Valley State Prison, Soledad, California
d: Jon Madsen, a correctional lieutenant at Salinas Valley State Prison in Soledad, pleaded guilty in October 2026 to conspiring to smuggle contraband into the prison in exchange for payments from an inmate. He worked for the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation from 2017 to 2025, and as a lieutenant often supervised a whole prison yard of about 1,000 inmates and 200 staff. He admitted that from January 2023 through February 2025 he worked with others, including at least one inmate and one person outside the prison, to bring in contraband, and that he received more than $95,000 in cash payments and wire transfers. Sentencing was set for February 2027.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Northern District of California, press release 20 October 2026
inside: An inmate's money reached a supervising lieutenant, so the officer in charge of a whole prison yard was working for the prisoner paying him.

n: Universal Aryan Brotherhood put two Oklahoma prison officers to work
rank: Two correctional officers, North Fork Correctional Facility, Sayre, Oklahoma
d: Micah Lynne Wascher and Travis Eugene Wascher were correctional officers at the North Fork Correctional Facility in Sayre, Oklahoma. In late 2018 Micah Wascher began smuggling methamphetamine and contraband mobile phones into the prison at the direction of members of the Universal Aryan Brotherhood, a prison gang whose leaders were incarcerated there, in exchange for money and narcotics for her own use. In spring 2019 she brought in her husband Travis to help carry the drugs and phones. Both pleaded guilty in September 2019 to possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, and in January 2020 she was sentenced to 96 months and he to 30 months.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Western District of Oklahoma, press release 28 January 2020
inside: A prison gang's incarcerated leaders directed two serving officers, so the staff guarding the prison moved the gang's drugs and phones for it.

n: South Carolina inmates' bribes reached 19 prison staff, one by one
rank: Corrections officer, Allendale Correctional Institution, South Carolina Department of Corrections
d: Joshua Cave, an officer of the South Carolina Department of Corrections, was sentenced in April 2019 to six months in federal prison and six months of probation after pleading guilty to conspiracy to commit honest services wire fraud. Evidence put to the court showed that inmates paid him bribes to smuggle alcohol into Allendale Correctional Institution, and that he received at least ten bribes amounting to more than a thousand dollars. The release said he was one of 19 former departmental employees, among them corrections officers, a nurse and food service workers, indicted on federal charges of accepting bribes and bringing contraband into South Carolina prisons; three others had already pleaded guilty and were awaiting sentence.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of South Carolina, press release 19 April 2019
inside: Inmates' payments bought officers inside the state prison service, so the staff meant to search for contraband were supplying it instead.

n: Montana State Prison officer took inmates' bribes for drugs and tobacco
rank: Correctional officer, Montana State Prison, Deer Lodge
d: Martin Reap, a correctional officer at Montana State Prison in Deer Lodge, was sentenced in October 2016 to 20 months in prison and five years of supervised release for accepting bribes. The charge arose from a scheme in which he smuggled contraband, including controlled substances and tobacco, to inmates at the prison in exchange for bribes. The investigation was carried out by the FBI, the United States Postal Inspector, the Montana Department of Corrections investigations division and the Montana Division of Criminal Investigations, with the prison's warden and his staff.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Montana, press release 18 October 2016
inside: Inmates' bribes reached a serving officer at the state prison, so the man guarding them brought in the drugs and tobacco they wanted.

n: Kansas City courier fed a jail officer contraband for an inmate
org_label: An inmate and an outside courier
rank: Corrections officer, Jackson County Detention Center, Kansas City, Missouri
d: Marion Lorenzo Byers of Kansas City pleaded guilty in December 2017 to a charge contained in a federal indictment of July 2017. He admitted conspiring with others, including a corrections officer and an inmate at the Jackson County Detention Center, to smuggle contraband mobile phones and other items to inmates between 2 May and 26 June 2017. He admitted that he delivered contraband to a co-conspirator, who passed it to a corrections officer at the detention centre, who was to hand it to an inmate. The prosecutors' release explained that the charge rested on the Travel Act, which covers the use of telephone calls to further bribery under state law.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Western District of Missouri, press release 6 December 2017
inside: An inmate's courier outside paid a jail officer, so the staff of the detention centre carried in the phones the prisoner had ordered.

n: A Taft inmate recruited the officer who then carried in his heroin
rank: Correctional officer, Taft Correctional Institution, California
d: Gerardo Alvarez-Montanez, an inmate at the federal correctional facility at Taft in California, pleaded guilty in June 2014 to conspiracy to provide and possess contraband in prison. According to court documents, between November 2013 and 27 February 2014 he recruited and conspired with a correctional officer to smuggle mobile phones, cash, alcohol, heroin and methamphetamine into the prison in return for cash payments. The officer, Ramon Cano of Bakersfield, was charged with acceptance of a bribe by a federal official and with possession with intent to distribute heroin and methamphetamine, and a change of plea hearing was set for July 2014.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of California, press release 24 June 2014
inside: An inmate recruited a serving officer with cash, so the federal prison's own guard became the supply route for his drugs and phones.

n: Atlanta penitentiary guard charged inmates $500 a smuggling run
org_label: Inmates of the United States Penitentiary, Atlanta
rank: Corrections officer, United States Penitentiary, Atlanta, Georgia
d: Dirk Antonious Engram Jr began working as a corrections officer at the United States Penitentiary in Atlanta, a medium-security prison holding about 2,000 men, in November 2013. In 2014 he began smuggling contraband into the prison for inmates who had befriended him, charging $500 each time he brought in cigarettes, marijuana or other contraband. He was arrested by the FBI on 11 September 2014 after accepting a bribe to smuggle in what he believed was heroin. He pleaded guilty in March 2015 and was sentenced in June 2015 to two years and four months in prison followed by three years of supervised release.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Northern District of Georgia, press release 3 June 2015
inside: Inmates' payments bought a serving federal officer, so the man searching for contraband was carrying it in at a fixed price.

n: Bronx juvenile centre worker charged with selling contraband to inmates
org_label: Residents of Horizon Juvenile Center and their associates
rank: Youth development specialist, Horizon Juvenile Center, New York City Administration for Children's Services
d: Federal prosecutors in Manhattan unsealed a complaint in June 2026 charging Joshua Smith, a New York City youth development specialist at the Horizon Juvenile Center in the Bronx, with conspiracy to commit bribery. Horizon is a secure detention facility for young people remanded as alleged or adjudicated juvenile delinquents or offenders. The complaint alleges that from at least about April 2023 through at least about July 2025 Smith received money for smuggling contraband into Horizon, meeting associates of the residents in the Bronx and elsewhere, taking marijuana, tobacco and pills from them, and delivering the goods to residents inside. On at least some occasions, it alleges, the residents or their associates paid him the bribes themselves.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York, press release 2 June 2026
inside: Detained youths and their associates allegedly paid a serving staff member, so the city employee guarding them trafficked for them instead.

n: Masonry contractor's gifts bought Amtrak's project manager at 30th Street
org_label: Masonry restoration contractor, 30th Street Station project
rank: Project manager, 30th Street Station repair and restoration project, Amtrak
d: Amtrak, the national passenger railway company, awarded a masonry restoration contractor a $58,473,000 contract on 10 December 2015 to repair the facade of 30th Street Station in Philadelphia, with federal funds supplying about 90 per cent of the money. Mark Snedden, the contractor's sole owner and president, admitted that from about May 2016 to about November 2019 he and three of his executives gave Amtrak's project manager gifts and other things of value worth about $323,686, including paid holidays, jewellery, cash, dinners and a dog. Court filings allege the manager passed internal Amtrak information to the firm and approved over $52 million in extra payments, with more than $2 million of overbilling. Snedden was sentenced in October 2025 to 90 months, a $250,000 fine and $2,062,374 in joint restitution.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania, press release 1 October 2025 (posting delayed by the federal shutdown)
inside: A contractor's gifts captured the Amtrak manager who checked its bills, so the railway's own approvals served the firm it was paying.

n: Metrorail contractor paid a Miami-Dade Transit supervisor $75,956
rank: Acting general superintendent and lead rail structure and track supervisor, Track and Guideway unit, Miami-Dade Transit
d: Dale Robinson was the acting general superintendent and lead track supervisor in Miami-Dade Transit's Track and Guideway unit. In about January 2021, while the contractor JB Railroad was working on a Metrorail fastener replacement contract and seeking a further welding contract, Robinson asked its principal Bledsoe for a large bribe, which Bledsoe agreed to pay to influence Robinson's choice of contractor for the welding work. Robinson had his wife Marcia set up Tailored Railroads & Consulting LLC in Maryland, and between February 2021 and February 2022 she sent four invoices to JB Railroad, which paid them by cheque. Robinson was sentenced in July 2025 to 18 months and had already paid a $75,956 forfeiture; his wife received three years' probation and Bledsoe pleaded guilty to paying the bribe.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida, press release 9 July 2025
inside: A track contractor's money reached the supervisor choosing contractors, so the transit system's repair work was awarded to the firm that paid.

n: Savannah transit contractor paid for two officials' home improvements
rank: Executive director and director of maintenance, Chatham Area Transit Authority
d: Anthony Florence, a contractor for the Chatham Area Transit Authority in Savannah, was convicted by a federal jury on 28 February 2018 of twenty-two counts of mail fraud, two of wire fraud and one of bribery of a programme receiving federal funds. Evidence at trial showed he paid bribes and kickbacks to two transit officials, Chadwick Reese and a director of maintenance named Morris, in the form of more than $100,000 of work on their own homes, and that although Florence and his company did little or no work for the authority, the two officials approved over $200,000 in payments to his company. The indictment had put the scheme from April 2014. Reese was sentenced to 84 months and Morris to 20 months.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Southern District of Georgia, press releases 3 December 2015 and 12 March 2018
inside: A contractor paid the transit authority's two senior managers in home improvements, so its payments went to a firm doing little or no work.

n: Builder's bribes inflated his own invoices at the Chester Housing Authority
rank: Director of public housing and his chief assistant, Chester Housing Authority, Pennsylvania
d: From about July 2014 through about March 2022 the contractor Coleman paid bribes separately to Wise, the Chester Housing Authority's director of public housing, and to Daniel, his chief assistant, in exchange for authority contracting work for his firm, Coleman's Contracting. The two officials generated the money by inflating the invoices Coleman submitted and making sure the authority paid the inflated amounts. He paid them about $76,400 while taking about $2.5 million in revenue from the authority. In a separate scheme the two officials billed the authority through a company of their own, Trinity Management Group, costing it about $544,967. All three were charged in August 2023, pleaded guilty, and were sentenced in May 2024: Wise to 37 months, Daniel to 13 months and a day, Coleman to a week.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania, press releases 29 August 2023 and 15 May 2024
inside: A builder's payments reached the two officials awarding housing authority work, so public housing money was spent on the firm that paid them.

n: Vendors' yearly 'donations' bought two Louisiana housing authorities' work
org_label: Vendors and contractors of the Lafayette and Opelousas housing authorities
rank: Executive director, Lafayette Housing Authority and Opelousas Housing Authority
d: Walter Guillory was executive director of the Lafayette Housing Authority from June 1998 to October 2010 and of the Opelousas Housing Authority from November 2005 to November 2010. Evidence at his guilty plea in February 2014 showed he solicited donations from vendors and contractors of both authorities for his baseball team, and that from 2006 to 2010 the vendors were expected to make yearly donations in exchange for doing business with the authorities. He solicited and received more than $100,000 in bribes from them in that period. He also took part in a conspiracy to steer bids to a preferred contractor in Opelousas, approving contracts from 2007 to 2009 knowing the bidding rules were not being followed. He was sentenced in June 2014 to 28 months.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Western District of Louisiana, press release 11 June 2014
inside: Suppliers paid the director of two housing authorities a yearly price for their business, so public housing contracts followed the payments.

n: Johnstown contractors roofed the redevelopment chief's house for work
rank: Executive director, Johnstown Redevelopment Authority, Pennsylvania
d: Ronald Repak, executive director of the Johnstown Redevelopment Authority, was convicted at trial of two counts of extortion under colour of official right and two counts of federal programme bribery, and sentenced in December 2015 to 42 months in prison and three years of supervised release. The court was told that in exchange for his official actions and influence in awarding the authority's contracting work he solicited and obtained from local contracting firms a new roof for his own house and building demolition and grading services at Evolution Gym, his son's private business. He was found not guilty of a further extortion and bribery charge concerning multiple Pittsburgh Steelers football tickets.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Western District of Pennsylvania, press release 8 December 2015
inside: Contracting firms paid the redevelopment authority's director in work on his property, so the body's contracts followed what the firms gave him.

n: Orthopaedic sales reps paid $80,000 inside a Tennessee veterans' hospital
org_label: Two surgical sales representatives and their own company
rank: Two employees, James H. Quillen VA Medical Center, Mountain Home, Tennessee
d: Eric S. Smith and Landon Chester worked as surgical sales representatives for an independent distributor of a nationwide orthopaedic company making replacement joints, and routinely sold to the James H. Quillen VA Medical Center in Mountain Home, Tennessee. In June 2018 they formed a separate company and began selling their own stock to the veterans' hospital at inflated prices, or when it was not needed, causing losses of more than $850,000. They agreed that they had paid cash bribes of more than $80,000 to two medical centre employees, indicted separately, for agreeing to collude in and assist the fraud. Both pleaded guilty on 25 January 2024 to conspiracy to commit bribery and honest services wire fraud and agreed to forfeit seized accounts holding over $156,000.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Tennessee, press release 25 January 2024
inside: Implant sellers paid staff inside a veterans' hospital, so its buying served the sellers' inflated invoices rather than the hospital.

n: Baltimore transit chief sold a $60,000 advertising debt for $20,000 cash
org_label: An advertiser owing the city for Circulator bus advertising
rank: Chief, Division of Transit and Marine Services, Baltimore City Department of Transportation
d: Barry Stephen Robinson, chief of the Division of Transit and Marine Services at Baltimore City's transport department, was sentenced in June 2015 to a year and a day in prison and ordered to forfeit $20,000. In spring 2013 he received a $40,000 cheque payable to the city's director of finance for advertising on Circulator buses; he returned it and proposed that for $20,000 in cash he would cancel the debt and provide paperwork saying it had been paid. In January 2014 he renewed the offer, this time to cancel $60,000 of debt for $20,000. Between 23 January and 11 March 2014 he took four cash payments of $5,000 and gave a signed letter on city notepaper falsely stating the debt was paid.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Maryland, press release 23 June 2015
inside: An advertiser's cash reached the official running the city's bus services, so the city's own paperwork wrote off the money it was owed.

n: United's loss-making 'chairman's flight' and the Port Authority hangar vote
rank: Chairman of the Board of Commissioners, Port Authority of New York and New Jersey
d: The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey operates Newark Airport, one of United Airlines' largest hubs. David Samson, its board chairman, pleaded guilty in July 2016 to bribery for using his authority over the board's agenda to pressure United into restoring a Newark to Columbia flight that suited his own travel to South Carolina. He twice had United's wide-body hangar agreement pulled from the agenda; after it was restored the board approved it on 8 December 2011. United reinstated the route on Samson's preferred schedule, flew it from September 2012 to March 2014, and he used it 27 times. United Continental Holdings was charged with conspiring to commit bribery, agreed to compliance reforms and paid a $2.25 million penalty.
cite: US Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, press release 14 July 2016
inside: An airline gave the chairman of the authority running its hub a flight he wanted, and the authority then approved the hangar deal he had blocked.

n: West Haven housing director took $1.5m from people wanting its contracts
org_label: Contractors and businessmen dealing with the West Haven Housing Authority
rank: Executive director, West Haven Housing Authority, Connecticut
d: Michael Siwek was executive director of the West Haven Housing Authority in Connecticut. From about February 2007 through February 2012 he received about $1.5 million in payments from individuals in exchange for awarding business and contracts with the authority and with entities it controlled, taking the money by wire transfer and cheque, both to himself and to Four Star Development Company LLC, a company he controlled. He pleaded guilty in September 2014 to conspiracy to commit bribery in connection with a programme receiving federal funds, to bribery and to tax evasion, and was sentenced in July 2016 to 48 months in prison, restitution of $1,503,096.91 and more than $363,000 in back taxes, penalties and interest.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Connecticut, press release 15 July 2016
inside: Contractors' payments bought the man who awarded a housing authority's business, so public housing contracts went to whoever paid him.

n: Chicago builder's $421,000 in kickbacks won $4.8m of housing work
org_label: Bell's Better Buildings, trading as Twenty Eleven Construction
rank: Director, Property and Asset Management Department, Chicago Housing Authority
d: An indictment returned in Chicago in June 2026 accuses Ryan Ross, a former director in the Chicago Housing Authority's property and asset management department, of taking more than $421,000 in kickbacks in 2023 and 2024 from Vanessa Rhodes, president of Bell's Better Buildings Inc, trading as Twenty Eleven Construction. In exchange, the indictment states, Ross used his position to award more than $4.8 million of construction and renovation work at authority properties to that company and another linked to Rhodes. It alleges they had Rhodes's husband pose to property managers as an employee who would do the work, and concealed Ross's interest with false proposals, scopes of work and invoices. Both are charged with eight counts of honest services fraud and are presumed innocent.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Northern District of Illinois, press release 9 June 2026
inside: A builder's kickbacks allegedly reached the director awarding housing authority work, so the agency's repair money went to the firm that paid.

n: Hempstead housing chairman took kickbacks on rigged repair bids
org_label: Devlin Mac Construction and other co-conspirator companies
rank: Chairman of the Board of Commissioners, Village of Hempstead Housing Authority, New York
d: The Village of Hempstead Housing Authority was set up to provide low-income families, disabled residents and senior citizens with affordable housing. Its board chairman, Cornell Bozier, was convicted by a federal jury in April 2019 of conspiracy to commit honest services fraud and three counts of federal programme bribery, and sentenced in March 2024 to ten years in prison. Prosecutors said he used bribes, threats and intimidation to push other board members into supporting his schemes, and took more than $100,000 in cash from the companies that prepared and submitted the rigged bids. In one instance the authority paid Devlin Mac Construction $273,900 to replace a roof; a subcontractor was paid $23,000 to patch parts of it and the rest was split, with Bozier taking $55,000.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York, press release 11 March 2024
inside: Contractors' cash bought the chairman of a housing authority, so its repair money was steered to their rigged bids instead of tenants' homes.

n: Firms' cash stopped environment-guard fines in Bihor county
org_label: company administrators inspected in Bihor county
rank: commissars, Bihor County Commissariat, National Environmental Guard
d: The National Environmental Guard is Romania's environmental inspectorate. Prosecutors charged three of its commissars at the Bihor county commissariat with taking money from the companies they were inspecting. On 23 and 29 February 2012 Gheorghe Ratiu and Gabriel Varga demanded sums and received between 2,700 and 3,000 lei in all so that three inspected firms would not be fined for environmental breaches found during checks. Varga took 1,000 lei and 20 litres of petrol from administrators of two other companies, and with Mugur Gheorghe Popa took 700 lei from a firm's administrator and wrote an inspection note recording untrue circumstances. Oradea's appeal court convicted Ratiu finally on 3 June 2014, four years and three months, for three counts of taking bribes and related abuse of office.
inside: Inspected companies paid commissars inside the state environmental inspectorate, which then recorded no breach and left the firms unfined.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 11/VIII/3 of 10 January 2013, and the conviction notice on Oradea Court of Appeal decision 268 of 3 June 2014

n: A guesthouse owner's 500 euros bought off a missing environment permit
org_label: a guesthouse and a company at Praid, Harghita county
rank: commissar, General Commissariat, National Environmental Guard
d: Lorant-Florian Osz-Strakator was a commissar of the General Commissariat of Romania's National Environmental Guard, the inspectorate's central body. Between 4 and 12 November 2009, while inspecting companies in Harghita county, he demanded 1,000 euros from the administrator of a guesthouse in the commune of Praid so as not to fine him for lacking an environmental permit, and on 16 November received 500 euros as a first instalment. On 4 November he had asked the administrator of another Praid company for 10,000 lei for the same reason. The High Court of Cassation and Justice convicted him finally on 22 September 2011 of two counts of taking bribes, three years in prison, and ordered him to pay the state the lei equivalent of 500 euros.
inside: Businesses facing fines paid a commissar of the national environmental inspectorate, who then held back the penalties their missing permits carried.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 61/VIII/3 of 10 March 2010, and the conviction notice on High Court decision 3200 of 22 September 2011

n: Alcohol firms' 27,000 euros bought Romanian customs antifraud protection
rank: officials of the Customs Information Centre, Antifraud Directorate, National Customs Authority
d: Romania's National Customs Authority policed excise goods, and its Antifraud Directorate ran a Customs Information Centre. Between February and November 2008 Sergiu Adorian Ignat, an official of that centre, took 27,000 euros in bribes from the representative of several companies producing alcohol, paid through two intermediaries, so as to breach his duties and give those firms illicit protection. From the same payer, between March and July 2008, Mihai Chioveanu of the tax administration's fiscal antifraud directorate and Marian Tutuianu and Adrian Modan of the customs authority each took sums of between 1,000 and 2,000 lei to favour his companies. Pitesti's appeal court convicted Ignat finally on 21 February 2014, five years in prison, and Tutuianu to one year suspended.
inside: Alcohol companies paid officials inside the customs antifraud service, which then shielded their operations from the controls it existed to run.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 765/VIII/3 of 29 October 2012, and the conviction notice on Pitesti Court of Appeal decision 75 of 21 February 2014

n: Customs brokers' payments ran the clearance queue at Ploiesti customs
org_label: customs broker Unitehnica SA and other declarants
who: customs brokers acting for importers and exporters
rank: sixteen customs officers, Ploiesti Customs Office
d: Sixteen customs officers of the Ploiesti customs office were charged with taking bribes in a continuing form. Prosecutors found that between 2004 and August 2006 they repeatedly demanded and took money and goods from customs declarants to speed up clearance formalities, and that the service itself was delayed when payment did not come. One payer was Lucia Simionescu of the customs brokerage Unitehnica SA, who gave money and goods to officers so that papers for her clients, firms importing and exporting, were finished quickly. Justina Stanila, a declarant at the brokerage Wim Bosman, took money from the firms she represented for the same purpose. The High Court convicted thirteen of the officers finally on 27 May 2013, each three years and six months suspended, and Simionescu of giving bribes.
inside: Brokers acting for importers paid officers inside the customs office, which then cleared their clients' goods ahead of those who did not pay.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 213/VIII/3 of 5 December 2006, and the conviction notice on High Court decision 1823 of 27 May 2013

n: A wholesaler's 5,000 euros won back its Romanian medicines licence
who: a medicines wholesaler whose licence had been suspended
rank: president, National Agency for Medicines and Medical Devices
d: Romania's National Agency for Medicines and Medical Devices licenses and inspects medicine distributors. On 8 September 2010 its inspectors made an unannounced check at SC Ioana Med Farm SRL of Stefanesti, run by Sandel Alexandrescu; the firm was fined and its wholesale distribution licence suspended. Rather than fix the faults, Alexandrescu and his wife Anca Elena decided to pay the agency's president. On 10 and 21 September 2010 Daniel Boda, the president, took 5,000 euros in all through the wife so that a fresh inspection would be approved and would record, untruthfully, that the faults were remedied, the suspension lifted and the licence returned. The High Court convicted Boda finally on 30 January 2014 of taking bribes, three years suspended, and Alexandrescu to five years and six months.
inside: A wholesaler whose licence the regulator had suspended paid the regulator's own president, who arranged an inspection written to clear it.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 535/VIII/3 of 31 August 2011, and the conviction notice on High Court decision 349 of 30 January 2014

n: An oil supplier's contract reached Romania's food-aid tender chair
org_label: S.C. Argus S.A. and S.C. Evalserv Standard S.R.L.
who: a cooking-oil supplier bidding for a state food-aid contract
rank: deputy director general, Agency for Payments and Intervention for Agriculture
d: Romania's Agency for Payments and Intervention for Agriculture ran the PEAD programme, which bought food for the needy. Between May and August 2013 Aurel Pana, its deputy director general and chair of the commission evaluating oil bids, acting with George Mugur Voinea of SC Evalserv Standard SRL, demanded from a bidder a commission of 10 per cent of the contracts awarded, about 5,200,000 lei, in exchange for using his influence over other commission members so the bids won. Voinea obtained a works contract obliging the bidder's firm to pay his company 516,871 lei plus VAT. Bucharest's appeal court convicted Pana finally on 31 August 2015, seven years and six months, and annulled the contract between S.C. Argus S.A. and S.C. Evalserv Standard S.R.L. as disguising the benefits demanded.
inside: An oil supplier's money reached the official chairing the state agency's tender commission, which then steered the award and payments its way.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 987/VIII/3 of 8 November 2013, and the conviction notices on Bucharest Court of Appeal decisions 343 of 18 March 2014 and 1030 of 31 August 2015

n: A businessman's firms paid the APIA director who moved farm money to them
org_label: companies controlled by Tudor Ioan Jurj
who: construction and services firms controlled by one businessman
rank: director, Caras-Severin county directorate, Agency for Payments and Intervention for Agriculture
d: Romania's Agency for Payments and Intervention for Agriculture passes European and national farm money to local authorities for work such as clearing pasture. Prosecutors found that in 2011 Romica Pavel Anculia, director of its Caras-Severin county office, used his influence over mayors to get backdated contracts signed with firms controlled by the businessman Tudor Ioan Jurj, for work partly or wholly not done, with the money then shared out. Jurj handed Socol's mayor Valentin Ghita 5,000 lei and later 50,000 lei; four contracts each under 15,000 euros avoided a tender. Otelu Rosu's mayor Simion Iancu took 15,000 lei. The High Court convicted Anculia finally on 28 January 2015, six years in prison, on a guilty-plea agreement, and confiscated 25,000 euros each from him and Ghita.
inside: A businessman's firms paid the director of the state farm-payments office, who then had communes award them contracts the agency financed.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 293/VIII/3 of 27 April 2012 and release 457/VIII/3 of 20 June 2012, and the conviction notice on High Court decision 147 of 28 January 2015

n: 67,000 lei bought Romania's contraceptive tender at thirty times cost
who: a medical-supplies company bidding for a ministry contract
rank: president of the national tender commission, Ministry of Health and Family
d: Romania's Ministry of Health and Family held a national tender in 2002 to buy contraceptives. Prosecutors charged Remus Virgil Baciu, the commission's president, and a member, Daiana-Elena Druta, with unlawfully easing the award to S.C. Vodimedicor S.R.L. of Targu Jiu of a contract worth 747,723.96 lei, about 223,000 US dollars, for 16,200 Cooper T 380 A intrauterine devices. The ministry paid 46.15 lei a device, against an import price of 1.54 lei and an average pharmacy price of 9.06 lei, and the indictment puts the loss to its budget at 597,116.80 lei. For easing the award, prosecutors say Baciu took 67,000 lei from Cristinel-Spiridon Vodislav, in cash and by bank transfer from the company. The release records the committal for trial and no later decision.
inside: A supplier's money reached the official chairing the health ministry's tender commission, which then bought its devices at many times their cost.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 257/VIII/3 of 19 October 2007

n: A hypermarket's 50,000 euros got a Craiova permit signed same day
who: a retail chain building a hypermarket
rank: mayor of Craiova and chair of the city's road and pedestrian planning commission
d: Between February and November 2006 Antonie Solomon, mayor of Craiova, took 50,000 euros in instalments from Gheorghe Cornel Penescu, majority shareholder of S.C. PIC S.A. of Pitesti. In exchange he eased, against the rules, the issue of a building permit for the PIC hypermarket in Craiova, the permit containing untrue particulars, and an approval for public transport to serve the site. Solomon signed the permit on the same day the company applied for it, after officials of Craiova city hall had twice refused an identical application because the matter was in litigation. A five-judge panel of the High Court upheld his conviction on 20 September 2013: three years in prison for taking bribes and forgery, three years for Penescu for giving them, and confiscation of the 50,000 euros.
inside: A retailer's money reached the mayor who signed its building permit, and the permit his own officials had twice refused was issued at once.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 75/VIII/3 of 19 March 2010, and the conviction notice on High Court decision 178 of 20 September 2013

n: A fuel supplier's Montenegro holiday for the mayor of Resita
org_label: SC IDN Grup Inc SRL and SC Petrodan Company SRL
rank: mayor of Resita and officers of the city's patrimony service
d: Between January and August 2005 Liviu Spataru, mayor of Resita, ordered a public contract for petroleum products with SC IDN Grup Inc SRL, owned by the businessman Danut Nelu Izvernari, in breach of the public procurement rules, and then approved advance payment for fuel invoiced but not fully delivered. In exchange he received a stay in Montenegro for himself, his wife and his daughter, worth 73,595,500 old lei or 2,085 euros, paid from the funds of Izvernari's other company, SC Petrodan Company SRL. Prosecutors put the loss to Resita local council at 130,000 euros. Craiova's appeal court convicted both finally on 28 March 2014, three years in prison each, Spataru for taking bribes and abuse of office and Izvernari for giving them.
inside: A fuel supplier paid for the mayor's family holiday, and the city then signed its contract outside the rules and paid for fuel never delivered.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 151/VIII/3 of 14 June 2007, and the conviction notice on Craiova Court of Appeal decision 438 of 28 March 2014

n: Two builders' instalments steered Cluj county's budget to them
org_label: Sinai Compimpex SRL and SCC Napoca SA
who: two construction companies holding local-authority contracts
rank: president of Cluj County Council
d: Horea Dorin Uioreanu, president of Cluj County Council, was charged with taking bribes from two businessmen whose firms held contracts with councils in the county. Prosecutors say he demanded 693,224 lei from Vasile Pogacean and received 134,500 lei in ten instalments between April 2013 and May 2014, to direct money from the county budget to the authorities that owed Pogacean's company Sinai Compimpex SRL; and demanded 300,000 lei from Ioan Bene, receiving 278,000 lei in seven instalments between October 2012 and March 2014, to direct budget money to pay contracts run by Bene's SCC Napoca SA. Cluj's appeal court convicted him finally on 31 January 2018, six years and four months, and confiscated 281,000 lei and 32,200 euros.
inside: Two contractors paid the head of the county council, who then pushed county money to the authorities that owed their firms.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 894/VIII/3 of 23 June 2014, and the conviction notice on Cluj Court of Appeal decision 170 of 31 January 2018

n: A maintenance firm's 43,000 lei bought the Cluj Arena tender from inside
who: a building-maintenance company bidding for a stadium contract
rank: vice-president of Cluj County Council
d: Cluj County Council holds 90 per cent of the company that runs the Cluj Arena stadium, and the council sitting in plenary runs that company, the vice-president included. In October 2011 Radu Vasile Bica, the council's vice-president, accepted Aspazia Droniuc's promise of 20,000 euros for information about the coming tender for the stadium's 2012 maintenance. The information gave her an advantage over other bidders. On 31 October 2011 Bica took 43,000 lei, the equivalent of 10,000 euros, and prosecutors caught him in the act. The High Court upheld his conviction on 4 October 2012: five years in prison for taking bribes, with 43,000 lei confiscated, and one year and ten months suspended for Droniuc, named as a partner in SC Frarom Import Export SRL, for giving them.
inside: A bidder paid the county council's vice-president for the tender terms before they were published, which put her firm ahead of its rivals.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 767/VIII/3 of 25 November 2011, and the conviction notice on High Court decision 3130 of 4 October 2012

n: An architecture firm paid a tenth of its fee to Ramnicu Valcea's mayor
org_label: an architecture firm holding the city design contract
who: an architecture firm designing a city square
rank: mayor of Ramnicu Valcea
d: Early in 2013 Ramnicu Valcea city hall gave an architecture firm the design at a fee of about 200,000 euros. In January 2013 the mayor, Emilian Valentin Francu, demanded from the firm's administrator 10 per cent of that sum in exchange for signing the documents his post required on the contract. On 22 April 2013, after a first instalment had been paid, he asked for 50,000 lei through an intermediary to sign the papers releasing the second instalment, and for a further 40,000 lei disguised as a sponsorship after the last one. On 25 April the administrator handed over the money as agreed. Bucharest's appeal court convicted Francu finally on 26 March 2014 of taking bribes, four years in prison.
inside: The firm holding the city's design contract paid the mayor to sign the papers releasing its own fee, which the city then paid out.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 459/VIII/3 of 20 May 2013, and the conviction notice on Bucharest Court of Appeal decision 368 of 26 March 2014

n: A Boston bus firm's 2,800 dollars kept its unsafe coaches on the road
who: a charter bus company undergoing a federal safety audit
rank: safety investigator, Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration
d: The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, part of the US Department of Transportation, sets and enforces safety rules for bus and lorry operators. L&W Travel Inc. registered as a charter bus company in January 2018. On several occasions in July and August 2018, during the agency's safety audit, its owner Le Wen Wu and its safety manager Yat Kuen Chan gave the agency's safety investigator 2,800 dollars in cash in all to influence the review. On 1 August 2018 Chan gave 600 dollars so that a bus with inadequate brakes and a defective emergency exit door would not be put out of service at once. Both pleaded guilty in October 2019 and were sentenced in 2020 to two years' probation with home detention.
inside: A bus company paid the federal investigator auditing it, and a coach with failed brakes was allowed to keep running instead of being grounded.
cite: US Department of Justice, District of Massachusetts, releases of 2 November 2018, 8 October 2019, 26 May 2020 and 15 October 2020

n: MJ-6's 800,000 dollars bought 21m in US Army subcontracts at Aberdeen
who: a subcontractor seeking US Army technology work
rank: two civilian officials of the Army Communications-Electronics Command
d: In 2006 the US Army Contracting Command at Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland awarded a ten-year, 19.2 billion dollar contract to seven prime contractors for technology services. John Kays and his wife Danielle Kays held leadership posts as Army civilians in the Communications-Electronics Command there. Matthew Barrow, who worked for a glass manufacturer in Toledo, set up a company called MJ-6; from August 2008 to June 2014 he paid the couple about 800,000 dollars, routed first through contracts with the glass firm and later in cash. They added MJ-6 to the Army's list of acceptable subcontractors, and steered it more than 21 million dollars of work. All three pleaded guilty; John Kays was sentenced to six years in 2018 and Danielle Kays to 18 months in 2017.
inside: A subcontractor paid two Army officials who then put its company on the approved list and steered it 21 million dollars of Army work.
cite: US Department of Justice, District of Maryland, releases of 13 July 2016, 25 January 2017, 9 November 2017 and 11 May 2018

n: Two vendors' money ran the purchase cards at Red River Army Depot
org_label: vendors Jeffrey Harrison and Justin Bishop
who: two suppliers to an Army depot
rank: equipment mechanic supervisor and the purchase-card programme supervisor, Red River Army Depot
d: Red River Army Depot in Texarkana, Texas, repairs and supplies army equipment. Jimmy Scarbrough, its equipment mechanic supervisor from November 2001 to May 2019, directed more than seven million dollars of depot purchases to two vendors, Jeffrey Harrison and Justin Bishop, by telling them what to bid and collecting fake bids from others so the buying looked competitive, and by certifying goods received that he had told them not to deliver. He took more than 300,000 dollars from the two, including postal money orders, car parts and firearms. Two other depot officials took smaller sums, one of them the supervisor who approved Scarbrough's purchases. All pleaded guilty and were sentenced in 2021 and 2022; the releases do not date the payments.
inside: Two suppliers paid depot officials, who then wrote the bidding so the depot's purchase cards went to them and paid for goods never delivered.
cite: US Department of Justice, Eastern District of Texas, releases of 18 May 2021 and 13 September 2022

n: A-TEK's 30,600 dollars reached the CDC officer who signed its contract
who: a company seeking business from the US public health agency
rank: senior contracting officer, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
d: Carlos Smiley was a senior contracting officer at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United States' federal public health agency. Between September 2011 and January 2012 he took six payments totalling 30,600 dollars from A-TEK, a Virginia-based holding company then seeking CDC business, presented as fees for real estate investment advice through a side company he ran, and he answered no when his financial disclosure forms asked about outside income. In 2012 A-TEK was awarded a single-source contract to staff CDC field stations overseas, and Smiley signed it as the approving contracting officer. A-TEK then turned the contract down on learning of the relationship. Smiley pleaded guilty to making false statements and was sentenced in November 2018 to three months in prison and a 5,000 dollar fine.
inside: A company seeking CDC work paid the agency's own contracting officer, who then signed the single-source contract awarded to it.
cite: US Department of Justice, Northern District of Georgia, release of 16 November 2018

n: Engineering clients paid the San Francisco inspector who signed off
who: a structural engineering firm and its construction clients
rank: senior building inspector, San Francisco Department of Building Inspection
d: San Francisco's Department of Building Inspection issues building permits and its inspectors decide on site whether work matches the permit. Bernard Curran was one of its senior building inspectors. Rodrigo Santos, co-founder of Santos & Urrutia Structural Engineers obtained permits for his clients from the department. The federal complaint filed in August 2021 alleges Santos asked those clients to write cheques of 500 to 1,500 dollars to a local non-profit athletic organisation favoured by Curran, that Curran knew of the donations and understood what they were for, and that he repeatedly gave Santos's clients favourable treatment. Curran pleaded guilty on 9 December 2022 to accepting illegal gratuities from developers and property owners whose projects he approved, and was sentenced in July 2023 to a year and a day.
inside: A permit expediter's clients paid into a charity the city inspector favoured, and the inspector then signed off their building work.
cite: US Department of Justice, Northern District of California, releases of 20 August 2021 and 17 July 2023

n: A businessman's firms split 1.2m dollars with a Navy approving officer
org_label: three companies run by Theodore Bauer
who: a businessman's companies holding Navy work orders
rank: master scheduler and approving official, Public Works Department, Naval Base Ventura County
d: Fernando Barroso Sr. worked for 22 years as master scheduler in the Public Works Department of Naval Base Ventura County in California, which covers Point Mugu, Port Hueneme and San Nicolas Island. As an approving official he could approve material purchases, service contracts, vendors and payments to vendors. From 2008 he had an arrangement with Theodore Bauer, a Ventura County businessman who ran three entities holding Navy contracts: Barroso issued and approved work and purchase orders for Bauer's companies, Bauer submitted false invoices, and Barroso approved the invoices and payments even though the work was not being done. Bauer gave Barroso half of everything the scheme produced, more than 1.2 million dollars. Barroso pleaded guilty in March 2019 and was sentenced in July 2019 to 70 months in prison.
inside: A contractor's payments bought the naval base official who approved its orders and invoices, and the Navy paid for work never done.
cite: US Department of Justice, Central District of California, releases of 7 March 2019 and 15 July 2019

n: A waste developer's casino chips bought a Gwinnett County planning vote
org_label: Mark Gary's waste transfer station project
who: a businessman developing a waste transfer station
rank: District 1 member, Gwinnett County Board of Commissioners
d: In October 2008 Mark Gary, a Gwinnett County businessman in Georgia, applied for county approval for a four million dollar solid waste transfer station. Gary had helped Shirley Lasseter get elected to the board, and she appointed him to the county planning commission in January 2009. In March or April 2009 Gary offered money to Lasseter and her son John Fanning, with sums discussed up to 100,000 dollars, for her vote. She told Gary to deal with her son. The commission approved the application on 28 April 2009 with Lasseter voting in favour, and in June Gary gave Fanning 30,000 dollars in chips at an out-of-state casino. All three were convicted; Gary was sentenced to two years in 2013 and Lasseter to two years and nine months in 2012.
inside: A developer paid a county commissioner through her son, and her vote carried the approval his waste station needed.
cite: US Department of Justice, Northern District of Georgia, release of 27 August 2013

n: A paving firm's weekly cash and 9.9m dollars of contracts in Catano
org_label: an asphalt and paving company in Puerto Rico
rank: mayor of the municipality of Catano, Puerto Rico
d: Felix Delgado-Montalvo was mayor of Catano in Puerto Rico. He pleaded guilty on 1 December 2021 to one count of conspiracy, admitting he enriched himself by taking things of value, including weekly cash payments, from a person whose business was then awarded municipal contracts. A separate indictment returned the same day alleges that from about June 2017 Mario Villegas-Vargas, who owned an asphalt and paving company with another man, paid kickbacks and bribes to the mayor, and that in exchange the mayor pressed Catano's municipal officials to award the company contracts, which came to more than 9.9 million dollars. Villegas-Vargas was charged with conspiracy and federal programme bribery, and those allegations against him had not been tried when the release was issued.
inside: A paving contractor paid the mayor weekly, and the mayor leaned on his own officials until the town's contracts went to that company.
cite: US Department of Justice, District of Puerto Rico, release of 2 December 2021

n: A camera firm's payments kept Crestwood's ticket approvals high
org_label: a red-light camera company serving Crestwood
who: a red-light camera contractor seeking more municipal work
rank: mayor of Crestwood, Illinois
d: A red-light camera company ran the cameras that let the village of Crestwood, Illinois, ticket motorists, and the mayor approved which recorded violations became tickets. Louis Presta, then mayor, pleaded guilty on 17 November 2021 to using a facility of interstate commerce in aid of bribery. His plea agreement states that while the company was trying to sell Crestwood further services, he asked for and accepted benefits from an individual with a financial interest in it, and told that person he would make sure the percentage of red-light violations he approved stayed high or rose, in exchange for a cash payment. The agreement describes a telephone call of 27 February 2018 in which Presta reported the higher share of violations the village had approved the previous week.
inside: A camera contractor paid the mayor who decided which violations became tickets, and he kept the approval rate up so the firm earned more.
cite: US Department of Justice, Northern District of Illinois, release of 17 November 2021

n: A contractor's 65,000 dollars drew 426,000 in Bayonne HUD grants
who: a general contracting company seeking federally funded repair work
rank: senior accountant, City of Bayonne Department of Community Development
d: Bayonne's Department of Community Development in New Jersey handed out grants of up to 20,000 dollars from the US Department of Housing and Urban Development to low-income families to repair their homes, and Anselmo Crisonino, its senior accountant, reviewed the applications and awarded the money. In September 2010 he asked Joseph Arrigo, owner of the general contractor Shadow Contracting LLC, for cash. From September 2010 to February 2013 Arrigo paid him about 65,000 dollars, and Crisonino helped award Arrigo about 426,000 dollars of those grants; he also awarded grants to contractors and plumbers whose bids he knew to be fraudulent. Both pleaded guilty. Arrigo was sentenced in November 2016 to 15 months and Crisonino in February 2017 to 21 months.
inside: A contractor paid the official who decided who got the federal home-repair grants, and the grants then came to that contractor.
cite: US Department of Justice, District of New Jersey, releases of 17 October 2013, 3 November 2016 and 27 February 2017

n: An IT firm's 330,000 dollars staffed a US agency's contracts office
org_label: a Virginia information technology and data management firm
who: an IT and data management contractor
rank: contracting officer, Office of Contracts, International Broadcast Bureau, Broadcasting Board of Governors
d: The Broadcasting Board of Governors runs America's state international broadcasting. Diane Sturgis was a contracting officer in its International Broadcast Bureau's Office of Contracts until September 2017, supervising several contracts held by a Virginia information technology and data management firm, including a blanket purchase agreement. In September 2014 the board and the Department of Defense used that agreement to issue a task order which became the route for buying millions of dollars of its services. In November 2014 Sturgis and the firm's owner used the same task order to fill several contracting posts in her own office in exchange for initial payments of at least 330,000 dollars. She pleaded guilty on 28 July 2020 to conspiring to defraud the United States through bribery and wire fraud.
inside: A contractor paid the agency's contracting officer and supplied the staff of her own office, while its task order carried millions in work.
cite: US Department of Justice, Criminal Division and Eastern District of Virginia, release of 28 July 2020

n: Builders' cash and cars steered Veterans Affairs construction work
org_label: construction contractors to the Veterans Affairs medical centres
rank: contracting officer and three contracting officer's representatives, Department of Veterans Affairs
d: Tracy Marasco was a contracting officer for the US Department of Veterans Affairs, which runs medical centres for former service members. She admitted that between 2007 and 2010 she took tens of thousands of dollars in cash, two used cars and paid trips to Disneyland and Las Vegas from private contractors and subcontractors, and used her position to steer valuable construction and maintenance contracts to certain prime contractors. Three contracting officer's representatives at the Palo Alto medical centre took cash, flight tickets, credit-card payments, car payments and roofing work on a home for steering contracts the same way; one was overseeing the installation of a new MRI scanner by the contractor who paid for his roof. Seven people were convicted, three of them contractors, the last in June 2016.
inside: Builders' cash and gifts reached the officials who awarded Veterans Affairs construction work, and the contracts went to those who paid.
cite: US Department of Justice, Northern District of California, release of 14 June 2016

n: An asbestos contractor's repairs for an Air Force contracting official
org_label: an asbestos abatement company working at Scott Air Force Base
who: an asbestos abatement contractor on an Air Force base
rank: contracting official, United States Air Force, Scott Air Force Base
d: Dennis Charles Toenjes Sr. was a contracting official with the United States Air Force at Scott Air Force Base in Illinois. Court records show that on 3 February 2009 he received and accepted gratuities from Stephen Keith Sweet, an owner of an asbestos abatement company that did work on the base, and that Sweet would not have given them but for Toenjes's position as a contracting official. The gratuities were car repairs and home heating and cooling repairs, 9,382.01 dollars in all. Toenjes pleaded guilty and was sentenced on 6 March 2014 to three years' probation and a 500 dollar fine. Sweet was serving 18 months for tax fraud and paying gratuities to a government official. The release identifies no decision by Toenjes that served Sweet's company.
inside: A base contractor paid the Air Force official who handled contracting there, a payment made because of the post he held.
cite: US Department of Justice, Southern District of Illinois, release of 6 March 2014

n: Contractors' kickbacks ran a 30m dollar ring in the Army Corps of Engineers
rank: programme manager, US Army Corps of Engineers
d: Kerry F. Khan was a programme manager for the US Army Corps of Engineers, the army's engineering and construction arm. Prosecutors described him as leading a ring of public officials and government contractors that used bribery and kickbacks and took more than 30 million dollars through inflated and fictitious invoices, on contracts awarded from 2007 to 2011 through the Corps and the Department of the Army. Six companies were involved, and Khan was paid over 12 million dollars directly and indirectly. Before his arrest he was trying to steer a planned one billion dollar federal contract to a favoured contractor in return for payments. Fifteen people and one company pleaded guilty. Khan was sentenced on 11 July 2013 to 19 years and seven months.
inside: Contractors' kickbacks bought the Army engineering manager who chose them, and the contracts and invoices he approved went their way.
cite: US Department of Justice, District of Columbia, release of 11 July 2013

n: A tow firm's bribes redirected wrecks from a Queens police precinct
who: a towing company seeking accident work
rank: officers of the 105th Precinct, New York City Police Department
d: The New York Police Department's Directed Accident Response Program sets which tow operators get vehicles damaged in crashes. Court filings in the Eastern District of New York state that between 2016 and 2017 two officers of the department's 105th Precinct in Queens, Robert Hassett and Robert Smith, received thousands of dollars in bribes for referring that business to a towing company, contrary to the programme. Smith resumed the scheme without Hassett in late 2019 and, when he retired in March 2020, brought in a serving officer, Heather Busch, to take his place. Hassett and Smith also sold the names and contact details of accident victims. All three pleaded guilty in 2021, Smith forfeiting 20,000 dollars, Hassett 10,000 and Busch 6,000.
inside: A tow firm paid police officers at the precinct that decided who collected wrecks, and the work went to it rather than down the official rota.
cite: US Department of Justice, Eastern District of New York, release of 7 October 2021

n: Businessmen paid 75,000 dollars to be sworn in as Culpeper deputy sheriffs
rank: sheriff of Culpeper County, Virginia, and auxiliary deputy posts in his office
d: Scott Howard Jenkins, sheriff of Culpeper County in Virginia, took more than 75,000 dollars in bribes in exchange for appointing Northern Virginia businessmen as auxiliary deputy sheriffs in his own department. A jury convicted him in December 2024 of conspiracy, four counts of honest services fraud and seven counts of bribery concerning programmes receiving federal funds, and he was sentenced on 21 March 2025 to ten years. The payments were cash and campaign contributions from Rick Rahim, Fredric Gumbinner and James Metcalf, who all pleaded guilty, and from at least five others including two FBI undercover agents. Each payer was made a sworn officer and issued official sheriff's office badges and credentials; none was trained or vetted or did any legitimate work.
inside: Businessmen bought sworn police positions and badges inside a county sheriff's office, which issued them the authority they had paid for.
cite: US Department of Justice, Western District of Virginia, release of 21 March 2025

n: Archive firms' sponsorships went to the Suceava archives chief
org_label: companies holding and processing archives in Suceava county
who: companies licensed to hold and process archives
rank: head of the Suceava County Service of the National Archives
d: The county services of Romania's National Archives, part of the interior ministry, inspect the private firms licensed to hold and process archives and can withdraw that licence. Prosecutors say that in 2011 and 2012 Simona Maria Palagheanu, head of the Suceava county service, used the office's headed paper and stamp to obtain benefits for herself and for an association she ran, the Friends of the Bucovina Archives, presented as sponsorship of archive conferences and exhibitions. Inspection teams she directed visited firms, some for the first time since they were founded in the 1990s, and the officials sent to inspect handed them sponsorship requests signed by her. The release records the opening of a criminal action in November 2014 and no later decision.
inside: Firms the archives service inspected and licensed paid into its chief's own association, with the requests handed over by her inspectors.
cite: Directia Nationala Anticoruptie, release 1572/VIII/3 of 4 November 2014

n: Developers' 1.9m dollars bought Hawaii County housing approvals
org_label: Luna Loa Developments, West View Developments and Plumeria at Waikoloa
who: three development companies and their owners
rank: housing specialist, Hawaii County Office of Housing and Community Development
d: Hawaii County's Office of Housing and Community Development approves affordable housing agreements, under which developers get land and housing credits in return for building affordable homes. Two Big Island attorneys, Paul Sulla and Gary Zamber, and a businessman, Rajesh Budhabhatti, conspired to pay a housing specialist in that office, Alan Scott Rudo, to use his position to make sure the county approved three such agreements for their companies, Luna Loa Developments, West View Developments and Plumeria at Waikoloa. The companies obtained more than 11 million dollars' worth of land and housing credits and built no units. They paid or tried to pay Rudo about 1,931,778 dollars. A federal jury convicted the three on 4 June 2025 and Rudo, who pleaded guilty and testified, was sentenced to 46 months.
inside: Developers paid the county official who handled their applications, and the county approved agreements that gave them land for homes never built.
cite: US Department of Justice, Criminal Division and District of Hawaii, release of 29 May 2026

n: Two small-business contractors' bribes drew 550m dollars of USAID contracts
org_label: Apprio, Inc. and PM Consulting Group LLC (Vistant)
rank: contracting officer, United States Agency for International Development
d: Roderick Watson was a contracting officer at the United States Agency for International Development, which runs American foreign aid. From 2013 he agreed with Darryl Britt, president of Apprio, Inc., to take bribes for using his influence to award contracts to that firm, which was certified under the Small Business Administration's 8(a) programme and so could take set-aside and sole-source work without competitive bidding. When Apprio left the programme, Walter Barnes's PM Consulting Group, trading as Vistant, became prime contractor and Apprio the subcontractor on contracts Watson awarded between 2018 and 2022. The Justice Department put the scheme at a decade and at least 14 prime contracts worth over 550 million dollars. All four men pleaded guilty in June 2025 and both companies admitted criminal liability under deferred prosecution agreements.
inside: Two contractors paid the USAID officer who awarded contracts, and the aid agency's work was set aside for the firms that paid him.
cite: US Department of Justice, Criminal Division and District of Maryland, release of 12 June 2025

n: Meal sponsors' bribes won approval for Arkansas child-feeding sites
org_label: sponsors of federal child feeding programmes in Arkansas
who: private sponsors paid to serve federally funded meals
rank: employees of the Arkansas Department of Human Services who approved feeding-programme applications
d: The US Department of Agriculture funds the Child and Adult Care Feeding Program and the Summer Food Service Program, which in Arkansas are administered by the state Department of Human Services. Sponsors apply to the department, which decides whether they qualify and approves their feeding sites, and they are then reimbursed for eligible meals. Gladys Waits and Tonique Hatton, departmental employees whose work was processing those applications and approving sites, each pleaded guilty in 2016 to conspiring to commit wire fraud and to receiving a bribe. Jacqueline Mills and Kattie Jordan were sponsors between about January 2012 and August 2014 whose programmes drew more than 2.5 million and more than 3.5 million dollars of federal money, and who paid the officials to secure approval for their programmes.
