inside: Meal sponsors paid the state officials who judged their applications, and the sites they wanted were approved and the federal money followed.
cite: US Department of Justice, Eastern District of Arkansas, releases of 30 March 2016 and 6 September 2016

n: Black Guerilla Family ran Baltimore's jail through its officers
rank: Correctional officers of the Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services at the Baltimore City Detention Center
d: A federal grand jury in Baltimore indicted 25 people in April 2013, including 13 correctional officers of the Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services, for conspiring to run the operations of the Black Guerilla Family gang inside correctional facilities. Prosecutors said the gang was dominant at the Baltimore City Detention Center and connected buildings. Officers admitted smuggling marijuana, tobacco and prescription pills for BGF leader Tavon White and others from 2011 to 2013; one met outside suppliers at the gang's direction and managed drug payments through her Green Dot account, and another warned inmates of impending searches. By June 2014, 24 of the 44 people charged had pleaded guilty, including 14 correctional officers. One defendant had died.
inside: A prison gang paid jail officers to carry its drugs and phones inside and tip off its members, so the jail's own staff served the gang.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Maryland, press releases, 23 April 2013, 5 February 2014, 27 February 2014, 27 June 2014 and 30 May 2014

n: Inmate's ring bribed staff at Maryland's Jessup prison for drugs and phones
rank: Correctional officer and correctional dietary officer, Maryland Correctional Institute Jessup
d: Correctional officer Janel Griffin pleaded guilty in October 2019 to a federal racketeering charge for smuggling narcotics, tobacco, cell phones and unauthorised flash drives into the Maryland Correctional Institute Jessup, a medium-security prison in Anne Arundel County holding about 1,100 men. Inmate Corey Alston admitted leading the conspiracy with four outside facilitators who packaged contraband and handed over bribes. Recorded jail calls confirmed Griffin met facilitators at least six times between 16 April and 14 August 2017 and took at least $2,800. A correctional dietary officer, Patricia McDaniel, admitted soliciting bribes for the same scheme. Griffin was sentenced to 27 months in November 2020.
inside: An inmate's outside helpers paid sworn prison staff, so officers of the state prison worked the contraband trade for his ring.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Maryland, press releases, 23 July 2019, 11 October 2019 and 30 November 2020

n: Bloods and DMI inmates bought officers at Maryland's largest prison
org_label: Bloods and Dead Man Incorporated prison gangs
rank: Correctional officers, Eastern Correctional Institution, Westover
d: Two correctional officers at the Eastern Correctional Institution near Westover, the largest state prison in Maryland, pleaded guilty in November 2016 to a racketeering conspiracy. Rachelle Hankerson admitted taking payments from inmates and outside facilitators to bring in narcotics, cell phones and tobacco, charging at least $500 a package, and smuggling for a co-defendant who belonged to the Bloods gang. Stephen Wise admitted accepting bribes from at least eight inmates, including a leader of the Dead Man Incorporated prison gang who had given him about $1,500. Both also pleaded guilty to deprivation of rights for their part in the stabbing of inmates who had crossed them.
inside: Prison gangs and their outside helpers paid guards at a state prison, so the officers supplied contraband and turned violence on chosen inmates.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Maryland, press releases, 18 November 2016 and 22 November 2016

n: Supermax sergeant in North Carolina sold phones to the inmates he guarded
org_label: Prisoners of Polk's high security maximum control unit
rank: Sergeant and supervisor, high security maximum control unit, Polk Correctional Institution
d: A federal grand jury in Raleigh indicted two former correctional officers of Polk Correctional Institution in Butner, North Carolina in August 2015. Prosecutors alleged that Gregory Dustin Gouldman, a sergeant and supervisor in Polk's high security maximum control unit, North Carolina's supermax for its most violent offenders, ran a scheme with a number of prisoners held there under which he smuggled tobacco, marijuana, mobile telephones and batteries to them for cash, and that he carried on after being transferred out in September 2014. The inmates used the phones to speak to people outside. The investigation was prompted by a kidnapping conspiracy alleged to have been directed by inmate Kelvin Melton using a phone in his cell.
inside: Prisoners paid the sergeant who supervised their unit to bring in phones they then used to direct crimes outside the prison.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of North Carolina, press release, 24 August 2015

n: Indictment: a Miami drug enterprise relied on corrupt county jail officers
rank: Correctional officers, Miami-Dade Corrections and Rehabilitation Department
d: A sealed indictment unsealed in December 2024 in the Southern District of Florida charged Vernell Syrethia Lawson, a former Miami-Dade correctional officer, and Gabrielle Nicole Bess-Mills in a continuing criminal enterprise led by Terrance Carter. According to the indictment, Carter led a drug trafficking organisation that relied on the corruption of Lawson and other Miami-Dade correctional officers, with trafficking associates, to bring narcotics and other contraband into Miami-Dade County jail facilities for sale. Lawson faces racketeering promotion through bribery and drug trafficking counts and a Hobbs Act extortion under colour of official right conspiracy count. A task force formed by the county's police and corrections departments investigated. An indictment contains mere allegations and the defendants are presumed innocent.
inside: Prosecutors allege a drug organisation bought county jail officers, so the officers moved its narcotics inside the jails it wanted to supply.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida, press release, 20 December 2024

n: Traffickers paid a Texas deputy $10,000 to stage a cocaine seizure
org_label: a cocaine trafficking organisation in the Rio Grande Valley
rank: Deputy, Hidalgo County Sheriff's Office
d: Baldemar Cardenas, a deputy with the Hidalgo County Sheriff's Office in south Texas, pleaded guilty in April 2022 to conspiring to possess cocaine with intent to distribute, and was sentenced in January 2025 to 46 months in federal prison. He admitted that in January 2020 he conspired with a drug trafficking organisation whose members stole highly pure cocaine from their supplier and replaced it with sham bundles of 1.5 per cent purity. In exchange for $10,000, Cardenas fed information to local law enforcement so that the fake bundles were seized, falsely claiming it came from a confidential source. About 33 kilograms of sham bundles were seized in Mission. The court noted the serious issues with law enforcement authorities assisting drug traffickers.
inside: A trafficking group paid a serving sheriff's deputy, who then used police powers to stage a seizure that covered the group's theft of real cocaine.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas, press releases, 1 April 2022 and 28 January 2025

n: Detainee's ring paid a Philadelphia jail officer to carry in drugs and knives
rank: Correctional officer, Philadelphia Industrial Correctional Center, Philadelphia Department of Prisons
d: Three Philadelphians pleaded guilty in April and May 2025 over a scheme to smuggle drugs, phones, chargers, cigarettes and knives into the Philadelphia Industrial Correctional Center between April and July 2021. Ahmad Nasir, who was then held there before trial, worked with Jawayne Brown, who was not in custody, and Breyanna Cornish, then a correctional officer employed by the Philadelphia Department of Prisons, along with other associates, to buy and assemble the contraband. Cornish carried it into the jail, Nasir sold it to other inmates at a profit, and Nasir then told associates to pay Cornish for her part. The charges included conspiracy to commit federal programme bribery and drug distribution counts.
inside: A detainee's outside associates paid a serving jail officer, so the officer supplied the goods he resold inside the jail that held him.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania, press release, 2 May 2025

n: Honolulu jail officer took cash to carry methamphetamine to an inmate
org_label: methamphetamine suppliers outside the Oahu Community Correctional Center
who: methamphetamine suppliers and an inmate customer
rank: Correctional officer, Oahu Community Correctional Center
d: Richard Ascencio worked as a correctional officer at the Oahu Community Correctional Center from 2000 until his arrest in 2020. He pleaded guilty in September 2022 to conspiring to distribute methamphetamine and possessing it with intent to distribute, and was sentenced in December 2023 to 42 months in prison and two years of supervised release. He had agreed to smuggle methamphetamine into the centre and hand it to an inmate for cash payments, obtaining the drugs from co-conspirators outside the jail, hiding them in his backpack and using his position as an officer to try to get past security. Investigators found 11 packets in his backpack when he reported for duty on 12 February 2020.
inside: Drug suppliers outside the jail paid a serving officer to be their carrier, so the jail's own security checks were the thing he bypassed for them.
cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Hawaii, press release, 13 December 2023

n: Militia factions split the directorates of Iraq's main intelligence service
org_label: Shi'a Coordination Framework militias, including Kata'ib Sayyid al-Shuhada and the Popular Mobilisation Forces leadership
rank: Director of Counterintelligence and Director of Surveillance, Iraqi National Intelligence Service
d: CTC Sentinel reported that from October 2022 the Iran-aligned militias of Iraq's Shi'a Coordination Framework purged officials promoted under the previous prime minister and installed their own in the Iraqi National Intelligence Service, the country's premier intelligence agency. The authors say the senior INIS directorates were, for the first time, split between the factions, which avoided putting a militia-linked figure at the head of the service itself. The Director of Counterintelligence appointed in early 2023 is named as Faisal Ghazi al-Lami, a nephew of the US-designated Popular Mobilisation Forces chairman Falah al-Fayyadh and a long-term protege of the Kata'ib Sayyid al-Shuhada leader Abu Alaa al-Wala'i; the Director of Surveillance, Wissam al-Mihyawi, was nominated by al-Fayyadh. The authors say liaison with Western intelligence agencies was downgraded as a result.
inside: Armed factions placed their own relatives and proteges in charge of counterintelligence and surveillance, so the spy service stopped working closely with Western agencies.
cite: Michael Knights, Crispin Smith and Hamdi Malik, 'Iraq's New Regime Change: How Tehran-Backed Terrorist Organizations and Militias Captured the Iraqi State', CTC Sentinel, December 2023

n: Militias nominated most 2023 recruits to Iraq's counter-terror force
org_label: Shi'a Coordination Framework militias, including Kata'ib Hezbollah and Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq
rank: Recruit intake and leadership of Iraq's Counter-Terrorism Command
d: Iraq's Counter-Terrorism Command was built with United States help and is described by CTC Sentinel as the country's most effective military force. The authors write that the militias of the Shi'a Coordination Framework moved quickly to penetrate and compromise it after the government formed in October 2022, and that the force is opening its doors to their recruits to an unprecedented extent. Research by Militia Spotlight, the project the authors run, suggests that 2,400 of the 2,900 new recruits taken on in 2023 were nominated by Coordination Framework players, among them the US-designated terrorist organisations Kata'ib Hezbollah and Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq, and also by non-designated figures such as Nouri al-Maliki and the Badr Organization. A wide-ranging leadership reshuffle was under way at the time of publication.
inside: Armed groups supplied most of a year's recruits to the state's best counter-terrorism force, putting their own people inside the unit meant to police them.
cite: Michael Knights, Crispin Smith and Hamdi Malik, 'Iraq's New Regime Change: How Tehran-Backed Terrorist Organizations and Militias Captured the Iraqi State', CTC Sentinel, December 2023

n: AAH fighter made deputy director of Iraq's security service
rank: Deputy director, director of operations and head of Baghdad security operations, National Security Service
d: The National Security Service is Iraq's domestic security service and has the largest authorised manpower of any Iraqi intelligence agency. CTC Sentinel reported that it was the next agency transferred to the control of the Iran-aligned militias after the government formed in October 2022, and that it had been strongly penetrated by their operators since its inception. The authors say the most significant of the director-level changes made under the new government was the appointment of an Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq fighter, Ahmed al-Tayyar, as deputy director of the service in January 2023, and that the posts of director of operations and head of Baghdad security operations also seem to have fallen to officials of the group. The United States has designated Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq a terrorist organisation.
inside: A designated armed group put one of its fighters in the second seat of the state's largest domestic intelligence agency and took two more of its command posts.
cite: Michael Knights, Crispin Smith and Hamdi Malik, 'Iraq's New Regime Change: How Tehran-Backed Terrorist Organizations and Militias Captured the Iraqi State', CTC Sentinel, December 2023

n: Airport security at Baghdad handed to an Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq-controlled official
rank: Official in charge of security operations at Baghdad International Airport
d: CTC Sentinel reported that after the government formed in October 2022 the Iran-aligned militias restaffed Iraq's airport, port, border and customs positions, which the authors describe as vital for counter-intelligence and for the suppression of dissidents because they tell the government who and what enters and leaves the country. The Iraqi National Intelligence Service lost its longstanding primacy for security operations inside Baghdad International Airport, and the role was given to an official the authors describe as controlled by Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq, Mazin al-Shibli, who had previously been Director of Operations of Iraq's Civil Aviation Authority. The United States has designated Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq a terrorist organisation.
inside: A designated armed group's man took over security screening at the country's main airport, deciding who and what passes through it.
cite: Michael Knights, Crispin Smith and Hamdi Malik, 'Iraq's New Regime Change: How Tehran-Backed Terrorist Organizations and Militias Captured the Iraqi State', CTC Sentinel, December 2023

n: Iraq's main port and land border posts divided among four armed factions
org_label: Badr Organization, Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq, Kataib Jund al-Imam and PMF Brigade 6
who: Badr, Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq, Kataib Jund al-Imam and PMF Brigade 6
rank: Control of security posts at Umm Qasr port and Iraq's land points of entry
d: Umm Qasr is Iraq's main deep-water port, on the Gulf south of Basra. CTC Sentinel reported that after the government formed in October 2022 control of the port and of Iraq's land points of entry was split among Shi'a Coordination Framework actors from the Badr Organization, Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq, Kataib Jund al-Imam and Ahmed al-Asadi's Popular Mobilisation Forces Brigade 6, with observers from the prime minister's office posted in each area. The authors place this in a wider restaffing of airport, port, border and customs positions, which they say the factions valued because the posts tell whoever holds them exactly who and what is entering and leaving the country, including through the Kurdistan Region.
inside: Armed factions took the border and port posts that decide what enters the country, so customs and entry control answered to them.
cite: Michael Knights, Crispin Smith and Hamdi Malik, 'Iraq's New Regime Change: How Tehran-Backed Terrorist Organizations and Militias Captured the Iraqi State', CTC Sentinel, December 2023

n: Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq ran Iraq's industry ministry and looted the Bayji refinery
rank: Ministry of Industry and Mines
d: CTC Sentinel reported that the US-designated terrorist organisation Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq entered Iraq's parliament from 2014 and gained control of the Ministry of Industry and Mines from 2014 to 2018, a period when the ministry had only an acting, part-time minister, Mohammed Shia al-Sudani, who later became prime minister and who the author says has a demonstrated close working relationship with the group's leader, Qais al-Khazali. The author writes that the group's well-documented exploitation of the ministry allowed it to corner the scrap metal market, then to loot the Bayji refinery, and finally to dominate the private sector metals industry. From there, he writes, it moved into the theft of heavily subsidised fuel oil allocated to state-run industries.
inside: An armed group took charge of the ministry that oversees state industry and used its paperwork to take the scrap trade, a refinery and the metals market.
cite: Michael Knights, 'Iraqi Oil and the Iran Threat Network', CTC Sentinel, April 2025

n: Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq picked senior grades in Iraq's ministries
org_label: Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq and other Shi'a Coordination Framework militias
who: Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq and allied militias
rank: 'Special grades' in Iraqi ministries: director-generals, deputy director-generals and general managers
d: CTC Sentinel reported that control of an Iraqi ministry now turns less on naming the minister than on what share of its 'special grades', meaning director-generals, deputy director-generals and general managers, goes to a given faction. The authors say the prime minister gave way on this after an argument with the Shi'a Coordination Framework, and that the horse-trading is arranged at the Prime Minister's Office, where factions send representatives to deal with a broker, Abdal-Karim al-Sudani, a relative of the prime minister. They write that he receives nominations on the hiring and firing of grades allocated to the US-designated Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq, delivered by Laith al-Khazali, a senior member and brother of its leader.
inside: A designated armed group chose who filled the senior civil service posts that sign off ministry spending, so its own contracts and jobs went through.
cite: Michael Knights, Crispin Smith and Hamdi Malik, 'Iraq's New Regime Change: How Tehran-Backed Terrorist Organizations and Militias Captured the Iraqi State', CTC Sentinel, December 2023

n: Iraqi oil officials kept their jobs only with a militia patron
org_label: Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq and the Badr Organization
rank: Director-generals and the deputy minister for upstream, Ministry of Oil
d: Iraq's Ministry of Oil earns about 85 per cent of government revenue. CTC Sentinel reported that from October 2022 every director-general was reviewed from the top down, and quoted a ministry employee as saying officials were left alone if they had a militia behind them and removed if they did not. The authors say officials who had looked to the cleric Ammar al-Hakim's faction for protection moved towards Badr and, most often, Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq, and that the head of the Petroleum Contracting and Licensing Directorate switched from Badr to Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq protection after October 2022. They write that the most powerful figure in the ministry is not the minister but a deputy minister, Bassim Khudair, whose power came from Qais al-Khazali, Hadi al-Ameri and the Iranian embassy.
inside: Armed groups made their protection the condition of keeping a senior oil ministry job, so the officials who award oil contracts worked for them.
cite: Michael Knights, Crispin Smith and Hamdi Malik, 'Iraq's New Regime Change: How Tehran-Backed Terrorist Organizations and Militias Captured the Iraqi State', CTC Sentinel, December 2023

n: Militia chief al-Kikli arranged the chairmanship of Libya's Waha Oil Company
org_label: Abdel Ghani al-Kikli's Stability Support Apparatus
rank: Chairman, Waha Oil Company
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Libya found that Farhat Bengdara, appointed chairman of the National Oil Corporation in July 2022 with the backing of the Haftar family, ran staffing and governance practices that weakened the corporation's capacity to act as an independent state body and enabled control by armed group actors or their associates. The Panel records that Bengdara also coordinated directly with the Tripoli armed group leader Abdel Ghani al-Kikli over the appointment of the chairman of the Waha Oil Company, one of the corporation's main production subsidiaries. That chairman was arrested in February 2025 by the Attorney General's Office on financial crime charges. Bengdara resigned with effect from 16 January 2025, and after his immunity was lifted the Attorney General issued an arrest warrant.
inside: An armed group leader helped choose who chaired a state oil subsidiary, so its contracts and payments could be steered to his network.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, S/2026/224, 24 March 2026, annex 9 ('Armed groups' footprint on the oil sector'), paras. 4-12

n: Iraq gave the militia-owned Muhandis company 1.2 million acres of state land
org_label: Popular Mobilisation Forces and Kata'ib Hezbollah
rank: Muhandis General Company for Construction, Engineering, and Mechanical, Agricultural, and Industrial Contracting
d: The Muhandis General Company, announced in November 2022 and named after the late US-designated terrorist Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, is officially owned by the Popular Mobilisation Forces, according to its articles of incorporation. CTC Sentinel reported that, uniquely among Iraqi state companies, it needs neither cabinet nor parliamentary approval to receive free land, state capital or state-owned enterprises, or to carry out construction and demolition. In December 2022 it received 1.2 million acres of government land along the Iraqi-Saudi border at no cost, an area half the size of Lebanon. The authors note that a Popular Mobilisation Forces unit had already seized and cordoned off the Muthanna land parcel before the company was formed. The government has since tried to bury the story and slow the company's growth.
inside: A militia-owned state company was handed a vast block of public land for nothing, without the approvals other state firms need.
cite: Michael Knights, Crispin Smith and Hamdi Malik, 'Iraq's New Regime Change: How Tehran-Backed Terrorist Organizations and Militias Captured the Iraqi State', CTC Sentinel, December 2023

n: Iraq's state tanker firm gave a smuggler a no-bid fuel oil deal
org_label: Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq and the Al-Iraqia Shipping Services & Oil Trading network
rank: Fuel oil marketing and export contract of the Iraqi Oil Tankers Company
d: CTC Sentinel reported that the Iraqi government of Prime Minister Adel Abdal-Mahdi, which the author describes as dominated by Iran-backed militias including Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq, moved the marketing of fuel oil away from the State Oil Marketing Organization and gave the task to the state-owned Iraqi Oil Tankers Company. Multiple reporting networks claim that the tanker company then awarded Al-Iraqia Shipping Services & Oil Trading FZE an exclusive, sole-source, no-bid and low fixed-price contract to buy, transport, store and export Iraqi fuel oil through the Khor al-Zubayr port in Basra. The Minister of Oil, Thamer Ghadban, calculated the loss to Iraq from under-valuing that fuel oil at $250 million a year. The scheme was shut down in 2019 and implicated ministry officials were removed.
inside: Militia-backed officials shifted fuel oil marketing to a state tanker firm, which then handed one allied company the export trade with no competition.
cite: Michael Knights, 'Iraqi Oil and the Iran Threat Network', CTC Sentinel, April 2025

n: Report: Iraq's top judge was groomed by a militia commander
org_label: Kata'ib Hezbollah, Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq and Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis's network
rank: Head of the Supreme Judicial Council and the Federal Supreme Court's bench
d: CTC Sentinel reported that Iraq's most senior judge, Faiq Zaydan of the Supreme Judicial Council, issued a flurry of rulings through the subordinate Federal Supreme Court in February 2022, during a tense government formation period, that damaged the effort by Moqtada al-Sadr's bloc to form a government without the Iran-aligned factions. The most important changed the rules so that a simple 165-seat majority was no longer enough and a two-thirds majority of 218 seats was needed, which made excluding those factions mathematically impossible. In the assessment of the authors' Militia Spotlight project, Zaydan is one of a number of judges groomed by the militias, specifically by Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis from around 2004, and traded made-to-order rulings for their support for his continued leadership of the judiciary.
inside: Researchers say armed groups cultivated the judge at the top of the court system, which then rewrote the rules so they could not be shut out of government.
cite: Michael Knights, Crispin Smith and Hamdi Malik, 'Iraq's New Regime Change: How Tehran-Backed Terrorist Organizations and Militias Captured the Iraqi State', CTC Sentinel, December 2023

n: Houthis seized Yemen Gulf Bank and made a custodian's nephew its custodian
rank: Judicial custodian of Yemen Gulf Bank
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen reported that the Houthis' seizure of commercial enterprises and financial institutions continued, and listed the seizure of Yemen Gulf Bank in July 2025 among recent developments. Raed Al-Shaer, a nephew of the former judicial custodian Saleh Mesfer Saleh Al Shaer, who is on the Security Council sanctions list, was appointed judicial custodian of the bank. A judicial custodian is an officer appointed to hold and manage property, and the Panel has reported in earlier years that the Houthi custodianship system was used to take over private firms through court orders made without the owners present. The Panel cited a Yemeni news report for the appointment.
inside: The movement put a relative of its asset custodian in legal charge of a private bank, so the bank's money was run by its own people.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2025/650, para. 124 (a)

n: Houthi decree moved Al-Amal Microfinance Bank inside a Sana'a ministry
rank: Al-Amal Microfinance Bank, placed under the Ministry of Social Affairs and Labour
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen reported that the Ministry of Social Affairs and Labour, under Houthi control in Sana'a, absorbed Al-Amal Microfinance Bank. The Panel published the decree that did it: Republican Decree No. 12 of 1446 AH, issued from the office of the prime minister in Sana'a, which sets out the ministry's objectives, duties and main organisational divisions and lists Al-Amal Microfinance Bank as one of the ministry's sectors, alongside the Social Fund for Development. The Panel reproduced five pages of the original decree in its annex and described it as the Houthi presidential decree of the takeover. The Panel places the step within a continuing pattern of Houthi seizures of commercial enterprises and financial institutions.
inside: A decree wrote a microfinance bank into the structure of a ministry the movement controls, so its lending sits under Houthi administration.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2025/650, para. 124 and annex 85 ('Decree on the takeover of Al Amal Microfinance Bank')

n: Houthi asset custodian made himself president of a Yemeni orphans charity
rank: President, Orphans Development Foundation (Al-Yateem)
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen listed the Orphans Development Foundation, also known as Al-Yateem, among the assets appropriated by Major General Saleh Mesfer Alshaer, the Houthi judicial custodian who was also assistant minister of defence for logistics. Its original owner is given as Hamdi Zayad of Islah. The Panel's table of entities appropriated by Alshaer records that Alshaer himself is president of the foundation. The Panel identified a transfer to the foundation from Save the Children and a deposit of 24 million Yemeni rials, about $48,000, for a project, and noted that the foundation and its subsidiary training institute had reported projects funded by Care International and Human Appeal Australia.
inside: The movement's asset custodian took the presidency of a charity he had seized, so its aid funds and projects ran under his control.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2020/326, paras. 88-89, table 4 and annex 26, tables 26.1 and 26.2

n: Houthi custodian's seizures ran through Sana'a's specialised criminal court
rank: Specialized criminal court, Sana'a, and its custodianship orders
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen found that Major General Saleh Mesfer Alshaer, the Houthi judicial custodian, used a Sana'a-based network made up of family members, the specialized criminal court, the national security bureau, the Central Bank of Yemen in Sana'a, the registrar services of the ministry of trade and industry and some private banks. The Panel found that the court orders in question were not issued after due legal process and were issued in the absence of the victims, and that it had seen nothing in them to suggest the seizures were demanded by the necessities of the conflict. The Panel described a method based on extortion, intimidation and the illegal arrest of company managers and bank directors, threatened with accusations of spying unless they complied.
inside: The movement used a criminal court to issue custody orders over private firms without hearing the owners, giving its seizures legal cover.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2020/326, paras. 88-89, table 4 and annex 26, tables 26.1 and 26.2

n: Yemen's security bureau arrested bank bosses for a Houthi custodian
rank: National security bureau, Sana'a
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen found that the Houthi judicial custodian Major General Saleh Mesfer Alshaer used a Sana'a-based network that included the national security bureau to appropriate companies and banks. The Panel named Major General Motlaq Amer al-Marrani, described as the former deputy head of the national security bureau, as having played a significant role by orchestrating the arrest of bank owners, managers and staffers. It listed the arrests and alleged torture of Ahmed Saleh Ali Arrahbi, owner of the firm Yemen Armored, across three spells between early December 2018 and late October 2019, and the arrests of the managing directors of Tadhamon International Islamic Bank, Yemen Kuwait Bank and the International Bank of Yemen, as well as owners of money exchangers.
inside: The movement's custodian had the state security service arrest bank bosses until they handed over their firms, turning policing into seizure.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2020/326, paras. 88-89, table 4 and annex 26, tables 26.1 and 26.2

n: Militia network recruited Iraqi intelligence officers in Baghdad
org_label: Kata'ib Hezbollah and Kata'ib Sayyid al-Shuhada operatives with the IRGC Quds Force
who: Kata'ib Hezbollah and Kata'ib Sayyid al-Shuhada operatives
rank: Director-generals of the National Security Service and the Iraqi National Intelligence Service; deputy interior minister for intelligence
d: CTC Sentinel reported that Mohammad Baqer al-Saadi, whom the US government alleges is a high-level member of Kata'ib Hezbollah, recruited Iraqi security officials to pass classified government information to Iran and to Iraqi armed factions. According to one Iraqi reporting network the authors consider credible, the work was supported by an IRGC Quds Force officer in Baghdad, the Kata'ib Sayyid al-Shuhada head Abu Alaa al-Walai and the head of Iraq's National Security Service, who brought officers to meeting houses to offer career help for information. They say that in late 2025 a deputy of al-Saadi and his wife, a director general in the service, allegedly gathered compromised officers at an MP's house in Jadriya, joined by two more director generals and the deputy interior minister for intelligence.
inside: Researchers say militia operatives signed up serving Iraqi intelligence officers, who then passed state secrets to the armed factions and Iran.
cite: Michael Knights, Crispin Smith and Hamdi Malik, 'Mohammad Baqer al-Saadi: Profiling an IRGC and Iraqi Militia Operative', CTC Sentinel, May 2026

n: Houthis installed the defence minister and ran Yemen's ministry from inside
rank: Minister of Defence and the senior staff of the Ministry of Defence, Sana'a
d: CTC Sentinel reported that after overrunning Sana'a in September 2014 the Houthis directly controlled the ministries of defence and interior for the first time, and that inside the defence ministry they progressively co-opted generals from the Saleh era to serve alongside, and quickly under, senior Houthis. The authors name the Houthi-installed Minister of Defence, Staff Major General Mohammed Nasser al-Atifi, as the most famous turncoat, writing that he attended Houthi ideological re-education, swore an oath of allegiance on the Qur'an and takes an active part in Houthi propaganda. They describe the power behind the minister as Staff Lieutenant General Mohammed Abdalkarim al-Ghammari, designated by the US and the UN in 2021, who from 2014 became the senior Houthi in the ministry with a team of deputies.
inside: The movement kept the ministry's name and staff but put its own men at the top, so Yemen's defence ministry took its orders.
cite: Michael Knights, Adnan al-Gabarni and Casey Coombs, 'The Houthi Jihad Council: Command and Control in ‘the Other Hezbollah’', CTC Sentinel, October 2022

n: Houthi leader's relative made Yemen's interior minister after the police fight
rank: Minister of Interior, Sana'a
d: CTC Sentinel reported that the Houthis took direct control of Yemen's interior ministry, which runs the police, after overrunning Sana'a in September 2014. Inside the ministry a slow-burning struggle for control of the police forces began with loyalists of the former president Ali Abdallah Saleh. The authors write that the struggle ended with Saleh's death at the hands of the Houthis in December 2017 and the appointment of Abdalkarim al-Houthi as Minister of Interior in 2019. The authors elsewhere describe Abdalkarim as regularly named among the top three power blocs within the Houthi movement, and cite one report placing him as the designated successor to the movement's leader, Abdalmalik al-Houthi.
inside: A senior figure of the armed movement took the ministry that commands the police, ending a contest for control of the force.
cite: Michael Knights, Adnan al-Gabarni and Casey Coombs, 'The Houthi Jihad Council: Command and Control in ‘the Other Hezbollah’', CTC Sentinel, October 2022

n: Houthi 'supervisors' sat inside every Yemeni ministry and major military unit
rank: Houthi supervisors (mushrifeen) attached to ministries, districts and military units
d: CTC Sentinel describes the Houthi movement's practice of placing local supervisors, known as mushrifeen, across all districts in Yemen and within all ministries and major military units, which the authors compare to a political commissar system of surveillance and parallel authority. They credit the senior Houthi commander Abdullah al-Hakim, known as Abu Ali, with a major role in establishing it, citing reporting by Al Masdar Online. The same reporting is cited for the Houthi shadow government, described as a parallel system of supervisory bodies in which real policy-making authority is vested, under which the formal Yemeni government architecture exists to execute Houthi orders. Those bodies include a General Council, an Executive Council and a Judicial Council, almost all run by the movement leader's hand-picked cadre.
inside: The movement attached its own watchers to each ministry and unit, so formal officials carried out decisions made in a parallel structure.
cite: Michael Knights, Adnan al-Gabarni and Casey Coombs, 'The Houthi Jihad Council: Command and Control in ‘the Other Hezbollah’', CTC Sentinel, October 2022

n: Yemen's presidential guard purged and filled with Houthi recruits
rank: Four Presidential Protection Brigades and the Central Region command, Sana'a
d: The Presidential Protection Brigades were the post-2012 renaming of the Republican Guards of the former president Ali Abdallah Saleh, and served under Saleh and his nephew until the Houthi-Saleh showdown of December 2017. CTC Sentinel reported that in the months leading up to and just after Saleh's death the brigades were purged of Saleh loyalists and bolstered with Houthi recruits, and that they are now led by a Houthi fighter, Abdallah Yahya al-Hasani. The authors assess that after seven years of re-staffing and indoctrination the brigades represent a fusion of Saleh-era elite equipment, selected Republican Guard officers, Houthi supervisors and fighters, and Houthi-recruited troops. They place tactical control of all military forces in Sana'a with Abdalkhaliq al-Huthi, a full brother of the movement's leader.
inside: The movement cleared the old guard out of the units that protect the capital and filled them with its own fighters and watchers.
cite: Michael Knights, Adnan al-Gabarni and Casey Coombs, 'The Houthi Jihad Council: Command and Control in ‘the Other Hezbollah’', CTC Sentinel, October 2022

n: Houthis emptied Yemen's army and refilled it through a new body
rank: General Mobilization Authority within the Ministry of Defence; Yemeni Army brigades
d: CTC Sentinel reported that since 2014, and particularly since the 2017 break with Ali Abdallah Saleh and his generals, the Houthi-run defence ministry has encouraged professional officers and personnel to take extended, partly paid home leave. The authors write that the resulting gaps in manpower were filled by a new General Mobilization Authority inside the ministry, with an estimated 130,000 recruits from poorer parts of society for whom about $30 a month was better than unemployment. The authority is run by Abdalrahim al-Humran, who instructs local Houthi governorate supervisors, neighbourhood affairs managers and neighbourhood sheikhs to comb households for military-age males. The authors add that Houthi militias were folded into the ministry's structure for legitimacy, payment and support, and that Houthi sub-units are nested within surviving army brigades.
inside: The movement pushed career soldiers out on leave and refilled the army through a recruiting body its own supervisors staffed.
cite: Michael Knights, Adnan al-Gabarni and Casey Coombs, 'The Houthi Jihad Council: Command and Control in ‘the Other Hezbollah’', CTC Sentinel, October 2022

n: AFC/M23 named the neighbourhood chiefs of Goma and Karisimbi
rank: Neighbourhood chiefs and deputy chiefs, communes of Goma and Karisimbi
d: The UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo reported that, under a provincial order of 1 April 2026, the armed group AFC/M23 designated an extensive network of neighbourhood-level authorities across the communes of Goma and Karisimbi, covering both primary and deputy positions. The Group listed the appointees by name: eight neighbourhood chiefs with their deputies in Goma commune, among them Himbi, Mapendo, Lac-Vert, Kyeshero, Les Volcans, Katindo and Mikeno, and ten more in Karisimbi commune, among them Mabanga-Nord, Mabanga-Sud, Katoyi, Kasika, Majengo, Virunga, Mugunga, Ndosho, Kahembe, Murara and Bujovu. The Group obtained the documents from a confidential source and sets the appointments within the group's parallel administration, which it has documented since 2022.
inside: The armed group filled the lowest tier of local government in the city it holds, so street-level authority answered to it.
cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, S/2026/466, annex 27 ('Additional information on the AFC/M23 governance structure')

n: US designated four Hezbollah officials sitting in Lebanon's parliament
rank: Members of the Lebanese parliament for Hizballah's Loyalty to the Resistance Bloc
d: On 21 May 2026 the US Treasury designated nine people in Lebanon for obstructing the peace process and impeding the disarmament of Hizballah, saying they were embedded across Lebanon's parliament, military and security sectors. Four are serving or former members of parliament. Mohamed Abdel-Mottaleb Fanich leads Hizballah's executive council, was elected for its Loyalty to the Resistance Bloc in 1992 and was later made Minister of Youth and Sports. Hassan Nizammeddine Fadlallah has been an elected Hizballah member of parliament since 2005. Ibrahim al-Moussawi heads Hizballah's media committee and is one of its elected representatives. Hussein Al-Hajj Hassan, a member since 1982 and an MP since 1996, is described as a key figure opposing the group's disarmament. All four were designated as acting on Hizballah's behalf.
inside: An armed movement's own senior officials hold parliamentary seats, which the US says they use to block the state's demand that it disarm.
cite: US Department of the Treasury, Office of Foreign Assets Control, press release, 21 May 2026, 'Treasury Targets Hizballah-Aligned Officials Obstructing Peace and Disarmament'

n: Sanctioned Malian figure paid as adviser to the transition council
org_label: Coordination of Azawad Movements-linked networks in Mali's north
who: Mohamed Ould Mataly, under UN sanctions for armed obstruction
rank: Special adviser to the President of the National Transition Council, Bamako
d: Mohamed Ould Mataly is listed under the Mali sanctions regime as MLi.008 and is subject to an asset freeze and travel ban. The UN Panel of Experts on Mali recorded that he was appointed special adviser to the President of the National Transition Council, the body that stood in for parliament after Mali's 2020 coup, in March 2021. He first told the Panel he had received no remuneration since taking office and that his bank account was almost depleted. In the following year's report the Panel recorded that he confirmed, contrary to what he had said before, that he received monthly remuneration from the Government of Mali in that capacity. The Panel found that there had been no effective implementation of the asset freeze by the Government of Mali.
inside: A man under UN sanctions for armed obstruction took a paid advisory post at the top of Mali's stand-in parliament, drawing a state salary.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Mali, final report S/2022/595, paras. 130 and 134, and S/2021/714, para. 114

n: Officer took more than $80,000 from inmates to run contraband into FCI Jesup
who: A contraband trafficking ring run by inmates of FCI Jesup and their outside associates
rank: Correctional officer, Federal Correctional Institution Jesup, Georgia
d: The Federal Correctional Institution at Jesup, Georgia is a US federal prison, and the Bureau of Prisons officers who staff it control everything that comes through the door. In the spring and summer of 2022 a trafficking ring operating inside the prison used one of those officers to get its goods in. Ashley Brown, 36, a Bureau of Prisons correctional officer, was paid more than $80,000 by inmates and people acting for them, and in return carried their contraband past the searches she was employed to run. She pleaded guilty on 3 February 2026 to 24 counts of a public official accepting a bribe and 16 counts of money laundering. The other seven defendants were inmates of the prison, and all have been found guilty.
inside: A prison trafficking ring paid the officer who searched the door more than $80,000, so the federal prison's own staff carried the ring's drugs inside for it.
cite: United States v. Ashley Brown et al., S.D. Ga.; Department of Justice press release, 3 February 2026
org_label: Inmate contraband ring inside FCI Jesup

n: Brooklyn federal jail officer charged with taking bribes to smuggle for inmates
who: Inmates of the Metropolitan Detention Center and those acting for them
rank: Correctional officer, Metropolitan Detention Center, Brooklyn
d: The Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn is the main federal jail in New York City, holding people awaiting trial. On 18 April 2023 prosecutors in Brooklyn unsealed a criminal complaint against Quandelle Joseph, a serving Bureau of Prisons correctional officer there, charging him with receiving bribes in exchange for supplying contraband to inmates. The US Attorney said he had accepted tens of thousands of dollars to carry goods past the jail's searches. Joseph was arrested that morning and released on bond pending trial. The figures and the conduct are the government's allegation in a charging document, not a finding of a court, and the case had not reached a verdict when this release was issued.
inside: Inmates paid a serving officer of the federal jail holding them to bring their goods through the door, putting the jail's own guard on their payroll.
cite: United States v. Quandelle Joseph, E.D.N.Y., criminal complaint unsealed 18 April 2023; Department of Justice press release, 18 April 2023
org_label: Inmate contraband network at MDC Brooklyn

n: Second Brooklyn federal jail officer indicted over inmate bribe payments
who: Inmates of the Metropolitan Detention Center running a contraband operation, and their outside helpers
rank: Correctional officer, Metropolitan Detention Center, Brooklyn
d: On 14 October 2026 federal prosecutors in Brooklyn unsealed an indictment against Melissa Brooks, a correctional officer of the US Bureau of Prisons assigned to the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, the federal jail for New York City. The indictment charges her with taking bribes as a public official and with conspiring to do so, and says she agreed to accept illegal payments from inmates and from others acting on behalf of inmates who were smuggling contraband into the jail. She was arrested that morning and arraigned the same afternoon. This is a separate case from the 2023 charge against another officer at the same jail, and both are allegations in charging documents rather than findings of a court.
inside: A second officer at the same federal jail is accused of agreeing to take inmates' money to let their contraband operation run through her post.
cite: United States v. Melissa Brooks, E.D.N.Y., indictment unsealed 14 October 2026; Department of Justice press release, 14 October 2026
org_label: Inmate contraband network at MDC Brooklyn

n: Jury convicted FCI Williamsburg officer paid $56,791 by inmates' families
who: Inmates of FCI Williamsburg and the family and associates who paid for them
rank: Correctional officer, Federal Correctional Institution Williamsburg, South Carolina
d: Angela Crosland, 51, worked as a correctional officer at the Federal Correctional Institution Williamsburg, a federal prison at Salters, South Carolina. A federal jury in Florence convicted her on 3 February 2025, after a two-day trial, of bribery, money laundering, distributing methamphetamine and suboxone, and filing false tax returns. The evidence included records of her Cash App account, a mobile payment service, showing $56,791 paid in over about nine months by the families and associates of inmates held at the prison. In exchange she carried contraband inside: suboxone, methamphetamine, paper soaked in the synthetic drug K2, marijuana, tobacco and food. She did not declare the income on her tax returns.
inside: Inmates' families paid an officer $56,791 through a phone app, and she carried their drugs into the federal prison she was employed to keep them out of.
cite: United States v. Angela Crosland, D.S.C., jury verdict 3 February 2025; Department of Justice press releases, 3 February 2025 and 2025
org_label: Inmate contraband network at FCI Williamsburg

n: MCC New York officer took $77,894 from inmates and tried to have an informer beaten
who: Inmates of the Metropolitan Correctional Center and their associates outside
rank: Correctional officer, Metropolitan Correctional Center, Manhattan
d: The Metropolitan Correctional Center in Manhattan was the federal jail beside the New York courthouses. Perry Joyner, a Bureau of Prisons correctional officer there, took about $77,894 in bribes from inmates or their associates between October 2019 and February 2020 and in return smuggled contraband into the jail. When he believed one inmate was reporting him to law enforcement, he tried to arrange for that inmate to be assaulted to stop him. Joyner pleaded guilty on 14 December 2022 and was sentenced on 25 July 2023 to 43 months in prison.
inside: Inmates bought the officer who controlled their wing, and he protected the arrangement by trying to have the inmate who threatened to expose it assaulted.
cite: United States v. Perry Joyner, S.D.N.Y., guilty plea 14 December 2022, sentenced 25 July 2023; Department of Justice press release, 25 July 2023
org_label: Inmate contraband network at MCC New York

n: MCC New York officer charged with taking $45,000 to smuggle for inmates
who: Inmates of the Metropolitan Correctional Center paying for contraband deliveries
rank: Correctional officer, Metropolitan Correctional Center, Manhattan
d: On 5 April 2018 federal prosecutors in Manhattan unsealed a complaint charging Victor Casado, a serving federal correctional officer at the Metropolitan Correctional Center, the federal jail in Manhattan, with taking bribes to smuggle contraband in to inmates. The complaint says that on multiple occasions he received more than $45,000 from one inmate, transferred by one of that inmate's own attorneys, in exchange for bringing in alcohol, mobile phones and other goods. He was arrested that morning and later pleaded guilty to conspiring to take bribes to smuggle contraband. This is an earlier and separate case from the 2019 to 2020 conduct of another officer at the same jail.
inside: An inmate routed more than $45,000 to a jail officer through his own lawyer, and the officer carried the inmate's goods through the checks he was posted to run.
cite: United States v. Victor Casado, S.D.N.Y., complaint unsealed 5 April 2018; Department of Justice press releases, 5 April 2018 and on the subsequent guilty plea
org_label: Inmate contraband network at MCC New York

n: Alabama state prison officer took bribes under a false name to supply inmates
who: Inmates of the William E. Donaldson Correctional Facility and those paying on their behalf
rank: Correctional officer, Alabama Department of Corrections, Donaldson Correctional Facility
d: The William E. Donaldson Correctional Facility is an Alabama state prison west of Birmingham. Wilson Brian Clemons, 32, a correctional officer of the Alabama Department of Corrections, was charged on 2 November 2022 with conspiring to smuggle mobile phones, controlled drugs and other contraband to inmates there. The charging document says that between 7 and 23 November 2021 he agreed to accept bribes to carry the goods in, and that he opened an account with the mobile payment service Cash App under a false name so that he could collect the payments without them being traced to him. The pseudonyms he used were recorded in the charge.
inside: Inmates paid a state prison officer through an account he opened in a false name, and he carried their phones and drugs past his own checkpoint.
cite: United States v. Wilson Brian Clemons, N.D. Ala., two-count information filed 2 November 2022; Department of Justice press release, 3 November 2022
org_label: Inmate contraband network at Donaldson Correctional Facility

n: FCI Texarkana officer forfeited $17,200 taken from an inmate he supplied
who: A federal inmate at FCI Texarkana buying deliveries through a serving officer
rank: Correctional officer, Federal Correctional Institution Texarkana, Texas
d: James Thompson, 55, was a correctional officer at the Federal Correctional Institution at Texarkana, Texas. He pleaded guilty on 5 August 2020 to conspiring to commit bribery and was sentenced to 46 months in federal prison, and ordered to forfeit $17,200 in cash and proceeds from the scheme. Gilbert Gomez, 54, an inmate at the same prison, pleaded guilty on 31 August 2020 to the same conspiracy and received the same 46-month sentence. The prosecutor described Thompson as having exploited his position of public trust and endangered the inmates and staff of the prison.
inside: A federal inmate paid a serving prison officer $17,200, and the officer used his post inside the prison to deliver what the inmate had bought.
cite: United States v. James Thompson and Gilbert Gomez, E.D. Tex., guilty pleas 5 and 31 August 2020, sentenced 5 March 2021; Department of Justice press release, 5 March 2021
org_label: Inmate contraband arrangement at FCI Texarkana

n: DC Jail officer took $6,400 to carry narcotics in for an inmate
who: An inmate of the DC Jail and an outside associate supplying him with narcotics
rank: Corrections officer, District of Columbia Central Detention Facility
d: The District of Columbia Central Detention Facility, known as the DC Jail, is the city's main jail. Beverly Williams, 52, a corrections officer there, took cash to smuggle narcotics inside for Andre Gregory, 31, an inmate at the time. A third defendant, Keywaune McLeod, 28, was charged with them. All three pleaded guilty in the federal district court for the District of Columbia. Williams was sentenced on 21 August 2023 to 18 months in prison and Gregory on 23 August 2023 to 42 months. The payments in the case came to $6,400. The US Attorney said Williams had undermined the safe and orderly operation of the jail.
inside: An inmate and his outside helper paid a jail officer $6,400, and she used her post to bring their narcotics through the jail's searches.
cite: United States v. Beverly Williams, Andre Gregory and Keywaune McLeod, D.D.C., sentenced 21 and 23 August 2023; Department of Justice press release, 23 August 2023
org_label: Inmate narcotics supply at the DC Jail

n: Victorville prison investigator took over $15,000 to carry drugs for inmates
who: Inmates of the Victorville federal penitentiary and the outside courier who paid for them
rank: Lieutenant, Special Investigation Services, Federal Correctional Complex Victorville
d: Paul James Hayes II, 52, was a lieutenant in Special Investigation Services at the Federal Correctional Complex at Victorville, California: the unit whose job is to investigate illegal activity by correctional officers and inmates. From early 2018 to September 2018 he met a co-defendant, Angel Marie Wagner, 44, in shop and restaurant car parks around Victorville and took cash bribes from her totalling more than $15,000. In return he accepted wrapped parcels of contraband, including methamphetamine, suboxone and mobile phones, and carried them into the complex's high-security penitentiary. He retired from the Bureau of Prisons in March 2019, pleaded guilty in January 2020 and was sentenced on 17 March 2021 to 15 months in prison.
inside: The officer paid to investigate smuggling inside the prison was taking the smugglers' cash in car parks and carrying their drugs in himself.
cite: United States v. Paul James Hayes II, C.D. Cal., guilty plea January 2020, sentenced 17 March 2021; Department of Justice press release, 17 March 2021
org_label: Inmate contraband network at FCC Victorville

n: FCI Bennettsville officer indicted over $60,000 from an inmate's network
who: A Bureau of Prisons inmate at FCI Bennettsville and the associates paying for him
rank: Correctional officer, Federal Correctional Institution Bennettsville, South Carolina
d: A federal grand jury in Florence, South Carolina returned a three-count indictment on 12 August 2026 charging Joseph Templeton, 30, with bribery, money laundering and possession of marijuana with intent to distribute. The indictment alleges that while employed as a correctional officer at the Federal Correctional Institution at Bennettsville he accepted more than $60,000 in bribes from an inmate and from others associated with that inmate, and in exchange carried mobile phones, phone accessories, cigarettes and THC into the prison. It alleges he disguised the deliveries by booking them falsely as contraband he had seized, before distributing them inside. He was arraigned the same day. These are allegations, not findings.
inside: An inmate's network allegedly paid an officer $60,000, and he logged their goods as seizures before handing them out inside the prison.
cite: United States v. Joseph Templeton, D.S.C., three-count indictment returned 12 August 2026; Department of Justice press release, 12 August 2026
org_label: Inmate contraband network at FCI Bennettsville

n: USP Atlanta officer convicted over contraband passed through a hole in the visit room
who: Inmates of the Atlanta federal penitentiary running a narcotics supply route through visitors
rank: Correctional officer, United States Penitentiary Atlanta
d: A federal jury in Atlanta convicted Patrick Shackelford, a former federal correctional officer, on 2 April 2026 after a six-day trial, of accepting bribes and conspiring with inmates to smuggle narcotics and other contraband into the United States Penitentiary Atlanta. The route ran through the prison's visitation area: visitors introduced the goods through a hole in the room, and the officer took payment from inmates to let the arrangement work. Large quantities of methamphetamine were among the drugs brought in for distribution to other inmates. The US Attorney said he had taken bribes from the inmates in his charge. He was taken into custody when the verdict was returned.
inside: Inmates paid an officer of the federal penitentiary to let visitors pass methamphetamine through a hole in the visit room for distribution inside.
cite: United States v. Patrick Shackelford, N.D. Ga., jury verdict 2 April 2026; Department of Justice press release, 6 April 2026
org_label: Inmate narcotics ring inside USP Atlanta

n: Camera firm paid over $3m to the school agency that bought its buses' cameras
who: Robert Leonard, president of Force Multiplier Solutions, a stop-arm camera supplier
rank: Superintendent and board president of Dallas County Schools, and a Dallas city councilman
d: Dallas County Schools was a Texas agency that collected property taxes and ran a fleet of about 2,000 school buses. Robert Leonard, president of Force Multiplier Solutions, wanted its contracts for stop-arm cameras, the cameras fitted to buses to catch drivers overtaking them. He funnelled more than $3 million in bribes to the agency's superintendent, Ricky Sorrells, and to Dallas city councilman Dwaine Caraway. A third recipient, four-term councilman Larry Duncan, a former president of the agency's board of trustees, took nearly a quarter of a million dollars routed as campaign contributions while Leonard was pursuing the contracts, and pleaded guilty to tax evasion on 22 October 2018. The agency was shut down in November 2017, about $103 million in debt. The investigation produced five convictions.
inside: A camera supplier paid more than $3m to the superintendent and board of the agency buying its cameras, and the agency bought until it collapsed in debt.
cite: United States v. Larry Duncan, N.D. Tex., guilty plea 22 October 2018, and related Dallas County Schools prosecutions; Department of Justice press release, 22 October 2018

n: Border Patrol agent fed traffickers intelligence and helped plan an informer's murder
org_label: Mexican drug trafficking organisations operating through Arizona
who: Drug traffickers buying US law enforcement intelligence
rank: US Border Patrol agent, and a state prison guard
d: Ivhan Herrera-Chiang, 31, was an agent of the US Border Patrol, the force that polices the land border. Michael Lopez-Garcia, 30, was an Arizona state prison guard. Both passed sensitive law enforcement information to drug traffickers, and both took part in a plot to arrange the murder of an informant. Having an agent inside the Border Patrol gave the traffickers what the agency itself held: the locations of sensors and surveillance, and the identities of people reporting on them. Both pleaded guilty, and on 5 November 2013 a federal judge sentenced Herrera-Chiang to 15 years and Lopez-Garcia to 9 years in prison.
inside: Traffickers put a serving Border Patrol agent on their side, so the agency's own intelligence told them where it was watching and who was informing.
cite: United States v. Ivhan Herrera-Chiang and Michael Lopez-Garcia, D. Ariz., sentenced 5 November 2013; Department of Justice press release, 6 November 2013

n: Developers' $15,000 bought a Cincinnati councilman's vote on their projects
org_label: Cincinnati property developers paying through a middleman
who: Developers seeking city approvals for their projects
rank: Member of Cincinnati City Council
d: Jeffrey Pastor, 40, was a member of Cincinnati City Council, the body that votes on the city's development approvals. In the autumn of 2018 he took a $15,000 cash bribe in return for official action advancing development projects in the city. The money was handled by Tyran Marshall, 38, a business partner who coordinated the payments and washed them through a non-profit he had set up for the purpose. In September 2018 the two flew to Miami on a private jet. Pastor pleaded guilty to honest services wire fraud and was sentenced in December 2023 to 24 months in prison; Marshall pleaded guilty to money laundering and was sentenced on 30 April 2024 to a year and a day.
inside: Developers paid a sitting councilman $15,000 through a sham non-profit, and he used his council vote to push their projects through.
cite: United States v. Jeffrey Pastor and United States v. Tyran Marshall, S.D. Ohio, sentenced December 2023 and 30 April 2024; Department of Justice press release, 30 April 2024

n: Cincinnati council president charged with selling her votes for money
who: People seeking favourable votes from Cincinnati City Council
rank: President Pro Tem of Cincinnati City Council
d: Tamaya Dennard, 40, was elected to Cincinnati City Council in November 2017 and became its President Pro Tem. On 25 February 2020 she was arrested and charged with honest services wire fraud, bribery and attempted extortion. The affidavit supporting the complaint said that between August and December 2019 she committed and attempted acts of bribery and extortion, trying to exchange her council votes for money. The investigation began when a member of the public who had dealt with her reported it to law enforcement. The charges were unsealed when she appeared in federal court. This is a separate case from the council bribery conviction in the same city a year earlier.
inside: A sitting council president is accused of offering her votes for cash, letting whoever paid decide what the council approved.
cite: United States v. Tamaya Dennard, S.D. Ohio, criminal complaint unsealed 25 February 2020; Department of Justice press release, 25 February 2020

n: Victorville penitentiary officer took a $1,000 bribe in a fast-food car park
org_label: Contraband supply arrangement at USP Victorville
who: A prisoner at the Victorville penitentiary and the person paying for his deliveries
rank: Correctional officer, United States Penitentiary Victorville
d: Ignacio Adrian Sobers Jr., 31, was a correctional officer at the United States Penitentiary in Victorville, California. He was arrested on 21 January 2017 after accepting a $1,000 payment and a gift-wrapped parcel of contraband in the car park of a fast-food restaurant in San Bernardino. The parcel held MP3 players, pornographic magazines and other goods he had agreed to carry in to a prisoner. He pleaded guilty in March 2017 to one count of acceptance of a bribe by a public official, and on 21 July 2017 was sentenced to six months in prison and six months of home detention. The judge said that when an officer corrupts the prison system, the system breaks down and the public pays for it.
inside: A prisoner's people paid an officer $1,000 in a car park, and he carried their parcel through the prison's searches for them.
cite: United States v. Ignacio Adrian Sobers Jr., C.D. Cal., guilty plea March 2017, sentenced 21 July 2017; Department of Justice press releases, 9 February and 21 July 2017

n: Officer at a private federal prison took twelve payments to run cigarettes in
org_label: Contraband supply arrangement at McRae Correctional Facility
who: An inmate of McRae Correctional Facility paying for deliveries

d: McRae Correctional Facility in Telfair County, Georgia is a private prison run under a federal contract. Michael Kerr, 30, a correctional officer there, was charged on 12 August 2019 in a 14-count federal indictment with 12 counts of bribery, one of providing contraband into a prison and one of making a false statement to law enforcement. The indictment alleges that on twelve occasions he accepted payments of between $400 and $640 in return for smuggling cigarettes to an inmate. Because the prison holds federal prisoners under contract, its officers are treated as public officials for the purposes of the federal bribery law. The charges carried up to 15 years in prison.
inside: An inmate paid an officer of a privately run federal prison twelve times over, and the officer carried his goods through the searches each time.
cite: United States v. Michael Kerr, S.D. Ga., 14-count indictment, 12 August 2019; Department of Justice press release, 12 August 2019

rank: Correctional officer, D. Ray James Correctional Facility, a private prison under federal contract
d: D. Ray James Correctional Facility at Folkston, Georgia is a private prison operated under a federal contract. On 18 September 2019 a federal grand jury indicted Micheal Eaddy, 23, a correctional officer there, on seven counts of bribery, one count of providing contraband in prison and one count of making a false statement, for accepting bribes from an inmate and then lying about it to investigators. The same indictment charged the inmate, Jean Civil, 24, a Haitian national held at the prison. Officers of a prison holding federal prisoners under contract are public officials for the purposes of the federal bribery law. The charges carried up to 15 years, and the federal system has no parole.
inside: An inmate paid a privately employed prison officer seven times to bring goods inside, and the officer lied to investigators to keep it going.
cite: United States v. Micheal Eaddy and Jean Civil, S.D. Ga., indictment 18 September 2019; Department of Justice press release, 18 September 2019

n: Northeast Ohio prison officer took bribes to supply an inmate she also abused

who: An inmate of the Northeast Ohio Correctional Center paying for a phone and tobacco
rank: Correctional officer, Northeast Ohio Correctional Center
d: Barbara Davis, 47, was a correctional officer at the Northeast Ohio Correctional Center in Youngstown. She pleaded guilty in January 2021 to accepting bribes, to providing a mobile phone and tobacco to an inmate, and to sexual abuse of a ward, and was sentenced on 29 April 2021 to five months in prison and five months of home confinement. A mobile phone inside a prison is the item that matters most to anyone running something from a cell, because it restores contact with the outside that the prison exists to control. The prosecutor said that taking bribe payments to smuggle contraband into a correctional centre undermines public trust in the justice system.
inside: An inmate's payments bought a serving officer, who used her post to put a phone and tobacco inside the prison holding him.
cite: United States v. Barbara Davis, N.D. Ohio, guilty plea January 2021, sentenced 29 April 2021; Department of Justice press release, 29 April 2021

n: Cook County jail officer took $200 to carry marijuana in inside sandwiches
org_label: Inmate smuggling conspiracy at Cook County Jail
who: Three Cook County Jail inmates and two civilian women who paid the officer
rank: Corrections officer, Cook County Department of Corrections, and a Chicago police dispatcher
d: Cook County Jail in Chicago is one of the largest single-site jails in the United States. In June 2013 three of its inmates arranged with two civilian women to pay Jason Marek, a corrections officer with the Cook County Department of Corrections since May 2011, to bring marijuana, cigarettes and tobacco inside. Nearly three ounces of marijuana was seized after it was found hidden inside two sandwiches he allegedly tried to carry in, for a $200 bribe. Seven people were charged federally on 21 October 2014 over the wider conspiracy: the officer, three inmates, two civilians and a Chicago police dispatcher.
inside: Inmates and their outside helpers paid a jail officer $200 a delivery, and he carried their drugs through the gate hidden in his lunch.
cite: United States v. Jason Marek et al., N.D. Ill., charges announced 21 October 2014; Department of Justice press release, 21 October 2014

n: Smugglers bought a lane at San Ysidro from the officer who inspected it
org_label: A cross-border human smuggling ring working through San Ysidro
who: Miriam Juarez-Herrera and Gilberto Aguilar-Martinez, smugglers paying for clear passage
rank: Officer, US Customs and Border Protection, San Ysidro Port of Entry
d: San Ysidro, between San Diego and Tijuana, is one of the busiest land border crossings in the world, and every vehicle through it passes an inspection lane staffed by a Customs and Border Protection officer. Jose Luis Cota, a fifteen-year CBP veteran, pleaded guilty on 10 January 2017 to bribery and alien smuggling. He admitted taking cash and other inducements from smugglers in return for waving undocumented people through his own lane without inspection. The two Mexican nationals who worked with him, Miriam Juarez-Herrera and Gilberto Aguilar-Martinez, pleaded guilty the week before. Cota was arrested in September 2016.
inside: A smuggling ring paid the officer who manned an inspection lane at the border, turning that lane into a route they controlled.
cite: United States v. Jose Luis Cota, S.D. Cal., guilty plea 10 January 2017; Department of Justice press release, 10 January 2017

n: DC jail officer charged with taking bribes to bring in weapons and drugs
org_label: Contraband supply at the DC Central Detention Facility
who: Those paying to get weapons and drugs to inmates of the DC jail
rank: Corrections officer, District of Columbia Department of Corrections
d: Johnson Ayuk, 31, an officer of the District of Columbia Department of Corrections, was arrested at his workplace on 24 February 2022 and charged in a federal criminal complaint with bribery and with providing or possessing contraband in prison. The complaint alleges he accepted bribes to bring prohibited items, including weapons and drugs, into the District's Central Detention Facility, the city's main jail. Weapons are the gravest category of prison contraband because they change who holds power on a wing. He was released on high-intensity supervision pending a preliminary hearing set for 10 March 2022. These are allegations in a complaint, not findings of a court.
inside: Payments allegedly bought a serving jail officer, who was to carry weapons and drugs through the door of the jail he guarded.
cite: United States v. Johnson Ayuk, D.D.C., criminal complaint, arrest 24 February 2022; Department of Justice press release, 24 February 2022

n: A gang trafficker put a Montebello police officer on his payroll
org_label: A Los Angeles-area gang narcotics operation
who: A gang member and drug trafficker paying a serving police officer
rank: Police officer, Montebello Police Department, California
d: Rudolph Petersen, 34, served nearly four years as an officer of the Montebello Police Department in Los Angeles County. From December 2018 to August 2020 he solicited and took repeated cash bribes, at least $14,000 in all, from a gang member and drug trafficker. In return he escorted narcotics shipments, using his position as a police officer to see them safely through, and searched a restricted police database to tell the trafficker which people were suspected of cooperating with law enforcement. The arrangement began with a dinner in mid-2018 at which the trafficker offered to put him on his payroll. Petersen pleaded guilty to bribery on 7 September 2021.
inside: A trafficker paid a serving officer to guard his drug shipments and to name the people informing on him, using police records against them.
cite: United States v. Rudolph Petersen, C.D. Cal., guilty plea 7 September 2021; Department of Justice press release, 7 September 2021

n: Towing firm gave a Hamtramck officer a car for access to the police database
who: A towing company operator buying restricted police information
rank: Police officer, Hamtramck Police Department, Michigan
d: Towing work in Michigan is dispatched by police, so knowing which vehicles have been stopped or recovered is worth money to an operator. Michael Stout, 60, an officer of the Hamtramck Police Department who left the force in 2020, was charged in a federal criminal complaint unsealed on 3 March 2022 with bribery. The complaint alleges that while serving as an officer he accepted bribes from a towing company operator, including a vehicle and $1,500 in cash, and in return supplied the operator with information from the Michigan Law Enforcement Information Network, a database restricted to law enforcement. He later pleaded guilty to bribery in a separate notice.
inside: A towing firm bought a serving officer with a car and cash, and got the police database that decides which vehicles are worth chasing.
cite: United States v. Michael Stout, E.D. Mich., criminal complaint unsealed 3 March 2022, subsequent guilty plea; Department of Justice press releases, 3 March 2022 and 2023

n: MDC Brooklyn officer convicted after an inmate's girlfriend paid him $15,000
org_label: Inmate contraband network at MDC Brooklyn
who: An inmate of the Metropolitan Detention Center and Alicia Alonso, his girlfriend, who paid the officer
rank: Correctional officer, Metropolitan Detention Center, Brooklyn
d: On 12 January 2017 federal prosecutors in Brooklyn unsealed a criminal complaint charging Armando Moronta, a correctional officer of the US Bureau of Prisons at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, and Alicia Alonso, the girlfriend of an inmate held there, with a bribery scheme to bring contraband into the jail. The outside partner is how these schemes work: an inmate cannot pay an officer directly without being seen, so a relative or partner outside carries the money. On 8 November 2017 Moronta pleaded guilty to bribery, narcotics conspiracy and four counts of sexual abuse of a ward, arising from two separate indictments, and agreed to forfeit $15,000 in bribes. The Bureau of Prisons had suspended him after his first arrest.
inside: An inmate's girlfriend paid a serving jail officer $15,000, and he brought the inmate's contraband and narcotics through the door for them.
cite: United States v. Armando Moronta and Alicia Alonso, E.D.N.Y., complaint unsealed 12 January 2017, guilty plea 8 November 2017; Department of Justice press releases, 12 January and 8 November 2017

n: Petersburg prison guard ran heroin to inmates for two and a half years
org_label: Inmate drug supply network at FCI Petersburg
who: Inmates of FCI Petersburg and the associates paying for their supply
rank: Correctional officer and recreational specialist, Federal Correctional Institution Petersburg
d: Jermaine Brown, 37, was a correctional officer and recreational specialist at the medium-security Federal Correctional Institution at Petersburg, Virginia. From the autumn of 2010 until 25 March 2013 he took part in a conspiracy to smuggle heroin, marijuana and cigarettes to several inmates there in exchange for bribes. A federal grand jury charged him with conspiracy to commit bribery and with bribery in May 2015, and he pleaded guilty to one count of bribery of a public official, admitting in a statement of facts filed with his plea that he had accepted payment for carrying contraband cigarettes in to inmates while employed as an officer.
inside: Inmates paid a serving officer for two and a half years, and he used his post to bring heroin and other goods into the prison for them.
cite: United States v. Jermaine Brown, E.D. Va., indicted May 2015, guilty plea 2015; Department of Justice press releases, 20 May 2015 and on the plea

n: USP Lee officer took cash from a prisoner to bring tobacco inside
org_label: Contraband supply arrangement at USP Lee County
who: A federal prisoner at USP Lee County paying for tobacco deliveries
rank: Correctional officer, United States Penitentiary Lee County, Virginia
d: Kimberlee Crabtree, 43, was a correctional officer at the United States Penitentiary Lee County in Virginia. On 27 February 2014 she waived her right to be indicted and pleaded guilty in the federal court at Abingdon to a one-count information charging her with accepting a bribe as a public official. She had taken cash from a federal prisoner and in exchange carried tobacco and other goods into the prison for him. Tobacco is banned in federal prisons and sells inside at many times its outside price, which is what makes it worth paying an officer to carry. She faced up to fifteen years in prison.
inside: A prisoner paid an officer cash, and she used her place on the staff to carry his tobacco past the prison's own searches.
cite: United States v. Kimberlee Crabtree, W.D. Va., guilty plea 27 February 2014; Department of Justice press release, 27 February 2014

n: FCI Aliceville officer took $5,695 and lied about it to the FBI
org_label: Contraband supply arrangement at FCI Aliceville
who: Inmates of FCI Aliceville and those paying on their behalf
rank: Correctional officer, Federal Correctional Institution Aliceville, Alabama
d: Eric C. Pendleton, 54, was a correctional officer at the Federal Correctional Institution at Aliceville, Alabama. On 19 June 2017 he pleaded guilty to accepting $5,695 in bribes to smuggle contraband into the prison, and to making false statements to agents of the FBI and the Justice Department's Office of the Inspector General when they asked him about it. The second charge is the common second act in these cases: the officer denies the arrangement to the investigators who have already traced the payments. He pleaded to accepting a bribe in return for violating his official duty as a federal correctional officer.
inside: An officer took $5,695 to carry inmates' contraband into the prison, then denied it to the federal agents investigating him.
cite: United States v. Eric C. Pendleton, N.D. Ala., guilty plea 19 June 2017; Department of Justice press release, 19 June 2017

n: Talladega prison cook supervisor took $4,000 for tobacco and synthetic drugs
