He pleaded guilty on 20 October 2015 to one count of accepting a bribe as a public official, having taken more than $4,000 to smuggle tobacco and synthetic marijuana into the prison. Kitchen staff are useful to a smuggling arrangement because deliveries of food arrive in bulk and are harder to search than a person. He had entered a plea agreement with the government the previous month and was listed for sentencing on 5 January 2016.
inside: Inmates paid a kitchen supervisor more than $4,000, and he used a job with access to bulk deliveries to bring their drugs in.
cite: United States v. Donald D. Johnson, N.D. Ala., guilty plea 20 October 2015; Department of Justice press release, 21 October 2015

The evidence at her plea hearing established that from 2013 to 2015 she accepted bribes from inmates and their associates and in exchange brought tobacco in to inmates at the prison. The maximum penalty for the offence is fifteen years. This is one of three separate prosecutions of officers at the same prison that the map holds, covering different officers and different years.
inside: Inmates and their outside associates paid an officer for two years, and she carried their tobacco into the prison for them.
cite: United States v. Angela McLeod, D.S.C., guilty plea entered 2016; Department of Justice press release, 14 September 2016

n: Earlier FCI Bennettsville officer brought in tobacco and mobile phones

She was sentenced in the federal court at Florence on 9 February 2015 to 13 months in prison and three years of supervised release. The case was investigated by the Justice Department's Office of the Inspector General. It is a separate case from the later prosecution of another officer at the same prison.
inside: Inmates' associates paid an officer, and she brought the phones that let them keep running things from inside the prison.
cite: United States v. Charlotte McLaughlin, D.S.C., sentenced 9 February 2015; Department of Justice press release, 9 February 2015

The court record shows that DeJesus and others were charged with conspiring to bribe him and with bribing him. The case was investigated by the FBI's Miami field office.

Charles Daniel Lynn, 34, served as a correctional officer there during the second half of 2016. Because the prison holds federal prisoners under contract, its officers fall within the federal bribery statute even though their employer is a company.
inside: Payers bought an officer at a privately run federal prison, and he carried banned goods to inmates in return.

d: Scottie Austin, 44, worked as a correctional officer at the United States Penitentiary Lee County in Virginia. On 5 January 2015 the federal court at Abingdon sentenced him to 12 months and one day of imprisonment. He is a different officer from the other member of staff at the same penitentiary whose case the map holds, and the two were prosecuted separately.
inside: Inmates paid a serving officer of the penitentiary, and he used his post on the staff to hand them goods the prison bans.

n: Huntsville officer took part in paying $5,000 to fix a cocaine prosecution

d: A federal grand jury indicted Lewis Bernard Hall, 45, a serving Huntsville police officer, on 29 December 2014 on four counts: conspiracy, bribery, obstruction of justice and making a false statement to investigators. The charges say he conspired with a person named in the indictment only as Individual B to pay a fellow Huntsville officer $5,000 to make the cocaine trafficking charges against someone that officer had arrested go away. Buying the outcome of a prosecution from inside the force that brought it is the point here: the arresting officer is the one witness the case cannot do without. These are allegations, not findings.
inside: A trafficking defendant's money allegedly reached inside the police force that arrested him, to buy off the officer whose evidence the case rested on.

n: Contractors paid a Texas county commissioner to rig their bids
org_label: Construction contractors bidding for Maverick County work
who: Construction contractors seeking Maverick County construction contracts
rank: Precinct Two Commissioner, Maverick County Commissioners Court, Texas
d: Maverick County sits on the Texas border at Eagle Pass, and its Commissioners Court awards the county's construction contracts. A federal grand jury in Del Rio indicted Precinct Two Commissioner Rodolfo Bainet Heredia, 54, on 23 January 2013 on six counts of receiving a bribe and one of paying a bribe to an agent of an organisation receiving federal funds. The indictment alleged that in 2010 and 2011 he manipulated the bidding process so that contractors he had chosen would win county construction contracts, and that those contractors then deposited money for him. He later entered a guilty plea.
inside: Contractors paid a sitting county commissioner, and he shaped the bidding from inside the body that awarded the work so they won it.
cite: United States v. Rodolfo Bainet Heredia, W.D. Tex., indictment 23 January 2013 and subsequent guilty plea; Department of Justice press releases, 23 January 2013 and on the plea

n: Bank fraud ring bought an ICE supervisor who made an arrest to order
org_label: A bank fraud conspiracy buying federal immigration enforcement
who: Members of a bank fraud conspiracy paying a federal immigration supervisor
rank: Supervisory deportation officer, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement
d: Henry Yau was a supervisory deportation officer at US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the agency that detains and removes people from the country. On 26 March 2026 he pleaded guilty in the federal court in Manhattan to conspiring to solicit and accept bribes and gratuities. In exchange for the payments he used his position to disclose confidential law enforcement information to people not entitled to it, to tip off an individual that the FBI was investigating them, and to arrest a particular person whom members of a bank fraud conspiracy wanted arrested. The last of those is the sharpest part: the power to detain someone was exercised on a payer's instruction.
inside: A fraud ring paid a supervising immigration officer, who then leaked investigations and used his power of arrest on the person they wanted detained.
cite: United States v. Henry Yau, S.D.N.Y., guilty plea 26 March 2026; Department of Justice press release, 26 March 2026

n: FCI Beaumont officer took bribes while delivering food to inmates
org_label: Contraband supply arrangement at FCI Beaumont
who: Inmates of FCI Beaumont paying the officer who worked their unit
rank: Corrections officer, Federal Correctional Institution Beaumont, Texas
d: Anqunett Vernetta Lewis, 34, worked as a corrections officer for the Bureau of Prisons at the Federal Correctional Institution at Beaumont, Texas, from 22 February 2015 to 9 November 2016, overseeing inmates and delivering food and other items to them. On 15 March 2017 she pleaded guilty, before a federal magistrate judge at Beaumont, to an information charging her with bribery of a public official. The routine access the job gave her to inmates and to the things carried in to them is what the payments bought.
inside: Inmates paid the officer who handled their daily deliveries, so what reached them was decided by who had paid her.
cite: United States v. Anqunett Vernetta Lewis, E.D. Tex., guilty plea 15 March 2017; Department of Justice press release, 15 March 2017

n: Pollock prison officer convicted by jury and jailed for contraband bribes
org_label: Contraband supply arrangement at FCC Pollock
who: Prisoners at the Pollock federal complex paying for deliveries
rank: Corrections officer, Federal Correctional Complex Pollock, Louisiana
d: Byron A. Wyatt worked as a corrections officer at the Federal Correctional Complex in Pollock, Louisiana. A federal jury in Alexandria found him guilty on 5 April 2018 of two counts of bribery of public officials and witnesses, after a trial that ran three days and a deliberation of about an hour and a half. The evidence at trial showed he had accepted payment to smuggle contraband to prisoners. He was sentenced the following year to 24 months in prison and two years of supervised release.
inside: Prisoners paid an officer of the federal complex, and he carried their goods inside past the checks he was employed to run.
cite: United States v. Byron A. Wyatt, W.D. La., jury verdict 5 April 2018, sentenced 2019; Department of Justice press releases, 6 April 2018 and on sentencing

n: Marketing contractors bought five Army National Guard officials
org_label: Contractors holding Army National Guard marketing and recruitment contracts
who: Companies seeking Army National Guard marketing, retention and recruitment contracts
rank: Five Army National Guard officials, four retired and one serving
d: The Army National Guard buys marketing, retention and recruitment services worth millions of dollars from private contractors, and the officials who run those contracts decide who wins them. On 1 October 2014 the Justice Department charged five Army National Guard officials, four retired and one on active duty, together with one civilian, over bribery schemes tied to the award of those contracts. Two of the retired officials and the civilian pleaded guilty to their roles. The case was brought jointly by the Criminal Division and two US Attorneys' offices, with the FBI's Washington field office investigating.
inside: Contractors paid the Army National Guard officials who decided its marketing contracts, so the force bought from whoever was paying them.
cite: United States v. five Army National Guard officials and one civilian, E.D. Va. and E.D.N.Y., charges announced 1 October 2014; Department of Justice press release, 1 October 2014

n: Toledo business owners bought four sitting city council members' votes
org_label: Toledo business owners paying for council votes
who: Local business owners paying for favourable votes on council
rank: Four members of Toledo City Council, and a local attorney
d: On 30 June 2020 federal prosecutors charged four sitting members of Toledo City Council and a local attorney with running a scheme in which they solicited and accepted cash, cheques, money orders and other things of value from local business owners in exchange for their votes on the council. Those charged were Tyrone Riley, Yvonne Harper, Garrick Johnson, Larry Sykes and Keith Mitchell. A grand jury in Cleveland returned a 13-count indictment on 21 July 2020. Riley and Sykes later pleaded guilty to Hobbs Act extortion under colour of official right and Harper to Hobbs Act conspiracy.
inside: Local business owners paid four of the city's own council members, so the council's votes on their matters were bought in advance.
cite: United States v. Tyrone Riley, Yvonne Harper, Garrick Johnson, Larry Sykes and Keith Mitchell, N.D. Ohio, complaint 30 June 2020, 13-count indictment 21 July 2020, guilty pleas 2022; Department of Justice press releases, 30 June 2020, 21 July 2020 and 2022

n: Army contracting official took $490,000 from the firms he helped win work
who: Contractors who paid for favourable treatment and federal contracts
rank: Contracting official, United States Department of the Army
d: In Seon Lim was a contracting official for the US Department of the Army, one of the people who decide which firms the Army buys from. On 31 July 2014 he pleaded guilty to federal charges over a scheme in which he accepted more than $490,000 in benefits from favoured contractors, including cash payments and holidays. In return he helped those businesses obtain millions of dollars in federal contracts. The case was announced jointly by two US Attorneys' offices, with the FBI's Washington field office and the Internal Revenue Service's criminal investigators involved.
inside: Contractors paid an Army buying official nearly half a million dollars in cash and holidays, and he steered millions in Army contracts to them.
cite: United States v. In Seon Lim, D.D.C. and E.D. Va., guilty plea 31 July 2014; Department of Justice press release, 31 July 2014

n: Army Corps official had a contractor bill $25,000 of work for him
who: Kenneth Hornsby, president and chief executive of HCS Group P.C., an Army Corps contractor
rank: Employee, United States Army Corps of Engineers
d: HCS Group P.C., a firm based in Montgomery, Alabama, held a contract with the United States Army Corps of Engineers to carry out work in Peru. Dennis Fails Jr., 55, an employee of the Corps, was indicted by a grand jury for bribery of a public official and made his first court appearance on 5 March 2014. The indictment alleges that he solicited a bribe from the firm's president and chief executive, Kenneth Hornsby, instructing him to submit billing for nearly $25,000 of work. The official overseeing a contract asking the contractor to pay for something through its own invoices is the mechanism alleged here. These are allegations, not findings.
inside: The Corps official overseeing a contract allegedly had the contractor bill the government for $25,000 of work done for him.
cite: United States v. Dennis Fails Jr., M.D. Ala., grand jury indictment, first appearance 5 March 2014; Department of Justice press release, 6 March 2014

n: Houthi-appointed customs officials took 994bn rials in duties at the ports they hold
who: The Houthi movement, through officials it appointed to the customs administration
rank: Customs authorities at Houthi-controlled ports, appointed by the movement
d: Customs duty is a state revenue, collected by a state body at a port. In Yemen the Houthi movement holds the main northern ports and has put its own appointees in charge of collecting there. The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen found that between 1 April 2022 and 30 June 2024 Houthi-appointed authorities collected about 994 billion Yemeni rials in the name of customs duties on fuel imports through ports under their control, and estimated the movement's total income from fuel at about 1.34 trillion rials once other illegal fees and profit margins were counted. The Panel's sources said a significant part of that went to military purposes, though the Panel could not independently verify how much was diverted.
inside: The movement's own appointees run customs at the ports it holds, so a state revenue is collected into the movement's hands instead of the treasury.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2024/731, para. 128

n: A Haitian armed group built with serving police officers in its ranks
org_label: Fantome 509 and the BLTS criminal group
who: Nenel Cassy, a former senator who controls the BLTS criminal group
rank: Serving officers of the Haitian National Police within Fantome 509
d: The UN Panel of Experts on Haiti found that Nenel Cassy, a former senator, controls the BLTS criminal group in Chalon, in the Nippes department, which the Panel records as specialising in illegal firearms, murder, kidnapping for ransom and armed robbery. It also found he contributed to the creation of Fantome 509, a violent armed group that emerged in 2018 and whose members include police officers. Fantome 509 took part in the disruption of public order, arson, the vandalisation of public and private property and the killing of police officers. The Panel further records that Cassy and his associates carried out an attempted kidnapping and the assassination of a Haitian diplomat in February 2021.
inside: Serving police officers joined an armed group that attacked public order and killed other officers, so the force held men working for the group inside it.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, report S/2026/714, paras. 53-55

n: Ex-rebel colonels inside Sudan's Rapid Support Forces ran its cross-border supply
org_label: Sudan Liberation Movement-Minni Minawi and Sudan Revolutionary Awakening Council veterans
who: Former rebel-movement colonels who joined the Rapid Support Forces
rank: Commanders of the Rapid Support Forces directing supply from Chad and Libya
d: The Rapid Support Forces grew out of Sudan's own paramilitary structures and remained a formally recognised force. The UN Panel of Experts on the Sudan found that former officers of armed movements had taken senior logistics roles within it. Abdallah Tijani Chaghab, a colonel in the Sudan Liberation Movement-Minni Minawi who joined the Rapid Support Forces in 2017, directed the movement of equipment from eastern Chad and Libya through Dar Zaghawa to Khartoum and front lines including El Fasher, travelling to oversee operations and drawing on his Zaghawa heritage and local networks. The Panel named two further commanders, Fadeil El Naji and Mohamed Bakhit Ajab al-Dor, both former members of the Sudan Revolutionary Awakening Council, as facilitating logistics between Chad, southern Libya and Darfur.
inside: Officers of armed movements took command of a state paramilitary force's supply lines, so its cross-border logistics ran on their own networks.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Sudan, report S/2025/239, para. 99 and footnotes 105-106

n: A rebel leader appointed his own local commander to head the Bria mixed brigade
org_label: Union pour la paix en Centrafrique (UPC)
who: Ali Darassa, leader of the Union pour la paix en Centrafrique
rank: Commander of the mixed brigade at Bria
d: A mixed brigade in the Central African Republic is a security unit meant to combine state forces with former armed-group fighters, so that the fighters come under state command rather than their own. The UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic recorded that in April 2020 the UPC leader Ali Darassa appointed the group's own local leader in Bria, who used the title general, Wada Oumda, to lead the mixed brigade there. The Panel found that Oumda commanded elements responsible for illegal detention and the use of violence against civilians, and headed its account of the change: a change in leadership, no change in behaviour.
inside: The rebel leader chose who commanded the joint state security unit in Bria, so the unit meant to absorb his fighters was run by his own man.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, report S/2020/662, para. 56

n: Demobilised fighters used as the Central African army's proxies
who: Former armed-group fighters serving alongside the national forces
rank: Proxies attached to the Armed Forces of the Central African Republic
d: The Central African Republic has been disarming armed-group fighters and taking some of them into its own forces. The UN Panel of Experts found the practice went further than the official scheme. The Ministry of Defence acknowledged that certain armed-group elements had been integrated into the national army but rejected the suggestion that any were used as proxies. National security and defence forces in the provinces told the Panel otherwise: army and gendarmerie officers in Bria said that 52 fighters demobilised at Sam-Ouandja in June and July 2022 were serving as army proxies, and a gendarmerie officer in Bambari described two demobilised men used as proxies who were wounded in an accidental grenade explosion at the Russian instructors' camp at Ippy in November 2022.
inside: Army and gendarmerie officers said demobilised fighters were being used as the army's own proxies, which the defence ministry denied.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on the Central African Republic, report S/2023/360, para. 119

n: Applicants paid North Charleston councilmen for their votes on rezoning
org_label: Applicants before North Charleston City Council
who: Aaron Hicks and the Core4Success Foundation's founder, paying for council support
rank: Two members of North Charleston City Council
d: North Charleston City Council votes on rezoning, which decides what a piece of land may be built on and so what it is worth. Four more defendants in a public corruption scheme there were sentenced by 30 June 2026. Jerome Sydney Heyward, 63, a former councilmember, got six years for extortion, bribery and money laundering. Mike A. Brown, 47, also a former councilmember, got two years for accepting a bribe from Aaron Hicks in exchange for his support of a rezoning application. Michelle Stent-Hilton, 58, and Donavan Laval Moten, 48, founder of the Core4Success Foundation, each got 18 months for paying Heyward $20,000 in kickbacks for his support of their own applications.
inside: Applicants paid two sitting councilmen for their votes, so the council's decisions on what could be built were settled by who had paid.
cite: United States v. Jerome Sydney Heyward, Mike A. Brown, Michelle Stent-Hilton and Donavan Laval Moten, D.S.C., sentenced by 30 June 2026; Department of Justice press release, 30 June 2026

n: A businessman paid the NYPD's school safety commander to steer work to his firm
org_label: A Florida company seeking NYPD business
who: Geno Roefaro, a Florida businessman whose company sought NYPD work
rank: Commanding Officer, School Safety Division, New York City Police Department
d: The School Safety Division is the New York Police Department unit responsible for safety in the city's schools, and like any NYPD division it buys equipment and services. On 12 February 2026 federal prosecutors in Manhattan unsealed an indictment charging its former commanding officer, Kevin Taylor, and a Florida businessman, Geno Roefaro, with bribery and related offences. The indictment alleges that in 2023 and 2024 Roefaro paid Taylor tens of thousands of dollars' worth of bribes, and that Taylor agreed to use his power and influence inside the NYPD to enrich Roefaro's company. Both were arrested that morning. These are allegations in an indictment, not findings of a court.
inside: A businessman allegedly bought the commander of an NYPD division, who was to use his influence over its buying to enrich the businessman's company.
cite: United States v. Kevin Taylor and Geno Roefaro, S.D.N.Y., indictment unsealed 12 February 2026; Department of Justice press release, 12 February 2026

n: An NYPD officer took bribes to distribute narcotics in New York
org_label: A New York narcotics distribution conspiracy
who: A narcotics distribution conspiracy paying a serving police officer
rank: Officer, New York City Police Department
d: Andrew Nguyen was an officer of the New York City Police Department. On 29 January 2026 he pleaded guilty in the federal court in Manhattan to conspiring to solicit and receive bribes, to conspiring to distribute narcotics, and to possessing a firearm in connection with that narcotics conspiracy. The US Attorney said that in exchange for bribes Nguyen used his power as a police officer to distribute deadly drugs in New York City. He was listed for sentencing on 22 June 2026. The combination is the point: the badge was not merely looking away but doing the distribution.
inside: A narcotics conspiracy paid a serving officer, who then used his police powers to move the drugs himself.
cite: United States v. Andrew Nguyen, S.D.N.Y., guilty plea 29 January 2026; Department of Justice press release, 29 January 2026

n: Contractors paid $1.25m to the Army official who directed their subcontracts
who: Brian Kent and Leonard Pick, defence contractors
rank: Civilian official, United States Army, Hawaii-Pacific Innovation Campus
d: The US Army Pacific Command's Hawaii-Pacific Innovation Campus was intended as a hub for testing new military technology. From January 2021 to October 2022 a civilian Army official, Carlos Duque, agreed with two defence contractors, Brian Kent and Leonard Pick, to accept a bribe of about $1.25 million over five years. In return he told prime contractors to award subcontracts to Kent and Pick's company, and helped them inflate government contracting costs fraudulently so that the inflated figures covered his own bribe payments. Duque received about $55,000 before the scheme was stopped. He pleaded guilty on 28 October 2026; Kent and Pick were arrested on 20 May 2026 after an indictment filed in Hawaii.
inside: Contractors bought the Army official who directed subcontracts, and the government paid their bribe back to them inside the inflated bills.
cite: United States v. Carlos Duque, guilty plea 28 October 2026, and United States v. Leonard Pick and Brian Kent, D. Haw., indictment filed 14 May 2026; Department of Justice press releases, 20 May and 28 October 2026

n: A driving school owner bought licences from a Massachusetts road test examiner
who: Carlos Cardoso, a driving school owner buying licences for his customers
rank: Road test examiner, Registry of Motor Vehicles, Brockton
d: A driving licence is issued by a state body after a road test, and the examiner who conducts that test decides who passes. Carlos Cardoso, 72, owner of a driving school in Brockton, Massachusetts, bribed a road test examiner at the Registry of Motor Vehicles there to issue licences to people who had failed their road test or, in some cases, had never taken one. He was indicted by a federal grand jury in May 2024, pleaded guilty in June 2025 to honest services mail fraud and to conspiring to commit it, and was sentenced on 6 February 2026 to time served, two years of supervised release with six months of home incarceration, and a $5,500 fine.
inside: A driving school paid the state examiner who decides who passes, so licences were issued to drivers who had never been tested.
cite: United States v. Carlos Cardoso, D. Mass., indicted May 2024, guilty plea June 2025, sentenced 6 February 2026; Department of Justice press release, 9 February 2026

n: Construction firms paid the federal official who directed their building work
who: Christopher Brackins and James Tillman, owners of construction companies
rank: Contracting officer's representative, General Services Administration
d: The General Services Administration is the federal agency that manages government property, and a contracting officer's representative is the official who oversees the work on it. Lennie Lamont Miller, 60, held that post. He pleaded guilty on 29 January 2026 to two counts of conspiring to commit bribery of a federal official, for agreeing to take bribes from construction companies. He conspired with Christopher Brackins, who owned one general construction company, to direct GSA federal project work to it, and separately with James Tillman, who owned another, in the same arrangement. On 22 September 2026 he was sentenced to three years in prison.
inside: Construction firms paid the federal official who assigned the work, and the agency's building projects went to whoever was paying him.
cite: United States v. Lennie Lamont Miller, D. Md., guilty plea 29 January 2026, sentenced 22 September 2026; Department of Justice press releases, 29 January and 22 September 2026

n: A New Jersey school district's administrator took kickbacks on a school build
org_label: Contractors on the Hillsborough Township school project
who: Contractors paid from a multi-million dollar school upgrade and building project
rank: Business Administrator, Hillsborough Township School District, New Jersey
d: Hillsborough Township School District in New Jersey won a 2019 referendum authorising a multi-million dollar project to upgrade its schools and build a new one. Aiman Mahmoud, 56, was the district's Business Administrator from 2008 to the end of 2021, the official who runs its money. A federal grand jury indicted him on 30 May 2026 over an overtime fraud and kickback scheme, alleging that he accepted tens of thousands of dollars in cash kickbacks in connection with that project, and that to oversee parts of the work, including safety monitoring, he arranged for particular people to be engaged. These are allegations in an indictment, not findings of a court.
inside: The official running a school district's money allegedly took cash from the contractors he engaged on its building programme.
cite: United States v. Aiman Mahmoud, D.N.J., indictment returned 30 May 2026; Department of Justice press release, 3 June 2026

n: An Alabama police officer charged with hiding evidence for violent men
who: Violent individuals paying to avoid prosecution
rank: Police officer, Prichard Police Department, Alabama
d: Emmanuel Naman Dotch II, an officer of the Prichard Police Department in Alabama, was arrested on 16 June 2026 on a federal criminal complaint charging him with civil rights violations, conspiracy, taking bribes, tampering with evidence and extortion, all in his capacity as a law enforcement officer. The complaint alleges he covered up crimes and concealed evidence for violent individuals so that they could avoid prosecution, and that he conspired with other officers of the same department to carry out unlawful traffic stops and detentions. Evidence in police custody is the thing a prosecution depends on, and the officer holding it is the one who can make it disappear. These are allegations, not findings.
inside: Violent men allegedly paid a serving officer to destroy the evidence against them, using the force's own custody of it.
cite: United States v. Emmanuel Naman Dotch II, S.D. Ala., criminal complaint, arrest 16 June 2026; Department of Justice press release, 16 June 2026

n: An Air Force contracting officer sold bidding secrets on $8.25m of work
who: Ryan Dalbec and Raihana Nadem, owners of Best Choice Construction LLC
rank: Contracting officer, United States Air Force, Alaska
d: Confidential bidding information tells a contractor what its rivals have offered, which makes winning a matter of arithmetic rather than competition. Brian Lowell Nash II, an Air Force contracting officer in Alaska, agreed in 2019 to accept more than $400,000 in bribes from a government contractor, Ryan Dalbec, who with his wife Raihana Nadem owned a construction company called Best Choice Construction LLC. In return Nash gave them confidential bidding information on more than $8,250,000 of military construction contracts at Eielson Air Force Base and Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson. A judgment under the False Claims Act secured the United States more than $1.3 million in civil damages and penalties, announced on 18 September 2026.
inside: A construction firm paid the officer who ran the bidding, and he handed them their rivals' confidential figures on $8.25m of military work.
cite: United States v. Brian Lowell Nash II, Ryan Dalbec and Raihana Nadem, D. Alaska, False Claims Act judgment; Department of Justice press release, 18 September 2026

n: A contractor paid an Amtrak official to change its station renovation contract
who: Mark 1 Restoration Company and its owner Mark Snedden
rank: An official of Amtrak, the United States' national passenger railroad
d: Amtrak is the United States' national passenger railroad, owned by the federal government. Mark 1 Restoration Company held a contract to renovate the facade of the William H. Gray III 30th Street Station in Philadelphia. The company paid kickbacks to an Amtrak official to obtain favourable changes to that contract. Its owner, Mark Snedden, pleaded guilty to criminal charges arising from the scheme, as did three Mark 1 executives, Donald Seefeldt, Lee Maniatis and Khaled Dallo. On 17 July 2026 the company and Snedden agreed to pay $7,257,232.12 to resolve the civil claims. A contract change order is where a construction job's price is really set, which is what the payments bought.
inside: A contractor paid an official of the state-owned railroad, and the railroad then changed the contract in the contractor's favour.
cite: United States v. Mark Snedden, No. 25-cr-120 (E.D. Pa.), with related prosecutions of Donald Seefeldt, Lee Maniatis and Khaled Dallo, and a civil resolution of $7,257,232.12; Department of Justice press release, 17 July 2026

n: A $550,000 bribery scheme ran through a South Carolina prisons officer
org_label: An inmate network inside the South Carolina Department of Corrections
who: Two South Carolina Department of Corrections inmates with their families and acquaintances
rank: Corrections officer, South Carolina Department of Corrections
d: A federal grand jury in Columbia returned a nine-count indictment, announced on 30 June 2026, over a $550,000 bribery scheme involving a corrections officer of the South Carolina Department of Corrections, two of its inmates, and their family members and acquaintances. Two people were charged in the indictment, among them Courtney Briggs, 39, charged with conspiracy to commit honest services wire fraud, and Larry Williamson, 51, a former inmate, charged with that conspiracy and five further counts. Five others waived indictment and agreed to plead guilty to their own roles. The figure is what marks this one out: most prison bribery cases run to thousands, not half a million.
inside: An inmate network put half a million dollars through a serving prisons officer, buying the state's own control of the wing.
cite: United States v. Courtney Briggs, Larry Williamson and others, D.S.C., nine-count indictment, with five further defendants agreeing to plead guilty; Department of Justice press release, 30 June 2026

n: A school board president steered $2.7m of air purifiers to her own company's client
org_label: An air purifier vendor to East Aurora School District 131
who: A school district vendor, and the company for which the board president was chief financial officer
rank: President, Board of Education, East Aurora School District 131, Illinois
d: An elected school board votes on what its district buys. An indictment returned in Chicago on 27 October 2026 accuses Annette Johnson, former President of the East Aurora School District 131 Board of Education, of steering the district to buy air purifiers from a vendor for about $2.7 million in 2021 and voting in favour of the purchase herself. It alleges that $1.3 million was directed to a company for which she was chief financial officer, as a kickback or bribe for the acts she took as president. The district paid for the purifiers with federal pandemic funds. These are allegations in an indictment, not findings of a court.
inside: The president of an elected school board allegedly voted through a $2.7m purchase while $1.3m went to the company she was finance officer of.
cite: United States v. Annette Johnson, N.D. Ill., indictment returned 27 October 2026; Department of Justice press release, 29 October 2026

n: A prisons contractor charged with taking bribes to carry contraband inside
org_label: Contraband supply at a federal prison in Orange County, New York
who: Those paying to get contraband to inmates of the prison
rank: Contractor working inside a federal prison, Bureau of Prisons
d: Prisons are not staffed only by officers: contractors work inside them too, and they pass the same gates. On 24 June 2026 federal prosecutors in Manhattan unsealed a complaint charging Terri Lynn Outer, a former Bureau of Prisons contractor working at a federal prison in Orange County, New York, with bribery, with providing or possessing contraband in prison, and with conspiring to do so. She was arrested that day. The contractor route matters because a prison's controls are built around its own staff, and a contracted worker is subject to the same bribery statute but not always to the same scrutiny. These are allegations in a complaint, not findings of a court.
inside: Payers allegedly bought a contractor working inside a federal prison, who was to carry their goods through the gates for inmates.
cite: United States v. Terri Lynn Outer, S.D.N.Y., complaint unsealed 24 June 2026; Department of Justice press release, 24 June 2026

n: An FCI Bastrop officer ran smuggling as a business for two years
who: Prisoners at FCI Bastrop and the friends and relatives who paid outside for them
rank: Correctional officer, Federal Correctional Institution Bastrop, Texas
d: Waldemar Perez, 49, worked as a correctional officer at the Federal Correctional Institution at Bastrop, Texas, from about 23 May 2021 to 11 May 2023. Court documents state that while employed there as a public official he developed a business and practice of smuggling prohibited items into the prison and giving them to prisoners in return for bribes, collecting the goods from the prisoners' friends and relatives outside. He pleaded guilty to one count of bribery at his first appearance in the federal court in Austin on 13 January 2026. The phrase in the court documents is worth keeping: not an incident but a practice, run as a business.
inside: Prisoners' families paid an officer who had made smuggling a standing business, so the prison's own staff ran the supply line.
cite: United States v. Waldemar Perez, W.D. Tex., guilty plea 13 January 2026; Department of Justice press release, 13 January 2026

n: A call centre paid two NYPD officers for crash victims' details
org_label: A call centre referring accident victims to lawyers and doctors
who: Mervin Rhymes, owner of an accident victim call centre referring victims to lawyers and doctors
rank: A supervisor and a traffic safety officer, New York City Police Department
d: When there is a road accident in New York the police record who was involved, and that record sits in a non-public NYPD database. Pamela Dillard, a supervisor in the New York City Police Department, pleaded guilty on 5 February 2026 to taking part in a conspiracy to solicit and accept bribes, admitting she passed the personal details of road accident victims from that database to a co-conspirator who owned a call centre referring accident victims to lawyers and doctors. Suzette Trimmingham, an NYPD traffic safety officer, and Mervin Rhymes, the call centre's owner, had both pleaded guilty in the same scheme on 29 May 2025. The buyer's business depended on reaching victims before anyone else did, which is what the police record gave him.
inside: A referral business paid two serving officers for the force's own records of crash victims, so its callers reached them first.
cite: United States v. Pamela Dillard, guilty plea 5 February 2026, and United States v. Suzette Trimmingham and Mervin Rhymes, guilty pleas 29 May 2025, S.D.N.Y.; Department of Justice press releases, 29 May 2025 and 5 February 2026

n: Defence contractors kept hundreds of millions in Navy work through a bought official
org_label: Defence contractors to the Naval Information Warfare Center
who: Defence contractors seeking and holding Navy contracts
rank: Public official, Naval Information Warfare Center, San Diego
d: The Naval Information Warfare Center in San Diego buys the US Navy's information and communications systems. James Soriano, a public official there, admitted in his plea agreement that he accepted hundreds of thousands of dollars in bribes from defence contractors, taken as lavish meals, jobs for his family members and friends, and tickets to major sporting events. In exchange he used his position to help those contractors win and keep hundreds of millions of dollars in government contracts. He also admitted filing false tax returns. On 9 September 2026 he was sentenced to 72 months in prison. Bribes paid as employment for relatives are harder to trace than cash and were part of the same arrangement.
inside: Contractors paid a Navy buying official in jobs for his family and hospitality, and he kept hundreds of millions in Navy work flowing to them.
cite: United States v. James Soriano, S.D. Cal., sentenced 9 September 2026; Department of Justice press release, 9 September 2026

n: Newark's deputy mayor and a councilman took bribes over city awards
who: Two Newark business owners paying for city awards
rank: Deputy Mayor and Director of Economic and Housing Development, and a member of the Newark Municipal Council
d: Carmelo Garcia, 51, was Deputy Mayor of Newark, New Jersey and Director of its Department of Economic and Housing Development, the arm of the city that decides which developers get land and money. He was also Executive Vice President and Chief Real Estate Officer of the Newark Community Economic Development Corporation. He took bribes and kickbacks from two Newark business owners, paid to influence the awards he controlled, and was sentenced on 3 June 2026 to 12 months and a day. Joseph A. McCallum Jr., 70, a member of the Newark Municipal Council who also sat on that corporation's board, was sentenced on 2 December 2025 to 18 months in the same scheme, alongside Malik Frederick, 65, a consultant for developers seeking Newark construction and real estate deals.
inside: Business owners and a developers' consultant paid the deputy mayor and a councilman who ran Newark's development awards, so the city's decisions followed their money.
cite: United States v. Carmelo Garcia, sentenced 3 June 2026, and United States v. Joseph A. McCallum Jr. and Malik Frederick, sentenced 2 December 2025, D.N.J.; Department of Justice press releases, 22 December 2025 and 3 June 2026

n: A housing company bought a San Leandro councilman's official acts
org_label: A housing company seeking San Leandro contracts
who: A housing company seeking favourable treatment and city contracts
rank: Member of San Leandro City Council, California
d: Bryan Azevedo, 49, was a member of San Leandro City Council in California. He pleaded guilty on 11 February 2026 to conspiring to commit honest services fraud and to making a false statement to federal investigators. He admitted that from the summer of 2023 he accepted bribes in exchange for using his official position to obtain favourable treatment and city contracts for a housing company. He had been charged by information on 20 October 2025. The second count matters as much as the first: when federal investigators asked him about the arrangement he lied to them, which is how most of these cases are finally made.
inside: A housing company paid a sitting councilman, and he used his council position to win it favourable treatment and city contracts.
cite: United States v. Bryan Azevedo, N.D. Cal., charged by information 20 October 2025, guilty plea 11 February 2026; Department of Justice press release, 11 February 2026

n: Louisiana's wildlife secretary took kickbacks over the contracts he awarded
org_label: Contractors to the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries
rank: Secretary of the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries
d: The Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries manages the state's hunting, fishing and coastal resources, and awards contracts for services on the state's behalf. Its former Secretary, Jack Montoucet, pleaded guilty on 31 March 2026 to conspiring to defraud the United States by corruptly soliciting and accepting kickbacks in return for being influenced in awarding those state contracts, and to wire fraud. He faced up to five years in federal prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. The head of a state department is the person who signs its contracts, so a kickback to him settles the award before any competition begins.
inside: Contractors paid the head of a state department, and he awarded the department's contracts to the people paying him.
cite: United States v. Jack Montoucet, W.D. La., guilty plea 31 March 2026; Department of Justice press release, 31 March 2026

n: Connecticut's school construction grants director jailed, then absconded
org_label: Contractors on Connecticut school construction projects
who: Contractors seeking Connecticut public school construction work
rank: Director, Office of School Constructions Grants and Review, State of Connecticut
d: Connecticut's Office of School Constructions Grants and Review is the state agency that administers the grants for every public school construction project in the state seeking state funding, which makes its director the person who decides which projects and contractors are funded. Konstantinos Diamantis, 70, held that post. On 30 September 2026 a federal judge in Bridgeport sentenced him to 84 months in prison and three years of supervised release for extortion, bribery, conspiracy and false statement offences committed in that role. He did not appear for his sentencing and was being sought by law enforcement when the sentence was announced.
inside: Contractors paid the state official who decided which school building projects were funded, so the grants followed the payments.
cite: United States v. Konstantinos Diamantis, D. Conn., sentenced 30 September 2026; Department of Justice press release, 30 September 2026

n: An Illinois police chief and a building inspector sold a liquor licence transfer
org_label: A Summit, Illinois business seeking a liquor licence
who: A local businessman paying for a liquor licence transfer
rank: Chief of Police of Summit, Illinois, with a village building inspector
d: In Illinois a village's police chief and its building inspector both sit between a business and a liquor licence: one reports on the premises, the other on the applicant. John Kosmowski, 58, Chief of Police in the village of Summit, conspired with a Summit building inspector, William Mundy, to accept $10,000 from a local businessman to help get a liquor licence transferred. A jury in Chicago convicted Kosmowski in December 2025 of bribery conspiracy, bribery and obstruction of justice, and on 15 July 2026 he was sentenced to three years in federal prison.
inside: A businessman paid the village police chief and its building inspector, the two officials whose sign-off a liquor licence needed.
cite: United States v. John Kosmowski, N.D. Ill., jury verdict December 2025, sentenced 15 July 2026; Department of Justice press release, 17 July 2026

n: Criminal networks paid a TD Bank insider to move $4.8m to Colombia
org_label: Criminal organisations moving money to Colombia
who: Criminal organisations paying a bank employee to launder their money
rank: Employee of TD Bank
d: A bank's controls against money laundering are worked by its own staff, so an employee who agrees to look the other way is the whole control. Gerardo Aquino, 40, pleaded guilty on 6 October 2026 to accepting bribes and to laundering more than $4.8 million to Colombia while employed by TD Bank. The US Attorney for New Jersey said that from inside TD Bank he facilitated the laundering of millions in exchange for bribes, and that by enabling crime instead of preventing it he provided a soft entry point into the banking system. A Drug Enforcement Administration official said corrupt financial insiders are as critical to criminal networks as the people who move drugs.
inside: Criminal networks paid a bank employee, and the bank's own defences against laundering were worked by the man they had bought.
cite: United States v. Gerardo Aquino, D.N.J., guilty plea 6 October 2026; Department of Justice press release, 6 October 2026

n: A Wisconsin prison officer took two $3,000 payments to supply an inmate
org_label: Contraband supply at Waupun Correctional Institution
who: An inmate of Waupun Correctional Institution paying for deliveries
rank: Correctional officer, Waupun Correctional Institution, Wisconsin
d: Luz Naranjo, 46, was a correctional officer at Waupun Correctional Institution in Wisconsin. On 15 January 2026 she pleaded guilty to conspiring to commit federal programs bribery, the offence that applies to officials of bodies receiving federal funds. Court documents state she received two bribe payments of $3,000 for smuggling contraband into the prison for an inmate: tobacco, mobile phones and controlled substances. She was listed for sentencing on 15 April 2026. The three items are the standard set, and the phone is the one that matters most, because it restores the contact with the outside that a prison exists to control.
inside: An inmate paid an officer $3,000 twice over, and she carried his phones and drugs into the prison holding him.
cite: United States v. Luz Naranjo, E.D. Wis., guilty plea 15 January 2026; Department of Justice press release, 20 January 2026

n: A DC school's budget officer took bribes from the vendors she chose
org_label: Vendors to McKinley Technology High School
who: Vendors seeking the school's supply contracts
rank: Administrative officer, McKinley Technology High School, District of Columbia Public Schools
d: Tracy Hatton, 60, was the administrative officer at McKinley Technology High School, part of District of Columbia Public Schools. Court documents state that she was responsible for managing the school's supply budget, selecting and awarding vendor contracts, and approving the invoices for them: the three steps that normally sit with different people so that no one controls all of them. She pleaded guilty to bribery in connection with a scheme that cost the District of Columbia government more than $40,000. The plea was unsealed in the federal court there on 9 July 2026.
inside: Vendors paid the school official who chose them, signed their contracts and approved their invoices, with no one else in the chain.
cite: United States v. Tracy Hatton, D.D.C., guilty plea unsealed 9 July 2026; Department of Justice press release, 9 July 2026

n: Cockfight organisers paid a Maui police lieutenant to keep his force away
org_label: Illegal cockfighting and drug operations on Maui
who: People organising illegal cockfights, paying for police non-enforcement
rank: Lieutenant, Maui Police Department, Hawaii
d: Michael Vaituulala, 53, a lieutenant with the Maui Police Department, was arrested and charged by criminal complaint on 6 August 2026 with conspiring to commit honest services wire fraud. The complaint alleges that over many years he used his position as a lieutenant for personal gain, accepting regular cash payments from people organising illegal cockfights in exchange for using his official position to ensure the department did not enforce the law against them. A lieutenant sets what his officers attend to, so buying one buys the absence of policing rather than a single favour. These are allegations in a complaint, not findings of a court.
inside: Cockfight organisers allegedly paid a police lieutenant a regular wage, and his force stopped enforcing the law against them.
cite: United States v. Michael Vaituulala, D. Haw., criminal complaint, arrest 6 August 2026; Department of Justice press release, 6 August 2026

n: Seventy New York housing authority staff sold $15m of repair contracts
org_label: Contractors seeking New York City Housing Authority repair work
who: Contractors paying for New York City Housing Authority repair contracts
rank: Seventy employees of the New York City Housing Authority
d: The New York City Housing Authority is the largest public housing landlord in the United States, and its staff award the small repair contracts that keep its buildings running. In February 2024 prosecutors charged 70 of its employees with accepting bribes for awarding those contracts. By 25 November 2025 all 70 had been convicted: three at trial, 56 by felony plea, 11 by misdemeanour plea. They had taken more than $2.1 million for contracts worth more than $15 million. Four superintendents drew the longest terms: Juan Mercado 48 months for over $300,000 in bribes, Joy Harris 41 months for over $50,000, Hector Colon 18 months, and Corey Gilmore a year and a day. The US Attorney called it one of the largest single-day corruption cases in the department's history.
inside: Contractors paid seventy of the housing authority's own staff, so who repaired the city's public housing was decided by who paid.
cite: United States v. 70 NYCHA employees, S.D.N.Y., charged February 2024, all convicted by 25 November 2025; Department of Justice press release, 25 November 2025

n: A Mississippi sheriff took $9,500 from a felon and gave him ammunition
org_label: A convicted felon paying the sheriff of Hinds County
who: A convicted felon paying the county's sheriff
rank: Sheriff of Hinds County, Mississippi
d: Marshand Crisler, 55, was appointed Sheriff of Hinds County, Mississippi in August 2021. The evidence at his trial showed that shortly after taking office he solicited and accepted $9,500 in cash bribes from a convicted felon over three months, from September to November 2021, and that he knowingly provided ammunition to a convicted felon, which is a federal offence in itself. On 11 February 2025 he was sentenced to 30 months in prison and fined $15,000. A sheriff is the senior law enforcement officer of a county and is elected or appointed to it, so the arrangement reached the top of the force rather than one officer in it.
inside: A convicted felon paid the county's own sheriff, who took the cash and handed him ammunition he was barred from having.
cite: United States v. Marshand Crisler, S.D. Miss., sentenced 11 February 2025; Department of Justice press release, 11 February 2025

n: Officers, a counsellor and a contractor jailed over corruption at Rikers Island
who: Rikers Island inmates and their associates paying staff
rank: Three corrections officers, a program counsellor and a contractor at Rikers Island
d: Rikers Island is New York City's main jail complex. Six defendants were sentenced by 10 March 2025 for conspiring to commit honest services wire fraud over corruption there: former corrections officers Jason Skeet, Chantal De Los Santos and Stephanie Davila, former program counsellor Shanequa Washington, former contractor Kenneth Webster, and former inmate Kristopher Francisco. The spread of roles is the finding: the arrangement did not rest on officers alone but reached a counsellor and a contracted worker, each of whom passed the same gates and was subject to the same bribery law.
inside: Inmates' money reached officers, a counsellor and a contractor at the same jail, so several separate routes inside were all on the payroll.
cite: United States v. Jason Skeet, Chantal De Los Santos, Stephanie Davila, Shanequa Washington, Kenneth Webster and Kristopher Francisco, S.D.N.Y., sentenced by 10 March 2025; Department of Justice press release, 10 March 2025

n: A separate Rikers officer pleaded guilty to smuggling narcotics for bribes
org_label: A narcotics supply arrangement at Rikers Island
who: Those paying to get narcotics to inmates of Rikers Island
rank: Corrections officer, Rikers Island
d: Ghislaine Barrientos, a corrections officer at Rikers Island, pleaded guilty on 8 January 2025 to bribery, for taking part in a scheme in which she accepted bribes in exchange for smuggling narcotics into the jail. She was listed for sentencing on 16 April 2025 before a different judge from the six defendants in the separate Rikers prosecution that concluded two months later, and hers was a separate prosecution with separate charges. Two unconnected prosecutions of staff at the same jail within a year is itself the measurement: the route inside was not one officer's arrangement.
inside: Payers bought a serving officer at the city's main jail, and she carried their narcotics through its gates for inmates.
cite: United States v. Ghislaine Barrientos, S.D.N.Y., guilty plea 8 January 2025; Department of Justice press release, 8 January 2025

n: A CBP officer at JFK sold immigration data and smooth passage at the border
org_label: A network buying preferential entry at JFK Airport
who: Hiu Kit David Chong, a former university administrator, and others paying for entry and data
rank: Officer, US Customs and Border Protection, John F. Kennedy International Airport
d: Every foreign national entering the United States through John F. Kennedy International Airport is processed by a Customs and Border Protection officer, who can wave someone through or send them to secondary inspection. On 17 December 2025 federal prosecutors in Manhattan unsealed a complaint charging Kevin Seto, a CBP officer at JFK, and Hiu Kit David Chong, a former administrator at a private research university, over a bribery scheme. It alleges Seto took bribes and gratuities from Chong and others in exchange for passing confidential law enforcement and immigration information and giving special treatment while processing the entry of foreign nationals and others. Both were arrested. These are allegations, not findings.
inside: Payers allegedly bought the officer who decided who came through JFK, getting both smooth entry and the government's own immigration files.
cite: United States v. Kevin Seto and Hiu Kit David Chong, S.D.N.Y., complaint unsealed 17 December 2025; Department of Justice press release, 17 December 2025

n: Companies bought a USAID contracting officer across $550m of aid contracts
org_label: Three companies holding USAID prime contracts
who: Three company owners and presidents holding USAID prime contracts
rank: Contracting officer, United States Agency for International Development
d: The United States Agency for International Development spends American aid money through contracts, and a contracting officer is the official who awards them. Roderick Watson, 57, worked as a USAID contracting officer. He pleaded guilty to bribery of a public official on 12 June 2025, and three owners and presidents of companies pleaded guilty alongside him, among them Walter Barnes, 46, who pleaded to conspiracy. The scheme ran for a decade and involved at least 14 prime contracts worth more than $550 million of US taxpayer money. The reach is what marks it: a single buying official, bought, across ten years of a foreign aid programme.
inside: Companies paid the USAID official who awarded contracts, and for a decade the aid programme's $550m of work went to whoever paid him.
cite: United States v. Roderick Watson, Walter Barnes and others, D. Md., guilty pleas 12 June 2025; Department of Justice press release, 12 June 2025

n: A defence lawyer paid a senior DEA agent for sealed indictments and arrests
org_label: A criminal defence practice buying law enforcement information
who: David Macey, a Florida criminal defence attorney building his client list
rank: Senior Special Agent, Drug Enforcement Administration
d: A sealed indictment is secret precisely so that the person named does not know they are about to be arrested. On 14 February 2025 federal prosecutors in Manhattan unsealed an indictment charging David Macey, a criminal defence attorney based in Florida, with bribery of a public official, conspiracy to bribe one, and honest services wire fraud. It alleges he paid tens of thousands of dollars to a senior Special Agent of the Drug Enforcement Administration in exchange for sensitive law enforcement information, including information about sealed indictments and impending arrests, which he used to recruit and represent clients. The prosecutor described it as secret payments for access Macey could use to enrich himself. These are allegations, not findings.
inside: A defence lawyer allegedly paid a senior DEA agent for sealed indictments, so he knew who was about to be arrested before they did.
cite: United States v. David Macey, S.D.N.Y., indictment unsealed 14 February 2025; Department of Justice press release, 14 February 2025

n: Two New York fire prevention chiefs sold faster safety inspections
org_label: Parties buying expedited Bureau of Fire Prevention approvals
who: Those paying to have fire safety inspections and approvals moved up the queue
rank: Two Chiefs of the Bureau of Fire Prevention, New York City Fire Department
d: The New York City Fire Department's Bureau of Fire Prevention inspects buildings and signs off their fire safety, and a building cannot open until it does. Two of its chiefs took bribes to move that work along. Anthony Saccavino pleaded guilty on 29 January 2025 to conspiring to solicit and receive bribes in that role, with the US Attorney saying he had repeatedly sold access to the bureau he was chosen to lead. Brian Cordasco pleaded guilty on 8 October 2024 to the same conspiracy and was sentenced on 31 March 2025 to 20 months in prison. An inspection queue is worth paying to skip, because a delayed sign-off holds up an entire building.
inside: Builders paid the two chiefs who ran the city's fire safety sign-offs, and the queue moved for whoever paid.
cite: United States v. Anthony Saccavino, guilty plea 29 January 2025, and United States v. Brian Cordasco, guilty plea 8 October 2024, sentenced 31 March 2025, S.D.N.Y.; Department of Justice press releases, 29 January and 31 March 2025

n: A federal inmate jailed for offering bribes to a corrections officer
org_label: A Bureau of Prisons inmate attempting to buy an officer
who: Robert Bibbs, a federal inmate offering money to a serving corrections officer
rank: Corrections officer, Federal Bureau of Prisons, Michigan
d: Most prison bribery cases on this map are prosecutions of the officer. This one is the other side of the same transaction. Robert Bibbs, 28, of Chicago, a federal inmate in the custody of the Bureau of Prisons, pleaded guilty in October 2024 to one count of offering bribes to a public official, and on 14 January 2025 was sentenced to 18 months in prison for offering bribes to a corrections officer. Federal law treats a corrections officer as a public official, which is what makes the offer itself a federal crime whether or not it is accepted. The case was investigated by the Justice Department's Office of the Inspector General.
inside: An inmate tried to buy a serving prison officer outright, which is a federal crime at the moment of the offer.
cite: United States v. Robert Bibbs, E.D. Mich., guilty plea October 2024, sentenced 14 January 2025; Department of Justice press release, 14 January 2025

n: An Energy Department specialist tried to bribe a colleague for a firm's contracts
org_label: A private company seeking Department of Energy contracts
who: A private company whose contracts the attempted bribe was meant to secure
rank: Security Specialist, United States Department of Energy
d: Edward Doherty, 34, was a Security Specialist with the US Department of Energy. A federal grand jury in Boston indicted him on 30 July 2025 for honest services fraud, payment of illegal gratuities and bribery of a public official, alleging that he tried to bribe another Department of Energy employee in order to secure government contracts for a private company. He had been arrested on a criminal complaint on 1 July 2025. The shape is worth recording even though the attempt failed: the route to a department's contracts ran through one of its own staff paying another, on a company's behalf. These are allegations in an indictment, not findings of a court.
inside: A company's interest allegedly reached inside the Energy Department through one official trying to buy another's decision on its contracts.
cite: United States v. Edward Doherty, D. Mass., indicted 30 July 2025; Department of Justice press release, 30 July 2025

n: Fraud defendants put a cash bribe in a bag at a juror's door mid-trial
org_label: The Feeding Our Future fraud network
who: Defendants on trial in the Feeding Our Future fraud case
rank: Juror in the Feeding Our Future trial, United States District Court for Minnesota
d: On 22 April 2024 seven defendants went to trial in the federal court in Minnesota over the Feeding Our Future fraud, a scheme that drew hundreds of millions of dollars from federal child nutrition programmes. During the trial, two of those defendants, the brothers Said and Abdiaziz Farah, took part in a plan to bribe one of the jurors with cash. Said Farah, 43, pleaded guilty on 21 August 2025, the fifth defendant charged over the juror bribery to do so. Buying a juror is the one route into a trial that does not require reaching a judge or a prosecutor, and the jury is the body that decides the facts.
inside: Defendants on trial paid a cash bribe to one of the jurors deciding their case, reaching inside the jury itself.
cite: United States v. Said Farah and others, D. Minn., guilty plea 21 August 2025, in the juror bribery prosecution arising from the Feeding Our Future trial; Department of Justice press release, 21 August 2025

n: An Alabama prison officer took a bribe at Limestone Correctional Facility
org_label: Contraband supply at Limestone Correctional Facility
who: Those paying the officer to act against his duties inside the prison
rank: Correctional officer, Limestone Correctional Facility, Alabama Department of Corrections
d: John Paul Ketteman, 28, was employed as a correctional officer at the Alabama Department of Corrections' Limestone Correctional Facility at Harvest, Alabama. He was sentenced on 24 September 2025 to 15 months in prison for receipt of a bribe by an agent of an organisation receiving federal funds, the offence that reaches officials of state bodies funded in part from Washington. His plea agreement set out the duties his post carried and the payment he took against them. The federal-funds route is how most state prison officers are reached by federal prosecutors at all.
inside: A payment reached a serving officer of the state prison, and he used the post he held inside it against the duties it carried.
cite: United States v. John Paul Ketteman, N.D. Ala., sentenced 24 September 2025; Department of Justice press release, 24 September 2025

n: An FCI Gilmer officer took $40,000 from inmates to carry contraband
who: Inmates of FCI Gilmer and those paying on their behalf
rank: Correctional officer, Federal Correctional Institution Gilmer, West Virginia
d: Hector Lopez, 41, was a correctional officer at the Federal Correctional Institution at Gilmer, West Virginia. He pleaded guilty, announced on 7 August 2025, to bribery of a public official, admitting in his plea agreement that he accepted $40,000 in payments from inmates or on their behalf as payment for smuggling contraband into the prison. He faced up to 15 years in federal prison. The figure puts this among the larger prison contraband arrangements on the map, where most run to a few thousand dollars.
inside: Inmates paid an officer $40,000, and he carried their goods into the federal prison past the searches he was employed to run.
cite: United States v. Hector Lopez, N.D. W. Va., guilty plea announced 7 August 2025; Department of Justice press release, 7 August 2025

n: An MCC New York inmate jailed for running a bribery and contraband scheme
org_label: An inmate contraband operation at MCC New York
who: Anthony Ellison, an inmate of the Metropolitan Correctional Center
rank: Staff of the Metropolitan Correctional Center reached from inside
d: Anthony Ellison was an inmate of the Metropolitan Correctional Center in Manhattan, the federal jail beside the New York courthouses. On 10 June 2025 he was sentenced to 29 months on each of two counts, to run at the same time as each other and after the federal sentence he was already serving in a separate case, for taking part in a wide-ranging bribery and contraband scheme at the jail. This is the buying side of the arrangement the map records from the officers' side in three separate prosecutions at the same jail.
inside: An inmate ran a bribery operation from inside the federal jail, buying the staff who controlled what came through the door.
cite: United States v. Anthony Ellison, S.D.N.Y., sentenced 10 June 2025; Department of Justice press release, 10 June 2025

n: A Memphis prison officer smuggled contraband over four months
who: Those paying the officer to bring contraband to inmates of FCI Memphis
rank: Correctional officer, Memphis Federal Correctional Institution
d: Bryan Miller, 32, was a correctional officer at the Memphis Federal Correctional Institution. The information presented in court showed that from December 2022 he began smuggling contraband into the prison while employed there, and that he continued over a four-month period. A federal judge sentenced him to prison for bribery, announced on 23 April 2025. A four-month run is the usual shape of these arrangements once they are found: the officer is detected not by the first delivery but by the pattern of them.
inside: Payers bought a serving officer of the federal prison, and for four months he carried their goods inside for inmates.
cite: United States v. Bryan Miller, W.D. Tenn., sentenced April 2025; Department of Justice press release, 23 April 2025

n: Oakland's mayor charged with promising official acts to two businessmen
org_label: A family recycling and waste business in Oakland
who: David Trung Duong and Andy Hung Duong, local businessmen
rank: Mayor of Oakland, California
d: An eight-count indictment filed on 9 January 2025 and unsealed a week later charged Sheng Thao, the former Mayor of Oakland, her partner Andre Jones, and two local businessmen, David Trung Duong and Andy Hung Duong, with bribery offences, and charged Andy Duong additionally with making false statements to federal agents. The indictment alleges that in the weeks before the Oakland mayoral election of November 2022, and after she won it, Thao promised to take official actions as mayor for the businessmen. Under ruling 21 a city mayor administers a government rather than sitting in an assembly. These are allegations, not findings.
inside: Two businessmen allegedly bought a mayoral candidate's promises before the election and her official acts after it.
cite: United States v. Sheng Thao, Andre Jones, David Trung Duong and Andy Hung Duong, N.D. Cal., indictment filed 9 January 2025, unsealed 17 January 2025; Department of Justice press release, 17 January 2025

n: Newark property owners paid the mayor's aide to speed their occupancy papers
org_label: Newark property owners seeking occupancy certificates
who: Property owners seeking Certificates of Code Compliance and Occupancy
rank: Senior Aide to the Mayor of Newark, reaching the Office of Inspections and Enforcement
d: Under Newark's rules a property owner needs a Certificate of Code Compliance from the Department of Engineering's Office of Inspections and Enforcement before certain changes of occupancy, and a Certificate of Occupancy to show the building meets the city code. Al-Tarik Onque, 49, a former Senior Aide to the Mayor of Newark, pleaded guilty on 4 September 2025 to conspiring to commit honest services fraud. He used his official position to approach people seeking those certificates and offered them faster issue in exchange for cash bribes, on multiple properties in and around the city, with others inducing the payments.
inside: Property owners paid the mayor's own aide, and the city's inspection certificates were issued faster for whoever paid.
cite: United States v. Al-Tarik Onque, D.N.J., guilty plea 4 September 2025; Department of Justice press release, 4 September 2025

n: A trader paid successive presidents of Venezuela's state food agency
who: Naman Wakil, a Venezuelan national controlling a group of companies
rank: Multiple presidents of Corporacion de Abastecimiento y Servicios Agricola (CASA)
d: Corporacion de Abastecimiento y Servicios Agricola, known as CASA, is Venezuela's state-owned food supply agency, the body that buys the country's imported food. Between 2008 and 2014 Naman Wakil, a Venezuelan national who controlled a number of companies, paid tens of millions of dollars in bribes to several successive presidents of CASA to win its food contracts. Through those companies he took hundreds of millions of dollars of proceeds into accounts he controlled in the Cayman Islands and Switzerland, and laundered money from the scheme into South Florida. On 8 January 2025 a federal judge in Miami entered final judgment forfeiting more than $20 million of those proceeds to the United States.
inside: A trader bought one state food agency president after another, so the body buying a country's food bought it from him.
cite: United States v. approximately $21,248,434.25 in US currency, S.D. Fla., civil forfeiture complaint filed 9 August 2023, final judgment 8 January 2025; Department of Justice press release, 10 January 2025

n: Three more San Ysidro officers charged over lanes left uninspected
org_label: A cross-border smuggling network working through San Ysidro
who: Smugglers who were told which lanes the officers would man and when
rank: Three officers, US Customs and Border Protection, San Ysidro Port of Entry
d: At San Ysidro, between San Diego and Tijuana, each vehicle entering the United States passes a primary inspection booth staffed by a Customs and Border Protection officer. An indictment announced on 6 May 2025 charged three CBP officers there, Farlis Almonte, Ricardo Rodriguez and Kairy Stephania Quinonez, with letting vehicles carrying undocumented people through their lanes without inspection. It alleges they revealed their lane assignments and the hours they were scheduled to work the booths, so that co-conspirators could send vehicles to the right lane at the right time. This is a separate and later case from the 2016 prosecution of another San Ysidro officer that the map already holds. These are allegations, not findings.
inside: Smugglers allegedly bought three inspection officers and their rosters, so they knew which lane would be unguarded and when.
cite: United States v. Farlis Almonte, Ricardo Rodriguez and Kairy Stephania Quinonez, S.D. Cal., indictment announced 6 May 2025; Department of Justice press release, 6 May 2025

n: Four Massachusetts troopers sold commercial driving licences to unqualified drivers
who: Civilian intermediaries and the applicants who paid for passing scores
rank: Sergeant and three troopers of the Massachusetts State Police commercial licence unit
d: A commercial driving licence is issued after a skills test conducted by the Massachusetts State Police, so the trooper running the test decides who may drive a heavy lorry. In January 2024 Sergeant Gary Cederquist, 59, was charged in a 74-count indictment with three other troopers, Calvin Butner, Perry Mendes and Joel Rogers, and two civilians, Scott Camara and Eric Mathison. On 2 May 2025 a federal jury convicted Cederquist of conspiracy to commit extortion, extortion, honest services fraud, falsifying records and false statements, and acquitted him on nine further counts. His co-defendants admitted their parts. They had given false passing scores to applicants who had failed the test or never taken it.
inside: Paid intermediaries bought the troopers who ran the driving tests, so heavy lorry licences went to drivers who had never been tested.
cite: United States v. Gary Cederquist and others, D. Mass., 74-count indictment January 2024, jury verdict 2 May 2025; Department of Justice press releases, 2 May 2025 and 4 September 2025

n: A lawyer bribed a police chief to get his client a cannabis licence
org_label: A recreational marijuana business seeking a Medford licence
who: A recreational marijuana business, through its lawyer Sean O'Donovan
rank: Chief of Police of Medford, Massachusetts
d: In Massachusetts a town's police chief sits on the bodies that approve a recreational marijuana licence, which makes his view of an applicant decisive. Sean O'Donovan, 56, a Massachusetts lawyer, paid a bribe to influence the Chief of Police of Medford to take official acts benefiting his client, a recreational marijuana business seeking approval to sell. He was convicted at trial and sentenced on 7 February 2024 to two years in prison. The chief had recently been appointed to the body deciding such approvals when the payment was made.
inside: A cannabis company's lawyer paid the town's police chief, so the officer whose approval the licence needed was working for the applicant.
cite: United States v. Sean O'Donovan, D. Mass., convicted at trial, sentenced 7 February 2024; Department of Justice press release, 7 February 2024

n: A border officer worked for two criminal organisations and got 23 years
org_label: Two separate criminal organisations moving drugs and people through the border
who: Two criminal organisations paying the officer who manned the lane
rank: Officer, US Customs and Border Protection, southern California port of entry
d: Leonard Darnell George was an officer of US Customs and Border Protection on the southern California border. A federal jury convicted him on 10 June 2024 of accepting bribes to let vehicles carrying methamphetamine and other drugs pass through the border into the United States, and of letting vehicles with unauthorised people through his lane. The evidence at trial was that he did this while working for two separate criminal organisations at once. On 25 October 2024 he was sentenced to 23 years in prison, by a distance the longest sentence among the border corruption cases the map holds.
inside: Two criminal organisations had the same inspection officer on their payrolls, and his lane carried their drugs and people through the border.
cite: United States v. Leonard Darnell George, S.D. Cal., jury verdict 10 June 2024, sentenced 25 October 2024; Department of Justice press releases, 12 June and 25 October 2024

n: A club owner paid a DEA agent to keep investigators away from his premises
who: Peter Gerace, owner and operator of Pharaoh's Gentlemen's Club
rank: Special agent, Drug Enforcement Administration, Buffalo
d: Peter Gerace, 57, owned and ran Pharaoh's Gentlemen's Club near Buffalo. Between 2005 and 2019 he conspired to defraud the United States and paid cash bribes to Joseph Bongiovanni, a special agent of the Drug Enforcement Administration. In exchange Bongiovanni protected Gerace and used his position to dissuade other law enforcement officers from investigating what went on at the club. From 2006 to 2019 Gerace maintained the club as a drug-involved premises where he and others distributed cocaine, Adderall, marijuana and heroin, and coerced dancers into sex acts there. A federal jury convicted Gerace on those counts and on witness tampering in December 2024. Bongiovanni had already been convicted.
inside: A club owner kept a serving DEA agent on his payroll, and the agent used his position to steer other investigators away from the club.
cite: United States v. Peter Gerace, W.D.N.Y., jury verdict December 2024, and the earlier conviction of DEA special agent Joseph Bongiovanni; Department of Justice press release, 27 December 2024

n: Cannabis companies bought Baldwin Park's permits through a councilman
org_label: Companies seeking Californian municipal marijuana permits
who: Companies seeking marijuana permits, paying through city officials
rank: Baldwin Park city councilmember, with the city attorney and a neighbouring city manager
d: Baldwin Park in Los Angeles County began issuing marijuana permits in June 2017, and its councilmember Ricardo Pacheco at once began soliciting bribes from the companies seeking them. Edgar Cisneros, 42, city manager of neighbouring Commerce, helped one company obtain a permit and related approvals through about $45,000 in bribes, and the company promised him at least $235,000. Robert Tafoya, 62, Baldwin Park's city attorney, facilitated a further scheme in which the Compton councilmember Isaac Galvan sought a permit for a consulting client, again through payments to Pacheco. Cisneros pleaded guilty to federal bribery and Tafoya to bribery and tax evasion, both unsealed on 5 December 2024, and both agreed to cooperate. Pacheco had pleaded guilty in June 2020.
inside: Cannabis companies paid a city councilman, its city attorney and a neighbouring city manager, and the permits went to whoever paid.
cite: United States v. Edgar Pascual Cisneros, guilty plea 6 November 2023, and United States v. Robert Manuel Nacionales Tafoya, guilty plea 5 December 2023, C.D. Cal., unsealed 5 December 2024, with the earlier plea of Ricardo Pacheco; Department of Justice press release, 5 December 2024

n: An Oregon prison officer jailed over a contraband smuggling conspiracy
org_label: A contraband supply conspiracy at a federal prison in Oregon
who: Those paying the officer to bring contraband into the prison
rank: Correctional officer at a federal prison in Oregon
d: Nickolas Carlos Herrera, 34, was a federal correctional officer at a prison in Oregon.
